Paulus.

...they might emulate in their way of life. Likewise, among the lower Indians, Pharaotes taught, if we believe Philostratus. Lysides the Pythagorean, writing to Hipparchus, also teaches that it is by no means pious to make the mysteries of true philosophy, which clearly savors of the divine, common to those who could not even dream of the purification of the soul: for neither can a bleary and unclean eye (as Hierocles drew from the storehouses of the ancients who followed these paths) gaze upon things too bright: Nor will anyone newly devoted to sacred rites, not well initiated, be able to immediately perceive those divine illuminations: because one awakened from sleep cannot immediately contemplate bright things. Therefore, the soul must be accustomed to beautiful studies and gradually purified, until the Divine light shines forth, and our intellect (as Plotinus says) shines forth within us: which may apply the soul to the Father and the true light: and place it unmixed in the understandings of the Creator: And let light (says Proclus) join light, not such as that which is said to belong to the sciences, but something more beautiful and more unified. Hence Abraham, the princes of the chosen family, and teachers of true wisdom, gathered with God, who, made gods, were vehemently elevated to receive that light: which, very far removed from mortals, the dark Jews considered a scandal, and the impious Gentiles, foolishness, but with eyes illuminated, it was seen as the most beautiful splendor, and the true storehouse of all treasures and most complete wisdom. Hence with great constancy, even at the risk of life, they tried with all their soul to defend it: To which treasures also (as Paul teaches) one does not arrive through philosophy, namely, this [philosophy] handed down by men, and empty deceit, but it is perceived by that light, through which, ascending from clarity to clarity, we are finally transformed into the same image of Him who is the splendor of the Father and His true image. But since the number of the illuminated who can receive that radiant light is very small, hence I think that those who wish to be initiated in this way should be led along those paths through which they can be more easily disposed to perceive that supreme light: And these paths are undoubtedly through these visible things to the invisible things of God, from the harmonic kinship which they have most consonant with each other. Therefore, concerning the consonance of both worlds and the archetype, and concerning the state of all things, and of all those things which each world itself (as it receives from the archetype) embraces with the greatest harmony, for such an easier guidance, we have opportunely thought it fit to treat: For those wishing to do this, we must take a journey through many paths, because all the artificial remedies of the disciplines must be met: Physics, Arithmetic, Astronomy, Geometry, Music, and Divine [disciplines]. Therefore, if there will be a treatment of things which are subject to the senses, then the Peripatetics with their sensible doctrine will support [us]: If we investigate celestial things, we will rely on the demonstrations of astronomers: If we examine the harmony of natural things, we will direct our path to the more secret philosophers: If a treatise is to be had concerning the variety of stars, and concerning that which is from diverse aspects, motions, and the harmony of sounds, it will immediately be resolved by musical reasons: If we attempt to explain the supreme intelligences and supercelestial mysteries in any way, having removed all these, and left them in the vestibule, we will approach the prophets and saints, to whom it has been given by a special gift to know the secrets of the living God, or we will implore that light which illuminates all and instructs best in such matters. If, however, for some reason we wish to be lifted from these visible things to the celestial and supramundane inner sanctuaries, that will be for us (error set aside) the unique path through numbers, by which these lower things, connected with the higher things by their harmonic proportion, present themselves most sweetly to those contemplating, and by mutual correspondence and inherent power, they offer the easiest way to those working: For all things are arranged by numbers, and thence so familiar to all, that nothing hinders them: for, related to the higher things, they ascend familiarly to the celestial: and again, when...

PROLOGUE.

they deal intimately with sensible things: and thence they assume diverse natures and diverse modes. For number, which (as Proculus says) always exists the same, is yet one thing in voice, another in the proportion of things, another in soul and reason, and another in divine things; and that which is bound in created things is found most absolutely familiar to God. [Marginal note: Proculus] But speaking of lower things, Themistius and Boethius so much prefer number that they believe no one can philosophize rightly without it. [Marginal note: Themi. Boëtius. Pythag. Academ. Theolo. Auenzo. Plato.] But the Pythagoreans, all together, and the Academics, but especially the more reclusive theologians, everywhere celebrate and venerate numbers: and not undeservedly, because, as Avenzoar the Babylonian reports, he rightly knows all things who knows well how to count. To whom Plato assents, saying in Epimonides: If anyone wishes to remove number from human nature, he by no means leaves them prudent or scientific: For the soul will perceive nothing without reason: Nor will anyone be able to give an account of things who is ignorant of number. Arts also, with number removed, entirely vanish: and what is greatest, he asserts that number is the cause of all good things, but of no evil. Hence, he who is to be blessed, who desires to explore celestial and divine things, ought not to be ignorant of number. Therefore, we must necessarily proceed through the paths of numbers and harmonic order, if we wish to ascend rightly and suitably through these lower things to the higher and the highest. For all things correspond to each other, and primarily with mutual harmonies, yet with different numbers: Which Orpheus sang, and after him Pythagoras taught, and also the Stoics confess, when they say the world was made by applying a certain harmonizing art. [Marginal note: Orpheus Pythag. Stoici. Plato. Porphy. Iablicus. Chalci. Proculus Syria.] Plato proposes it, Porphyry asserts it with many reasons, Iamblichus, Chalcidius, Proculus, and his teacher Syrianus declare it, and as many as are of the Pythagorean and Academic family interpret and affirm it to the best of their ability, believing that nature had nothing more ancient or more suitable than harmony, both in things produced and in things to be produced, by which all parts of this harmonious machine might be rendered. But divine prophets, leaving lower numbers far behind and introduced to divine and more secret inner chambers, contemplated many things not to be revealed, hiding the better parts of which in their heart, lest they should transgress, and offered some, and a few, for us to contemplate, as much as was permitted to them. From whom Isaiah says: I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, [Marginal note: Iſaias.] namely, over this whole worldly house, whose heaven is his seat, and this full of the glory of its maker: which shines harmoniously in the series of distributed ranks with his divine exemplary offices. Whence the harmony and mutual love between the artisan and the fabric, sung by two seraphim crying out to each other with alternating voices: Holy, Holy, Holy Lord God Sabaoth, The whole earth is full of his glory, communicated to each by a harmonious proportion through related numbers, by which all things are arranged. Therefore, absorbed in these measures and most consonant harmonies, the celestial prophets, leaving vocal numbers and their reasons in the vestibules, philosophized in better and divine numbers, in the species and forms of nature, indeed, in the exemplars themselves through all genera of ideas, proceeding in a certain order known only to those who have seen. To this also Ezekiel, Isaiah's colleague, applied himself, when he beheld the divine tribunal, which the Hebrews call Mercava, [Marginal note: Ezechiel Hebræi.] composed of divine ministers, Seraphim, Ophianim, and animals of holiness, made to be brought into the harmony of all things, concluding the whole matter, he said: And their appearance was like האופן בתוך האופן haophan betoc haophan, that is, a wheel within a wheel, as for now we follow our translation, because this spherical worldly house is in the middle of that intelligible and supreme wheel and sphere, that is, in the Word, which in that supramundane wheel...
a iij

--- Page 8 ---
**PROEM.**

[Marginal note: Ioannes] ...it possesses the middle, as John says: "That which has been made, in him was life." In him, as if in the Word, by which the Father carries and sustains all things, and which John, a true prophet, saw on the two-peaked Parnassus, namely Christ's breast, in which the two pinnacles of divine and human nature, respectively, stand out. [Marginal note: Moſes.] Moses, the first revealer of these sacraments, saw the same thing on the two-peaked Sinai, from which that truly happy Arabia (I will not name it, but it obtained the thing) derived its blessing. Hence, he spoke face to face with the divine countenance very often, and contemplated the peaks of subsequent effects. But he enclosed these in most hidden enigmas in his weighty and most fruitful description of the mundane fabric, deeming the rude and unlearned common people unworthy of the secrets of both worlds. For the most sublime light was not to be presented to the duller eyes of a people so weak that they could not gaze upon the face of Moses, glowing with that light from divine communion, unless he suppressed the splendor itself with a veil drawn over it (as their blinking eyes required). Therefore, he delivered the deepest sacraments to the unlearned people under the coverings of narrated history, leaving a place apart for the wise, so that they might approach the innermost sanctuaries of profound wisdom and supreme doctrine with the curtain drawn aside and the face unveiled, to contemplate that storehouse openly at times, and at times to proceed from the weak and visible to the invisible through those related numbers and harmonic proportions, from which both the wiser Hebrews and our own have added moral, allegorical, and anagogical senses. Hence, these lower things are moved by higher things with greater efficacy, inasmuch as natural and divine things are more excellent than those which are acquired by art. For by this [Marginal note: Pythag. Cicero. Boëtius. Terpan. Arion. Iſmeni. Dion.] musical art, Pythagoras (as Cicero and Boethius relate) restrained a raging youth by changing the modes. Terpander and Arion of Methymna, Lesbians and Ionians, and Ismenias the Theban cured very many afflicted with most severe diseases with harmonies. The song of trumpets and clarions also incites the spirits of soldiers and horses. Dion also relates concerning Alexander the Macedonian that he was sometimes so incited by Timotheus's modes that he would leap to arms as if raging. For sacred purposes also, King Saul's madness was so tempered by David's lyre that he was restored to his former peace, the evil demon having been put to flight, who, collapsing from that harmony, cannot endure any true harmony, as if it were hostile to him. Hence, I believe that singing and harmonic sounds were introduced into sacred rites by the royal prophet himself, the true restorer of sacred things, and by those fathers who perceived these sacraments of God and nature. What power, therefore, and what delight is to be thought to be inherent in the harmony of natural and divine things? Hence, truth, which is the agreement of things, even when explained in lower things, is most efficacious and brings delight, filled with wonderful pleasantness, to those who perceive it. But in divine things, it so exhilarates and moves the soul that it seems to transform it entirely into another state, especially in David's hymns, which, repeated so often, are never tiresome to well-composed souls, but rather delight and favor them greatly. For in them, as if in a certain singing of the whole law, are chanted the measures of both worlds with their archetype, and that consonance which has been restored to all things by the Messiah, and by what sweet step his most perfect work returns to the maker. And not only this royal prophet, but all who contributed to the sacred page were such that in them we can admire both an ample knowledge of true harmony and divinity, and a profound study of other doctrines. For who does not see all the prophets instructed in true poetry? Who does not recognize the most exact geometric measures in Moses, Ezekiel, and John? And again, in Moses, Ezekiel, Daniel, and John, the proportions of numbers, and

--- Page 9 ---
**PROEM.**

...in Davidic hymns, and Solomon's epithalamium, and in the entire description of both testaments, as if in a full epithalamium, the sweetest harmony of perfect music? Of music, I say, more sublime than that of Orpheus, Amphion, and such: but everywhere, and widely from them, you will imbibe draughts of true philosophy of both kinds, provided you have learned to philosophize well. These, therefore, are the leaders to be followed by us; these are the teachers to be imitated, and whatever we undertake is to be formed according to their measure. But truly, Most Blessed Father, what has been handed down by most to memory is that Mercury, Aglaophemus, Orpheus, Hesiod, Pythagoras, Archytas, Plato, Parmenides, Charondas, Zalmoxis, Lycurgus, and finally all those who followed them and philosophized brilliantly, or gave laws, did not derive what they taught from any other source: We have also deemed these (so that we may make all agree, as far as is right) to be admitted insofar as they appear to be in harmony with our harmony, which we have decided to undertake; but if they should be dissonant anywhere, they are to be rejected no differently than useless strings. Therefore, following those ancient fathers in their footsteps, among other names of things, but most especially that of the Creator himself, we shall endeavor to render them into our Latin, as they themselves handed them down, or at least as close as possible: so that we may more clearly express their profound meanings and sacraments, which lie hidden in those described characters of theirs, so much so that Origen believes that when translated into another idiom, they retain very little of their proper force. [Marginal note: Origen.] Therefore, I ought not to be considered a trivial or curious author of novelty, if we use the original words themselves, or those very close to them. Nor let it be judged superfluous and useless if we seem to repeat some things often, because the same things, needing to be fitted with different ones, are necessarily repeated as often as they are fitted: For different things are to be combined with different things, and the same things with many, so that all things may be shown to be harmonious with each other: and from every part of all the works of the Lord, the sweetest agreement may be drawn, with the divine spirit, the artificer of all things, inspiring (as we pray). This all-encompassing harmony we have judged capable of being embraced by three diapason canticles: hence each canticle will be completed with eight tones, that is, a perfect diapason. Therefore, in the first canticle, we shall resound the consonance of both worlds with each other, and of both with the archetype: In the second, concerning the agreement of all things with Messiah as head, and concerning the harmony that has been restored through Christ himself to all things broken and dissonant by sin: In the third, concerning man, the most harmonious bond of all things, to be recalled to harmony with all things that are bound in him, and with the Creator, with whom it is innate for him to agree, indeed, to be united: In these (unless I am mistaken) is contained the whole business of both worlds, and the sum of many disciplines. But Holy Father, and although according to the common adage all new things please, nevertheless, new things themselves often excite rivalry: they also offend eyes unaccustomed to new light, which are blinking: whence, turned to hatred, they often begin to attack what they have not yet well understood: Hence I am not unaware that I am exposed to many sharp-nosed and easily slandering individuals, both because of the new method of proceeding, and because of some sparks, long hidden under ashes, or newly struck from flint: Therefore, Most Blessed Father, this work, whatever its nature, and all other new things which we undertake with God's help, and all things that are in me, we have deemed to

--- Page 10 ---
PROLOGUE.

truly harmonious, unless by your virtue and authority it is rendered a sweet and harmless food to those who partake, for all members of the ecclesiastical body. Therefore, I have dedicated it to you, who hold the place of Christ, in whom are all things, and through whom are all things, in this Catholic body: so that just as all things receive life and beauty from Christ, the Word of God, so this work, which treats of all things, may live more successfully through you, and be beautiful, and a secure and pleasant feast for all. Farewell,
Most Holy Father, and live long.

PROEM TO THE FIRST CANTO.

[Decorative element] First Canto, in which
ALL DIVINE, HUMAN, CELESTIAL,
SUPRA-CELESTIAL, AND INFERIOR
things are shown to be distributed in fitting
proportion and harmonious sweetness.

PROEM TO THE FIRST CANTO.

[Large decorative initial C] O Most Blessed Father, when we are about to discourse on the sonority of the world, it is fitting that we take the path through those harmonious steps, through which that supreme Arch-Musician entered upon his work: Who arranged each individual thing, and the whole world itself, with sonorous numbers: Nor did the hand of the artist himself grow weary, until he had brought the work to a perfect consonance through due numbers into itself, so that a full octave symphony might be completed: which is then finally completed, when, with six intermediate steps passed, the last (which is the same, and not the same, as the first) recalls itself to itself. Indeed, by this octave the whole fabric of the world is perfected: by this it is arranged: by this, finally, it is completed. For it is perfected when the supreme Creator arranged this whole fabric through six steps of things full of sacraments, revealed by Moses under the veil of six days, and rested on the seventh. Which, if it is counted with the first, while existing in itself, is the eighth: And the perfect work, arranged by this harmonious succession of days, endures: so that it always returns after the seventh to the eighth, which is the same as the first and not the same. Thus at last will the most consonant work of God be completed, when in the perfect octave (of which we shall speak in its proper place) all things will be restored to their original state. We also, following the Creator's footsteps, will complete this harmonious work through that octave, returning to the same point from which we also take our beginning: so that both extremes may be from the supreme God. For the First Tone will be from Him, inasmuch as He is the beginning: The Last from the same, inasmuch as He is the end: And the intermediate ones concern the progression from the first to the last, in which (if I am not mistaken) are contained the elements of worldly and supra-worldly speculation.

--- Page 140 ---
PRIMI CANTICI TONI.

[Decorative woodcut initial V containing a figure] Who is the progenitor of the world, and in what harmony of super-excellent unity He rejoices. Tone I.
In what concord the principles of things, and their describers, agree or disagree. Tone II.
By what consonant number the supreme artificer descends into all created things. Tone III.
By what mutual harmonies the first kinds of things agree among themselves, and with the Archetype. Tone IIII.
By what consonance their intervals are filled. Tone V.
In what concord all things are contained in man, as in a small instrument. Tone VI.
By what sonority all things, even particulars existing in this earthly world, agree with the Archetype. Tone VII.
What is the ultimate, into which all diapason consonances are reduced. Tone VIII.

PRIMI TONI CAPITA.

What we can learn about God from holy men illuminated by divine light, which we discuss. Chapter I.
That without such light, all who spoke about God erred through very many deviations. Chapter II.
And if we cannot understand what God is, nevertheless we are taught that God exists both by oracles, and by prayer, and by the consent of all. Chapter III.
How through the trace, or image, of created things, and their consonance with the Archetype, we can arrive at the knowledge of His fecundity. Chapter IIII.
That God is full of the fecundity of all things and numbers, so that He can produce all things most consonantly. Chapter V.
That God is one. Chapter VI.
That that most fecund first mind, which is called God, produced both within and without. Chapter VII.
That God fabricated the world. Chapter VIII.
The condition of the world does not allow philosophers to conclude against its generation. Chapter IX.
Nor does motion achieve the same. Chapter X.
Its governors likewise contribute less. Chapter XI.
Nor by proceeding from the artificer do they prove what they intend. Chapter XII.
Why philosophers erred from Catholic truth. Chapter XIII.
Reasons for the world's newness. Chapter XIIII.
Why God did not make the world before or after what Moses narrates. Chapter XV.
Philosophers fail while they strive to prove that God necessarily acts externally. Chapter XVI.
Progress for contingency in the divine work. Chapter XVII.
God knows particulars. Chapter XVIII.

TONE ONE. 2

WHAT WE CAN LEARN ABOUT GOD FROM HOLY MEN
ILLUMINATED BY DIVINE LIGHT,
Which we discuss. Chapter I.

[Decorative initial C] AS WE DESIRE, according to what the undertaken work demands, to
investigate who the progenitor of this world is, it undoubtedly happens,
what Plato, inspired by some divine power, used to say: "The maker
and generator of the universe is as difficult to find as, once found, to
worthily declare," since inaccessible light dwells [there]. Hence, very many
speaking about Him erred through many byways, all those indeed whose eyes He
Himself had not illuminated. Therefore Pythagoras commands that no one presume
to speak about divine matters without light: [Marginal note: Pytha.] without that light, I say, about which the
Psalmist sings: "In your light we shall see light." [Marginal note: Dauid] Bathed in this light, the first man
saw God Himself walking at midday: he recognized His voice: and he duly observed
the natures of all created things, so that he might impose a fitting name on each one.

By this light, Seth (after Enos was born) began to invoke the name of the Lord,
still hidden, and Enoch to predict future events, and to be translated to God Himself.
By this light, Noah, as not only the monuments of the Hebrews, but also of the
Chaldeans and Scythians (if we believe Berosus) [Marginal note: Bero.] relate, predicted the future flood:
he built the ark: he saved the seed of men and animals. [Marginal note: Abrahā] Afterwards, he taught the
Armenians and Scythians, then the Italians, whom scripture calls Chittim, the secrets
of nature, theology, and sacred rites: and he distinguished the courses of the stars,
and years according to the sun's movement, and months according to the moon's course:
Whom poets celebrate under the name of Janus. Indeed, Noah is called Janus (who
signifies "wine-bearing") in the Aramaic language.

This light, the later it came, the more brilliantly it later infused Abraham's mind,
so that he taught better rites: gave a sign to the chosen family: was the first to
recognize the one God diffused in the Trinity: concerning the revealed name of God,
and concerning the sacraments of His solitary eminence, and how He diffuses Himself
into others through sacramental vestments or channels, he wrote before all others
(as the Cabalists assert), [Marginal note: Cabal.] or taught what others wrote.

For this, Alexander [Marginal note: Alexan.] and Eupolemon [Marginal note: Eupol.], being cited, depose thus: "Abraham, most
excellent of all in holiness and wisdom, first taught the Chaldeans, then the
Phoenicians, and finally the Egyptian priests astrology and divine matters." But
Julius Firmicus, the astronomer, [Marginal note: Iul. firm.] calls him divine on account of his wonderful
wisdom: "Who testified to the one maker of all things not without risk to his life,
and preserved and taught to posterity all things pertaining to wisdom and divine
worship: Which he left to Isaac as if by hereditary right: and Isaac to Jacob: and
Jacob himself handed down such records to his family, so that all wisdom emanated
from that family: With which Moses was imbued above all others, on A ij

CANTICI PRIMI

in whom the doctrine of all his fathers is not doubted to have converged. And this is the
wisdom of the Egyptians, by which (according to Luke's testimony in the Acts of the
Apostles) he had been instructed. For Abraham had taught this to the Egyptians: which
they afterwards committed to writing after their Io, daughter of Inachus, whom the
Egyptians worship as a goddess: because they believed they had received letters from her:
But falsely, because Inachus began to rule the Argives, at which time Abraham's grandsons
were already receiving this light. [Marginal note: Eupole.] But Eupolemon writes that Moses was in the times of Inachus
and Ogiges, and this wise man, who taught grammar to his Hebrews (to whom he gave
the name from עבר, which means "to pass over") and all wisdom: Who afterwards
bestowed it upon the Phoenicians [Marginal note: Plinius] because of their proximity: from whom the Greeks also
received the system of characters. Hence Pliny said that the primordial letters were Assyrian:
and that Cadmus transferred sixteen from Phoenicia to Greece: from which Assyrians the
Egyptians also learned: although they boast of their antiquity: For Moses (as we said),
initiated into their institutions, taught them better things: [Marginal note: Strabo] so that he was called an Egyptian
Priest by Strabo. There were also, in writing about Athenian affairs, famous Helanicus,
Philochorus, Castor, Thales, and Alexander Polyhistor, and Diodorus, easily the foremost
of all historians, who diligently surveyed almost all of Asia and Europe with his own eyes.
All these proclaimed the most ample signs of antiquity, and about Moses, the most excellent
leader, and author of divine things. For neither before him is anyone found who committed
anything to writing: unless perhaps Abraham (as we touched upon) and Enoch: whose
doctrine Moses, as a legitimate heir, most fully collected in his volumes, adding what he
had received from the mouth of the living God in daily oracles, or embracing everything
in them. Hence [Marginal note: August.] our Augustine speaks with great boldness. "No nation," he says, "should
boast with any unjust vanity about the antiquity of its wisdom above our patriarchs and
prophets: since not even Egypt is found (which usually boasts falsely and vainly about the
antiquity of its doctrines) to have surpassed our patriarchs' wisdom with any of its doctrines
during their time." Nor did any of the philoso- [Marginal note: Pytha.] phers precede them: since the name of
philosopher drew its origin from Pythagoras the Samian: who began to flourish at the time
when the captivity of the Jews was ended. Nor should the Sages be brought forward, who
long preceded the philosophers: who themselves were after Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and
Joseph, indeed even after Moses himself: as [Marginal note: Augusti. Cicero] Augustine most accurately calculates. Thales,
who (according to Cicero's testimony) first disputed about the nature of things, flourished
at the time when Hezekiah ruled the Jews, and Numa Pompilius ruled the Romans. And
after him followed Solon the Athenian, Chilo the Lacedaemonian, Pittacus the Mytilenaean,
and the other Sages, even the most ancient of the Greeks, are younger than the Hebrew
prophets: For Moses wrote three hundred and ten years [Marginal note: Au. Eus. Cicero] before the destruction of Troy:
as Augustine and Eusebius calculate. But Homer and Hesiod (as Cicero says) followed
Troy by one hundred and fifty years: by which a little

TOMVS PRIMVS. 3

the earlier Orpheus with his sacred rites, namely in the time of Gideon, but about three hundred years after Moses, flourished. Moses therefore was the first who committed to public writings those sacred mysteries which, illuminated by divine light and communion, he had learned: mysteries by which his progenitors had also been instructed, at least in part. But, wrapping these things in histories for the unlearned common people with whom he dealt, he presented himself as one of them; entrusting more secret sayings to the wiser ones; and leaving for wise posterity, in a hidden place, under a veil, the most splendid light of divine and natural things to be gazed upon, like that dove which the Prophet commemorates as most simple in appearance, but with its hinder parts shining with the gleam of gold. By this splendor, the eyes of the Wise, undefiled by sensible things or any other impurities, gazed into the deepest mysteries of God and nature. Among these, the great Trismegistus was the first: who followed Moses's teaching to such an extent that Moses was called by those ancient wise men. For Artabanus [Marginal note: Artaba.] showed that whatever is said of Trismegistus, the same was found in Moses: Plato also, the master of philosophers (so that I may agree with Cicero, Augustine, Apuleius, Proclus, and many wise men [Marginal note: Plato / Cicero] [Marginal note: August. / Apule.], let others say what they will), agrees so much with Moses that Numenius Pythagoras [Marginal note: Procul. / Nume.] says Plato is nothing other than Moses speaking in Attic Greek. Pythagoras, from whom the Academics learned [Marginal note: Plato] (as Hermippus the Pythagorean testifies [Marginal note: Hermi.]), transferred much from Moses's doctrine into his own philosophy; so that it is true what Iamblichus [Marginal note: Iambli.], the great priest of the Egyptians, says in the volume he compiled about their mysteries: 'Pythagoras, Democritus, Plato, Eudoxus, and many others approached the Egyptian priests, where from the pillars of Mercury, which were inscribed with all kinds of doctrine, they learned a more secret philosophy.' But Mercury (as we have said) drew from Moses. This, then, is the teacher from whom all Syrian, Egyptian, and Greek wisdom emanated. Ambrose, Eusebius Pamphilus, and Cyril also testify to this among our own writers, beyond Augustine [Marginal note: Augu.]; the last of whom says word for word: 'Pythagoras and Plato, when they devoted themselves to studies in the land of Egypt [Marginal note: Ambr. / Eus. Pã.], did not ignore the doctrine of many illustrious men, and especially that of Moses [Marginal note: Cyrillus], according to their diligence. For at that time, the name of Moses was held in no small admiration among the Egyptians; hence we do not doubt that they received the understanding of God, that is, of the First Cause, from him: whom Numenius Pythagoras followed, writing many things from Mosaic doctrine in his books, as the great Basil testifies [Marginal note: Basilius / Clemens].' And so that I may free myself from these, Clement of Alexandria, Atticus the Platonist [Marginal note: Atticus], Eusebius, and Aristobulus [Marginal note: Eu. Ari.] prove that the Gentiles (if they had any excellent doctrines and mysteries) usurped them from the Jews and wrapped them in coverings of fables: such as that of Deucalion from the history of the deluge, and the fiction of Phaethon from the retrogradation of the sun, which occurred in the time of Hezekiah. Whence also, that they fabricated stories about giants who piled mountain upon mountain and tried to reach heaven, it is doubtless that they drew this from the Tower of Babel. From here, the Sulmonian (Ovid) [Marginal note: Ouid.], from where he sang of the origin and fabric of the world, usurped. Homer also, Hesiod, and Linus, from where they sang of the seventh day to be sanctified, undoubtedly received this from here: For Homer indeed says.

**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

Home. The seventh light was present, and all things were complete and perfect. Whom others, following, agree on the same point: and before them Orpheus, from whom he would extol the author of the universe with the highest praises, took it in his work "On the Divine Word": for (as Artabanus testifies) Orpheus learned many things from the doctrine of Moses. After whom Virgil learned to restrain the winds under Aeolus from Noah's ark: in which all kinds of animals were ruled by Noah's command. From the happy state of Adam also they sang, and very many wrote in prose about the golden Saturnian reigns. It would be long to recount how many kinds of secrets of inferior and supramundane nature poets learned to wrap in the veils of fables and enigmas from those, who, taught by sacred oracles, concealed the mysteries entrusted to them: lest they expose holy things to be trampled by pigs. But because some do not think that Peripatetic philosophy can stand with Hebrew philosophy: indeed, from this they take occasion for ridicule, let them say where they found, or rather fabricated, it to have been said by their Aristotle about Moses: "This man said many good things: but he proved nothing?"

Clear. Therefore, let Clearchus the Peripatetic, cited on his behalf in the book "On Sleep," say how much the prince of the Peripatetics (Aristotle) deferred to the Hebrews. For he says that when Aristotle was debating with Hyperochides, he said: "There was a Jew who, descending from the higher regions of Asia to the maritime cities, was Greek both in language and in spirit: And when it happened that at that time we too were staying in the maritime regions of Asia, he came to us voluntarily out of love for philosophy: who brought us much more than he received: these things Clearchus says." To which places the same Aristotle sailed, persuaded by a short letter of Plato, written from Egypt in commendation of the Israelite wise men: as we found in Hebrew records. Megasthenes, moreover, in the third book of "Jewish Affairs," declares not only Aristotle but all philosophers to be disciples of Hebrew wisdom. "All things," he says, "which the ancient Greeks wrote about nature, others also handed down before them: For the Brahmans among the Indians (who are also called Jews) philosophized much earlier." Nor should anyone wonder that Jews were Indians: since Aristotle also says in Clearchus: "The Jews are the Calani from India." But they were called Jews from the father of a principal tribe: and Israelites from their divine Prince and progenitor Jacob: and Hebrews from their passage, to which they were always devoted as strangers. To this Numenius assents in the first volume "On the Good." "Plato," he says, "and Pythagoras expounded in Greek what the Brahmans, Egyptians, and Jews had discovered." There are also those who assert that the mysteries of Numenius, Philo, Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus were received from Paul, Dionysius, Hierotheus, and John. Indeed, it would be tedious to cite all who assert that the Jews and our fathers (from whom we too received the first principles of wisdom) were the first teachers of wisdom, from whose founts all mortals have drawn: For this not only our own people believe: but also most distinguished historians and eminent philosophers testify: To these let us also add the oracles of the Gentiles: if they do not believe the witnesses brought forward: For Porphyry relates that the oracle of Apollo handed down these things concerning the Jews.

        That all who spoke about God without this kind of light erred through very many

**Q** How necessary this light is for those who wish to speak about God, experience will sufficiently
prove: if we wish to recall what delusions those who claimed the name of wise for themselves
invented without this very light: As Eusebius, Augustine, Laertius, and very many more recent authors well gather, but especially      Eu. Aug.
                                                                                                                                                Lae. Cic.
Cicero. For Thales of Miletus, who held the first place among the wise,      Thales.
said that water was the beginning of all things: but God was that mind which fashioned all things
from water. Anaximander asserted that the Gods were born, rising and setting at long intervals,
and also that there were innumerable worlds. Afterwards, Anaximenes established air as God:      Anaxi.
and that it was generated, and was immense, and infinite, and always in motion, as if air
without any form could be God. Anaxagoras, who received instruction      Anaxa.
from Anaximenes, was the first of all to wish the description and manner of all things to be
designated and completed by the power and reason of an infinite mind; nor does he proceed
further from that, so that it might be understood what this mind is and how it completed all things.
Alcmaeon of Croton gave souls and divinity to the Sun, Moon,      Croton.
and other stars. Pythagoras thought the soul was      Pythag.

**OF THE FIRST SONG**

Democ. Democritus speaks, to know. Democritus counts images and their circuits among the gods. But since he denies anything to be eternal (because nothing always remains in its own state), does he not entirely abolish God and leave no opinion concerning Him?
Epicurus Epicurus, who watered his gardens from the springs of Democritus, thought of God as clothed in human form: because that [form] is the most beautiful of all, and alone suitable for reason and mind.
Cicero Whom Cicero demolishes with lengthy disputations and assails with many jests.
Aristote. Aristotle confuses many things, disagreeing with his sole master Plato: for at one time he attributes divinity to the mind, at another he says the world itself is God, at another he places a certain other [being] over the world, and attributes to it those parts, so that by a certain unfolding of the world, it may govern and protect its order. Then he says the ardor of heaven is God, not understanding that heaven is a part of the world,
Xenocr. which in another place he designates as God. Xenocrates says there are eight gods: five who are named in the wandering stars; One who [is formed] from other constellations as if from scattered limbs, the seventh the Sun, and the eighth the Moon.
Theoph. Theophrastus, with a certain inconstancy, at one time attributes divine supremacy to the mind, at another to heaven, then moreover to the signs and celestial constellations.
Strato Strato the philosopher considers all divine power to be situated in nature, which possesses the causes of generating, increasing, and decreasing, but lacks all sense and form.
Zeno Zeno considers natural law to be God, and that it possesses the power to command what is right and to prohibit what is contrary. And elsewhere he calls the aether God;
Aristo and in other places, a certain reason diffused through the nature of all things. His disciple Aristo says that the form of God cannot be understood, doubting entirely whether God is animate or not.
Cleantes Cleanthes, also a listener of Zeno, now says the world is God, now the mind, and judges this ultimate and highest ardor, diffused everywhere, and encompassing and embracing all things (which is named aether), to be the most certain God.
Perseus Perseus, another of his listeners, says that useful and salutary things are designated by the names of gods.

He had spoken of such gods. Following him, Diogenes the Babylonian dreams many things about Minerva and the birth of Jupiter, and the origin of the Virgin. Cicero's Cotta seems to refute and mock all who speak of the gods: and his boat sails through so many waves that, as if submerged, having abandoned the sea and despaired of the harbor, almost shipwrecked, he struggles to conclude that the gods have obscure and difficult explanations.
I will omit those things which, poured forth by the voices of poets, more absurd, have harmed by their very sweetness: who introduced gods inflamed with anger and raging with lust, and made us see their battles and wounds: moreover, hatreds, dissensions, births, deaths, complaints, effusive lamentations, in all intemperance lusts, adulteries, chains, sexual intercourse with the human race, quarrels, hatreds, and many such insanities. But many have also descended to such madness: that they fashioned with their own hands the Gods whom they adored: as Hermes Trismegistus says of the Egyptians. Thus did the Assyrians, for whom the statue of Bel constructed by his son Ninus (as some believe) provided a reason for idol worship: whom the Moabites, Palestinians, and many peoples emulated, and they too fashioned their statues at will: and erected altars for themselves: and named them by a word of their own idiom.
      And if we cannot understand what God is, yet we are taught that God exists both by oracles, and by reason, and by the consensus of all.          Chapter III.
Therefore, speaking of God, we deem that saying of Dionysius to be observed, in which he says: That it is indeed permissible to ascend to higher things: as much as the ray of divine eloquence shall deign to insinuate itself: And that our powers must be prepared to absorb those divine splendors: moreover, that divine things ought to be revered by us innocently, soberly, piously, and chastely: lest if we wish to proceed by natural inquiry, we fall into various errors: just like those wise men of the world whom we mentioned above. Or let that happen which Simonides, whom Aristotle and Cicero sufficiently celebrate, experienced, who, when asked by Hiero the tyrant what God was, requested the space of one day: And returning the next day, when asked, Simonides requested two days. Then, as the tyrant asked more frequently, Simonides always doubled the number of days. But to Hiero asking why he did this, he replied: because the longer I consider it, the more obscure the matter seems: because He inhabits light inaccessible to human intellects. Hence the heavenly teacher testifies in the Gospel, which is titled according to Matthew, saying: No one knows the Son except the Father: nor does anyone know the Father, except the Son: and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him. Therefore, concerning this supersubstantial and most holy (as the Areopagite continues) it is not to be presumed to say anything or to think otherwise than as the sacred scriptures have very piously and chastely handed down. From these most sacred discourses, therefore, we have some things: to which some philosophers come with ready feet. But some things, which since they cannot attain, they either do not admit, or they evade them, or they leave them untouched as doubtful. Treating each of these, we will propose them thus: so that the pious may admit them with fair ears: but the impious, even if they do not admit them, at least cannot reject them. For these are placed in the first category of impiety by Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus, who deny God

For all created things, whose nature it is to depend on another, teach that there is something from which they themselves are: and that [something] from nothing, lest there be an infinite regress. And those things which are moved conclude that there is one [thing] from which all things are moved,

And that [thing] is perfect, needing nothing: which is God, whether principle, or fount and origin of all things, or the highest, or infinite, or that than which nothing greater can be conceived, or the prime mover, or the first cause, or that which is from itself, or the Archetype, and containing all things, or by whatever other name it may be called, he

[Marginal note: Epicurus] For from that divine volume of Epicurus *On the Rule and Judgment*, we have received that there is a certain pre-conceived notion for the reason of the soul, which we understand here: in which the nature of all agrees that God exists: and that he governs the world: To which he adds
[Marginal note: Pythag.] the illustrious deed of the Athenians, who burned the book of Pythagoras the sophist, in the beginning of which he seems to doubt whether God exists, having expelled him from the city and territory. But

How, through the trace or image of created things: and their consonance with the Archetype, we can arrive at the knowledge of His fecundity. Chapter IIII.

[Large initial V]
In order that we may grasp that most divine fecundity, which is found shadow-like in all His handiwork, from these domestic things which we have at hand, at least individual things must be sketched: since there is nothing in the nature of things (according to Mer-
[Marginal note: Mercu.] cury) that does not bear some image of divinity. For all living things generate their offspring within themselves: and harmoniously bringing forth into the open what they conceived in their innermost parts, they utter the praises of the supreme artisan with a certain voice of their own.
To these hymns, all things invite [us], including the boys purified in the Babylonian furnace, and David, when he would bring his hymns to an end. For trees and plants, when they sprout

--- Page 149 ---
**FIRST THEME. 6**

...their shoots, or produce buds, they generate seed as if a fetus in their body. But when they yield fruit, as if by a kind of birth, they praise God with their own voice. Hail and snow are congealed in the air, and rains are prepared in the clouds, and then their conception occurs: but when they descend to earth, as if a completed offspring, they too bless the Creator. Animals generate a better offspring. But when they bring forth into the light, they too burst forth in praise of God. The sensitive faculty also conceives within itself the image and intention of things to be made, afterwards, by applying its limbs to the work, it brings forth what it had conceived. Which offspring of Imagination is closer to the soul than to the vegetative [faculty], which only occurs in the body: Therefore it more clearly shows the offspring of the divine mind. Thus the rational soul, when it receives power from the imaginative faculty, which measures all things to be done with due prudence, first by fabricating an exemplar of them in the mind, produces as it were an offspring in that same mind: which it brings forth externally: Where what has been conceived in the mind, it brings into its proper figure or form. Which conception, as an operative life, expresses (according to Augustine) the divine creative life, in which all things pre-existed before they were unfolded into their proper forms.
[Marginal note: August.]
But the work demonstrates the craftsmanship of the creator: Which, brought forth in harmonious order, sings praise to the creator himself, to whom it is assimilated in its operation. There is also another offspring of rational life similar to this, namely reason and discourse, which, formed in the mind from that thing which we know, is called the Word by the same Augustine.
[Marginal note: Idem]
Each of which offspring is closer to the soul than the conception of imagination or the vegetative faculty, because the rational faculty reflects into its own understanding, and through that, into itself. To these succeeds holy and free love: which Imagination does not effect. But it brings forth this offspring into the open: when it manifests what it had conceived by a sounding word. But since the angelic state is more perfect than that of those who still struggle in the arena, it brings forth a more excellent conception, unchanged by any interval: which, in bringing forth, it continuously perseveres in praises of God by a certain utterance. From all these things in the Creator, whose image they hold, we contemplate all things in their degrees: both the Word and the conception of creatures in the ideal life. But it reveals the essential Word when it manifests it in the sacred page: and the ideal Word, when it makes what it had fabricated in the mind shine forth in the work. Which is a certain way of saying and manifesting what has been conceived. Hence Moses and David, of whom the one wrote the secrets of God, the other sang them, declare all things to be produced by the Word.
[Marginal note: Moses David]

That God is full of the fecundity of all things and numbers: so that He can produce all things most harmoniously. Chapter V.

Mercury affirms that the elements and principles of nature, and also the whole beautiful world, have emanated from Him who is most full of the fecundity of all things and of both sexes, containing the whole power of generating without any external aid.
[Marginal note: Merc.]
Hence by the Poets He is called Pan (which means 'all'): whom the Arcadians, believing to be the sun, adored.
[Marginal note: poets]
He is indeed the true sun, not this celestial one, but supramundane and divine. And if it is permitted to pursue what [the poets] feigned about this Pan

Antiquity, which always handed down divine mysteries under enigmas, we will also examine its typical depiction. They first placed horns on its head, denoting the kingdom which it holds in the heavens and the underworld; for Jerome proves in a long series in the prayer of Habakkuk that a horn is accepted as representing a kingdom even [Marginal note: Hiero.] among those who wrote our sacred texts. But a long beard, extending down to the lowest parts, represented rays of light, or of its divine power. The lower part was shaggy because of trees, shrubs, mountains, rocks, and wild beasts; but the upper part was smooth. Whence it is also said to ride upon *haravah*, that is, plains; which our translation renders as "setting" (or "west"). A pipe of seven reeds sounds, that is, the harmony of the seven planets, in which are seven-fold sounds, which complete the perfect diapason, namely, consonance. The rod in its hands is power, by which it moderates all things. They depicted him laughing, hinting at his eternal happiness. And they asserted that he delighted in echo, which is a voice emitted in hollow places, or resounding from any arranged objects. For voice expresses word and the concept of the mind; therefore, by voice or word, God fashioned the world and all its parts, and by voice he governs, commanding. Therefore, he also manifests love to us with many cries; but he delights in reciprocal love (which is a resounding echo). And these are the delights which he has with the children of men. He wore a starry fawn-skin on his chest, because he contains the confluence and [Marginal note: Poete Philo.] power of all stars in a single skin, and by a single act or nod. But whom the Poets called Pan, that is, the whole, and containing all things, Philosophers called the first cause, and the principle of all [Marginal note: Procul.] causes, giving to all causes that they may flow forth; because whatever the second cause does, it acts in the virtue of the first, which is more influent than the second, says Proculus. And granted that a secondary universal cause also removes from a thing the power which it bestowed, the first cause by no means removes it. And further down it says: All things have their essence from the first being, and the first cause, and live from the first life, and immediately from the first and highest intelligence. It is necessary that this (intelligence) be fruitful of all those things which others bestow. [Marginal note: Speusi. August. Bo.tius Plato] And it is supremely happy and blessed in itself. But Beatitude (as Speusippus defines it) is a good accumulated from all goods. But blessed is he who needs nothing, and who has whatever he wills, if Augustine, Boethius, and Plato teach well. [Marginal note: Hermes] Therefore, nothing is lacking to him who contains all things, as the true sphere of all things, as Hermes said. And since nothing is outside the sphere of the world, so nothing is outside the divine embrace, which encompasses all things; to whom belongs that inexplicable name, where all the letters contain circular numbers, namely, ten, five, and six, each attesting that it is the truest sphere, which they name, containing all things within its embrace. The meanings of these letters also indicate the same thing: for *Ioth* is interpreted as knowledge or principle; *He* as being; *Vau* as "and itself," in which, namely, all things rest; so that [Marginal note: Procul.] it is the principle of all essences, providing to all that they may be, and being itself is the first of created things, as Proculus teaches. Therefore, it emanates from the first cause, to which alone is attributed the giving of being itself. Therefore, elsewhere it concludes with open mouth that all things pro- [Marginal note: Peripa.] ceed from one cause, which, first of all, must be pregnant with all things, if the Peripatetic (philosophy) is true.

TONVS PRIMVS. 7
Peripatetic maxim: No one gives what he does not have. Nor is anything produced by nature, or fabricated by art, unless it first pre-exists in the maker. An animal, or a human, is generated from a seminal virtue, which contained that which was generated: and from a seed is generated a plant which pre-existed in the seed by potency (as the Peripatetics say) or by some virtue. Hence the wisest philosopher Moses, when speaking of producing plants, [Marginal note: Moses] says: "Whose seed, namely, of the plant, is in it," that is, the seminal virtue for producing another plant. There also exists in the mind of the artisan an ideal form, from which he derives the external one: as Augustine explains at length, interpreting that passage of John, [Marginal note: August.] "what was made, in him was life," life indeed being creative, and the idea [Marginal note: Ioan.] of all things to be made. For just as a work of art lives in the mind of the artist before it is brought forth: so the world lived in that divine mind before it was brought into being. Moreover, it contains every number, being itself the true unity: which is the principle and root of all numbers, giving to all that they may be numbered. For every multitude (as the same Proclus says in his theological theorems) is from the one. [Marginal note: Procu.] Nor would anything be one, making a multitude together with others (as he continues there) unless through the participation of the one it acquired unity for itself. That one, and most ancient [being], no one doubts to be God, who, before communicating a particular unity to lower things, diffused himself into the first number: And hence into the denary (if we admit the theology of the Hebrews) as into ten ideas, and measures [Marginal note: Hebraei.] of all numbers, and of all things to be made: for this reason, a further number cannot be given, although Aristotle attempts to assign other manifold reasons. [Marginal note: Aristo.] Which denary, accumulated into one, returns to that from which it had its beginning. So that the denary is the end of numbers, and their completion, and the principle of decads. All things, imitating this series of numbers as a true exemplar, strive to return to that one from which they proceeded: As our Proclus somewhat further adds, saying: that every order beginning from unity proceeds [Marginal note: Procul.] into a multitude co-elemental with unity: and that same multitude of order is finally reduced to unity. And all things that are under the lunar sphere, through man as through the tenth genus of those things which are subject to corruption: And the nine heavens through the tenth heaven: which they call the Empyrean: and the nine orders of Angels through their decad are restored to the primary unity: Which we will discuss more broadly in its proper place.

They also add concerning the power by which He can do all things: Hence, if there were two, one could destroy what the other had built: and if he could not, he would not be God: who is omnipotent. And proceeding, they reason that since each would enjoy the other, being supremely enjoyable, and one unwilling to enjoy would be deficient. But one enjoying would receive something from another, as if imperfect: and thus the most perfect God would be imperfect: and still further. If there are two, which of them built this machine? And which of them governs it? And if he who made it, also rules it, what does the other do? But if one made it, and the other governs it, how did the governor enter a house not his own? Therefore, from the order and governance, let us conclude [Marginal note: Diony. Plato Philo. Aſtro.] with Dionysius, Plato, with all true philosophers and astronomers, that the maker and ruler of so many things agreeing with each other is the same: who is the craftsman of all, having all power, foreseeing all things.

That that most fertile first mind, which is called God, produced both within and without. Chapter VII.

[E] LED by these created images to the most eminent and most fertile divine mind, illuminated by its light, we shall see a progeny most similar to itself, who is the true image of the Father: whom it first generates in itself by a unique and never-interrupted act: by which it always understands itself to be the supreme good by essence, without any intermission or change.

**FIRST CANTICLE**

From this results an offspring, which is full intelligence, a full image of itself, and a complete exemplar of the world.
[Marginalia: Io. Mer. Plato] Which offspring John and Mercury named the Word:
[Marginalia: Orph.] Plato [named] the Son of God the Father: but Orpheus [named it] Pallas, that is, wisdom born from Jupiter's head. From which full intelligence, love of its supreme goodness is produced, binding intelligence with mind, and all the more so, by how much an immense proportion it is more intimate to itself than other offspring are with their parents. Hence it is the most exact image of the parent, yet by a certain distinction, or by some intrinsic absolute, as if generated, distinct from the generator. And unless there were generation in that supreme Prototype, there would not be an image of generation in created things: Nor would a sterile and unfruitful [being] have given
[Marginalia: Isaias] fecundity to its creations: as through Isaiah, concerning the unbelievers, it complains with a certain impatience, saying: "I who grant generation to others, shall I be sterile?" Therefore,
[Marginalia: Ricar.] in the supreme artisan, there is a seed and fecundity: Because (if it exists, says Richard, most delightfully happy), nevertheless, from its inherent goodness, that most happy mind willed to openly produce this offspring of its own by constructing a fabric full of its image: In which, spreading itself out in an ordered series of degrees, it made some capable of its propagation and happiness: Of whom, some by only momentary subjection, others however by a longer struggle, it ordained to become sharers of its happiness, assigning to each their due habitations. But because those [the former] were to soon after attack the creator of things, it did not assign to them hospices for pilgrimage, nor any other field for instantaneous battle except the palace of triumph. To mortals, however (for whom it had declared a long war with various enemies), it gave wide spaces for struggle and opportune lodgings. And because united with an alterable and fallible nature, it took care to provide fodder and sustenance, by which they might draw the course of life to its due end. All these things, prepared at an opportune time, it committed to the elements and the heavens, as most obedient ministers, commanding also, for the delight of this very dwelling, that fields be extended, valleys exist, forests be covered with foliage, stony mountains rise: And other things of that kind: which we perceive to be ordered more for beauty and adornment than for necessity: So that from these delights, which the guest would feel in such hospices of servitude, he might ascend to contemplate those most exquisite ages, which are prepared in the triumphal hall. For it recognized the unhappiness of this bodily prison: in which those most absolute goods, free from all degenerating matter, can only be conceived through sensible things, unless they are revealed by a particular light. Therefore, with supreme artifice, it arranged harmonious images of those celestial things: so that through these, the veil of ignorance or sin being easily drawn away, we might be drawn to the celestial things themselves:
[Marginalia: Orige.] and from the beauty of the works and the adornment of creatures (as Origen writes in Periarchon), we might understand the parent of the universe. This especially, since a more proper nature of the image is found in man: who alone among mortals (as the Platonists say)
[Marginalia: Platoni] possesses the likeness of the divine mind. But the animal holds the likeness of man: the zoophyte [holds the likeness] of the animal: but the plant [holds the likeness] of the zoophyte: and metals [hold the likeness] of the plant: stones [hold the likeness] of metals. That God created the world. Chapter VIII.

**I**NTER those things which lie hidden from human intellects and transcend natural reasoning, is the generation of the world: whether it exists, if it had a beginning, and if necessarily, or by some free outpouring of the divine mind. Hence the wise are divided into various factions. Aristotle, with that crowd [Marginal note: Aristo.] who admit nothing unless they are able to investigate it with their own strength and intellect, being unable to understand whence and why this generation occurred, rejects it: and as an ungrateful disciple, he falsely accuses Plato, saying that he alone posits the world to be generated. But Plato himself, with other wise men enlightened by a better light, professes the creation of the world: [Marginal note: Plato.] and this (creation) to be most harmonious and arranged with the fullest numbers: under the veil of which, and by obscure indications for those whose senses are receding, he concealed the mysteries of the world from those not yet well initiated. He deemed it better to skillfully unravel what has been received through divine oracles, than to labor in vain with his own intellect to apprehend those things which escape the grasp of rational discourse: and are only received by a pure, joyful, and festive harmony of mind. Hence Mercury, embracing the mind and introducing these inner mysteries, [Marginal note: Mercu.] hints in a few words in his Pymander at the creation of the world, and its governors, and all composite things, and the pure artifice of nature from the elements tending downwards, yet united to the mind of the Creator. He teaches that these elements, cast forth, pre-exist by God's will alone in a lower condition than in the Creator. But Empedocles of Agrigentum, and Heraclitus of Ephesus, [Marginal note: Emped. Heracli.] assert that the world is generated and corrupted not once, but continuously. Which, according to parts, or a certain renewal hidden from those not enlightened, could be admitted into the bosom of truth. But Democritus teaches that the world is generated: and will perish once, [Marginal note: Democ. Hesiod Orph. Thales. Pythag. Hiero. Auicena Algazel Philo. Alcinous] and will never be repaired further. Hesiod also and Orpheus sing of the world as having been brought forth. Thales, one of the seven wise men, asserts this orb to be the work of God. Pythagoras, and his interpreter Hierocles, profess God as the maker and father of things. Avicenna the Arab, Algazel the Saracen, Philo (most famous no less for his doctrine than for his Greek eloquence), Alcinous the Platonist, who says: "This entire world must necessarily be the most beautiful work of God," agree. And many later ones, whom it would be tedious to recount. Hence Plato does not alone generate the world, [Marginal note: Plato] but he himself, with many, testifies that it was generated. But omitting external authors, let us come to those,

Moses. For Moses is the father of theologians, and the chief teacher of philosophers, "In the beginning," he says, "God created heaven and earth, and the other things which follow." To this most complete God, and holy, vitalized divine power, who in many places proves those things which he said, more belief is to be given than to Aristotle, who confirms his trifles of this kind neither by reasons, nor by miracles, nor by oracles. The consensus of the parts of the whole doctrine, the weighty authority of those who confirm his doctrine, and approve it by interpreting. Miracles are manifest. matter, which the natural agent requires; nor because it operates from contrary to contrary, that the supreme artisan should also proceed in the same way. From where, I ask, did those learn these inferences, who taught that art is distinguished from nature, and that natural things belong to one kind of doctrine, and eternal things, separated from motion, to another? For the artisan introduces an artificial form, and presupposes a natural one. But the natural agent introduces a substantial form, and presupposes matter, which is an effect of God: And if God in operating required something beforehand, He would also require a prior God, who would have produced that; and thus there would first be something prior. What then are these monstrous arguments? They also reason fallaciously, while from the possession of a new place which something newly generated acquires, they wish to exclude the world from generation, because it acquired no place. But granting that it acquired a place for itself, I would say it acquired the same place in which it now is. For it is around the center either of the earth, or of the world, or of that intellectual sphere, whose center (as Hermes says) is [Marginal note: Hermes] everywhere. Moreover, that they maintain every new thing must be reduced to something ancient, we grant to them. And that ancient thing is the divine mind, by which all things are contained, before they are unfolded into their proper forms; and when unfolded, it moderates and preserves them. That they add that every natural transmutation occurs from matter into matter, we admit: but in the primal production, and absolute from all laws of nature, by which the ruler is not bound by right, this is not required. Moreover, that every product first pre-exists in some potentiality, we grant: but natural things in matter; but the world itself, and the species of things, in ideas, or in those exemplars [Marginal note: Platoni. Nor are the ideas of Plato monsters, O Aristotle; but they are the eyes of a bat (as you say), if they do not see those things which are most manifest in nature, or in nature's author. And so that we may dissolve the strongest knot of natural philosophers: that from nothing, nothing is made: I would wish them to be asked to explain this opinion of theirs, since it is ambiguous. For if its sense is, that from nothing, nothing is made by art or nature, which require a subject in which they operate: we readily agree. But what does this have to do with the supreme artisan, whom nature emulates at a great distance; just as art (emulates) nature itself, as Aristotle with his Averroes agree? [Marginal note: Aristo. Auerrois] And just as in being, so also in operation, the determined natural agent, subject to motion, time, and succession, falls short of Him who is absolute from all laws of nature. If, however, they understand "from nothing," that is, "after not being, nothing is made," they have left this to posterity to prove; whence a wide field for denying is left to us, since it is neither proven, nor is it evident in itself. If, however, they mean that that "nothing" excludes every kind of cause, even this we grant: But in the generation of the world, we presuppose an operative and supreme cause: which contains matter, subject, forms to be given, instruments, disposing qualities, and all things which are required for bringing about any work, by its own infinite power.

to flow: yet it says "before the sky, which covers all things." It also signifies the front part of a place: hence *anteambulones* (those who walk before), and *antesto* (I stand before). It also signifies a higher rank, from which *Antistes* (a prelate), who is superior to others, comes. And since that "before" has so many meanings: why do they want to restrict it to signifying only a part of time? Would they not also concede that matter exists before form in a certain order, even if it did not precede it in time? Thus God was before the world in eternity, and in a certain order. But what they add, that an instant is the end of the past and the beginning of the future, Algazel resolves by saying: [Marginal note: Algazel] As a point exists in continuous things, so an instant exists in successive things: a point, however, is sometimes the end of part of a line, and the beginning of another part; sometimes it is the beginning of an entire line, and not the end of a preceding part. Thus that instant, in which the world had its beginning, was the beginning of the time that followed, and not the end of a past time. The Arab denies the similitude: because time passes, a line remains. [Marginal note: Auerrois] Oh, what a ridiculous solution: since the similitude is not about transition and permanence, in which they differ: but about the indivisible part in which they agree. For all things that agree in something, differ in another: as is trivial even to novices in their doctrines.
They add something seemingly obvious: "That which flows," they say, "has something before it and something after it." But (to bring forth something from the storehouses of nature and God) we say more: namely, that everything that flows returns to that from which it had the beginning of its flow. For water returns to the sea from which it drew its origin, as the wisest Solomon teaches: [Marginal note: Salomon] and experience proves. The body to the earth, from which it was taken. The spirit, and all things made by God, return to the same from which they were begotten. "All things produced," says Proclus, [Marginal note: Procul.] "make a circle, beginning from God, and ending in God Himself." Thus also time returns to the same eternity from which it flowed: which will remain when time ceases, just as it pre-existed before time. Hence, to Avicenna asking how the Creator preceded the making of the world, [Marginal note: Auicen.] we will say with Augustine, [Marginal note: Auguſt.] certainly a most upright philosopher: that He preceded it by that eternal duration. Plotinus also (although he taught many things beyond human understanding, [Marginal note: Plotinus] as he drew from the springs of Ammonius, [Marginal note: Ammo.] and he from those who were taught by divine oracles) makes a paralogism concerning this duration of the world, when he says: "That which is resolved into another is dissected; but since there is nothing beyond the world into which it can be resolved, it will endure forever." To whom we say: The world is resolved according to its parts, so that it may persevere in a better state; but we are not presently disputing about its resolution, since the discussion is about its generation: nor does it disagree with our religion that God's creation should endure perpetually, so that we may agree with Plato [Marginal note: Plato] and Plotinus: [Marginal note: Plotinus] who consider it an impiety for those things to perish which proceeded immediately from blessed God. Hence we also assert the soul to be immortal, because it was produced and inspired by God. The body will also attain eternity, if it takes on the nature of the soul: as we will discuss elsewhere.

Likewise, its governors attribute less. **Chapter XI.**

[Marginal note: Astro.] [Decorative initial O containing a figure of a scholar] The supporters of the world also believed that the intelligences moving the spheres attain happiness in the perpetual revolution of the heavens: as Aristotle seems to suggest in his higher philosophy, where, repeating higher principles, he contends more fiercely for this eternity of the world. To whom John Scotus concedes more, perhaps interpreting his words better than he himself conceived them: because they are blessed not only by moving the orbs, but while (by means of that revolution) performing the office of God, they communicate perfection to lower things. What Plotinus says, discussing the heavens and the soul of the world, agrees with this: For it is indeed absurd to think that the soul, which contained the heaven for a time, would not also always do the same, as if it had contained it by violence. And having progressed a little, he says: What can be the cause for the world to cease at some point? For the elements of the world are not worn out like wood and other things of this kind; and since these always remain, the universe also remains. Here, speaking of future permanence, he presupposes that it has always existed. Hence he further infers that it will always endure, because the dominion of its soul cannot be dissolved, nor its nature weakened: And Aristotle also considers this important: because the ruler of this worldly house, since he is eternal, not undergoing change, his house also seems to be eternal. And since its governors do not labor, nor are they tired by revolving, being devoted to eternal motion, they will never rest. To refute these things, we say there is an error of equivocation, arguing from the immediate to the ultimate end. Almost all things are ordered to diverse ends, but only to one ultimate end. For animals, the immediate end is to live and to feed, but the ultimate end is to serve man: who (in the opinion of many wise men) is the end of all lower things. But the immediate end of man is to govern the house, the republic, the family, to trade, to study, and things of that kind; but the ultimate end is to come to God, or to happiness, whether through Stoic virtue, or Peripatetic speculation, or through Academic purification, or through faith and grace, as our Catholics assert. But for intelligences separated from God and from corruptible matter, the immediate end is to govern the heavens and men, and other things committed to them; but the ultimate end is in the contemplation of the first substance, where they are blessed: as Aristotle himself states in his Ethics. Let it be, therefore, that they rest from motion and from a lower end, yet they will not cease from blessedness: just as man will not be less happy if he does not govern the republic and lower things. For it is indeed astonishing that anyone should think those minds are blessed in continuous motion: since all motions (as they themselves also teach) tend towards rest: and greater progress in wisdom is made by resting in studies and on benches, than in motion. Nor will they cease because they labor, but with the work perfected and completed, and having rendered to lower things the favor they owed. Nor will the soul, of which Plotinus speaks, cease to provide life to the universe by ceasing from motion. Nor do we assert the annihilation of its elements or parts, but rest from motion: so that it may finally be brought back after many revolutions into the sabbatical

rest, closed off even to many wise men. Nor do they prove the intention by proceeding from the Creator. Cap. XII.

**C**UM again, from this new generation of the world, a new relation seems to be introduced into the Creator from the novelty of the work, and consequently a certain change in nature or will, which cannot happen to the most perfect and unmoving being: neither from within, because nothing can move itself, nor from without, because it would suffer from it with the defilement of the most perfect and infinite being. Many arguments of this kind are brought forward by Aristotle, Averroes, Moses Aegyptius, [Marginal note: Aristo. Auerrois Mo. egy. Cicero] and their followers: which Cicero, inveighing against Plato, wove together into one in his eloquent speech: "With what eyes of the mind," he says, "could your Plato behold that fabric of such a great work, which he makes to be constructed and built by God? What effort? What tools? What levers? What machines? Who were the ministers of such a great task? How could air, water, fire, and earth obey the Architect? From where arose so many suitable forms for producing the mind and generating the senses?" And having progressed a little from these points, I ask: why did the builders of the world remain dormant for innumerable ages? For even if there was no world, there were some ages: even if not those which are completed by the number of days and nights in annual courses (for I confess that these could not have been made without the world's revolution), there was certainly from infinite time a certain eternity, which no circumscription of times measured: However, of what kind that space was, cannot be understood: for it does not even fall within the realm of understanding, that there was some time when no time existed. Therefore, in such an immense space, why did providence cease? Was it fleeing labor? What was it, moreover, that God should desire to adorn the world with signs and lights like an architect? If so that God himself might dwell better: before, he dwelt in darkness as if in a hovel: If we think he delights in variety, because we see he adorned heaven and earth: What kind of delight of God can this be, which he could have lacked for so long? Or are these things, as you generally say, established by God for the sake of humans? For the wise, or for the foolish? If for the wise, then such a great effort of things was made for the sake of a few: If for the foolish, then first there was no reason: that he should deserve well of the wicked. Then what has he achieved, when all have become foolish? What can we say is more miserable than foolishness? Thus far Cicero. Alcinous adds: "Since nothing remains outside the world that could inflict force, [Marginal note: Alcinous] it will not suffer disease or any dissolution: And since it will endure perpetually: therefore it was also perpetual."
