[Marginal note: Paulus] And if it is contended that good by nature tends towards communicating good: here, ascending higher than philosophy inquires, we will say: That highest good always diffuses itself into its offspring, and co-eternal spirit: in which offspring it continuously produces those eternal exemplars, that measure which is always present, and the whole possession at once. Nor was He inactive in idleness before the generation of the world, who, as the Son testifies, always works a work which no one knows, just as no one knows the worker, except the Son: and to whom the Son wishes to reveal it. These things were not revealed to Aristotle, nor to Averroes, nor to those who are content with only an Aristotelian or Ciceronian torch. Nor was He inactive (to speak with you) who was most happy in Himself, nor for Himself, who needs no external thing, did He build this worldly house with such ornament: but for man, the chief, not foolish or wicked, but just and wise: or at least, that in the same house he might be instructed in wisdom and goodness: that he might be a worthy citizen of the super-mundane palace. This play He had with the orb of lands, and with the sons of men: Which Cicero or Aristotle did not know: Because as Trismegistus says: God (whom they name nature) by mixing Himself with man, brought forth a miracle, which surpasses the reason of all miracles. [Marginal note: Triſme.] In whom, beholding His own image, He smiled upon him with immense love: and congratulating Himself as if on a son, He granted all his works for his own use: that he might bring all things back to Himself through him, with whom He was mixed, but him first of all: provided that, purified and recognizing his divine origin, he might be made worthy of God: But to this, the greatest impediment is brought by the delight in corporeal things, and the erroneous love of inferior things: By which hindered minds recognize neither themselves, nor even God, whose image they bear. Nor did He need instruments, who accomplishes all things by mere command. Nor did that Archetype, existing as the giver of all forms (as that thrice-greatest one teaches), and most full of all fruitfulness, need assistance to produce forms.

--- Page 168 ---
CANTICI PRIMI

Nor is it strange if the elements obeyed him, which were cast forth by his sole command. Nor did he dwell in a hovel, but in the most spacious dwelling of that immense sphere, whose center is everywhere: There he resided through those eternal ages, which neither you nor any mind apart from him can comprehend. Therefore, it is no wonder if you and other mortals struggle in conceiving those things which lie hidden in the archive of the supreme architect, revealed to very few. And to turn myself to Alcinous, there is nothing outside the world into which it might be resolved, nor do we say it itself is to be resolved: granted that it had a beginning of its duration. And if it is resolved, it requires nothing beforehand into which it might be dissolved, just as it did not seek anything beforehand from which it might be made: since its creation or dissolution is independent of the laws of natural generation and dissolution. Nor did he await co-workers, [Marginal note: Avicenna] O Avicenna, who accomplishes all things by his own power and good pleasure, as we shall presently declare. And not by nature or necessity, as those believe to whom the eternal power of God and the love by which he created the world is hidden.

Why the Philosophers erred from Catholic truth. Chapter XIII.

[Illuminated initial H containing a figure of a man at a desk] These and similar forces and machines the philosophers directed in vain against the walls of supernal truth, Whose teaching is not usurped by human pride, but diffused by the clarity of divine power: which mocks those who are wise in their own eyes and despise others, leaving them in the darkness of their obscured arrogance, but those whom it illuminates, it leads to contemplate the inner sanctuaries of God and nature with clear light. And so that I may expose, even in part, the madness of those who arrogate to themselves the name of wisdom, I would like to ask them this one thing: how they recognize the blessed God. They will certainly respond: "From motion and these sensible things, by which we are led to those things which can be known by us, because all our knowledge has its origin from sense; and the test of true statements is (says [Marginal note: Averroes] Averroes) that they agree with sensible things." And that is more known in which more senses agree. These are their most common doctrines: but let them say, I ask. Do these sensible things have a univocal or an equivocal proportion with the supreme God? Not indeed univocal, if we follow their teachings, by which they teach that God and created things do not agree in any [Marginal note: Porphy. Aristo.] univocal concept of substance or being. Hence Porphyry, pursuing their doctrine, says: "If anyone calls all beings, he will name them equivocally (says Aristotle, of course)." Whom many more recent (philosophers) follow, although some, holding a univocal concept of God and creature, substance and accident, try to interpret Aristotle's mind to their own purpose, perhaps fearing to contradict such a highly esteemed man without necessity. But if they are equivocal, it is no wonder if by proceeding through these lower things they err in the knowledge of God. For what can they [Marginal note: Aristote. Averroes] imagine about God through their motion or these sensible things, who is entirely alien from senses and motion? For he is entirely removed (says Aristotle with his Averroes in the discourse on the heavens) from the modes of creatures. Hence, that he is the first mover, who is not moved, they only know, all other knowledge about him through creatures being excluded: since him

--- Page 169 ---
they remove [Him] from the modes of creatures. Therefore, it is not surprising if they try to take away many things, as if closed off to themselves, from the supreme Creator. Namely, that He created the world, that He fashioned it with free generosity, and that He established it when He willed. What He produces according to nature, or out of His innate benevolence: How He foresees all things, even the smallest, what He requires from His creations, why He constructed this machine, how He conducted Himself in its making. And it is indeed strange, that while on the one hand they completely remove God from the modes of creatures, on the other hand, through those things they observe in these lower realms, they wish to restrict God's omnipotence and virtue.

Let them hear, I ask, what the great Dionysius, first imbued with their [Marginal note: Diony.] discipline, and afterwards illuminated by the rays of divine power, says about Him. God (he says) is all things eminently. For whatever good we observe in these domestic things, let us dedicate it to the sublime God, in the most excellent way we can: because all things that are beautiful in a work of art ought to flourish more beautifully in the Artist. And whatever is commended in mediocre things, and in the lowest, it is fitting to be found in the best. For good is always better in the better. Wisdom is good in a Citizen, better in a Praetor, best in a Prince. Power is good in a Soldier, better in a leader, best in a King. Let the same be held for clemency, liberality, and other virtues and adornments. But since fecundity, power, vigor, piety, beauty, munificence, and other things of that kind shine in lower things: they ought to vibrate with supreme splendor in that divine mind. For in this worldly populace, all these things paint the soul like adventitious colors: but in the super-worldly Prince, they gleam with the rays of His infinite essence (which unites all things attributed and dedicated to Him).

These people admit God is the first and best of all, but that other things are inferior and ministering to Him. And if they commend fecundity, liberty, generation, and similar things in this manner: why do they deny them to the best God, who says to His own household: "If I grant generation to others, shall I be barren?" They will perhaps say: We remove from God not only what savors of imperfection, [Marginal note: Iſaias] but everything that falls short of perfection. Hence we take away external fecundity from Him: lest anything new, or any change, be ascribed to that eternal and immutable being. We also remove the liberty of contingency from Him: lest He seem to act as if imperfect, hoping for retribution: nor do we deny the liberty by which He acts, according to what is fitting for Him. These are indeed subtle arguments, yet they do not restrict. Do not, O wise ones, all schools teach: that these lower things strive to hold the image of God to the best of their ability? This the Platonists everywhere, this the Catholics with great [Marginal note: Platoni. Cathol. Ariſto.] consonance echo. But even the Peripatetics agree on the same point: as their master says word for word in the second discourse on the Soul: "It is the most natural of operations for living beings: that whatever are perfect, and not deprived, or have spontaneous generation, to make another like itself." An animal indeed, an animal: a plant truly, a plant: so that they may participate in that divine and immortal being, as far as they can: For all things desire that, and for its sake they do all things whatsoever they do according to nature: and they cannot imitate it continuously, nor with perpetual reason for it,

**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

As for the fact that nothing corruptible manages to remain identical and numerically one, but rather each thing participates and communicates [in this permanence] to the extent it can, some more, some less: thus far, Aristotle. The gist of whose words is: that each member of this earthly body, the more perfect it is, the more it strives to emulate the maker. [Marginal note: Averroes] What faithless Arab interprets this concerning heaven? For how, according to the faithless one, is heaven that eternal thing which all things emulate, when this eternal thing is that for whose sake the elements, and heaven itself, and all things act?

[Marginal note: Aristotle] Do not Aristotle's dogmas everywhere resound, that God is the end of all things, for whose sake, as beloved and desired, all things are moved? But these are the least among many things which the faithless dog, barking against the truth, distorts and destroys the master's meanings: in which the name of destroyer rather than commentator could be ascribed to him. Nor should anyone wonder if I rage against this slanderer, because the zeal of the living God burns me: for this wretch dares to blaspheme, and makes very many others (alas, to be lamented) blaspheme.

Listen, I beg you, what this dog barks there about the best God. Divine solicitude, he says, since it could not make this remain as an individual, took pity by giving the power so that they could remain in species. Be silent, faithless dog, nor presume to speak of God, you fugitive from light. With what audacity do you dare to measure the power of the Almighty? Why could He not give permanence to man and other inferior things, which He gave to Saturn, and all the Planets, and stars, as you assert? How did He become impotent in inferior things, who was so powerful in the highest things? What dignity of the Most High God, who, when He could not provide one benefit to His inferiors, took care to provide another. But if you attribute this solicitude to heaven, I truly wonder, while you ascribe the providence and work of the highest Prince to ministers. And if the heavens could not do this, why could the highest Prince not do it?

But returning to where we digressed, these people confess that all things are divine and emulate perfection: elements in being, plants in life and fecundity, animals in a better life, and in whatever their condition. Man, however, who rejoices in the peculiar gift of liberty, in the same way emulates God. Hence also liberty is proven in God, because He contains all things which He bestows upon others. Nor does the highest perfection fail in lower degrees; nor is its simplicity destroyed in many things, by which it contains all things with infinite power. Nor indeed does the intellectual soul degenerate, if it exercises the power of sensing, vegetating, and moving according to place, according to their dogmas.

For God senses (that we may ascend to higher things) with His own senses, which the sacred scriptures attribute to Him. He moves all other things, remaining stable, gives life, and is nourished by His own food of wisdom. But all these things in their manner, and perfection, and power, lie hidden from human intellects, unless they are illuminated by His light.

For liberty is not an election according to nature (as some think), nor indifferent to good or evil, but to good according to its own free will. In man, however, the most perfect of living beings, this liberty has somewhat degenerated, so that it can even be carried towards evil; but in this it least emulates God. But in a better way, perhaps above all things, it bears His image. And it is in God Himself

fertility without labor, as Mercury says: God, endowed with the fertility of both sexes,

And let them remove whatever denotes weakness in the operator: and then they will see that the

harmony, which we have proposed. For neither do the singers, sub-singers, and counter-singers enter

notes, produce the same harmony: For all things are in the Maker, as it were,
in a certain likeness: which are contemplated in these lower things as in an image or a trace:

represents. Nevertheless, from these things, through analogy and a certain symbol, we arrive
at the knowledge of the Maker: Which agree neither by a different reason as equivocal terms, nor
exactly the same as univocal terms: but by a certain similitude, representing
that most perfect characteristic of higher things, each according to its degree, with its own
somewhat inferior and less refined quality.

nevertheless wrote it with this law, that no one should understand the enclosed
mysteries, unless they are led by the same divine power with which they themselves
were imbued.
    Philosophers fail, while they strive to prove that God acts necessarily
        externally.                                           Cap. XVI.

[Large decorative initial E] Having concluded the discussion on the world's creation, another battle remains for us to settle with the Philosophers, before we enter into the innermost secrets of God and nature: Namely, whether God is led to action by a certain necessity, or by a free and contingent choice. Philosophers were of the opinion that the condition of necessity was better than that of contingency, and for this reason they attributed it to God: To which reasons seem to assent, especially this, because He acts through His own substance and not through a borrowed power: Also because the effects of the world seem necessary, which in no way seem to proceed from a contingent cause: Also the seemingly invariable and necessary order of things, lest the universe be confused or disturbed. Nor could they deem it consistent that the divine intellect should act necessarily, and the will freely, since that divine mind and will is no less perfect than the intellect. We too could direct some arrows from the quiver of rational discourse at the philosophers, but since a matter of this kind pertains to God, we believe, with Plato, that it is not to be investigated by reason, but learned from oracles. The great lawgiver thunders: "God said, and it was done,"  Moſes.
with whom also his successor David: "He spoke, and they were made." But what  Dauid
seems to disturb those wise men is absolutely nothing. They presuppose a necessary
disposition to be more perfect than a contingent one, which they left to their successors
to prove. Do we not rather commend a Prince who directs all things according to his
will, than if he were to direct the work by nature or by any other impulse or stimulus?
                                                         C iiij

--- Page 178 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

Who would condemn freedom, which (as it is commonly said) is not sold cheaply for all gold? Which wise men consider to be a special good granted to men. What perfection, I ask, what praise would there be in exalted minds, if they were always compelled to one side? What dignity would there be in a Prince, if he did all things by nature, and nothing by a generous spirit? Since by common consent we acknowledge God as the Prince of the world: What glory concerning governance, wisdom, justice, or clemency could be ascribed to Him, if for all things entrusted to Him, He were led by inevitable necessity? What thanks, or what worship, would we owe Him? Why, O Aristotle (as you say), is sacrificing innate to nature? Why are we bound, Averroes (as you teach), to magnify God the Creator with prayers and sacrifices? If God acts necessarily, to what end are sacrifices? To what end are prayers? Nevertheless, secondary causes are so bound to the primary cause that they operate only as much as the primary cause commands. But the same (as Augustine says) administers the things which it has created in such a way that it allows them to perform their own proper motions. Which, because it rarely happens, and because the order decreed from the primal institution persists in most cases and frequently, therefore Aristotle judges it to be natural and necessary. Natural (as he himself [Marginal note: Aristo.] teaches in *On Physical Hearing*) is that which happens in most cases, and frequently. Nor could he investigate further from sensible things. But the operations of God, and the connection of inferior things with the primary cause, are not to be investigated by rational discourse, but to be learned from oracles (as we have said). Hence, no progress from that necessity which is seen in effects to the necessity of the cause is proven, since the necessity of effects depends on the order of the primary cause. Nor indeed are they necessary, since all are particular: because the work of nature is not limited to the universal, but to the singular, which they themselves report to be more contingent than necessary. As for what they add, that God's will has equal perfection with the intellect, which acts necessarily, we admit, while it operates in its innermost parts in conformity with the intellect itself, but it unfolds external effects, which the intellect depicted from eternity in the Word, at will. Indeed, I wonder at those philosophers who confess God to be most simple and perfect, with all externals excluded, and immediately forgetting their own dogma, they think God has a necessary connection with inferior things, as if He could not exist or be blessed without them. How is He most simple, if He has a necessary connection with others? How is the prince of all (as they say) necessarily enslaved to the service of inferiors? What dignity, what condition is this for the supreme prince? Nor should they fear that the order of celestial things and the universe would be destroyed if the craftsman disposes and varies at will, since He knows how to reduce to order what He has made and ordered. Nor indeed is the destruction of the work to be feared when the craftsman applies his hand, by whose touch it is perfected rather than destroyed.

Progress for contingency in divine workmanship. Chapter XVII.

Up to this point, we have taken up the shield for the defense of truth and divine majesty; but now, beyond those things which divine oracles have taught, we will direct some arrows against the enemies of truth, who believe God acts necessarily. And if they are rather to be scorned than refuted—
[Marginal note: Procul.] those whom Proclus, following Plato's mind, places in the third class of impiety, and decrees that one should not deal with them when speaking of divine matters—nevertheless, so that they may be pierced by their own darts, we will run through some points. And I would like to ask them to explain whence monsters arise in nature. For they will say: Because matter was deficient or superfluous; or qualities do not correspond in due proportion; or because of the container's fault; and things of this kind, which are subdivided into various members. But if these causes act necessarily, why do they not prepare everything properly, since nature (as they say) does not fail in necessary things? How then do they act necessarily, if they fail? "You wish to infer," they will say, "that natural causes operate contingently." And if they were to say: What would follow? Nevertheless,

--- Page 181 ---
**TONVS PRIMVS.** **22**

to remove superfluous argumentation, let them remember what is common in schools: that necessity has a twofold manner of existing: one indeed absolute, the other truly conditional. The former (unless the truth of the sacred scriptures deceives me) must be attributed to God alone, the Blessed. The latter, however, to inferior things, so that they are necessary by the order given by the Creator. But because perhaps the philosophers would deny this, let us come to the work of these causes. For if they err and produce monsters, that is because the order decreed for them by nature (as they say) or by the supreme Creator is deficient: as is the truth. And if they deviate from the order, that [order] was not simply necessary, but given by the first cause, to which other [causes] are subordinated and act in its virtue: from which if the first withdraws itself, not only do they fail, but they accomplish nothing. And if some things seem to lead necessarily, that proceeds from the law given to them, as he full of God sings: *You have set a boundary, which they shall not pass.* [Marginal note: David] Nor is he bound by the law, who imposes law on others. But they will say: Therefore, knowledge will be about things that can be otherwise: the opposite of which Aristotle teaches? To whom we will say: If your Aristotle understands those things which are known to be necessary [Marginal note: Aristo] by the order of the universe, thus it will be about things impossible to be otherwise. But if he understands things absolutely necessary, let him remember what he taught at the end of the book *On Physical Hearing*: that it is not enough for the wise man to state something, unless he assigns a reason for what is stated. Nor let them adduce experience: because from that it will be easily concluded that that necessity proceeds from order, which failing, those things fail: Therefore they are not simply necessary. If they say: therefore they can be otherwise: What is that to me? Let them solve it themselves: For fire can not burn, as was actually the case: And any effect can be removed from the cause that produced it, while the inherence (as we said) of the predicate to the subject, about which their knowledge exists, remains. But having progressed further, I would like to learn from the Peripatetics: Whence do those things necessarily inhere? They will say: They have it from nature, as we prove by experience. But what is this nature of theirs? Nothing certainly, unless the author of the universe, who is true unerring intelligence, since (as they teach) the work of nature is the work of unerring intelligence: By whose order all things succeed: because all things serve Him, says the Prophet. [Marginal note: David] Nor let them say, What concern are the Prophets to us, since we do not consider anything to be known, unless it is proven by demonstration? But where, I ask, does demonstration have its origin? Is it not from principles, to which, once the terms are known, we assent, or which we prove by experience? But if we believe demonstrated things through principles and experienced things, therefore other things are known more than demonstrated things. O execrable vice, which has grown among our people, who bear the Christian name, that they do not admit as certain, unless it is proven by demonstration: which Aristotle [Marginal note: Aristo.] painted, but uses minimally in his natural progress, where he always proceeds from presuppositions made by him: so that what they believe to be demonstration, is a deduction by way of authority, or from things pre-accepted by him. If they are Catholics, let them believe the sacred pages more than Aristotle: If they are Academics, let them know that many things, especially divine ones, are known through illuminating rays, or through the agreement of what is said with an intellect inclined to truth. If they are Peripatetics, let them hear their Aristotle, that other things than demonstra-

...that things can be known with certainty: From where does he get that to know is to understand by demonstration? Is it not from Aristotle, speaking thus? And we have our doctrines from the [Marginal note: Prophets.] Prophets, taught by divine oracle: who prove what they teach by wonders and the peril of their lives. And if we were to say that to know is certain knowledge about anything whatsoever, would we sin against the Holy Spirit, or against Aristotle? Not against the Holy Spirit, certainly, and I care little for Aristotle: because he is neither my lord, nor shall I come to his tribunal to be judged if I do not adhere to him. But they will call me rash or ignorant: because I dare to depart from Aristotelian institutions, which so many brilliant minds follow. Hence pain, hence tears (alas, a horrible deed) after they fear more to deny Aristotle than Paul, in whose breast Christ resonates: indeed, Christ himself, who is the wisdom and truth of God, who will judge all, especially those who in name follow Him, but in doctrine and life follow Aristotle, whom the Greeks call a cacodaemon, or the insane and impious Averroes. We consider it a small thing (to speak with John Scotus) to deny Aristotle in those matters which [Marginal note: John Scotus.] are against the doctrine of truth that we defend: And although he was most sagacious, and a diligent reader of other doctrines, and a careful collector, yet he was a cunning accuser of the ancients: whose poorly presented opinions he by no means refutes, proceeding rather (as [Marginal note: Simplicius.] Simplicius, his auditor, says) against words than meanings, and obscuring many things: so that he alone might seem wise. Proclus.] by which Aristotle is weighed down: Who (as Proclus, professor of Academic and Peripatetic dogma, says) together with Theophrastus and other Peripatetics, extended the light of their speculation even to the forms moving the universe. [Marginal note: Plato.] Plato, however, takes his beginnings from that which has dignity among beings, far removed, and indeed more worthy: whence also his progress is more sublime. Aristotle also accuses countless others, whose sayings, if pondered, will perhaps not be judged worthy of censure: for from these very men he learned all that he wrote. Nor does he claim for himself, compelled by truth, anything but refutations (elenchi). The rest, however, receiving from the ancients, he weaves into his syllogistic processes: so that he delivered an artificial art and a debased method of proceeding, rather than science: as he himself tacitly admits, where he treats of the Posterior Analytics, teaching that science is by demonstration, and this by quiddities (as they say) and the proper differences of things hidden from us: From which the principles of demonstration are shown to be unknown, and that no, or very little, demonstration can be had from them. Moreover, he condemns circular demonstration, and yet teaches that demonstration is made from those things which are "of every per se" and "according to that which is itself," to speak in his manner: Which propositions are convertible and infer each other. They will say, "There is no circularity in demon-"

demonstration from causes. But let them note that a little above he had said that circular demonstration is sometimes found. But these things being omitted, since he teaches nothing in his doctrines that he has not received from the ancients: why should he be believed more than the ancients, who taught before him?

They will say: We accept what has been weighed in the Aristotelian balance. And would that it were not corrupted to the detriment of Christian religion and truth! Yet some insolent individuals, new to doctrine, dare to say with most impudent mouths: I do not cite Genesis, Jeremiah, or Isaiah to you; but I bring forth Aristotle: as if Moses and the prophets were not wise and learned in letters: although he [Moses] was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians: afterwards, by God's oracle, he was led to contemplate the innermost secrets of God himself and of nature: which neither Aristotle nor his most zealous followers ever considered.

And the Prophets, inspired by divine light [Marginal note: Prophets], which those who shun the light and are darkened cannot see, not only prophesied: but also handed down many things from the innermost storehouses of God and of lower things (though under their own enigmas).

Some more modest people say: We honor the prophets and holy men in divine matters: but in natural things, this [Aristotle] is the rule we must follow.

But I truly wonder how they could have known divine and supreme things: and yet the lower things, through which one arrives at the supreme, were closed off to them.

And since God is a mirror in which all things shine, how did they know Him without knowing the images that shine in Him?

Hence, they would not have thought that those [prophets] knew the archetype without knowing what is contained in it, if they had perceived the connection of the archetype with this mundane machine and the human world: of which each holds the likeness and image of the other: and from the knowledge of one, the other is easily recognized.

Hence, both by divine oracle and by many wise men—Mercury, Plato, Socrates, Zoroaster [Marginal notes: Mercury, Plato, Socrates, Zoroaster]—and by Aristotle himself [Marginal note: Aristotle], self-knowledge is commended in a wonderful way: because from it, a more perfect knowledge of God and of this machine [the universe] is more easily attained than Aristotle himself teaches.

Indeed, it was necessary for those prophets to contemplate divine and human things, and their correspondence: who spoke of divine matters through enigmas and veils of lower things, so that God's sacraments might be hidden from common and nocturnal eyes.

But if anyone reads the prophets with the veil removed, he will see that they explored the secrets of nature and God better than Aristotle.

Nor is the sun to be blamed if the eye does not see.

When (says Jerome) [Marginal note: Jerome] I was devoted to Cicero: if any prophet was taken into my hands, the language seemed uncultivated and rough: and I thought the defect was not of the light, but of the sun [i.e., the source, not the perception]. But being corrected, and with the veil removed, he saw in the prophets what he had not read before in gentile authors.

But let us return to the contingency of things.

Here Algazel [Marginal note: Algazel] argues more sharply, from the fact that the parts of this machine [the universe] are arranged in such a way that they could have been situated differently without any contradiction, hence they are contingent: and are arranged not by necessity, but by choice.

The Arab [Averroes] [Marginal note: Averroes] responds: We say that the parts of the world could not have been arranged differently: because the world is an animal.

From where did you faithlessly learn this kind of arguing from your Aristotle? For you want your authority to be for the principle of demon-

**FIRST CANTICLE**

demonstration. From where, moreover, this inference? Are you dreaming, or are you suffering from a frenzy? If the world is an animal: is it sensible or insensible? Deprived of sense, therefore not an animal: If it is sentient: does it see, hear, smell, taste, eat? If it eats: who, I ask, prepares food for it? From where does it obtain it for itself? In the world itself, or outside? If in the world: it eats itself: If outside the world: there is therefore another world. And it is doubtful, lest by eating each other, they destroy themselves. But setting aside jest in such a serious matter, if it is granted that it is an animal (as
[Marginal note: Plato] Plato, Aristotle, & many wise men seem to imply)
[Marginal note: Averroes] it is certainly not an animal contained under the genus of animals: because those things which are in that machine are divided by a prior division, before one arrives at 'animal'. But let it be said that it is called an animal according to a certain analogy & similitude: Why could its dispositions not have been ordered differently? From where does it contradict man, that he should have only one eye in his forehead, as is said of certain beings? Why could the upper jaw not have been made movable in other animals, and the lower fixed, as we observe in the crocodile? Why could other animals not have double knees, like the Camel? What contradiction would there be, if man had four arms, & only one ear? These things are so coordinated by the supreme moderator, that they could have been arranged differently without any contradiction, unless a specific condition of nature is presupposed: which the same creator himself established. But let us come to the world-animal. By what necessity is the sea, & land, arranged so that the ocean enters through the narrowest straits of Abila, & the high promontories of Calpe: which antiquity called the Pillars of Hercules? From where is it necessary: that from there it immediately spreads far and wide: which again extends into the Tuscan sea (which they call the Tyrrhenian): now it narrows into the Adriatic gulf: now it widens into the Syrian: now it flows around through the Aegean: which is called an archipelago from the beautiful multitude of intervening islands: and from there, constrained by the narrowest straits, it becomes the Hellespont: and the Propontis, where it expands: and where it is again pressed by the Thracian Bosphorus: when it again pours forth, the Pontus Euxinus, that is, the hospitable (the customs of the wild peoples having been softened) is formed: which was first called Axenus, that is, inhospitable, from the very cruel nature of its inhabitants: And again, when it mixes with the Maeotian swamp, it is named the Cimmerian Bosphorus? What also is the necessity, that the Nile, passing through the Ethiopians, & Arabs, arriving at Egypt, & the Tanais (Don River) running through both Scythias, & flowing into almost the middle of the Maeotian swamp, should distinguish the three principal parts of the world? What also is the necessity, that some part of the earth should be depressed into a valley: another should be spread out through plains: another should rise into hills, & higher mountains: and that rivers should flow with perpetual course, & torrents in their seasons? By what necessity are some clods of earth fertile, others sterile, some arid, & others marshy? Could we not imagine the entire circuit of the earth, without any contradiction, as flat, soft, and fruitful? And if God can do what we cannot think, as wiser men than Averroes affirm, why can He not do what we imagine? But if He is able to accomplish this: then things are not necessarily arranged in the way we perceive them.

**FIRST TONE. 24**
**That God knows particulars. Chapter XVIII.**

Now also other javelins must be hurled back against the natural philosophers, so that, fortified by the unshaken shield of truth, we may proceed to other matters. They were of the opinion that blessed God only looked upon higher and universal things, with particulars either being disregarded or entrusted to secondary causes, as if the divine intellect would disdain, or act more basely, if it were to behold such things. Not to see (says Aristotle) certain things is better and nobler than to see them. [Aristo.] The Arab, interpreting him, says: To be ignorant of base things is better than to know them. [Averroes] What (I ask) are those base things which it is better if they are not known than if they are known? Those things which do not exist, cannot be known. Those things which exist, are certainly good. If good, how are they base? And if you contend that some good things are also base, what, I ask, are those good base things? If you understand an Angel: why not heaven? And if heaven: why not man? And if man: why not the elements, where man lives? Why not horses, and oxen, and all things serving man, and certain known things that are part of man? Where shall we place the limits of His understanding? In heaven, or on earth, in the elements, in plants, or in living creatures? Where, I ask? And (to speak with Cicero) [Cicero] if God cares for heaven, and for the island which we call the globe of the earth, He will also care for its inhabitants, and for the parts of the island, Europe, Asia, and Africa, and their inhabitants: and that He may prefer the great (because no one is great unless inspired by divine will) and that He may sustain the small: For He made the small and the great (as that wise man says). [Wise man] Of these, and of the whole world, since they themselves confess Him to be the ruler: what will He do in His rule unless He exercises governance? And if He rules all things: how is it better that He should be ignorant even of the lowest things which He governs, than if He should know them? Who forced Him into ignorance of physical things, mathematical things, and other things, even if they are most minute? Who measured His capacity? [Aristo.] Aristotle, or Averroes? He commends the opinion of the Chaldean fathers, [Chaldeans] who with shrewd intellect investigated the knowledge of God: and yet he does not agree with them: that God understands all things. Nor does the intellect of a wise man become base (good sirs): if he knows the degrees, qualities, and even the most minute powers of herbs, juices, and stones. Nor if he knows the degrees of celestial bodies, minutes, seconds, thirds, and hundredths of minutes. Solomon is commended by the voice of all, to whom the surname "wise" [Salomon] (is given): because he discoursed from the cedar of Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall: and who spoke of beasts, birds, creeping things, and fishes: Did his intellect and wisdom become base because of this? Did Aristotle and Theophrastus [Aristot. Theoph.] become base, who, imitating him, the one discoursed on the nature of animals, the other on the nature of plants? And if we wish to recall older figures: did not Hermes, greatest in wisdom, [Hermes] write of a singular harmony of certain stars, stones, and herbs? His grandfather Aesculapius (as some believe) [Aescula. Apollo] was held as a god together with Apollo: because they were the first, having learned the properties of herbs and roots, to apply their juices, leaves, and powders to heal human bodies. Who, I ask, are wiser, those ignorant of these things, or those who, because of their knowledge of these very things, (were held in such great honor...)

--- Page 186 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

...knowledge of these things, claimed the name of wise men for themselves? But they will say: They were wise, not because they contemplated particulars, but because they contemplated the species of things and universal nature. And how did they investigate the species of things, unless by a pre-existing (as they teach), that is, particular experience? Nor could they know species without particulars: since the universal is nothing else (as they assert) but one out of many. How can this one be understood, unless the many are also understood: from which that one is extracted by them: or through ideal reasons, which they themselves do not sustain?

Nor if he understands all species, will it be contradictory. Therefore, he will be able to know animals, small fish, worms, ants, and plants. But why, I ask, will he be ignorant of man, the prelate of the world? How will he rule him as a prince, provide for his necessities, judge, unless he knows all his needs, and his deeds, both good and bad? The wisdom of God thunders forth, to which it is better to believe than to Aristotle or Averroes: [Marginal note: Christ David] "Your Father knows what you need." And His prophetic trumpet thunders: "My frame was not hidden from you, when I was made in the secret place: your eyes saw my unformed body, and in your book all of them will be written: so that they may receive worthy rewards for good or ill deeds."

They bring forward another argument: which they consider their strongest point. Namely, that that supreme mind cannot understand these lower things: lest, moved or perfected by them, it fall from its simplicity. Indeed, I wonder how they equate the knowledge of the Most High God [Marginal note: Aristotle.] with ours, when Aristotle says: that the intellect of God is simple, and perfect, and from itself. And thus, from itself, it understands all things that are in the world: [Marginal note: Averroes] Averroes, interpreting his words, posits a difference between God's knowledge and ours: because ours is caused by being: but that [God's knowledge] is of being. Nor does he wish to say openly: that it is the cause of being: as Catholics freely profess: yet compelled by truth, he cannot remain silent. For above he had said through obscure words, which I do not know whether the Barbarian uttered barbarically, or deliberately obscured: which he was unwillingly compelled to confess. Listen, I ask, to these monstrous words: "Truth," he says, "is: first, that it knows all things: second, that it knows itself only by knowledge in being, which is the cause of their being." And to pursue the Barbarian in his barbaric speech: If knowledge in being, in things, is the cause of those things which are: therefore, by understanding, it causes those things which are: And if it understands them: is not their understanding in its own intellect?

Why then do you, and your teacher, deride ideas: which are nothing other than the cognitions of things, and the exemplars of things to be made in that first intellect: which produces all things by knowing and commanding? Nor does it take knowledge from the produced object, or is it moved, or perfected, or does it beg to understand, or be excited: as our intellect does. Nor does that supreme intellect fail by contemplating so many particulars: Rather, that unique intellect of Averroes would fail by informing, or directing, or illuminating so many individuals. Oh, what foolishness and madness! Do you think the intellect you fabricate is stronger than God, who fabricated all things? Since God is moreover the end of all things: towards whom all things are directed, as towards the beloved and desired: by whom are all these things directed? "By nature," they will say. But what is this nature? By no one yet...

--- Page 187 ---
TOMVS PRIMVS. 25

I have ascertained what that nature is, about which they speak: whether it was made by God, or whether, like God's spouse, it produced the world together with Him; since they say, God and nature do nothing in vain, as if they together bring forth the offspring of this world. Nor can nature of this kind be matter or form, which do nothing, order nothing. Nor reasons, nor degrees of things, because they hint at something universal through this nature of theirs: that it acts together with God. But what that is, they have nowhere explained. Nevertheless, they profess that God acts together with it, and has disposed all things well; and elsewhere they assert that God does nothing except as an attracting end. And if the secondary causes, with which it co-acts, are this nature, who ordered them? Who established that they should cooperate together? Nature (they say) is the principle of motion and rest. But what is this principle of motion and state, unless an inclination inherent in those subjected to motion itself by some agent? And whether they wish or not, they must agree on one thing, from whom all motion and order proceeds, as they themselves teach. And if I did not fear exposing myself to the Peripatetics as a rash person to be torn apart, I would ask, what is this nature, to which they say universals are first known? What mutual process is there from nature to us, and vice versa? Who answers us in this game of balls? What again is this nature, which provides us with principles, through which we may know conclusions? Is it some general agent? Or something aggregated from natural things? Or their order? Is it something capable of reason, or an element, a stone, the sky, or something of this kind lacking sense? If it does not perceive, nor understand, how are principles known to it? But if it is intellectual, what is this nature? Is it us, or intelligences, or God Himself? If it is us, how will the same things be known to us beforehand, from which we may pre-receive knowledge? If intelligences are this nature, how are they outside natural and physical speculation (as they themselves teach) because they are not moved while they move? And why do they not say: these principles are known to separate or conjoined intelligences? But if God is this nature, why do they name it as something separated from Him, while they say God and nature? Is this nature again some intellect outside the universe, or a fifth, or sixth essence? Perhaps the Averroists will say: Nature is a single, perfect intellect, understanding all these things. But how will this intellect be the principle of motion and rest, insofar as it is what it is? Therefore, this intellect will be in living beings, fleas, and flies, and tiny plants, and elements, moving them with their own motions. Therefore, this single intellect will be not only in humans, but also in all things: why then do not all things understand? Because it admits no superfluous member, nor heaven, nor the vilest speck of dust, nor any superfluous motion, since it has disposed all things in the best possible way. But who is ordering all these things, unless He whom we profess to be God? Why then, speaking of nature, do you hint at something separated from God Himself? Perhaps lest you confess that God made the world, which you impiously denied: You have conceded, however, that God with nature si-

**HOW GREAT A DISSONANCE IS FOUND AMONG THE DISCORDANT WISE MEN OF THE WORLD IN THEIR DOCTRINES. Chapter One.**

[Large decorative initial T] O great a dissonance do those who are called the wise men of the world both handle and agitate this worldly instrument, that their schools are unable to agree neither in doctrine, nor in morals, nor in religion, nor in the end for which they do all things. And they resound with such dreadful horror that no one can listen to them sounding together, with harmony utterly broken: which (as musicians define it) is the concord of strings or voices harmonizing in complete modes without any offense. But these men, nourished in the same school, taught under the same teacher, utterly disagree. The Socratic disciples Aristippus and Ariston so greatly disagree on the end: that the one placed our end in pleasure, while the other placed it in virtues. [Marginal note: Aristippus. Ariston] Aristotle's chief followers, Alexander and Averroes, splitting his doctrine, create a divergence, [Marginal note: Alexander] especially in the matter of the soul: since the former asserts it to be mortal, but the latter asserts a unique intellect in all things; [Marginal note: Averroes] who disagree not only among themselves, but also from the truth. But Aristotle, a student of Plato for more than twenty years, [Marginal note: Aristotle] so greatly disagreed with the doctrine and morals of his teacher that he accused him and pursued him with false slanders. The Saracen Algazel [Marginal note: Algazel] rises up against all philosophers: and the Arab Averroes strives to attack him, [Marginal note: Averroes] but like a snake, he is broken in the very attempt. Lucretius the Epicurean [Marginal note: Lucretius] disagrees both with his fellow students and with himself, now proclaiming that God has fellowship with mortals, now denying that he has it; thus in many other things, he pursues manifest dissonance. But the Pythagoreans, [Marginal note: Pythagoras] concerning the transmigration of souls, are utterly divided into many dissenting factions. Hiarcas the Brahman and Apollonius of Tyana [Marginal note: Hiarcas Apo. Th.] asserted that transmutations occurred even into beasts. From which arose those celebrated metamorphoses, in which they sing of one changed into a wolf, another into a nightingale, another into a laurel, and similar transformations. Iamblichus and Porphyry [Marginal note: Iamblichus Porphyry] utterly rejected such transmigrations into beasts, not admitting that the soul, once fixed in its center, could be torn out. But also Proclus, Hermias, and Syrianus [Marginal note: Proclus. Hermias Syrianus] considered it a horrible crime for a celestial soul to be cast down into beasts. Timaeus Locrus, a most noble Pythagorean, [Marginal note: Timaeus] asserts that these transmutations were introduced for the terror of men. Chapter II. That Catholic writers agree.
**V**But those who confess one God, the maker of all, and the fount from which all waters of true wisdom emanate, all made as one voice, Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, with the greatest harmony, both praise the same God and lay the foundations of the world's edifice. Moses, Job, David, Solomon, and all the Prophets, with those who wrote the Gospels, and Paul with the whole Apostolic company, together with the supercelestial intelligences, in God's assembly produce the sweetest harmony: indeed with diverse voices, yet with the same sound: For dissimilar voices do not produce dissonance, but harmony, provided they converge into one: For what harmony would there be if all the strings of a lyre produced a low or a high sound? Or if (to touch upon the principles of music) hypate, perhypate, lichanos, mese, paramese, and all subsequent strings of the instrument, so named by musicians, produced the gravest tone, that of the hypate, by which it represents Saturn? And what consonance of the planets would there be if all moved with the gravity of Saturn, or ran with the swiftness of the Moon? What beauty of the body also would there be if all members were eyes, or ears? For just as beauty (as the Peripatetics teach) results from various members harmonizing with each other: so from various voices arises diapentic, diapasonic, diatessaronic, or diatonic harmony: Which is not founded in various voices, but in a concordant sound, which results from those diverse voices.
Therefore, those sounding in the divine lyre do not generate dissonance: If John and Augustine are elevated to the fervent and acute seraphim: If Ambrose and Matthew utter voices among the grave thrones of maxims: If Luke and Gregory delight in cherubic sweetness: If Jerome with Mark, with the more robust voice of powers and virtues, suppresses and suffocates the dissonant blasts of heretics: If Solomon and Bernard sing epithalamia of the bridegroom and bride of the heavenly nuptials with Gabriel: And turning to the Greeks, Basil with Ezekiel always brings forth divine things with the higher minds. Gregory Nazianzen with Jeremiah, with a tragic voice, sympathizing with the patient bridegroom and bride, also laments the slaughter of those invited to their nuptials. Isaiah and John, whose surname is Chrysostom, resonate with the Archangels with wonderful eloquence. Daniel and John Damascene treat the sacraments of God with a clearer voice: but the latter describes lower and domestic influences, while the former describes the supercelestial fount, from which these lower things flow. And other harmonious singers have followed in this divine instrument.
Scotus and Francis correspond to the high-sounding Augustine: but the former with a slower movement makes a graver and more robust sound: while the latter with a swifter course resonates more acutely. Albert with weighty judgment, and by diligent investigation of the secrets of both natures, emulates Ambrose. Thomas Angelicus in voice and doctrine, and in ineffable sweetness, follows Bernard, but in breadth, follows Augustine. [Marginal note: Lactan.] For, as Firmianus says, dissonance happens to them because they have departed from that unique master of all truths and giver of harmony (as we said), rashly presuming to investigate by their own powers those things which God willed to be obscure rather than hidden, namely, the nature of heavenly and earthly things. These, far removed from us, can neither be touched by hand nor perceived by the senses; and yet they dispute about the reason of all these things in such a way that they want what they assert to seem proven and known. From this, not only have they themselves fallen into error, but they have also led very many others adhering to them, blind, with themselves into the pit of darkness and errors; and (alas, sad to say) daily lead still others.

From this, his principal followers, Alexander [Alexan.] and Averroes [Auerrois], made a crossroads: and how far each of them is removed from all piety, religion, and truth is now evident. Pythagoras [Pytha.] believed the soul to be a certain divine kind of being inherent in humans, full of forms indeed, but submerged and hindered by the corporeal forest: so that it seems to have drunk from the Lethaean river, that is, oblivion. Timaeus Locrus [Tim. lo.] and Plato [Plato] with the other Academics imitate him. However, they strove to conceal the essence and nature of this soul as if they were divine sacraments, as was their custom; or they did not express what perhaps they themselves had not understood: as Plato [Idem] testifies in *Laws* 10: "What kind of soul it is," he says, "and what power it has, almost all seem to have been ignorant." If they did transmit anything about it, they proceeded through numbers as if these were more known to them: not perceiving the fourfold nature of these numbers, and how one ascends from the vocal to the formal, and thence to the rational, from which to the divine number, they either judged this progression through number to be a kind of delusion; or, treading with longer and more circuitous steps, after Pythagoras [Pytha.] and Plato [Plato], they deviated into various paths. Anaxander [Anaxan.] said the soul is a number; Aristoxenus [Aristo.] said it is a number moving itself. Others believed the soul to be from unity, as from the indivisible; and from duality, as from the divisible. Severus [Seuer.] asserts that it has a geometric essence, composing it from a point and distance: the latter indeed divisible, the former truly indivisible. Plutarch [Plutar.] and Atticus [Atticus] say that its passible part is irrational; the impartible part is divine: the divine part indeed emanating and composing; the other truly holding the place of the subject. They add, moreover, that the soul is unbegotten according to its subject, but begotten according to its form. Plotinus [Plotinus], speaking more physically, places it midway between intellect and sense: the former indeed individual, the latter truly divisible even through bodies. Asmeus [Asme.] and Theodorus [Theod.] ascend higher, and drawing (according to Porphyry [Prophy.]) the origin of their opinion from Persia, they posit two intellects before their soul: one indeed containing the idea of universals, the other of particulars, and the soul as the middle ground between these. Proclus [Procul.] posits it as unique and manifold, individual and multiplied according to the number of subjects: Nor did he explain Plato's [Plato] opinion about it, emulating the same master who in many places (especially when writing to Dionysius) protests that the sacraments of God are not to be made public. Nor do these wise men of the world agree with any consistency on where the soul is located. Hippocrates [Hippo.] asserts that the principal power of the soul has its seat in the head. Epicurus denies this: because many animals live for a time with their heads cut off, as if no damage were done to the whole; such as bees and drones. Empedocles [Emped.] established the principal force of the soul in the heart. But Epicurus also denies this: because crocodiles live for some time with their hearts torn out, and resist violence. The Stoics [Stoici] place it in the heart, not mediated by blood (as Empedocles said), but by spirit, so that it is located in the spirit rather than in the heart: as Chrysippus [Chrysi.] implies. Others [place it] in the blood, which seems to be drawn from Moses [Moses]: who (by divine oracle commanding) forbids the eating of blood: because the soul of the animal is in it. Philosophers and physicians still dispute this matter, awaiting judgment.

**Of the First Canticle**

That they disagree no less in describing that end which all things seek. Chapter V.

[Decorative initial L]ong and tedious would it be to present all the various opinions concerning the end of this our life and condition. Augustine mentions two hundred and eighty-eight opinions collected by M. Varro. Six are also mentioned by Plotinus in his 'On Beatitude'; omitting these, we will more briefly survey those which are more frequently discussed in schools and in public places. Zeno of Citium, Cleanthes, Posidonius, Hecato, Dionysius the Babylonian, all Stoics, considered our end to be laborious virtues; but Antisthenes expressed that it is in the virtue of the soul. The Epicureans, however, especially Aristippus, Eudoxus of Cnidus, and the Cyrenaics, placed it in pleasures, which are contrary to toil. The Peripatetics in contemplation. The Platonists, always recalling divine decrees, gave decrees sufficiently akin to the Christian religion. These decree the union with the highest good as the end of man, as Plotinus in the cal[ce].

you may be ignorant of to whom you should award the palm, until (as Firmianus says) someone descends from heaven to pass judgment on the opinions of individuals. But in the meantime, since we cannot tolerate those who are dissonant, let us leave them aside and return to our own.

Whence our people derived consonance, and those others dissonance. Chapter VI.

[Decorative initial Q] As many as have handed down the principles of music teach that the foundation of consonance is one: into which many similar and dissimilar things converge. And the harmonious sound, which many singing together make, poets and grammarians call Polymnia, as if it were a convergence of many songs into one. Hence it is necessary for this harmony to proceed from instruments, strings, pipes, or suitable voices, if sounds or harmonious voices are to converge into one. For no one will make the roar of lions, the lowing of oxen, the neighing of a horse, or the braying of an ass converge. Nor can strings made from the sinews of a wolf and a lamb (as we have learned by experience) be brought into any consonance, because their foundations are dissonant. Nevertheless, the voices of men of different languages and nations converge easily, because their foundation is unique according to species. And many musical birds of different species converge, because their genus is uniquely related, and they share a symbol from above. And artificial instruments converge together, and with natural voices, because in both there is a similarity, either true and expressed, or through a certain analogy. Our doctors also agree, for whom the canon of sacred letters is fixed and determined (says Augustine), so that they do not dissent for any reason: because they laid the foundations of all wisdom with one and the true author [August.]: upon which innumerable doctors, variously arranged, in different climates, in successive times, with diverse temperaments, and multiple languages, have with the highest consonance erected diverse edifices. Which could in no way have happened, unless they had been illuminated by the rays of the same divine intellect (as the Platonists say), or (as Catholics assert) had been taught by the same Holy Spirit [Plato.], who makes the harmonious dwell in the house, and who easily grants to all one heart and one soul. Filled with this Spirit, the ancient prophets, Apostles, and true sounding instruments of the divine, did not prattle in schools or gymnasia with litigious disputes: but in fields, and in cities, and in crowded multitudes, acting with the learned and the unlearned, with princes and peoples, they proposed those doctrines with such constancy that they confirmed those truths with the sanctity and splendor of their lives, with many miracles, and with their own blood. But the world's people, I will not call them harmonizers but dissonant ones (because they disagreed in their foundation), became utterly discordant. These therefore, having become wise in their own eyes, either partly or entirely abolished religion: they scorned oracles: relying on their own strengths and inventions, each one re-echoing with his own voice, they so disagreed that some assert one world, others innumerable worlds. And among those who confess it to be one, some assert it has no origin, others no beginning; some that it will perish, others that it will always exist; some that it is moved by a divine mind, others by chance and accidents; some that souls are immortal, others mortal; others that they are reborn into beasts.

...others by no means (revolved into beasts): But those who (believe the soul to be) mortal, some (say it) perishes soon after the body, others even live afterwards, either for a short while, or longer, but not always: Some established the end of good in the body, others in the soul, others in both. You will find these, and other almost innumerable dissensions of philosophers: so that you may perceive them to have built not a harmonious consonance, but a Babylonian confusion: The builder of whose citadel, Nimrod, under whom the first confusion of tongues occurred, wishing to attempt things higher than his strength, decided to build the tower itself up to the heavens: so that, removed from alteration, and surrounded by a veil subject to alteration, he might contemplate heaven and supermundane things by his own strength. Following him, these wise men of the world have become either citizens of Babylon and confusion: or, flying higher than they ought, like Icarus, they have been drowned in the waters, as the supreme craftsman protests through the oracle of [Marginal note: Isaias Paulus Abdias] Isaiah, Paul, and Obadiah, who says: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent." If, however, they handed down any truths among the many falsehoods they opined: they learned these without any doubt from divine voices: because the secrets of the most high God cannot be apprehended by our strength. [Marginal note: Plato] Therefore Plato often warns: that young people, and those not yet initiated, should not rashly pronounce judgment on divine matters: but should believe the laws: until, with age maturing, through the due degrees of disciplines, and through a certain separation of the soul, their eyes may be revealed: which all possess, but very few truly use: Or (as Plo- [Marginal note: Platonus Procul.] tinus and Proclus say) a light more united to itself than natural may shine forth from God: by which we know God himself and the father of all: and his primal [Marginal note: Plato] making, and immediate, and hidden operation: Which light Plato called the Sun, but the natural (light) the Moon. By this solar light, a great multitude of our harmonious ones, some preceded by a certain prelude, such as Moses, Job, Solomon, Isaiah, and the other prophets: Who divinely personified the sweetest precention under the figure of a worldly instrument with such sweetness, that purified ears are never offended, and never grow weary. But the Apostles and Evangelists made a more explicit sound: Whom innumerable Hebrews, Chaldeans, Greeks, and Latins followed, filling the world with most consonant books.

Which doctors in the divine and worldly instrument have harmoniously personified concerning the innermost secrets. Chapter VII.

Why the ancients studied to hide the dogmas they handed down under metaphors
& enigmas. Chapter VIII.

[Large decorative initial S] It was always the study of the ancients to envelop and cover the mysteries of God, & nature,
and to hide the words of God entrusted to them in their heart: lest they sin:
Which law was observed by the Brahmins from India, Ethio- [Marginal note: Mercury.] pians, Persians, & Egyptians.
Hence their illustrious Mercury said: 'It is of an irreligious mind to publish to the consciousness
of many a treatise most full of the entire majesty of the divine.' This Orpheus, & all ancient
seers, this Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Aristoxenus, Ammonius preserved with inviolable faith.
Hence Herennius, Plotinus, & Origen (as Porphyry writes in 'On the Education &
Discipline of Plotinus') swore that they would not publish the dogmas of Ammonius: And because Plotinus,
having violated the oath sworn to Ammonius, published the mysteries, as punishment for the transgression
(as some assert) he was consumed by a horrible affliction of lice. Glo- [Marginal note: Alexander. Themistius.] ries

--- Page 201 ---
**TONVS SECVNDVS. 32**

God teaches his disciples not to give what is holy to dogs, nor to cast pearls before swine to be trampled underfoot. These teachings of the master, which the disciples were to preserve, they either did not write down, or they handed down for all to observe only those things which pertain to miracles, the ordering of morals, and the institutions of the law. Thus did all the Apostles and Evangelists, with the exception of Paul and John. For John, with three Gospels already published and many years having passed, in order to extirpate the heresy of the Ebionites, who asserted that Christ was a man but not God, pronounced some things briefly and obscurely concerning the eternal generation of the Son of God and concerning man's union with God through Him, after our first animal nature was mortified. The Apocalypse, however, involves so many mysteries in enigmas that neither Oedipus, who alone solved the Sphinx's riddles, nor Solomon, who solved the riddles of the Queen of Sheba, nor anyone else could unravel them, unless imbued with the same spirit with which he who wrote it was full.

But Paul, since he perceived that the fashion of this world was passing away, chose some, or rather a few, disciples, about whom he says: *But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord*, [Marginal note: Paulus] regretting that he did not have very many well-initiated disciples to whom he could entrust these mysteries. And he complains about the Hebrews, who were still particularly rude and uncultivated, saying: *We have a great discourse, and one that is difficult to explain, because you have become dull of hearing. For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again what are the elementary principles of the oracles of God. And you have become those who need milk, not solid food. But solid food is for the mature, for those who by constant practice have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil.*

But note what follows. *Therefore, leaving the elementary doctrine of Christ, let us go on to maturity, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, of spiritual gifts, of doctrine, and also of the laying on of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. And this indeed we will do, if God permits. For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have also tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance.*
In these words two things are to be noted. The first, that the Apostle hints that he holds in the treasury of his heart doctrines beyond those concerning repentance, baptism, the resurrection of the dead, judgment, and suchlike, about which theologians write most fully. The second is, what is the case from which he judges it impossible to be relieved by repentance, if one has revealed to the unworthy those things which ought to be hidden, or if someone, unworthily receiving such a great sacrament, inflicts injury upon it. Therefore, the Apostle distinguishes more perfect disciples: among whom he speaks those things which pertain to higher wisdom, having become a disciple of the true master: who revealed the name of God the Father only to those whom the Father himself had given; and he chose those to whom he spoke the mystery of the kingdom of God, apart from those whom he taught in parables.

Thus to Ezra (as we read in his fourth book) [Marginal note: Ezra.] God declared in these words: *Revealing, I was revealed upon the bush, and I spoke to Moses, when my people served in Egypt; and I brought him upon Mount Sinai; and I kept him with me for many days; and I narrated to him many wondrous things,*

--- Page 202 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

& I showed him the secrets of the times, & the end: & I commanded him, saying: These words, O God, you shall make public: & these you shall hide. For he made public the precepts of the law, the genealogy of Christ, some very brief histories of the ancient fathers, yet with their mystery kept secret: Likewise, sacrifices, ceremonies, the construction of the ark, the war with the Amalekites, & with the other kings of various nations: and the wiser Hebrews call this the written law: in which higher meanings are contained than many might conceive: The knowledge of which meanings the aforesaid wise men call the law from mouth to mouth: Which, according to the precept of the living God, Moses reserved by word of mouth to seventy elders: whose succession lasted until the captivity made by Nebuchadnezzar: at which time it ceased, or was diminished until Cyrus: for then (the divine spirit suggesting, five thousand four hundred vessels of the temple having been assigned, and the captivity having been dissolved, & families having been sent back to the number of forty-two thousand, three hundred & seventy, except for servants, & maidservants) under the hand of Zerubbabel, Nehemiah, & Ezra, the temple of the Lord began to be rebuilt: Which having been restored, & the sacred rites having been restored (the Lord commanding), he reduced that doctrine into seventy volumes, according to the number of the elders, lest they should be dispersed: yet with this law of the living God, that they should not be expounded to the unlearned. For the first things (he says) which you wrote, namely the text of the law, you shall make public, let the worthy, & the unworthy read them: But the seventy newest books you shall preserve, so that you may hand them over to the wise among your people: For in these is the vein of understanding, the fount of wisdom, & the river of knowledge: which are enclosed under a bark by divine & inconceivable artifice. And lest these things be scorned as Apocrypha, let us see what Dionysius states in favor of this matter: It was most fitting (he says) that divine, & incomprehensible things should be hidden by enigmas: & to place the sacred, & hidden truth of supermundane understandings out of reach for many. For not everything is sacred, nor is knowledge for all (as the oracles say): & having progressed a little, he says: O Timothy, made divine in divine doctrine, guarding in the secret of your soul those things which are holy from the impure multitude, keep these as uniform. For it is not right to cast before swine the unconfused, & luminous, & beneficial adornment of invisible pearls. Therefore, not departing from that law of the Most High God, celebrated with such observance by the fathers of the Old, & New Testaments, & by the wise men of the world, we shall propose the solid food of wisdom to more solid souls with gravity & reverence: so that the worthy may receive it: & the brutal swine, & the rest of the unworthy, may not trample upon it. Therefore we shall philosophize about God (as Nazianzen teaches) to whom, when, how, & as much as shall be necessary, committing to scripture as much as the Lord shall permit: & shall judge worthy of revelation, reserving those things which are only to be communicated by word of mouth among the wise.

How the Dissonant Could Be Harmonized. Chapter IX.

[Decorative initial 'U' containing a figure playing a stringed instrument]
So that we may not admit anything harsh, & dissonant into our harmony, which is the concord of all strings in complete modes without offending consonances: we shall introduce the philosophers of the world, as harmonizers, into it, making them consonant: provided that their instruments, or elements—

--- Page 203 ---
**TONVS SECVNDVS. 33**

...are willing to adapt their matters to the strings. Indeed, they will do so if they are willing to confess God (as nature teaches, religion persuades, reason approves) as the author and maker of the universe: because all human wisdom is placed in this alone (says Firmianus) that one may know and worship God. [Marginal note: Lactan.] Therefore, let us embrace Him as the one true [source] of all things, and the one principle, the free creator, and the supreme fount from whom all truth emanates. Then easily the sounds of all dissimilar voices will come into the same harmony: which results from similar and dissimilar voices: just as so many very diverse members, bound by a single life, are consonant in the same body: just as the parts of the earthly body also come together in the sweetest concord: because they are permeated and bound by a single life: For there is one spirit of life in them, rendering all most consonant. Moreover, all members of the mystical and ecclesiastical body come together in the sweetest melody: when they live that one life, which says: I am the way, the truth, and the life: [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] By whose spirit the early fathers were imbued, and it was made for all of them (says Luke) one heart and one soul. [Marginal note: Lucas.] And all those of diverse languages were instructed by the single voice of the Apostles, not without the admiration of those present. By this same spirit, our doctors, imbued and enlightened, though with diverse instruments and various songs, nevertheless resounded most harmoniously. And to begin with the principal ones, four Greeks and four Latins sang in God's assembly, as bases and foundations of our Theology, along with those four who handed down the evangelical elements in four distinct, yet consonant, songs. For Jerome [Marginal note: Hiero.] and Chrysostom [Marginal note: Chryso.] unravel the literal shell. Both Gregory the Roman [Marginal note: Gregor.] and Nazianzen [Marginal note: Nazian.] pursue the matter of the soul hidden beneath the bark. Damascene [Marginal note: Damascen.] with Ambrose fixes weighty sentences and allegorical meanings. Augustine with Basil [Marginal note: Basili.] soars in an Anagogical song to proclaim the highest things: And those who preceded up to the times of Jerome, he himself in *De Illustribus Viris* commemorates as known to him, seven and thirty beyond a hundred: [Marginal note: Hieron.] To whom Gennadius, the presbyter of Marseille, adds one above ninety. [Marginal note: Genad.] And many countless others followed these, up to the times of Peter Lombard: [Marginal note: Petr. lōb.] who, emulating Damascene, [Marginal note: Damasc.] reducing and distinguishing theological doctrine into four volumes, provided material for disputation to posterity. In this disputative genre, members of the Minorite friars wrote, up to Bartholomew of Pisa, who commemorates them as a hundred and more. But those of diverse professions, nations, and languages grew so much, resounding with wonderful concord, that we can assign neither an end to the sound nor a number to the strings: of whom it may be said: I saw a great multitude: which no one could number except Him who numbers the multitude of the stars. All, however, come together in wonderful harmony: because they are enlightened by the supreme teacher and the supreme light, from whom all light and truth emanates. But those who rely on their own strengths feel that prophetic saying proven in themselves: Every man is a liar: For God alone contains the fount of truth, from which it is necessary to draw: if we intend to hand down true and harmonious doctrines: since there is nothing concerning separate substances,

Agreement of the wise concerning the time of the world's creation. Chapter X.

**P**resupposing the fabric of the world, which we proved above, let us also acknowledge this new point: as both the sacred scriptures teach and all mathematicians confirm, while from the very Genesis of the world, those events which are to be in it are predicted; therefore, let us see in how much time it was made. It is the doctrine of the wise: that He who remains in eternity created
[Marginal notes: Idem
Albertus
Mag. sen.] all things at once. To this agree Augustine, Albertus, the Master of the Sentences, with the Hebrew doctors, and all who think correctly. For finite and determined power requires time in acting, but infinite power by no means does, such as that of the supreme craftsman – not indeed well measured by the accursed Arab, and by others who said that God does not work with infinite power, because an infinite work was not produced. For He used His boundless power in creating, although He did not unfold that infinite power into the work, but enclosed it within the limits He wished, which He also produced by commanding. Since therefore He produced all things by command and
[Marginal note: David] word, as the Prophet says: "He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created." For the word having been spoken, "Let there be light," or "Let there be a firmament," or "a globe of the heavens in the midst of the waters," or "Let the earth bring forth green herb": why was light made with such delay, until the space of the day passed and evening came? And why was the germination of the earth delayed until the third day, and the production of the Sun, Moon, and Stars until the fourth? And why was the generation of water creatures given only on the fifth? And why was the formation of man celebrated on the sixth? And why was the seventh appointed for rest?
[Marginal note: August.] Let them say if they have anything. Augustine laughs at these, deservedly to be laughed at, who think that God requires time in acting.
