they wanted this cloud of theirs: since the ethereal region in no way admits it, being alien from every foreign impression? Nor could a small cloud in the air near the earth illuminate the whole hemisphere: for the magnitude of the Sun, and its proper altitude, cause the whole hemisphere to be illuminated, and a pyramidal shadow to be cast in the other hemisphere: which causes night and darkness in the entire space of the pyramid. And because the pyramidal shadow does not cross the orbit of the Moon, therefore the Stars, not being occupied by that shadow of the earth, suffer no Eclipse: but continuously receive the light which they direct towards us. How, moreover, could this cloud illuminating the air cause day from evening and morning: since the air was not yet distinct: nor was there a firmament, or a globe of the heavens, nor were the supercelestial waters divided from the lower ones? Indeed, that all things were in confusion is stated in the text, up to the second day.

They also inflict no small calumny upon the supreme Creator with this cloud of theirs, believing that God fashioned an imperfect world, and lit an adventitious light until He should light His own proper light: just as our architects do: who sometimes build a wooden tower where they may place bells, until they construct their own tower, which they intend, out of bricks: All of which ascribe no small imperfection to the Craftsman. In the same way, those are to be rejected who dream that God fashioned the sun imperfect on the first day: and afterwards on the fourth day gave it the form of light itself. Let these people say, I ask: If the sun on the first day was imperfect, and not endowed with its own light, how did it cause day and night by illuminating the world, as they had said a little above? And if it was first made formless, like matter: why did Moses not say, 'The sun was imperfect,' just as he had said of the earth, 'But the earth was without form and void'? Afterwards, concerning the perfection bestowed, he added: 'Let the earth bring forth green herb.' Let them also note that on the fourth day God said: 'Let there be, or let there exist, two great luminaries:' Nor did He say, 'Let the two luminaries bring forth their light:' as He had commanded the earth a little before: that it should bring forth. These people imagined that God, in the manner of painters, first sketched the figure with a stylus, so that afterwards He might paint it with suitable marks and colors. Indeed, that which mortals seek from imperfect virtue is unfitting for God. But because it is said of matter that it was first formless, and afterwards depicted with its own figures [Augustine.], let this be understood to signify the order of nature, and not of time: so that not only Augustine [Ancient Theologians.], and ancient Theologians agree, but also distinguished Philosophers, and more skilled Poets [Trismegistus. Alcinous.] concur: For Trismegistus, Alcinous the Platonist, and other wise men [Hesiod. Euripides. Ovid. Plato.] say: Hesiod also, Euripides, and Ovid sing that heaven and earth were once mixed, and a certain chaos, afterwards separated, generated individual things: trees, birds, wild beasts, and the race of mortals: Which is most clearly demonstrated by Plato in the Timaeus, and by Philo, most celebrated in both Greek and Hebrew languages: and we are taught to refer that division of days not to time, but to the order of production [Augustine.], and of the things produced. Why the number six was assigned to creation, and the seventh day to rest. Ch. XI.

[Decorative Initial E] And if all the works of the supreme craftsman are said to have been made with great mystery and great sacrament, no less is this true of the number six, by which
t

--- Page 208 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

nothing is superfluous, nor deficient, nor does anything exceed, nor flow out, nor flow in, nor does it need foreign aids: but it is equal and temperate, and relies on its own parts and strengths, and stands firm. And the generating parts render the begotten similar to the begetter: Therefore, when God had produced His work by dividing it into this number, [Marginal note: Moses] Moses said: "Therefore the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them." Hence also Orpheus commands hymns to be ended with the sixth generation: because nothing further can be sung about created things, since all perfection is terminated therein. [Marginal note: August.] Thus Augustine teaches that God perfected His works in six days: in which number he believes a mystery is signified rather than parts of time. Therefore we also need numbers to perceive the sacraments of God and nature, not indeed the numbers of a merchant, but those distinguished by their own numbers. Proceeding further, let us say: that from a triangular figure this number is best suited to the structure: for its base is the ternary, the summit is one, the intermediate are two, as is clear in the figure presented [three dots in a triangle]: For the entire structure emanates from three persons, since their external works are undivided: They also tend towards one end, to which all things are directed: but the transition is through the binary, namely matter: For the first principle of this emanation was matter, which savors of the binary: and it tends to be reduced to one through form, which bears the image of the ternary: just as from every part in the preceding figure the ternary tends towards the monad through the binary: To which, all things being reduced, follows the sabbatical rest of the seventh day, closing and terminating the course of all days. Therefore, the structure is divided by this senary, far more excellent than that which is numbered by the succession of days. If, therefore, it is admitted that God, the supreme craftsman, proceeded to work in His perfect order, the agreement of Catholic wise men with [Marginal note: Plato.] philosophers, especially the Academics, will be easy: Whose Prince (Plato) said in the Timaeus, that God, the propagator of the world, having produced the twin matter of heaven and earth, immediately afterwards produced light, by which things might be distinguished and, being distinguished, might be known: or commanded it to be inherent in things: Therefore it is notably said (as the truth of the letter has it) "let there be light upon the matter," namely, informing it. First, therefore, the matter of heaven and earth is said to have been fabricated simultaneously with light, through which the matter itself would be painted with the image or likeness of the craftsman. And this necessarily was: and it is called the first emanation of the craftsman into the work: and the first illumination, or light seen by the darkened matter, from which, a composite being made simultaneously with light, the first day appeared, completed from the evening of matter and the morning of form. But because the whole influx of divinity was by no means suitable for matter, therefore on the second day Arachiah said that a curtain, or Mass of the heavens, was placed between the super-excellent fount of light and waters, and the darkened matter, and a few waters of goodness, lest the influx of waters and goodness be greater than was suitable for the matter itself: But this is said to have been done on the second day, namely, an inauspicious one. Hence the Hebrews read this separation mournfully, with the accent placed above, which they call Zarco, [placed] on וַיַּרְא (vayyar), as if grieving over the obstacle established between the flowing goodness and the receptive matter: And this as regards the primeval production. But we too must lament concerning this inauspicious day: on which was interposed

--- Page 209 ---
**SECOND TONE.**                                                                    36

There is also between us and God a tribunal balancing how much grace and how much divine influx should be admitted to each. For the fount of divine goodness is most exuberant, from which it would flow more than those receiving might deserve, if there had not been an intervening obstacle preventing it: as ordering justice requires. But on the third day, indeed according to the formal number of things, forms are unfolded, and are said to be separated from the inner and earthly things, therefore it is said: Let the waters that are under the heaven be gathered together unto one place: that is, let the generative forces be collected together, and let the dry land appear: which may be made fruitful by the virtue of those collected forces: as is subjoined: Let the earth bring forth grass, the green herb: and the fruit-bearing tree, and those things which follow. Therefore, the forms having been produced, and the earth depicted, so that those pictures might appear and be seen, in the fourth place it was said: Let there be two great lights in the globe, or mass of the heavens: and let them divide, that is, let them cause to discern between the dark and the light: and let those things be seen, which have been illuminated by their forms: and let them be separated from those things which still lie in their darkness and more obscure figures. But on the fifth vital day, from the fifth character, namely ה signifying life, a full communion of life is described, while it says: Let the waters swarm forth, or produce swarms of living creatures, and the fowl that may fly above the earth, as well as upon the face of the heavens. God also created on the same day great dragons, or great whales, as our translation has it: and every living soul creeping upon the earth: whence God is understood to be the author of all life, both superior and inferior. Great mysteries are here: First, why the waters are said to produce living things and animals, just as their seed is also watery: and why those animals are first said to be produced by the waters, afterwards fashioned by God, insofar as the waters had swarmed forth and produced, and what is the fowl flying above the earth, and upon the face of the heavens. But access is not given here to such intimate sanctuaries: since our purpose is to run through why, and how those works are said to be distinct through five days, and on the sixth day, indeed perfect and vital, from the letter ו signifying six and life, again beasts are introduced, produced in their kind: and man in the most perfect form, with the image, namely, and likeness of God. Also why the seventh is said to be ascribed to rest: so that, namely, rest and the day of the Sabbath may agree: just as their names agree in the mysterious Hebrew language.

**VOLUME TWO. 33**
**On the general agreement of the Peripatetics, and also of all others in essential matters. Chapter XIV.**

[Large decorative initial S] We establish that the Peripatetics and very many others agree in a pleasant harmony of the wise: This will indeed seem all the more difficult, the more their prince (Aristotle), in order to be considered singular and more excellent, wished to dissent even when not disagreeing with others, especially from Plato, pursuing an opposite process. For there is a twofold process: just as there is a twofold nature: as Plato himself recalls. One is sensible: concerning which there is reasoning based on opinion: which they call science: [Plato] The other, however, is the incorruptible nature of superior substances, immutable, constant, continuous, always the same, which is not perceived by discursive thought: but is seen by the keenness of the mind. This is called divine science: because it deals with divine matters, and is divinely taught. The preceding (science), however, is called daemonic: because it is about earthly things: and because it is suggested by those inferior intelligences: whom Marcus Tullius calls Lares, Apuleius sometimes Lares, sometimes Genii, and others indeed call Daemons: [Tul. Cic. Apul.] who are contained below the lunar orb, busying themselves with the understanding of earthly things. Hence the Greeks, both Peripatetics and Platonists, called Plato himself divine, but Aristotle a daemon: because the former always made it his concern both to deal with divine matters and to learn from those who had received from divine oracles: The latter, however, relying on his own powers, wished to admit only those things which he judged he could prove by his own senses and reasons: For by this path he pursued multiple motions, fourfold qualities, three principles of things, four causes, and suchlike: which are easily apprehended from the senses. Nor does the teacher of sensible things progress further: unless he transgresses (as he himself says) the limits of his sensitive doctrine. Which he also sometimes does, confessing God to be the maker of things: [Aristo.] although, content within sensitive limits, he asserts the world to be unbegotten, and takes away the making of things from God. If, however, we wish to lead him into the assembly of Platonists and divine wise men, this alone seems to me the way. that (just as it sometimes happens with musicians) we observe the former seeking the highest from the lowest: [Idem] but Plato, with John, descending from the highest progenitor to the lowest: [Plato. Ioan.] For the latter, beginning from the Word, says: In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and the Word was God. Afterwards he descends through the Idea, and the light granted to us, to know divine things, even to the flesh assumed by the Word itself: Such a twofold progression we shall also demonstrate in the discussion concerning divine things with elementary and inferior things: For from God, one arrives at the heavens through the ternary: and one ascends there from the elements through the quaternary: where the converging and combined numbers constitute a duodenary (twelve) through each other: by which number heaven is divided and manifoldly adorned: as we shall explain in its proper place (God willing): Which progression these two principal leaders among philosophers observe. Plato, therefore, following the footsteps of the Pythagoreans and ancient [Plato] wise men, wishing to describe the fabric of the world, began from the Creator through the way of numbers: Concerning which with the greatest difficulty (as

Aristotle, however (especially in the book *On Physical Hearing*), begins from lower and elementary principles, ascending through various motions to investigate the first mover, God. Plato, in turn, from oracles and from those things which he learned to hunt out from the ancients, lays the foundations of his doctrine from numbers: since numbers are native to divine, terrestrial, and human affairs. In the same way, let them conduct the business of the soul (as far as is right) through their senses, leaving those things that transcend physical limits to divine wise men. And if some dissonance appears among them, let the strings be loosened by the higher teachers: but by the lower ones, let them be tightened, and the sound softened: as is accustomed to happen with instruments: and their harmony will be found. To achieve which harmony, we would apply effort and industry: were it not that the business distracts us too much from our purpose: which is to reconcile not only the wise, but all things contained in this machine.

**SECOND TONE. 39**
**HOW ONE IS EXTENDED THROUGH TWENTY-SEVEN. Chapter One.**

**M**ONAD diffused into multitude is clear to all wise men: But how the nature of unity may agree with multitude, and without discrepancy may cohabit in it, this labor must be undertaken by us here. Nor can it agree in any other way, except through the harmony of unity: which is found in multitude. Hence Plato, imitating Timaeus of Locri, describes the fabric of the soul and the world through the accepted monad: and through doubled, tripled, and quadrupled proportions he arrives at twenty-seven, namely the cube of the first number, adding that all intervals were filled. **[Marginal note: Plato]** So that his interpreters Proclus, Chalcidius, and later thinkers may do this, they place the senary, the first perfect number, in the place of unity: **[Marginal note: Procul. Chalcid.]** which, by doubling and tripling in the same order, they reach 162: And then they fill the intervals with diapentic and diatessaronic harmony, also with a tone, semitone, and leimma: so that the whole soul and the whole world may be harmonic: and may contain all divine harmony: For the first and highest monad is diffused into the first number, namely the ternary: which, if squared, completes the novenary: By which number the orders of separate intellects, the heavens, and all elemental things are distributed with the highest harmony: as we intend to demonstrate below: Which number, if reduced to a cube, yields those twenty-seven mentioned above: But before these harmonic degrees of things are distributed, the prime matter (which poets call Chaos, the Greeks Hyle, and the Hebrews תהו, that is Hiuili or Tohu) was pre-required: which was not counted among the numbered things: just as the prime agent and the highest monad does not enter into the number of others: although through its unity it enables all to be numbered. Hence, most wisely, Moses, before the fabric of things, prefaced the production of matter, saying: **[Marginal note: Moses]** "In the beginning God created heaven and earth," namely the matter of both: which were afterwards formed: For he gave form to the former on the second day, when he said: "Let there be an *arachiba* in the midst of the waters," that is, the extended or expanded thing of all heavens: Whence it follows: "and he called the *arachiba* heavens." For *arachiba* is not the firmament, as our translation has it: but the globe and mass of all heavens: Which is proven by that which follows: "God made two great lights, and the stars: and he placed them in the *arachiba*:" For those lights were not placed in the firmament, that is, the starry heaven: but each one in its own orb: from which it is concluded that *arachiba* signifies something gathered together from all the orbs. But he gave form to the earth on the third day, in that he said: "Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear:" which dry land he called earth: So that he might express this more clearly, he had said above: "But the earth was *tohu*," which is explained as chaos, or a certain rude mass, or matter. With what order the progression from the triune God through the ternary occurs into all created things. Chapter II.

[Large decorative initial P] YTHAGORAS, the Father of Philosophers, and the most diligent investigator of natural order and harmony, [Marginal note: Pythag.]
who had no predecessor in natural philosophy, and saw no equal, [Marginal note: Chaldæi]
not only drew his doctrine from the Chaldeans and [Marginal note: Assyrii]
Assyrians, but, imbued with the more hidden wisdom of the Hebrews, attributed
so much to the ternary number (as we have from his followers) that he asserted every principle
of Divinity, and consequently the universe, is perfected by the ternary: For every number
grows by a threefold increase, namely, in length, breadth, and depth,
beyond which no further progression is given. Moreover, perfect dimension in a body
is completed by the same threefold increase, and by a threefold intersection at a right angle. Nor indeed
can more right angles be caused in any figure, although very many obtuse and acute ones can.
Therefore, the production of numbers and continuous quantity is threefold: For if a number
is added to unity, it becomes linear: And if a point is extended in length, it constitutes a line.
But if a number grows in breadth, it becomes superficial: and if breadth is added to a line,
it is changed into a surface. If again a number is led into depth, it becomes corporeal,
solid, and a cube. And if depth is joined to breadth, a body is constituted.
But to a three-dimensional body, and to a cube number, nothing can be added, as all Pythagorean
philosophers and mathematicians teach. Hence Aristotle celebrates this number [Marginal note: Pythag. Mathe. Arifto.]
at the beginning of his discourses on the heavens: saying, "We have the ternary number
from nature: and we uphold it as a law, according to which, namely, all things are ordered."
Hence, according to the same number, we are bound to magnify God, the maker
and creator of all things. All spiritual and corporeal things also consist of three,
namely, beginning, middle, and end: which trinity they draw from that most
excellent ternary: from whom are all things, in whom are all things, and through whom are all things: as Paul
teaches. Moreover, by three (as Trismegistus says) the world is perfected: fate (himarmene), necessity, [Marginal note: Paulus Trifme.]

**TONUS TERTIUS. 41**

How Angels are distributed through our ninefold system corresponding to the simple ternary. Chapter III.

[Large initial N] That there are nine orders, or grades, of Angels among Dionysius, Iamblichus, and more recent Theologians is most accurate: And they are completed by the ninefold number (not indeed simple, but in some way composite): Because they themselves, separated from the most simple intellect (whence they are called "separated intellects" by philosophers as well as by Hebrew sages), admit some composition: because in them is essence and the virtue perfecting them; or (as they say) Metaphysical matter and form. For neither, receding from pure act, are they entirely stripped of matter: since it is evident in the breadth of things that whatever recedes from pure act necessarily inclines towards matter. Whence Dionysius, the principal doctor concerning Angels, asserts that they are unmixed, namely with matter. But because in them there are degrees of perfection, those nearer to God are distributed into the first ternary, bearing a more express image of the simple ternary: And the subsequent ones by a doubled ternary: And the last ones are concluded by a tripled ternary. Therefore, the first ones, rejoicing in a more express image of the triune God, represent that diffusion of the supreme monad into a trinity: For God and Father of all, having His essence presented to His intellect (which is called "fecund memory" by Theologians), by understanding Himself, generates wisdom, or the Word, or knowledge of Himself, which is called the Son. Hence it acquires the name of Son of the Father: For the wisdom produced, since it is most similar to the producer and emanating from Him by natural progression, obtains the name of Son. But love, springing forth from the knowledge of both (who are the supreme good), is named the Spirit and the bond of both: To this love, connecting parent with offspring, the Seraphic order corresponds. But the Cherubic (order), full of wisdom and beauty, corresponds to supreme wisdom and to the Son, who is the Father's delight and the beauty of all things. But the Thrones themselves serve the Father, in whom, sitting, He glories in the continuous production of the Word and the Spirit: In whom also He judges the world, as is read in the psalm: "He has prepared His throne for judgment." To whom also He calls the Son, bestowing upon Him all-encompassing power of judging, as He Himself testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: "I have conquered, and I sit on the throne of my Father." But since the supreme good easily diffuses itself into others, hence He also produced another threefold order, by which it would relate to producing and governing creatures: To these orders and ministers, as a magnificent craftsman and prince, He decreed to work and to rule. But one thing must be guarded against here: that God (as Augustine and the entire school of Theologians agree on this point) always operates as triune and undivided externally: so that none of the persons ever operates without the others: Which is also proven by examples: "we have," says Origen, "from the Father, that we exist; From the Son, or the Word, the communion of reason or order; But life from the spirit of life, who presides over mundane and supercelestial wheels." Because therefore God the Father gives to all that they exist, He is deservedly called Lord of all: concerning whom it is read in sacred scripture: Lo-

And this is what the Psalmist sings: "By the spirit of his mouth is all their strength." Chapter IIII.
[Marginal note: Diony.] [Decorative initial N containing figures of people in a landscape] It is very well known in Dionysius that not only inferior intelligences, but also we ourselves, are enlightened, purified, and perfected by superior beings. If we assent to these things, we easily ascend to the rank and order of Angels, which is nearer to us; from which, by acting rightly and being purified, we are deservedly preferred to others, and Archangels, that is, Angelic princes, have care over us. Among these prelates and subjects, Principalities intervene, so that they subject the former and elevate the latter by a certain hidden power. And neither of them perceives it, yet the subject feels a certain yoke of the one presiding, from which he cannot easily free himself; indeed, he fears and reveres that power which Principalities infuse into prelates, just as they themselves draw it from the terrifying seat of divine majesty, which, situated in the north, binds all minds, both angelic and human, under the yoke of servitude with terrifying and fiery laws. The transgression of which is the evil of guilt, and
[Marginal note: Ieremias] punishment is the evil of penalty, as Jeremiah, subject to the divine spirit, prophesies: "From the north every evil shall break forth." Hence that murderer, who did not stand in the truth from the beginning, burst forth with stubborn arrogance, saying: "I will place my seat in the north, and I will be like the Most High," namely, the prince of the evil and confused forest, just as that one rules in the kingdom of peace and quiet. Hence the prince of the world, that is, of things separated from God, is often named by the true prince, as in the Gospel, whose title
[Marginal note: Ioan.] is according to John: "The prince of this world comes," he says, "and has nothing in me." the punishment of their transgression: where the terrifying sons of Elohim, that is, of God the just judge, severely judge, and execute judgment most sharply, so that they may strike that fear of God into demons and men, which the Hebrews call *pahad* (פחד). [Marginal note: Iahacob] Concerning which Jacob, the master of these sacraments, speaking with his father-in-law Laban the Aramean, said: "Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the fear of my father Isaac, had been with me, perhaps you would have sent me away naked." And again: [Marginal note: Idem] Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac: To whom God had granted power from that tribunal of strength and justice, just as to father Abraham from the south of mercy and piety: Adorned with whose symbol, Jacob sits in the midst of the throne of glory. From the north, therefore, all evil, both of transgression and of punishing justice, proceeds with severity and a certain terror, by which inferiors may be led into fear of their superiors. Is not a prince a man similar to other men? How would others fear and revere him, unless divine terror elevated him, and striking fear into others, suppressed them, so that they might revere him as their prince? All of which the supreme prince executes through these principalities. Moreover, all presidency is considered exceedingly deformed, unless there is an adornment and grace in the president, by which he may deservedly be considered a prince of others. Therefore, the ministry of superiors is also necessary for the president, by which impediments, namely vices and the pleasures of the corporeal world, may be shaken off. And the order of virtues achieves this: By whose favor, with constancy and strength acquired, we are made strong against vices and effeminating pleasures. But so that we may also prevail against these aerial powers full of envy and malice, the protection of powers is also necessary for us: so that we may say with [Marginal note: Eliseus] Elisha: "There are more with us than against us." Lest we also be hindered by worldly affections, but that it may dominate all of them, intelligences assist with their virtue, which are called Dominions: By whose favor we may be able to reduce the body to servitude, and to subdue the earth, according to the Imperial decree, which says: "Fill the earth and subdue it." Therefore, having obtained dominion over all inferiors, it remains that, turning to God, we devote ourselves to Him alone: Which can be done if we retain the memory of supercelestial things through the aid of the Thrones, and contemplate them with Cherubic illumination, and, fused by Seraphic ardor, unite with the supreme kinsman and parent: Whence, just as the supreme creator descends to us by His power and influx through the angelic ranks, so also through the same ranks may we return to Him from whom we proceeded. Nor shall I omit those things which Augustine discusses concerning this return to God by the same steps. And first he enumerates four affections, namely fear, sorrow, joy, and hope: which he believed to proceed from the irascible and concupiscible parts (of the soul): to which he adds sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence, adapting this ninefold division to the nine orders of Angels, he attempts to lead the whole man to God: although he leaves this to the prudent reader to complete: yet, as we can gather from the same, he assigns the senses to the Angels, who are called messengers: just as the bodily senses themselves are messengers.

CANTICI PRIMI

He assigns to Archangels the intellect of the inner virtues, namely, of reason, and the imagination of the soul's senses, which perceives more than the senses. To Virtues, fear. To Powers, sorrow. For he who, strengthened by inner virtue through fear of vices and grieving over sins, can, with the Powers, put demons to flight, and with the Virtues, perform miracles. He makes reason correspond to Principalities: just as they preside over spirits, so reason presides over senses and affections. To Dominations, love or joy: for he rightly dominates others who loves all and rejoices in their progress. To Thrones, the intellect, which are called the seats of God. And he attributes intelligence to Cherubim, who are so much more full of perfect knowledge as they contemplate God's majesty more intimately and clearly. For intelligence is a power of the soul which is immediately subject to God. But to Seraphim he equates hope, since they lead into God, who is the hope of all the ends of the earth.

And from the same earth which stands forever, with no variation intervening and no cultivation, various effects are produced, namely, herbs, flowers, and those things which are produced by the earth itself, putrefied by solar virtue. And if they say: 'Various effects are brought about by other particular causes working together,' they have left this to be proven, whether this variety proceeds from diverse causes, or from the same sun fertile with multi-faceted power. How much more so: the first and true Sun, about whom Trismegistus [Trisme.], rightly called the father of philosophers, states in these words: My God, existing most full of the fecundity of both sexes, life, and light, by His word begot another creative mind, namely, a son fertile with all ideas and exemplars of things to be made, which pre-existed in Him as the life of all things. For all things (as Mercury [Mercu.] continues) are in God: not indeed as placed in a location, but situated in the mind: from which, producing all things, He is called the parent of all. He alone, freed from the laws of nature, with no subject presupposed and no matter, produced all things, and even matter itself, by His most complete fecundity. But a secondary or natural cause (as they say) requires a subject and matter produced by God, upon which they may act: And in these matters, what the prince of the Peripatetics states holds true: namely, that it is agreeable to the common understanding of the mind that nothing comes from nothing. Hence Augustine [Augusti.], rightly called the father of Latin Theologians, with his entire school, openly asserts that Angels can by no means create nature: And that Angels are no more creators of things than farmers are of crops: Which opinion more recent Theologians, Aegidius Romanus [Aeg. Ro.], Henry of Ghent [Hē. Gā.], Richard [Ricardus], and most vehemently John Scotus [Ioā. Sco.], have striven to fortify, all of which I leave to be read in their books. Here I am struck with the greatest astonishment, because such great men deny that God is the maker of all things; and that nevertheless secondary causes produce from nothing, contrary to the philosophy they profess, in which the more celebrated assert that neither by the supreme maker himself was the world, or anything, produced from nothing. But those who have received the light of truth, profess God alone to be the author of all things. He is the author of the entire world (says Alcinous the Platonist [Alcinous]), of gods and demons: and this universe, by the gift of divine will, will never hereafter be dissolved. Plato [Plato.], moreover, presupposing the highest good to be the cause of separate substances and their duration, thus introduces it addressing them: 'You are indeed not immortal, nor entirely dissoluble: nevertheless, you will not at any time be dissolved: For if all things which have been constituted can be destroyed and dissolved: to dissolve and destroy those things which have been rightly constituted and are in good order, is the mark of a perverse and self-contradictory mind.' Mercury [Mercu.] also, when he spoke of the rulers of the planets, says: 'Then he fashioned seven governors:' and thus enumerates all things produced by God. Nor is it to be thought that in such great harmony of the universe there were many progenitors, and many rulers, and that many things consist of themselves: Because from that would arise confusion, dissonance, and consequently easy dissolution in the universe.

**How the artisan fabricated the heavens by the second square of three. Chapter VI.**

[Large decorative initial E] By the same number, by the same degrees, the supreme governor distributed the heavens, namely by the second nonary: as the opinion of the ancients and the common opinion holds: although some more recent thinkers assert a tenth, not understanding how the motion, which they call trepidation, is preserved in the eighth sphere without a tenth circle: Nor does it seem consistent to them that the eighth sphere itself, which revolves with three motions, should be annexed to the prime mover: which is driven by only one rotation: For it has a diurnal motion from east to west above the poles of the world: And it has a motion from west to east above the poles of the zodiac, or of the signs, by one degree every hundred years, as pleases [Marginal note: Ptolem.] Ptolemy: But in sixty, as others assert: And it also has that asserted motion of trepidation: whence they believe there is a ninth heaven: which moves only with a double motion between itself and the prime mover: which revolves with only a single motion: so that all things may be reduced in due order to the prime mover: which, by revolving with a single motion, carries all other things with it in a regular and ordered circuit: And that which [Marginal note: Aristo.] Aristotle teaches in his higher philosophy may be preserved, namely that it is necessary for all things to be reduced in due order to that which is their cause.

But since eight orbs are observed: and are proven distinct by armillary spheres and other instruments: and that beyond these there is a ninth (which [Marginal note: Astron.] astronomers call the prime mover, but others, for some reason I know not, call crystalline) manifest reason concludes. These we admit: But a tenth, since it has nothing for itself, except that that asserted motion of trepidation may be preserved, we do not admit: since it can be preserved in another way. Indeed, all the motions of the eighth sphere itself are preserved (as I have observed with an instrument, and confirmed by very clear experience) under that ninth circle without a tenth. [Marginal note: Ptolem. Hermes Aratus] Nor would this tenth orb have escaped Ptolemy, Hermes, Aratus, and other most diligent ancient investigators of the heavens, and their motions, and aspects: who are content with the number nine.

But because Theologians assert a tenth, which they call the Empyrean, vital, fiery, and divine: where those are received who have led a more divine life: as [Marginal note: Plato. plotinus] Plato, and his Academics (Plotinus especially in that which he published concerning the world) agree with our theologians: Therefore we say: granted that a tenth is spoken of, yet properly it is by no means numbered with these nine: Because these are mobile, but that is stable: These are from one material, that from another: [Marginal note: Moses.] Which we can easily learn from Moses, easily the chief of all philosophers, theologians, and prophets, indeed from the true Artisan himself: Where, being asked by Moses to dwell with him: and to instruct him with continuous oracles: which were sought for leading a very numerous people, and for delivering the law: "I will come," he said, "but make for me a wooden ark: which indeed bears the type of the world in which I dwell: Which you shall complete with a cubit and a half, namely nine palms: For a cubit contains six palms: and half a cubit three palms: By which he would represent the nine heavens." But the tenth, namely the covering, he commanded to be made of gold, a material indeed very distant from wood: Which tenth is not fully numbered with those nine—

--- Page 225 ---
**TONE THREE. 44**

...is not fully counted with those nine: but it is the principle of another combination: For the denarius (number ten), although it completes the first numbers, is nevertheless the principle of tens; just as the centenarius (number one hundred) completes the tens, and is the beginning of thousands. So also that covering (which they call the propitiatory), terminating the ark, provided the principle of a better thing: For upon it sat the cherubim, whence propitiations were had. But in the ark, the law, manna, and the rod stood hidden in deep mystery. In like manner also the empyrean heaven, although it completes the number of nine heavens, is nevertheless the principle of spiritual and divine things, redolent of angelic and divine nature, so that it may be proportionate to those things placed there. So also all tenths, having I know not what divine quality, are demanded by God as His own, together with the firstfruits: so that the principle of numbers, or the beginnings and ends of things, or the tenths, may be rendered to Him who is the beginning and end of all things. But we, intending to treat of separate natures, and of those things which, counted together, agree with each other, will omit those things which, as their perfection, connected with a more perfect one, lead lower things into that perfect one. Concerning which union of any ennead into its tenth, we will (God favoring) discuss the perfect harmony of those enneads.

There are therefore nine heavens: the Primum Mobile, through which the prime mover moves all things; afterwards, the heaven of the stars, through which the Creator diffuses Himself into numerous instruments for the effecting of things; and He executes through seven principal ministers, upon whom sit those seven principal spirits, or intelligences: Who, existing before the throne of God, enjoy His presence, and contemplating all things to be accomplished in that divine face as in a mirror, they execute all the same things at the nod of the prince. Their names (if we believe the Hebrew doctors) are these: Zaphchiel presides over Saturn; Zadchiel over Jupiter; Camael over Mars; Raphael over the Sun; Honiel over Venus; Michael over Mercury; and Gabriel over the Moon. Who, through the heavens as through instruments, having accumulated the influences of all stars and signs, operate in these lower things, concurring in the production of metals, stones, plants, and animals: But especially in all things that are in man, and pertain to him, whether they appear good or evil: But how they operate evil or good, I think should be somewhat examined.

**How planets or stars operate good or evil in lower things. Chapter VII.**

**S**tars influence good and evil, both Ptolemy and all who deal with astrological matters assert. Through Saturn is given firm and unshaken prudence: From Jupiter, upright justice: From Mars, constant strength and fortitude: From the Sun, fervent charity and love: From Venus, delightful and sweetest hope: From Mercury, penetrating faith: From the Moon (which is most facile in motion, and in nothing persistent), moderate temperance. Nor do these planets influence the above-mentioned things as sources or masters of these virtues: but by disposing the body and its powers, they easily lead to the increase of the aforesaid virtues: provided that the soul, by moderating those powers, disposes them to achieve

those things which the giver of all good things decrees to flow in through his ministers or instruments. From Saturn again, as from a more weighty and sublime patron, we are drawn to more secret things, namely theological and divine matters, a more secret philosophy, the hidden things of both natures; and we are led by a certain disposition to the accumulation of all things to be gathered, both temporal and divine, without which no one is truly great. For what will a scholar be, unless he has gathered many opinions? What will a Saint be, unless he is crowded with merits and manifold graces? Through Jupiter, led by due temperament, we establish and observe the law; we provide what is just; we govern subjects with due authority in peaceful order and tranquil quiet, lest we be worse than bees, cranes, camels, goats, and other such creatures, which recognize their leader. From Mars we have strength and impetus to accomplish work, so that we may be fortunate in our works. For [Aristotle] the cause of fortune is the impetus of nature, if Aristotle thinks correctly, where he wrote about good and bad fortune. Whence evils arise, whether from the malice of influences, or from the bad disposition of the recipient. Chapter VIII.

[Decorative initial V] Since the supreme craftsman saw all things which he had made were very good, not without admiration and prostration of spirit do we hear of so many evils, which some assert concerning the stars, ministers of the best God, decreeing planets (which they call malevolent) to be rather wicked than celestial: namely, that Saturn devours all his children, four excepted; that, troubled by some misfortune, he is voracious, tenacious, difficult, inducing exile, dangers, deceit, wickedness, treachery, moreover, violence, captivity, damnation, perfidy, stubbornness, anger, hatred of all good, fear, distress, sorrow, funerals, mourning, bereavement: Likewise, that he causes witchcraft, thefts, undertakers, embalmers, and magicians.

And concerning the signification of Mars, that Firmicus Maternus, with his ready eloquence, presents these things [Marginal note: Firmicus]: which are treachery, battle, slaughter, audacity, rashness, arrogance, sedition, controversy, plunder, ambushes, robberies, wounds, captivities, flights, difficulties of perfidy, obscenity, incautious love, easy offense, varied thought, no counsel, violent princes, fierce, inhuman, always desiring the slaughter of others, perjured, deceitful, inconstant, slanderous, disordered, contaminating all things, polluting all things: It also signifies the deformed, the shameless, pernicious to childbirth, abortion of children: And in whatever part of the sky it is, it always threatens some evil: If in Aries, it makes thieves, clamorous people, fraudsters: In Taurus, audacious, rash, slanderers, for whom right and wrong are just, provided they satisfy their own lust: In Gemini, devoted to malice, and seeking out hidden crimes with vigilant sagacity: And so he continues concerning other signs. In like manner also concerning the houses: so if it is in the ascendant (horoscope), it makes cunning, audacious, furious, squanderers of patrimony: If in the subsequent house, it still decrees the greatest evils, great misfortunes, estranged from parents, and always strangers from their own home, wounds, chains: And wherever it may be, they always slander him with tireless speech: To this is corroborated what Ptolemy had said before: after whom Alcabitium and Albumasar [Marginal note: Ptolem: Alcabi. Nor is it wonderful, if those who profess knowledge of these things predict so many evils to follow daily in the world: since the heavens, stars, or presiding Angels seem to lead us to commit them. But those who are not dabblers, but lovers of true wisdom (August.) think entirely differently: "From the ears of all (says Augustine) such follies must be repelled: not only of those who hold the true religion, but also of those who wish to be worshippers of any gods whatsoever: For what else does this opinion do, but that no God should be worshipped or adored?" Indeed, they do great injury to heaven: when they suppose that crimes are decreed to be committed there, as if in a most illustrious senate and a most splendid court (Orige, Hiero. Ambrof. August.). I could also cite Origen, Jerome, Ambrose, and very many of our own [authors] who agree with Augustine: But since Christian authority carries less weight with the superstitious, let us come to external [authors]: indeed, to those who were the foremost in handing down the precepts of these prognostications: and we will prove that they themselves handed down their doctrines differently than the common people and the crowd of dabblers imagine.

Let Ptolemy's (Ptolem.) text be read at the beginning of the Apotelesmatics: who is deservedly preferred in such matters and others: and it will be seen what he attributes to the stars, what to birth, what to the parents' seed, what to food, what to place, and what to customs. "The born (he says) greatly imitates the seed and blood of the parents: as is obvious." He also attributes much to place (Porphy. Ptolem.): "which is the principle of generation," says Porphyry, "just as the father is." Hence, even if Jupiter or Venus signify [it] (Ptolemy continues), one born in Ethiopia will not be white, the region and place being an impediment. Customs and food are added (Hali.): "because very often (says Hali, his interpreter) those born are drawn to the nature of customs and foods." Therefore, little is left to the stars: Which did not escape him (Virgilius) who said: "Few, whom righteous Jupiter loved, or ardent virtue raised to the heavens. Those born of gods were able." By which words he implies that not only the stars, but also birth and customs elevate men to sublime things: From which the prince of Astronomers (Ptolem.) himself concludes: "Just as we praise physicians who inquire into the origin of infirmity and its many kinds of causes, in the same way we ought not to be held up to ridicule if, in judging one born, we seek [information] from region, birthplace, foods, customs, and other circumstances:" And in that book, which is called Alarba, he concludes that these accidents very often occur in the born, so that he cannot receive celestial influence: sometimes indeed little, and sometimes much, which very many are ignorant of. Hence in the volume of Apotelesmatics he complains about many: who, not having a complete cause for prognostication in the stars, take [it] from another source, namely necromancy and geomancy (as his interpreter explains), from which they divine, leading men into sophistry and error, when they wish to predict things which a mortal cannot perceive: because nothing certain, but only opinion from many dissimilar things, can be gathered in this art. And when they wish to assert something with certain knowledge, they make that doctrine abominable, which is good and useful. These things, scattered, [says] the Leader of Astronomers. But I will say more: that if all things were disposed by the ruling heaven: they would certainly be very good, moderated by good causes.

from the best God: and transgression of the law from the supreme moderator:

deformity, but to the underlying act: as they say: in which the secondary cause inducing deformity is to be blamed. For it is commonly held that when multiple causes concur to the same effect, the effect itself always follows the weaker and worse cause; which if it were to agree with the supreme (cause), a good effect would always follow. Hence, not the primary, but the secondary cause is to be blamed. There are also those who presume to blame the presiding intelligence. But let such people say: does this intelligence itself do this by the command of the supreme prince, whom all confess to be the sole moderator of the universe, or against his mind and command? If they accomplish something by his command, it is certainly not evil; because nothing is evil unless it is perpetrated against the order of the supreme moderator. But if, opposing the prince, they do it: then indeed there is great confusion in the supreme ruler, if he allows ministers so rebellious and insolent to go unpunished. Nor should they look to evil prelates, who are wayfarers and endowed with their own free will, so that they may merit (reward) by obeying the prince's command, and demerit (punishment) as transgressors, soon to render an account of their stewardship.

Which also happened among the Angels, before they were given stability. Hence, many were punished and expelled from the ministry of God, as not only our most divine Theology teaches, but also the doctrines of the Assyrians, Arabs, Egyptians, and Greeks confirm. [Marginal note: Pherecy.] Pherecydes the Syrian describes the fall of demons, and Ophion, that is, the demonic serpent, as having been the head of the rebellious army. The splendor of the Egyptians, [Marginal note: Trism.] Trismegistus, touched upon the same case, teaching that the fallen Angel and man (as is clear to one who observes well) descended from the diapason of divine harmony into a lower harmony, or dissonance, and became a most wretched servant, indeed an outcast. [Marginal note: Home.] Homer, the chief poet of the Greeks and painter of mysteries, sings of the fall of the first rebel under the name of Atar in his poems. The theology of the Arabs, also emulating the Hebrew, asserts the same. And the demons themselves have often unwillingly confessed their fall.

Therefore, with those having fallen and been excluded, the rest are fortified with such stability that they cannot fall thereafter. But, to speak with the wise and well-initiated, do they not say that all those motions are invariable and removed from error in their continuous revolution? If, therefore, those orbs revolve with such diligence that no error ever occurs, why are they not faithful in the significations and influences of the stars? And if they are obedient and faithful ministers, they will not cause evil, nor will they dispose badly by executing the command of the supreme good. How then do ministers, who never transgress the commands of the ruler himself, lead to transgression against the king? How also do those causes, which never fail, propel towards defect? But if someone contends that they do fail: since the supreme moderator leaves no evil unpunished in the universe, and without coordinating punishment: when will they be punished? Will they cease from motion, or will they be corrected from error? If they cease, how will that motion be perpetual (as they say)? But if, corrected, they desist from error, why are they not corrected quickly? Why is correction deferred? Why does God entrust the perpetual administration of his house for so long to uncorrected, indeed rebellious, ministers? How will it stand?

perpetuity with error, since error is almost nothing and tends towards nothing? But to those

**That neither Saturn, nor Mars, nor any other star whatsoever is evil: as was previously stated. Chapter X.**

[Decorative initial A] Let the accusers of the stars hear what the prince of astronomical doctrine [Marginal note: Ptolem.] first states about Saturn in the third book of Apotelesmata. "If Saturn," he says, "should be the sole significator in the state of the soul, and Lord of the place of Mercury and the Moon, and filled with good irradiation at the angles of the world, he will be a lover of good things, of great and firm counsel, a seeker of secret and [Marginal note: Iul. Fir.] divine matters." But Firmicus also, pursuing him with many praises, says: "that his leadership in matters of deliberation is a most keen intellect: certain speech, stable friendship, long foresight, and royal counsel: He also signifies deep understanding and profound knowledge of things." And concerning him, younger authors state: "that while common life is decreed by Jupiter, Saturn claims for himself a separate and divine life." But to those who feign this life, he is more hostile than to others: those whom Jupiter, scorned by them, has abandoned: nor does Saturn acknowledge them as his own: he who loves true solitaries and divine men. Hence the ancients feigned: that Jupiter usurped the kingdom for himself, with Saturn put to flight, namely by those who are hostile to good Saturn. But he lay hidden in Italy: when he began to elevate the intellects of the Italians: Yet he is said to have come from Greece: because sublime and profound speculations reached the Italians from the Greeks. But formerly from the higher and more distant regions of the East, where, according to the Arabs and Persians, the most subtle demons dwell, of long-lived, Saturnian life in those regions, namely those subject to Saturn: But (to speak more truly) sublime speculations were taught by divine ora- [Marginal note: Albu.] cles. Albumasar, perhaps emulating the Arabs, says that in the regions of India subject to Saturn, men are long-lived: and for the most part die of extreme old age: because Saturn harms his own least of all. But the ancient [Marginal note: Ovid.] philosophers and poets sang of Saturn as the best: and that the golden age ran its course under him. But the Sulmonian (Ovid), imitating the Pythagoreans and Platonists, sang these things in verses:
The Golden Age was first sown, which with no avenger
Of its own accord, without law, cultivated faith and righteousness.
And he continues that many good things ran their course under Saturn: and that mortals, freed from his patronage, declined: whence concerning the succeeding course he continues, saying:
After Saturn, sent into gloomy Tartarus,
The world was under Jupiter: and the silver progeny succeeded,
Worse than gold, more precious than yellow bronze.
[Marginal note: Virgilius] To whom another poet assents, singing:
Before Jupiter, no farmers tilled the fields.
And to Pollio, as if auguring something great, he says:
Now the virgin returns, the Saturnian kingdoms return.

Of these elements, the poets called Jupiter fire, Juno air, Neptune water, and Pluto earth. Whether stars act upon us or not, and if they act, whether by knowing, or by disposing. Chapter XI.

**C**ontend some, and assert that we acquire nothing from sidereal influences: Whence they reject this dogma about the influence of the stars as absurd and utterly alien to philosophy. They add that the most serious philosophers, whose care and diligence was in scrutinizing the causes of things, borrowing truth (if any there be) from medicine, from mathematicians, from every art and science, yet never use astrological causes. And to prove this, they send us to Favorinus the Academic, Panaetius the Stoic, Carneades, Posidonius, Timaeus, Pythagoras, Aristotle, Plato, Plotinus, Avicenna, Averroes. Let them send, I beg, also to Galen, Hippocrates, Aesculapius, and Apollo: because they will be easily answered. For let them remember that in favor of the dogmas invented by them, they recalled the agrarian precept: by which it is commanded in Deuteronomy [Marginal note: Deuter.]: that no one should reap the entire field, but should leave an untouched portion for the poor, who might take gleanings and sheaves for themselves to relieve hunger. Whence if someone were to attack you saying, Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, Origen, Damascene, Rabbi Solomon, and both Rabbi Moses, and the other Hebrew, Greek, and Latin doctors have scrutinized the meanings of scripture with the most diligent labor: and what you write they have not touched: therefore, what you have said is not true. What would he conclude against you? Is it not a common saying in schools: that by arguing from a place of negative authority, nothing is inferred. The wise do not condemn those things which you have devised with your keenest intellect—

**CANTICLE ONE**

(unless we are in Biria) the cunning Mercury will not persuade us that we are not altered by the luminaries: which even common rustics perceive. And other stars produce effects no less known to the wise than the effects of the luminaries are to common people: (Ptolemy) as the Prince of Astronomers wisely said in the beginning of the Apotelesmatics. Yet the influxes of the stars do not produce full effects: since to these same effects concur food, customs, nativity, place, but most especially, the freedom of the soul. (The Same) Hence the same Ptolemy teaches in the same place, and in "Fructus": how some bodily extremity, when offended, can be tempered; and how the freedom of the soul represses the influx, lest we be drawn by bodily inclinations as if by force, like cattle. "The best astrologer," he says, "will be able to prevent much evil that would proceed from the disposition of the stars, when he has foreknown their nature, by forewarning lest it occur; and lest a badly disposed subject receive harm from which it ought to receive benefit, since every celestial influx is good, as we have said." Therefore, do not attribute vicious sadness or superfluous rigidity to Saturn, nor fierce rashness to Mars, nor fraudulent malice to Mercury, nor lustful loves to Venus, nor unstable progress to the Moon: just as a bleary-eyed person ought not to impute calamity to light, nor the burning of temples or houses to fire, nor bad striking to a stone, nor should chains, prisons, and the slaughter of the wicked be attributed to the severity of the judge, but to those who act wickedly: so too, bad effects which follow from the indisposition of the receiving subject ought not to be attributed to the stars. And that we may seek examples from higher things: What is more excellent than the sacrament of sacraments? Yet to those who receive it unworthily and are badly disposed, it becomes for judgment and condemnation. And if it pleases to come to the particular decrees of the stars (if any truth underlies the opinion of the astrologers): Saturn disposes the intellectual virtue; Saturn is dedicated to prudence and the contemplation of divine and human things, and penetrates even to the splendor of true philosophy. But if a profound intellect directs itself to evil, and to satisfy its own lust, entirely applies itself to frauds, deceptions, simulations, with the superior and divine (which they call synderesis) resisting: then, filled with black bile, it feels anxiety and weariness, by which it is so oppressed that it renders good and profitable things into harmful ones. To one thus oppressed, many delusions occur: namely, apparitions of the dead, lemures, larvae, manes, terrors of tombs, frights of burial places. And to the inner eye occurs the wrath of God, the provocations of demons, blasphemies, desperate and hated salvation. I once knew a man agitated by such things, to whom, while praying, there appeared heads of the dead, black and long beards, horrible eyes, terrifying in aspect. To these things, it was not Saturn that led the wretched man, though he was naturally pleasant and festive, but black bile, which arose from a pressing bad conscience and the recollection of a life badly lived. The same must be said of a Martial person: who, if he excites Martial force and impetus not for the zeal of justice (as he ought), but for satisfying lower pleasures, then there are plunderings, then rapines, then many evils. the influences of those planets which are called benevolent can be led to evil: For Jupiter's disposition, arising from its hot and humid, or benevolent nature, which leads to clemency, could be so augmented that the mind, thus inclined, might be led to complete dissolution. Thus Venus's soft influence, though benevolent, if not moderated, makes one effeminate and enslaved to lust; whence often follow adulteries, incests, rapes, sacrileges, and moreover, deaths, fires, plunders, the overthrowing of cities, and perpetual hatreds. The Sun also, father of life and giver of light, who is also called Apollo, leads to true wisdom and royal dignity. If anyone, however, abuses this splendor of mind obtained from the Sun—indeed, from God through the sun—he will fall into evil pride, haughtiness, arrogance, and contempt for others; thence many evils arise from good, just as from wine gulped down will arise oppression of the heart, weakening of virtue, and many things of that kind, which, however, taken moderately, gladdens the heart and strengthens the powers. Water is a good element, very useful for many things; yet it suffocates the unwary and throws down buildings not well fortified. All influences are therefore good, provided that the subjects are well disposed, as we shall discuss more particularly below.

**How the Craftsman of all things produced all elementary things by the third squared ternary. Chapter XII.**

[Decorative Initial A] Lexander (according to Laertius) relates in the Successions of Philosophers, [Marginal note: Alexan. Lucre.] and in the Pythagorean commentaries, that he noted the monad to be the principle of all things: And that from the monad, an indefinite duality, as matter to the author, was subjected to the monad: and that from the monad and duality, numbers are generated; from numbers, points; from points, lines arise, from which plane figures consist; and from planes, solid bodies consist: Of which the principal are the four elements, from which all elementary things emanate. But since we have already discussed the supercelestial and celestial fabric and its matter, it remains that we speak of the elements, and of the compounds made from them which are subject to corruption. Therefore there are four elements, and primary foundations of things, from which all things are composed: Whose superior forms the ancients said brought aid: To Water, Neptune; to Air, Juno; to Fire, Vulcan. Here some wonder that Augustine, and before him Pliny, [Marginal note: August. Plinius] derided these forms and their proponents. For Augustine indeed derided those who taught that these forms should be adored as certain deities favoring mortals; nor did he deny the archetypal exemplars of things to be made: For there are in the heavens, and in the supramundane world, elements of a better kind, and images of animals: Whose primary kinds, distributed in a quaternary, Ezekiel saw before the tribunal of God, [Marginal note: Ezechi. The. he.] as pertaining to Him, as is taught in the theology of the Hebrews. There also exists another quaternary, of which this fourfold kind of animals stands for one corner; to which are joined three others, namely the Ophaninim, Seraphim, and angels of service, who, together with those animals of holiness (as they say, with Abraham as author in the book of formation), complete the tribunal of God: Who, even if He delights in the ternary number, is nevertheless diffused into created things by means of the quaternary: Therefore through those fourfold, supreme elements,

Why the elements are distributed by the quaternary number. Chapter 42.

[Illuminated initial V] That we may bring forth some things from the storehouses of the Pythagoreans and more secret Theologians, all foundations must be laid by the quaternary number: since it itself is the root and origin of all numbers: For the accumulation from the monad up to four yields ten: [Marginal note: Aristote.] Beyond which number (as Aristotle mentions in his Problems, and Hierocles in [Marginal note: Hierocl.] the verses of Pythagoras) no region, nor any language, ever progressed: For the Hebrews, Greeks, Latins, and all barbarians, when they reached ten, again resuming the monad, say eleven, and so forth, imitating leading nature, which by the decimal law divided the fingers on the hands and feet, indeed, the supreme Creator: who willed to distribute the supercelestial world and archetype (as the Theology of the Hebrews teaches) by that [Marginal note: The. he.] number: Which number contains all kinds of numbering, even and odd, square, quadrantal, long, plane, cubic, pyramidal, prime and composite: By which number also, namely by ten proportions, four cubic numbers are completed: just as the quaternary itself is the root of the denary, and through the denary of the centenary: and through these of the millenary: for one, two, three, and four complete the decade: In a similar way, through tens one arrives at a hundred, and through hundreds at a thousand. Moreover, the quaternary contains all musical harmony: since in it is the double, triple, quadruple, sesquialter, sesquitertia proportion: Whence the octave, double octave, fifth, fourth, and octave together with the fifth—

Nor can any more elegant reason be adduced why water does not suffocate the earth, even though it is above it, unless it is because it does not wish to depart from the harmony by which the Creator bound them together in themselves, and in compounds, the more perfectly, the more perfect the compound is in its parts.

**That the elements are found in all worldly members. Chapter XIV.**

[Decorative initial Q] Therefore, the four elements correspond to four kinds of perfect compounds: stones, metals, plants, and animals. The first of these is founded upon the earthy corner of this worldly house: For stones imitate the earth, always descending towards the center, unless they have been burned, like pumice stones made spongy with air-filled caverns. But when reduced to powder, resuming their proper stony nature, they descend. And with stones are numbered crystal and beryl, which, although generated from water, are so congealed that, having become earthy, they descend: Which does not happen with frost and snow. Also, stones generated in the bladder, imitating earthy nature, descend, although they are generated from watery humor. And all of these are concreted by a certain astringency, so that they cannot be liquefied like metals, although they descend, like stones. Upon the second, watery corner, metals are constructed: which, although they are made from all elements (according to Hermes), [Marginal note: Herm.] nevertheless, most especially, being melted from water, they partake of its nature and liquefy: so that in this we have as witnesses Timaeus Locrus, Plato, Plotinus, Aristotle, Avicenna, and the more recent ones following them. [Marginal notes: Timæ. Plato. Plotinus Aristo. Democ. Albertin.] Nor does Democritus disagree, whom some imagine to have taught that metals are generated from lye and lime: For it would dry out like cement, nor could it be liquefied. This matter is pursued at length by Albert the Great, but more concisely by Abubacher. We see (he says) in mines, that due to the continuous heat of certain mountains, the grosser parts of water are so much boiled down and thickened, that in time it becomes quicksilver. And from the fatness of the earth, by the same boiling down and heat, sulfur is generated: and with continued heat, metals are generated. For gold, having no defect, is generated from quicksilver and pure, fixed, clear, and red sulfur. Silver from the same mobile quicksilver and fixed, pure, clear, and white sulfur, which lacks color, some fixity, and consequently weight. Imperfect tin from the same imperfect parts, with sparse boiling down and digestion intervening. Lead from the same earthy and dreggy quicksilver, lacking purity, fixity, and from coarse, somewhat red sulfur, which lacks fixity, purity, and boiling down: Whence it becomes very imperfect. Copper, moreover, from the same impure, unfixed, earthy, burning, unclear (quicksilver), and from such combustible sulfur, which lacks fixity, purity, and weight: Whence it is imperfect and unclean. Finally, iron from the same impure, fixed, partly earthy and burning, white, unclear (quicksilver), and from less fixed, earthy, and burning sulfur: whence it is imperfect and unclean: from which purity is absent: and weight is lacking. Since all these are from quicksilver, and that is watery, therefore they partake of the nature of water. G iij supports this.

[Marginal notes: Auice. Gilgil.] Avicenna, both in his *Physics* and in in his letter to Hazem the philosopher. But Gilgil of Seville was of the opinion that metals are generated from ashes: because they sink in water, and liquefy, like glass, which is extracted from earthy ash and fused stone. But this does not conclude [the argument]: because metal sinks from its earthy [nature], incorporated with moisture, its porosities closed, retaining air. Nor is nitre derived from earthy matter, but from the radical moisture intrinsic to the ashes and stones themselves: for in every compound there are four elements. Upon the third angle, namely the airy one, plants are constructed: which (unless under the open sky) do not sprout: nor do they coalesce. And although the other elements intervene in the composition of the plant itself, and of all other things, it nevertheless savors of an airy nature. For the plant always seeks air related to itself: and wood deprived of air immediately corrupts: and rots: unless aqueous humor, which participates with air, comes to its aid. Upon the fourth angle of this fourfold edifice, which is fire, the zoophyte is fabricated: or animal, whose life (as many wise men teach, Plotinus especially) is fiery, derived from the fiery heaven: and life from the spirit, [Marginal notes: Ezechi. Virgilius] which is fiery, vivifying all the mundane wheels: as we are taught by the oracle of Ezekiel, where he says: "And the spirit of life was in the wheels." With this, Maro (Virgil), imitating the footsteps of the ancients, or seized by poetic frenzy, sings: "Fiery is their vigor, and celestial their origin." Therefore, upon the four elemental bases, five principal kinds of compounds are fabricated: which complete the ennead, namely stones, metals, plants, zoophytes, and animals, which are in the fiery angle. However, the zoophyte, since it is a certain mixture and imperfect: does not have a determined angle: but is received in the bosom of the others.

On another division of elemental things: by which many objections that could be made concerning the aforesaid are removed. Chapter XV.

**E**T if to each angle, or element of this square house, its universal genus has been assigned, they are nevertheless distinguished from one another. For although stones are earthy, all are nevertheless sometimes denominated by another element intervening more strongly. Undoubtedly all elements concur in composing stones, but especially earth and water: Hence opaque stones are called earthy, while transparent ones are called aqueous.

Some liquefy with the strongest fire: so that they are converted into glass. Some are generated drop by drop from falling rain in shells: like pearls in the Indian and British seas. Cry- [Marginal notes: Augusti. Aristote.] stal and Beryl (as Augustine and Aristotle write, and experience teaches) are made from congealed water, with their porosities evacuated: so that they can neither absorb heat nor liquefy. Fire is also present in the composition of stones: which is also extracted from flint struck by steel: and sometimes resolves itself within it: unless Hermes is deceived: who in his arcana teaches that stone ascends from earth to heaven, that is, fire: and from heaven returns again to its nourishing earth: To which heaven (as he says) the wind carried it, enclosed in its belly. Metals also, even if they are aqueous, by their very—

...some of them, however, partake of a fiery nature: such as gold and iron: of which the one imitates the solar fire, the other the Martial fire. But tin and copper are airy: the former receiving its airy nature from Jupiter, the latter from Venus. Silver, however, is earthy with the Moon; lead with Saturn; and quicksilver in water agrees with Mercury: who is (as they say) the lord of the waves. All, however, are endowed with a watery nature: so that they liquefy and differ in weight. For just as water differs from water in weight, so metal from metal, not only by specific kind, but individually. For in weight, barbaric gold differs from refined gold: Tharsian from Indian and Hungarian: and this from Spanish: but that from Eiulat gold: which, coming through the Gihon river, when it perceives the virtue of the fountain existing in the garden of delights, is the best of all: just as water, the closer and more perfect it is to its source, the lighter it is. For waters differ by region and situation in goodness and weight: by which (as Vitruvius states) the goodness of the air is recognized: and there he orders places for constructing buildings to be decided. Plants also, although they are of an airy nature, nevertheless the roots, sap, leaves, and flowers of some are said to be hot, in the first, second, third, or fourth degree: some cold, or dry, and of this kind: concerning which the present place does not permit discussion. That diversity, however, arises when a plant more or less takes on the nature of some element. Animals also, although they are fiery, some, however, being more earthy, delight in the earth: such as the mole, worms, and commonly all reptiles: All aquatic fish are nourished by water: the chameleon by air: the salamander by fire, and some of them are fervent with heat: such as doves, lions: Some are depressed by moisture, such as the lamb: some by dryness: such as the hare, the fawn: All fiery things, however, are distinguished by degrees: whence they borrow names from the elements: or from their qualities.

**That elements are found not only in this terrestrial world, but also in the celestial, supercelestial, and archetypal. Chapter XVI.**

[Illuminated initial E] There are most ample witnesses that elements are found in all things: But those which are found in this lower world are dregs-like and coarser: Those in heaven: bright and pure: Those above the heavens: living, and beneficial in every part. And, to begin from the lower things, this earth around the center is a stable foundation for the feet, the most fertile mother of all seeds. There is density in heaven: which can be seen especially in the Sun, and Moon, and stars: which (as Plotinus states) repel the solar rays. There is (earth/density) in angels: so that they may be firm seats of God: and fertile for us, giving fertility to this dregs-like earth as ministers of God. There is in the archetype of all things a firm and most fertile nature: concerning which it is said: Let the earth open: and bring forth a savior. This water is light and most watery, cleansing and washing all things. There is (water) in the heavens, irrigating the earth with its flow: and a commingling virtue (as Basil discusses in a long discourse). There is (water) in angels, teaching and cleansing: concerning which, when speaking of heaven, it is sung in the psalms: "Who rules over the waters above..."

On the figure of the elements according to the Pythagoreans, and Pla-
tonists. Chapter XVII.

<span style="font-size: 3em; line-height: 0.8em; vertical-align: -0.2em;">T</span>imæus Locrus, from the Pythagorean school, and after him Plato, ascribed [Marginal note: Timæ. Plato.]
figures of this kind to the elements: First, to Earth, a cube of eight
angles and six sides, in the form of a die: And this because of its sta-
bility, heaviness, and difficulty of motion. But they form Fire into
a pyramid of four bases and four angles: so that it may have an easier ascent. They construct Air into an octahedron, that is, a body of eight faces: namely, from eight bases and six solid angles, and twenty-four plane angles: And this because it follows fire in ascent. Finally, they say Water holds an Icosahedral figure: which has twenty bases and twelve angles: because water, by its flexible nature, is mobile and very easy to divide: All these figures are derived from the quaternary: For earth from the first two squares: Fire from four bases and as many angles: Air from twice four bases: For they are doubled, so that it may be penetrative from both sides, and of easier motion. And the plane angles from six quaternaries: But water from twenty bases and twelve angles, which make 32: Which number is from two squares, whose root is four-

**FIRST CANTICLE**

four. Again, there are bases from five quaternaries, and angles from three: And
all these they place universally in a dodecahedral figure, that is, in a solid with twelve
faces: which consists of twelve pentagonal bases, twenty solid angles, and
sixty planar angles: All of which arise from the quaternary: twelve from three qua-
ternaries: twenty from five: sixty from fifteen. Moreover, the fullest harmony
of all these elements is gathered from those bases and angles. The proportion of Air
to Fire is double in the bases, sesquialtera in the solid angles, but double in the pla-

which again, a diapason and a diapente. But the proportion of Earth to Water in the bases is
triple sesquitertia: in the angles sesquialtera: whence a diapason, a diapente, and
a diatessaron in the bases: but in the angles a diapente results. But the proportion of Water to Air
in the bases is double sesquialtera: but in the angles double: whence a diapason, and a diapen-
te in the bases: but in the angles, again a diapason arises. However,
the harmony and proportion of fire to water, and of air
to earth, in which there is a full contrariety in qualities,
is somewhat lacking from that proportion which the elements
have when placed in their proper order: and where two always

participates in both: as
