CANTICLE ONE

HOW THE FIRST ANGELS
of the order agree with the first heaven which is called the *primum mobile*. Chapter One.

[Large decorative initial P depicting a figure in a landscape] OSTQUAM we have discussed the generation of the three enneads, let us come to their harmony, namely the particular consonance of one fabric with another. And starting from the highest spirits, so that we may presuppose something solid, we will approach our Areopagite Dionysius, a true contemplator of mysteries: Who, bringing forth those mysteries which Paul (as some think), [Marginal note: Diony.] but Hierotheus (as he himself confesses) had entrusted to him, [Marginal note: Hierot.] says: that all inferior intelligences are illuminated, taught, and purified by the superior ones, and finally sent to execute the works of God: The supreme ones, however, are destined by God alone: and all are ministering spirits sent for service. But there is a difference: because the first are commanded by God alone: while the subsequent ones are destined and impelled by God and the superior ones, yet by God's command. Here Paul, teaching that all are sent, and Dionysius, saying that [Marginal note: Paulus Diony.] the superior ones are not destined by others, namely intelligences: but by God alone: as we have in the heavenly oracle of Isaiah: where it is said: One of the Seraphim, [Marginal note: Iſaias.] that is, of the supreme ones, flew to me, commanded namely by God, to whose throne and majesty he had been brought for contemplation: from whence that Seraph was destined. But because Dionysius [Marginal note: Diony.] teaches that "seraph" is a name of office, not of person: then some, deceived, said that he was not of the supreme ones, but had performed the office of a superior: Which (unless I am mistaken) is not according to Dionysius's meaning, since all Seraphim are named from שרף (saraph), that is, *saraph* in Hebrew, which in Latin means "to set on fire": And their office is to ignite not only themselves, but also the inferior ones: to whom they are sent: Nor does an inferior perform their ministry: nor does he claim the name of the superiors for himself. Therefore, when that Seraph came to ignite Isaiah and purify his lips with a burning coal: he was a Seraph by office, name, and supreme order. These supreme ones, therefore, who are destined by God alone, agree with the *primum mobile*: which is moved and revolved only by the first mover: Which first mover is either the first of the intelligences: to whom the heavens are entrusted: or the first moderator of all things: Which [Marginal note: Procul. Platon. Triſme.] Proclus and other Platonists, agreeing in like manner with Trismegistus, teach, as [Marginal note: Boëtius] Boethius sings.

but from inferior intelligences by a particular motion and its own sphere: And just as the first is moved by a single impulse, so it receives a single influx: But others receive various influxes according to the variety of movers and motions. Hence the Arab, though barbarically, yet truly [Marginal note: Auerroi] states, saying: The best has its perfection from itself: But that which is near to this (the best) is by few, or one operation, and only one motion: But that which is far removed is by many: for the higher one is, the greater is its motion in virtue, but lesser in number: And the lower one is, the greater is its motion in number, but lesser in virtue, all other things being equal: For the Sun, although it is in the middle of the planets, yet in virtue it is the greatest, and king of the wandering stars: whence, like a king, it holds the middle position. That order is also evident in a civil republic and in the supercelestial realm: For in a civil republic, ministers are agitated and troubled about many things, so that they may fulfill the commands of the ruler: But the chief stewards, being commanded, give commands and are moved to few things: But the lords, with a certain gravity, almost immovably command, not departing from their place, nor from their purpose. Also in the supercelestial republic, the inferior intelligences are called in Hebrew מלאכים [Marginal note: Mala-] Malakhim, in Greek angeli (angels), but in Latin nuntii (messengers) or missi (sent ones), because they are more frequently destined to us to carry the commands of the supreme (being). But the superior intelligences, because they are rarely destined, are called "assistants" by Daniel. [Marginal note: chim] [Marginal note: Daniel] Nevertheless, they are sent sometimes, if what Paul states is true, [Marginal note: Paulus] saying that all are ministering spirits sent for the salvation of those who are capable of eternal inheritance. But the intermediate (intelligences) are sent more frequently to the superior ones, and more rarely to the inferior ones: So also in the celestial Republic, the superior circles move more slowly, the lowest ones more quickly. The Moon, the lowest of all circles, completes its own motion in twenty-eight or twenty-nine days. Saturn, higher up, in thirty years: The Sun and Venus, intermediate, in one year: The starry heaven, the supreme of all spheres which are seen, completes its revolution in many thousands of years: although all are carried along by the first mobile, whose motion is immediately from the first mover: whence it is unique and simple: But those of the inferior circles are multiple. But if it pleases (us) to run through the particular correspondences which that first mobile has with the supreme order of intelligences, which is that of the Seraphim: let us see what that great Dionysius states about these Seraphic minds from the workshop of his teacher: [Marginal note: Diony:] For he attributes sixteen (qualities) to them, saying: The surname of the Seraphim is "always moving around divine things," "incessantly hot," "acutely superfervid," "of inflexible perpetual motion," "reducing the placed ranks," "active exemplar," "reheating those lower things," "reducing to a similar heat, by that fiery celestial vigor obtained, those things which as holocausts, it purifies with the utmost force of fire:" "Not existing veiled, but lucid," "inextinguishable," "always illuminating," "expelling all dark obscurity:" And let us see how much the first mobile agrees with the Seraphim in these respects: For since it is the first thing that is moved, and immediately by the first mover, it is deservedly always carried in its revolution towards that very first (mover), so that, seizing its commands, it may fulfill all things in others according to the will of the commander. Secondly, it is necessary that it be strong with incessant heat, by which it may be moved without interruption, and with such force draw with it

**How the Cherubim correspond to the starry heaven. Chapter II.**

<span style="font-size: 2em; line-height: 0.5em; vertical-align: -0.2em;">S</span>ucceeds the Cherubic order, and let us see how much it agrees with the starry heaven.
A cherub is (if the now common Chaldean interpretations are true) an immaculate picture:
hence Cherub is said to be a Phrygian work, or a fiction:
or (as Abraham ben Ezra prefers) it is a picture, or
image of any separate form: But what more beautiful picture in the entire machine of the
world than the eighth heaven? where there are many images not from Phrygian
Indians, or from Arachne of Lydia: but from Pallas herself, and divine wisdom: which of heaven

--- Page 251 ---
TOMVS QVARTVS. 57

he painted that with figures always living (as some prefer) and full of virtue: just as he had painted the species of ideas in the Cherubic minds. Therefore, by another interpretation, Cherub is called multiplied knowledge, or fullness of knowledge, or many knowledges, and orders, or much order: from כרה *cara*, which means 'he ordered', and רב *rab*, which means 'much'. For in them is multiplied knowledge, and manifold species of things, and in heaven many images. In both places, moreover, the picture is without blemish, and indelible: which will not be consumed by any destructive flood of envious time: nor will it receive any foreign picture or impression, both being filled with full images from the fount of ideas: from which also, as from exemplary forms, this earth is composed with such a living adornment of flowers and herbs. For just as the earth is adorned with flowers, heaven with stars, so the Cherubic mind is adorned with various scientific forms. Therefore it is called multiplied knowledge, its contemplation extended to knowing the most diverse things. Likewise, the starry heaven is multiplied light for cherishing the most diverse things. The Cherubim also cherish these lower things through the same heaven, the first cause giving them the source from which they flow. Hence the psalmist sings: He ascended upon Che [Marginal note: Dauid] rubim, and flew: that is, to arrange all things most swiftly through their all-encompassing knowledge and virtue. And this is that first operative virtue (to use the words of Dionysius) by which the Cherubim are filled and disposed to adapt lower things: [Marginal note: Diony.] as Hugo and Albertus understand in their exposition. And what the supreme artificer does through the Cheru- [Marginal note: Vgo Albertus] bim, as through ministers and secondary causes, he likewise brings about through the starry sphere, as through an instrument: as many Catholics agree with the Academics.

Moreover (says Dionysius), the Cherubic order is filled [Marginal note: Diony.] with divine beauty and wise tradition, and communicative to secondary kinds: So also the eighth sphere is full of most beautiful stars and virtues to be communicated to the second kind, namely, the wandering stars. It is common among [Marginal note: Astron.] astronomers how much power the signs exert on the planets when they receive them in their domiciles. Also manifest is the disposition which they induce in the horoscope of someone born, nor less in arranging other things of the lower world: so that they seem to moderate this mechanism beneath the lunar sphere, yet drawing favor from the supreme parent and his holy name: as is sung in the Davidic hymn: O Lord our Lord, [Marginal note: Dauid] how wonderful is your name in all the earth: which through those sidereal figures, and virtues imbibed from the holy name, draws life, beauty, and virtue. To these intervene the seven wandering stars: which themselves, from the seven measures or circles of the fabric (as Hebrew theology teaches), through their seven [Marginal note: The. he.] regulating intelligences, receive whence they flow. That starry circle is divided into twelve principal images: each of which disposes both a part of the earth subject to it, and some member of the lesser world: Whence both worlds are regulated by that heaven itself, whose middle circle is called the circle of Minerva, or Justice, by the Memphitics, and the king's guide by the Arabs. For by that, as by a certain rod, [Marginal note: Aegyp. Arabib.] the supreme king moderates lower things through the Cherubim, as through ministers:

And if we wish to accommodate all interpretations: we can indeed from the Symbol of all things which are contained in one mysterious name of the sacred language. For if its meaning is sea: since water is the seedbed of things together with earth, what is more suitably adapted for arranging matter than the watery virtue supplied by the Ophaninim? But if by Tarshish the prophet understands carbuncle (which is called anthrax in Greek, and by another name is red, but it shines in the night; yet it is not red [in its light] at all; and it imprints a figure on all stones, but does not receive one; and is said to be the most precious of all by Pliny, Calistratus, Aaron, Archelaus, Aluredus, and Arnoldus) [Marginal note: Pliny, Calistratus, Aaron, Archelaus, Aluredus, Arnoldus, Thethel also] this indeed is most suitable: For the Ophaninim, by arranging darkened matter, illuminate it, and dispose it to receive form and figure: whence their operation is precious. But if by Tarshish hyacinth ought to be understood: it itself is watery (as Arnoldus agrees) and, being in harmony with the sea and water, extinguishes ardor with its coldness. It also compares grace and glory, says Thethel, whence it is also suitable, with the Ophaninim arranging matter by watery virtue, from which grace, form, and glory may be drawn into the subject. But if they interpret chrysolite well: as it is held in common usage, it itself is similar to gold, with a somewhat marine color, as Pliny, Arnoldus, and Bochus write: [Marginal note: Pliny, Arnoldus, Bochus] whence for arranging, that virtue is most suitable, from its softening watery nature, and its golden color most apt for depiction, especially of stars. But if we wish to follow Bachai: [Marginal note: Bachai] that it is a stone favoring digestion and fattening: this also is most suitable: since the office of the Ophaninim is to digest and to fatten matter. [Marginal note: Ezekiel] The interpreter of sacred texts adds: that there were four Ophaninim for arranging matter which was to receive the forms of the four elements, before the composite was brought together. But because in composites only one face is perceived: therefore it follows, that their appearance was a single likeness: as if there were an Ophaninus within an Ophaninus: because in composites each element is in another: and if the composite is resolved, it returns to those four elements. Therefore it follows: "And when they went," namely, from the friendship of the composite towards themselves, they advanced in four directions: and "they did not turn back when they went": because the elements, coming to resolution, do not return into the composite: unless they are led back by a superior cause: whence it adds: "To the place whither the head, or their leader, tended, the elements themselves followed in obedience to the superior cause." But that the flesh, back, hands, and wings of the Ophaninim are said to be full of eyes, is most beautiful: since in arranging the elements, as many eyes are required in those who arrange, as there are forms to be introduced into that subject matter. For forms are eyes, and the splendors of composite things. And that the Ophaninim are called wheels in the ears of the prophet is consistent: because generations,

**FOURTH TONE.** **60**

Lastly, it concludes that, given their complete disposition, proximity, and customary nature, they are made God-bearing by the immediate mystery of God. Indeed, the best description by which the seats of God are first declared to be removed from all unworthiness and most sublime, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: "I dwell in the highest places." Afterwards, that the seats are joined together by truth and love, where the most just judge ought to sit; and that they always tend towards Him whom they serve, and from whom they draw, so that they may be worthy seats; which so imbibe that divine power that they lead the purified to God Himself, but terrify and offend the defiled. Hence, concerning such things, the divine John says in his Patmos vision: "From his throne proceed lightnings and voices, namely, threatening ones, and terrifying thunders." And concerning the favor granted to us by them, Paul, the inspector of sacraments, states: "Let us approach," he says, "with confidence to the throne of God, to obtain from there what we seek." Nor should that of the Psalmist offend anyone: "Who sits upon the Cherubim," because, as Lord of all, He sits at will in the Cherubim, Seraphim, and even in the souls of the just. For it is written: "The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom." But most especially is He said to sit in the Thrones, as the name indicates. Since these are joined together by Seraphic love and illuminated by Cherubic splendor, therefore, He is said to sit in the Cherubim and Seraphim. And since the whole heaven is joined together by the glue of golden charity (as John testifies), therefore, through Isaiah, He says: "Heaven is my seat:" And since this lower mechanism is always ready for Him, He adds: "And the earth is the footstool of my feet." In which He operates and distributes all things, dividing to each as He wills, just as the soul moves all members of the body at will; yet its primary seat is the heart, just as God's more powerful seat is heaven, and within it, the order of Thrones.

[Marginal note: Isaias]

  *How great is the consonance by which Saturn is equated with the same properties. Chapter V.*

**S** But let us see if this order of thrones agrees with Saturn. The Thrones are said to be exalted above the lower orders: Hence they are familiar to God, who through them judges all things contained in His handiwork. Saturn is also the seventh of the planets in ascent, a kind of seat: So that not without mystery God is said to have rested on the day dedicated to it; and commanded His people to rest on the same day; which is called Sabbath, that is, rest, named from Saturn, which in Hebrew is שבתי (shabbatai), which can be interpreted as "my rest" or "my seats." Nor should it be argued from this that that most divine law is Saturnian, or taught by Saturn, since in it its observers are commanded not to fear the stars, and in the same (law) they themselves are declared not to be subject to the stars, although anyone can obtain favor for themselves from God through celestial instruments and through His ministers. But if we wish that those to whom that law was given received influx directly from God, as is hinted in many places of the same law, nevertheless Saturn is not excluded, since they themselves say they received the law from a place, or measure, of divinity: which is called twofold: to which Saturn corresponds, and the intelligence presiding over it. From which place flows rest, remission of sins, and that exuberance which jubi-

**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

The Jubilee is called, after the square of the number seven: which agrees with Saturn, the seventh planet. It was said in the second place concerning Thrones, that they are bound together by
[Marginal note: Iul. Fir.] truth and love. And concerning Saturn, that Firmicus Maternus [says] that he is tenacious: and makes his
[Marginal note: Alchabi.] Saturnians well-compacted: Whence they delight in silence and solitude (as Alchabitius
[Marginal note: Ptolem.] testifies). And they are of firm and solid counsel, as Ptolemy testifies: And they are of a most tenacious nature from that composition, therefore they eagerly gather and with difficulty dispense, and separated from society, and collected within themselves in silence, and with elevated intellect, they more keenly scrutinize the secrets of God and nature: so that with the Thrones they become living
[Marginal note: Democr. Plato. Ariſto. Auicena] seats of God. Whence the aforementioned Astronomers continue, and with them Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and Avicenna, saying: Saturn favors high intellect, and a profound knowledge of things, a more secret Philosophy, and Theology: of which kind is that of the Hebrews: which savors of the influx of supramundane Saturn: And in this he is best equated with the thrones: in which a judge sitting ought to shine with intellect, knowledge of laws, stable speech, long foresight, and royal counsel: Rectitude is added, untainted faith, and agreement with the sitting Prince. And concerning Saturn it is said, that if he rules alone, troubled by no impediment, he gives most faithful friendship. Moreover, Thrones are called God-bearing, and pouring forth wisdom, and God-like dispositions. And Saturn is God-bearing, receiving divine inspirations: which he diffuses into his Saturnians. I will not omit what
[Marginal note: Ianus] antiquity relates about Saturn: that he taught Janus wisdom, and yielded a part of the kingdom to him, in this implying that the outflow of wisdom comes from Saturn: filled with which, one has the greatest part for obtaining a kingdom: and he diffused God-like dispositions in the times dedicated to him, therefore they are proclaimed most happy: and then was the
[Marginal note: Verſus] golden age, in which neither theft nor anything wrong was committed: There was no helmet, no sword, no use of a soldier: nor was it lawful under him to divide the field by boundary: nor for anyone to be oppressed by servitude: nor then was anyone troubled by the injury of war or famine:
[Marginal note: Macro. Nouius Mũmi. Maſuri. Mallius] Therefore, dedicated to him were (as Macrobius relates) solemn rites and sacrifices, which were called Saturnalia: which were celebrated for seven days. In confirmation of which, Novius and Mummius are cited: although Masurius and Mallius thought otherwise: Of whom the former consecrated only one day to him, the latter three: For its
[Marginal note: Cæſar Auguſt.] solemnity was for a day: But by Caesar first, afterwards by the decree of Augustus, it was extended up to a three-day festival: Moreover, the added celebration of the Sigillaria extended the public procession and joy of the religion to seven days. Indeed, the number seven is appropriately attributed to Saturn: who is the seventh planet: who signifies rest: to whom the seventh day is ascribed: which indicates the seventh millennium: in which (as John testifies) with the instigator of evils held in chains, mortals will rest, leading a tranquil life: Which, through the septenary year of rest, and through the great year of
[Marginal note: Leuitico.] Jubilee, after the squares of sevens, is sufficiently prefigured in Leviticus. And since Saturn strives to make his Saturnians God-like: he, indignant, those who with evil morals, by deeds more than by words, slander his good influence,

--- Page 260 ---
**TONVS QVARTVS. 61**

deservedly depresses, and chastises: as we see proven many times in the Hebrews:
Who, more than others, incomparably received the most divine abundances of the true Saturn.
From which the exulting Prophet says: He has not dealt thus with every nation: and his judgments [Marginal note: Dauid]
he has not made manifest to them. Hence also they were oppressed by servitude, captivity, and many
plagues so much more severely, the greater the gifts of the Prince and true Saturn they despised.
Another adaptation of Saturn follows, with the seventh order in the ascent of Angels.
Messahala and Alcabitius write that all planets are joined with him: but he, [Marginal note: Messa. Alcab.]
because he is supreme among all, is joined to none: thus also to the Saturnian religion (which,
however, belongs to the supramundane Saturn) all adhere, either according to the true fulfillment
of the mysteries contained in that divine law, or by imitating Moses, its lawgiver, like apes:
and boasting that they received from Apollo, Jupiter, Mercury, Minerva, the Nymph Egeria,
Vesta, and a good deity, what they stole from Moses. But the Law itself adheres to no one:
nor did it receive anything from anyone, except from God himself: And this Law, pregnant with the divine birth of the Gospel,
seems to be cast out as if barren: although it is held in the highest honor by those who think rightly:
because the Gospel does not abolish the Law itself: but fulfills it even to the smallest iota and tittle.
Thus all orders of Angels are joined with the Thrones to fulfill the judgments of God: but the Throne itself is joined to none.
For Seraphic love, zeal for truth and justice, concurs: Cherubic knowledge also intervenes: which arranges
degrees in distributive justice: and decrees retributions and scourges in retributive justice,
according to merits and misdeeds. Dominations are present, that is, freedom of mind (for thus [Marginal note: Diony.]
is domination declared by Dionysius) so that judgment may be pronounced free from affection and
passion. Virtues assist the judges: so that they may be manly and constant in pronouncing judgments.
Powers are at hand: so that they may execute the judgment pronounced, coercing (to use the words of Dionysius) [Marginal note: Idem]
all tyranny, and those abusing the strengths of their power. Principalities, Angels and Archangels,
presiding over Princes, particular men, and provinces, convene: so that they may approve and favor
the judgment and distribution brought forth by the judge. Nor do others take on the Thrones to fulfill
their offices: Not Seraphim to love: not Cherubim to understand: not Angels to announce: nor others
to execute those things to which their offices are appointed.

**Dominationum proprietates decem. Cap. VI.**

**C**um Saturnum (whom the ignorant call malevolent) with the most holy seats of God
we have made agree: where no concordance appeared: we will easily adapt Jupiter to the Dominations,
especially those things that are stated about both by their authors.
About Dominations, the great Dionysius writes this: I consider the manifest designation of the Holy Domination [Marginal note: Diony.]
to declare a certain absolute and anagogical ascent, free from all pedestrian diminishment: and into no tyrannical

dissimilarity, in no way universally inclined to it; a liberally severe Dominion, placed above all diminishing servitude, superior to all subjection, and removed from all dissimilarity, and incessantly desiring dominion; and conforming itself and what is after it most excellently and beautifully to the virtue and likeness of that which naturally subsists, as much as possible; turned not to any who see vainly, but properly to the universal Being; and made always in participation of the Lord's Deiformity, as far as is possible for it. Thus far Dionysius.

Whose meaning is (as he himself states beforehand) to declare the names, or full denominations of the holy Dominions and mysteries. And the first of these is, that they have a certain absolute elevation, free from all crushing depression, which diminishes the dignity of the ruler. And secondly, their mind is free from all tyrannical dissimilarity, so that it feels no inclination towards it. And indeed, what could more properly be ascribed to tyranny than dissimilarity from true principality, since the latter rules by right, and the tyrant against right: The one strives to favor and uplift subjects; the other, however, to oppress and plunder: The one breathes truth, piety, munificence, justice, and clemency; the other squanders everything with lies, deceptions, impiety, avarice, cruelty: The one a certain divine image; the other a diabolical one. Therefore, the tyrant is dissimilar to the legitimate Prince, but much more so to God, whose place the Dominions hold. Thirdly, a true Dominion is liberal with severe equity, and freed from all servitude and diminishing service. Nor should anyone think that severity contradicts liberality, since severity is an equitable distribution without distorting affection, so that a judge relying on truth may be able to restrain insolence, and with due munificence honor the well-deserving. Which he cannot do unless he has a mind free from avarice, hatred, self-interest, and such things, which lead the mind into a servitude that diminishes from the right balance of justice. Hence so often the supreme Prince of all exclaims, commands, and protests to judges and those holding his place, that they should have hands free from all gifts, because gifts, having torn out the eyes of the mind, lead into the most miserable servitude. Hence, in the fourth place, it is inferred that the ruler is superior to all subjection, which may be contracted from gifts, blood, affinity, clientage, country, friendship, custom, ambition, or from wherever. Fifthly, it is added that Dominion is removed from all dissimilarity to the supreme Prince, who is truth itself:
[Marginal note: CHRIST.]
But sin introduces this dissimilarity, by which one differs from the primal truth. Hence concerning the first rebel, the supreme doctor says: "That murderer did not stand in the truth from the beginning." But I think that 'slayer' could be more aptly translated than 'murderer,' because he was not then a slayer of man, but a slayer of himself. Nor is this word 'homicida' (murderer) in use among the Hebrews, in which idiom John wrote his Gospel, where those words are recited. Therefore, they are, and ought to be, so conformed to God that they may rightly be called Gods, just as it is said of them in Exodus: "You shall not revile gods," that is, judges. [Marginal note: Dauid] ...judges. And the Psalmist, when singing of such men, or of the Apostles appointed over the twelve tribes of Israel, says: "The mighty gods of the earth are greatly exalted."
Sixthly, it follows that they ought incessantly to desire dominion. Here, the weak might be offended: how can those holy intelligences be said to aspire to dominion with unwearied desire, when in this Church, of which that heavenly one is a type and exemplar, they are condemned by the supreme hierarch [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] Christ, who burn for pre-eminence? As it says in the Gospel, whose title is according to Luke: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority among them are called benefactors; but you are not to be so. Instead, whoever wishes to be great among you must be as a minister and a servant." To these, we will give a satisfactory answer by bringing forth a truth known to the wise: For the appetite for dominion and pre-eminence, since it is innate in nature, does not seem blameworthy. Nor can we immediately desire subjection and the lowest rank, just as we cannot extend our will [Marginal note: Augusti.] to pain; since pain (according to Augustine) arises from things we do not want. Thus, to desire the lowest things is against the instinct of nature, which is always drawn to greater and better things.
Hence, one who desires great things should be called not proud, but magnanimous, [Marginal note: Aristote. CHRI STVS.] if Aristotle teaches correctly in his Ethics. And if the appetite for pre-eminence were blameworthy, the supreme teacher Christ would not have proposed it as a reward to those who renounce earthly things, saying: "You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel."
[Marginal note: Apocal] And again in the Apocalypse, to lead us to struggle and victory, he promises a high seat, saying: "To the one who conquers, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne."
Therefore, the appetite itself is not to be blamed, but the wrong object: namely, when we wish to be exalted in these momentary things of our earthly pilgrimage with the loss of heavenly things, to which we ought to aspire. The manner is also to be blamed, presuming to obtain by one's own strength what ought to be acknowledged as coming from the giver of all good things.
Hence, he erred who said: "I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High." He commits as many sins as he utters words. He claims a higher seat for himself with no existing merits. Again, he wished to ascend a more eminent throne uncalled, when he ought to have sat in the lowest place until he heard the Prince saying: "Friend, go up higher." And he had decided to sit on the mount of assembly, on the northern side, from where the law was given, from where the insolent are punished, from where [Marginal note: Ieremi.] falls and many transgressions spring forth, according to that of Jeremiah: "From the north every evil will be unleashed."
Hence, he deservedly experienced the sentence and judgment of God, when he tried (though in vain) to place himself in the place of judgment. He again ambitiously sought to ascend above the height of the super-celestial clouds, from where all things are irrigated through God-bearing channels. And he had impiously thought to make himself like the Most High, to whom he was not even worthy to be a servant.
Hence, he became the lowest of all, and most remote from the Most High. If, therefore, he had wished to obtain the sublime degree of blessedness from the supreme dispenser, he would certainly have achieved it (as it pleases [Marginal note: Ansel. Bernar.] Anselm, Bernard, and other wise men), concerning whom, to God...

In what harmony Jupiter imitates all the same properties. Chapter VII.

[Decorative initial Q containing a figure] How harmoniously Jupiter obtains these attributes assigned to the Dominations, it will be easy to judge: if what the Astronomers state about him is true. For that Julius Maternus says, from Ptolemy's school: [Marginal note: Iul. Fir. Ptolm.] The significance of Jupiter is dignity of form, nobility of spirit, sound wisdom, and intellect: Then rights, laws, statutes, religion: Then piety, modesty, grace, faith, and whatever an excellent mind of a well-instructed man can conceive. All these things he effects, especially when he is in the Horoscope: or in his domiciles, or in his bounds, or in his exaltation, and in signs and places where, rejoicing in his connatural property, he receives favor: so that he may dispose (people) to those things which the Dominations enjoin by the command of the Prince. Also, being constituted in such places, he makes noble, illustrious, great, and distinguished governors, or prefects of cities: and, according to the measure of their nativity, good, modest, benevolent, joyful, and rich. And all these things (to speak physically) he effects from a hot and humid nature: rendering the temperament tractable from the humid; friendly from the blood; disposed to wisdom from the proportionate heat; generous from the abundant influx. Hence in him are piety, benevolence, faith, modesty, grace, and whatever pertains to what is just and right: for a well-tempered complexion easily disposes one to all good things. But if we wish to ascend higher, this influx is drawn from the Dominations, which dispose the soul, while the star (planet) only disposes the body: But God, as the primary cause, provides both the influx and the increase to all things. But let us come to agreement. It has been said of the Dominations that they are free from all earthly baseness: and of Jupiter, that he disposes to nobility of form. Who, I ask, ascends to a higher place, man or beast? Man or woman? Angel or man? He, indeed, who is more elegant in form, is worthily preferred to others. For among all living beings, it was said to man alone, who is more beautiful in form than all others: "Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and the beasts of the earth." [Marginal note: Genesis. Psalm.] And of the Prince of all it is said: "You are fairer than the sons of men." Nor is that form, which merely soothes bodily eyes, sought in those who are to predominate: But that which Paul earnestly desired in the Thessalonians, so that they might deservedly be leaders and princes of others, saying: [Marginal note: Paulus] "having become imitators of us, so that you might be a pattern to all believers." Of which form the Law boasted (as the Hebrews explain), or the Blessed Virgin, saying, as our people assert: "I am black, as far as outward appearance is concerned, [Marginal note: Cantic.] but beautiful in inner beauty:" If, however, both beauties coincide, a form more worthy of command will result. Concerning the three co-equalizations of the fire of Mars with the Virtues. Chapter VIII.

**T**hat we may treat of the harmony of the fifth order of the enneads themselves, let it [Marginal note: Dionysius.] please us to examine what our God-filled Dionysius teaches concerning the holy virtues. He says that it is a certain strong and immutable virility of the holy virtues in all operations according to their Deiformity, not weakly infirm for any reception of indwelling things, or of divine illuminations, but powerfully reduced to the imitation of God, not abandoning its Deiform motion through its own weakness, but firmly bearing itself into superessential and pontifical virtue, and made similar to the image of virtue itself (as far as is permitted): and indeed powerfully turned to it, as the principal virtue: but giving rise to a second virtue in a Deiform manner. Thus Dionysius: And before we proceed: we will endeavor to declare why this fifth order is called by the particular name of virtues, Although all angels are called virtues by the same Dionysius: and rightly so, since every operation requires an operative virtue. Therefore, since no order of angels, or particular intelligence, languishes in idleness: but all execute the commands of the prince: in each of them virtue is required: by which they can be denominated virtues. Therefore, to remove this difficulty, we will recall what has been said concerning the Seraphim, Cherubim, and other orders. For although the Seraphim understand: and all other spirits love: yet from love, by which they are most ardent, they are called Seraphim, that is, burning ones: And granted again, that all understand: yet the Cherubim are denominated from the fullness of knowledge. Thus also from the gift, by which it most flourishes, this order is called virtues, although all rejoice in their own virtue and their own fortitude. And here also pleases the opinion of Albert: [Marginal note: Albert.] that although superiors are adorned with nobler lineages, they yield to inferiors in this denomination. For presbyters, although they hold the rank of deacon, yet claim for themselves the name of Priest from a more dignified one. The same is true of Bishops, and Patriarchs, and the like. The Virtues therefore are denominated from the gift by which they most shine: Which gift is described as adorned with multiple properties: namely seven, which they receive from the supreme virtue: and two, by which they communicate themselves to inferiors. For this is proper to all ministers of God constituted in the hierarchy: that they communicate to inferiors what they receive from superiors. The first gift, therefore, is virility, and unshaken fortitude to conquer those things which are hostile to the supreme prince. This sacrament is wonderful, how that most happy supreme emperor in the kingdom of peace, where he broke powers, the bow, the shield, the sword, and war: and himself being true peace and the blessedness of all, still contends through his virtues and fights: and when that warrior, who had undertaken the Lord's battles, in his [Marginal note: David]

The supreme Emperor acts through virtues, as through ministers: likewise he acts through Mars, as through an instrument: It is trivial that he favors all warriors, from his nature (to speak physically) always inflamed with fiery favor, so that he makes his Martials choleric, irascible, impetuous, strong, virile, and unshaken. Secondly, it follows concerning the holy virtues: that they undertake and perfect all their operations, as deifying and deiform, just like all other intelligences: which, having been made deiform, degenerate in nothing from that uniform and deifying beauty itself. Which Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and whatever celestial instrument effects, in this praising the supreme craftsman, who made all things very good [Marginal note: David]. Hence the deiform lyre-player sings: Praise him, sun and moon: Praise him, stars and light, indeed both fixed and wandering stars, and the light of all of them in this most resounding theater praise the craftsman. Thirdly, it is sought: that they are in no way weak to draw in the influx of divine virtue: lest they succumb when their own strength fails: which tends to nothing, unless favor is continuously supplied from that supreme source for themselves, and for those whom they favor. Hence Moses helped the people fighting with the Amalekites with virtue, which he continuously drew in by praying with arms outstretched in a cross [Marginal note: Moses,]. Which Mars also provides with his fiery power: as Ptolemy [Marginal note: Ptolem.], Hermes [Marginal note: Hermes.], Firmicus [Marginal note: Iul Fir.], Alchabitius [Marginal note: Alcha.] and all astronomers agree, whence it is called Empyrois: For fiery power is indeficient: and operates without interruption. It is also always increasing, and receiving increment in proportion to the increase of matter: And that it may always operate as if defective in itself, so that it may always draw in, is necessary: Therefore Mars, together with the presiding virtues, must always imbibe from a higher virtue, so that they may always succor their own, over whom they preside in battle.

**How they still agree in six other properties. Chapter IX.**

[Decorative woodcut initial V] Further, Dionysius, progressing concerning the deifying virtues, says: that with strong powers they imitate God: and lead true soldiers, who fight for the kingdom of God, to Him: so that they may receive a crown in Him: because he will not be crowned (the heavenly trumpet sounds) unless he has fought lawfully [Marginal note: Dionysius]. And what is perfected through warlike virtues, is arranged through Mars, the signifier of war [Marginal note: Paul]: Which war, if we undertake it with right intention, is certainly good and holy: But if we commit it out of ambition, hatred, envy, and pride, it is certainly evil and diabolical. For if Mars (says Firmicus) [Marginal note: Iul. Fir.] is well disposed in the ninth house, with Jupiter favoring, and the house itself, and the Horoscopal irradiation, he makes people fortunate: and those who easily obtain all things. But what is "with Jupiter favoring," if not with the justice of war favoring, and the zeal of the Lord, for whom we must always fight? Fifthly, it is added, that they do not abandon the deiform work and the battle they have undertaken out of any weakness: lest they be driven from the kingdom and the military service, together with Saul, who fought not with the faith he ought to have. Sixthly, it is brought forward, that they are carried firmly and incessantly into the most powerful and superessential virtue, by which they can acquire for themselves the perfect image of the prince. And here is no- I

--- Page 269 ---
**CANTICI PRIMI**

stagnation, or repetition: but declares that they themselves always ascend to higher things: For first, they have manly constancy: Second, they perform every heavenly and God-like work: Third, lest they be weakened, they always draw from the supreme fount: Fourth, they have God before their eyes as an example: Fifth, they persevere in the work they have begun: Sixth, always tending towards the supreme hierarch, they acquire for themselves his complete likeness and image: To do this, they are turned towards God himself with all affection and all their strength: And thus, like most holy vessels filled with all charisms, in the eighth place they communicate virtue and strength to those inferiors entrusted to them: Finally, they strive with all diligence to make those whom they favor God-like: To all these things, the fiery element seems to dispose by its fiery power. And since five have been spoken of, let us proceed to the sixth. Fire (as our Dionysius [Marginal note: Diony.] testifies) always tends upwards, but Plotinus [Marginal note: Plotinus], going further, says: Fire, reaching up to heaven, since it cannot be sluggish, returns to other things, seeking its amplification everywhere. And since it cannot be carried downwards, nature resisting, it is most easily led and by natural attraction is drawn by the soul to life: so that through communion with superiors, acquired from a single life, it may make a transition into the highest things. If Plotinus transcends the bounds of philosophy or truth, let the readers judge. However, we hold this as constant, that fire always moves upwards: and seeks the highest rather than the lowest. What, I ask, could be said to be more fitting with the sixth property of virtues, by which they are always carried upwards, so that serving the heavenly beings, they strive to be transformed into their likeness: No less so with the seventh, by which, to do likewise, they are turned with all their strength towards God, just as fire, which always strives to transform upwards into the highest, not only itself, but all things it can ignite. But stones, earth, metals, and whatever things refuse to yield, it leaves in their lowliness. And what has been said of fire, Mars likewise accomplishes by his nature and fiery impulse, concerning which Ptolemy [Marginal note: Ptolem.], proceeding no less physically than mathematically in the first of his *Apotelesmata*, says: "The star of Mars dries and burns, and its heat is assimilated to fire." Hence, through the fiery properties accommodated to Mars, we have made them agree with the most holy virtues: from which, those whom Mars and the virtues favor are rendered ready and skillful for all things. But since good happens in one way, but evil in many ways: hence an impulse not moderated by any bridle of reason, not directed by any inner eye, rushes, like a wanton horse, into manifold precipices: tyranny, oppression, unjust homicides, thefts, robberies, immoderate wantonness, and other evils, which dabblers are accustomed to prognosticate with too broad a license through the signification of Mars: For this proceeds not from Mars, who merely provides the impulse, but from the soul badly regulating that impulse: But if it is well regulated, Mars (Mauors) is rendered stronger and more powerful with fiery or Herculean vigor: whom the wise (especially Boethius) celebrate in their songs, and here, having been celebrated, he exhorts us to imitate him, adding:

Go now, brave ones, where a higher exemplary path leads; why do you, being inert, expose your backs, when the earth, once overcome, grants stars? To achieve these things, among natural gifts, choleric fervor is required: Among celestial things, the favor of Mars: Among supercelestial things, the vigor of virtues: Among divine things, the grace of God, or the inflammation of spiritual fire: By which the saints were made strong in war: they conquered kingdoms: they wrought righteousness: they obtained promises: they stopped the mouths of lions: they quenched the violence of fire: they escaped the edge of the sword: they recovered from infirmity: they put to flight the armies of aliens, and other things, which Paul, in his Epistle to the Hebrews, mentions. Nor is Mars alone (as pure mathematicians opine) the cause, therefore so many errors boil forth in their prognostications: because, namely, they do not consider cooperating causes with the heavens, which their leader Ptolemy teaches should be considered. [Ptolem.] And because the conjunctions of stars, and their virtues, are not fully known by us, as is very well known to all wise people: hence also a certain judgment about their effects cannot be given, with the added freedom of will, by which we can reject many things, and accept many things according to our wish.

Nor should sharper minds be moved by the fact that the stars seem to provide complete life and form to plants and animals generated by putrefaction: and some of those forms appear good, some bad: so that they conclude that good and evil proceed from celestial influence. Into which heresy if they fall, they will easily be removed from it, if they consider (besides those things which we have adduced above) how absurd it is for any turbid things to emanate from those most limpid fountains of celestial or supercelestial waters.

And concerning this Mars, Ptolemy in the third book of his Apotelesmatics decrees: [Idem] that if it alone presides over the disposition of the soul, the native will be most strong and powerful: But if it is badly disposed, he attributes this not to the sidereal influx, but to repugnant qualities arising from a certain antiparastasis of influxes. But (to speak more accurately) this arises from a badly disposed subject: just as medicines, the best wines, and more delicate foods harm those who are unwell. And concerning such matters, Iamblichus draws these things from the columns, or storehouses, of the great Trismegistus: [Iamblic.] [Trism.] All celestial influxes are good and beneficial, as they themselves receive only the good: And acting thus, they are immutable in their eternal gaze: although operating in mutable nature itself, they degenerate, yet in perpetual order they are always beneficial: Therefore, from the flow of heaven into matter full of discords, something dissonant sometimes results, yet the celestial powers remain always good. Therefore, a harmful quality on earth is different from the celestial influx, which, while it exists in itself, and is influenced by the Giver of good things, is good as long as it reaches the lowest parts, as if in the first degree. Secondly, when it is received in a viler subject: it itself becomes vile. Thirdly, because of the diverse nature of the recipient, it is received in diverse ways. Fourthly, by qualities differing among themselves in the same subject, it itself is varied. Fifthly

--- Page 271 ---

the recipient enduring, it suffers. Sixth, from all things comprehended in the subject, something else finally results. Therefore, celestial and immaterial influences, which extend themselves into the containing power of Saturn and the moving power of Mars, frequently cause harm by accident: The former, when it is received in colder matter: the latter, however, when in hotter. Which entirely happens according to the disposition of the matter: For the Sun, although it seems to offend some with its heat and light, is nevertheless necessary for life: similarly, all celestial influences come as salutary, although either the perversity of the subject receives them perversely, or weakness cannot easily tolerate the efficacy of the superiors. All movements contribute to all, even the smallest parts of it: although meanwhile the smallest particles may be affected by this or that movement, or may not easily receive it, just as in a dance, while individuals dance harmonically and their gestures agree with each other and with the whole chorus: yet a finger and a foot are struck and pressed: And if anything weak has moved, it is ruined.                                                                                                      Cap. X.

**A**nd so that we may make the most holy powers agree with the king of the planets, it must be seen what Dionysius teaches about them. Of these (he says) holy powers, the equally powerful, well-ordered, and unconfused arrangement of divine dominations and virtues regarding divine receptions, And the ordered power of the supermundane and intellectual. Nor tyrannically precipitated into those things which are inferior by their virtues of power. But powerfully led back into the divine, after well-ordered things, and after it, leading back in a deiform manner, and assimilated to the powerful causal power (as far as is right), and revealing it (as is possible for angels) in well-ordered ranks through its powerful virtue. Thus Dionysius. Among the principles of whose discourse he includes the most worthy privilege of the holy powers, that they are those who restrain all evils, and at the same time, evil-doers.
[Marginal note: Grego.] Which Gregory and Bernard openly relate, of whom the former says: Powers are called those Angels who have received this more powerfully than others in their order: so that adverse virtues may be subject to their dominion: by whose power they are restrained, lest they be able to oppress or overshadow the hearts of men.
[Marginal note: Bernard] The latter, however, says: Those spirits who are named Powers, while delighting to magnify the divine power of our crucified one, reaching it everywhere: from this they receive power to disturb the forces of demons and men for the righteous, who inherit salvation. All of which Dionysius touches upon in that he says they shine with the gifts of divine dominations and virtues: by which they can restrain rebellious virtues and powers. Nor is there confusion of the celestial orders: because the gifts of one are communicated to another: For just as all love and understand: yet two supreme orders are adorned with this particular privilege, so that one is called the order of lovers, and the other of intelligent ones. No less do all angels oppose evils, and fighting against them, resist them: nevertheless, the fight is particularly assigned to the Virtues, and resistance to evils by a certain authority to the Powers.

is attributed: All these things we observe in the lower Republic, which bears the type of that super-celestial one. For in this one, the king commands, soldiers fight, and the powers, or praetors, suppress crimes: they restrain rebels, and resist evils with the moderation of justice. In the higher republic too, the emperor commands: the Seraphim are the household and familiars, the Cherubim are the wise moderators, and the Thrones are the assessors; the Virtues fighting under Prince Michael suppress evils and put to flight the darkness of the wicked. There are Powers shining with the sun, and truly favoring the Sun, who said: "All power is given unto me in heaven, and in earth:" Which, free from all envy, He communicated to His more secret friends, saying: "Behold, I have given you power to tread on serpents, and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy."
<br/> [Marginal note: CHRIST.]
He also gives power, that they may become sons of God: And this through the light, which illuminates every man who wishes to be illuminated, and does not oppose the darkness of sins, or the gloom of dark powers. Hence the order of Powers sweetly agrees with the true Sun, illuminating all things: of whom it was said: "God made the sun, that it might have power over the day." But returning to the sidereal sun, it thrives here with the fervor of Mars, and the benignity of Jupiter: thus the Powers are filled with the strength of virtues, and the rectitude of dominations: And the Powers put to flight dark demons: lest they inflict harm on the elect: just as the sun puts to flight the darkness of night, and all dark things, as we read in Job, "When the dawn suddenly appears, they consider it the shadow of death."
<br/> [Marginal note: Job. David]
And David, when speaking of the lion cubs seeking permission from Elohim to devour, adds, "The sun has risen, and they are gathered, and will lie down in their dens." When these are put to flight, it follows, "Man will go out to his work." The Powers are said to assist the true crucified Sun with such fidelity, that they strive to subject all things to Him. And this sun (the sidereal sun) responds to the supreme Sun with such consonance, that Plato calls it the visible son of the highest good, not indeed the first, but the second, through whom we may arrive at the knowledge of the first.
<br/> [Marginal note: Plato.]
We will leave the declaration of all other congruities of both suns for elsewhere.
<br/> [Marginal note: Diony. Iamblic.]
For Dionysius, along with certain Platonists, calls this sun which we see a clear statue of God: But Iamblichus calls it an image of divine intelligence.

Secondly, it follows concerning the order of Powers, how well adorned and unconfused it is. And the sun, the ornament of all, sits like a king in the midst of the wandering stars, adorning and beautifying all, and by whose course all are regulated and disposed, so much so that their movements are thence called diurnal or nocturnal, meridional or northern, eastern or western. The Powers are certainly ordained to receive from God, from which they dispose of lower things. And our sun is ordained to the first (principle), so that from it, it may receive light and virtue, by which it may illuminate and vivify other things; whence the sun is called the father of life.

Thirdly, it follows that their order is of supramundane and deifying power, as Hugo explains.
<br/> [Marginal note: Hugo]
But (unless I am mistaken) they are an ordered image of the deifying empire, and not the order itself, since lower things do not order higher things, but bear their image. The sun also among

**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

The Sun also, among all stars, is an image and statue of the highest prince: just as the powers are an image of the supramundane power: who is the Sun, and the true light of both the celestial and terrestrial world. Fourthly, it follows that they exercise power internally without any tyrannical impiety: so that we may be taught what kind of equity the highest prince demands from those who hold his place in the celestial and mundane republic. For concerning dominations and powers it is said: that they are without tyrannical force. And thus the former with just Jupiter, and the latter with the benevolent Sun most excellently agree: Both of whom dispose towards empires and dominions with equal favor: The former (to speak physically) from his well-tuned airy nature, and the latter from his tempered, and always benevolent warmth: Whence (as Ptolemy and Firmicus teach) from a moderate influx they dispose towards the most honorable reconciliation of men: strength of soul and body: great victory over all: highest expectation: and whatever seems to pertain to royal pomp. Its signification is also a principate not cruel, not difficult, not unjust: but most splendid from justice and beneficence. But what they add, that solar spirits are a little inflated with the spirit of pride, and desirous of honors: this could be referred to their magnanimity (which is commonly called pride): For the Sun and Phaethon decree their offspring to be just, good according to the quality of the dominations and powers to which they correspond: They also make (especially the Sun) clear in doctrine. Hence antiquity said that Phoebus, or Apollo, favors true philosophy and clear knowledge, which ought to flourish in a prince: Whence Plato teaches in proverbs that no one rules worthily unless they philosophize from a certain divine lot. Therefore, since the Sun decrees its solar (followers) to be mature in counsel, weighty in eloquence, zealous in justice: to what does it invite them, if not to celestial things by which they ought to be confirmed: so that they may agree, sixthly, with the powers, which lead the multitudes that are after them to the imitation of God?

But what is added, seventhly, concerning the powers, they agree so much with the Sun that nothing is more fitting: For they, as far as they can, strive to express the likeness of that potentific cause, from which they received power: And the Sun, a true statue of God and image of the supreme light, leads so much to the knowledge of God, that the Academics do not have anything by which they could more expressly teach that Deific nature, Whose essence reveals the Father, splendor the Son, heat the Holy Spirit, and whose beneficent virtue (reveals) God's munificence towards us. Hence the highest doctor taught the beneficent nature of the Father through the Sun, saying: "Be perfect as your heavenly Father: who makes his sun rise on the good and the bad." Most beautifully, in the eighth place, it is added that through the powers (by which all things can be governed with God's favor) is represented that Deific power, which Dionysius calls 'potentific,' that is, making his ministers powerful: If they burn, they are inflamed by that divine fire: If they know, they do so illuminated by the supreme light: If they judge others, this is by the authority of Him who said, "I will make you sit on my throne": If they rule, this is by the dominion granted by Him who said: "Rule..."

**In five, principalities participate with Venus. Chapter XI.**

[Marginal note: Diony.]
Indeed, the heavenly principalities manifest that principal, God-formingly educing [power]: And this, with sacred order, and most fitting principal virtues: And that they are universally converted to the super-principal principle: And to hierarchically lead others to that same [principle], as far as possible, to be formed as a principle of principles, and to manifest its super-essential ordination, and the adornment of principal virtues. Fire [represents] strength, and love: Water [represents] clemency, and piety: Air [represents] a subtle spirit: Earth [represents] the stability of essence. From composite things, man [represents] intrinsic operations, and all that is in God, rejoicing in His perfect image: The starry heaven [represents] multiple exemplars, or ideas: The Primum Mobile [represents] the first mover: Seraphim [represent] the fire of love: Cherubim [represent] scientific power: And so concerning each one. **By what song Mercury sings with the archangels. Chapter XII.**

[Marginal note: Diony.]
[Decorative initial A]pproaching the archangels, our Dionysius says: But the very virtue of the holy archangels is indeed equal in power to the celestial principalities: For their and the angels' hierarchy and disposition (as I said) is one: Indeed, there is no hierarchy unless it has primary, middle, and ultimate virtues. The holy order of Archangels, established in a communicative middle, embraces the extremes by a certain common and social right: For it communicates with the higher principalities and the holy angels: To the former, indeed, because it is especially directed to that supreme principality itself, and is formed in its image (as far as is right): and it unites and joins the angels by most orderly and invisible guidances: But in the archangels themselves resides the prophetic office: that they may hierarchically receive divine illuminations through the primary virtues: and announce them in a God-like manner to the angels: and manifest them to us through the angels, according to the sacred analogy of each illuminator. This is what our Dionysius says. He brings forth a most celebrated secret: that there is no hierarchy unless supreme, middle, and lowest virtues and charisms shine within it: so that every hierarchy, proceeding from the triune creator, is connected to three orders: and the whole multitude is distributed into three hierarchies: The first of these, always looking to God himself, serves Him immediately, namely, the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones: The next, however, is for conferring God-like virtue upon us: which has been declared in the Dominions, Virtues, and Powers: But the last is dedicated to human disposition, so that man may be made God-like: And not only for leading provinces, princes, and particular men, as is trivial to all, but also for bringing certain more secret things into us: For the explanation of which we will approach the threefold return of the soul to God:
[Marginal note: Academ. Plotinus.] about which the Academics (Plotinus especially, drawn by I know not what spirit) diligently discuss. This return happens (as they say) through amatory music and philosophy. So that through music, by numbers and measures, we may be aroused to the melodious harmonies of the universe and the archetype: Through amatory love, we may be affected by the most beautiful modes: But through philosophy, aided by the benefit of reason and discourse, we abstract universal reasons: or (as the scholastics are accustomed to say) the quiddities of things. The first of these occurs through a certain sensible reason, by which we perceive the consonance of things: The second through concupiscible reason, by which we are affected by that perceived numerous consonance: The third, however, through intellectual reason, abstracting from all sensibles, by which steps, elevated and ascending to higher things, we lead the soul to the ideas of all beauty and consonance: Finally, to the Good itself and the Beautiful, to which all its ministers and instruments invite and attract. For Mercury impels us to number, Venus to love, but Phoebus to abstract contemplation: And sometimes the Moon, familiar to the Sun, performs his office, and claims for herself the name "Phoebe," called from Phoebus:
[Marginal note: Iul. firm. Mathe.] Which (as Firmicus and other mathematicians assert) makes cultivators of good arts, and of all things—

Hence, to one asking why the angels of the Persians, Chaldeans, and other nations did not lead those entrusted to them to the knowledge of the true God, Dionysius responds, saying: [Diony.] "We cannot accuse the Dominions or righteous and just Archangels if the nations entrusted to them have fallen to the worship of those who are falsely called Gods, but it must be imputed to those who, by their own customs, of their own accord deviated from the straight path leading to God:" The cause of such a pernicious error was self-love and pride. Hence, the same crime is sometimes imputed to the rebellious Hebrew people by the prophet saying: "You have rejected the knowledge of God: and you have walked after your own heart." In which order also the angelic minds succeed: For angels have an earthly nature with the Moon: Archangels a watery nature with Mercury: Principalities an airy nature with Venus: Powers a fiery nature with the Sun: Virtues again a fiery nature with Mars: Dominions an airy nature with Jupiter: Thrones a watery nature with Saturn: Cherubim an earthly nature with the firmament: Seraphim a fiery nature with the Primum Mobile: and with the archetype in fiery power they agree with the Holy Spirit: But Thrones with the Son, who is the supermundane water, concerning which of all philosophers and theologians,

praising David: There is also the highest abundance of divine goodness, which, lest more than the degree and works of inferiors deserve should be poured out, that celestial container is interposed: in which, as if in a certain tribunal, it is judged how much of that water ought to be given to each. But Moses concealed such mysteries under a veil from those fathers and peoples, to whom all things happened in figure: From these manifold and most hidden sacraments, ancient philosophers and seers, extracting some outer layers, claimed many things for themselves: so much so that the wisdom of Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, and others is believed to be that which emanated from the highest source, God, through Moses to mortals, so that Moses himself, and not Socrates (as Cicero writes), called wisdom from heaven, and was the first to commend it in public writings. And so that with Mercury we may reveal something from the inner and divine storehouses, there is in the higher coordinations a supreme water: Which is called wisdom and the Son of God: The middle is piety, mercy, and peace: And the lower is a milky udder, which all the prophets sucked, and Paul together with others, to whom it was given to ascend to the third heaven, so that they might offer to those coverings: to whom it is permitted to know the mystery of the kingdom of God only in parables. The Same] And again: All things that I have heard from the Father, I have made known to you. Nor do we say that the star of Mercury does this, except insofar as it can operate either by disposing, or as an instrument of the presiding intelligence. Moreover, Mercury is named from merchandise, over which he presides: which are exchanged for the price of metals, which are watery: so that the merchandise itself may flow by elemental and celestial watery virtue.

Air with Jupiter and Venus resounds. **Chap. XVI.**

[Decorative initial A]er, to Venus, corresponds its nature (as we speak physically in the stars) humid and hot: Hence they dedicated aerial animals to her. And just as air and spirit couple and join things that are separated, so does that Venereal virtue. But the Academics teach with an open doctrine that there are two Venuses: one indeed ethereal, the other truly aerial: The superior one is pure, chaste, ordered, agreeing with Jupiter, connecting higher, divine, and spiritual things: The inferior one is disordered, slippery, varied, and lascivious, joining animals and things inferior to them. And concerning this Venus, so many obscene things are sung by poets: because she is the cause of all evils, just as the other (superior Venus) is the cause of all good things. Hence Augustine says: "Two Loves made two cities: the love of God, regulated and good, and the love of neighbors even to the contempt of self, made the city of God: But inverted love of self even to the contempt of God made the city of the devil." Whence the power of this star is called Venus by grammarians: because it comes to all things, evil, namely, and good: Which Orpheus sings in his hymns: "You generate (he says) all things whatsoever are in heaven and on earth, urging mortals and the immense race of wild beasts with the raging love-potions: And all things are filled with love: and nothing is empty of it, just as all things are filled with air, which fills the appetite of nature abhorring a vacuum." For by love (says Boethius) the heavens are joined: and the elements come together in composite things. By love animals cohabit: The city is preserved: and every Republic receives increase. By love God fashioned and governs the world: and the sum of all things that He requires from us is love itself. Divine love (says Dionysius) did not permit the king of all things to remain without offspring in himself: And just as by love He diffused Himself into all things outside Himself, so by love He delights to draw all things to Himself, especially man: in whom all things are contained: Therefore, with him united, all things will be united. And Dionysius concludes all these things from the mind of Hierotheus, saying: "Whether we speak of divine love, or angelic, or spiritual, or animal, or natural, let us understand it as a certain inherent and mingling virtue: which indeed moves superior things to the providence of inferior things: reconciles equals to social communion with each other: and finally admonishes all inferior things to turn towards better and higher things." And because love and Venus are sought in all things, therefore the Cypriots painted her with both sexes, indeed with a long beard and feminine clothing. And Aristophanes called her Aphroditon, not Aphrodite: because she is found in every sex and every soul. She is also called Lucifer, as if "light-bearing": namely, the light of the Sun, or bearing us to that light, therefore she is called Phosphoros: For love and the appetite for truth lead through all things, however arduous, so that we may attain truth itself. She is also called Hesperos, when she follows the Sun: because having obtained virtue, we are affected by no less love for it than before. But that which precedes is (as the poets imagine) the daughter of heaven and day, i.e., a small light and a new clear truth, which we seek: otherwise we would not be moved to seek it. But that which follows is the daughter of Jupiter and Dione, i.e., the daughter of humidity: which is ethereal and shining. But the poets imagine another

...provided that it restores itself. Heavenly fire puts to flight dark princes and their hosts, as sung in the psalms:
[Marginal note: Psalm] The Sun has risen, and they are gathered, and they will be placed in their chambers. And in Job it is said:
[Marginal note: Job] When they see the dawn, they consider it the shadow of death. And this lower [fire] also puts them to flight, so that it may serve as an ally. Hence, not without reason, the wisest founders of the nascent church ordered lights to be lit for the bodies of the dead, from which they should not be removed until, the sacred rites completed, they are committed to the sacred earth. And they taught that public prayers and psalmody should be performed with a light kindled: which God also, to whom these sacred rites are offered, requires, namely, that all sacrifices
[Marginal note: Pythag.] be offered by fire, and that fire always burn on the altar. Hence Pythagoras in his symbols: Do not speak of God without light. Which, however, others, and even we ourselves elsewhere, have interpreted according to analogy: for this lowest light-giving fire contributes to sacred rites, as does also the celestial, angelic, intellectual, and divine [fire]. But dark fire by no means [contributes], not infernal heat, not the burning of evil desire, not immoderate passion, not burnt-out understanding: for this dark fire consumes all things, fills all things with barrenness, so that no one can accomplish anything in that nocturnal flame. Hence some wished to interpret fire [as such]: because nothing is begotten by it. There is, however, a good and natural fire, heat giving life and fertility. For eggs are not changed into chicks, nor caterpillars or silkworms into chrysalises, nor do plants grow; nor are animals nourished and fostered, except by heat, whether superior, or animating, or elemental, which are in some way congenate by a certain analogy through a symbol. And fire is so fertile that it begets itself, and enables others to generate, not by heat alone, but by the power of light, which it draws from Him who said:
[Marginal note: CHRIST] I am the light of the world. And so that Moses might declare that all things were produced by the benefit of light,
[Marginal note: Moses. Plato] after matter was created (which he calls earth) covered in darkness, he said that light was immediately created: by which life and form would be given to all things, and by which (as Plato says) all things could be seen. This vigor of life is in that divine fire: which, called the spirit of life, incubating upon the face of the waters, bestowed life and forms upon all things, by which each thing, separated from another, might be discerned by observers. For neither from matter (as some suppose) is there (as they say) individuation or determination of a particular thing: but each thing is distinguished by its own singular form (as the more acute teach). But if we wish to look more acutely into whence this determination comes, it will be found that it proceeds from matter, form, and spirit: which is hinted at by the letters, vowel points, and accents of the sacred idiom, as is held in the most recondite mysteries of Hebrew theo-
[Marginal note: The same] logy. Plato, wishing to imitate these in Cratylus, fell short as much as the Greek idiom, a spurious offspring (so to speak) of the Hebrew language, falls short of that sacred and mysterious eloquence itself: in which, according to the properties of things, names were imposed by Adam, at God's command.

Stones sing in harmony with the heavens. Chapter XVIII.

**C**Since they have a mixed, multi-faceted nature, they do not easily agree with one heaven: especially because in each of the primary kinds, many subordinate kinds and species intervene, which [are] of diverse stars

--- Page 288 ---
TOMVS QVARTVS. 75

they partake of nature. For in the genus of stones there are diverse species: just as in metals, plants, and animals. And although stones are earthy, supported by a certain stability: and metals are fluid, and are liquefied by the power of fire, so that they seem to pass into a watery nature: In both, however, very diverse species are contained: and they agree not only with diverse planets, but also with fixed stars: Diamond with the head of Algol, garnet with the heart of the lion: And the magnet agrees with the tail of the bear: Emerald with the horn of the wing, achamee jasper: Sardonyx with the heart of Scorpio: chrysolite with the falling vulture. And many such things are discussed by Mercury, and by some more recent authors, perhaps to be more widely explained in their proper place. There are also many kinds of marbles: There is Theban marble, more lively than others, green, spotted, sprinkled with serpent spots: whence in Latin it is called Serpentinus, in Greek Ophites. And this is manifold, Lacedaemonian, Augustean, and Tiberian. Porphyry is red with intervening white spots, called Leucostictos, Basalt is of iron color and hardness. Onychites was found in Arabia in ancient times, afterwards in Germany. Alabastrites draws its origin from Thebes, Damascus, Carmania, India, and Asia: which they hollow out for unguent vessels, and crush when burnt for plasters. There is also Ligdinus of exceptional whiteness, Theban, interspersed with golden drops. Coral of black, white, and red color, which some call Pyrites. Simires, which they previously called Pyropaecilium: because it is varied with fiery flames. There is also Tuscan marble of snowy whiteness, and distinguished by various veins. Magnet of five kinds. Tasio, flint whetstone, tufa, and very many kinds, which are mentioned by Pliny, Albert, Vitruvius for making buildings [Marginal note: Plinius Albert. Vitruu.]. There are also many kinds of precious stones, which partake of diverse natures. If, however, we wish to reduce them from their common property to their one primary genus, assigning them to one element and one planet, we will say that they are earthy: and they agree with Mars, with Saturn underlying, from their harder and earthy nature, well cooked by fire, and so compacted that they live with a very subtle spirit: Nevertheless, they live, whence not undeservedly are they called living stones: yet enjoying life alone, deprived of reason, sense, and all movement, except for growth and alteration: For they grow and are altered by the heat of fire and sun. There is also in them an appetite for tending towards the center, either from gravity or from their own nature. And from their beneficial temperament with Jupiter: from weight, stickiness, and astringency with Saturn, from hardness with Mars, but from life with the Sun they agree. And if there is any grace in them, it is with Venus, from hidden virtue with Mercury, and from common benefit with the Moon.

The Romans, however, not heeding the sacraments and the subordinate power of Mammon, in order to summon to themselves the lord of gold, dedicated a temple on the Aventine Mount to Jupiter Ammonius, that is, to the Ammonian God from Ammo, who is called Mammon: and not from sand, nor from Ammon the shepherd, as some think.
