For he waged the first for himself on the mountain of the desert: the second for us on the cross: In which, despoiling the principalities and northern powers and these powers of darkness, he led away the spoils, teaching us with great confidence not to care about gathering these inferior treasures: whose prince is Mammon: but that we should seek treasures in heaven: whose prince is He, in whom (as Paul says) are all hidden [Marginal note: Paulus] treasures. Into which treasures we ought to exchange these inferior riches. Up to this point we have proceeded, discussing metals and treasures: lest, by establishing these dregs and scum of true treasures as an idol for ourselves, we fall together with their prince, having lost the true treasures: in which we can be most fully rich.

Herbs respond to the heavens with a more vibrant sound, especially to Jupiter. Chapter XX.

[Decorative initial D containing a landscape scene]
Two things occur, both in herbs and in metals, worthy of no small investigation: namely, whence and how virtue is drawn from them. Not indeed from hot, cold, humid, and dry, as the Peripatetics [Marginal note: Peripate.] assert, easily excusing themselves from assigning the cause of effects and operations of things: For we prove a virtue in them exceeding all quality, whence they may benefit or harm. Nor are we content to depart from the theologians: who say, and truly, that this is implanted in them by God. It will be beautiful to somehow traverse by what means that power is infused into things, which the Hebrews call כח (coah). The Academics teach, together with Tris- [Marginal note: Hebræi. Academ. Trism. Hiarch. Philost. The. ho] megistus, and Hiarchas, prince of the Brahmans, hints in Philostratus, But in the more secret Theology of the Hebrews it is asserted everywhere, that all things which are under the lunar sphere, and in this world subject to generation and corruption, are of a better nature in the celestial world, more perfect in the intelligences, most perfect in the archetype: and that each one, in the same series, responds to the superior and the supreme according to its kind: and from them receives, from the heavens indeed that celestial force which they call the fifth essence, from the intelligences a spiritual and living vigor transcending all qualitative virtue, but from the archetype, through these intermediates, according to its degree, the original force of all perfection. intelligences, and from them each thing can be aptly reduced to the archetype: From the series of which thing emanates all natural magic, and the more secret, and true philosophy. Hence the consonance of things in this manifold world, and a mystical understanding in explaining that which is not said by that which is written: Since it is our purpose to reveal this in the whole of our progress, now we will only generally survey how herbs agree with the heavens: just as we touched upon metals: Although each of these (metals) is led to its own planet (as we said), nevertheless it is reduced to Martian dominion, both in the heavens, and in angels, and in the archetype: thus herbs, in which there is a more benign spirit of life, agree with the air and aerial Jupiter in general: but in particular, each with its own planet and fixed star. For since stones are earthy, metals watery, plants, proceeding in a direct series, are proven to be aerial. The sign of this is: because they sprout, coalesce, and grow under the air: but deprived of air, they not only do not coalesce, but die. For herbs live and sprout under the benefit of God, Venus, and Jupiter, with the Sun nevertheless infusing a certain seminal force: For lower things draw animal force from the Sun, generative force from Venus, natural force from Jupiter, so called because it always helps. For any star, indeed all of them together, foster and strengthen natural forces in us less than Jupiter. Hence it is always auspicious to receive him: the Sun perhaps (as some please) is not always safe: because that immense vigor sometimes harms the weakness of the recipient. Therefore, because plants coalesce especially by the benefit of Venus and Jupiter, we say that they are aerial and Jovian, although each is subject to its own star: Hence some, from an excessive influx, tend towards a harmful poison. For these, however, Jupiter, indeed the supreme artificer, has prepared good antidotes: Therefore, herbs, nor the fruits of trees, nor their cultivation, have ever been forbidden for human use: For man was placed in the garden of delight, that he might eat of the fruits of the trees and cultivate them: although the matter ascends higher than it presents itself in the literal shell: from which place, man having been cast out, before and after the flood, and under both the Mosaic and Evangelical laws, the same vegetables were always permitted, except for those which, by some grave excess, became poisonous and harmful in their roots, stems, leaves, or fruits, thus rendering themselves to be avoided. But meats were not in use before the flood, indeed (as some assert) forbidden: But metals (by which treasure is stored in this pilgrimage) are denied in the Gospel: which are contained under the dominion of Mars (as we said): Thus the blood of animals, carrion preyed upon, torn by beaks, or claws, or teeth, and such things, which are Martian, and are forbidden on the left side in the law to those who are to be placed on the right: from which (lest we proceed further than is permitted) we have deemed it necessary to abstain.

Those who investigate the more secret origins of nature assert that animals born through putrefaction, in waters, on land, and in the ruins of buildings, are generated by the favor of Saturn, and are Saturnian. And although this is attributed by some to the Sun, as if among the stars, from its beneficial heat, to the common parent of all, it has nevertheless been investigated with more subtle diligence, and asserted that this comes from Saturn: Who, feeling the virtue of the superior and contiguous heaven, if he cannot arrange or bring forth perfect animals, at least, as far as the nature of the star permits, the dregs of animals and imperfect things coalesce by his virtue, yet compared from the superior, indeed from the supermundane heaven, and from the presiding intelligence. For each planet has its own intelligence, and in divine matters its own measure: by whose rule it is regulated: and these are called the measures of the fabric. Saturn, therefore, is regulated by that measure (as is taught in Hebrew theology) [Marginal note: The. He.] where they say Elohim resides: who is introduced as the craftsman and commander in all the works of the six days. But since he falls short of the creative cause, and of every kind of instrument of the starry heaven, his virtue extends even to imperfect animals. Hence to him are attributed mice, worms, scorpions, and such things born from putrefaction: likewise oysters, sea sponges, shells, and things of this kind, which are called zoophytes by the Platonists. Hence perhaps antiquity, [Marginal note: Antiqui.] redolent of that primeval wisdom, feigned Saturn to be born from heaven: not to generate as a father, but with his virile parts cut off and cast into the sea, from there Venus was generated, that is, the generative force from heated moisture.

Antiquity. These animals, since they are many and varied in nature, are deservedly placed in the eighth sphere: and true animals are subject to it: which is wandering in a threefold motion, and most diverse in the figures of its stars: Whose number, just as it is known to God alone, so are their effects concerning birds, animals, reptiles, fish, and plants: And even if we make them agree with Jupiter, nevertheless they are not deprived of the benefit of the star-bearing heaven. For the planets execute those things which the superior stars influence. Hence there is great harmony of each with its own sign, house, or triplicity, and particular stars: From which effects proceed no less than from the wandering ones, although they are attributed to these, as being nearer, and more distinct, and more manifest to mortals. And if we wished to ascend higher still, and to investigate more deeply the causes, origins, and forms of animals: perhaps we would prove that these do not proceed from the bosom of matter, as natural philosophers dream, but from elsewhere: Since not without reason is the production of animals repeated three times by [Marginal note: Moses.] Moses: Of which, first water, then Elohim, in the third place earth is introduced as the author. And repeating again, in the last place it concludes that Elohim made all those things. Nor must it be overlooked that a bird is introduced as produced from the waters upon the face of the heavens, and not under heaven, as our translation has it: For this was touched upon, so that it might be intimated to us that the images of both birds and animals were produced first above the heavens, before they sprouted forth on earth: so that their origin might be not from earth, but from heaven, and from super-mundane sources. Therefore, it was not without reason that we made animals agree with the superior heaven, which, even if they proceed with all other things from the author of all, nevertheless, they are fashioned through the star-bearing heaven, as if through a principal instrument. [Marginal note: Mathematicians.] Mathematicians also assert that in the *primum mobile* there are images of things and signs of greater power, according to which prognostics are made in nativities.

They echo the same things especially with the super-celestial world. Chapter XXIII.

**C**ontinuing from the first and one principle, it is necessary that all things depend on it and correspond to it. For concerning the Creator, it is written in Wisdom, that by the spirit of his understanding he embraces all power, he foresees all things, he contains all spirits of understanding: and remaining in himself, a unique power renews all things. By which spirit also he fills the entire orb of the earth, vivifying, uniting, and causing all things to resound, reaching all things from end to end, and disposing all things sweetly. Which things we defer to discuss more broadly in their proper place.

What things in particular agree with Saturn. Chapter XXIV.

**H**aving established the general agreement of things, let us run through how their species also agree with superior things: so that we may be able to receive from all sides, in what ways we may praise the Creator. And so that we may begin from the lower composite things, from the elements it (Saturn) has earth: Among stones, those that are black agree with Saturn: Onyx, ziazaa, as their color indicates, and their tingling effect on the wearer, especially when better spirits are lulled to sleep in dreams. And to it, together with Mercury and the tail of Scorpio, agrees chalcedony, as its sub-sapphire, dusky, and pale color indicates: and it has from good

TOMVS QVARTVS. 78

to Saturn, that it may expel fantastic illusions: preserve and bind together the body's strength: but from Mercury, that it may prevent hoarseness: and clarify the voice, especially the blacker one. Among minerals, it rules lead: It also subjects to itself jasper, and magnet, and camoinum. Among herbs, the serpentary corresponds to it and to the celestial Serpentarius. It also rules rue, cumin, hellebore, asafoetida, which the Greeks call Silphion: Likewise, opium, mandrake, and those things which are styptic. Among animals, it possesses the camel, pig, ape, bear, especially the black cat, mule, donkey: But birds, those which have long necks and coarse voices, cranes, ostriches, peacocks, and that kind: whence the poet sings of Argus transformed into a peacock: "The Saturnian bird receives these eyes on its feathers." [Marginal note: Ovid:] Moreover, serpents, scorpions, and creeping things in the earth, waters, and ruins of walls or roofs: such as mice, ants, and various worms. Among humors, it rules moist black bile, both native and adventitious, except for the burnt kind. Indeed, of colors, black, leaden, and livid follow it. Also, sour, sharper, and heavy tastes imitate its heavy nature. Likewise, those things which smell heavily. In seasons, however, it presides over autumn and winter, and over stronger and heavy winds. Likewise, to Indians and Ethiopians: as their color testifies. So also to dark, subterranean, and solitary places. Moreover, to fishponds, stagnant pools, and marshes, and dreadful places. Also to hidden treasures, and those acquired through long journeys and with difficulty. What it possesses in man, however, we will reserve for the harmony of both the greater and lesser worlds.

What harmonizes with Jupiter. Chapter XXV.
[Decorative initial E] From the elements (as we have said), Air corresponds to Jupiter, and all things in which it dominates: Tin among minerals, and things hot and moist: also all things pertaining to the nourishment and growth of life, especially those which are masculine: And those things which are found sweet and pleasant in odors and tastes. In all living beings, blood, and in this part, the changeable winds of the air, which strengthen the natural and vegetative heat of living beings: which are (as some prefer) principally northerly or septentrional: where fire resides, and that supreme vigor: which vivifies and strengthens without burning: But in my judgment, southerly winds correspond more aptly to Jupiter: and that to the supramundane south wind: concerning which it is said in the Canticles: [Marginal note: Canticles.] "Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out." Therefore, from the north wind it draws strengthening power: and from the south wind, beneficial temperament and abundance of all good things. Also, clear green colors, and those which strengthen, are dedicated to it: Whence, among stones, the green emerald, although elsewhere it may correspond to Mercury and Venus. All green gemstones, and valued saffron-colored ones, are dedicated to it, and some white ones, like crystal. But sapphire (is associated) with Jupiter and Saturn: but it has from Jupiter that it makes one charming: and resists envy and fraud: and makes one placable and desirous of peace: from Saturn, that it cools heat: and favors the understanding of hidden things and magic. But in higher things, it agrees with Alaiot, some (attribute) tutty to the same

they assert is dedicated, although from the favor it grants to lights, it seems to be suited to luminaries. Among trees, the oak is primarily sung by poets as dedicated to him. Also ruled by him are the olive, and oil, and wheat, barley, raisins, egg yolks, white sugar, licorice, pheasants, partridges, and similar things most suitable to nature: and all things whose sweetness is manifest and subtle, and which have a slightly astringent and sharp taste, such as nuts, almonds, pine nuts, hazelnuts, pistachios, starches, bugloss, basil, white and red ben roots: Moreover, elecampane, spikenard, mace, manna, if only it is made firm by the virtue of myrobalan: which is entirely Jovial. To him, with Phoebus, are mastic and mint. But with Venus, rhubarb, which prevails against cholera, and expels it, just as Jupiter and Venus expel Martian impetus. Orpheus attributes storax to him. From flowers are the lily, and the violet. But from birds, the eagle especially, the emblem of emperors: who ought to administer the justice of true Jupiter with clemency to their subjects. Also hens, quails, and birds of temperate complexion. Among quadrupeds: elephants, sheep, lambs, and all tame animals: To him, with his fish, is subjected the second climate, and the regions existing therein, namely Lycia, Pamphylia, Phazania, Garamantica, Nasamonitis, and similar ones. If we wish to descend to human activities, he favors religious people, prelates, kings, judges who judge rightly: Hence, by the Hebrews, Jupiter is named צדק, that is, Zadic, which among us means 'just': and subsequently, he predominates over profits arising therefrom, and lawfully acquired. Some subject Arabs to Jupiter: because they are obedient, faithful, and of inviolable faith, clean, pure, desirous of kingdom, and their region, especially Arabia Felix, is sprinkled with various perfumes. Others, supported by Ptolemy, subject them to Mars: because they delight in living by plunder and rapine. But let these and Ptolemy think whatever they wish: In all Arabs who are truly Hagarenes, the voice of the oracle to Hagar holds true: that her son and all his posterity should pitch their tents beside his brothers, and his hand against all, and the hand of all against him: All of which is fulfilled to the letter up to this day. But returning to Jupiter, his is the spirit of life: which is found in all living things, and in this whole mundane animal, if it is permitted to call the world an animal. To lead this spirit, the Sun and Venus also intervene, for it arises from the Sun, and in an animal from the heart, which is solar. It is infused when Jupiter tempers the immense power of the Sun within himself. It overflows, flows forth, is transferred, propagates offspring, and expands itself to the pleasure of every sense, with Venus favoring.

What things receive strength from Mars. Cap. XXVI.
[I] We have already concluded that fire is dedicated to Mars: in the same way, all burnt and sharp things are suitable for him: pungent and bitter tastes that burn the tongue: such as castor, euphorbium, radish, and similar things. And colors: fiery, violet, and purple. From stones, amethyst is dedicated to Mars with Jupiter [Marginal note: Ptolem.] (Hermes being the author): And it has from Mars that it favors the capture of fe-

wild beasts: and renders one victorious in battle with them: and makes one vigilant: and experienced: but from Jupiter, that it may increase good understanding, and an equitable mind: as we can learn from Aaron [Aaron Arthe.] and Artephius. To the same (planets) is subjected the multifaceted Jasper: Which has from Mars, that it may render one powerful: but from Jupiter, that it may expel fevers, and distemperatures: and induce an equitable constitution: and in the aforementioned (properties) it agrees with Alramet. Hellebore also corresponds to Mars and the head of Algol: And to both (as Hermes [Hermes] teaches) hellebore is equal. To Mars again (are attributed) euphorbium, ammoniac, laureola, napellus, scammony, and commonly hot poisonous things, from an overabundance of heat. Likewise cultivated or wild garlic (which Dioscorides calls ophioscorodum, or elaphoscorodum) onion, shallot, and all things of this kind: whose taste is said to be lachrymose (tear-inducing). [Disco.] Moreover, among animals, horses are pre-eminently suited for war, mules, goats, kids, wolves (as Augustine also testifies) [August.] leopards, wild asses, and commonly predatory animals: and also those hostile to man: such as flies, fleas, and the like: Also serpents and dragons that attack with venom. From minerals, indeed, glass, yellow bronze, and iron, masters of the oven, furnace, and mill, phlebotomists, surgeons, barbers, butchers, and all soldiers, who are commonly called "Mauortian" from Mars. From regions, Ptolemy [Ptolem.] subjects to Mars himself with Scorpio: Syria, Cappadocia, Metagonitis, Commagene, Mauretania, and Getulia. But with Aries: Britain, Galatia, Germania, Barfania, Coele-Syria, Idumaea, Judea. In particular, lands and warlike peoples. Also impetuous winds, especially those tending from the northern quarter towards the west, and all things impetuous and violent. Not indeed these things from the malice of the star thus decreeing, but from ill-moderated impulse: For the origin is from the celestial Mars, and also the supercelestial: but the disorder is from us who regulate poorly: hence to him are attributed spoils, rapine, plunder, depopulations, deceptions, and all abominable things which are perpetrated by violence and impulse. But if that force and impulse were moderated by the bridle of reason and laws: all these things would be justly directed.

Things that harmonize with the Sun, or Phoebus. Cap. XXVII.

**T**HE SUN holds the middle seat among the planets, as king of all, exceeding all in light, magnitude, virtue, and beauty, illuminates all: and consequently intervenes in arranging all inferior things. But those things which especially follow its motion, among the elements is fire, among metals is gold, and all gilded things: Consequently, those things which shine with the same color, both in flowers and in small stones, the carbuncle glowing at night, the stone which is called the Sun's eye, having the shape of a pupil: from which light shines forth. Chrysolite, topaz inclining to its golden color, hyacinth, ruby, balagius (spinel), and things of this kind filled with golden or reddish color. Panthaura, or Pantheus, so called because it resembles the spotted animal, the panther: For it has certain black, red, pale, green, rosy, purple, and varied markings: hence it contains (says Albertus) [Albertus] as many virtues as colors: and especially renders the bearer victorious: or whoever looks at it (as he says) at sunrise. Hence all poets proclaim it dedicated to the Sun itself. Also the Ash, which by the same Phoebean virtue keeps poisons far away. Peony, as not only its virtue but also its name indicates, not indeed that which [Marginal note: Diosco.] Dioscorides calls Chelidonia or [Marginal note: Romani] Cratea, the Romans Fabium, [Marginal note: Galli] the Gauls Tona, [Marginal note: Aegypt.] the Egyptians Mothon; But that which [Marginal note: Gręci.] the Greeks call Glycisides, and [Marginal note: Theod.] Theodorus among us Dulcisida, and [Marginal note: Antiqui.] the Ancients called Ephialtion, as being very powerful against nocturnal oppressions of incubi and fauns. From its seed, loaves are made by Egyptian shepherds, kneaded with water or milk; than which food they deny anything to be healthier; whence they are called Lotophagi. To the same also belong all herbs and flowers called Heliotropes, which close when the Sun departs, and conversely, open immediately when it returns, and continuously follow it. Moreover, its movement is followed by the citron tree; saffron, which is solar in all respects, although its scent is dedicated by astrologers to all graces. Also musk, amber, yellow honey, aromatic reed, aloes wood, cinnamon, pepper, clove, ginger, and other aromatics; Frankincense also, and marjoram, and those things in which there is a sharp taste mixed with sweetness; And also (according to [Marginal note: Orph.] Orpheus) Libamomana, which, pursuing his magic, he calls the Sun's Incense. Among Phoebean animals are, first, the Lion, king of beasts, so that not without reason the Sun increases its power in the sign of Leo. Among birds, however, is the Rooster, whom the Lion fears, since it is superior in the Phoebean order. For the same reason, [Marginal note: Procul.] says Proculus, an Apollonian demon, who sometimes appears in the form of a Lion, immediately flees when a rooster is presented. Also Phoebean are the swan, the goshawk, and the raven, as some believe; The hawk, as [Marginal note: Porphy.] Porphyrius states in *On the Mystical Theology of the Egyptians and Greeks*, because it is a symbol of light and spirit among them, and because it seeks higher and brighter places by flying. But among animals, after the Lion, is the Ram, in whose sign the Sun is exalted; the crocodile, and the sea-calf, which is also subject to the heart of the Lion; from whose hide a belt made relieves kidney pain and hoarseness, restoring Phoebean harmony to the throat, as has often been proven. It also mitigates the force of lightning. All these things reflect solar influences.

Things that delight with Venus. Chapter XXVIII.

[Large decorative initial V] Enus, mistress of coupling, has an affinity with all well-composed things: and with those whose taste is sweet and unctuous, and whose odor is delightful, and whose color tends towards whiteness. She delights in moist things: and increases strength: whence she claims waters rather than any other element for herself. From metals, saffron-colored bronze, and red (copper/bronze): From stones, Beryl is especially dedicated to her: which (says Aaron) makes the wearer cheerful: rich: magnificent: [Marginal note: Aaron] very prompt to union and conjugal love: It comforts the desolate: favors pregnant women: lest their offspring be contaminated. And water, in which it lies, removes sighs and all infirmities of the liver. Mixed with silver, however, it frees from leprosy, that is, Martian contagion. In these things, how beautifully they agree with Venus, it is very easy for one knowing its nature to judge. Chrysolite, however, favoring wisdom (as is asserted) and resisting foolishness, is said to belong to Venus and Mercury: Which (as Plotinus and other Platonists believe) bestows genius and an aptitude for the harmony of things: [Marginal note: Plotin. Platoni.] by which it also makes the mind desirous of understanding the things themselves that are harmonious, especially with the intervention of Phoebean vigor: which purges from material and coarser things. Emerald also corresponds to the same (Venus and Mercury), and to Jupiter (as we said): Hence (according to Aaron) it bestows the power of eloquence and grace: and is most pleasing to the eyes: And [Marginal note: Aaron] with the superior stars, Athimot Alaata. Also Sapphire, Carnelian, Lapis Lazuli, Coral, and all of beautiful and delightful color. From herbs, to Venus, that is, to Lucifer (the morning star), is given the rose; to Hesperus (the evening star), the myrtle. Also well-scented and sweet-smelling Thyme, Labdanum, Amber, Incenses. And with the Sun is given Musk and Sandalwood: but with Saturn, Coriander. Also sweet and delightful fruits: Figs, the Musa grape, which is a kind of fig, as some assert, sweet Pears, the Pomegranate, having its name from Punic Carthage, where it is most praised: whence poets feigned that the pomegranate was first sown in Cyprus by Venus. [Marginal note: Poëtę] Among birds, the dove is dedicated to her by common consent. Also the turtle-dove, which contains such an affinity with the dove, that in the purification of childbirth, either of them is commanded to be offered without distinction. Also the sparrow, which is given, by command of the law, for the purification of leprosy, indeed a Martian infirmity: against which nothing is more beneficial than Venusian things.

For it favors philosophy, the investigation of scriptures, the investigation of enigmas, metrical poetry, geometry, disputative arithmetic, sophistry, painting, sculpture, and all things in which figures and characters are to be formed. How all these things, with the Moon, bring about a perfected harmony of consonance. Chapter XXX.

[Decorative initial V] The Moon is not inappropriately called another Sun by some: because those things which the Sun generates above by masculine power, she, receiving the offspring of the Sun itself and of other planets, brings forth to the lower world near her. Therefore, her motion is observed above others, as if giving birth to the conception of all things: For from Mercury she receives the power mixing humors; from Venus, that which leads to suitable forms of generation; from Mars, strength and impetus; from Jupiter, natural spirit and the nourishment of all things; from Saturn, structure and stability: But from the Sun, which contains all-encompassing virtue (as Iamblichus, Julianus, Proculus, and very many others assert), all-encompassing offspring and light. [Marginal note: Iambl. i] [Marginal note: Iulianur. Procul.] All these things she variously unfolds according to her varied complexion, orbit, and diverse aspects, both with planets and with other stars: For in the first quarter, Peripatetics think she is hot and humid; in the second, hot and dry; in the third, cold and dry; in the fourth, cold and humid. Now she is in apogee, now depressed, now at the extreme of her epicycle she is distant from it: now full of light, now half, now barely seen, afterwards totally hidden: And now she is in conjunction with one planet, in sextile with another, and with that one in quadrature, or opposition. And this same (Moon) governs the head in Aries, the neck in Taurus, and so proceeding. Which we do not doubt she also does in the greater world, namely, governing diverse things placed in diverse signs, so that thus, being varied, she may always produce varied effects: and through frequent conjunctions with planets and other stars, having become the wife of all, she receives from them those things which, as the mother of all lower things, and a medium between both, namely the superior and inferior, she communicates to all these. Therefore, not without reason is she likened to that mother full of all graces: who bestows upon the lower beings, according to the disposition of the recipients, those things which she draws from the supernal founts through diverse channels: But returning to the Moon, and if she receives from all stars, she does so most especially from the Sun: to whom as often as she is conjoined, so often she is filled with offspring and vivifying virtue: which she infuses into the moistened and disposed lower things. From her also in the heavens begins to re-

Among these Lunar animals (as I seem to see) are especially faithful dogs, and domestic above other living beings, just as the Moon is above other planets, although we have enumerated them among Mercurial animals according to the opinion of some. But we consider them Lunar themselves, not only because they are familiar, but from their varied nature, by which they excel both in love and in hatred. They are also varied in size, color, and manners above all animals. For some are faithful guardians, Others are greyhounds, Others are bird scouts, Others attack bulls, Others [attack] wolves, Others [attack] birds, Others [attack] strangers, Others offend no one: But they rejoice in all human companionship. Likewise, among Lunar things we can count the Chameleon: which, due to the variety of the object's color, seems to take on a new color, just as we prove the Moon takes on a varied nature, according to the variety of the sign in which it is found. From the crafts, they are commonly plebeian, and vulgar, and lowly, just as it (the Moon) is the lowest of all stars: yet it explains all the concepts of the superior [stars]: Therefore (as [Marginal note: Thebit.] Thebit teaches), if anyone wishes to capture the virtue of any star: let him take the stone and herb of that star: from which he desires to attract power: when the Moon approaches that star: or looks at the same with a trine or sextile aspect, as if without the Moon itself as a medium, we cannot attract the power of the superior [stars]. Hence we say that it introduces into the most consonant effects of all superior [stars]: and their harmony in these lower things...

        What things resonate in particular with certain particular
                stars. Chapter XXXI.

[Decorated initial N]ot content with the influence of the planets, those who desire to operate in natural things have also tried to attract the effluences of the stars, namely, of those whose knowledge they were able to attain. How beautifully all these things are depicted in the ark, which Moses built by heavenly oracle. Chapter XXXII.

When a great burden was laid upon the shoulders of holy Moses by God, and human weakness was not hidden from him, he refused to undertake it: but God, having decided that he should lead the people out of Egypt, promised his angel for their guidance and protection: Not content with this, Moses, with great confidence, protested to God, saying: "Unless you come, I will not go": For he knew that God's presence was necessary for many things, hence, not content with the promised angel, nor with the power given for performing signs and wonders, he demanded God himself as leader, "Unless you (he said) go before us, do not make us ascend from this place." And again: "How shall we know that I and your people have found favor in your eyes, unless you come with us?" To him the Lord assented, saying: "Make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in your midst": and this according to every likeness of the tabernacle, which I will show you, namely, of this earthly house, which is God's own dwelling: as He Himself testifies through the oracle of Isaiah in plain speech, when He says: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool." When He showed Moses the whole structure, He added: "See, and make it according to the pattern,"

which was shown to you on the mountain. But since it would be too long to recount all the things demonstrated, which pertain to building the ark conformable to the world, we will run through some or a few. And first, the division, of which it is said: Its height, likewise [Exodus] and breadth shall have a cubit and a half. i.e., nine palms: For a cubit is divided into six palms: and a half into three: Which division, by means of the number nine, represents the nine heavens: Over which presides the empyrean, indeed of another and nobler material: And this is denoted by the golden covering: for the entire structure of the ark was of nobler material: which was commanded to be made from shittim wood, or cedar wood: which is the same according to Hebrew doctors: And that wood is (as some assert) what we call larch: although our translation has cedars for larch. There was also another threefold division of the entire structure: one part of which, defended by no roof or shade, was subjected to rains, snow, sun, heat, and cold: which signifies this structure subject to all change: Which not only clean men, but also unclean and profane men, and all kinds of animals inhabit: And in it, because of sacrifices and constant immolations, just as in this one, there was a perpetual vicissitude of life and death. The remaining two parts, both covered, and everywhere free from all foreign injury, just like both worlds, the celestial and the supercelestial, incapable of either injury or insult. Both likewise honored by the name of sanctity, and the more secret part, the Holy of Holies, the rest merely adorned with the title of holy: And this both signifies and represents the celestial world, where angels dwell: in whom after the fall of Lucifer (as our theology teaches) neither sin nor any stain is found. The supercelestial, however, is denoted by the interior and more secret place: into which come those who, truly made priests, have consecrated themselves as a living and pleasing sacrifice to God: so that they may deserve to be united with that very one: who is truly the Holy of Holies. And here (as I believe) is the true garden of delights, in which are planted and flourish all the chosen trees of Adonai, which the Heavenly Father planted, no longer to be uprooted by anyone: Over which presides, not without mystery, the cherubic power, just as by God's command they presided over the ark, which was placed in that spot which was called the Holy of Holies: but in this figurative sense, there were remissions and intimate conversations with God: There, however, in the true dwelling, for those who have entered, already expiated, there is perfect union with God himself, and full delight in every part. Seven golden lamps were also commanded to be made: which would represent the seven shining stars in their orbits. But also a candelabrum is named separately with three branches on each side, and with their cups, spheres, and flowers: Which signifies the Sun in the midst of the planets, having three planets on each side in spherical form: which, like cups and receiving vessels, receiving what flows from above, produce flowers by flowing down to the lower regions. And thus, that which was now numbered among the seven lamps, also separated, is said to have been made together with the adjacent stars: so that these may be understood to receive light from the Sun, and to arise in a certain way. With what great mystery all enneads converge in their tenth. Chapter XXXIII.

[Decorative initial N] Not without mystery does the maker of all things require from us the primary
and tenth portions of all things: namely, the first and the last:
since he himself is the beginning and end of all things: To which beginning we ought to offer
primary fruits: and to which end, tenths. For the number ten
is the end and completion of all numbers: beyond which neither ingenuity nor
any nation has devised: because no further (number) is given. And because the number ten
is a completion: therefore he not only requires the tenth of works and fruits produced by us:
but in the natural series and genealogy of men, by a more celebrated choice,
he wished to appropriate the number ten to himself. For Noah was the tenth from Adam:
and Abraham was the tenth from him: But Christ, most gracious of all,
according to the legal genealogy woven by Luke, is the tenth of the seventh denarius
(group of ten) starting from God: so that by the revolution of the ten and the seven,
by a more secret mystery, returning to God, he might bring others with him by leading them.
But in Matthew's natural texture, and according to the flesh, he is the sixty-third from God,

This also must be noted: that the tenth always partakes of a double nature: both of the number, of which it is the end, and of that, of which it is the beginning: For ten is the end of numbers, and the beginning of denarii: For when you reach ten, you say, one denarius, two denarii, and so on: as the Hebrew characters indicate in their numerical significations. Thus the tenth in each of the primary kinds partakes of both natures. For the first novenary, namely of corruptible things, terminates in man: who is composed of the incorruptible and the corruptible. But the novenary of the heavens terminates in the Empyrean heaven: which, because it is material, agrees with the heavens: but in the dignity of its matter, it has a symbol with higher things. Therefore, in the ark, which represented the structure of the heavens, the tenth portion, namely the covering, was made of gold: indeed, a different material from that of the whole ark: which was divided into nine parts (as we said a little earlier). Also, nine [Marginal note: Paulus] angelic orders terminate in Christ their king: who embraces both the nature of angels and of God: in whom also all things terminate: as the Apostle says: Because it pleased God, namely, to make all fullness dwell in him: and in him to reconcile, or to recapitulate all things: as the Greek text has it. These [Marginal note: Idem] things we will attempt to explain in the second volume (with divine grace assisting). **FIRST CANTICLE**
**WHY THE FIRST DESCRIPTION IS MADE BY PLATO WITH THE TWENTY-SEVENTH NUMBER. Chapter One.**

[Marginal note: Timaeus.]
[Decorative Initial O]f all Pythagoreans and Academics, it is most manifest that the world and the soul were first described by Timaeus of Locri, and afterwards by Plato, according to certain laws and musical proportions, as a kind of heptachord composed of seven limits, beginning from unity, doubling up to the cube of two, tripling up to the cube and solid of three: by which numbers and proportions it was believed that the fabric of the soul and of the whole world was arranged and completed, according to the records of Pythagoras. And this from the odd, as from the male; and from the even, as from the female: from which complex virtues all things are propagated. But they said that the work was terminated in the cube of each; because beyond the three dimensions, namely length, breadth, and depth, no further progress is given. Therefore, in these numbers and proportions, all the force of the active and passive is contained; and all consonance is gathered. Of these numbers,

[Marginal note: Adrastus. Calcidius.]
we will form a triangular figure (if we wish to follow Adrastus and Calcidius): At the vertex of this triangle, unity is placed: six other numbers divide the parts on either side. Indeed, on one side is the order of all the doubles; but on the other, the series of triples

[Marginal note: Porphyry. Severus. Proclus.]
is laid out. However, following Porphyry, Severus, and Proclus, we will arrange both sets of numbers in straight lines in a triple order from unity, | 1. 2. 4. 8. | Or mixed in the same line, as Proclus believes was Plato's intention | 3. 9. 27. | 1. 2. 3. 4. 8. 9. 27.

**Which intervals of the same number can be filled, and which cannot. Chapter II.**

[Marginal note: The Same]
[Decorative Initial H]owever, of these numbers, or limits, some are filled; but some cannot be completed: especially that which is between one and two: since no mean lies between them, unless we wish to divide unity, as Proclus suggests. Therefore, the means are not well filled, nor are they harmonically joined, unless the numbers are increased, as we shall presently declare. However, between two and four, only the number three intervenes, with a sesquialtera proportion to the smaller number, and a subsesquitertia to the larger: hence, this interval also cannot be harmonically completed. Likewise, between four and eight, the number six lies, with the same diminished proportions for completing the harmony. On the other side, however, where there are odd numbers, between one and three are two, with a double proportion to one, and a sesquialtera to three. And between three and nine is six: from which, in the same way, to three is a double proportion, and to nine a sesqualtera. By the same rule, 18 occurs between 9 and 27. And up to this point extends the proportion of these numbers.

--- Page 310 ---
**FIFTH TONE. 86**
**Why this coordination is reduced to larger numbers. Chapter III.**

[Decorative initial E] And if in the number 27 all primary kinds of things, and some intermediate ones, are contained, yet not all: since there are no spaces in which those more important intervening kinds can be placed: Therefore another figure is assigned with the same limits, and the same proportion, but with a wider field and larger intervals to be filled. Therefore, in place of unity, the number six must be assumed, doubling through 12, 24, & 48; and tripling through 18, 54, & 162. In which figure all intervals are filled with their kinds: For the intermediate terms placed between 6 & 12 are 8 & 9, where 9 is exceeded and exceeds by an equal numerical portion: But 8 itself exceeds by the same part, and is exceeded by the extremes themselves. Hence we find unity and duality by multiplying numbers by six, receiving the aforesaid means: which the former number (system) could not do. And between 12 & 24 are 16 & 18; and between 24 & 48 are 32 & 34. Indeed, some of these means are harmonic; others are arithmetic and geometric: which nevertheless all pertain to harmony: For from the greater extreme to the lesser, the proportion is double: and it makes a diapason: But from the lesser extreme to the greater mean it is sesquialtera: and it makes a diapente: But from the same extreme to the lesser mean the proportion is sesquitertia: and it yields a diatessaron. And the same is true from the greater mean to the greater extreme. But it makes a diapente from the lesser mean to the greater extreme: But from the mean itself to the mean it is sesquioctava: and it makes a tone: From which the whole harmony resulting from tones is obtained: And in a similar way it is from the other side multiplied by triple, where the first extremes are 6 & 18, between which are the means 9 & 12. But other extremes are 18 & 54, between which are found the intervening means 27 & 36. Again there are 54 & 162, between which extremes fall 81 & 108: Which means correspond with the extremes, and among themselves, by the same proportion: by which the means between the doubled extremes agreed. And what geometric, arithmetic, and harmonic means are, from the many things that various authors have written, I will briefly add these few points. Indeed, the arithmetic mean is the proportion of excesses: the geometric, however, is the proportion of proportions: from both of which the harmonic results. And how they relate, we will imitate Proculus thus deriving it. Between 12 & 6, 9 itself is the mean, I say, according to the arithmetic mean: For in the number three, the excess is found, both of the greater to the mean, and of the mean to the lesser: Again, I take the difference of the extremes: which is 6 itself, and I multiply this with the lesser term: let it be 36 for me. I divide this by 18: which is made from the extremes themselves: and let the breadth of this comparison be duality: I add this to 6, and from this I have the resulting harmonic mean, 8 itself. For by whatever part the greater is exceeded by the greater itself: by the same part of the lesser it exceeds the lesser term itself: For it is separated by a third from 12, and it exceeds 6 itself by a third: Again, the interval and its

--- Page 311 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

Let us set a triple proportion, as for example 18 and 6: combining these, I make 24: taking its half, namely 12, I have the arithmetic mean. But taking again the excess of 18 over 6, namely 12, I multiply it with the smaller term, namely 6, and then 72 results for me. I divide this by 24, which is composed from the extremes: the breadth of the whole composition, namely three, arises for me: I add this to the six itself: and I have found the harmonic mean, exceeding the smaller extreme by the same part by which it is exceeded by the larger extreme: By which rules he teaches all intervals to be filled, except for semitones and dieses. Others, however, define the harmonic mean in this way: indeed they take two terms, and a mean between them behaving thus, that just as the greater term relates to the smaller, so the excess of the greater to the mean, relates to the excess of the mean to the smaller term, such as these numbers 3, 4, 6. For there, from 6 to 3 is a double proportion: The same is the excess of 6 over 4, which is 2, to the excess of 3 over 2, which is one: And it gives me a double proportion: which is derived from the excess, as if from an arithmetic mean: and from the proportion, as if from a geometric mean. Proculus, however, imitating Timaeus and Plato, derives the harmonic mean from the arithmetic mean with a more renowned method, by which all intervals may be filled. And some wished to arrange all these things in a triangular figure thus. But if we wish to follow Proculus, Porphyrius, and Severus, we will arrange all things thus in the same line.

Why in this kind of description Plato used the diatonic genus more than the chromatic and enharmonic. Chapter V.

[Decorative initial T] Hree genera of harmony were in use among the ancients, as many
authors report, namely diatonic, enharmonic, and chromatic.
The diatonic, however, consists of a semitone, or lemma, and a tone, and another
tone: The enharmonic of a diesis, and another diesis, and a ditone: The chro-
matic, however, of a semitone, and another semitone, and three semitones. A diesis, however, is
like a fourth part, but not exactly: just as a lemma is not an entire semi-
[Marginal note: Proclus. Plato. Aristox.] tone: granted that some ancients (according to Proclus) called a diesis a semitone.
Therefore, Plato describes the business of the world and the soul through the diatonic: although Aris-
toxenus, not without the admiration of the wise, says that the ancients did not
know the diatonic figure: Which he did not assert as true: but, as is his custom, always seemed to
[Marginal note: Adrastus. Plato.] bring something new (as Adrastus says) into the midst. Therefore, Plato uses the diatonic
genus in the reason of the world and the soul, believing it to have taken up the reins
of rational life, leaving the enharmonic to preside over all life that is shared with
bodies: and the chromatic to the corporeal idea itself. This genus, however, is distinct,
and least noble. The enharmonic, however, is suited for teaching and instructing:
But the diatonic is fuller, simpler, and more noble than the others.
Therefore, with this genus, as being more suitable, he describes especially the soul's
primary office, and that of the universe.

By what wonderful artifice in the first of all creatures, which the Hebrews call מטטרון
Metatron, are contained those three nines: which complete twenty-seven,
namely their cube. Chapter VI.

Nor should anyone therefore think that Mary, the mother of Christ, spoke to Moses: since this (as we have said) is a name not of a person, but of an office: let whoever it may be perform that office. But who then performed that office, the Hebrews say many things: but however the matter stood, it was he who spoke immediately, either an angel, or a man made angelic, or transformed into an angel, as Paul says with the Galatians: [Marginal note: Paul] "the law was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator." But God, or the Lord, or the Tetragrammaton is introduced speaking to Moses himself: because whatever the angel did, it was by the command, power, and influence of God Himself sending, as if He Himself were working: Who truly worked by the influence or power which (as we said above) Moses had demanded, not content with bare and sole angelic power.

That the same number, and in the same order, is contained in higher things by a certain super-excellent power. Chapter VII.

[P] Ostquam Moses described the fabric of the whole world, he added: "The heavens and all their host were completed," for which we have, "And all their ornament." The numbers of whose letters, when calculated, yield 999: ת, 400. שׂ, 300, and ר, 200. צ, 90, ו, 6, ב, 2, א, 1. Therefore, He is called the prince of the entire army: which is contained in those three nines: all of which are contained by the power of aleph, and of the millennium itself. Moreover, those three nines are also contained in the full letters of the great name of God, together with the letters that signify fire, water, air, or spirit, or wind, and dust: From which four elements, through the mediating power of the great name (as the Hebrews say), all things were produced.

**In what way the described heptachord agrees with the soul. Chap. IX.**

**A**ND because Plato, through this heptachord of his, seems to describe the workmanship of both the human soul and the cosmic soul, it must also be investigated how it is adapted to the human soul itself, where this is first presupposed: that the soul itself, removed from all corporeal laws, is not a number in the quantitative sense: whence it is neither divided nor multiplied by parts. But it is a substantial number, uniform, self-reverting, and rational, surpassing all corporeal and material things by a long interval: Whose division is not according to matter: nor from inferior and coarser things: but proceeding from an efficient cause (says Proclus). From these, I say, perfect measures of all things, to which the creator looking back operates, he divides the soul, just as he divided this whole universe according to intelligible exemplars. Therefore, in the soul, there is this mode of division, immaterial, intellectual, unmixed, perfecting the living substance, generative of the multitude which is in it and under it, and collecting it into one order through harmony: which gathers diverse parts: and existing as the cause of unmixed purity, and bestowing upon the soul itself a confluent communion of principles of multitude, so that the soul itself (as Timaeus and Plato teach) is both divisible and indivisible. **How those three nines are found in man. Chapter X.**

[Large decorative initial H containing a figure] Man, existing as the most perfect image of the world, contains all those things which are gathered in the great world, in the same proportion: And first, a nine of hundreds in the inferior part, which is the twofold body: as Plato asserts: [Marginal note: Plato] Each of which (parts) is from four elements: For the corruptible (part) is from four alterable (elements), and the incorruptible (part), at least after resurrection, will be from nobler elements, by no means subject to corruption: these two fours give me eight: To which (so that the body may be joined together and live) a certain unique life is inherent: Let that be the soul, which the Hebrews call נפש, that is, nephes; or let it be the vital spirit, or the rational soul supplying the place of all lives: as the more recent (thinkers) say. From it with those eight, the first nine results: which terminates in the tenth, namely the superior proportion.

But in the soul is the second nine, collected from the five exterior senses, and the four interior (senses), namely the imaginative, cogitative, phantasy, and common sense: and it terminates at the intellect, as if at the tenth:

And in this is another, purer nine in simple numbers: which corresponds with the nine orders of angels, and superior enumerations: so that in it there may be a full image of angels and of God: as we shall discuss in its proper place: and it terminates in that tenth, namely the supreme fount, and parent of all: To whom all operations and prayers are due: as taught by the Son of God who said: When you pray, say Our Father. [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] And to whom finally, having turned, we ought to be united. However, the intervals of these enneads (groups of nine) are completed by operations (which they call secondary acts). For man has a threefold operation: and this (is) consonant and harmonious: with this inferior world in nature: with the heavens in the senses: with angels in the superior part, namely the rational, intellectual, and voluntary: Unless he had this consonance with all things, he would not be able to operate in all things, nor understand all things. And among all living beings, man alone rejoices in this honor: that he may act with all things: and may be able (to act) in all things, even in the supreme artificer, by understanding and loving.

But if we wish to precisely trace man to the figure of Plato and the Pythagoreans, which is contained by seven principal terms collected from the first even and from the first odd (number), as from the active and passive, [Marginal note: Plato Pytha.] we will recall that most common (saying) among the Peripatetics: [Marginal note: Peripate.] that there is in man, namely, the possible intellect receiving all things, and the agent intellect producing all concepts: which are received in that passive intellect. Moreover, man himself is composed of both parts, namely from the spiritual, that is, the mind, and from the coarser, that is, the body: from which a certain mixture of both results, especially the interior senses: which are partly animal, partly intellectual, connecting both.

What those three proportions, Musical, Geometrical, and Arithmetical, by which the soul and the whole world are ordered, mean. **Chapter XI.**

**Aristo.** [Illuminated initial C]elebrating, Aristotle draws the number three from Pythagorean principles, because we have it from nature and uphold it as a law. For from nature is the progression of multitude from one, and the return to the same, which happens through the ternary itself. For the Creator, content in Himself and enclosed, is the supreme unity; but into the many things produced by Him, which are called "other," the binary is diffused; but by recalling all these same things to Himself, He completes the ternary. And that unity is most perfect and most propitious; but the binary is unpropitious; but the ternary, converting the multitude, is itself a happy number, in which God rejoices, the work being brought, namely, to its proper end with a perfect image of Himself. For in it is that most perfect generating unity, whence it receives the name of father. The second, who makes the binary in divine things, is the begotten son, yet not unpropitious, because he is contained not outside that all-encompassing perfection of the divine essence, but within its embrace. Whence he is neither entirely other, nor second, except in person; for in essence he is entirely the same. The third is love connecting the parent with the offspring, and vice versa.
**Pythag.** Hence (as the Pythagoreans say), wherever one is found, that is fruitful and generating; but that which is generated is the binary, or second; but that which connects both makes the ternary. For neither does the binary, and the other, rest until through the ternary, that is, form, it returns to the first. Therefore, the identity of all things existing in the Creator is declared by musical propor**Procul.** tion (says Proclus). But the otherness of produced things by Arithmetical proportion; but the union of othernesses by Geometrical proportion. In the same series, the business of the soul (as the **Idem.** same Proclus says) proceeds, existing the same in itself, manifold in powers and senses, collected again to itself; the same again in the Creator, but manifold in itself, always tending towards union with the same Creator. For the Creator assigned three containing unions to the soul itself and to the world, which **Plato** Plato called "mediations," because he seems to bind the order of the universe. The Geometrical indeed comprehends substances

**Why the Pythagoreans and Academics embrace the business of the world and the soul with seven limits. Chapter XII.**

[Marginal note: Timaeus. The Same]
**I**t seemed good to Timaeus, and to Plato emulating him, to embrace the soul with seven limits: In the first, placing unity first, as the supreme [aspect] of the soul itself: by which, containing the highest unity in the Creator, it may be the same with Him: because all things pre-existing in the Word were the same with the Word itself: as our Theologians say [Marginal note: Orpheus]. But imitating Orpheus, we say that the soul places its head in the first intellect. The second limit, which contains a double proportion to the first, indicates the soul's progress from God. The third, indeed, its egress to the same. The fourth, moreover, its egress from itself, so that it may be occupied with performing other things. The fifth, a retrocession to itself, so that the process from itself is connected to the progress it makes from Him who precedes it: and its return to itself depends on its own return to the Creator preceding it. The last limits, indeed, which are constituted from solids, teach the conversion of bodies, to which the soul itself is connected. I said "of bodies," because the world consists of a twofold body, incorruptible and celestial: and corruptible and earthy: And in a similar way, so that it may contain a perfect image of the world, man is perfected from a twofold body, according to the Platonists [Marginal note: Plato], elementary and celestial: The elementary, moreover, is denoted by the cube, or solid of the binary, which signifies matter; the celestial, indeed, by the cube of the ternary.

Therefore, the harmony of the world, that which is in the mind, and soul, and in the whole human being, follows: as is held in many places by the Academics [Marginal note: Academics. Proclus], especially Proclus: but here he says the world partakes of harmony in ten ways: the soul, however, in four ways. And just as unity itself is the cause of the quaternary: here, however, of the denary: so intellectual harmony produces the animal [soul]: this, however, the sensible [soul]. Hence the Hebrews say, from their most recondite secrets, that the soul proceeds from the great name of God of four letters, and the whole world proceeds from ten enumerations, and is governed: But by the three supreme ones by command, and by the seven remaining ones by execution: hence they call these seven, the enumerations of the fabric [Marginal note: Syrianus].

According to unity, therefore (as it pleases Syrianus), the perfect and whole world is represented. According to the binary, however, multitude and variety are indicated in it: And through the division of even and odd, masculine and feminine, beginning from the Gods themselves down to roots and plants: For according to the binary and ternary, that which is in the Gods: and according to the quaternary and novenary, that which is in the genera superior to us and better: and according to the cubes, proceeding down to terrestrial and ultimate species of life, and reducing them to the first [Marginal note: Pythagoreans].

Therefore, perfect harmony is completed by cubes: which the Pythagoreans were accustomed to call harmony: because they alone among figures have angles proportionally equal to their sides and surfaces. How in the soul of the world (speaking in the Platonic manner) the intervals of their limits are filled. Chapter XIII.

**That those things which have been said about beings in the spheres seem to agree with sacred scripture. Chapter 14.**

[Marginal note: Psalm.]

For to each orb, the entire school of the wise, even the Peripatetics, assigns at least one intelligence. But since each star has its own power and influence on lower things, it is necessary that it also has its own presiding intelligence, which confers power so that it may act, since operation can by no means proceed from a pure body.

Regarding our souls, however, a difficulty remains, and it would be considered ridiculous by many that souls themselves are placed in the spheres. Yet it does not seem strange to those who truly understand. For even some Catholics of no mediocre genius have proclaimed that human souls are carried up to various spheres: which is not to be understood only of corporeal spheres, but of those supramundane wheels, to which souls return just as they proceeded from them, as is most fully handed down in the more secret Theology of the Hebrews. And these are, no doubt, the various and many mansions in the Father's house, as the supreme truth proclaims. [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.]
But the Pythagoreans assert that they (souls) make a passage while they descend through those intelligences and spheres, to which they return after the perfected course of a well-lived life. [Marginal note: Pythag. Astron.]
And from this, astronomers (if they have any truth) determine by prognostication that this one is Saturnian, or Martian, another Jovian, Venereal, or Mercurial, or Phoebean (solar), or Lunar. For indeed, there are various affections, inclinations, and customs in humans: not indeed proceeding only from matter variously disposed (as some think), but from various influx and diverse form: not indeed by specific diversity, but by particular and proper (diversity): Whose degrees, even if they are variously distributed by Him, who remaining the same divides (says the Apostle) to each as He wills, [Marginal note: Paulus]
nevertheless, secondary angelic and celestial causes cooperate, disposing the body and other things which God has committed to them. Nor should anyone say that the Apostle was speaking there about the division of graces: because (as Gregory rightly thinks) minds, both angelic and human, are assimilated in receiving gifts, just as they agree in the participation of natural degrees.

**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

**What can be said about the complements of the intervals of the three enneads. Chapter 15.**

[Decorative initial P] After we have dealt with the filling of intervals, whatever can be said about the complements of the first kinds, twenty-seven, or of the three enneads, must be discussed. They are indeed filled according to superparticular proportions, as the Pythagoreans say. And this is [Marginal note: Pythag.] according to only one portion imparted to things. Yet that unique life is not divided; but just as the sun is unique in itself, yet manifold and varied in its rays and effects, and influencing more effectively in one time and place than another, so too the soul, existing as one in the body, has very diverse effects. And to begin with the nobler parts: In the intellect, or in the head, it understands; in the heart, it wills; in the eyes, it sees; in the ears, it hears; in the hands, it works; in the feet, it walks; in the intestines, it digests, and intervenes even to expel feces. Where, although it operates as a whole, since it is not divisible, it nevertheless acts not according to its whole self, but according to a part of its power. For if the power were always the same, the work would consequently also be the same. Nor does the variety of organs suffice to bring about such varied effects, because, separated from the body, it could only bring about a single work. Nevertheless, removed from the body, it wills, understands, moves according to place, and uses the senses, which are according to the inner man. It is therefore varied in its effects, and unique in itself, which engages itself with its organs and instruments according to a part (of its power); whence results a superparticular proportion, namely, of the whole to some proportioned part. So too the life of the world is unique, of which it is said: God, to whom all things live. And [Marginal note: Paulus Aratus Orph.] Paul, celebrating the saying of Aratus, says: In Him (namely, God) we live, and move, and have our being. From the hidden recesses of whose unity (says Orpheus) a numerous multitude proceeds. Whence the tree of life situated in the midst of paradise, which bestows life on all, is unique; and yet it is called עץ חיים (etz chayim), that is, "tree of lives" (or "tree of living things"); because that unique tree diffuses diverse rays of life into other things. Just as Paul says [Marginal note: Paulus] concerning the life of the mystical body: "The one and the same Spirit divides to each one as He wills." This Spirit of life, [Marginal note: Ezechi.] existing as one with the tree of lives, also vivifies all things, as we are taught by the oracle of Ezekiel, where he says: "The spirit of life was in the wheels." In the wheels, I say, mundane, or celestial, and terrestrial. For all things, rejoicing in their spherical form, imitate that supreme and divine sphere. This life, therefore, existing whole in itself, communicates itself according to a certain portion (which is by no means cut off from it), to one indeed in a sesquialtera proportion, to another in a sesquitertia proportion, to another in a sesquioctava, to another in a sesquisextadecima; whence result the diapente, diatessaron, tonus, and lemma. But with what particular kinds and species, by this or that proportion, that first life, diffusing itself, disposes all things by its numbers, weights, and measures, no one has yet even hinted in particular. Nor do I think it can be expressed or perceived, except by those purified and filled with wisdom, by which they are able to know all things and embrace all things. [Marginal note: Sapien.] Just as it is said in the Book of Wisdom: "He Himself gave me true knowledge of the things that are, that I might know the disposition of the world..."

secrets, and the virtues of the elements: the beginning, and the end, and the middle of times: the changes of successions: the completions of times: the changes of customs: the dispositions of the stars: the natures of animals: the rages of beasts: the force of the winds and the thoughts of men: the differences of shrubs: the virtues of roots: and whatsoever are hidden, and unforeseen, I have learned. Therefore, let us here pursue our subject.

[Marginal note: Plato.] For what the wise man hints at through number, weight, and measure, Plato describes through numbers, figures, and solids: For by numbers he wished to signify the specific forms of things, which Aristotle also compared to numbers:
[Marginal note: Aristote.] But by measures he indicates the powers bestowed upon each thing: about which even the highest Truth speaks in the Gospel, saying:

But by solids, the weights of things are understood, and the heavy elements, which always lead us downwards: or the inclinations of things, which,
[Marginal note: Augusti.] like weights, draw and impel us either to good or to evil. Hence Augustine calls love a weight, saying: My weight is my love; I am carried thither, whither I love.
Again, by numbers the arithmetic mean is designated. By dimensions and measures, the geometric mean. But by weights, the musical mean: which, in a balanced proportion or likeness, comprehends the speed and slowness of movements, and the sharpness and gravity of voices, and the heavier or lighter inclinations of things. And just as in strings, or pipes, or any sounding instruments, temperaments derived from weights are necessary. So in all things, especially in man, the bond of all things, so that he may be well-tempered, appetites must be moderated: and natural inclinations must be moderated towards the goal of reason, or of the divine law inherent in human minds. Foods also, and all things which we convert to our use, must be moderated by their own weights: just as in this greater machine, the elements, the heavens, and all things rejoice in their proper temperaments: so much so that innumerable species and forms, balanced by their measures, harmoniously agree: Whose subject bodies, although all are composed of four elements, are nevertheless found to be innumerable. Nor is it wonderful: For if from a cube, which is formed from three numbers, namely linear, plane, and solid: and is figured by four surfaces, diverse and almost infinite lines are drawn from the center to the circumference: how much more in the mundane cube, derived from the ternary (as we wrote above) into twenty-seven, will innumerable forms and innumerable composite subjects be found? although all things are composed of four elements, as if from four principal surfaces, through their better numbers, by which multiplied forms correspond to the subject bodies. Which are led through the seven stars, and through the seven intelligences presiding over them: and through the seven divine powers, from which the intelligences receive whence they flow. And how excellently that septenary, resulting from four surfaces and three numbers, is led into a composite through the celestial, angelic, and divine septenary, with the intervention also of the duodenary of signs: which is led through the parts of the septenary. For three times four, and four times three, constitute the duodenary. Whence such great consonance results: that musical artists, following nature as their guide, have striven to adapt their harmonic instruments to such harmonious causes. *How all these three novenaries are still contained in the supreme name of God, and emanate from it. Chapter XVIII.*

[Large decorative initial S] But so that we may ascend to the first and supreme principle, beyond which no access is given, we will outline with what mystery, and with what sacrament, those three novenaries, or the cube of the supercelestial ternary, from which the entire cube of created things descends, are contained in the supreme name of God: and in the super-excellent measure of God: to which that name is attributed: and from there emanate all things which are contained in that linear square, or superficial, and cube: For from that supreme measure, and fount of all emanations (which the Hebrews call the Superior Crown, and we, taught by Christ, call the Father) [Marginal note: Hebrews] first emanates the Son: who is called Wisdom by the Hebrews and by us: And from both [Marginal note: CHRIST. Hebrews.] the spirit is produced: which completes the first and true ternary. Nor, because it reached the ternary, was that first unity exhausted and unfruitful: on the contrary, the whole Trinity was most fruitful: and squaring its ternary, it produced nine choirs of angels: and again squaring, it fabricated nine heavens. And through repeated squaring, it brought forth the novenary of lower things: From these novenaries results the cube 27: beyond which the ternary does not extend. Therefore, arriving at that cube, there is no further progress: since number by its very nature, when it has grown in length, breadth, and depth, cannot be extended further. Through which relation, or in which, those two numbers are joined: & their conjunction is expressed: just as through relations are indicated all operations which God has internally, & externally. For the supreme teacher Christ Jesus, when he wished to explain those most holy persons produced, & producing, expressed [them] in no other way than through certain relations, calling [them] Father, Son, & Holy Spirit. Likewise, & in all things which he does with us, he takes on some relative name: by which his work also may be indicated. For when he fabricated the world, he took on the name of fabricator, or creator: & that in respect to the created creature. Similarly, while he rules, & orders the world itself, he is called ruler, & governor: & through rule, & governance he is joined with us: just as also through creation, when he created, or produced. Thus finally you will always find God acting, & being joined with us through certain relations: whether these are real, or rational, as is disputed by Theologians, let it not be a contention for the present. And while also in reality he diffuses himself in us not only by grace, but in a better way, from this diffusion results the relation of the filler to the filled. Having enumerated as many hundreds as there are numbers and tens, he gathers all into a millenary, which is signified by א, aleph. This letter, in the lines by which its character is formed, comprehends (as we have said) all the numbers of the letters of the tetragrammaton. Each of these letters, not without great mystery, signifies a circular number, so that all those numbers are circular, and all circular numbers are comprehended in these same letters. These are the quinary (five), senary (six), and denary (ten). And the quinary is denoted by the letter ה, he; the senary by ו, vau; and the denary by י, iod. These individual numbers, and all of them together, properly signify that true intelligible sphere, God, who also gave His own image in a circle to all things produced by Him, so that, the course of the world completed, they might strive to return to that from which they proceeded.

Another mystery, which is contained in these same letters, must also be observed. For ה, he, signifying the quinary, indicates the fifth essence (quintessence), inherent in all things composed of the four elements. And ו, vau, signifying the perfect senary number, denotes that life by which all things live. And י, iod, signifying the perfect denary number, represents divinity itself, by which all things are filled, as has often been said, and which all things represent either by image, or by trace and likeness. If, however, we return to the supreme name, in which א, aleph, is placed instead of ו, vau, and this at the very beginning of the word, so that it may be understood that the named (God) never departs from His circular property: and א, aleph itself, signifying unity, which is the principle of all circular numbers. For it (Aleph/unity) also returns into itself, and potentially contains all numbers, and brings them into actuality through multiplied unity. And finally, it leads to the unity of the denary (ten), centenary (hundred), and millenary (thousand), which is again signified by א, aleph. In this, most fittingly figuring God: who, existing as supremely one, potentially contains all numbered things, and unfolds all things into particular and numbered forms, and finally recalls all those same things into Himself: so that the whole mundane enharmony, proceeding from the One, most consonant by a single life and breath, may tend towards and return to the One.

[Large decorative initial P]
**Apollo** [marginal note] **P**ainters, most accurate emulators of nature, diligently imitate, as far as they can, those things which they depict. For painting (says Apollonius the Pythagorean) is a certain imitation of a natural thing, prepared by nature; but the composition of colors is from art. In the former, however, the more powerful force of painting is placed. And what they do with colors, likewise the describers of truth strive to do to the best of their ability, whether they be poets, or orators, or historiographers. In all of these, imitation and a full description of things, which nature bestows, is more commended than an artificial composition of characters. Therefore, since we are describers of the works of the supreme artist, it is right that the manner of writing for those things which we compose should correspond to our abilities. Of this, our Moses, full of God, stands as a most clear example, who, writing the creation of both worlds, wove it together with fitting care, as each of them required. For he narrates the parts of the macrocosm (as the order of nature demanded) as produced by a mere command. But coming to the lesser world (which nevertheless is greater in virtue and mystery), he describes its creation with a more celebrated artifice, inasmuch as it itself was fashioned with a more excellent gift. Which is manifest in those things which were done concerning him. For he had prepared a dwelling for him beforehand, into which he led him, now completed and ready. Afterwards he bestowed dominion over all living things. He planted a place of delight, adorned with all pleasures, for his enjoyment. He gave him a most pleasant companion. And he gave all things to his will, as to a legitimate heir, with only one tree excepted, so that from it he might recognize a superior Lord. For in this, as in his own form (say **Mercur** [marginal note] Mercury and Solomon), he delighted. But also, in creating him, with a most solemn assembly summoned—either of the Most Holy Trinity, as Catholics say; or of the holy angels, as some Hebrews assert; or of supramundane deities, or of the measures of things to be made (which we can call ideas, along with attributes and persons), as more secret Theologians affirm—with a certain prelude having been sent before, he fashioned him not by mere command, but with his own hands and power. Observing this, the wisest **Moses** [marginal note] Moses narrates the creation of man with a longer and more celebrated discourse. For he repeats his formation twice, now created, now made, now having breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, not without mystery, distinctly setting forth all things which were done by the artist concerning him. He also discusses other things pertaining to him with a most solemn narration. Rightly therefore do the creator and the writer pursue man with such diligence, since in him is placed the whole force of nature and the most sublime divine power, as that wise Saracen **A'gazel** [marginal note] Algazel says: Coming to the composition of man, nature ceased, as if nothing more honorable was to be composed at hand.

**That man imitates the world in circular figure. Chapter II.**

[Large decorative initial E]
There exists a saying of the wise, that lower things always emulate higher
things: so much so that, if it were possible, they would even attain the perfection
of the highest: but since this cannot be done, one pursues the type of the other.
Hence metals (have the type) of plants, and plants (of) Zoophytes, and this (Zoophyte) of an animal,
but an animal (of) man, and man has the image of God: as the Platonists teach. [Marginal note: Platonists.]

and that eternity of God, and at the same time, the whole fullness: Which, since they cannot equal, from the whole
