Therefore, all inferior things imitate superior things, even the supreme maker: who is deservedly called the archetype, as if the first type of all things, holding primacy in all things, indeed existing as the idea of all images which are seen in inferior things, assimilates more perfectly those things which approach Him more closely. Since therefore God is an intelligible sphere, and this world presents itself entirely to be seen in a spherical figure, man also, who holds the middle ground between God and this world, must necessarily be bounded by the same figure: and imitate that intellectual sphere in the soul, but the sensible one in the body: as this present picture can teach: From whose navel, according to some, but from the chest (as is truer), if a compass is drawn, that circle is perfectly formed: Whence the entire measure of the body is known to originate from roundness and to tend towards it. We could also pursue many other things about the numbers and proportions of the human body, both evident and hidden: but I fear that while we discourse on numbers, we may exceed number and measure: and that our slender strengths may succumb to such a burden: since these things lie hidden (yet harmonically arranged) in veins, nerves, and internal organs: which no one has ever found, says Augustine, nor even the cruel diligence of anatomists: [Marginal note: Augusti.] who dissect the bodies of the dead, to examine all hidden things: and from there, learn how and in what places to cure: Yet no one has been able to find the complete numbers by which this harmonic adaptation, as of a certain organ, both internally and externally, of the whole body consists: which perhaps no one has dared to seek. Nevertheless, they exist (as Augustine continues, and Hippocrates and the Pythagoreans teach) [Marginal note: Hippoc. Pythag.] Whence we may at least outline some things (if not all) in this harmonic work.

For the proportion of the whole body to the trunk is sesquioctave (9:8): From the trunk or
chest to the whole legs down to the soles, sesquitertia (4:3): But of the chest from the neck
to the navel, and to the loins or belly down to the end of the trunk, dupla (2:1): The
width of the ilia to the width of the coxa sesquialtera (3:2): In which a tone, a diatessaron,
a diapente, and a diapason result. There is also a triple (3:1) proportion of the head to the neck, where there is a dia-
pason and a diapente simultaneously: And again, of the head to the knee, triple: And the same to the thigh,
or petasus: And thus all members of the human body are proven to be arranged with most exact measurements,
as Hippocrates wisely teaches his son Thessalus: And [Marginal note: Hippoc: Boëtius Moses.]
Boethius discusses this in a longer discourse: Indeed, the Creator was pleased to explain this through Moses
under the type of the ark built by Noah: For it says: The length of the ark shall be
three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits: so that the
proportion of length to width is sextuple (6:1), and to height decuple (10:1): By which
measurements the structure of our body is taught: as is not only my opinion, but that
of divine Augustine: Reading whom, after my own discoveries, I rejoiced at the testimony, and favor [Marginal note: Augusti.]
of such a great man: but (to tell the truth) I grieved that someone had stated my discoveries
before me. Thus, the same proportion exists in that ark as in the human body:
But if we also wish to adapt the number, attention must be paid to the measurements
by which some microcosmographers measure the human body itself: For they divide
it by six feet, which are somewhat smaller than common ones: and they call the measure
of one of these feet a hexiped: and they divide this into ten degrees: whence from
six hexipeds sixty degrees result: But they divide each degree into ten, according to some:
but better, as others say, into five minutes: so that all degrees together yield three hundred
minutes: which Moses calls cubits: If these were understood as common cubits, they could not
apply either to the ark or to the human creation: For if referred to the ark, it would have been
very small by common cubits: which are only two spans, having a foot and a half, or six
palms. Therefore, Augustine and Origen wisely opined (so that the ark might be capacious
enough to hold all kinds of animals) that these were Geometric cubits: For a Geometric
cubit contains six common ones: And he was not ignorant of this, who was instructed
in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, among whom this doctrine flourished most greatly.
If we also wish to refer this to the creation of the human body, such a measurement can by no means
be suitable. Therefore, the minutes, and the proportion from

**The Harmony of its Members and Features with Each Other. Chapter IV.**

ET unless we hesitated to be accused of excessive curiosity (which, however, would only happen among common people), we would proceed also to the very features of the face and hands: All of which the most sagacious artisan does not permit to occur by chance in such an elegant body, but with a precise seal, just as he forms the soul and body: and in a similar way, he seals and imprints all things that are adjacent to the body: so that by that artistry, by which he represents this machine with its archetype through the most ordered parts of the body and soul, he might also reveal the art, mastery, and most secret structure and disposition of the human animal by an indication so much more secret, as those very things which it indicates are enclosed by a more obscure veil. Hence many errors in the prognostication of metoposcopists, and more in chiromancy: because in the hands there are inferior and weaker signs. Nor should anyone think that these lead to vices and virtues: because such things absolutely nothing by means of—

...operate, but indicate the force and dispositions of nature; all of them certainly good, provided
that the mind, as the guide of the whole body, directs them to good by its prudence. And since
man is led by his own free will; hence prognosticators err a second time, if they wish to divine
beyond the disposition of nature, the very morals and effects themselves. That this was proven
in the judgment of Zopyrus [Marginal note: Zopy.], has now become common in schools and public places: Who, when from his

necessary for propagation, and hence by those vices which usually arise from bad governance,
and was therefore ridiculed by Socrates' disciples, because they did not recognize such vices in
their teacher [Marginal note: Socrates], Socrates silenced them saying: "Do not ridicule the man: For I would indeed be such
as Zopyrus judged me to be, had I not overcome nature by reason and the precepts of philosophy:
but he would have said better, 'I had directed it to good'." In which sense perhaps is that saying
of the Savior: "Judge not according to appearance." [Marginal note: CHRIST.] Nor is such a doctrine to be entirely
scorned, which proceeds not from superstition, but from the harmonious correspondence of all
parts. Hence also we are compelled to admire and praise the most accurate diligence of the
artist: who also brought together the lineaments and colors of this corruptible body with such art
and such a mystery. Hence men of most serious judgment dedicated themselves to such a
doctrine. Aristotle [Marginal note: Aristote.], leader of the Peripatetics and most sagacious investigator of nature, wrote
much on this subject in a particular treatise, and to Alexander, and in the first book "On the Parts
of Animals". Constantine the African also produced an excellent volume on this matter [Marginal note: Constant. Rasis Galen. Avicenna. Alber. m. Micha. Scotus. Concilia. Pythag.].
Rasis in the second book to Almansor. Galen, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus, Michael Scotus,

ancient and most serious men), looking at adolescents who offered themselves to undertake his
discipline, inquired into their *physiognomonika*, that is, their morals and natures, by a certain
conjecture from the character of their mouth and face, and from the build and habit of their
whole body: And whom he judged suitable, he ordered to be received into his discipline. This
was also practiced by Pharao [Marginal note: Pharao.], king of the Indians: who advised that young men to be admitted to
philosophy should be examined as to what parents they were born from, what morals they were
imbued with, what modesty and affection they were filled with. Therefore, speaking with
Apollonius, he added: "For the eyes indicate most of men's morals." Many things are also placed
in the eyebrows, cheeks, and the whole face: from which wise men and those skilled in nature,
looking as if in a mirror, contemplate what mind and what character they possess. For Lucius
Sulla and Caesar the dictator (as Horace sings and Livy narrates) [Marginal note: Lu. Sy. Caesar. Horat. Livy. Plautus Martial. Juvenal.] often conjectured the hidden
morals of their adversaries, like a fox, by this judgment. Nor without reason do Plautus in his
Comedies describe pimps and criminals, and Martial describes the most wicked Zoilus from a

forehead and hand to the seer." But lest this be believed alien to due piety, let us adduce Job,
approved by the testimony of God [Marginal note: Job], who says: "He seals in the hands of men, that each may know his

Our teachers, attending more to instructing souls with morals than to the mysteries of nature and the Creator, interpreted [them] in another sense. It is also a common judgment among natural philosophers regarding temperament and the nature's property through colors. For an earthy color, derived from cold and dry, indicates black bile and a Saturnine nature. But a blue color, or one tending towards whiteness, signifies phlegm:
[Marginal note: Avicenna.] For cold (according to Avicenna) makes humid matter white, and makes dry [matter] black. But a reddish color, like thick air reddened by the sun's rays, indicates blood: but a fiery [color], like an inflamed flame, [indicates] choler: Although it (choler) is predominant over others due to its very sharp active virtue, yet due to its subtlety it is easily mixable with another, especially with blood and black bile. Hence if it is mixed with superabundant blood, it is vibrant with redness. But if choler superabounds, it makes [the color] reddish-brown. But if with an equal mixture, reddish-brown: but if choler is burnt with blood, it renders an ash-colored [complexion]; rubicund if blood predominates, and somewhat reddish if choler prevails. But if bile is mixed with black bile, it stains with blackness: if with black bile and phlegm in equal mixture, the color will be ash-colored: If phlegm superabounds, yellow: but if black bile is dominant, grayish-blue: But if it is mixed with phlegm in equal proportion, the color will be lemon-yellow: If by the superabundance of the other, pale or somewhat pale: Hence choler is called red, lemon-yellow, vitelline, black, and similar. Also from actions and operations, the nature of man is conjectured: For slow and solid movement signifies earthy black bile: Fear and inertia, and sluggish work, [signify] phlegm: Cheerfulness and friendly manners [signify] blood: Sharp impulse and fiery strength [signify] choler. Many things of this kind are also handed down by those instructed in the work of nature: but we have touched upon these few things to indicate with what order and what correspondence the supreme Creator constructed this tabernacle and outer shell of the true man dwelling within it: so that from there we may be raised up to contemplate the harmony of that better man himself, which he has within, and with the archetype, just as the exterior figure [has harmony] with the interior man himself.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*That all things are included in man, a general discourse. Chapter V.*

[Marginal note: Moses.] [Large decorated initial Q containing a seated figure] With what fullness and what harmony all things were concluded in this man by the supreme Creator, our Moses, a most upright philosopher, indicated with a single and mysterious word, saying: *The Lord God formed man from the dust of the earth: and breathed into his face, or into his nostrils, the breath of life.* He touches both extremes of all things, so that all intermediate things, which are contained between those extremes, may also be understood as included in man: in whose creation he describes the highest and the lowest reconciled: For the lowest and most diminished of all is the element of earth. But the highest is He [Marginal note: CHRIST.] who said: *I am the life,* namely, diffusing the rays of life into all things.

the breath of lives, he says, converged in him. And just as in the greater world divine things are united with earthly things by flowing through the heavens, and conversely, by receiving those [earthly things] through the same heavens, which understand the nature of both extremes: so that divine [element] is communicated to man through a certain celestial [element] marked by dust with a secret indication, as also the name of man first expressed indicates, which is אדם (Adam). Where א (Aleph) signifies divinity, ד (Daleth) celestial nature, and ם (Mem) indeed the corruptible body, according to the experts. Therefore, in man there is the corruptible, the celestial, and the divine, or life of every kind: For man lives with the life of elements and stones: to which the vigor of being, growing, and changing is continuously supplied. He lives with metals by a higher life: which have a certain most hidden spirit: therefore, it is either never, or very rarely, found by artisans, however diligently it may be sought. He lives with plants by a vegetative life, with animals by a motive life, with separated minds by a rational or intellective life, and with God indeed by a divine and eternal life: concerning which John [says]: "The life was the light of men." And again: The Supreme [Marginal note: John. CHRIST.] Truth [says]: "I came that they may have life, and have it more abundantly." Rightly, therefore, it is said that the breath of lives, namely of every kind, was breathed into this man, And what Moses secretly hinted at through the two extremes and the middle, Solomon, or Philo, expresses in plain [Marginal note: Solomon Philo.] language, saying: "God brought man out of the mud of the earth, or dust from the earth: and gave him the power of containing all things:" To whom Trismegistus assents: who, when [Marginal note: Trismegistus.] asked by his son about the generation of man, replied: "Man is a certain all, and a certain whole in all, that is, in God, who consists of all things by power, not indeed by composition: but man, consisting by composition, is made of all the powers of things." Augustine, however, contemplated this all-encompassing [Marginal note: Augustine.] containment of things not only in the whole man, but only in the soul: "The soul, made in the likeness of all wisdom," he says, "bears within itself the image of all things, whence it was defined by the [Marginal note: Philosopher.] philosopher as the likeness of all things:" "For it has within itself powers by which it comprehends all things, investigates all things, and is similar to all things:" "For although it is one, it is similar to earth through sense, to water through imagination, to air through reason, to the firmament through intellect, to the heaven of heavens through understanding." And just as God is comprehensible and participable by all: so the soul is capable of all things. But let us return to man himself: who contains all things not only by likeness, but by power and act, with such dignity and consonance: so that Boethius, imitating those ancient fathers, rightly calls him a second kind of music, [Marginal note: Boethius] thus distinguishing concerning him: "that incorporeal vivacity of reason is mixed by a certain co-adaptation: and just as the effective tempering of grave and light voices results in a single consonance." But Mercury calls this a higher harmony, namely, in relation to that which belongs to the body, [Marginal note: Mercury. Zoroaster.] or the corporeal world. Zoroaster (perhaps in the solitude which he inhabited for twenty years) rightly perceived that, so that he said: "Man rejoices because of the harmony in which the mortal body exists, tempered, namely, together with the soul." Of this (as it pleases [Marginal note: Origen.] Origen) Moses makes mention, when he says: "Male and female he created them," understanding, namely, that divine [element] through the male, and through the female this animal body: which is subject to the spirit and that divine [element]: so that, with it (the spirit/divine element) brooding, it may conceive and give birth to such great con

How great elegance the elements are found in this man. Cap. VI.

[Large decorative initial H] Man, the most perfect and most absolute work of God, and also the Lord of all things, contains those things which are suitable for his composition, as if chosen portions for the Lord, with a more perfect seasoning and sweeter consonance, than those things which are contained in his subordinates. Hence the elements, and all other things composing man, are seen in him as if in a head, with a certain more sublime dignity. Therefore, elements are found consonant even in all coarser things, yet in man, [they are consonant] to a much greater degree, inasmuch as he himself is endowed with a better life: For he is (as we have said) alone among all living beings, a partaker of celestial and divine life. Therefore, elements and all other things in this supreme work attain a certain supreme status. It is not surprising, therefore, if beyond the common consonance which bodily portions and qualities have with each other, and in other composite things, some other modulation, I know not what, is perceived in the well-proportioned complexion of this man, in his colors, figures, and well-arranged features: Which is more clearly discerned by wise and experienced men, [and is] far more pleasing than the harmony of a voice heard by even well-judging ears. And since we have touched upon the proportion of elements and their qualities above, now, omitting those, we will examine that which they hold in a well-constituted man: To whom, so that he may be well-composed, these weights of complexions and humors have been assigned: to Blood eight, to Phlegm four, to Bile two, to Black Bile one, so that everywhere there is a double proportion: but from the first to the third, a quadruple, and to the last, an octuple:

What in man himself corresponds to the elements. Chapter VII.

To these let certain mixed minerals sing with wondrous art. Chapter X.

[Large decorative initial V] Beyond the humors are their internal vessels, which hold the middle place between bones

With which plants may grow green and be nourished. Chapter X. I.

**P**ost metals, the primary kind is that of plants: Whose virtue in flesh and blood, with the vital spirits passing through them in this small world, is quite clearly seen. For a plant is by its very nature (through the mediation of the vital spirit) nourishing and growing. There is also in flesh a vegetative power providing nourishment and manifest growth, in both of which what is lost is most easily repaired: For a cut plant sprouts again, even a rather hard bark: So flesh and skin, when cut, grow again, although often both the skin in flesh and the bark in a plant bear an eternal scar: And both live by a certain most secret spirit: but this plant grows and produces various effects in its leaves, fruits, or root for one who eats it: Flesh, however, not only grows, but is moved by multiple motions, by expanding, contracting, and moving according to place, due to the diversity of muscles existing within it. And if flesh does not grow in those already adult, and brought to the limit of growth, nevertheless, they are continuously nourished, as Galen, Avicenna, Albertus, and others extensively discuss. [Galen. Avicenna Albertus] Therefore, in man are the powers of plants, not only terrestrial, but also celestial. Concerning terrestrial ones, the perceptive doctor Aristotle, speaking in his discourse on the soul, says: that [Aristotle. David] man is an inverted tree, extending the hairs of his head like roots into the upper part, and existing in the upper parts, he takes nourishment through the mouth, just as a plant extends its roots into the earth and downwards, and is nourished from below. And concerning celestial trees, the celestial doctor, after he sang of celestial bread, wine, and oil, he adds: "The trees of Adonai shall be satisfied," for which we have "the trees of the field, and the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted." For he plants these trees, of whom it is said: "Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted." What the ancients thought concerning the transmigration of the human soul into beasts, and what the truth of the matter is. Chapter XIII.

**M**etamorphoses of this kind, sung about by Pythagoras and Plato, [Marginal note: Pythagoras, Plato] are well known even to children in schools. For many have sung of this one into a laurel, that one into a wolf, another into a nightingale, another into a swallow, and similar transmutations: But whether Pythagoras, Plato, and the sacred authors from whom they learned, believed these transmutations happened in reality, or merely in affection, is debated by their followers: For some contend that Pythagoras thought so: Others, however, considered those writings handed down by Plato in a poetic manner, such as Xenocrates, Archelaus, and Carneades among the Athenians; and Ammonius and his followers among the Egyptians. [Marginal note: Xenocrates, Archelaus, Carneades, Ammonius, Archelaus] But Carneades, observing the footsteps of Plato himself in the manner of the Sceptics, thought that he wrote rather by questioning than by determining: Archelaus, however, believed that truth was rather described by Plato: Xenocrates, however, [Marginal note: Xenocrates, Ammonius] and Ammonius believed that he spoke some things, or a few things, as true, both concerning the soul and providence, and other such most hidden matters: but that he strove to conceal the rest under various enigmas: Among these, the circuit of souls, and the restitution of things in thirty-six thousand years, according to the complete revolution of the eighth sphere: But he received the transmigration of souls into beasts not as something conceived by himself, but from Egyptian priests, [Marginal note: Egyptian Priests] fabricated (as they say) for the expiation of souls: Then sung about in verses by Orpheus, Empedocles, and Heraclitus. [Marginal note: Orpheus, Empedocles, Heraclitus, Plato, Iamblichus, Porphyry, Proclus, Hermias, Syrianus] Those, however, who thought correctly, and pursued the true opinion of Plato, utterly rejected the transmigration of the human soul into beasts. Iamblichus achieved this, and Porphyry, who does not permit the soul to be torn from the center in which it is once fixed. But Proclus, Hermias, and Syrianus considered it a horrible crime for a celestial soul to be cast into beasts: because a human body does not receive any other soul than a human one: nor is a human soul inclined into any other body than a human one. Nor is it right (they say) for a rational soul to fall into the body of an animal lacking reason, as such an impious generation is forbidden by divine law: Whence Porphyry and Iamblichus, [Marginal note: Porphyry, Iamblichus] having refuted their error, conclude that a man corrupted in morals should by no means be called an ass, but ass-like; nor a lion, but lion-like. Whence each of the signs of the zodiac has its denomination, and what those animals signify, from which they are named, along with the Sun. Chapter XVIII.

[Marginal note: Macro.] [Large decorative initial P] Macrobius touched lightly upon the reasons for a few denominations from Academic sources; to which we will add those things which have been drawn from better streams. Therefore, the first sign is called Aries: because that animal (the ram) leans on its left side for six winter months, but from the vernal equinox, on its right: So also the Sun at the same time traverses the right Hemisphere, and for the rest, the left. Moreover, the ram is the head and leader of sheep, and that sign
[Marginal note: Astron.] named after it is the head of the signs, and the leader of the months of the year. Whence Astronomers prognosticate the events of the entire year from the Sun's entry into the first part of Aries. From the same also rural philosophers prophesy, who (as Isaac reports) if they see older rams more inclined to copulation than younger ones at the appointed time: from this they infer a happy and prosperous course of the year, and the best temperament. Taurus succeeds, which Egyptian worship shows to be related to the Sun for multiple reasons, either because in Heliopolis they especially worship a bull consecrated to the Sun (which they call Nerites): or because the Apis bull in the city of Memphis is received as an image of the Sun: or because in the town of Herminth they worship a bull consecrated to the Sun in a magnificent temple of Apollo, calling it Pachim, notable for miracles suitable to the nature of the Sun: For it is asserted to have changed colors every hour, and it is said to be shaggy with bristles growing in the opposite direction, contrary to the nature of all animals: whence it is held as an image of the sun shining on the opposite part of the world. But since these things savor of rather pure fables, other reasons must be sought: For the bull is the king of herds, just as the ram is of flocks, the lion of wild beasts, and man of all rational creatures: whose images the Sun, king of planets, claims for its dwellings: And from Aries, whose virtue is in the head, it ascends to Taurus, which chiefly contains its power in the neck: and from the king of flocks to the king of herds, and from there it proceeds to the king of those using reason (man): And from here they call Gemini, always succeeding with alternating deaths, as antiquity feigned concerning Castor and Pollux: For whether life pursues man or death succeeds, he always lives in the better part, which remains eternal, while the souls of beasts dissolve into nothing: Man himself also lives this mortal life through a perpetual succession of individuals. Of Gemini

--- Page 362 ---
**TONUS SEXTUS.** 112
moreover it is called a sign, either because, when the Sun has arrived there, it doubles its strength: or because it then doubles its journey by descending, just as it had ascended. Therefore Cancer follows, an animal indeed retreating, because when the Sun has reached its first threshold, it begins to retreat to the lowest points. Cancer is also, above all animals, lunar, deservedly the domicile of the Moon: And this is like the breast of the sky, while Gemini are the arms. Leo succeeds, like the shoulders and sides of the same sky, in which sign, as if in its own domicile, and an image especially dedicated to itself, the Sun burns above all seasons, although its rays are more bent than when it passed through Cancer and Gemini: For from there it receives strength, as if from a place named by Leo as preeminent among the solar animals: For here it seems to derive its nature from the substance of the sun: whence from the intemperance of heat it often languishes, just as our bodies do, when the Sun is in the same sign: Therefore then physicians forbid medicines, phlebotomy, and the diminution of blood, unless necessity compels it. The succeeding sign is rightly called Virgo: because then the Sun, from which the principal denomination of the signs is made, seems to lose all power of producing: and to arrive at a certain sterility: because as it passes through there, already the crops, wine, and fruits of the earth are ripe, and seem to close the fertility of that part of the earth. The sign that follows afterwards is rightly called Libra: because then the weighing or measuring of collected fruits begins: And the Sun's course is divided into equal diurnal and nocturnal portions: The balance also seems to weigh the time, rejoicing in the greatest temperance between heat and moderate cold. To this is added Scorpio, a venomous animal, more troublesome than others, by how much more severe a torment it inflicts: It has venom in its tail: it always strikes with an oblique blow: And it seems wonderful that it never lacks venom, especially at midday, when the Sun burns with ardors, although Phoebus is a physician bringing healing to all: Which, however, to those who inspect it sanely, ought not to seem at all absurd, since all things, the more pernicious venom they have, so much the more efficacious an antidote (they also have): For the flesh of the viper or tiri, from which theriac is made, offers a remedy for virulent things: although it itself boils with poisonous ichor: Likewise, the flesh of the scorpion itself is effective even for those poisoned by it: Thus, wherever one extreme arises, another proceeds from it: For God himself, supremely good, brings forth these testimonies about himself: "I will strike, and I will heal: I will kill, and I will make alive." [Marginal note: Deuter.] And we have said of the Sun, that sometimes it is Dionysius, tearing apart, and sometimes Phoebus, reuniting: Nor is it wonderful, therefore, if for its domicile it sometimes takes on the scorpion. Here perhaps there is an allusion to that scorpion, about which we read in Joshua and in the book of Numbers: [Marginal note: Iosube Nume.] "The boundary of Judah will be from the end of the Salt Sea, from the gulf that looks towards the south, and it goes out from the south to the ascent of the scorpion, or scorpions, as the Hebrew truth has it:" Which ascend higher than the letter on the surface presents: For Scorpio is earthly, celestial, and supercelestial, from which the sun receives some power. There are also scorpions in the lower abyss, about which the highest Truth says: [Marginal note: CHRISTUS.] "Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy:" For not concerning the sign

Sagittarius is added, where the Sun, being present in winter, directs arrows of hail and rain at us. It is also called a monster, degenerating in its hinder part, because the sun, proceeding thither, seems to degenerate in light, influence, and effect. Capricorn follows, whom the Hebrews name with the express word גדי, that is, gedi, which we can interpret as "kid," which is an animal: it always tends towards high places while it feeds, indeed a house suitable for the sun, while it begins to ascend. For entering there, it changes its path from descent to ascent, and therefore that place is called "tropic" according to τροπὴν, which is "conversion." Finally there are the Fish (Pisces), in which the zodiac terminates, which the Sun also consecrated, so that it may be known to provide life not only to aerial and terrestrial animals, but also to those whose existence is immersed in the waters: For so great is the power of the Sun, that by penetrating even the most hidden things, it vivifies them even to the lowest parts of the earth. Indeed, happily for man, the sun's course ends in the fish, whom the redeemer of the human race and the true Sun of the world ate, having completed the course of life, and transformed into a better lot. In the same series also, the Divine life and influence, signified by the Sun, descends into
[Marginal note: Psalm.] man, beginning from the head down to the feet and fringes: as the Psalmograph sings under another type, saying: "Like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard: that went down to the skirts of his garments." Therefore it begins from the head, or from Aries, it passes through Taurus, because through the strength of the neck it is diffused to the arms, and the twin parts of double virtues and operations. And it passes through the Cancerian breast, and the virile, and Leonine strength of the shoulders and sides: But coming to the loins, it renders those fountains sterile from the works of the flesh: If, however, the preservation of nature demands it, at least the succeeding Libra moderates pleasure, and by the influence of the superior Scorpion, it restrains the extreme sting of the tail of this scorpion, that is, by preferring the ultimate (things), by which it mortifies the ultimate pleasures. Why those signs, and the principal joints in man, are distributed in the number twelve. Chapter XIX.

[Decorative initial I containing a coat of arms] N the archives of the wise, we find two progressions of things: one indeed through the ternary, seeking the lowest from the highest; the other, however, through the quaternary, ascending from the lowest to the highest. And Plato followed the former, from divine things to inferior ones; [Marginal note: Plato.] while Aristotle, pursuing the latter from the lowest to the highest, proceeded only as far as he could be led by hand through his senses from these things. [Marginal note: Aristote.] The quaternary, therefore, is an elemental number, and is also found to be divine with great mystery, according to the fitness of the thing: as Orpheus [Marginal note: Orph.] and those wiser than him said. And this (quaternary) gives birth to the indefatigable and immutable number ten (as the same Orpheus continues), beyond which no number is given. The quaternary itself, however, complicated by the ternary, leads to the number twelve, the first increasing number, and more celestial and divine than terrestrial: whence all increasing things, and very many divine things, are distributed by it. This number is also composed of two first perfect sixes, namely: and it is the first increasing number, and this abounds in sixteen by four, whence that happy increase comes, because it is made by the square of equilateral sides, and the parent of ten: Therefore, deservedly, Plato in the Phaedo, and in many places, [Marginal note: Plato.] venerates this number, and by it divides the supernal world into twelve faces, and as many colors, yet with a more perfect mark: For he asserts that stones, fruits, trees, flowers, and such things are found in the supernal region with such perfection that they have not yet come to our knowledge, nor can we even imagine them: For these things they had received from those who were taught by divine oracles: John, [Marginal note: Ioan.] also instructed by these things, at the end of his Patmos vision, relates that the tree of life produces twelve fruits every month: He also describes that supernal city constructed with twelve foundations of precious stones, with the twelve names of the Apostles, and distinguished by twelve gates, over which as many angels presided: and he mentions the names of the twelve tribes inscribed on them. Moreover, on every side of it, he completes a measure of twelve thousand stadia, as the prophet Ezekiel had done before. Plato, therefore, following these, in order to conform his Republic to the celestial city, arranges the fields in his 'Laws' with this number, and in the book 'On the Republic', he solidifies the duodenary, and reduces it to a body, namely 1728, to which, when a Republic or dominion arrives, if discipline flourishes, it achieves its end (as he asserts): and if it progresses further, it gradually declines for the worse by a fatal law, especially as discipline degenerates: And he considered the solid of this number to be the end of the Republic, since it is the first increasing number, and beyond a solid, no further progress is given: then

...then because it draws the whole celestial influx: For by the millenary, which is the solid of the denarius, is denoted the manifold thousandfold influx of the star-bearing heaven, corresponding to the number of stars residing therein. But in the seven hundred are designated the powers of the seven planets, and by twenty-eight the favor of the Moon. For its motion, distant from the course of other wandering stars, is considered as solitary, completing its revolution on the twenty-eighth day, when it returns to the same point of the Zodiac; but on the twenty-ninth to the sign [Plato.], at which time it has advanced nearly one degree. Plato therefore celebrates this number, emulating Mercury; and both (Plato and Mercury) emulate Moses, and the deifying prophets, indeed God Himself: who chose that Israelite family of twelve, which He always commanded to stand thus divided, and to have twelve princes set over it; and as many stones to be placed in the bottom of the Jordan, while they crossed through it to the promised land; and commanded stones of the same number to be fixed on the breastplate of the high priest. Moreover, twelve loaves of faces, for which we have the loaves of proposition, are placed in the ark; and the altar is constructed with as many stones. By which number also the bronze sea [Salomon] made by Solomon for the washing of offerings, was supported by oxen. Also, after crossing the Red Sea, twelve springs were prepared for that chosen family in Elim; and twelve scouts were sent to explore the promised land. To the goal of which number Christ, the wisdom of God, separates the Apostolic family, and sets them over the twelve tribes. And those sealed and chief elect are enumerated by John by twelve thousands. He also describes the Queen of this people crowned with twelve stars. When the loaves multiplied, fragments are collected in twelve baskets. Moreover, the day is divided by twice twelve hours, and the Moon daily traverses twelve degrees; and Jupiter, balancing all things, completes its own course in twelve years. Hence not without cause Timaeus Locrus [Tim.lo.] describes the whole world with twelve faces. And if we descend to lower things, many growing things proceed by this number. The hare and the rabbit, most fertile, generate twelve times a year. The camel carries its fetus for twelve months. The peacock [Plato] lays twelve eggs. Furthermore, Plato squares the millenary and solidifies the hundreds into ten times a hundred thousand, so that he may also enumerate the supernal, and ministering, and assisting intelligences, according to Daniel's prophecy. Of which (intelligences) the chief princes, by the duodenary multiplied by its half, namely the senary, are distributed into seventy-two: By which number both the elders in the figurative people, and the disciples in the true, are represented, according to the number of languages [Sapien. Hiero.]. To which languages (as we can learn from ancient wise men) as many angelic princes preside: Which things are somewhat discussed by Jerome concerning that psalm verse, "clothed in varied raiment". But by assigning to each its senary, not [Procul.] without mystery, twelve more powerful princes remain: Therefore Proclus asserts this number to be consecrated to the Gods, and to those kinds (of beings) which proceed from them. Hence heaven, the seat of divinity, is divided into twelve signs, over which preside twelve chief angels, supported by twelve irrigations of the great name of God.

Correspondence of qualities with the planets, and the eighth heaven. Chapter XX.
[Decorative initial E] There exist in the human body qualities and complexions having their own consonance with the planets and the starry heaven: For, postponing that manifest consonance which this (body) has with them in its triplicities, let us come to that which Saturn has a correspondence with black bile: so that those in whom this prevails are called Saturnine, and so closely follow its motion and influence, that Saturn seems to be present in all their operations: And, drawn by the same (Saturn) by a certain consonant force, they always delight in Saturnine things, in solitude, contemplation, deep imagination, an appetite for gathering (things) from fear brought on by a cold and dry earthly nature, and in such decrees of Saturn. Jupiter, however, has its own harmony with blood, and with humid and warm air, and consequently with life, which especially resides in such (conditions): And who, by its harmonious expansion, with an equalizing force, makes its Phaethonteans tractable...

...to things which we understand, and full of ideas of what we are about to do. And so that heaven itself might be shown to embrace all things not only by revolution, but by virtue, the wise divided those signs into four ternaries, according to the four elements and the foundations of all things, assigning to each ternary the beginning, middle, and end of the element suitable to it: From which the generations, states, and resolutions of all things are made: For they gave the beginning of fire to Aries, its increase or progress to Leo, and its end to Sagittarius: But the beginning of earth to Taurus, its progress to Virgo, and its end to Capricorn: The beginning of air to Gemini, its process to Libra, and its end to Aquarius: But Cancer possesses the beginning of water, Scorpio the middle, and Pisces the end. Thus the intellect comprehends the beginning, progress, and end of all things produced and to be produced from these elements, beyond which nothing is found that can be understood: because outside them there is nothing. And just as in the intellect of the divine or human craftsman all things to be made by him are conceived, so the future of all things is conceived in heaven: but it is unfolded and produced by the planets, just as by inferior powers those things which our intellect conceives are brought to effect: which especially resides in the brain, and this in a skull full of innumerable hairs: Thus that power of generation is (as the Theologians of the Hebrews say) in the sacred name of God diffused through heaven, and filling it like a skull, and a certain shell full of innumerable stars: However, their number is known to Him who numbers the multitude of stars, as also the hairs of the head, as the highest Truth says: [Marginal note: CHRIST.] All the hairs of your head are numbered. Not indeed those which are cut off and perish (says Origen), but those which were in the Nazirites filled with the Holy Spirit: so that they might cast down others: concerning whom it is said in the Canticles: [Marginal note: Origen. Canticles.] "The locks of your head are like royal purple joined to channels," those, namely, supernal ones, through which all effusions of graces flow, by cutting off which a weak man is overcome by a woman, that is, by the sensitive part, as we read of Samson: Which hairs receive influx and power from a supernal source, just like the stars. But let us return to the intellect. For it composes concepts and images, which it contains, and prayers and sentences, by which it is instructed: and all knowledge is generated, just as when the influxes of the stars are combined with the virtues of the planets and elements: whose power is contained in the heavens, especially with the intervention of a great name, or the virtue of the craftsman himself, diverse species and particular things are produced, whose names (as they say) result according to the property of the influxes and the influencing entities: Knowing these, the Protoplast (first created man) imposed names on things according to their quiddities: To which perhaps tends that saying of the highest Truth: "Your names are written in the heavens." [Marginal note: CHRIST 3.] For the Hebrews divide the twenty-two letters of their alphabet into three parts: of which three signify the three elements, seven as many planets, and twelve the twelve signs, as their characters, they assert: And they call those seven letters double, both because they are pronounced in two ways, softly and sharply: and because they represent the planets, which, according to the diversity of the signs in which they are found, remit, and P iij

The first mobile carries away with the heart, or the freedom of the spirit residing there.

Cap. XXII.

[Large ornate initial E] The ninth circle, which is called the first mobile, the leader of the heavens, carrying all the heavens with it, leads them along: and it itself is led by no inferior circle, but by the sole intelligence moving it, or by God commanding it: Into which, as into the first mover, lest the whole harmony of heaven be confounded, all motion is led, as [Marginal note: Aristotle.] Aristotle proves at the end of his Organon. Thus in this our small world, the will is the mistress of all other powers, and their leader at will: To which, deservedly, kingdom and principality are due, because it always tends towards the good, as towards an object adequate to itself: even if sometimes, by error or by animal force impelling it, it chooses evil, believing or foreseeing it to be good: And then it becomes not a mistress, but a most wretched servant, as the highest [Marginal note: Christ.] Truth says: "Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin." Rightly, therefore, and tending towards the good, it is justly preferred, just as in Polities, he who has stood firm for the better and greater good is deservedly placed first. But this will, or synderesis, together with the superior part of its nature, like the first mobile, leads all inferior powers with it at will: but it itself, when upright, is led by no one, except by the highest mover, or by that influx which [Marginal notes: Theologians. Christ. David] theologians call grace, charity, or infused love. Concerning which again the highest Truth says: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him:" And the royal prophet says that he then runs in the way of God's commandments, when his heart has been enlarged and moved by love. To its (the will's) ordered motion also follow the progresses of the other inferior powers, just as all the motions of the orbs are regulated by the revolution of the first mobile itself. Nor let anyone say that the will, as if blind, is led by the intellect: because we can love nothing unless it is first known: towards which alone the will itself is carried, as [Marginal notes: Augustine. Aristotle.] Augustine and Aristotle agree: For just as light shows the eye the way, yet by no means leads it, so the intellect demonstrates paths to the will, but does not lead the will itself along them, but the will remains mistress of its own operation. Thus also the starry heaven in a certain way represents to the first mobile the degrees and names of things to be produced by it and the planets, and for executing these, the first mobile is approached: and it willed all things by [Marginal note: The Same.] diurnal motion. Therefore, in man there is will and heart (as Aristotle says) like the first intelligence—

way in the sphere, the first namely, and having the likeness of the first sphere, it revolves and draws all things, just as the first mobile [draws] the other spheres. And just as sin follows in nature, when lower causes deviate from the first, and lower spheres from the first mobile: So when the law of the members and lower powers, repugnant to the mind, leads man captive into the law of sin. But the slowest of all motions is that of the starry heaven, which moves one degree in a hundred years, as Ptolemy holds: [Marginal note: Ptolem] which is the square number of ten, which is made up of parts of the quaternary elementary number: From which it is hinted that that heaven represents the elementary body: and also because it is integrated from a fourfold kind of signs, according to the nature of the four elements, just as the body is composed of the same. Nor let anyone criticize me, that a little above we made the starry heaven correspond with the intellect, but now we equate it with the body: For the serpent sometimes holds the type of the devil, sometimes of Christ: and this, while He himself says: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." And any planet is sometimes equated with some element, sometimes with some order of angels. Many such things are also found compared with different things due to the symbolism that different known things have to each other: For with respect to superior minds, that heaven behaves as a body: and with respect to producing lower things, it has the likeness of an in- [Marginal note: Porph.] tellect producing ideas. So also in the coordination of things assigned by Porphyry and Aristotle, [Marginal note: Aristo.] the same thing, compared to what is superior, has the nature of a species, but compared to what is inferior, the nature of a genus. Therefore, in our proposition, the motion of the first mobile is like the motion of the soul/mind, and the motion of the starry heaven, having the likeness of bodily motion: but the revolutions of the planets represent the motions of the powers existing between the body and the soul. But if we wish to equate these things with the lowest and the highest, in the heavens, the first mobile is the most fervent of all, in the microcosm the heart and will, in the angelic [hierarchy] the burning Seraphim. Again, there is a fiery power inflaming in the Seraphim, carrying along in the first mobile, a fervent virtue in our will and heart: Therefore, this dwells in the heart, the warmest of all members, indeed, with both natural and a better heat: concerning which [Marginal note: Dauid] the Psalmist says: "My heart grew hot within me." And again: "My heart was inflamed." There is also an earthly power in the Cherubim, a most beautiful figure of ideas, in the starry heaven, a splendid picture of stars, but in the lowest element, an adornment of various herbs and flowers.

The stomach is also most appropriately governed by Saturn, which by its nature, with prevailing nervous parts, is cold and dry: therefore attracting humidities, like earth, Saturn, and the Moon. But it heats and digests from the inherent warmth in its flesh, fostered by the warmth of the adjacent members, namely the liver, heart, [Marginal note: The Same. Galen] spleen, gall, and hymen, as Avicenna teaches: from which aids it is rendered warmer than the liver, although it has received the opposite from nature: which (according to Galen) has placed heating agents near its belly. And just as the stomach is constrained by Saturnian power to contain food, so is the womb to contain the fetus, and both are joined together by nervous parts. **Things that are active with Mars. Chapter XXV.**

**M**ars has its seats in the kidneys, veins, and the course of semen through the back, and in the gallbladder. But these indeed alone; with Jupiter, however (according to Firmicus), in the liver and nostrils.
[Marginal note: Iul. Fir. Auicena]
Therefore, it fittingly rages in the kidneys, since they themselves (according to Avicenna) are hot and dry; although others consider them hot and humid. But this is because the hot, humid, and radical (innate principle), informed by life-giving heat, thrives in them, but by their simple nature, they are dry and Martian. Of which thing the calculi (stones) generated in them provide a sign, because they are most active especially in Martian individuals, and with Mars favoring. And the disposer of nature combined these, just as many members of the body,
[Marginal note: Galen. Auicen.]
as Galen and Avicenna discuss. But these are given for concocting the superfluous watery and sanguineous (humors), just as the gallbladder for a receptacle of bile, and the spleen
[Marginal note: Galen.]
for a receiver of gross melancholic humor, as the same Galen determines. It is also preferred to the course of semen and the back, through which it descends, so that the semen may be warmed by its heat and receive vigor for generating offspring. Moreover, those who treat of such matters judge that the same (Mars) presides over the veins, although by their nervous, membranous, and ligamentous nature they are cold and dry, so that perhaps (notwithstanding their cold nature, which is required to constrict them) warmed by it, they may preserve the blood in its heat. And (so that we may draw a more secret reason from the storehouses of nature) we will also conclude this from their location. For they have their location between the Jovian liver and the solar heart, just as Mars is between both. **Things moved by the Moon. Chapter XXIX.**

[Decorative initial T]hough the Moon disposes the whole body and individual members according to the variety of signs and aspects with the Sun and other planets, it is nevertheless said to have the greatest power in moving certain members that respond to it with a peculiar affinity: For it presides over the left eye, just as the Sun presides over the right: so that the two luminaries in each world may mutually agree. Frequently also it predominates over all humors, which in both worlds, and also in trees and living beings, ascend and descend following the Moon itself: Which is quite evidently proven in the fluxes of women: which are therefore called menstrual, because they follow the course of the Moon: which is completed almost monthly. In other humors also it is likewise manifest to those who observe well, since they are more prone (to flow) when the Moon is in a watery sign, than when in a fiery or earthy one. And therefore, experts in this kind of business order these things to be observed when giving medicines. It is also judged to be preferred to the lung, which like a fan cools the heart and those things that are inflamed by the heart itself, and

**On the admirable harmony of disordered things, and of both worlds within themselves. Chapter XXXI.**

[Large initial E containing a woodcut illustration of a figure] And before we ascend to the harmony of man with the supercelestial world, we will also survey the agreement which the dregs of both this corporeal world and the lower one, and the infernal parts, possess. For in this sensible world there is an earthly dwelling, there is a celestial house, and finally, there is a lofty and supercelestial one, where the supreme Moderator resides: But beyond all these are purgative places, where the dregs of both this domestic and the celestial world flow together, as something superfluous, and the refuse of the food of the supreme life, which is nourished by angelic minds and human souls: as He Himself testifies in the Gospel, which is titled according to John, saying: [CHRIST] "My food is to do the will of my Father, who is in heaven." And what this will is, declaring elsewhere, He says: "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me: For this is the will of Him who sent me, [The Same] that I should lose nothing of all that He has given me, but should raise it up on the last day." Therefore, the soul and the angelic mind are the food of God and Christ, who eats and receives all of them: so that by purifying and cooking them with His warming and divine power in the depths of His mercy, with which the dawn from on high has visited us, He may make them worthy of God. Therefore, digesting this food which He has taken, He transforms that part of the better substance into Himself as nourishment, not of necessity, but of pleasure. "We are transformed (says Paul) [Paul] into the same image, so that we also may be called and be children of God (as John says)." [John] Nor does He only receive human souls as food, but also angelic minds, so that He may purify them, and as the mediator of all, unite them to God, as we can learn from Dionysius and Grosseteste: [Diony. Lyncon.] For the former says: "angels are purged from pride and ignorance:" And the latter interpreting says: "For those first substances, divine knowledge, which is the Word and the Son of God, is as it were a cleanser, not from filth which was inherent, which among us is usually called true purgation: but lest there be any hindrance, which kind of purgation is, according to truth, the best and most sufficient." Therefore, the superfluous parts of the final digestion have been sent down, and are sent down, to the foul and dreggy places of hell: Where, falling without any order, enveloped in that most confused mass and most horrible chaos of darkness, they pay the due penalties for their insolence, by which they were unwilling to feed Him, who complaining threatens, saying: [CHRIST] "I was hungry, and you gave me no food to eat: Therefore, cursed by me and cast out, go into eternal fire, to which you have been given as perpetual food, after you were unwilling to be food for me and my members, just as I offered myself as food for you, so that you might live in me." That Man Harmonizes with Angels, Containing Them. Chapter XXXII.

[Decorative initial H] Man is (says the wise man) to whom is given the power of containing all things:
Therefore, beyond lower and middle things, namely mutable and celestial,
he also apprehends angels and God Himself: so that he is in a way the bond of all things,
and nearest to all, and a true world containing all things, and conversing with all:
with the higher indeed through faith and wisdom, with the middle through reason and discourse:
with the lower through sense and dominion: And let him have a symbol with all things,
with matter in its proper subject, with the elements in a fourfold body, with plants in vegetative
power, with the heavens in the influx of superior parts to inferior ones, and in circular motion
tending to the same from which it came: with angels in mind and wisdom: with God in the
containment of all things, which man has by composition, but God by a certain sim-
[Marginal note: Mercu.] plicity. Hence Mercury says: "Man is even superior to the heavenly inhabitants,"

--- Page 384 ---
**VOLUME SIX.** **123**

or at least enjoys an equal lot: For whoever of the heavenly beings descends to earth, abandons the threshold of heaven: but man ascends into heaven, and measures it: Nor do those things which are lowest, and those which are highest, and all other things, escape him: and what is greater, not leaving the earth, he is raised into heaven: so vast is human power.

Wherefore it must be dared to say that man is indeed a mortal earthly God, but God is an immortal heavenly man: Hence by the virtue of these, individual things are governed: yet all things are subjected to one. Therefore, that angels exist, not only do the sacred scriptures teach, but also natural philosophers assert and prove it, [Marginal note: philoso.] especially Plato with all his Academics, Chrysippus, and Aristotle: The latter [Marginal note: Plato Academ. Chrysi. Aristo. Chry.] indeed says, it would be absurd for that part which is most apt for generating animals, such as the stars and ethereal regions, to be deprived of its fullness: Hence he judged that generations were necessary there, and that these were intelligences. Chrysippus, however, asserted that perfection is found in each thing: For a puppy is imperfect, but a dog is perfect in its kind: Thus a foal becomes a perfect horse, and a boy a man. In the same series, it also happens in parts, since the hand is more perfect than the foot, and the eye than the hand: Hence, since the parts of the lower world are imperfect, because the earth only generates: beasts thrive with sense and motion: man is governed by reason, and drawn by appetite to lower things. There is therefore reason unimpeded by the senses, and this must be in angels. Hence Plato asserted that between Gods and men there were certain divine powers, intermediate by nature and place, and that these governed all divinations, miracles, and individual men: And if by the gentiles they are named genii, by us however they are named angels. But how they relate to us by influencing and interacting, from which a most sweet harmony results in operation, because these things escape the sight of the eyes and other senses, it is not easy to discuss them, therefore we ought to consult not Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, or Ari- [Marginal note: Zeno. Clean. Chryf. Aristote. Diony.] stotle, but our prophets and pontiffs, Dionysius, and other fathers illuminated by divine light in this matter: but especially that greatest pontiff, who says: All things whatsoever I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you: For he says: Their angels, that is, of the little ones, always see the face of my Father: from whom they draw: that they may influence us, so that, joined like leaven with our mass, yet by the power of the supreme craftsman, they do not indeed corrupt, but transform us into a divine lot: Hence, according to that prophetic [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] saying: With the holy you will be holy, it can also be said to us, with an angel you will be an angel. Therefore, when man receives their influx and vigor, he is called Seraphic, Cherubic, angelic, and the like, according to the nature of the influx received. Thus man has a conformity with all of them, and from all he receives (according to the writings [Marginal note: Diony.] of Dionysius) purifications, illuminations, and advancements. But descending to particulars, man receives from angels, that he may be a good messenger of God, and an interpreter of the divine mind: From archangels, that he may rule over all to whom it is given to preside: From principalities, that also the powers of all subjects

Man is attuned with God, existing as His temple and image. Chapter XXXIII.

It was given enough, and more than enough, to man, that he himself, having become another world, should embrace all parts of that world within himself; yet this seemed little to the most munificent Giver, unless He also offered Himself to man, as to a beloved son. Which I would by no means dare to assert, unless the wise, and the Giver of all good things Himself, testified to the same. [Marginal note: Xistus.] Xistus [Marginal note: Pythag.] the Pythagorean judged the soul of man to be the temple of God, and therefore immortal, like a sacred host, [Marginal note: Paulus] so that the place might be proportionate to what is placed there: But Paul proclaims this with an clear voice, saying: "You are the temple of God." Which could be proven in many places of sacred scripture: But let us first consider how man is the image of God, made in the likeness of God and with His similitude, as the Creator Himself reserved before He brought him forth: For he is the image and likeness of God, containing all things that are in God: And in this the image differs from the trace, because the latter represents a part, while the former represents the whole (as our theologians teach). Hence, those who have dealt with this image have tried to investigate all things that man can represent in God: For all commonplace thinkers, striving to adapt the three powers of man to the three persons, have said that in memory the Father, who is called fertile memory; in intellect the Son, the Word and wisdom of God; and in will the Holy Spirit, indeed divine love, is revealed. But more acute theologians, progressing further, teach that also in operations (which they call secondary acts) those divine properties or actions are represented: or (as they say) notional and essential [attributes], or by whatever other name divine things can be called: For we do not know, nor is it permitted to those who know to speak of those secrets of God, removed from all modes of creatures; and who is (says [Marginal note: Diony.] Dionysius) all things eminently: so much so that these words which we use cannot express those things which are in Him, except through a certain similitude and analogy: according to which, progressing further, we will say that also in our passions we represent something in God, which, although they are not passions in God, yet analogically we call them by the name of passions: such as anger, wrath, and desire...

Nor are we conformed only to the Son, but also, bearing the image of the Father and of the whole Trinity, we can be conformed to them:

Trism.] For God had said (as Moses narrates), "Let us make man in our image and likeness": Trismegistus, echoing this doctrine, expresses the Trinity, whose image we bear, not under the names of persons, but with other terms, saying: "But the Father of all, existing as intellect, life, and splendor, created man similar to Himself: to whom He rejoiced as a son: for he was beautiful: and bore the image of his father:" This Father is intellect,
[Marginal note: Theol.] having (as theologians say) essence as its object: The Son is life, as He Himself teaches, when He says: "I am the life": The Holy Spirit is splendor, indeed, He is fire itself, shining and inflaming: To all these we are conformed by right understanding, right life, and right love: And they are conformed to Him in certain particulars, which Scripture is accustomed to call by the names of members through analogy, concerning which let us see in detail.

**On the harmony of the members of God and man. Chapter XXXIIII.**
[Decorative initial V] What then are the members in God, to which man can be conformed, we shall survey by sketching rather than by painting, bringing forth from many things some which sacred scripture attests concerning this matter:
[Marginal note: Antiqui] and the ancients described them in the type of a super-exalted tree: For all, both rational creatures, and the Redeemer, and God Himself, are called trees,
[Marginal note: Moses.] as Moses hints in his garden of delight, which he describes as planted and filled with diverse trees, that is, with many kinds of ranks and conditions of rational creatures: But in the middle, the tree of lives is said to be placed, from which all life, both angelic and human, and whatever other life there may be, emanates and flows: and in which all things live, and lived before they were unfolded into their proper forms, as John says: "What was made, in Him was life." There also is said to have been the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which (unless I am mistaken) is Christ man, who alone simultaneously and once tasted the good of blessedness and the evil of our passions.
[Marginal note: Theolo.] For (as all theologians exclaim) there was no one else who was simultaneously blessed and a wayfarer, except Christ Jesus: Whose rank was forbidden to Adam, all others being granted. Hence, by a great mystery, the wicked, who are to receive Christ's harsh sentence, are said to be placed at the judge's left; while those who are to obtain mercy are placed at the right. Therefore, the left arm had been revealed to the fathers in the harsher law; but the right arm has been opened to us through the Son of God, concerning whom Isaiah, wishing to prophesy, cried out: "Lord, who will believe our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord [Marginal note: Isaias] been revealed?" or "through whom has it been revealed?", as the Hebrew truth has it: Certainly through Him, or above Him, who ascended like a shoot from a thirsty land, namely, the Jewish people then made dry by their sins. **OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**
**IT IS PROVEN BY REASONS AND AUTHORITIES THAT**
**ALL THINGS HAVE SOMETHING IN THE ARCHETYPE**
**to which they correspond. Chapter One.**

[Large decorative initial S] The most proven and no less common dogma of the wise is that all created things pre-exist prudently in the artisan, and not by chance, the artisan creating: In the same way, a house in an architect; so also a speech pre-exists in an orator; nor otherwise offspring in the begetter and pregnant one: So this machine of the universe in the supreme progenitor God, as a creative life, presided, to whose measure it would form all members. For number, weight, and measure, by which all things are numbered, established, and measured (as Augustine most wisely teaches), are not in the things produced, just as neither the measure by which cloth is measured, nor the weight by which heavier things are weighed, nor the number by which all things are numbered, is found in the things measured, established, or numbered, but undoubtedly outside them. Therefore, number, weight, and measure, by which all things are measured and weighed, are necessarily outside all those things. And since there is nothing outside all produced things except God himself, it remains that in Him are number, weight, and measures.
[Marginal note: Prisci. / Theolo. / Abrahã] Therefore, the Ancient Theologians most excellently and elegantly celebrated that most ancient dogma, first (as it is said) revealed by the patriarch Abraham, by which we are taught that measures and enumerations are in the archetype, by which all things are arranged and numbered.
[Marginal note: August.] And concerning these things, Augustine most excellently continues, saying: In God are numbers without number, since all things that are in Him are God himself, the unique one. And there is weight without weight, by which the Creator himself is not burdened, but established, allowing all other things to be moved and finally established. So also our soul is a certain number
[Marginal note: Academ.] and rational measure, called so by the Academics, by which we measure all things to be understood and done by us, so that we may be able to avoid error, foolishness, and deformity in our works. Nor indeed would this harmonious fabric of the world, balanced by due weights, subsist unless numbered and weighed by its Creator and Governor. So neither would a house or a Republic enjoy its peace and tranquility, unless it were governed by him who rules it: Whose measure and balance is in the governor, to whose standard all things entrusted to him are arranged. Necessarily, therefore, in blessed God are understood measures and enumerations, by which He measures and numbers all things,
[Marginal note: Ecclesia. / Dauid / CHRI / STVS.] as it is read in Ecclesiasticus: "Who has numbered the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the world?" "Who has measured the height of the sea, and the depth of the abyss?" unless, of course, that creative and governing wisdom, concerning which it is also sung in the psalm: "Who numbers the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by their names." But also, "He numbers all the hairs of the head," as it is said in the Gospel.
[Marginal note: Ezechie. / Ioan.] But by what measure the Creator measured this worldly house, we are seriously taught by Ezekiel and John, of whom one with a reed of six cubits and a palm, the other as

--- Page 392 ---
**SEVENTH TONE. 127**

Indeed, he reports that he saw the city measured with a golden reed, or this worldly house, as we will discuss more broadly in its place. To Belshazzar also it was said through Daniel: God has numbered your kingdom, and finished it: so that it is also hinted that the course of life is numbered, beyond which we cannot transgress, just as Job speaks with open mouth, saying: [Marginal note: Job] The days of man are short, and the number of his months is with you: you have appointed his bounds, which cannot be passed, though they may be shortened. Also, the merits and misdeeds of all are numbered, so that they may be rewarded and punished in due proportion by Him who speaks through Zechariah, saying: [Marginal note: Zach.] I will measure Jerusalem, that is, the soul (as it is explained in a moral sense), and I will see how great is its length and its breadth. Which Christ states more clearly, saying: [Marginal note: CHRIST.] With what measure you have measured, it will be measured to you again. And through another Evangelist he says: [Marginal note: Luke.] Give, and it will be given to you: A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, will be given into your bosom, for with the same measure that you have measured, it will be measured to you again. But the misdeeds of men are said to be weighed with a double measure, namely, a greater and a lesser. The greater is compared to mountains, when it is said: Your justice is like the mountains of God: [Marginal note: David] Which by the Hebrews is called Din, which signifies a hard and strong judgment, so that no one can be justified by it, as the Prophet says: Enter not into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for no living person will be justified in your sight. And in Isaiah [Marginal note: Isaiah] it is said: We have all become unclean, and all our righteousness is like a menstruous cloth. With which Gregory agrees: [Marginal note: Greg.] "All human justice," he says, "is proven to be injustice, if it is strictly judged." But concerning the lesser justice, the prophet Micah [Marginal note: Mich.] says: Is there yet fire in the house of the wicked, and treasures of iniquity, a lesser measure full of wrath?

Also, the charisms granted to us are called a measure, and faith given, as the Apostle says to the Romans: [Marginal note: Paul] As God has distributed to each a measure of faith. And again to the Ephesians: [Marginal note: The Same] To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. He also declares there that we will have a perfect and determined measure of the body to be resumed in a happy and blessed state, when he says: We shall all come to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. Also, the spiritual body and its members are measured, [Marginal note: Ibid.] as he added a little later, saying: Speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together by every joint with which it is supplied, according to the working in the measure of each member. From these and many other passages of sacred scripture, it is proven that measures and weights exist in the archetype, by which all lower things were measured when they were created, so that each one might stand harmonious in its own degrees, and now also they are weighed and pondered, so much so that there is nothing in creation, or that is done, which does not correspond to and is not examined by those eternal measures, and each thing exists and acts only as much as has been granted by those supernal measures, and they receive for deeds well or ill done only as much as has been decreed by those measures to be fitting. But let us descend to the correspondence of particular things.

**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

To whose majesty prime matter responds harmoniously. Chapter II.

[Decorative initial O inside a square frame depicting a landscape with a building] To God the highest, who makes all things and is the first act, so that omnipotent matter and the first receptive potency may respond, it is fitting that between those two extremes all intermediates should result, from Him who is omnipotent in leading all things, and from that which is most disposed to receive all things. Concerning their agreement, Eusebius Pamphilus discourses elegantly in his work on the Triad and Monad. "To the first being," he says, "matter is always opposed: for the former alone acts, the latter alone suffers; the former alone moves, the latter alone is moved:" Which, as the receiver of all species, some physicists have called "pandoche"; but Pythagoras and Empedocles, with the Peripatetics, called it "sylva"; Plato, however, called it the formless receptacle, mother of the world, container, subject, nurse of forms, and a potency capable of all of them, just as God is potent to make all things, the shaper of all these same things, the first efficient cause in all things, the father of the world, a fount flowing in all things. And again they said that matter is the receiver and expeller of all species, just as the Creator distinguishes them according to divine and causal exemplars. This is non-being, and the passive principle of beings, just as God is the active principle of all things, existing in all things and outside all things. From which it has images, and obscure manifestations, and exact representations of the first being: whence every essence is led to action through potency, and rightly so: for things placed diametrically opposite to each other project certain images of similarity. The first being, incomprehensible to the intellect, also constitutes the extreme (matter) incomprehensible to the intellect: And if anything of them can be apprehended, it will be discovered by negative reasoning: For the first is defined by negation, as Dionysius teaches, that it exists as none of the beings, but as the efficient cause, and better than them. By negation also is the other extreme defined, that it exists as none of the beings, but is inferior to them. The first is most simple, and the last is also most simple. But the latter vacillates, leaping from species to species, while the former is always the same, and always acting, just as the latter is always receiving as long as successive generation endures. The intermediate intervals, however, are found to be less and more perfect by participating in both extremes, the more they approach one of the extremes. Hence Zeno of Citium, son of Mnaseas, posited two principles of things, God and matter: of which he said the former was the cause of acting, the latter of suffering. But Plato and Socrates added a third, the idea, namely in the divine senses and visions of God, or in the divine mind, or word: as our Theologians are accustomed to say, which nevertheless is the same. But here the sequence of things must be observed. Matter and its pure potency respond to the omnipotent Father: whence not without mystery Moses introduces God as the creator and maker of this matter, which corresponds to Him without any intermediate cause. But other produced things he recounts through intermediate causes, yet by the command of the first parent and supreme maker: so that the production of matter, and matter itself when produced, differs from the production of other things, and from those things brought forth into light: so much so, that Timaeus Locrus and Plato do not—
