With which the earth is established. Chapter III.
[Large decorative initial E] We have revealed that all elements are found in the heavens, angels, and God, each with its proper mark: Now, however, it occurs to us to explain with what harmony these same elements agree with the archetype. For indeed, the paternal mind is most fruitful of all, so that it might produce those two offspring, namely the Son, and simultaneously with Him the Holy Spirit: by whom it produced all other things of this universe, and the whole globe itself: Which filial offspring, having completed the decreed course of times by itself, it gave for the salvation of the nations. Concerning this, Isaiah, [Marginal note: Isaiah] conscious of these Sacraments, prayed, saying: Let the earth be opened, and let it sprout a savior. [Marginal note: Theologians] Our Theologians interpret this concerning the blessed virgin, the Hebrews concerning the ultimate measure of the archetype (which they call Shekinah, that is, the mediated and domestic habitation of God in us). But (if I am not mistaken) it can rightly be understood concerning the paternal mind: which is primarily the first producer of the Son, and consequently of all other things. For concerning the Son, who is called the Word and Truth of God, the Prophet [Marginal note: David] sings: Truth has sprung from the earth. Who is also called the water of salvation gushing forth from the same earth. This earth, therefore, is receptive of all fecundities, and consequently, as it were, the first parent, also generative of all things: so much so that (according to Plutarch) [Marginal note: Plutarch. Physicists. Moses.] physicists believe that God auspiciously began the creation of the world from the earth as from a center, and the mother of all. Which Moses also indicates, narrating the production which God commanded to be made, having laid the elemental foundations, saying: Let the earth bring forth green herb, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after its kind. And just as these earthly [Marginal note: CHRIST.] trees, unless they are planted in the earthly element, certainly do not live: so concerning the better, and rational tree, the supreme Truth says, that unless it is planted by the Father, the supreme farmer, namely in that supernal earth, it will be uprooted. This earth also stands eternally, never torn from its center, nor destined for another place, while all other elements and elementary things are agitated by a certain succession, and seeking diverse spaces. And that paternal mind is always stable in itself, neither sent, nor moved from its center, even if the Son, the Holy Spirit, and all intelligences are said to be sent to execute diverse things. Again, the earth is the center of the universe: and the Father is the center of the intellectual sphere, existing everywhere through His essence and power: but appearing with open presence in the celestial palace, as their earth and habitation. To which the Prophet, [Marginal note: David] sighing, said: I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

With which the other elements resonate in the same way. Chapter IIII.

Moses.] saying: All things were made through the Word. And this is what Moses said on the part of the commanding Creator: Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing, or the brood of a living soul, and the flying [creatures].

Judgment belongs to the Son, who says: The Father has given all judgment to me. Ardor [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] however is referred to the Holy Spirit, who perfects and cleanses those things which the Son had moistened by purifying and washing: To this ardor corresponds this elemental fire, which cooks raw things and heats them: which purifies gold and other metals, and melts diverse things into one: which finally transmutes one nature into another; thus it cooks and seasons those raw and dreadful things: so that they can be presented as dishes of God at the table in a heavenly and deifying symposium. For when he spoke of the Samaritans beginning now to whiten and to be cooked like harvests through the disposition of the Holy [Marginal note: Idem.] Spirit, he said: I have other food to eat, which you do not know, namely, the prepared souls of the Samaritans: and which were already being cooked within by the operation of the Deifying fire: It heats and expels all coldness of sin and fear, because grace cannot coexist with sin. And charity, if it is perfect (says John), casts out fear. The power of that sacred [Marginal note: Ioan.] flame in the time of the Apostles melted the hearts of the people hearing those inflamed words, so that soon for all there was one heart and one soul. And it melts so much that it cannot be separated, as Paul says: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? That fiery spirit [Marginal note: Paulus] poured into us also purifies all the dross of sin and concupiscence.
It also transmutes, so much so that it rendered a shepherd boy and lyre-player into a most exquisite prophet and Psalm-writer. It fills fishermen, and constitutes them teachers of nations, and lights of the world. It pours over the persecutor Paul, and changes him into a vessel of election, and into Paul. It happens therefore, that as many as are turned from evil into good, it is by the benefit of this heat. But air (as Abraham teaches in the book on for- [Marginal note: Abrahā] mation) is not numbered among the elements: but is held as a medium, glue, and bond connecting diverse things together: therefore it rightly corresponds (to use his words) to the spirit, which is of the spirit. But lest pious ears be offended, thinking that two holy spirits are asserted, we will say that it agrees with the power of the spirit uniting all things that seem discordant, and resounding in all the pipes of the worldly instrument. And this is what is said through Ezekiel: And the spirit [Marginal note: Ezechf.] of life was in the wheels. And what is taught here about the worldly instrument, Paul teaches about the human instrument, [Marginal note: Paulus] while he says: But the same spirit divides to each one as he wills. And in many places it is held that the Holy Spirit fills men, who is called fire, because he purifies and melts. But air because it connects, binds, glues, and fills all things to be filled by it.

What stones signify therein. Chapter V.

**A**D elements coming, let us begin with stones, which are earthy, and being suited for foundations and buildings, correspond to the Father and the Son. Hence sometimes for one, sometimes for the other, sometimes for both, rock or stone is taken. For the Son showed himself to be the rock, [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.]

R

--- Page 397 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

when he said to Peter: "And upon this rock I will build my church." i.e., upon
[Marginal note: Paulus] himself, as all explain. He indeed is the foundational stone, as the Apostle says: "No
one can lay another foundation, except that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus:" Who also
is called the cornerstone, indeed rejected by those who build according to the flesh and blood:
but placed by the supreme architect in the head of the corner of that structure and building
of the holy Jerusalem, which is built from living stones. He also was that rock
struck by Moses, from which waters flowed for the drink of the Israelite people, if well in-
[Marginal note: Idem] terpreted by Paul when speaking with the Corinthians. "All (he says) our fathers were under the cloud,
all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and the sea:
and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink:
For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, but that rock was
Christ." But if by water we wish to understand the wisdom of God, who is the Son,
as we referred to above: the rock from which that water of saving wisdom flowed, rightly
signifies the Father: Which is called סלע in Hebrew, which we can interpret as strong, or rocky mountain,
or refuge. And who is strong, and omnipotent, and the supreme refuge
of all, except the eternal Father? Nor should anyone wonder that we now take rock for
the Father, now for the Son: because in sacred writings it is sometimes placed for both si-
multaneously. For אבן (even) in Hebrew signifies stone, of which word if the first two
letters are taken, they make אב (ab), which signifies Father: But if the middle with the
last is joined, they constitute בן (ben), which is interpreted as Son. Therefore אבן, which
we call rock, signifies both Father and Son, who are the same, indeed rejected
by those who build and construct doctrines and statutes for the Hebrews, or
Gentiles: who do not confess God the Father, and His Son Jesus Christ: Which
now is called water flowing from the rock, now the very same rock: because it proceeds
from the Father, yet always existing as the same with the Father. But how, and why Moses struck this
rock, and why from that striking God, angered against Moses
himself and Aaron, said: "Because you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me
before the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this people into the land
which I gave them," this matter would require a deeper investigation. He struck twice, with a double
error, namely: One, because he believed less than he ought: The other, indeed,
because he transgressed the command: For the Lord had commanded that they should speak
to the rock: and Moses, with Aaron's consent, struck it: And therefore God complained
that they had not believed, namely that His word alone would suffice, and
that they had transgressed the limits of the command by striking the rock, to which the Lord
had commanded that they should only speak. And this was their sin, not however,
because they claimed for themselves what they ought to have attributed to God, as many ex-
plain. Nor was it a small transgression to carry out God's work through severity (for
striking implies this), which God by piety, so that He might be more sanctified among the
people, had determined to accomplish, commanding that with a pious and sweet word, without striking,
they should draw water from the rock: since the waters of mercy were not to be drawn out

--- Page 398 ---
TONE SEVENTH. 130

through the harsh pipe of justice. Therefore, after they wished to deal with the people with an iron rod (as they say), they deserved to feel the divine, and iron, sentence, by which it was said: "You shall not bring this people into the land which I gave them." Perhaps it would be too long and mysterious for this place to inquire into, to unravel all the secrets that could be revealed about the rock: and why it is sometimes called אבן eben, sometimes סלע selah, sometimes צור zur, concerning which David says in the psalm, בצור bezur, that is, "He exalted me in the rock": which word perhaps also [Marginal note: Dauid] signifies the name of God. But omitting these things, let us come to our topic, concluding that in the archetype, from which all strength and virtue is drawn by any inferior thing, is the idea and virtue of the rock, to which this inferior subjection is suitably equated.

What place metals hold there. Chapter VI.

[Large decorative initial M] Etals, which are watery, correspond to that supreme water: concerning which it is said in Ezekiel: "I will pour upon you living water," [Marginal note: Ezechi.] namely God the Son: who is also called the water of life and wisdom, and full of hidden treasures: which, as a true leader and commander of the entire spiritual army, he most copiously dispenses according to the need of each, giving to all who are newly enrolled in his army a most opulent gift, as it is said through the prophet Hosea: "I multiplied silver and gold," [Marginal note: Osee.] namely, in a gift. But he complains that his soldiers dedicated it to Baal, polluting the divine gifts and charisms, as he continues with a more open complaint in Joel, saying: "You [Marginal note: Ioël.] have taken my silver and my gold: and you have brought my desirable things and my most beautiful things into your temples." Just as we read about Belshazzar in Daniel, who [Marginal note: Daniel] profaned golden and silver vessels and all precious things by abusing them with banqueters, harlots, and gluttons: Whom (alas!) very many imitate, abusing the gift of grace and the gifts of the Holy Spirit in the worst things, forging an idol and a calf of their prostitution, just as those transgressors of old, whom God led out of Egypt with much silver and gold, with which they should have bought necessities and offered for the building of the Lord's tabernacle, forged it into an idol of scandal and perdition. Therefore, grace and divine charisms have been imparted to us through God the Son, true gold and silver: of which God is the rightful owner, who through Haggai [Marginal note: Aggeus] protests, saying: "Mine is the gold, and mine is the silver." Yet he willingly communicates it to us, having a certain pleasing exchange, concerning which it is said in Revelation: [Marginal note: Apocal.] "I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, that you may be rich." Nor do we have anything that we can exchange, except our transgressions, sins, and free will. But sometimes it is freely imparted for necessary food and clothing, so that we may appear in the royal presence and at the heavenly wedding feasts: But if we lose it, woe to us, for being cast out from the wedding feasts, we shall be thrown into outer darkness. And this is what Jeremiah [Marginal note: Ierem.] lamented in his Lamentations, saying: "The noble sons of Zion, clothed in the finest gold, how they have been turned into earthen vessels." And again: "How the gold has become dim." And through Isaiah it is said: "Your [Marginal note: Isaias] silver has turned into dross," namely, with spiritual knowledge obscured, charity grown cold, and charisms defiled or put to flight.

--- Page 399 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

Regarding divine matters. And the heavenly Emperor is the possessor of so much gold that we read in the Apocalypse that even the pavement of the supernal city, rebuilt by Him, is made of gold [Marginal note: Job]. But Job goes further, saying that even the clods of earth of that supernal region are made of gold, so that the earth may agree with the pavement, and with the unique foundation [Marginal note: Paul], who is Jesus the Son of God Himself, as the Apostle says: Upon which He persuades us also to build with gold, silver, and precious stones: Which signified all the offerings that were commanded to be made in the old law. But also, with this treasure imparted to us, He commands that we gain super-mundane riches with five, two, or [Marginal note: Matthew] one talent given to us, as Matthew relates: or ten, or five, or only one mina, [Marginal note: Luke] as we read in another evangelist, threatening most severely unless we take care to increase the money and multiply the heavenly treasures, into which we ought to transform these dregs of treasure.

Nor does this God the Son claim for Himself only the more precious metals that pertain to treasure, but also all other molten and fusible [metals], which are of the same kind, prepared by the craftsman for various purposes, but especially for waging war and preserving empire. For this, iron is necessary for the punishment of evildoers, and for the stable strength of the kingdom and empire of the Son of God Himself: concerning whom it is said in the psalm [Marginal note: David]: The Lord said to me, You are my Son, today I have begotten you: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession: [Marginal note: The same.] And you shall rule them with a rod of iron. And again in another psalm: To bind their kings with fetters, and their nobles with iron manacles. But also concerning [Marginal note: Apocalypse] iron for military matters it is said in the Apocalypse, that a sword proceeded from His mouth, sharp on both sides, namely, for conquering and suppressing rebels. And if the time for vengeance or justice is not at hand, yet iron is still [Marginal note: Jeremiah] sought, with which sins to be punished may be written, as we read in Jeremiah: The sin [Marginal note: Job] of Judah is written in an iron book. So also Job says, That they may be engraved in an iron book.

Bronze is also necessary for casting the vessels of the temple: therefore not without [Marginal note: Exodus] mystery are all the vessels of the tabernacle commanded to be made of bronze in Exodus, similarly also the [Marginal note: 3 Kings] vessels of the temple, and the sea (molten sea), as we read in the third book of Kings: Which very abundant bronze holy David, who bore a most elegant type of the Son of God, full of the Holy Spirit, receiving from the cities of Betah and Beroth of Hadadezer the Assyrian, prepared for casting those vessels, the sea, the altar, and the columns. Indeed, he took bronze from the Assyrians, who are interpreted as merchants, a good merchant: so that he might convert it to a better use, [Marginal note: CHRIST] and to the ministry of God, as the highest Truth teaches, saying: Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, namely, by exchanging this bronze, iron, and these stones, which are called precious, for those of the supernal city: in which not only gold, [Marginal note: Deuteronomy] but also precious iron and bronze are found, as Moses speaks typically in Deuteronomy, saying: Its stones are iron, and from its mountains bronze is dug. For neither in this lower land, which is called Canaan or Charam, possessed by that wandering people according to divine promises, are there (as we know and have seen) iron stones: nor is bronze or any metal dug from its mountains: whence concerning a better region—

...or a servant, a citizen, or a countryman, an artisan, or even a woman: For both sexes are found as much in trees as in living beings: And sometimes God plants them most beautiful even in the celestial paradise: and sometimes He uproots them, as He says through Jeremiah [Marginal note: Jer.]: "Those whom I have planted, I uproot." But through Ezekiel [Marginal note: Ezek.] the whole series of a tree planted in the garden of delights, and irrigated, nurtured, and uprooted, is described under the name of Assur by a certain hyperbole, as Jerome [Marginal note: Hiero. Ezechie.] understands it: For Ezekiel says: "Behold, Assur, like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in branches, and leafy in foliage, raised on high: The waters nourished him, the deep exalted him, its rivers went around its planting, and it sent its streams to all the trees of the field:" Therefore it was exalted and raised above all the trees of the field: And it describes that tree as so lofty that in paradise, where it was planted, neither cedar, nor fir, nor cypress, nor any other tree of God's paradise could be compared to it. But lest it trust too much in such great height, he adds: "According to its impiety, I cast it out, and strangers shall cut it down:" And pursuing many things concerning its ruin, he finally adds: "Behold, I have made you descend with the trees of pleasure to the lowest parts of the earth:" From which we are taught that even those planted with whatever sublimity in the paradise of delights fall, just like the first man, and those intelligences that fell: since no one can stand or be raised by himself, as the supreme Truth says: "If anyone (He says) [Marginal note: CHRIST] does not remain in me, he will be cast out like a branch, and will wither, and they will throw him into the fire, and he burns." Therefore there are vegetable trees: there are human trees: there are angelic trees: and there is a supreme, and divine tree. Nor do these vegetable trees flourish, nor do they produce fruit, unless endowed with life and fruitfulness by the supreme [tree] through intermediaries. Nor do human or angelic trees live, or are they stable, unless preserved by that which alone is stable in itself: and from the same they draw life, and are irrigated from that supernal fount, from which comes all good: as Job [Marginal note: Job] relates concerning angels, saying: "Behold, those who serve Him are not stable, or do not believe, that is, firmly: and in His angels He placed change," which some have interpreted as depravity, but others as splendor. And concerning human trees, the supreme Truth said: "He who remains in me, and I in him, [Marginal note: CHRIST] bears much fruit: because without me you can do nothing." Therefore all inferior trees have that supernal tree, to which they correspond: and from which they receive life, growth, and fruits: concerning which it is often hinted in sacred scriptures under the type of these inferior ones. Therefore, concerning that [tree] and other lofty trees (as I believe) taught by the prophets, Plato [Marginal note: Plato] in Phaedrus, speaking through the person of Socrates above human paths, describes that higher and purer world, separating at the same time all things produced for human use from this common condition. For he asserts that those things are purer and more perfect: and that there is true heaven, and true light, and also true earth: From which, if anyone should come to this earth, stones, trees, flowers, fruits, and suchlike, which are cultivated by us, all things would seem gnawed away and corrupted by a certain saltiness of this sea. He also declares how great the difference is between that contemplation which true Saturnians, and from the crowd se-

inspired, and divine men have, and that which they possess who, entangled in earthly cares of this kind, are contaminated by falsehood, that is, by the wisdom of this worldly sea. For there are (he says) there trees, flowers, fruits, mountains, Sardian stones, Jasper, Emerald, and other things of this kind: of which these (things here) are certain deformed particles, and to the contemplation of these, and clear intuition, we arrive dead, as he very openly revealed above, not indeed by the death of the body, but through a complete sequestration of the senses, and purgative virtues from everything external and alien. But until all those things are offered to us to be seen with clear intuition, and to be contemplated with unveiled face, through these lower things a discourse must be held among us, from which we may be able to hint at supermundane and divine things, and finally, by the auspices of these (lower things), to be carried up to those (higher things), not unmindful of our lot.
      With which our plain may be made equal.            Cap. VIII.

[Decorative initial letter 'IN' in a square frame with floral motifs]
      IN the celestial region there are not only stones, metals, trees, and fruits, to which we can be led by these lower things, but there is also a flat, and mountainous, and rough terrain: and it is fruitful, irrigated, and cultivated: and conversely, wild and arid, just as this lower world is divided. For we see this earth as tripartite, of which one part is flat, habitable, and irrigated: another is desert and arid: the third, however, is mountainous. And some of the mountains, especially the hills, are fertile and rich: and some are deserted and arid. But for now let us proceed concerning the plain, which the Psalmographer testifies is found in that supernal region, saying: He who ascends, or rides upon the plain, the Lord is His name: for which a faulty translation has "setting": For ערבות, that is *haravot*, signifies pleasantness or a plain: which our translator renders "setting," perhaps thinking that word comes from ערב, which denotes evening and that hour when the Sun tends towards its setting: But this (haravot) is pointed with two *segol*, while that (erev) is pointed with *patah* *het* *qamets*, and they differ entirely in meaning. Well then, the Prophet says that God rides upon pleasantness and a plain: since He is most blessed in Himself, containing nothing rough, nothing bristly. But others (and perhaps better) interpret that *haravot* as the empyrean heaven, supremely flat and smooth: in which neither swelling of stars, nor anything humped or rough is found: but it is entirely flat, entirely pleasant, and delightful. But if we wish to ascend still higher to the supermundane plain, namely, we shall find that just as there are supercelestial waters which continually praise the Lord, and waters, and divine fire, as we touched upon above, in like manner, in that archetype, there are plains from which all pleasant, smooth, sweet, delightful, and enjoyable things proceed. And this among ancient Theologians is called the supermundane southern region,      Ant. the.
concerning which it is sung in the Canticles: Tell me, where you feed your flock, where you rest at noon. Et   Canti.
And again: Awake, O south wind, and blow upon my garden, that its spices may flow out, and all delightful things: From which quarter comes He, at whose advent (as Isaiah together with the Baptist testifies) the crooked were made straight, and the rough places into plain ways. came the Redeemer, if Habakkuk truly foresaw, who said, "God מתימן that is, from Teman

All of which John touches upon, saying that He Himself is light and truth, and that grace was made and diffused through Him. And just as He came from the shining South and a smooth plain, so by His followers this smooth path must be followed, namely, of peace, gentleness, patience, quietude, equity, piety, and equanimity, so that (if it were possible) nothing harsh, nothing horrid might be found in them. Hence He commanded injuries to be forgiven, peace to be proclaimed and brought to all, [Marginal note: CHRIST]
all things to be patiently endured, saying: "Blessed are the merciful, Blessed are the peacemakers, and blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake." Indeed, He also commanded all instruments of war and occasions for fighting to be laid down, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, who says: "And they shall beat [Marginal note: Isaiah]
their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up [Marginal note: CHRIST]

Hence He Himself, teaching better by deeds than by words, stood as if mute before those who sheared Him, not opening His mouth, and like a lamb led to the slaughter. Which so many true Christians observed, who for three hundred years, and more than that, endured innumerable kinds of martyrdom with an undisturbed spirit: Among whom neither murmur nor complaint resounded, for they had become imitators of that true Lamb placed at the right hand of God, who was led silently to the sacrifice, not opening His mouth in blasphemy, insults, or any complaints: But alas, unhappy times, when among Christians only the name remains, with all Israelite, indeed Christian, gentleness and mildness put to flight; the pruning hooks and plowshares, into which swords had been beaten, they have again beaten into spears and very sharp and harmful javelins, having become like Esau and the Idumaeans, rough, horrid, and contentious above all nations and peoples, so much so that neither in temporal nor in spiritual matters do they ever cease from disputes, everywhere addicted to perpetual contentions, so that Christ [Marginal note: The same.]
no longer recognizes them as His own, but says to them: "I do not know you," and excludes from the most peaceful, gentle, and pleasant kingdom those who have always pursued rough paths and a harsh life. "We possessed (said Moses in his typical discourse) all the cities [Marginal note: Moses.]

mountains, and their inhabitants are commended in sacred scriptures; therefore, what these

        By what means mountains are exalted.        Chap. XIX.

**A**ll the chosen sons of Israel, entering the land of promise, possessed not only plains, but also mountains, their inhabitants having been conquered and expelled, as we read in
[Marginal note: Iosue] Joshua, where it is said: And Joshua took all the mountainous and southern land, and the land of Jesse, and the plain, and the western region, and the mountain of Israel, and its lowlands, and part of the mountain which ascends Seir as far as Baal-gad through the plain of Lebanon below Mount Hermon, distributing each and every thing to those tribes and families, as it is pursued in a long discourse: All these things happened in figure to those fathers, who held the type of those entering the true land of promise under the leadership of Jesus, whose figure Joshua preceded. For the heavenly land (as we have said) is a true plain, where there are also mountains, both irrigated and arid, and both are necessary. Of the former it is sung in the
[Marginal note: Psalm.] psalms: Watering the mountains from his upper chambers, or his heights, just as these material mountains are watered by higher clouds: but these do not produce spices like those, of
[Marginal note: Cantic.] which it is said in the Canticles: Flee, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of spices. Nor do they distill sweetness like those, of which
[Marginal note: Ioël.] Joel says: And Jerusalem shall be holy, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, when the number of the elect is complete, or its gates are opened by the Redeemer, so ordered that strangers shall not pass through it, and in that day (as follows) the
[Marginal note: Canti.] mountains shall distill sweetness, and the hills shall flow with milk, just as it says of the whole land of Zebi, that it will flow with milk and honey, not indeed with milk that is pressed from the udders of goats, cows, and sheep, but from those exalted udders, of which it is said: Your breasts are better than wine: Nor with honey that the busy bee extracts from flowers, but with that, of which it is again said: Honey
[Marginal note: Dauid Salomon] and milk are under her tongue: And by David in the psalm: He satisfied them with honey from the rock, that is, with honey flowing from the rock, which is God: For צור, that is Zur, which we have translated as "rock," perhaps signifies the name of God. Therefore those mountains yield both milk and most sweet honey and most fragrant spices: therefore he yearned for them, who said: I will go to the mountains of myrrh. There is, however, among them a preeminent mountain, to which the most merciful God himself often leads us by his kindness,
[Marginal note: Isaias] provided we carry out what he has commanded us: as he declares through Isaiah, saying: Those who keep my Sabbath, and hold fast to my covenant, I will bring to my holy mountain,
[Marginal note: Dauid] and from this, as from a treasury of all treasures, David asserted that he obtained what he sought, saying: He heard me from his holy mountain. And this mountain is sometimes taken for a host, and sometimes for a dwelling place. Of this again the
[Marginal note: Idem Itidem.] Prophet sings: Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? And elsewhere: Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy mountain? God himself is also a host, the supreme mountain, whose summit is
[Marginal note: Isaias.] raised to an immense height. There is also the exalted mountain, Messiah, of whom Isaiah open-

--- Page 406 ---
**SEVENTH TONE. 134**

he says in his sermon: And it shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above all hills; and all nations shall flow unto it: and many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, that is, to Christ, and the Church, and he will teach us of his ways: and we will walk in his paths, for out of Zion shall go forth the law, where he poured out his Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, who suggested to them all things that were contained in the law.
It follows: And the word of the Lord from Jerusalem: For the eternal Word of God, made human, frequently spoke in Jerusalem, and in that temple of Jerusalem. This mountain, therefore, was also sometimes called a plain, when in his advent he made all rough places into smooth paths. But it was also called a mountain, exalted above others, because of the eminence of its nature: the fullness of grace, and the summit of virtues and merits. There are also other intellectual mountains, who, as ministers, assist and serve the supreme mountain, of whom Isaiah says: The mountains and [Isaias] hills shall sing praise, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands. For stony and earthly mountains do not sing, nor do combustible trees clap their hands, but rational trees and mountains, of whom again in the psalm: The mountains shall exult together [Psalm.] before the face of the Lord, for he comes: And again: The mountains exulted, or leaped [Psalm.] (according to the Hebrew truth) like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep: All these things refer to the higher mountains, hills, rams, and lambs, whose image they bear, and to whom they correspond, if they are to be rightly understood. There are also evil mountains, great in strength and malice, as the Lord speaks in Jeremiah, saying: [Ierem.] Behold, I am against thee, O destroying mountain, or desolate, or corruptor: says the Lord, who corrupts the whole earth: I will stretch out my hand upon thee, and roll thee down from the rocks, of which you are composed, and will make thee a burnt mountain, where, according to the wise man's saying, the mighty shall mightily suffer torments. [Sapien.] And to Satan, who opposed Zerubbabel building the temple, the Lord says through Zechariah: [Zacha.] Who art thou, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel? But the Lord easily demolishes and scatters these, either by himself, or through mountains chosen by him, as he says to Isaiah: Thou shalt thresh the mountains [Isaias mō-] and beat them small: and shalt make the hills as chaff. And into the lot of these mountains was placed Seir, that is, Sehir, given into the possession of Esau, and the chiefs who came forth from his loins, that is, of the carnal man and all things that pertain to him, as is described in Genesis under a figurative account in a long discourse. For this is indicated by the name Sehir, [Genesi.] which signifies not only that mountain, but also a whirlwind, baseness, evil thought, evil mind, crime, hair, goat, and the devil, not without mystery: To which mountain had ascended he who was the head of all rebellion, baseness, pride, and evil thought, saying: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north. And these are mountains deservedly to be explained, as Isaiah infers concerning [Isaias] that prince of arrogance, saying: Nevertheless, thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the lowest parts of the pit. And in particular concerning Mount Seir, the Lord says through Ezekiel: I will give [Ezechie.]

OF THE FIRST CANTICLE

Mount Seir desolate, and I will take away from it him who goes and him who returns. And concerning this whole
[Marginal note: Abacuc.] multitude, Habakkuk says: The mountains of the world are broken, and the hills of the world are bowed down by its eternal ways. By these mountains of the world, demons are
[Marginal note: Hieron.] understood (as Jerome thinks) who raise themselves against the knowledge of God, and by the hills, other demonic strongholds, which make men admire the beauty of bodies, dignities, the riches of the world, nobility of birth, and other good things of the world. And with these demons and princes of darkness, puffed up and darkened evil men, and they themselves with the princes of obscurity, are called misty
[Marginal note: Ierem.] mountains, concerning which the Lord says through Jeremiah: Let not your feet stumble on the misty and darkened mountains. For these are the mountains and high places where the incense of pride is offered with the greatest indignation of God, as the Lord laments with manifold
[Marginal note: Regum] complaint in the books of Kings, both concerning the people still sacrificing on the high places, and concerning the kings who had not removed those high places. These are also the
[Marginal note: Hiero.] mountains and high places where Saul (as Jerome says) killed the priests of God, puffed up and elevated by the desire to reign against God and against David, when God himself had already handed over the kingdom. For he was in Gibeah, which is interpreted as "high place" or "elevated." From these mountains we must turn away, as from those that will most swiftly fall and be reduced to nothing,
[Marginal note: Apocal. Dauid] whence in the Apocalypse we read that when the cup of God's indignation is poured out, mountains are not found, as also the Psalmist speaks under the figure of a tree, saying: "I saw the wicked greatly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of God, and I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found."

There are indeed also other mountains for us to ascend, namely the pinnacles of
[Marginal note: Pſalm.] virtues, so that we may meet with divine virtue, concerning which the divine Psalmist says: "Your righteousness is like the mountains of God." For in righteousness, which is a common virtue, every
[Marginal note: Dauid] troop of virtues is found. And concerning our virtues, the same Royal Prophet says: "high mountains for deer," that is, the pinnacles of virtues are for those strong
[Marginal note: Hiero. Orige. Canti.] deer who know how to kill the serpent, as Jerome thinks in his commentaries, and Origen in the Song of Songs. But here he adds that mountains also signify eminent cognitions, saying: "One comes leaping upon mountains of high sense and sublime understanding," concerning which it is said: "Behold, here he comes leaping on the mountains, skipping over the hills." And again: "Flee, my beloved, to the mountains of spices." Ascending to which, would that we might deserve, with Elijah and Moses, to hear the voice of the Lord, caressing, teaching, and feeding with that milk and honey with which he fed Moses, and through him
[Marginal note: Ezechil.] all the people from Mount Sinai, so that we may be those sheep, concerning which the Lord says through Ezekiel: "In the richest pastures I will feed my sheep on high mountains." Thus Christ from Mount Tabor fed the three Apostles with such sweetness that Peter, forgetting all other things, exclaimed, saying: "Lord, it is good for us to be here." He also fed from Mount Zion all the Apostles and those who were with them with the supreme food of his Holy Spirit, with which he so refreshed them, suggesting all things to them, that, drenched with a blessed fullness and spiritual intoxication, they proclaimed the mighty works of God in various tongues to the peoples.

And for this reason, and others to be passed over for now, the royal prophet celebrates this Mount Sion, saying: "Mount Sion, which I have loved." [Marginal: Dauid Psalm. Psalm. Psalm.] And again: "The Lord loves the gates of Sion." And again: "The God of gods shall be seen in Sion." And elsewhere: "The Lord has chosen Sion, He has chosen it for His dwelling." Thus in many other places. But also through [Marginal: Isaias. Ioëlis. Abdias Ioan.] Isaiah, the Lord Himself says: "I will give salvation in Sion." And in Joel: "I am the Lord your God, who dwell in Sion." And from Obadiah: "In Mount Sion there shall be salvation." John also in his most famous vision: "I saw the Lamb standing on Mount Sion, and with Him a great number of those who were sealed, to all of whom was imparted from His fullness, which we all receive." But (as I think) he speaks of that supreme Sion, to which this lower one, existing in the middle of the world, is perpendicularly subjected, so that from both, the true mediator and supernal fount may distribute to all manna, honey, milk, the water of wisdom, and all good things: so that we may possess not only the plain, but also the irrigated mountain, that is, the eminence of glory and of degrees in that meridian of graces, and Gessem, a region, namely, drenched and moistened by those supernal channels and streams, or that supernal rain, of which in the psalm: "O God, you will set apart a voluntary rain for your inheritance," [Marginal: Psalmus] for Gessem is interpreted as rain. Let us also possess the Plain, and Haravah, of which we spoke above, and the countryside, and the mountains of Israel, not indeed wild and arid, but fertile and excellent, and that part of the mountain which ascends Sehir: For Mount Sehir is the summit of worldly prosperity given to Esau, a part of which was also given to Israel, although a portion of divine things was given to him as the cord of his inheritance, yet they were not destitute in temporal goods, which are called goods of fortune: Which goods true Israelites did not possess separated from their patron, who is God: but together with Him, who said to Abraham: "I will be your exceeding great reward." And of whom the prophet said for himself and [Marginal: Genes. Dauid.] his Israelites: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." Therefore, Joshua pointedly said that their part extended to Babalgad, which is interpreted as "patron" or "lord of fortune." There are also arid and desert mountains, which come into lot with the arid land, of which we shall speak presently: Therefore, we shall pass through such dry mountains with dry foot, even to the uncultivated and infertile wilderness, where we shall treat of both.

What is desert, and arid. Chapter X.

[Decorative initial V] Since there is nothing in this lower world without its presiding intelligence (as many wise men agree) and without an idea or measure in the archetype, to which it corresponds and by which it is governed, it is fitting that even the desert and arid places, even those fashioned by the hand of the Lord, should have their intelligences, and something in the supermundane court, by whatever name it may be called: from which they receive their aridity, or are excluded from the irrigation of the supreme fount, from which comes all true irrigation. Therefore, the desert (to begin with the etymology of the word) is a place destitute and abandoned by celestial favor, just as the Hebrew word, which is מדבר, that is midbar, also sounds, and this is said to be without anything fertile according to the etymology of its language: It is also called arid or dry, as be-

--- Page 409 ---
**CANTICLE THE FIRST**

nor does the Hebrew word sound like 'waters gathered in one place'. Therefore, when the super-mundane waters are gathered into one place, other places remain with a dry influx, not irrigating nor moistening those things they care for: therefore all those places remain parched and dry, deprived of celestial benefit, as it is sung in the
[Marginal note: Psalm.] psalm: "When you turn away your face, they will be troubled: you will take away their spirit, which is given by heavenly irrigation, and they will fail, and return to their dust." And
[Marginal note: Leuiti.] in Leviticus the Lord says: "If you do not listen to me, I will give you a heaven above like iron, and an earth like bronze: Your labor will be consumed in vain, the earth will not bring forth its seed, nor will the trees yield fruit." Conversely, however, let us hear what the
[Marginal note: Deuter.] supreme ruler promises to those who do good in Deuteronomy: "The Lord himself says, 'He will open his best treasure, heaven, to give rain to your land in its season: And he will bless all the works of your hands.'" But it must be noted that desert and dry places are of multiple kinds: For some are only deprived of heavenly irrigation, not indeed entirely, because they would tend to nothingness: but some more, and others less, according to the suitability of those receiving, or according to the command of the irrigator.

Some are also dried up not only by the deprivation of the supreme irrigation, but by the Chaldean fire of that furnace, whose flame ascended forty-nine cubits, namely the square of the number of remission and punishment: and such places are so parched that they become habitations for Tartarean citizens, just as
[Marginal note: Ioannes] John says in the Apocalypse concerning Babylon, deprived of heavenly favor and consumed by its own fire: "that it has become a dwelling place for demons, and a prison for every unclean spirit." No less does God threaten concerning another Babylon, and wretched Rome,

Through all these, diverse kinds of unclean spirits are understood: The prince of these is עזאזל, that is, Azazel,
[Marginal note: Leuiti.] for whom we have, I know not in what sense, 'emissary' translated in the book of Leviticus. Therefore, to this one dwelling in the desert, and to the prince of desert spirits, was sent the goat of lot and sin: and it was commanded to be released there not without great mystery, namely, that sin, and whatever pertains to it that is dry and bristly, might be released to the devil dwelling in the uncultivated wilderness and squalid desert. also in the Gospel we have that the desert is the seat of evil spirits, with Luke [Marginal note: Luke.] narrating that that wicked man, vexed by a spirit, with broken chains, was driven by a demon into the desert. Also said to dwell in the desert are those who are deprived of heavenly irrigation, either serving sins, or expurgating them through penance, not yet worthy of heavenly dew. Therefore it is notably said in Genesis [Marginal note: Genesis.] that Ishmael, expelled from Abraham's house, and serving with bow and arrows, dwelt in solitude in the desert of Paran. And for those not yet well initiated and disposed to heavenly showers, it is said that John the Baptist preached the baptism of repentance in the desert, where the boy (he) dwelt, not yet well-sprinkled. And Moses, already a partaker of heavenly influences, fed the flock not within the inner chambers, but beyond the desert. But also through the desert he led the entire Israelite people, bearing the type of all those who strive through penance to ascend to the super-heavenly homeland. Christ also, the example of all, and leader of penance and the beginning of evangelical life, wished to act in the desert, where he was led by the Holy Spirit: so that he might fast, and enter into battle with the prince of this desert world, and (with those) abandoned by super-heavenly irrigation. Thus also David, a figure preceding Christ himself and the future church, before he came to the kingdom (which prefigured that kingdom which is within us), dwelt in the desert, he himself, and the men who were with him. In the desert is also every soul newly entering into the prison of this body, where it is abandoned by wisdom, virtue, knowledge, and the performance of good works, according to that of Zephaniah [Marginal note: Zephaniah.]: "And he will make the beautiful (place/soul) into a solitude and a wilderness, as in a desert." But the more the soul is separated from the desert of this body, the more it is disposed to heavenly influence, and is filled with an abundance of all fragrant good things, like spices: as it is said in the Song of Songs [Marginal note: Song of Songs.]: "Who is this who ascends from the desert, like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh, and frankincense, and all the perfumer's powder?" But also, seeing her fortified by the favor of the most beloved Son of God, from whose fullness we have all received, again it says [Marginal note: Ibidem]: "Who is this who ascends from the desert, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved son?" And sometimes she is so imbued with such charisms that it overflows even into the body, which was a desert, as the Psalmist says [Marginal note: David Psalm.]: "The beautiful places of the desert will grow fat." And again: "You have made the desert into pools of water." And through Isaiah [Marginal note: Isaiah.], to the needy and poor seeking water, the Lord says: "I will make the desert into pools of water, and the pathless land into springs of water." But often the opposite happens, that a fruitful soul, adhering to a dry body, is itself abandoned, with Zechariah [Marginal note: Zechariah.] saying: "They have made the desirable land into a desert," a land indeed good and suitable for receiving heavenly seed, so that it might yield a hundredfold fruit. These rebels the Lord hates and abandons, as he himself says through Malachi [Marginal note: Malachi.] concerning Esau, who signifies our animal nature, hated by Him, and to be hated by us. "Esau," he says, "I have hated, and I have made his mountain Seir into a solitude, and his inheritance into dragons of the desert." What of the fruitful earth. Chapter XI.
[Marginal note: Genesis] [N]o one doubts that all earth is dry by its own nature, as it is said in Genesis: The earth was formless and void: And again: God called the dry land earth: and this until it is irrigated by its own springs, as it follows in the same place: A spring ascended, irrigating the entire face of the earth. Therefore, moistened by this irrigation, the earth becomes good, which we have proven above to be of many kinds,
[Marginal note: Job] elemental, human, celestial, angelic, divine, and infernal: which by Job is called the land of misery and darkness: where the shadow of death, and no order, but eternal horror dwells. But setting aside this [earth] as always dry and scorched by eternal fire, let us pursue what is fertile and whence it is irrigated. For this elemental earth is only fertile as much as it is irrigated by supernal springs, not indeed by common rain only, which descends upon sterile mountains, rocks, dry land, and entirely into infertile sand: but from superior waters, and celestial, and supercelestial ones. For the fruitful earth does not receive natural fertility from elsewhere, as we can easily prove from many places of sacred scripture, but from very many I will adduce even a few. Therefore Moses says
[Marginal note: Deut.] in Deuteronomy: If you hear the voice of the Lord, he will make you abound in all your works, with the fruit of your womb, the fruit of your livestock, and the fruit of your land, which the Lord swore to give to your fathers, that he might give it to you. The Lord will open the excellent treasure, heaven, that he may give rain to your land in its time.
[Marginal note: Ezechi.] And through Ezekiel he says: I will give a blessing around my hill, and I will bring down rain in its time, and there will be rains of blessing: And the tree of the field will yield its fruit, and the earth will yield its produce.
[Marginal note: Zacha.] Also in Zechariah he says: These things I will do for the remnant of this people: the vineyard will yield its fruit, and the earth will yield its produce, and the heavens will give their dew. And if he does this, as in many cases, through causes

What are fountains? Chapter XIII.

[Decorative initial N] O much labor is not required of us to declare that God is a fountain, since He Himself proclaims and complains in these words: "They have forsaken me, the Fountain of living waters, the Lord." [Ierem. Dauid] This also the royal prophet and he who was privy to divine secrets have testified: For one says: "With you is the fountain of life." But the other introduces Him saying: "To the thirsty I will give from the fountain of living water freely." [Ioan.] Which fountain (as it says a little further down) sent forth a river proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb. But Isaiah testifies that there are many divine fountains, [Isaias.] saying: "With joy you will draw water from the fountains of the Savior." Which fountains are the Father Himself, the first origin of all things, the Son of God Himself, and also the Holy Spirit: And He, although He is fire, nevertheless sometimes takes the name of a fountain or a river. From which John, explaining that word of the highest Truth: "It will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life," says, "But this He spoke concerning the Spirit, which those who believed were to receive." Or fountains are (as Jerome explains) evangelical teachings and divine words, [Hieron.] which wash and purify souls better than the waters of a fountain wash the body, according to that saying of the Savior: "You are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you." Concerning these fountains, the prophet says: "In the churches, bless God the Lord from the fountains of Israel," [CHRISTVS. Dauid] that is, of that universal Israel, concerning whom it is said: "I have not come except..."

It is also a fountain sealed with the seal of the living God teaching it, so that it is not without mystery said that the sum of the law, comprised in ten precepts, was written by the finger of God. But sometimes (alas!) the fountains have dried up, the supreme fountain withdrawing its influx, [Marginal note: Peter.] of whom Peter says: "These are fountains without water, and clouds agitated by a whirlwind, to whom the mist of darkness is reserved forever," after they delighted in the aridity and dryness of broken cisterns, having abandoned the fountain of living waters, may He continually nourish us by watering us with His clemency.

**What are rivers, or channels. Chapter XIV.**

[Marginal note: Solomon] [Large decorative initial F] That rivers have their origin from the sea is most clearly evident from the testimony of Scripture, Solomon saying in Ecclesiastes: "All rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full, more indeed than it was, or it does not overflow, as our translation has it. To their place the rivers return: and behold, they return to go." For they return to the fountains, so that they may flow again, and they return to the sea, from which they have their origin. In these rivers fish are generated, and from them regions are irrigated, and to

--- Page 418 ---
**TONE SEVEN. 140**

...for navigation, being passable, they are useful to men through various services. Indeed, great are the mysteries of rivers: For the sea and the infinite ocean is God Himself, and fountains are of multiple kinds: but rivers are rational souls emanating from that very sea, and returning to the same. But these elemental rivers flow and reflow with perpetual course and circuit: while those better rivers, signified by these, tend once and for all, and with a single course, to their origin, unless the opinion of the Pythagoreans about the transmigration of souls is true, which the Catholic faith does not admit: [Marginal note: Pythag.] Concerning these rivers, it is sung in the psalm: The floods of the Lord have lifted up, the floods have lifted up their voice: the floods have lifted up their waves. [Marginal note: Psalm.] For neither are the Eridanus, Danube, Tagus, Nile, Euphrates, or Indus called rivers of the Lord, but of lands and regions: nor do they cry out, or lift up their voice. Therefore, these are the rivers of the Lord, endowed with mouth, tongue, ears, eyes, and hands: concerning which it is again said: The rivers shall clap their hands: And their impetus gladdens the city of God, while through the earthly channels of this body they have flowed from the eternal sea to the fountains, from which, still through earthly channels, but openly operating publicly in the body of the world, they return to the sea itself, giving in their passage due fruits: irrigation to the land, generation to fish, and passage to navigators, not suffocation, not inundation of lands, not ruin of buildings: Because those doing this are not called rivers of peace gladdening the city of the Lord, but Babylonian rivers, concerning which it is said in the psalm: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, and wept: [Marginal note: Psalm.] Because with excessive or disordered impetus they suffocate and destroy: or they are dried up and wither, according to that of Isaiah: And [Marginal note: Isaias] the water shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up, and the rivers shall fail. The streams of the embankments shall be diminished and dried up, and the bed of the river shall be laid bare from its source: and all irrigated seed shall be dried up. He also pursues many things, all of which it would be long to recount and explain. But these dried-up channels are sometimes refilled with the fire of punishing justice, which causes the rivers of mercy and piety to dry up, which the impious do not deserve to receive. There are also rivers of eloquence, as the adage is now worn out. There are also rivers of wisdom, as it is said in plain language in Ecclesiasticus: [Marginal note: Ecclesia:] I, Wisdom, poured out rivers as a conduit of immense water: I am like a river's diorix, that is, a river of a pool, or a derivation, and not a river dorix, as faulty codices have it: and like an aqueduct I came forth from Paradise, and I said: I will water good plantations, and I will make drunk the fruit of my offspring. And concerning Solomon it is again said: [Marginal note: Idem] He was filled with wisdom as with a river. Job also says concerning one seeking wisdom: [Marginal note: Iob] He has searched the depths of rivers, and brought hidden things to light: Which rivers especially [Marginal note: CHRIST,] flow from a land flowing with milk and honey. They also flow from human earth, if the highest Truth speaks truly, when He says: He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly. And these are the rivers, upon which the spiritual world is ordered, as the royal prophet sings, saying: [Marginal note: David] The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof, the world, and all who dwell therein: for He has founded it upon the seas, and prepared it upon the rivers. For neither is this world of earthly things,

**What are pools, lakes, and ponds. Chapter XV.**

[Illuminated initial 'E' containing a figure of a man, possibly a saint or scholar, seated at a desk with a book]
From the sea, springs, rivers, and waters gushing from the bowels
of the earth, sometimes aided by rain, arise ponds, lakes, and pools:
which, however, in sacred scripture are of the greatest difference. A pool,
for example, which among the Hebrews has the name of blessing, is always
auspicious: For ברכה *beraca* signifies both blessing and pool. A lake, however, a name,
as in many cases derived from בור *bor*, which signifies a pit, or a certain place of hell,
is always inauspicious. A pond, however, which in Hebrew is called אגם *agam*,
is sometimes taken in a good sense, sometimes in a bad sense. But ascending
to the better things, which are signified by these lower things, it must be noted:
that a pool, just as it receives water, so also it diffuses it, with no putrefaction
of the waters ever occurring in it. And these are they who communicate the talents
they have received, and profit in blessing, imparting themselves to others, according
to the apostolic saying, where it is said: "I have become all things to all people, that I might gain
[Idem] all for Christ." So also those who communicate the wisdom or doctrine bestowed upon them,
as the highest Truth teaches: "Freely you have received, freely give." And of these speaks
[CHRI STVS.] the Wise Man, who [Salomon] communicated that wisdom which he received by divine gift, teaching and writing.
"I built for myself," he says, "pools of water, to irrigate a forest of growing trees."
But this is the lower pool, of which Isaiah says: "You gathered the waters of the
[Isaias] lower pool." There is also a higher and exalted pool, of which in the same Isaiah
[Idem] God speaks, saying: "Go out to meet Ahaz, you and your son Shear-Jashub,
at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road, or the beaten path of the fuller's field."

**What the Red Sea is. Chapter XVI.**

[Decorative initial M in a square frame with foliage] The Red Sea is not without reason so celebrated in sacred writings, because *Yam Suph*, that is, *suph*, truly signifies a finite sea, or a marshy sea: For God alone is the infinite sea. But other seas, lakes, and pools are finite, determined, and disturbed, or are rendered marshy and muddy, permeated by saltiness, or by earth and mud. And these are the seas we must cross, along with the adjacent desert, so that at last, having passed through hills and mountains, we may reach that clear and most sweet sea, from which true milk and honey continuously flows,
leaving Pharaoh, that is, the destroyer and shaker, with his Egyptians: who are interpreted as distress, or those who cause distress: and they are in that very marsh, which is formed from the mixing of water with earth: From which it becomes marshy, and in many places, a reed-bed: as we have that text well interpreted, when Moses' mother placed her son in the reed-bed on the river bank, where in Hebrew it has *b'suph* (בסוף), which elsewhere we have interpreted as red: and together with *yam*, which signifies sea, it is interpreted as the Red Sea. Yet this reed-bed is not that Red or marshy sea, which is called the Arabian Gulf, crossed by the Israelite people, since it is far from the royal city by a long journey. Therefore, by *Zuph*, it is well interpreted as a reed-bed, or marshy, where (alas, wretched us) we are all placed together with Moses, when, emanating from that most clear and immense sea, we enter this bodily prison, destined to return again to the same supreme ocean. Therefore, we must make a passage through this narrow and marshy sea, but indeed, this one is split: so that we may obtain a free passage, leaving its inhabitants to be enveloped in that mud, and with their most stubborn leader, to be overwhelmed by their marsh, in whose mire they were entangled.

After crossing this sea, the true Pasch, that is, the true passage, with God as our leader, must be celebrated by us with the greatest solemnity, and with the Psalmist it must be said: We have sinned [Dauid] with our fathers, we have acted wickedly, we have committed impiety, while we dwelt in Egypt, in the marshy sea, in the dry land, and in the desert. Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders, nor were they mindful of the multitude of your mercy: Nor do we understand the work which you continuously perform with us, leading us out of this muddy ocean. They provoked, or (to speak more truly to the letter) rebelled against the Red, or marshy, sea: and we rebel in this bodily marsh, which is the cause and incitement of all rebellion. They deservedly praised the great four-letter name, in which they were saved: and we ought to praise the name of Jesus, in whom alone (says Peter) [Petrus.] we must be saved: and in whom the power of that great four-letter name is contained. Therefore, in this struggle with the sea, and the Egyptians, with the dry land, and enemies of many kinds, our Creator has placed us, so that he might make known his power among the peoples, freeing us from manifold snares. And he does this by rebuking this marshy sea of our body, and by teaching us to mortify it, so that it may be dried up from all softening moisture; and foul-

--- Page 423 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

...defiled by mud, leading us through its dry land, and through the desert of penance more happily than through soft luxuries: Those who flee these, and live austerely in solitude, and in [Marginal note: David] that very desert of penance, are saved: as the prophet adds: "And He saved them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of their enemies," who easily succumb in battle against the austere, but conquer against the soft. But those who rashly presume to cross it, trusting in their own virtue, entangling themselves in that marsh, are suffocated, as it is written of the Egyptians: "He enveloped the horse and its rider in the sea," that is, He permitted them to be enveloped, instead of which we have "He cast them out." Whence it follows: "and the waters covered those who troubled them: not one of them remained." This, therefore, is the sea which all those [Marginal note: Paul] fathers (according to the Apostle's opinion) crossed in the cloud and in the sea, namely, being baptized in the highest sense: Which we all also must cross, if we wish to reach the harbor of salvation.

**What are clouds, and rain. Chapter XVII.**
[Large decorative initial D containing a landscape scene] **T**WO benefits are conferred upon us by clouds: One is covering; the other is rain: and both mitigate the sun's intensity: For its excessively excellent light strikes eyes that are less prepared, or not accustomed to such great light: and its drying and scorching heat sometimes burns: Yet both are necessary: For the tempering of these, the highest regulator commands clouds to be interposed for a time, which may suppress the light, and moisten what is dried, and sprinkle it. No less do those better clouds, of which these are a likeness, interpose themselves as veils, when the weak eyes of mortals cannot gaze upon the glory and splendor of the Creator, who is indeed the true sun: Into which [Marginal note: Plotinus] most brilliant spectacle (says Plotinus), if an eye infected with impurities, not yet purified, or weak from idleness, attempts to gaze, it will immediately be blinded, and discern nothing. Therefore, lest eyes thus infected be offended, a cloud is interposed: just as to the murmuring people the [Marginal note: Exodus] glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud, as we read in Exodus. And again: "I will come to you in the thick cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking to you." So also, when Moses ascended to the Lord to the top of the mountain, a cloud covered the mountain, lest common eyes gazing upon the glory of the Lord, which was like a burning fire [Marginal note: Ezekiel] upon the top of the mountain, should be offended. And speaking to Ezekiel, He filled the court and the house, where they were, with a cloud [Marginal note: Kings]. So also in the third book of Kings we read that God, speaking to Solomon in the temple, lest His glory appearing there should offend squinting eyes, filled the temple and the house with mist. In this way, therefore, God presents Himself to inferiors [Marginal note: Psalm.], as it is sung in the psalm: "Clouds and thick darkness are around Him." Which He also observed with the apostles, for when He appeared glorious to them, He sent a cloud before, which might overshadow them, lest their still weak eyes should be offended by the splendor of His glory shining like the sun. Another benefit is that just as we are cooled in body by the covering of clouds when the sun grows strong, so also when the heat of divine wrath rages upon dried-up souls without heavenly dew, the most merciful [Marginal note: Isaiah] judge protects them with a cloud of clemency, just as He speaks through Isaiah to a scattered and parched nation.

**What Dew and Frost Are. Chapter 18.**

[Large decorative initial P depicting a figure, possibly a scholar or saint, seated at a desk with a book] Dew and frost descend from the sky in clear weather, but with a very great difference: For the former is pure, fertile, blessed, and always beneficial; but the latter is ill-omened and harmful, descending with very great cold, and when things are dried up and rivers fail. And it is indeed surprising that the former (dew) nourishes, but the latter, wintry, dries up and burns plants, and in a way consumes the very earth. For thus from the same sky proceeds benefit and harm: For by the sun mud is hardened, and wax melts according to the varied disposition of the recipient. From the most beneficent Christ some received benefit, others harm, according to Simeon's prophecy: "Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel." Finally, from the best God proceeds both good and evil, as Isaiah says: "I am he who makes good and creates evil, making lig..."

hat piety might be diffused into our apostolic ancestors, and that we might be inflamed with the love of Christ, who suffered so many and such great things for us. Hence greater is the sin of Christian priests, teachers, and leading men, who in the multitude of benefits rather become frozen into most savage hail, and provoke the hail of punishing justice, as we read happened to the Egyptians in Exodus and likewise in the psalm: [Marginal note: Psalmi] "And he killed their vines with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost: And he delivered their cattle to the hail, and their flocks to coals of fire." Afterwards, he raged against the five kings of the Canaanites, and their army in Gibeon, as it is written in the book of Joshua, where it is said: [Marginal note: Iosue] "Far more died by hailstones than those whom the children of Israel struck with the sword:" because far more perish from ingratitude, and their own malice, by which the water of graces is frozen into hail, and into their own ruin, than those whom pursuing enemies kill. For sin has it that it is a punishment to the perpetrator, and by its own weight it draws to something else, and brings on God's wrath, and punishment, and lack of charisms, as the Lord speaks in Haggai, saying: [Marginal note: Agge] "I struck you with scorching wind, blight, and hail, and all the works of your hands:" But better according to the truth of the letter: "I struck you with drying up, drought, and hail:" For 'aurigo' is the royal disease (jaundice), doing nothing to the purpose. And thus, wherever mention is made of hail in sacred scripture, you will undoubtedly find it to have been brought forth for vengeance. But those who are less powerful, and less hardened in evil, are compared to small hailstones, and they, that is, come to be punished with a milder vengeance.

Snow, however, which is a soft and gentle coagulation of water like wool, is not read to be given for destruction, nor is it harmful unless it is frozen more strongly; indeed, it is often beneficial, providing nourishment to sown wheat: and it is adorned with such whiteness, that even spiritual things to be whitened are compared to it, as it is found in the psalm: [Marginal note: Psalmus] "You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow." And again: "They shall be whitened with snow in Salmon." And in Isaiah: [Marginal note: Isaias] "If your sins are red as scarlet, and as crimson, they shall be whitened like snow." Also in the Gospel [Marginal note: Euange.] we read that the garments of Christ, when transfigured, became white as snow. And in Revelation, [Marginal note: Apocal.] the hairs of him who was clothed in a long garment are said to be white like snow. Also, those Nazirites in Lamentations [Marginal note: Treno.] are said to be whiter than snow, although the whiteness of spiritual things is purer than the whiteness of snow, even though snow itself holds the highest degree of whiteness among corporeal things. To this (snow) also, as something auspicious, Solomon in Proverbs [Marginal note: Salomon] equates happy things, saying: "As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to him who sent him, for he refreshes the soul of his master." This is brought forth for the Easterners, who are accustomed to keep snow as a faithful guardian of the gift which the highest provider has bestowed upon them, so that in summer and at harvest time they may somewhat cool the sun's fires, and temper their burning limbs, so that they may rest from that fiery agitation. Thus a faithful messenger tempers the anxious cares of his prince: Which also held true for the evangelical speakers, who were sent to that harvest, concerning which the Lord said: "The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few:" From which returning, seventy-two faithful messengers (as

--- Page 429 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

(Luke narrates) with joy about the work done in the harvest, and the prince who had sent them also rejoiced, whence it follows: "In that hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit, saying: I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth," and the rest that follows. Behold how much the Lord was refreshed by the faithful execution of the messengers whom he had sent. Moreover, snow is cold, but its cold, which is preserved in straw filled with good tempering, indeed, rather tending towards warmth, is not a cold that expels the warmth of charity, but rather one that restrains the ardor of concupiscence: and it is cherished by the garment of twofold love, or the charity of God and neighbor, according to that saying of the Wise Man in Proverbs: "She will not fear for her house from the cold of snow, for all her household are clothed with double garments," that is, supported by both charity, or by a good mind and good work simultaneously, as Jerome touches upon in his commentaries. If, however, snow dissolves into water not boiled by fire, it harms: Similarly, if this cold, and the zeal of chastity, dissolves into the flowing water of worldly glory, and not boiled by the fire of the Holy Spirit and divine love, it harms, and condemns, and causes one to return to a greater ardor of concupiscence, according to that saying of Job: "They will pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat." Snow, therefore, is the zeal of good works, which suppresses the ardor of evil concupiscence; let it burn for God and for neighbor, and let it shine with the whiteness of good example, and grow white with purity. Frost, however, since it is frozen snow, indeed signifies those who receive the word of God hard as a rock, whence the power of the divine word itself is frozen for them. And concerning such it is said in the Gospel, where the seed of the word of God is discussed: "Another fell upon a rock, and when it grew, it withered away, because it had no moisture," the power of the divine word being frozen by the hardness of the receiver, so much so that it bears no fruit in them.
