[Marginal note: CHRI STVS.]

**What is ice and crystal. Chapter XX.**

[Marginal note: Sapien.]
<G> Ice and crystal, no doubt, are frozen water, but they differ, because ice is of very easy dissolution, as it is said in the book of Wisdom: "It was easily dissolved like ice." Crystal, however, is so compacted, that with its porosities completely emptied and removed, it can no longer admit heat internally so as to be dissolved. And these too are stored in the treasury of the Lord, and are commemorated in sacred writings by a mysterious type, and are invited to the praise of the Creator by those boys sprinkled with divine dew in the burning furnace: "Bless the Lord, ice and snow:" because they themselves also do his word, and execute the command of the prince. But let us come to man, for whom all things were made, and for whom all these things are commemorated. Ice holds the image of the sinner, for whom the water of divine benevolence is frozen by the cold of sin, and by the north wind, whence all evil is spread and revealed, as it is said in Ecclesiasticus: "The cold north wind blew, and the crystal froze from the waters." But would that this frozen water, transcending the limits of ice, not turn into crystal, so compacted and compressed within itself, that it cannot admit God as a guest, and a stranger...

--- Page 430 ---
TOMVS SEPTIMVS. 146

...foreign heat, nor be dissolved, unless there is a virtue exceeding all the power of nature. However, human ice is resolved by the heat of serene and pure love for God and neighbor, as we read in the same Ecclesiasticus: "As ice in the clear sky, so shall your sins be melted away." [Marginal note: Ecclesia.] But crystal, even if it requires greater strength, yet lest those frozen in the abyss of sins despair, the prophet, full of the Holy Spirit, [Marginal note: David] comforts them, foretelling those things which the Word and the Holy Spirit themselves, sent by the Father, will do for the restoration of the heavenly Jerusalem, saying: "He sends his crystal like a morsel, which is very porous and receives a foreign moisture, making it wet." And wondering whence this happens, which nature cannot do, the prophet himself adds: "Before the face of its cold, namely the crystal's, who shall stand, able to dissolve it?" But immediately, illuminated by holy light, he added: "He will send his word, and will melt it; his spirit will blow, and the waters of tears will flow, and floods of graces into the place of sin, according to that of the Apostle: 'Where iniquity abounded, grace also superabounded.'" But let us pass on to better things.

What is the paradise of delight. Chapter XXI.

[Decorative woodcut initial L] A broad field of discourse has indeed been offered to us: But because those things which pertain to that garden of delights and place of happiness lie deeply hidden from human senses, therefore the Wise describer of it, Moses, [Marginal note: Moses] touched upon a few things under metaphors, always hinting at an anagogical sense, since that garden is not terrestrial (as is commonly said) but celestial and divine, planted by the heavenly farmer and supreme artisan, not indeed in this fertile earth, but in the land of the living, figured by that promised land, of which it is said: "You brought a vine out of Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it; and you [Marginal note: Psalm.] planted its roots, and it filled the land." And lest anyone be deceived into believing that he was speaking of this crude earth, a little further down he adds: "Visit this vine, and perfect it, which your right hand has planted, and over the son whom you have strengthened, or confirmed for yourself." Behold how clearly it hints that that better vine, and consequently all the trees of the sacred garden, are planted in the Son and in the divine Word, which says: "If anyone does not abide in me, he will be cast out like a branch and will wither, and they will [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] throw him into the fire and he burns." And so that we may open something of the hidden mysteries beneath the veil of history, we will briefly touch upon a few things (lest pearls be exposed to the unworthy). For in the Word and Son of God, not only trees, but all things are planted and founded, as John says: "What was made in him was life." With him Paul says: "Upholding all things by the word of his power." Which is also called the book of life by the divine composer: "And in your book all will be written." For there all are described under images and eternal exemplars: But he himself, with all things contained in him, is in the Father: And therefore we are also planted in the Father, in whom he himself is, who says: "As you, Father, are in me, and I [Marginal note: Idem] in you, and they are one in us." Hence we said above that the garden is planted in the Father, since it is planted in the Son, who is from the Father, and from whom (as he himself confesses) all things have been received.

--- Page 431 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

...ceived. And in these are true delights and pleasures, whence it is rightly called paradise, or a garden of delights irrigated by that river of pleasure, of which the divine psalmist says: "They shall be inebriated by the abundance of Your house, and You shall give them to drink from the torrent of Your pleasure," from the fountain, namely, of which it follows: "For with You is the fountain of life." This garden is therefore planted with all trees most beautiful to behold, and most sweet to taste, since all things contained in it are beautiful and pleasant, especially rational minds, which bear His image, although plunged into this bodily mire they may be defiled, yet they may emerge from it more beautiful.

In this paradise not only man, but also an angel was placed, as Ezechiel speaks to the cherubic prince of Tyre, or Assur (who was not a man, but an angel, as Origen says; or a certain strength [Hiero. Ezechi.] of Tyre, as Jerome thinks) saying: "You are the seal of likeness:" Towards which perfect likeness man also strives to attain, when we shall be like Him [Idem.], seeing Him face to face: as He is. Then we too shall be in those delights, in which the cherub had been, of whom the prophet continues: "You were perfect in wisdom, and full of beauty in the delights of paradise." And this until iniquity was found in him, because then it was said to him: "Your inner parts were filled with iniquity, you sinned, and I cast you out from the holy mountain of God: I destroyed you, O cherub:" For the discourse is not directed to him who is placed to guard the tree of life, because this one is one of the cherubim placed above the propitiatory, whence the remission of sins was expected: Which is denoted by that turning sword in the hand of the cherub guarding the tree of life: For man must be turned from creature to God through true repentance, which is called *teshuvah* in Hebrew, and *versio* (turning) in Latin, if he wishes to return to the paradise of delights, just as he had been cast out by turning away from God, and by conversion or (as we better say) by falling towards the creature, and by his fall, just as it is said of another transgressing prince: "You have fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning," [Isaias] or as the truth of the letter has it, "How have you fallen, O howling son of the dawn?" as Jerome [Hieron.] asserts in his commentaries, that that word הילל (*heylel*) comes from ילל (*yalal*), which is an interjection, or a verb of lamenting, just as a little earlier, "Howl, for the day of the Lord is near," has הילילו (*heylilu*). And indeed, it was right for him to howl, when he was cast out from all manner of pleasure to all manner of calamity. It follows: "You are broken to the ground, who wounded the nations." For envy was the beginning of his sin, by which, envying [Sapien.] man who was to be exalted, he tried to destroy him, as it is said in the book of Wisdom: "Through envy death entered the world." Therefore, man was granted a return to paradise itself, because, deceived by some ignorance, and drawn by fragility, he fell. But he, enveloped by no ignorance, nor surrounded by the fragility of the flesh, sinned by his own malice with an unforgivable sin, and entirely against the Holy Spirit. A return, however, is given to us through repentance, and turning back to God, and to the place of delights figured by that land flowing with milk and honey: And the return is figured in that Israelite people, who were first oppressed in Egypt with great suffering for many years under the burdens of mud, and bricks, and carrying

the manifold pressure which we suffer in this bodily mass, especially while we strive to return to God: And we must pass through a muddy and marshy sea, as we said a little earlier. The vine, therefore, brought out of Egypt is the entire number of those to be saved, who are to be led into the true land of promise, and into the land of the living, from which the nations were cast out, concerning whom it is said in the Apocalypse: The great dragon was cast out, [Marginal note: Apocal.] that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan: and his angels were cast out with him, nor was their place found any more in heaven. The elect, however, have been replanted, just as material and vegetative plants are transplanted so that they may produce better: For those who were planted in the Word from eternity, were afterwards transplanted into the Messiah, as He Himself clearly testifies, saying: Just as [Marginal note: CHRISTUS.] a branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me: For I have chosen you, and placed you in my garden, so that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain, and that you may never be cast out of the garden. And this is the garden, or vineyard, concerning which He says again: Go also into my vineyard, [Marginal note: Idem] so that you may work by my grace, just as the first man was placed to work that righteousness, and the light given from the beginning, but lost through sin. And although God the Son is the garden and the vineyard, He is also the tree of life, because He grants life to all: and he who believes in Him does not perish, but has eternal life. He is also the bread of life, as He Himself testifies, saying: I am the living bread who came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Therefore, He is the fountain of life, the tree of life, the bread of life, and life itself. He is also the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, according to what was said above and what will be said below: Which the Devil envied, and by his persuasion, the first man also envied, believing he could obtain a rank granted to no one, and specifically denied to him, when he was forbidden to eat from that tree, as some well interpret that word of Jonah, who bears the type of Christ (by His own testimony), [Marginal note: Ionas] "because of me this tempest has come," indeed, in angels and men: since both presumed to claim that rank for themselves, from which they were cast out. Therefore, paradise of delight is a place and dwelling in the archetype, furnished with all delights, where there are the ranks of all creatures, and in the midst of all, Christ as the tree and fountain of life, and most full of all good things, from whose fullness all receive: Into which the first man was introduced, and all the angels: And after the rebels were expelled, some faithful ones were at some point introduced, to whom access was given to the innermost chambers of the Most High King, as is the common opinion concerning Enoch and Elijah. Nor is it otherwise to be thought concerning Moses, Abraham, and many prophets. To whom the secrets of the Most High God were so revealed that some of them boast that they saw God the King face to face, and Christ, whom they preached would come in many ways. Nor is it less to be considered concerning the intimates of Christ Himself, already destined by the Father for the world, to whom He Himself said: I am the door: [Marginal note: CHRISTUS.] If anyone enters through me, he will be saved: and he will go in and go out, that is, at will into paradise itself of delight: Which is not terrestrial (as is commonly said), but was planted before the creation of the world, as he rightly believes

**Symmachus.** Gan Abeden, that is, "garden of delights": For which Symmachus translated "flourishing paradise".

Thus far Jerome, whom I have cited word for word, lest some, deceived by misuse, should think me to be dreaming when I have said that that paradise is not terrestrial, as is said by scholars, but celestial, indeed divine, into which entrance is given when man, turned away from sin and created things, returns to God with a whole and pure heart: For then he sees God, acquires understanding, possesses the kingdom of heaven, which is within us: and delights in that very paradise. All of which (unless I am mistaken, nor do I think I am mistaken) are the same thing. And this is the turning sword, which the cherub holds for the guarding of paradise itself, namely, turning away: Which if it is from God towards creatures, then it thus expelled the one turned away from the tree of life and from the delights of paradise itself. But if this turning away is from sins and creatures towards God, then through the cherub one obtains remission and return to the same paradise from which he had been expelled. And for this reason, the cherubim were commanded to be placed upon the cover of the ark of the covenant, which was called the propitiatory (mercy seat), because from there propitiations and remissions of sins were made: Which cherub, for many reasons, prefigures Christ, in whom true propitiation and remission of sins was made. And the twin cherub indicates the twofold nature of the same Christ. I omit many things which could be adduced in corroboration of this opinion through the numerical values of Hebrew letters and their interpretation, lest they seem strange and fictitious to those unaccustomed and not having the rudiments of that study: But since insistence is made with the description of the rivers flowing out from there, since they seem to flow through this habitable earth and to have their origin from a terrestrial place, let us therefore see what the rivers themselves signify.

**What Gihon, Pishon, Tigris, and Euphrates flowing from paradise itself signify. Chapter XXII.**

[Large decorative initial 'A' featuring a landscape with a building]
From that fountain of paradise, water is said to emanate, or a river, which immediately divides into four heads: Which, if we wish to understand according to the true sense, we will remember that from that divine fountain of life flows water, namely the essence and being of all things, which by its first division is divided into four elements as into the principal and primary material principles of things: Which river of essence flowed out from delight, that is, from the most blessed Godhead, to irrigate and pervade the entire earth, that is, matter: which, when first produced, was called earth. And it is well said to be divided in its first course into four heads, namely into four elements, with which the names of the rivers also agree: For the name of one is Pishon (פישון), which some interpret as "revolution of the mouth": But it would be better to say "mouth" and "dentition" from שן (shen), which is "tooth": lest we think it changed from שן, i.e., "sana" (healthy), by way of derivation. Hence it also indicates the earth, of which it is said,

--- Page 434 ---
TOMVS SEPTIMVS. 148

¶ it circles all the land of Havilah, which they interpret as 'bringing forth' [or 'parturition'], because the land of Havilah, that is, fertile and fruitful, is surrounded by an arid shore, from which, by those words, both lands are expressed: the arid and the fruitful. And rightly is the earth first expressed as arid, since it is said in Genesis: 'And God called the dry land Earth.' [Marginal note: Genesi] Which would thus remain arid, unless it were irrigated by that river flowing out of the paradise of delight to irrigate (as the text states) the whole earth. Therefore, having received fertility from God according to its capacity, it produces not only herbs and plants (as is clear to all) but also metals and precious stones. Therefore it follows: 'And there is gold, and the gold of that land is good, and there is born Bedolach (הבדולח) and Even ha-Shoham (ואבן השהם).' Some interpret Bedolach as Bdellium, others as crystal or talc; and Aven asobam as the onyx stone. Nor without reason are these three said to be born in the earth, so that, in a few words, it may be indicated what good and evil we have from the earth itself. For we have gold and other metals, all of which signify perishable and contemptible treasures, granted however for our uses, while we sojourn in this defiled earth: and that through them we may acquire heavenly ones. But Bdellium, that is, crystal or talc, are not dissolvable by any heat, as we have proven by clear experience. And the onyx stone is called wondrous, inwardly, around the center, of an earthly color, but on the circumference, of a heavenly color: Which two denote the crossroads of mortals journeying or dwelling upon the earth. For there are those who savor earthly things so much that their mind and their watery soul become hardened, like crystal or talc, over which no fire can prevail. I said 'watery soul,' since not without reason is it said in scripture: 'Let the waters bring forth every living soul.' But especially the rational soul is watery, so that it may be capable of the water of saving wisdom. But sometimes it is so hardened by malice and sin, that it is not dissolvable by any natural heat. But lest mortals thus hardened despair, it is said through the prophet [David]: [Marginal note: Dauid] 'He sends forth his crystal like morsels before the face of his cold; who can endure it? He will send forth his word, and melt them; his spirit will blow, and the waters will flow.' But others are made onyx stones, who, even if they are earthly in their central nature, yet contemplate heaven with their mind and affection, and tend towards heaven. As for the etymology of the river [Pishon], we have said that it signifies a toothed mouth: because while we are on earth, all food which we take with our mouth for the soul, must be pressed, ground, and ruminated by teeth, that is, by certain powers of the soul. And if anyone does not do this, he is considered unclean in the law. The second river is called Gihon (גיחון), and it signifies the breast, which was commanded to perform the office of feet for the serpent: The flowing water holds its likeness, without feet and hands, over the earthly channel, as if with its breast upon the earth; and the water of the sea creeps over the shores in the same manner. This river, moreover, circles all the land of Cush (כוש), which they interpret as Ethiopia, and also 'covered': For Cush (כוש) comes from 'cassah' (כשה), which means 'covered.' For water circles the entire earth, covering and enveloping it all around, except for this small portion which we inhabit. And the name of the third river is Hiddekel (חדקל), which by our people is interpreted as 'tiger': But it comes from 'chad' (חד).

badad, which means sharpens, and `חד chal` (chad kal), which is interpreted as light, so that its meaning is sharp and light: And it denotes air, or an airy spirit, which is light, and more penetrating than fire: because fire can be excluded from entering anywhere more easily than air. And here it anticipates Assur, that is, the rich man, who is inflated by wind and air. Or it goes against Assur, that is, against one who speculates by himself: For Assur signifies both the rich man and the speculator: For he who wishes to speculate on divine things by himself, remains full of wind. And finally that airy spirit will so sharpen the body, already made light by grace, that it can penetrate the heavens, and whatever is opposed to it, better than this thick air.

Coming to the fourth river, Moses says: The fourth river is `הוא פרת hu` (hu perat), that is, *ipse perat* (he, Perat), for which we have, it is Euphrates: For Euphrates is interpreted as multiplying, or fructifying, or fruit-bearing, just as *perat* also means to fructify: Whence it denotes heat and igneous power, which provides fertility to all things, as we prove by experience: For with the arrival of heat, all things begin to germinate, and as it (the heat) intensifies, they ripen: and with its departure, the earth is stripped, and trees shed their fruits and leaves: For the Sun, who is called the father of life, provides life to lower things through heat, and agrees with God, who, being fire, gives fertility and fruit to all things: Which God, containing not only igneous power, but that of all elements, exists as a true source, from which all elemental power emanates. And this is hinted at (as more secret Theologians assert) by the four letters of His great name: For by the first, for many reasons which I pass over in silence, fire is indicated: By the second, which is the mark of aspiration, air: By the third, water, and by the fourth, earth, and all terrestrial things, with which that divine igneous power is united. And this is hinted at in the figure of that letter in which `י` (Yod), which is the first letter indicating divine igneous power (as we have said), is placed in the belly of that letter which is called `ר` (Resh), and imports two hundred, namely, two deduced by a hundred, which is the number of material things. But these things, as foreign to our Latins, and to those not initiated into such matters, we will omit.

The source therefore and the super-excellent sea, from which these four rivers flow, is the great four-letter name of God (as the [Marginal note: Hebrews] Hebrews say) or the power imported by that name, which the [Marginal note: Pythagoreans] Pythagoreans call Tetractys: and it indicates that the divine is fertile of all things, and from which are all things: Which Orpheus and Homer call Ocean, the origin of divine and human things, first always existing, second emanating in the generation of the Gods, third irrigating earthly things, fourth dripping into all fluid matter: Whose emanation again is found by form indeed in angels, by true participation and image in rational souls, by imaginary (participation) in those lacking reason, by shadow in the figures of bodies: Which four-fold emanation is also hinted at by the four-fold animals [Marginal note: Ezekiel] seen by Ezekiel, of which the Lion is fiery: the Eagle airy: Man, especially in soul, and in seed watery, as we have declared elsewhere: The Calf indeed earthy, and always dedicated to the cultivation of the earth: Which elements, composed together, show a single fa-

-ce, and virtue, therefore it is said: Four faces to one, and four wings to one: Of which we have spoken enough above. And because some truth is contained in the literal description of those rivers, it must also be said concerning them, from where they originate, and where they flow, as we have learned from the most diligent Geographers. Pishon (as some assert, to whom Jerome assents) (Geographers) is the Ganges, a river of India, pre-eminent among rivers bearing gold. For these are counted among the gold-bearing rivers: the Tagus in Spain, the Eridanus in Italy, the Hebrus in Thrace, the Pactolus in Asia, the Ganges in India: its source is in the Median mountains, according to Artemidorus. (Artemidorus) And concerning this, the text says: "And the gold of that land is excellent." Gihon, however, which is considered to be the Nile, passing through all the land of Ethiopia and from the furthest bounds of the southern land, flows northward with a wonderful and varied course: For although for a long time its sources were uncertain, nevertheless, in the time of Nero, its origin is said to have been discovered on a mountain in Lower Mauretania, (Nero) not far from the Ocean, where a lake called Hilis stagnates. Then it hides itself for a journey of several days, and again bursts forth from another larger lake in Mauretania Caesariensis: And again received by the sands, through deserts of twenty days, it is carried to the nearest Ethiopians: Then it springs forth into a fountain, which is called black: From there, separating Africa from Ethiopia, it cuts through the middle of the Ethiopians by the name Astaplus, which in the language of those peoples means "water flowing from darkness." And here it forms many islands, the most famous of which is Meroë, named after the city Meroë, founded by Cambyses, and called by his mother's name: And finally, reaching the Egyptian sea through many mouths, it makes Egypt itself an island in the shape of the Greek letter Delta (Δ). Here, therefore, it originates in Africa, separated from Asia by the Arabian Sea, in which other rivers draw their origin: For the Tigris, which flows towards the Assyrians, originates in the region of Lesser Armenia from a conspicuous spring in a plain, where it flows more slowly, being called Diglito up to the borders of the Medes: then it begins to be called Tigris, because it seems to fly like an arrow: for the Medes call an arrow "tigris". And it flows into Lake Arethusa: and from there, carried along, meeting Mount Taurus, it plunges into a cave, and having flowed beneath, it bursts forth from the other side of it: which place they call Zeroarda. Then it crosses another lake, which is called Thesbitis, and again it plunges into subterranean channels, and after twenty-five miles, near Nymphaeum, it is returned so close to the Arsanias, that they flow together, but do not mix: for the lighter Arsanias floats on top. Soon, after a space of nearly four miles, divided, it plunges into the Euphrates. And finally, flowing with a vast channel, it is carried into the Persian Sea through ten mouths. The Euphrates, however, is said to originate on Mount Pariedrus in Greater Armenia, running through the same region, it distinguishes Greater Armenia from Cappadocia, and flows into the Arabian or Persian Gulf (which is called the Red Sea). Hence no conjecture remains as to how these four rivers could have the same origin, since they appear to originate from very distant places. Nor are there lacking those who assert that all of them have a single primary origin, but that they run through subterranean passages to different places, from which they seem to begin their course. What the Jordan, and the river Ieor of Egypt. Chapter XXIII.

[P]ost those four elementary rivers, from which all things consist, two other rivers are celebrated in scripture, one in the holy land of promise, which is called Jordan, and the other in the reprobate land of Egypt, named Ieor: Which, with great mystery, signify propitious and unpropitious emanations from the supermundane tribunal: The sign of which thing is, that all things done in the Jordan were good and beneficial: and those things done in the Ieor, on the contrary, were unpropitious and harmful. For in the Jordan were placed memorial stones of the passage of the children of Israel coming from Egypt and from the Moabites: In it Naaman the Syrian was healed at the command of Elisha: In it Christ was baptized, and John, who, preceding Christ's baptism, had himself also baptized in it. Therefore, from this and other causes, it is sung by the prophets, especially by the Psalmographer, in many places. In the Ieor, however, many evils are commemorated, perpetrated to the destruction of various people: For there the infants of the Hebrews were seen to be drowned. Afterwards, those waters, [Marginal note: Psalm.] by God's command, through Moses, were turned into blood so foul-smelling that the fish died, and the Egyptians were afflicted when they wanted to drink them, and that putrid gore spread throughout the entire region. It also brought forth frogs, which covered that Memphitic land, and finally, having died, collected into immense heaps, they infected the entire surrounding air. Therefore, the water of the Jordan is beneficial, while that of the Ieor, on the contrary, is harmful and destructive. But let us come to the names, which ought to be consistent with the things themselves. For Jordan is written in its own proper Hebrew idiom ירדן (yarden), which, reversed, makes נדרי (nederi), that is, "my vow", namely, a spontaneous offering which everyone makes of himself, wishing to perfectly serve God: With this offering made, all things succeed propitiously and happily. The other river, however, which was formerly called יארה (yorah) in scripture, was afterwards called היאור (haior) with a letter transposed, a great mystery now to be passed over in silence. But for now, lest we pass over the meaning of the changed word entirely in silence, we will only bring forth יאר (yor): For Ior signifies light, to which word, the letter ה (he) prefixed, according to the property of Hebrew grammar, has the force of an interrogation, so that the meaning of היאור (haior) is interpreted as, "Is it light?" Which interrogative sentence [implies] a negative

--- Page 439 ---
TOMVS SEPTIMVS. 105

implies, so that the meaning is: There is no light, and consequently neither good nor anything divine is there, but it remains named pernicious to those among whom it flows. Yet these rivers both emanate from heavenly tribunals, Jordan from the tribunal of mercy, and Haior from the tribunal of justice, so that in the former the sheep to be placed on the right may be washed, but in the latter the goats to be condemned and punished may be submerged.

What wine, milk, butter, and honey. Chapter XXIIII.

[Ornate initial H] These are not without mystery: wine, milk, butter, and honey, so often celebrated in sacred scripture. And so that we may come expeditiously to the interpretations of these words, which, like other things, are held metaphorically in sacred utterances, wine signifies the wisdom of lower things, milk and butter of higher things, and honey is the taste and sweetness that is had from tasting them. For Solomon was filled with wine and the wisdom of lower things above all who were before and after him, just as he had asked from God, who offered and promised to give whatever he might ask: For he said, "Give your servant an understanding heart, so that he may be able to judge your people and discern between good and evil: For who will be able to judge this great people of yours?" To whom the Lord (said): "Because you have asked for wisdom to discern judgment, behold, I have done for you according to your words, and I have given you a wise and understanding heart, so much so that no one like you has been before you, nor will rise after you." Nevertheless, although he was full of that wisdom, he still seems to seek another, grieving that he could not obtain it, as he says in his book of sermons, which in Greek is called Ecclesiastes, and in Hebrew Kohelet: "And I applied my heart to find wisdom." And again: "I thought in my heart to withdraw my flesh from wine, so that I might transfer my mind to wisdom." For from what wine does he withdraw his flesh, if not from the wisdom of earthly things, which do not well agree with heavenly things, just as neither does the wisdom of both? For this wisdom of lower things is signified by wine, born from an earthly vine, that is, from human intellects, although sometimes it is bestowed by God, as we recently said about Solomon: But that (wisdom) of divine things is offered from those exalted breasts, about which it is said in the Song of Songs: "Your breasts are better than wine." And this teaches the true discernment of good and evil, as it is said in Isaiah about Christ: "He shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know to refuse the evil and choose the good." For no one will know how to make a distinction between good and evil in cow's butter, but in that better wisdom, which is figured from above by the better part of milk, from which butter is made. And because for acquiring this wisdom, a separation of the better man from the animal (part) is required, and a certain ecstasy of the mind, which is called the "death of the kiss" by more secret Theologians, therefore, aspiring to it, he prefaces: "Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth." But why this better and divine wisdom is compared to milk, while that lower (wisdom) to wine, I deem it necessary to explain. For wine is drawn from a plant, but milk from an animal, which is better. That (wine) also intoxicates, but milk not at all, although both nourish. Wine also, when preserved and exposed, does not easily change;
[Marginal note: Ecclesia.]
[Marginal note: Isaias]
[Marginal note: Theolo.]

--- Page 440 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

or is corrupted: But milk, the longer it exists outside the udder, the worse it becomes, and most easily undergoes corruption, just as the wisdom of divine things and the secrets of God, the more it is revealed, the greater harm it suffers, like blood outside the veins: Therefore, it is to be communicated only among the perfect, and preserved in the heart according to that prophetic saying: "I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you." But if milk is pressed into butter, it is preserved for a long time, but boiled, for longer. So too, divine wisdom, pressed and well-formed in the mind of its possessor, and boiled by the fire of love, is preserved for a long time, even as a seasoning for other foods, namely those teachings given by true teachers. But because both kinds of wisdom are good, provided that the wine-like wisdom is directed towards God, and is not perverted in a woman's heart, as was permitted in Solomon, lest anyone [Marginal note: Isaias] trust in it: And that both are given by God, Isaiah testifies, who in the name of God himself says: "All you who thirst, come to the waters," that is, to saving wisdom, "and you who have no money, hasten, and buy wine and milk without any exchange:" because, of course, they are given by God's generosity without any suitable recompense: Although both wine and milk are good, yet when mixed they are corrupted and putrefy: So too with lower and supreme wisdom. Therefore, whoever wishes to be wise in divine matters, it is necessary that he be stripped of lower wisdom, God speaking through Paul [Marginal note: Paulus Isaias] and the prophet, when dealing with the sending of higher wisdom: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise." In the same way, when someone is too deeply immersed in lower wisdom and cunning, he is stripped of the higher. Therefore Adam was found naked, because he wished to know too much at the persuasion of the serpent, which is called *arum* [ערום], which means naked and cunning: so that we may be taught that the overly cunning is always stripped of divine [Marginal note: Salomon] wisdom: Hence, Solomon, who wished to mix both according to that saying, "I drank my wine with my milk," did not succeed well: But it turned out better and more fortunately for David, who was nourished with milk and honey, just as it was decreed for all the elect, that they should be nourished in a land flowing with milk and honey, as has been repeated so many times in scripture. And if only Solomon had not mixed wine and milk, but had been content with butter and honey with the Messiah, or honeycomb with honey and milk, as is said of the true bride: "Your [Marginal note: Canti.] lips distill honeycomb, honey and milk are under your tongue:" Which happens to all cultivators of that true land of promise.

What is the land flowing with milk and honey. Chapter XXV.

**P**ost we have explained what milk and honey are, it remains to unravel what that flowing land is. For it is not to be thought that God promised a land flowing with cow's milk, or sheep's milk, or bee's honey to his most chosen people, after so many labors traversing the desert, after the most burdensome observance of the law, after many wars waged in the name of the Lord. But there is another land (unless I am mistaken) truly flowing with divine milk and honey, which is celebrated with great renown and frequency in many places by the Law and the Prophets. For it is the promised land of the living, which flows with true milk and honey, for which the divine [person] sighed

--- Page 441 ---
**SEVENTH TONE. 151**

the psalmist, who said: "I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living." Of which that land bore the type, to which the Israelite people were led after a long wandering in the desert: In which, above all regions, the prophetic spirit flourished, and the investigation of the secrets of the law, and wisdom, and the taste of divine things: so much so that that land is called by Daniel צבי Zebi, that is, glorious, as our translation has it [Daniel.], or renowned, as Jerome says, or land of strength, as it pleased Symmachus [Hieron. Symmā.], or pleasant, and pre-eminent above all others, not indeed by the fertility of corruptible things, because (as God testifies in Deuteronomy) [Deuter.] the land of Egypt is more fertile: Nor does it exceed others in breadth or pleasantness, because it is small and quite rugged. It is therefore pre-eminent, glorious, and renowned, because it is subject to the most abundant influence of prophecy, wisdom, and all divine things. For there the Patriarchs were raised, Abraham having been called from Mesopotamia of Syria: To the Israelite people going there, the law, most full of all wisdom, was given, so that the future inhabitants would be suitable for the place: There almost all prophecy was poured out: There very many prophets, powerful in deed, word, and wisdom: There Christ, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom, was conceived, born, and raised: And there he preached, and filled many with wisdom: Nor did he ever depart from that place, except when, still a child, he was taken away into Egypt, so that he might yield to Herod's cruelty. There he suffered, rose, and from there ascended into heaven, he gave the Holy Spirit there to his disciples, who would fill their hearts with all wisdom and all skill in languages, and feed them with milk and honey drawn from the most excellent land. There also was born, raised, and filled with the spirit, he who said: "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth": To taste which sweetness he invited others, saying: "Taste and see that the Lord is good." [David]

But if we wish to ascend to the allegorical sense, and perhaps one more intended by the Holy Spirit, this land flowing with milk and honey is the flesh and body of Christ, from whom flowed both water for the washing of sins, and milk and honey for the true food of life and spirit: indeed, the body itself was shown to us as bread, and the blood as wine. But the milk offered by him is now given to beginners, according to that of the apostle: "To you, as to infants, we offer milk." [Paulus] Now, however, it is given to the perfect, as it is said of the apostles and primary founders of the church under the name of the bride in the Song of Songs: "Honey and milk are under your tongue." [Cantic.] For then honey and milk were under the tongue of the bride, that is, of the apostles, whose assembly Christ accepted as his bride, so that through them he might generate other children, when that spirit of truth poured over them and fed them, so much so that throughout the whole world they spread the milk and honey received from him, that is, doctrine and the taste of divine things. And truly, milk is the food of the perfect, and of those who are children, that is, in cunning and malice, as that chief distributor of milk and honey says: "You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones." [CHRI STVS.] This food is therefore for the perfect, who, according to the king's decree, become like little children, so that they may enter the inner chambers of the kingdom of heaven, where they may be fed with true milk offered from those breasts, of which it is said in

--- Page 442 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

In the Canticles: "There I will give you my breasts." And again: "My beloved is mine, and I am his; he will dwell between my breasts." This milk always follows honey, because taste and delight lead to wisdom and the knowledge of divine things.

**What is Oil. Chapter XXVI.**

[Marginal notes: David, Joel, CHRIST.]
**O**il also is most celebrated in sacred writings, and necessary for many things: namely, for anointing kings, priests, and prophets; for anointing those cereal offerings that were offered; for maintaining lamps; and for healing infirmities. Nor do I believe that priests, kings, prophets, and sacrifices are sanctified by olive oil, but by a better virtue, of which that material oil was a sacrament. Therefore, the better and true oil is a certain divine virtue, indeed, divinity itself, represented by the oil we use.
[Marginal note: Canti.]
And concerning this better (oil) it is said in the Canticles: "Your name is oil poured out," that is, divinity, and the virtue of divinity itself indicated by oil. With this virtue, kings, prophets, and priests ought especially to be filled: Kings, because they bear a special representation and image of God on earth; prophets, because they perform miracles and foretell future events, which is proper to God, as Isaiah says: "Declare to us what is to come, and we will say that you are gods;" priests, because they perform the office of God by judging souls and remitting sins, and because they exist as mediators between God and men. But the middle (as is common in schools) ought to partake of both extremes. And because Jesus was King of kings, the highest prophet, and the greatest high priest, therefore he ought to have been filled with divinity above all, as the Psalmist sings: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." Indeed, it is rightly called the oil of gladness, because there is no true joy except where God dwells. He who serves Him ought always to be joyful. Hence Christ says: "When you fast," that is, when you devote yourselves to God through fasting, "do not be like the sad hypocrites." But
[Marginal notes: CHRIST., David]
rather at that time "anoint your head," so that you may be joyful, that is, according to that prophetic saying: "That he may make the face cheerful with oil." And this is "the cheerful giver, whom God loves." Nor let that evangelical saying be brought forward: "Blessed are those who mourn," because that mourning pertains to the carnal man, which must be taken up so that consolation may follow; therefore it is immediately added: "For they shall be comforted." Therefore, just as by the water of baptism that super-mundane water is indicated, so by oil and chrism is denoted oil, chrism,
[Marginal notes: John, Paul, Peter.]
and that anointing of divinity, about which John says: "You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things." And Paul: "God, who has anointed us, and who has sealed us, and given the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts." By whom also Christ, as man, was anointed, as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: "God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power."

**What are the Palm, Cedar, Shittim wood, Hyssop, and Willow. Chapter XXVII.**

**A**mong plants, however, the palm, cedar, and hyssop are greatly celebrated: the former as the most excellent of all trees, and the latter as the most excellent of all smaller plants. For the palm is so celebrated that in two respects it holds the image of an animal. The first is, because it does not bear fru-

--- Page 443 ---
**VOLUME SEVEN. 152**

It fructifies without coitus, but its branches are impregnated by male buds, as if by a certain seed. The other is because in its upper part it has a kind of brain, which the Hebrews call הַלּוּלָב (hallulab), and the Arabs call chedar or gemar: If this is destroyed, the tree dies, just as an animal dies if its brain is destroyed: which indeed happens to this plant alone among all plants: and it is so famous that in the solemnity of the seventh month, its fronds were commanded to be offered, which the Hebrews properly call כַּפּוֹת (caphot), that is, palms, together with willows of the torrents, and branches of the עָבֹת (habot) tree, which we have translated as "of dense foliage": but Jerome and others wish to interpret that habot as myrtle. And all these things together with the fruits of the most beautiful tree, which is the citrus, or citron, always green, and bearing fruit at all hours, as is the common opinion of the Hebrews, who celebrate that solemnity to this very day with its fruit, which Galen calls citrinum, along with the fronds mentioned above: Emulating these Hebrews, the Lacedaemonians used to crown their gods with those fruits which they call oximala persica, as Aristophanes is the author. Nor is it without mystery that that solemnity is celebrated with this fruit, which is effective against poison when placed in wine that is drunk, as Dioscorides writes. Nor are the other trees without mystery, which made the day joyful in the same solemnity. For the palm (as we have said) holds a quite express likeness of an animal in its reproduction, and brain, and also in that it has a crown of foliage extended around its top, and branches stretched out like fingers, and fruits formed almost in the shape of fingers, whence they are called dactyli, that is, fingers. The pulp of these fruits is also called "flesh," indeed very medicinal and of the highest nutritional value, either from a certain quasi-animal force, or from a Phoebean nature: And it is of such great nourishment that certain Anchorites were content with only that food, just as to this very day many in Africa do not use other foods: And it is a fruit of many kinds, and more varied than all others. Moreover, it is a glorious tree, and has an express symbol of victory, because its branches never bend, but laden, they rise against the weight, as Aristotle and Plutarch write, and as we have learned from experience: Therefore, this is a type, likeness, and sign of glory, just as it has its power from the seat of glory, as is known to those who are initiated in such matters. The cedar, however (as those who deal with plants, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Pliny, sufficiently agree), is that which is called tya, providing the most excellent resin, which is called cedria and cedrium, most useful for toothaches; when inserted into cavities, it subdues them and soothes the pain: It also takes away life from the dying, because it assumes strength when vital heat is added, but it preserves dead bodies incorrupt by expelling and consuming harmful humors. Those who have written about plants also relate many things concerning the cedar, such as that when applied with salt to the bites of a horned viper, it is a remedy: It cures elephantiasis, and it is beneficial to drink a cup of it for lung ulcers. When injected as an enema, it is a safeguard against worms and moths, and against the mange of quadrupeds, dogs, and oxen: and that it burns like a torch. Also, its oil,

--- Page 444 ---
**OF THE FIRST SONG**

That which comes from it is much celebrated, perhaps indicating the source of true oil, namely, the place of divine mercy and piety, to which that tree corresponds: But whether this is the tree [Hebrews] from which the Ark of the Covenant was made, or whether it was a larch, as many Hebrews [Pliny] assert, or a cedar of another kind, from which (as Pliny and others relate) precious tables of nobles were made, we hold as uncertain. But in this all the wise men of the Hebrews agree, that shittim wood and the cedar, which they call ארז erez arezim in their idiom, are entirely the same, indeed a tree most famously sung about by the divine lyre-player [David], because it is, namely, the tree of Adonai, planted by Him in Lebanon, that is, in the true supramundane forest and garden of delights, or in that most eminent pure divine mind: For Lebanon signifies both, namely a forest and white or pure. Therefore, this tree is sacramental, as are the palm and the myrtle, with which, by God's command, the feast days of the seventh month were celebrated: For cedars signify the more eminent saints, and God's chief leaders planted by Him: But palms signify the victories which they achieve in God's warfare: But the myrtle, bestowing in manifold infirmity, a multi-faceted grace of healings, which God bestows on those who overcome. And those legitimately celebrate God's feasts who are planted by the Father: for they conquer and report triumph with the Son, and are beneficial to the needy and succor them with the sevenfold spirit: or (following the theology of the Hebrews) those celebrate the true feasts of God who are beautiful trees adorned by Tipheret and the glory of God, and strengthened by true celestial strength, which is called Geburah, and anointed with the oil of piety and divine benignity for their own and others' health and salvation. To these, however, are added the willows of the brook, not because (as I think) unfruitful trees belong to these, on which the prophet says instruments were hung, lest the songs and harmonies of God be heard over the unworthy rivers of Babylon: [The same] For he says, "In the willows in its midst we hung our instruments." But as far as another meaning, they can agree with those sacramental trees and feasts: for where we have "and willows of the brook," in Hebrew it is said וערבי נחל uehirbe nachal, which can signify "and the delights of inheritance": For ערב harab is interpreted as "willow" and "pleasant" or "delightful." But נחל nachal signifies "torrent" and "inheritance," so that both senses can exist, namely, "willows of the brook" and "the delights of the supernal, namely, and celestial inheritance," of which a taste is made by those who rightly celebrate the true solemnities: Therefore, for those who celebrate thus, the prophet [David] sings: "Exult to God our helper, shout for joy to the God of Jacob: take a psalm, and give a timbrel, a pleasant psaltery with the harp: blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the glorious day of your solemnity." But if the willows of the brook, signified by that hirbe nachal, are understood in another sense, by these are indicated our bodies, which are unfruitful; indeed, we ourselves are barren, unless we are irrigated by the upper waters, and planted beside the watercourses, so that we may be able to bear fruit in its season: Therefore, not without reason are these willows called "of the brook," which are set apart for celebrating the festivities of God. Nor without mystery do these celebrants, now through

benign promise and of the promised thing, and fear of punishing justice:
Which, like two spurs, drive to every good work, or, like bread and wine,
refresh the mind of the worker. But if these two are disordered, and that which
ought not to be loved or feared, is loved and feared, they become spurs driving
to every evil, and lethal food and drink. Hence Augustine adds the opposite
sentence to the former, saying: [Marginal note: Idem] To every sin, love and fear lead: For just

world drive to every evil. Which we can learn from the Savior, who, just as he

those who abuse such things, loving and fearing [Marginal note: Paulus] what they ought not, while

...while through the same wound he obtained for us such grace and pardon. Thus also, leading the mystical body to action, he finally decided to render to each according to his works. And lest man, instead of fearing and loving God, should fear and love the world, He strove to separate him from the world itself with all diligence. And this is what the prophet sings under the type of the vineyard: "You brought a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations, and planted it." For he led us out of the darkness and distress of this world into his wonderful light, from which those had been cast out who were called angels of light, but now are [angels] of darkness.
[Marginal note: David] Or, following the truth of the letter, in which there is 'vine' and not 'vineyard', this vine of Egypt is the human race subject to sin, and confined in the darkness and distress of this world, figured by Egypt: which he shattered, or permitted to be shattered or trampled. For the word 'tasiah' is a present tense verb of the third mood or conjugation, and it signifies not 'you brought out' (as we have in our translation) but 'you permit to shatter, or to trample,' or

--- Page 449 ---
**TONE SEVEN. 155**

invasions and slaughters, which ought to be inflicted by enemies in that vineyard, he said: "Why have you destroyed," that is, "permitted to be destroyed, its wall or hedge, and all who pass by the way, namely diabolical and worldly enemies, harvest it?"
Concerning the former, it follows, saying: "The wild boar, or pig from the forest, which signifies the devil, has exterminated or devastated it:" since it is a demonic animal: whence the devils, who were cast out by Christ, said: "Send us into the pigs, as into a place suitable for them." And concerning worldly enemies, it adds: [Hebrew: רוח שדי] sadai, that is, the vapor, or smoke of the field, has grazed and demolished it: For which we have: "and a singular wild beast has grazed it:" For the vapor and smoke of the field signifies all worldly enticements, which consume and dissipate the human vine, lest it grow for God and bear fruit. Therefore, for the repair of this vineyard thus demolished, the prophet prays, adding: "God of hosts, turn, now look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vineyard: And perfect it, which your right hand has planted, and upon the Son of Man, whom you have confirmed, or strengthened for yourself." But who this Son of Man is, is clear to all, to whom the Father has handed over all power of cleansing and perfecting that vine, as we read in John: "Every branch that bears fruit, he will prune it, so that it may bear more fruit:" [Marginal note: John.] Which, although it is said of the Father, is also understood of the Son, who is one and the same with the Father, and who is now called the true vine, now the vinedresser, and now the lord of the vine and vineyard, also having the power to constrain those who demolish it, and having the right to reward all who work in it. Therefore, either the Father, or the Son himself, has leased this to vinedressers, that is, to ourselves, so that we might work and guard it, rendering due fruits in their season. The vine, therefore, is a tree, which we are: and the vineyard is the place in which the vines are, that is, this world, or the place in which we are planted by the distribution of divine justice, which is the super-worldly vine, by which this lower vine is cultivated and cherished, whose trunk is Christ, and we are the branches, or shoots, bearing as much fruit as we receive from it by remaining in the vine itself, from which we may produce fruit, as the vine itself says: "Just as a branch cannot [Marginal note: CHRIST] bear fruit from itself, unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me."

**What are roe deer, stags, & fawns. Chapter XXX.**
[Decorative drop cap C] We see stags, fawns, roe deer, and goats celebrated excessively in sacred scripture, not only in the Canticles, but in the law, and Davidic hymns. [Marginal note: Exodi.] For in the law it is commanded that the tabernacle be covered with dyed skins of goats: And with the kidneys and fat of any animal forbidden, stags and roe deer are granted to be eaten entirely as clean, as we read in Deuteronomy, where it is said: "But just as you eat the roe deer, you shall also eat the stag." [Marginal note: Deuteri] And again: "They shall eat of them, as of the roe deer and the stag," of which, namely, all intestines are eaten, except the blood: because in it is the soul, which ought not to be eaten together with the flesh, because the soul of an animal does not turn into nourishment for man, but into his depravation, defilement, and destruction (as they say). In the title, however, of the twenty-first psalm, where we have, "For the Chief Musician; upon Aijeleth Shahar" (literally "At the end, for the morning reception"), it is found in the truth of the letter, "For the hind of the dawn." And in many other places, the prophet here celebrates stags so much that we clearly understand them to refer to something better and hidden, just as Origen also agrees, when he says: [Marginal note: Orige.] "The stag, or roe deer, animals indeed according to the reason of nature, which they corporally bear, are referred to certain causes of corporal things, and to those invisible stags seems to apply that which is written: 'The voice of the Lord preparing the stags.'" [Marginal note: Psalm.] For what preparation from the voice of the Lord is there for these visible stags? Or what doctrine from the voice of the Lord ever descended to them? Therefore, stags are spiritual, whose form and image that corporal animal holds, which by the voice of the Lord is disposed to pursue the race of serpents: By that voice, indeed, of the law and of evangelical doctrine, which disposes and prepares stags—that is, those who have truly been made clean by the washing of baptism and by the words of Christ—to fight under Michael, indeed under Christ, against the serpent and that ancient dragon, who is the devil: In which fight, both from labor, and from inflamed zeal, and also from the expelled venom of the serpent, they are rendered thirsty, and desiring the fountain of true water, as it is said in the psalm: "As the stag desires the fountain of waters, [Marginal note: Psalm.] so my soul desires You, O God." Whose young or fawns are those who are newly initiated in the way of the Lord, that they may run to the mountains, of which it is said: "High mountains for the stags." For mountains are the pinnacles of virtues, to which run those who are inflamed with the love of virtue, and ascend above, who have already reached the pinnacle of virtue. In the archetype, however, stags and roe deer represent those divine powers and influences, from which those animals, and men signified by them, receive that by which they can be, and are called stags, or roe deer: Of which sublime stags, the fawns are called by more secret theologians those lower measures, which are beneath those fuller measures of piety and justice designated by stags and roe deer. Through these divine powers, therefore, or divine properties, Solomon adjures [Marginal note: Salomon] V iiij

--- Page 452 ---
**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

the wisest in the Canticles when he says: "I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the fields, that you stir not up, nor awake my beloved." The bond of this oath is, by the tribunal of grace, from which the good are rewarded, and by the tribunal of justice, whence the wicked are punished. Hence, swearing by these and adjuring by all censures and sentences emanating from the supernal tribunals, he submits and binds himself, so that he cannot in any way be absolved, but may receive a reward for the observance of the oath, and punishment for its transgression. And because the lower measures, which are called fawns, are also called breasts, namely those which nursed all the prophets, therefore in the same Canticles it is said: "Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle." What are sheep, and shepherds of sheep. Chapter XXXI.

**S**heep are also always blessed in sacred scripture, so much so that eventually those to be placed at the right hand of the judge, who will receive a reward for their good deeds, are called sheep: and many of those who were raised to higher ranks pastured sheep. For Abel the just was a shepherd of sheep, Abraham the chief patriarch, Jacob a shepherd of sheep, and the twelve sons, princes of the twelve tribes: Who are also taught by Joseph, so that when asked by Pharaoh about their occupation and industry, they should answer, "We are shepherds of sheep, and our fathers from our infancy even until the present." Nor is what follows devoid of mystery: "The Egyptians detest all shepherds of sheep:" For the worldly and evil have always detested those who walk in simplicity in all things, and in the straight way of the Lord, [Marginal note: CHRIST] according to what the supreme Truth says: "If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you:" For Egypt always signifies the worldly and oppressors of the good. Moses also pastured sheep, when he was called by God to accomplish greater things. David was also a shepherd of sheep, when, by the Lord's command, he was anointed king of Israel by Samuel. But what is greater, the shepherd of sheep [Marginal note: The same] is God, and Christ and the Messiah himself, who says: "I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep." But concerning God himself, clothed in no flesh, the Psalmograph says: "You led [Marginal note: David, Ezekiel] out your people like sheep." More clearly however in Ezekiel: "I myself (he says) will seek out my sheep, and I will visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock: and I will deliver them from all places where they have been scattered: I will feed them in the richest pastures, on the high mountains of Israel shall be their pastures: There they shall rest in green grass, and in fat pastures they shall feed upon the mountains of Israel: For I will feed my sheep, says the Lord God." Indeed, sheep are pastured, cattle are pastured, goats and kids are pastured, and pigs are pastured, but no mention is made of these in sacred scripture, because they are entirely unclean: But sheep, cattle, and kids, or goats, contain their own mysteries: For sheep are very simple animals, and always most useful, full of all gentleness, and removed from all harm. Therefore, those who pasture sheep, that is, are meek and simple, harming no one, and always benevolent, are loved by God and exalted: But kids and goats harm the vine itself, provoking-

--- Page 453 ---
**SEVENTH TONE. 157**

...king the vine: Which vine we recently said signifies divine justice, which is diminished and provoked by those who offend God and sin. And therefore, like wanton kids, they are said to be placed on the left hand of the judge, to receive punishment for their misdeeds from Him, just as the gentle and benevolent sheep are said to be placed on the right hand. Therefore, God entrusts His better sheep to the shepherds of these sheep, as to those trained in good deeds and faithful ministers, whom He Himself, as the true and principal shepherd, feeds and governs. Therefore, the true shepherds of the sheep are those who, simple, harmless, and always doing good, follow gentleness and piety. But if kids are to be pastured by us, it must be observed what is said in the Canticles: "Feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds," **[Marginal note: Canticles:]** that is, of the sheep: Beside which tents we pasture the kids when we restrain our anger and passion, and the furious impulses of wantonness, guiding them with sheep-like simplicity: For then the kids, having been pastured and initiated into the ways of the sheep, can, placed with them at the right hand of the judge, await blessing and the reward of good works.

**What are clean and unclean animals, fish, birds, and plants. Chapter XXXII.**

**Q**uatre kinds of living things the Supreme Creator produced for human food: plants and their fruits, fish, birds, and quadrupeds: In each of these kinds, He created clean and unclean, just as among those who eat them, some are clean and some are unclean. For animals and humans feed on plants, but the foods are distinct, as God says: **[Marginal note: GOD.]** "Behold, to you humans I have given every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of the earth, and every fruit-bearing tree, and every tree bearing seed; these shall be for your food." "But to every beast of the earth, and to every bird of the heavens, and to everything that creeps upon the earth, in which there is a living soul, I have given every green herb for food." And so it was established. Therefore, He distinguishes foods, although our translation speaks confusedly of such things: For He gave seed-bearing plants and fruit-bearing trees to man, who has the industry for sowing and gathering: But to beasts, who do not know how to sow, He allotted the greenness of herbs, which grow spontaneously, as the Psalmograph sings, **[Marginal note: David]** producing hay for cattle, which comes from herbs that grow spontaneously, and grass, namely cultivated grass, for the service of men. Indeed, He granted this along with fruit-bearing trees to man, as clean and better: But those wild herbs He tacitly prohibited as unclean, by giving them to animals for food: Which things, spoken enigmatically, indicate that unfruitful works, which have neither seed from which fruits can be sown and gathered, are left to beasts as unclean: But those things which have fruit and the seed of doing good are assigned to man as clean. Concerning animals, fish, and birds, however, making a clear distinction between clean and unclean, He forbade the former and permitted the latter, as we read in Leviticus and Deuteronomy: **[Marginal notes: Leviticus. Deuteronomy:]** For He first distinguishes clean animals from unclean by a twofold sign: Of which, one is to ruminate, or (as it is in Hebrew) to raise the cud: The other is un-

On the other hand, it appears that hostile and evil things proceed from him, who says through Isaiah: I am he who makes good, [Marginal note: Isaias] and creates evil; I make light, and create darkness: Which can be understood thus: Since to create is from nothing, and is terminated at the subject, or matter, which has the nature of evil, therefore it is said "creating evil": And since to make is terminated at the form, which has the nature of good, therefore it is said "making good." Therefore, whatever things, insofar as they decline towards matter, have the nature of evil, and those which approach the highest form more, the more they have the nature of good. And this is what is said in Ecclesiasticus: Against evil is good, against life is death, and against the just man, [Marginal note: Ecclesia:] who is devoted to God, is the sinner always declining to the lowest things. It follows: Thus behold all the works of the Most High, two against two, and one against one, because there is no good in the world without its contrary: For there are angels of light, and angels of darkness: angels of life, and angels of death: a dwelling of light, and a dwelling of darkness: A cup of the clean, and a cup of the unclean: Which indeed were made by God and are good in their order, although unclean to us: Which uncleanness they derive either from a fierce and rapacious spirit, Mars influencing (as the Astronomers say) or Samael, his intelligence, as the Hebrews assert: Or they have it from Saturn, so that infected by bad melancholic humor, they become seats of uncleanness, just as good joy is the seat of a good spirit, indeed of God: From which the prophet [Marginal note: Dauid] says: Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and in many places he teaches to serve the Lord in joy. Or let this influence be from a higher divine power, through secondary causes, favorable or unfavorable.
