**What Jerusalem, Sion, & the temple are. Chapter 34.**

[Large decorative initial S] But if we come to the dwellings of that most sacred region, which is not without reason called the Holy Land, even it, with its adjacent places, are sacramental. And among other places of that promised and figurative region, the most celebrated of all cities is Jerusalem: which by common opinion indicates and prefigures that super-celestial city, in which all the blessed ought to dwell. Sion, however, where was the citadel, and the royal palace, and the priesthood of the prince, signifies the more eminent mansions of that supernal city, which (as CHRIST testifies) are many there. Therefore, the congruence of these must be examined: First, indeed, they agree in name, as is trivial, and also in the meaning of the name itself: For Jerusalem (as is commonly said) signifies a vision of peace, which most perfect vision and enjoyment of peace, and of its prince, is had in that supernal city: Or (as others say) Jerusalem can be translated as "inheritance to them," so that the word is derived from *iaras*, which is "to inherit," and *lemo*, which is "to them": Whence Jerusalem is well called as if *Ierus lemo* ירוש למו. Which interpretation well suits the supernal Jerusalem, in which an inheritance is given to each one, concerning which the prophet DAVID says: "My inheritance is glorious to me." Also the king and founder of this lower city was Melchizedek: and the king and founder, and the chief foundation of that supernal Jerusalem was He who was constituted by God a priest according to the order of Melchizedek. But co-reigning and co-workers with Him in building the city out of living stones are all who, according to the commands of the prince, govern themselves well: so that each one can be called Melchizedek, which means "my king is righteous." This also is situated upon mountains with a temple, and in the middle of the world. That also, upon the revolution of the outermost sphere, having a temple in the middle, erected perpendicularly above this lower temple, as witnesses of no mediocre faith assert: Among these temples is a celestial, or angelic one, responding to both in a straight line: Concerning these three temples the Jerusalemites used to boast, saying: (as is found in JEREMIAH) "The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this!" Yet Jeremiah rebuked them, saying: "Do not trust in lying words, saying, 'The temple of the Lord!'" Not indeed attributing it to a lie that they asserted it to be the temple of the Lord, and this threefold: but because they wanted to trust in the temple without works, which great lie was ingratitude, and a sin all the greater, the more effective was the influx of charisms upon the place, and the temple, and the city, which was preeminent in a region flowing with milk and honey: And in which flowed the milk of prophecy, of celestial hymns, of gospels, and of all celestial doctrine: And in which was the most celebrated temple of God, corresponding to the upper temple described by EZECHIEL, and mentioned by ISAIAH, who said: "The house was full..."

--- Page 457 ---
TONE SEVEN. 159

His majesty, and those things which were under Him, filled the temple. Therefore that place, next to the supermundane temple, was specially chosen by the Lord, who says in Second Chronicles: "I have chosen and sanctified this place, that My name may be there [Paralip.] forever: and My eyes and My heart may remain there all days." He also commanded that all sacrifices signifying the sacrifice of sacrifices, which the high priest Christ offered on the altar of the cross outside the gate of that city, be offered there. Hence it is asserted by Hebrew doctors that the sin committed in Jerusalem, and in the temple fortified with such excellences, and rejoicing in the special presence of the prince, is greater. Hence it was said not without mystery to David ascending from Hebron to reign in Jerusalem: "You shall not enter here, unless you remove the blind and the lame," that is, ignorance and sin. But the holy king himself not only removed the blind and the lame who hated his soul, and were hateful to him (as it was widely spread by proverb: "The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple"), but he dwelt (our text says) in the citadel of Zion, or its fortification, as the literal truth has it, that is, in a special influx by which he strengthened and fortified himself, so that he would not sin: And he called it the city of David, and built it around from the Millo, and within [David], as our translation has it: Or according to the Hebrew truth מן המלוא min amilo, that is, he fortified it from the fullness of charismata. And that the text speaks of a better fortification than that of walls, appears in what follows: "And he went on and grew great, and the Lord God of hosts was with him:" because, namely, he had fortified himself with divine gifts and emanations. But that temple was built after the manner of the ark, or the tabernacle of the covenant, representing both worlds, namely the greater and the lesser, after whose example (as we said) the ark and the temple were built: In these figurative rites, figurative sacred acts were performed until true sacred acts should succeed, which would not be perfected in a man-made temple, but in a better and more perfect one, concerning which the Apostle says: "You are the temple of God" [Paul]. In this, if we perform sacred rites well by purifying it, we shall ascend to another temple, concerning which the Apostle again says: "A tabernacle not made with hands" [Idem] which is Christ Himself: into whom entrance is given to us through the door, which is He Himself: Having entered into Him, and united with Him, we ascend to the supermundane temple, concerning which it is said in the Apocalypse: "The Lord God Almighty is its temple," [Apocal.] namely, of the heavenly city. Thus, therefore, working so that we may deserve to reach the supreme temple, then we shall be able to say joyfully and without falsehood: "The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord it is:" Into which temples may God in His clemency grant a happy entrance.

What Egypt, Babylon, & Damascus. Chapter 34.
[Decorative initial C containing a figure] Since the human race has always been bipartite, namely into the family of God and that of the devil, as Augustine posits in the proem of his volume [August.] 'On the City of God,' and pursues throughout the entire context, it was fitting that in that mysterious and typical region, the sacred scriptures cele-

--- Page 458 ---
CANTICLE ONE

...designate places which would be habitations for both families. And just as Jerusalem with all surrounding places had, without any doubt, been ordained for God's family (concerning which it would be long to narrate in detail), so Egypt, Babylon, and Damascus always sustained that hostile family by which the people of God were often vexed.

Egypt had received a great benefit from the Israelite people, whence Pharaoh called Joseph צפנת פענח Zaphnat pahaneah, which is an Egyptian word found nowhere else in scripture, as Rabbi Salomon says: [Marginal note: Rabbi Salomon.] for which our translation has "savior of the world," but as others wish, it signifies "revealer of secrets": for *zaphan* in Hebrew means "to reveal," but *pahaneah* is purely Egyptian, and signifies "hidden" or "unknown future." But whatever may be about the words, Joseph the Israelite saved Egypt by revealing the secret of the vision, by which those evils had been shown to Pharaoh which were about to come upon his people, thus guarding against them. Nevertheless, Egypt itself oppressed the people for two hundred and ten years, who had descended there under Joseph's auspices. Whence they rightly interpret Egypt, which in Hebrew is called מצרים *Mizraim*, as "distresses" (or "straits"), although some, I know not for what reason, add that it also signifies "darkness": for the Egyptians were always distresses and oppressors of good things.

The Babylonians also, as ministers of God, led captive the best of Jerusalem, their king Jehoiakim also having been transferred to Babylon. Afterwards again they captured King Zedekiah, besieged with his whole army, his sons having been killed, and the temple having been burned: and they held the people captive for seventy years. Damascus also afflicted the people of God many times, but did not lead them into captivity.

Let the difference between these oppressors be noted here, please. Egypt graciously received the people, afterwards afflicted them, and finally dismissed them by force. Babylon led them captive by force, and always acting more mildly, finally dismissed them voluntarily. Damascus, however, harassed them many times without captivity. For Egypt, the oppressor, is the devil, who cunningly receives man, and having received him, subjugates him: nor does he release him, unless he is drawn away by divine power. Babylon is the confusion of the flesh, which, receiving the soul captive, immediately holds it, and confused for seventy years, that is, the common course of human life: But it always acts more leniently, as day by day the soul, which at first was so oppressed that it could understand nothing, is freed from the oppressing and obscuring flesh, so that it may act more freely successively: finally, after the course of life, it is completely liberated, freed from bodily chains. Damascus, however, which is interpreted as "drinking blood," is the world: which feeds only on those things which are according to flesh and blood, sometimes it harasses man, sometimes it dismisses him without harassment: And Damascus is called the head of Assyria, like Assur, which they interpret as "riches," of which, not indeed heavenly but earthly, this world is the head and receptacle.

But the burdens, or pronouncements, or divine sanctions of these places are described by Isaiah: [Marginal note: Isaiah] Which in summary are these: The burden of Egypt, [Marginal note: CHRIST.] that is, of the devil, is that its idols will be moved and will waste away, namely at the coming of Him who said: "Now the prince of this world will be cast out." The burden

--- Page 459 ---
**SEVENTH TONE. 160**

The burden of Babylon, that is, of the flesh which confuses the mind, is that every hand, and heart, and corruptible body will be dissolved, and man will be transmuted for the better, more precious than refined gold. The burden of Damascus, that is, of this world, is; because it will cease to be a city, and will be like a heap of stones: For with the inhabitants removed, all the buildings of this worldly city will be destroyed. Many other things, which are said there, could be brought to this meaning, which we omit, lest we proceed further than is fitting.

**What Arabia, Mount Sinai, and Mesopotamia of Syria. Chapter XXXV.**

[Decorative initial H showing two figures]
It was fittingly in Arabia, which rejoices in Mount Sinai, blessed with frankincense and various gums, that the law was given: Nor without mystery did Abraham, full of the Holy Spirit, demand by an oath given from the elder servant of his house, that he should by no means take a wife, except from his own kindred, which was in Mesopotamia of Syria: Whom Isaac followed, and he himself full of God, commanded Jacob, while blessing him, saying: Do not take a wife from the race of Canaan, but go, and proceed to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's brother, and take for yourself thence a wife from the daughters of Laban, your uncle. Concerning the mystery of Arabia, the Apostle says: Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman, and one [Marginal note: Paul] by a free woman: He who was of the slave woman, was born according to the flesh: But he who was of the free woman, through promise: Which things are spoken by allegory: For these are the two covenants: One indeed on Mount Sinai, generating unto servitude, which is Hagar. Mount Sinai is in Arabia, which is joined to her who is now Jerusalem, and serves with her children. But that Jerusalem which is above, is free, which is our mother. Here it must be noted, how the Apostle says Mount Sinai is contiguous to Jerusalem, when it is distant from it by fifteen days' journeys, with a vast desert interposed. Therefore he does not speak of a local conjunction (because they are separated by a great distance), but of a conjunction of influence, just as the Psalmographer metaphorically says of the dew of Hermon, which descends on Mount Zion, although [Marginal note: David] those mountains are distant by eighty thousand paces. Therefore they are understood to be joined by influence, which is the same on Mount Sinai, where the written law was given, and in Jerusalem, where it was kept with great favor by King David, who amplified the worship of God according to that law itself, and Solomon, who built the temple, and of many prophets, who flourished in Jerusalem and the surrounding places. This law of servitude is figured by the son of the slave woman, who was cast out by Abraham, by God's command, to the wilderness of Beersheba; which is joined to the desert of Arabia: nor is Sinai far from there, where Moses pastured his flock after the desert, as we explained a little earlier. Therefore on this mountain the law of servitude was given to those who came out of Egypt, figured by those who came out of Hagar, the Egyptian slave woman, as the Apostle hints in the words recently adduced. [Marginal note: Paul] And because the same law of servitude was kept in the lower Jerusalem, therefore it is said to be joined with Sinai: because both places were oppressed by the same yoke of servitude, until that new, free Jerusalem descended from above, which is our mother, concerning which John in Revelation says: I saw [Marginal note: John] the holy city, new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, prepared by God as a bride adorned for her husband, that is, to our Father Christ, to whom she was a bride, but to us a mother.

Mesopotamia of Syria, which in Hebrew is called Padan Aram, is a place between the Chaldeans and the Canaanites, blessed more by its lineage than by its location: For from there Abraham and the entire Hebrew nation drew their origin from Terah, who had come from Ur of the Chaldeans to Haran, a place and region which was Padan Aram: And from there Abraham proceeded to Canaan, eventually to possess that region, as a worthy inhabitant of that special place.

Therefore Abraham commanded, saying to his son Isaac, and Isaac to Jacob, that they should not take wives from the daughters of Canaan, whom Noah had cursed with all his posterity, saying: "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brethren." Nor indeed ought a wife be taken from a servile seed for the son of a free woman, or for Jacob, in whose blessing it was said: "Be master of your brethren." Therefore, when the father again repeated the blessing, he said: "Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan," as if implying, "If you mix yourself with a cursed and servile seed, you will not be able to obtain the blessing by which it was said, 'Be master of your brethren.'"

And so both were sent, this one by Isaac, and that one by Abraham, to the land and people of their own lineage, which had descended from Shem, the son of Noah, who was by no means cursed, so that from there they might take wives, from whom they would produce offspring who would drive out the cursed ones and possess that entire region occupied by an unjust possessor: In which, so that it might dwell worthily, that family was expiated by law and sacrifices. But if we wish to transcend to a mystical sense, this lineage came out of Ur, that is, from the fire of the Chaldeans and the Babylonian confusion, and a still small family came, namely Terah, Abraham's father, with his son, and Lot, the son of Haran, and Sarai, Abraham's wife, so that they might come to Canaan. But when they had come to Haran, Terah, Abraham's father, died there, unable to reach Canaan. But after he died, it was said to Abraham: "Go out from your land, and from your kindred, or your lineage, and from your father's house, and come to the land which I will show you." By this context we are taught that that family, in order to possess the beautiful and God-beloved region, ought first to depart from the confusion of sin and the fire of concupiscence, and proceed to Haran, which signifies indignation, anger, or zeal, with which one ought to be armed against sin and evil. But care must be taken lest this indignation be excessive and unbridled, so that one does not die there with Terah: But let him correct it with meekness,

And so that this family of the Amalekites may be shown to be utterly diabolical, it is introduced without a genealogy, just as, conversely, to denote the divinity of Melchizedek, he himself is described without lineage. Also Moab and Ammon, although they were of the lineage of Shem, yet were always hostile to the family of God, and never to be mingled with it. Why then was Ruth the Moabitess admitted not only into the family of God itself, but also into the genealogy of the Savior? This is because that prohibition, which in Deuteronomy commands that eunuchs and those with a mutilated member should not enter the temple of the Lord, except until the tenth generation, and Philistines until the third, was not made for women. But for Moabites and Ammonites, that access is forbidden forever.
[marginal note: Deuteronomy]
Peace and mingling with them are also forbidden as utterly unfruitful, just as can be seen in a plant, whose shoot, if grafted onto the same trunk from which it is torn, produces no fruit at all. Thus, neither can the seed of a son with a mother, nor of a father with a daughter, produce good fruits worthy of the family of God: as happened with the Moabites and Ammonites, who were born from the obscene mingling of daughters with their father. The Philistines, however, came forth from the lineage of Ham along with the Egyptians: For Philistim was the son of Casluhim, and he the son of Mizraim, who is Egypt, and he the son of Ham. This Philistine people, though small, was nevertheless long hostile to the Israelite family, and never destroyed. so much so that some are still considered Philistines, who are called not indeed 'falling' but 'enveloped' or 'enveloping' from פלש *palash*, which means 'to envelop': For with much revolution and varied fortune they fought against Israel, and were enveloped in very many things. But reducing these peoples to a mystical sense, Amalek signifies the devil, against whom a continuous war has been declared for us, as God says: 'I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.'
[marginal note: GOD.]
Moab and Ammon, born of their father Lot, who is interpreted as 'enclosed,' signify the flesh, which is generated from animal spirits and the seminal virtue enclosed in the paternal viscera. The Philistines, however, signify the world, with which we play in continuous revolutions, now freed from it, now again enveloped in it. Hence, against Amalek, and against Moab and Ammon (of whom the first represents the devil, and the latter the flesh), a continuous battle must be waged, and no peace, no concord, no commerce should be had, as commanded by law. With the world, however, sometimes we must fight, and sometimes converse: so that, drawing its lovers away from it, we may lead them into the service of God, just as Christ taught us: who ate and conversed with tax collectors and sinners, so that he might recall them to repentance. We could adduce many other things from natural objects, plants, and stones, mountains, and valleys, particular places, and peoples, through which, as through certain enigmas, the sacred scriptures indicate better things and those pertaining to the spirit. But lest we proceed further than is fitting, let these few suffice out of many.

TONE EIGHT. 163
GOD FILLS ALL THINGS WITH BREATH, AND
a most sweet life. Chapter One.

[Large decorative initial P] AFTER we have shown this earthly home with its guest, arranged with the highest harmony for you, both in enneads and in filled intervals; it remains for us to make its melody heard, which results from the living and unfailing breath of its Maker, who fills all things, in an inexplicable harmony: concerning which Orpheus [says] (Greek: you attune all the heavens with your many-stringed lyre), that is, you attune the whole heaven with your melodious lyre. But going further, Dorylaus Pythagoras says that the world is the instrument of God: Likewise Alexander Milesius with Gregory Nazianzen: The world (he says here) is praiseworthy for each and every species, but much more praiseworthy for the harmony of all, and the structure of the universe, in which there is the highest and most astounding concord from contrariety in the same life and sound, while things are diverse among themselves, and all things agree with each individual part, just as the pipes or strings of an instrument come together in the same sound. Hence the fabric of the world remains (as Timaeus Locrus testifies) most excellent in its very harmony and indissoluble reason. Also one (says Apuleius, emulating those wise men) is the revolution of the earthly sphere, one harmony, and one chorus of stars and other things from diverse occasions and risings: For just as in dances the leader of the song sings a hymn before, and the singing crowd of men and women, with mixed grave and acute cries, resounds one harmony, so the divine mind reveals earthly variations as if they were a single harmony: This co-adaptation and harmony of all things, men (says Augustine in his volume 'On Order') cannot grasp and consider with a weak mind: just as if someone were placed like a statue in the corner of a very spacious and harmonious building, he would not perceive the beauty and harmony of its structure, of which he himself was nevertheless a part, nor can a soldier existing in battle view the order of the entire army: And this is because the soul, dwelling among the lowest things, polluted by the love of inferior beauty, has lost its order and beauty, so much so that it cannot gaze upon the beauty of the universe and the archetype, unless it is again made beautiful and deiform, and recovers its pristine eye, deprived by the thickness of this deadly and darkening gloom: so that, with it purified or recovered, wherever it turns, it may perceive this most harmonious earthly instrument, and, with God modulating, its harmony to be so much sweeter than sound produced by musical arts, as nature and the Maker of nature are more excellent than art itself. If therefore one applies oneself to the first kind of formal music (which Boethius calls "mundane") and inclines one's ears to its foundation, one will perceive in the contrary elements a moderate antiparistasis, and in the things composed from them, a tranquil song led by the highest harmonizer, and

Whence again Job: [Marginal note: Iob] When we have scarcely heard a small spark of his speech, who will be able to behold the thunder of his greatness? Therefore, just as he fills all things, he makes all things resound, for that reason it follows: Under every heaven is his harmony and modulation: That this may be perceived rather by a better eye than by ears, he prefaced by saying: He extends his light over all the extremities of the earth, by which, of course, these recondite mysteries may be seen by the purified. Therefore, in this great instrument of the universe, he resounds in the voices of his greatness: but wonderful harmonies cannot be comprehended by weak intellects, when a purified mind, not only these lower things, but if it raises its ears to the highest interval of this worldly organ, it will feel the concord, and harmony, or peace, which God made (Job himself being the author) in his sublime places: [Marginal note: Idem] Which should be explained, setting aside error, not about the heavens, but about the angels: Whence he then adds: Is there a number of his soldiers, or of his troops, over whom his light does not rise, or his eye scrutinizing all things, numbering all things, and fitting them together: so that they themselves, together with the celestial circles, by running through with the most modulated succession and most ordered turns, with a singular variety, may complete a most consonant course? Who, now with heat, now with cold, now with moisture, now with dryness, and with many kinds of influences, by suffusing the earth, render it now despoiled, now adorned with flowers and herbs, and fruits according to the quality and opportunity of the seasons, always reducing it to the same (yet with continuous succession): so that the unique moderator of all things, at whose nod all things are most clearly arranged in turn, just as notes or strings, moved by the same resonating force in a certain succession, produce one harmony, indicating a unique leader of the song. If again we direct our ears to the singers and those chanting in this psalmody, we will perceive him, the high-sounding one, making all things resound with a certain proportion (says Albertus) [Marginal note: Albert.] discovered by the Creator's wisdom, nor devised by any intelligence from itself, but drawn from the fount of super-mundane wisdom: For if there is a temperament of the parts of the body, which is called health, is this not from him, who from the beginning arranged all things very good and temperate, and again, by tempering dissonant things, makes them sound? Hence the Psalmist sings: He sent his word, and [Marginal note: Dauid] healed them. And if the affections of animals lacking reason agree among themselves, and for their necessary pasture, did not the artificer of nature instill this, that like things delight to dwell with like things, and having rejected harmful foods, they take for themselves suitable ones prepared by him? About these things Job continues, saying: Who prepares food for the raven, when [Marginal note: Iob] its young cry to God, wailing, because they have no food? With whom the royal prophet sings: Who gives food to all flesh, namely, that which is suitable for it. [Marginal note: Dauid] If also those using reason are fitted together in morals, does not he do this, about whom again it is sung in the psalms: Who makes those of one mind dwell in a house? If again harmonious people gather in a city or some republic, is this not from him, who through angels of peace commanded peace to be announced and given to people of good will: and who, through his apostles and messengers, commanded peace to be offered to all who wish to receive it, into whatever city, house, or place they enter? **Who this one is, who completes all things, and what we can know about Him. Chapter II.**
**T**hat there is a being, from whom all things have proceeded, who completes all things, and towards whom, as a beloved and pre-elected end, all these same things tend, is doubtful to no one: And that this same one is called God by all, though by different names according to the diversity of languages. But this is He,
[Marginal note: Isaiah]
who says through Isaiah: "I am He, I am the first, and I am the last: My hand founded the earth, and my right hand measured, or enclosed the heavens with a span." The "I" is repeated three times, not without mystery (as the Hebrew text has it), to denote that some Trinity is contained in that supreme unity. Therefore I (He says) am He, who indeed is from Himself: or I am that which is: as the Hebrew words clearly sound. It follows: "And I am the first, and the origin of all things: and I am the last and the end, towards whom all things tend:" And as the first efficient cause, with my hand I founded the earth, the stable foundation of the whole machine which was built upon it or around it: And with my right hand I measure, order, direct, or enclose all things with a span, calling and drawing them to myself, from whom all these things have proceeded: whence it follows: "I call them, and they stand together," that is, gathered into myself: But who, how great, or of what kind this God may be, since He escapes all human comprehension, it will be difficult, indeed impossible, to investigate:
[Marginal note: Paul]
because He dwells (as Paul testifies) in inaccessible light, whom no man has seen, nor can see: This was not hidden from those ancient fathers, who constantly asserted that two supreme divine measures or dignities, of which they call the higher one the fount, crown, origin, from which indeed all things emanate, and the other wisdom, the firstborn, and by many other appropriate names, were not known to mortals, nor even to Moses himself: who (as they say) did not even enter the fiftieth gate of the preceding measure. Therefore no one could understand the Father or the Son, until He came, who said: "No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him."
[Marginal note: John]
Likewise, John also says: "No one has ever seen God; but the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him to us."

of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. For there is a threefold progress in knowledge
especially celebrated among the Peripatetic philosophers: the resolutive or defining, the dividing, & the composing:
None of which pertains to God, who can neither be defined, nor divided, nor composed.
Hence, Peripatetic theology is too diminished, & that doctrine is less sufficient for divine things,
which are perceived by a pure intellect, or by a purified spirit. Therefore, another method must be sought by us, by which
we may receive divine things. For there is one, and that a sublime one, which is called intuitive, when
man with a pure heart & eye looks into those clear & eternal mirrors, & spectacles:
to which all the prophets arrived, and hence were rightly called seers. Thus Isaiah,

**FIRST CANTICLE**

I would rightly consider all as one, namely, the agreement of the truths which those who saw announced, to our intellect, which is capable of all truths; whence the passible intellect is so called, that is, receptive of all intelligibles, nay, most desirous of all truths: This intellect, when purified, while it assents to declared truth and rests in it, acquires for itself a great judgment, that it is true, that which so well fits with its own intellect, just as a key with a lock, which if it does not fit the mechanism of the lock itself, is proven not to be that key; but if it fits, it passes through, opens, and closes, and is judged to be its own: No less so, the meaning or interpretation of anything announced by the prophets, if it fits a purified intellect without any disagreement, is proven true; but if not, false and not its own. This, therefore, is the way to be sought by us, who cannot, like the prophets and apostles, intuit divine things, so that we may obtain understanding and interpretation of the scriptures, which those who saw with a true eye what they say, have set forth: We shall long declare that interpretation true, when it has been balanced and harmonious with our purified intellect.

Therefore, with this truth and doctrine, we have said that blessed God was not only the maker of this machine (as we discussed at the beginning) and the end towards which all things tend, as we shall immediately declare, but that He is the one who, filling all things, makes all things resound around Him, [Marginal note: Jer. 23.] just as He declares with an outstretched voice in Jeremiah, saying: "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" namely, with spirit, voice, and harmonious power, and glory [Marginal note: Isaiah]: as Isaiah testifies he saw, when he says: "I saw, and the house was full," namely, the heavenly house, with His majesty, and those things which were beneath Him filled that exalted temple. [Marginal note: Haggai] But the Maker, not content with that fulfillment, promises through the prophet Haggai, at the coming of the Messiah, that He will better fulfill the same, saying: "The desired of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory [Marginal note: Isaiah]." And lest the earth be thought empty of His majesty, the Seraphim are introduced, having first uttered the Trisagion, crying out: "The whole earth is full of His glory [Marginal note: Ezek.]." Ezekiel also, when he treated of the earthly and heavenly wheel, or of the ophanim, through whom the elemental wheels are arranged, adds: "The spirit of life was in the wheels." He also adds that he heard the sound or voice of the animals of holiness, by whom the wheels or ophanim following them were governed. "And I heard," he says, "the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters, like the sound of the sublime God, or שדי Shaddai, as the Hebrew truth has it." He says he heard a sound in the wings of the animals, which he made with the wheels or ophanim, like the sound of waters, from which, as from a seminal power, all things are produced. And since all things are from God, therefore he says "as the sound" or "voice of Shaddai," which we sometimes interpret as "the Almighty," sometimes "God of heaven," but here we have it interpreted as "the sublime God," although perhaps we could better interpret it as "sufficient cause" or "God fully operating [Marginal note: David]." For He is the one of whom it is sung in the psalm: "When You open Your hand, all things will be filled with goodness." And again: "The earth is filled with Your possession and Your influence." Therefore, in His absence, all things are disturbed and return to their dust. But if all things remain filled, although they succeed one another in a reciprocal transformation,

Truly all things tend towards God. Chapter III.

<span style="font-size: 200%;">F</span>abric this universal, the motion of the spheres, the successive generation and corruption of things, all of which are circular, bear the trace of the Creator: by which we are taught that, just as God is to Himself the beginning and the end, and a complete sphere, so all things which hold His likeness tend towards the same (source) from which they proceeded: For this is proper to each: as
[Marginal note: Ecclesia] Ecclesiastes says concerning rivers: "To the place from which they go forth, the rivers return, that they may flow again." So also concerning the earthly body, the Creator said to sinful man: "Dust you are, and
[Marginal note: Genesis] to dust you shall return." Which also Solomon himself teaches all things do, saying:
[Marginal note: Salomon] "All things go to one place; all things that are made of earth, and to earth they equally return." And let these things be said of earthly matters. But concerning the two parts of man,
[Marginal note: Idem] he continues at the end of the volume, saying: "The dust returns to its earth, from whence it was, and the spirit returns to God who made it." For this (spirit) which is from God, freed from the body, immediately returns to the same (God), unless it is detained by violent impediment: But the earthly part is returned to the earth, from which it immediately proceeded. And since the earth is from God, who created it, and it, following the due order with all things sprouting from it, must at some time return to God. He who moves all things,
[Marginal note: Aristot:] and draws all things into Himself (says Aristotle with his Peripatetics) as a heart—

desired, and greatly beloved by all with a love and longing innate by nature: Who, proceeding also by a mathematical path, had previously said that all things are reduced to one, just as they had proceeded from one. Which the Academics (especially Proclus in his Theological Elements) most clearly teach. Thus, and not without a small mystery, the Hebrew characters signifying numbers proceed in the same order: For א (Aleph) is a character signifying one, but with the complete progression through all characters, some of which signify units, some tens, some hundreds, one arrives at last at the same א (Aleph) which, pronounced by saying Aleph, signifies the millenary complement of all numbers, and the cube of the supreme number ten: so that just as the character itself signifies one, so when pronounced it signifies a thousand: and the same character also signifies the same with an added point א̇: But this Aleph also signifies a leader, and is the seal of the highest crown, or of the supreme Father, containing in its figure two י (Yods) and one ו (Vav), which letters in numbers yield 26, like the great four-letter name of God. Therefore, with great mystery, that which represents the divine name in numbers contained by a certain hidden mystery, in the simple character itself signifies the one God, and the first principle of all, and in its pronunciation, the end of numbers. But another sacrament must be observed in that great name of God: in which all the letters signify circular numbers: For י (Yod) gives ten, ה (He) five, and ו (Vav) six: which are all and solely circular numbers: so that it is intimated that God is the true sphere: and proceeds in every spherical progression, reducing all things into Himself, just as they had proceeded from Him: which is testified by Isaiah [Marginal note: Isaias] saying: "I am the first, and the last: my hands founded all things, ordering them, namely, into Myself, so that they might follow a spherical order." Whence this mass of created things cannot tend towards anything else, except towards Him whose image it holds. Moreover, all lines of a circle proceeding from the center to the circumference, and from it to the center, denote that all creatures emanating from the center of the supreme sphere tend towards the circumference of the same sphere, as to their end: And just as the same lines never exceed the limits of the sphere or circle, so too creatures do not exceed the boundaries of that divine sphere: so much so that they are from Him, and in Him they remain, and towards Him they tend: Just as all accidents depend on substance, which is their subject and support, so all created things, which are like accidents with respect to the first and supreme being, which is from itself, depend on Him from whom they depend: and in whom they are contained as in a support: and in whom they were, before they were unfolded into their proper forms, and to Him they look, and tend as to their proper place and home: whence without Him, like strangers, they cannot long remain: but strive to return to Him, especially man: who contains all things by virtue and power, as Trismegistus teaches: Who, dying, as reported by Chalcidius, said: "Hitherto, my son, driven from my homeland, I have lived as a stranger and an exile: [Marginal note: Trism. **By what appetite they proceed to the same [goal]. Chapter IV.**

[Decorative initial D] All have asserted that there are two appetites in things: natural, and
free: But in man (if I am not mistaken) we could add a third,
which is external and supernatural, and divine, drawing by its
effect, and leading to the performance of divine, meritorious works pleasing to God himself.
And that is what always aspires to the best things, not
indeed a natural discourse, as very many think, but that higher part,
[Marginalia: Plotinus.] which Plotinus calls intellect, distinct from the rational faculty: By which we mediately understand God
and divine things: and we tend towards Him in mind and deed: as he discusses
at length in his work 'On Man'. And this [intellect], residing in the citadel of the soul, always resists the law,
which is in our members, leading to what natural virtue and affection can least
[Marginalia: Paulus] accomplish. This, therefore, is 'I', but that is 'grace', according to the teaching of the Apostle, who
says: "Not I, but the grace of God with me." This divine [part], therefore, tends towards the best and divine things:
But that inferior and animal part of us always draws towards the lowest things, from matter
most distant from the supreme. But our soul, or rational faculty, is in the middle, now
carried here, now there: or adhering now to this, now to that, by indecision, or by the choice of the will,
although by its own nature it tends towards that principle from which it proceeded, unless
[Marginalia: Boetius] matter, the mother of error, distracts it: as that common saying of Boethius is apt: "There is
in the minds of men a certain desire for the true good, but wandering error leads them astray to false things."
Which is either from matter (as we said) drawing to the lowest things, or from corporeal
images and manifold present objects distracting: For a present
and sensible object more strongly moves a man who is still natural, and one who
does not have senses trained for the discernment of good and evil: and who does not
taste true honey, milk, and butter, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good.
He who does not hear what the Lord God speaks within him, nor tastes, nor sees,
[Marginalia: Paulus] nor feels, nor perceives (as the Apostle says) the things that are of God, being a natural man himself:
but is enticed by the allure of these apparent goods, which are shadows of the true ones.

On what course they are carried. Chapter V.

**A**LL those things which have no free movement ascend no other
course by which they are carried to the first (principle), from which they departed, except
instinct, which they call natural, because it is implanted by nature, as the
Peripatetics say, or (to use their words) because it happens in many cases and [marginal note: Peripate:]
frequently: For thus they defined natural things. But, as the truth of the matter is, they were thus endowed by the Supreme Creator.
But those who are partakers of reason and liberty by God's gift,
these ascend the course of their will, or of love, according to that saying of Augustine: [marginal note: August.]
"My love is my weight, or my course; I am carried there where I love." To this, however,
with nature often contributing great force and divinity attracting, they run more
easily: For to the progress of wisdom and doctrine come more readily men
well-strung in body, and endowed with a good soul, and disposed to doctrine,
with Phoebus, Venus, and Mercury favoring them, if we wish to follow the Platonists. And [marginal note: Platoni.]
this either by disposing the body, or because the intelligences presiding over them favor them with their
influence, or (as the Pythagoreans say) because in descending the soul takes on the [marginal note: Pythag.]
nature of those intelligences, just as light seems to take on the color of the glass through which
it passes, be it red, blue, green, or yellow. Others run more easily to dominion,
if birth and virtue grant it; and if the Sun, and Mars, and such like have
favored them: if what the Astronomers teach is true. Others run to diverse virtues by a [marginal note: Astron.]
natural course, according to the varied disposition of body, and mind, and the favoring sky;
but they attain nothing good, unless the supernal virtue favors them, from which comes all good: For
wisdom is not acquired by one's own strength, as testifies he who is rightly called wise
by surname: "And I applied my heart to know wisdom; and I understood that man [marginal note: Solomon]
cannot find the reason for any of the works of the Lord that are done under the
sun; and the more he labors to inquire, the less he will find." And this is because
wisdom is given by God, according to the saying of James: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask [marginal note: James]
of the Lord, who gives to all generously, and alone gives." Nor to come to dominion

who will be able, unless God grants it, as Paul says, and with him Dionysius the Platonist in his volume on the kingdom: There is no power except from God. But also the supreme Truth itself says to the Roman prelate: You would have no power over me, unless it were given to you from above. Nor is man able for any good work without divine favor, as He Himself everywhere declares, saying: Without me you can do nothing. And he, in whose breast Christ Himself resonated, says: We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as if from ourselves: but all our sufficiency is from God.

Hence Joram (as we read in the fourth volume of Kings), trusting in his own strength, having scorned divine oracle and favor, ascended a war chariot to engage with the Assyrians, by whom he was wounded by an arrow shot at random between the stomach and the lung, or between the chest and the breastplate, as the literal truth has it, and fell from the chariot in a miserable accident: These things are not without mystery: For he falls from the chariot of his own strength, in which he trusted: he is wounded between two artifacts woven by human ingenuity, to signify that the weaving, and every work conceived by human cunning, or labored by ingenuity and one's own strength, is frustrated: and is turned to the ruin of the one laboring without divine favor, as He speaks with a clear voice through Isaiah, saying: Woe to the rebellious children, that you would take counsel, but not from me: and weave a web, but not by my spirit: that sin might be added to sin: Who walk to go down into Egypt, that is, to inferior virtues and cunning: and you have not asked my mouth, nor sought my favor, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh: who is interpreted as 'uncovering' or 'scattering,' and signifies that most cunning and naked serpent who by his cunning scattered the human race, and stripped the first-formed, so that he would blush before the face of the Lord. It follows: And the strength of Pharaoh shall be to you for confusion, and the trust in the shadow of Egypt for ignominy.

Therefore, he labors in vain who thinks to attain divine things by natural course or inferior favor: Which we can confirm with the example of the eunuch of Queen Candace, who was reading Isaiah in his chariot with vain labor, until, by the command of the Holy Spirit, Philip joined himself to that chariot, teaching what he could not understand: and providing light, and a sign of faith: so that from then on he could do what he was not able to do before: And then by the presence and favor of Philip, indeed of the Holy Spirit sending and assisting, that chariot became like that of which it is said in the psalm: The chariots of God are ten thousands, thousands of those rejoicing. Indeed, to the divine chariot, for the favor of those ascending it, there is present not only the Holy Spirit, but many thousands of ministering powers, called ten thousands hyperbolically, as Jerome says. Therefore, these are present, joined to those assisting and working, and sometimes they advance the chariot, as we shall say immediately: Which chariot of God is of many kinds: One of which Peter had ascended, the other John, as it is said in the Gospel: They ran two together, but he [Peter] in the chariot of faith, this one [John] truly of charity: Which, being fiery, therefore leads more swiftly: Whence it follows: But he who was younger ran more quickly than Peter: Not indeed because he was younger, but because he was more fervent in love. Peter, however, entered the tomb first: because the first gate

From whom this chariot is drawn. Chapter VI.

**S**INCE this chariot is of God, it is necessary that it also be drawn by divine power, because an inferior power would not suffice: Therefore, the highest Truth says: [Marginal note: CHRIST] No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him: Knowing this, he who obtained the name of the wise man by a special privilege, [Marginal note: Solomon] said: Draw me after you. Indeed, he draws in two ways, as he says through Hosea in plain speech: [Marginal note: Hosea] I will draw you with cords of a man, with bands of love: The cords of men pertain to the humanity of the Messiah, but the bands of love to his divinity: Did not Christ as man attract us by his presence, doctrine, prayer, manifold example, and various works, especially those which he suffered for us in flesh and body? Did he not also attract by a certain divine power? Feeling this, Peter said: You have the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go? And again: You are Christ, [Marginal note: Peter] the Son of the living God. Therefore, embracing at the same time the bonds of humanity and divinity, especially at the end, where acting in an orderly manner he usually operates more powerfully, he said: [Marginal note: CHRIST] When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself. And so truly did he draw to himself, that for many years, those whom he had bound with love, he led fearlessly to every kind of martyrdom. But he also granted this power of drawing to his apostles and legates, when he said: Come after me, I will make you become fishers of men, so that you may draw them into the net of the word of God. And he also taught them in what part they should cast the net [Marginal note: The Same] after the resurrection, not without mystery, saying: [Marginal note: The Same] Cast the net on the right side of the boat: In which right side are charity, piety, love, mercy, kindness, and other things of that kind; but on the left are fear, terror, threat, severe justice, punishment, and similar things. Hence hinting that the divine preacher ought to attract souls more by soothing than by terrifying, and rather by bonds of charity than of terror, as he himself did with the adulteress, the sinner, the publican, the tax collector, and such, leading them with kindness, and not terrifying them with threats. And although sometimes the divine orator ought to announce their crimes to the people with a loud voice, nevertheless he ought to do it not by reproaching, but by admonishing with charity, proposing those things which are prepared by the rectitude of justice for their crimes. Therefore, casting their nets into this part, those Apostles were unable to draw them in because of the multitude of fish, so that we may be taught how great a harvest is made in love and charity. Nor without reason is it added: And though there were so many, the net was not torn: because virtue and the office of preaching in

--- Page 478 ---
CANTICLE ONE

...charity exhibited, with God's help, is strengthened and corroborated, so that it cannot be broken or torn apart; [Paulus] but it can accomplish all things, according to that saying of the Apostle: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me." Angels also draw, and ministering spirits, so that they may carry out those things which the highest ruler commands, as it is said of them in the psalm: [Psalmus] "Bless the Lord, all his angels, his ministers, who do his will," not only among men, but moving all things, and influencing in all things, however small. Hence we see many things stirred up and working beyond that which their nature provides; and mortals, not knowing whence these things happen, wonder. This, however, happens in many ways: For sometimes they anticipate, by a certain prescience and movement, those things which are to come to man, as we can prove from the most weighty external and Catholic authors, and by the clearest experience. [Cicero] Cicero relates in the first book of 'On Divination' that for the Lacedaemonians, a little before the Leuctrian disaster, arms sounded in the temple of Hercules: [Calisth.] But at the same time in Thebes (as Callisthenes says), in the temple of Hercules, doors closed with bars opened by themselves; and arms, which had been fixed to the walls, were found on the ground. And at the same time, by many signs, the Lacedaemonians were announcing the calamities of the Leuctrian battle: For on the head of the statue of Lysander, who was the most famous of the Lacedaemonians, which stood at Delphi, a crown suddenly appeared, made of rough and wild herbs: And golden stars, which had been placed at Delphi by the Lacedaemonians after that naval victory in which the Athenians fell, a little before the Leuctrian battle, fell down, and were not found. [Ioseph] Why should I mention those many portents recounted by Josephus which preceded the Jerusalem disaster suffered under Titus and Vespasian? The moon for many days seemed to suffer an unusual eclipse, sympathizing with the future ruin: Lightning for half an hour, as if it were midday, surrounded the temple: Its bronze gate, which was scarcely moved by twenty men, at the sixth hour of the night, opened of its own accord: Chariots and an army of armed men seemed to be carried around the region with great impetus: [Euseb.] All these things Eusebius of Caesarea confirms in the third book of his 'Ecclesiastical History'. And to briefly conclude, almost all significant disasters have been preceded by some portents and prodigies from God's ministers. [Myda Cicero] Many also were preceded by signs at their birth, as Cicero relates in the same place concerning the boy Midas, to whom, while sleeping, ants carried grains of wheat into his mouth, an omen said to be of [Plato] great riches, which came to pass. But when bees settled on the lips of Plato, sleeping in his cradle, it was answered that he would be of singular sweetness of speech; thus his future eloquence was anticipated in the infant: Which we read happened to Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, in our histories. To Hecuba, wife of Priam, about to give birth to Paris, it seemed that she gave birth to a burning torch, which would set Troy and all Asia ablaze. [Heracl.] To the mother of Phalaris (as Heraclitus Ponticus, a student of Plato, writes), it seemed that a statue of Mercury poured blood onto the ground, with which the whole house overflowed: Which offered a sign of immense cruelty in the son she was bearing. [Philistus] To the mother of Dionysius (as Philistus says), while pregnant, it seemed that she gave birth to a satyr. But to the mother of Clare of Assisi, a gardener, not only did it seem, but by a clear voice of a sign

--- Page 479 ---
VOLUME EIGHT. 170

by a clear voice it was signified, that she should safely give birth to a very bright light. The portent, which was at the birth of John the Baptist, is known to all: by which it is proven what angels do with us, both by anticipating and celebrating birth: although among the gentiles evil angels were at work. To the father Zacharias, Gabriel appeared: Speech is withheld from the unbeliever: the barren woman is made fruitful: when the boy is born, speech is restored to the silent father: so that the neighbors and those aware of the events were compelled to exclaim in wonder, "What do you think this boy will be?" Ascending to older examples, Isaac is anticipated by a most famous oracle: he is conceived by a barren and old woman: he is begotten by an old man: His son Jacob quarrels with his brother in his mother's womb: from which the parents are taught by a divine oracle that two nations are contained in that maternal womb. The ancient legislator is exposed to be killed by the river and reeds: and is taken up by Pharaoh's daughter not by chance, but by God's arrangement: who, through his angel, led her to that place, so that the boy might be saved, and be called Moses, i.e., 'taken from the waters,' and who, by angelic favor, would continuously be the leader of that most famous and celebrated exodus of the Israelite people from Egypt. Sampson, the strongest of the strong, is conceived by a barren woman made fruitful by an angelic oracle: and is consecrated to the Lord as a Nazirite, that is, dedicated to the Lord, before he is born. It would be too long to recount all the examples that could be adduced from sacred scriptures and very many gentile histories: by which it would be proven that God's ministers anticipated many either before or at the very birth, or favored war, or other arduous matters, or dealt familiarly with humans in many ways: But let these few things be said, so that unbelievers, and those who only want to admit what they apprehend with their animal senses, may learn how angelic ministers are sent for our service: who not only persuade us to do things in an insensible way, but have shown themselves in many visible and sensible ways, leading people, even those not yet born or not yet adults, to various things: and warning by various portents of future destruction, or leading to strenuous work: Which we can still prove from sacred scriptures.

What the angelic ministers of God accomplish in this attraction is proven from sacred scripture. Chapter VII.

**M**inisters of the most resounding tribunal, and of the supreme Arch-Muse, in order to be faithful, strive with all their might to bring everything into harmony with the Prince, as Dionysius very often repeats in his work on the angelic hierarchy: [Marginal note: Dionysius] For these (says the prophet) [Marginal note: David] come before, joined with those who sing psalms, and harmonizing themselves, like skilled choristers adapting all strings and voices in God's supreme monochord, so that they may render it harmonious and most sweet. And if there are any useless strings, or measures, or those wishing to dissent, they cast them out, cut them off, and overwhelm them: lest in the mundane, and celestial, or human instrument, anything dissonant be found through their idleness. And to begin from higher places, to the leader of the Israelite people, lest he be found discordant or dissonant in so great a province, an angel was assigned by the supreme God with great solemnity, leading and guiding. "Behold, I (He says) send my angel, who shall go before you, and guard you in"

This angel therefore, now going before, now following, defended the camps, taught, guarded, led out of Egypt, and guided the leader and the people whither they were going. An angel also was a companion and guide to the father of the chosen family, Abraham, in Egypt, in Haran, and wherever he went. An angel saved Isaac from sacrifice, guarded him in the pilgrimage made in Gerar and in various places, and from the dispute had with Abimelech. An angel also led Jacob into Mesopotamia of Syria, enriched him, and protected him from the envious Laban, and from the persecution of his brother Esau who pursued him. But also what angels accomplish in us, he foresaw in dreams, not yet well initiated in this manner, so that the animal senses, enemies of angelic custom, which he had not yet fully mortified, might be lulled to sleep by slumber. Indeed, great is the mystery of the ladder, and of the angels ascending and descending: but let this suffice for the present, that from it we are taught that all are led by the ministry of angels to whatever degree of virtues, merits, and dignity, and the unworthy are cast down to the lowest degree of misery: according as their evil merits demand: For this signifies the ascent and descent of angels: And the ladder, distinguished by steps, reveals the order of the universe, and the degrees of all things. Nor is further faculty given for speaking in so great a mystery.

Nor was an angel wanting to Joseph, the son of this patriarch, while his brothers pursued him with much hatred even to his sale: For a man appeared to him in the field, who in Hebrew is called איש [ish], by which name in many places Gabriel is said to have been the constant companion and teacher of that Joseph, as the Hebrews assert.
[Marginal note: Hebrews.] Indeed, it would be long to adduce all things which are read to have been done by angels for men in the sacred writings: but let us conclude with that sentence of the Psalmist, sung for any righteous person (as Jerome rightly understands):
[Marginal note: David]
[Marginal note: Jerome.] God has given his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways: They shall bear you up in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon. I know not what clearer could be adduced concerning the protection, guardianship, and guidance of angels.

But lest those who are under the evangelical law, and the Gentiles, should seem to have been abandoned by angels, and that angels served only the circumcised, as the Hebrews falsely boast, let us see what is treated in the evangelical and apostolic scriptures. To Philip, who by the command of the Holy Spirit joined himself to the chariot of that eunuch of Queen Candace (as we said a little before), an angel had first spoken, commanding him to go there, teaching that they also have care for the Gentiles. And to Cornelius the Centurion, a Gentile, he showed himself visibly, commanding and Peter, not to despise the Gentiles and the uncircumcised, who seemed unclean. We also read that an angel was given as a visible guardian to Agnes and Cecilia, and through her intercession, to her husband Tiburtius and brother-in-law Valerian, after their bodily eyes were cleansed by baptism, he offered himself to be seen, and filled their nostrils with odor and fragrance—

Therefore the angel protects the simple common people, and through them often wards off the cursed teacher, and him who attempts wicked deeds. In the camp of the Assyrians, demonstrating how detestable blasphemy is to God, he utterly destroyed and cast away eighty-five thousand from the blaspheming army. He consumed the Sodomites and Gomorrahites with fire. He overwhelmed the Egyptians with waters. He burned the Chaldeans with fire, preserving the boys in the furnace from the blaze. He killed seventy thousand of those numbered by David in Israel, extending his hand to destroy Jerusalem, unless the Lord, pitying him, had commanded the striking angel himself to hold back his hand. For this is the office of God's ministers, when the measure of wickedness is complete, not to permit discordant notes in God's most harmonious instrument, [Marginal note: David] as the divine Lyre-player sings: "The angel of the Lord constraining and pursuing them." But sometimes the Supreme Governor executes this through evil angels, as through ministers of justice, as the same prophet testifies elsewhere, saying: [Marginal note: The same] "And sendings through evil angels." Our heavenly John also mentions those to whom it was given to harm the earth, [Marginal note: John] and the sea, and other things. Up to this point, we have digressed to a few examples from many, to prove that leadership and attraction to good, and to punishment, according to merits and misdeeds, were given to angels: who are also appointed to arrange all things, as Origen explains at length in his book on Numbers, saying: [Marginal note: Origen.] "The world itself needs angels to preside over earthly armies, kingdoms, provinces, heavens, men, beasts, the birth and growth of animals, shrubs, plants, stones, and other things, bestowing upon them that power which they say is inherent in things from..."

How all things proceed from God through the number six. Chapter VIII.

[Large decorative initial P]
[Marginal note: August.]
After we have discussed a little concerning those things attracting us to God, the numbers, through which we came forth and again return to God (as I agree with Augustine), are also not to be despised: since in many places of the sacred scriptures their significance seems to be magnified, and deservedly so: since God made all things in number, weight, and measure. We read therefore, not without mystery, that the supreme Creator, having proceeded to produce creatures, did so through the number six, which is indeed primarily perfect, and gives a triangle by a great sacrament, as we explained above: Which perfection it has from itself, not however because God created the world in it, as the same Augustine affirms elsewhere. Here therefore, the most perfect artisan first chose the perfect number for the perfect fabric of the world: And so that it might be harmonious, he chose that number which corresponds to the middle diapasonic intervals of perfect consonance: For there are six with seven intervals, after which one arrives at the eighth, which itself completes the octave: By which same order proceeds the weekly revolution, returning to the same eighth, from which it began: so that Sabbath returns to Sabbath, Sunday to Sunday, and the intermediate days are always six: Which six, if it is squared to 36, and simultaneously, with the denary number, is brought to a cubic form, they complete all degrees of the Zodiac, 360. It would also complete the days of the year, unless the sun sparingly passed one degree each day: For it extends its course up to 365 days, as many as there are joints in the human body. If indeed the number six is combined, it yields the signs of the Zodiac itself, and the principal joints in our body, and brings about many other things mentioned above, where we treated of the number twelve. And moreover, the number six, designating twice three, a binary-ternary, by which the Creator proceeded to work: For first he perfected the structure, secondly its adornment: For in the first three days he created all elementary things, and the foundations of this worldly fabric, and distinguished them: First the super-celestial from the terrestrial through the globe and mass of the heavens, afterwards the waters from the earth, bestowing upon the latter its fecundity: But in the remaining three days he adorned the fabric with its inhabitants, placing in the heaven two luminaries and stars: On earth, four-footed animals: In the waters, fish and their creeping things: In the air, birds and winged creatures. And thus the triune God, acting with material things, of which the binary, or duality, is from matter, communicated himself in a twofold manner: The Spirit in fire, light, and heat, vivifying all things: The Son in waters, and generation proceeding from them: But the Father existing as the principle and origin of all things, in the primordial foundation and in the base, upon which all things are established. But on the sixth day he produced man, the high priest of the whole world, all those things

**EIGHTH TONE. 171**

embracing: Who also, growing through six ages, would progress, so that in the seventh and in the true Sabbath he might rest.
      How through the number six they return to the same, and especially into Christ, who is true rest and the true Sabbath. Chapter IX.
[Large initial S] Just as through the number six all things came forth from God, so through the same number, and in the same order, they return into Him, resting and blessed in the true Sabbath: Which Augustine touches upon somewhat in his *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*. [Marginal note: Augusti.] But we shall proceed further, as far as the spirit suggests. On the first day light was made, and for us returning to God it is necessary that that light appear, which illuminates every man coming into this world: and that light of faith, which is the beginning of progressing into God. On the second day the sphere of the heavens was placed, dividing between the waters above the heavens and the lower waters, signifying that discretion and spiritual prudence by which we may know to reject evil and choose good: and to separate spiritual and higher love from carnal and lower love: For those loves meet, and by a certain symbol an easy passage is given from the spiritual to the carnal, unless a curtain and a firmament of prudence, supported by divine grace, be interposed, which may divide between them. But the waters, which are gathered into one place on the third day, denote natural and voluptuous passions: which together ought to be gathered under the dominion of reason, so that our mind may appear dry, naked, and stripped of all earthly affections: Which so much pleases in the eyes of the Lord, that looking upon it, He delights in it, because it is good: And then He commands the earth of our mind, that it may sprout and produce green grass, and wood, or a fruit-bearing tree, according to its kind, that is, multifaceted virtue. But because light placed on a mountain cannot be hidden, nor should a lit lamp be hidden under a bushel, but placed on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all, namely, light and an example of good works: Therefore on the following day, which is the fourth, two great luminaries are commanded to be made in every well-doer: The greater luminary is a meritorious work done in grace, shining before God and His angels. The lesser luminary is prudence and wisdom in arranging lower things: which are a kind of night with respect to supercelestial things, to which, being free, it shines like the sun. But in arranging these lower things, since the examples of doctrine and the favors of saints and angels, who are like stars in the firmament of the heavens, are very helpful, therefore stars are added, placed there in favor of the Moon. But on the fifth day, to those progressing from virtue to virtue, it is said: "Let the waters bring forth swarms of living creatures, and flying fowl flying over the earth, and over the face of the firmament of the heavens," and not "under the firmament," as our translation has it. It follows, that God created התנינים הגדולים hataninim hagadolim, which we have translated as "great whales." It follows: "And every living soul, which the waters had brought forth according to their kind." Great are the mysteries concerning these whales, or *hataninim hagadolim*: For it does not appear why whales should have been expressed more than other fish, who are perhaps larger than them. Finally, on the sixth day, he said: "Let the earth bring forth a living soul" (which we interpreted above as the mind), that is, better fruits of life: And this when we are somehow freed from this mortal body, living to God, conformed to him: In which God is so pleased that he not only praises and says that it is good, but cooperates with us, saying: "Let us make man in our image, with our likeness." For when man applies himself to God and virtue, he is transformed, and passes into his image in act, which he first had in potential: and is made male and female: Female indeed by receiving seed and conception from the true agent, according to that of Isaiah: "From your face, O Lord, we have conceived, and brought forth the spirit of salvation."
[Marginal note: Isaiah] But male is made, when he works according to the grace received. Therefore, when our intellect is coupled with divine light, the mind and man become complete, producing fruits, concerning which it follows: "Be fruitful, and multiply" producing much fruit, not content with little, "and fill the earth," that is, the earthly animal, with the outpouring of the higher man, or with charisms received from above: so that you may reduce that animal to the due servitude of the spirit: and then rule...

you shall have dominion over fish, birds, and beasts, that is, over all living virtues, whether they be watery, airy, or earthly: For fiery virtues, as heavenly and divine, ought to preside. And when man passes through these six steps, he will immediately reach the seventh, where he will obtain true rest: and Jesus, who by his own name is called YHV (יהו), in which are two letters of the great name of God, Y (י) and V (ו), with H (ה) interposed, which is the beginning of Sabbath (שבת), that is, true rest: so that we may understand Jesus to be not only the redeemer of men, but their true rest and refreshment, making us rest from our works and labors, and feeding us with himself, the living bread, who descended from heaven, and giving us to drink wine converted into that new wine, which is drunk in the kingdom of his Father. Moses kept silent about the eighth day, whose province it is to lead his Hebrews through the types of the law up to Christ, their rest, yielding to Him in the work to which He intended to lead us after that rest: For the shadowy law ought to lead us to the end of the shadow, and not carry us further, but that perfect executor and opener of the law (of whom Moses said, [Marginal note: Moses.] "Send, Lord, whom you will send") as the most perfect teacher instructs us to what works we ought to apply ourselves after rest, saying to the Apostles, that in the regeneration, which will be after the resurrection, they ought to sit judging the twelve tribes of Israel, exercising the office of God, having become his co-workers by his grace. And concerning all, he said that after the resurrection they will be like angels of God, who continually serve and minister to Him, executing what He commands: Which work differs greatly from the first, because that was with labor and anxiety, but this is without labor and with delight: That tends towards rest, but this seeks no rest, since it is itself to itself rest and the highest delight, which man can desire and have.

How the human race is led into God himself through the six ages. Chapter X.

**A**s the work of the world in six days, so also the course of the world itself, through six distinct times, as through six ages, comes to the sabbatical millennium described by John in the Apocalypse: For on the first day, [Marginal note: John.] the earth and heaven are said to have been made with a certain common light, and its division from darkness: and that the spirit of Elohim hovered over the waters. Thus man in the first age of the world is said to have been fashioned from soul and body, as from heaven and earth, with some light of natural law, and with divinity illuminating, especially while he was in a state of innocence: But light was divided from darkness, when man was expelled from that paradise of delight: and when the shining and divine Enoch was taken away from the dark multitude: And at the end of that age, it is said that the sons of Elohim approached the daughters of men, impregnating them. Indeed, there are here very great mysteries concerning the correspondence of the sons of Elohim impregnating the daughters of men, so that giants, or "the fallen ones" (as it is in the text), might generate men of renown and powerful from old with the spirit of Elohim: who, hovering over the face of the waters, made them fertile amidst the darkness that covered the face of the abyss. The second age began in Noah, who was as a certain middle and firmament, dividing in-
