between that long-lived first age, and the second, in which the confusion of tongues occurred: denoted by the lower waters: And that medium was called heaven: because Noah was heavenly, dividing, and righteous in his generations, that is, to the extent that period of time permitted: For in that age the family of God was divided, in Shem and Japheth, from the family of the devil, in Ham with his descendants: For from him came Cush, that is, the Ethiopian; Mizraim, that is, the Egyptians; and Canaan, from whom the Canaanites, indeed inferior and reprobate generations, marked by the lower waters: and separated from those who were irrigated by the upper waters: And this divi-
[Marginal note: Jerome.] sion remains to this day, as Jerome wisely and well discusses in Genesis. Or the firmament, or globe of the heavens, distinguishing between waters and waters, was Saint Abraham, in whom, in that age, he was distinguished by a particular sign of the covenant with his family from the waters, that is, from earthly peoples and animals: For to him first was given a sensible and distinctive sign between family and family, and he was called the father of faith, that is, of the faithful: Yet it was not said on this day, or in this age, that it was good: because it was entirely subjected to troubles and calamities: For then the nations were scattered and divided on earth, and the confusion of tongues occurred, and the world was always in turmoil then, even in Abraham himself, the father of the chosen family: who suffered so many and such great things from the Chaldeans, that he was barely rescued from the fiery furnace: And from there he journeyed to Egypt, to Haran, and was greatly oppressed, until the familiar hospitality of angels comforted him: who also announced to the old man a son, and to his barren and aged wife a birth, namely Isaac, which means laughter, because in him the father rejoiced, and a happier age began. In this age, therefore, the waters began to gather, that is, the chosen people and the family of God, to one place, and to be separated from the Gentiles deprived of divine charisms, so that then the dry land might appear. Also in that age the Israelite nation was separated from the Egyptians: and like land moistened by the waters of law, doctrine, wisdom, and sacrifices, it was prepared, so that it might be said to it: 'Let the earth bring forth green herb, and fruit-bearing wood,' which before was empty and void without law and legal sacrifices: and this age proceeded up to David through fourteen generations, namely a double septenary. One was from Abraham to Amminadab, in which the people served, oppressed by burdens, crossed the sea, wandered through deserts, ascended mountains. In the other, from Amminadab under Salmon to David, it received the law, waged wars, and by military labor obtained the promised land to possess; moreover, it was adorned with kingdom and prophecy: And this third age was, as it were, double, consisting of two septenaries: of which one was dedicated to purification through servitude, the sea, the desert, and various oppressions: The other was ascribed to fruit and increase in the promised land and the obtained kingdom. And rightly both are done by the septenary, since purification, and remission, and good work are perfected by that very number (as we shall declare elsewhere, with God's favor): Which is hinted at in the mystical description of the fabric (of creation), when these two things are described as having been done on the same day. For first the waters were gathered, and

--- Page 487 ---
TOMUS OCTAVUS. 174

the dry land appeared, just as the waters were gathered during the people's passage through the dry land, and the dry land of the Red Sea: In these waters (says Paul) all were baptized, and initiated into [Marginal note: Paulus] the service of God: And they made various dwellings in the desert, which signify the progress of [Marginal note: Hieron.] penitents and those advancing in the way of God, as Jerome explained in a long treatise, which he named 'On the Forty-Two Dwellings,' in which the whole person is chastised by due penance. But in the other [septenary] (as we said), the sprout and fruitfulness of the land, now obtained in possession after the sea and desert had been traversed, is attributed. But when all these things had come to evening in the depraved Saul, and this day was closed, it is therefore necessary that another succeed. Therefore, in the fourth [age], the kingdom shines in David, Solomon, and the other kings: the priesthood gleams with the temple erected and sacred rites most famously instituted, like the Moon and the Sun: very many prophets flash like stars in the firmament. And this most splendid day, through a double septenary, succeeded, until evening came, and an unhappy night, with those depraved and worst kings, Manasseh, Amon, Jeconiah, and the others: so much so that they were led to a most miserable captivity in Babylon: From which it was necessary for another day to be renewed. Thus, the fifth age began under captivity, among a wandering and vagrant people, having no determined seat, like the birds of the heavens, which were produced on that day: But for comfort, they had heaven, which they could contemplate. Nor were there lacking great whales, namely great men like Jeremiah, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, Tobias, and similar ones: who excelled in captivity and amidst all the shaking waves: nor were they inclined to the worship of idols, nor to the rites of the gentiles, among whom they were wandering captives: To these adversities, as if properly cultivated with ploughshares, hoes, and rakes, it was said: 'Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth: and quickly dominate, to be freed from captivity:' For from them was produced that seed of salvation, Jesus the Son of God, the Blessed Virgin, and the apostles, and other apostolic and evangelical men generated from that stock. But when this age also began to draw to evening because of evil, avaricious, and hypocritical priests: and with princes given into the dominion of the Romans, the sixth age and day succeeded: This, therefore, was the most fortunate and auspicious [age], beginning under the Son of God and Redeemer of the world: and in whom, by God's grace, it will end with the most fortunate success, although it has suffered and still suffers various things: In this [age], man, produced from the earth, is led to the true image and likeness of God, so that he can even become a son of God himself, provided he believes in His name, not living according to flesh and blood, but if he is reborn of God in profession and deed. In this [age] also, serpents, reptiles, and all unclean things have been pacified and cleansed, as was shown to Peter, lodging with Simon the Tanner, in that vessel full of reptiles and unclean animals: To whom it was also said: 'Arise, and eat:' and to him resisting, it is said again: 'What God has cleansed, you must not call common and unclean:' For He has cleansed all things in His blood. In this [age] it is also said: 'Male and female He created them:' because the betrothal of the soul and the Church with Christ has been made by that sacrament, of which in—

--- Page 488 ---
CANTICLE THE FIRST

[Marginal note: Paul] Paul says: This is a great sacrament of Christ and the Church. In this, dominion is again given to man, and he is placed over cattle, serpents, and birds: because, having become a Son of God and co-heir with Christ, he rightly rules over all things, unless man willingly reduces himself to the servitude of sin, flesh, and the devil. Moreover, for food, all seed-bearing plants and fruit-bearing trees that have seed in themselves are prepared; but for all other living creatures, every green plant. Here, Augustine rightly doubts in his *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans* [Marginal note: August.] whether this literal meaning can be saved, since lions, tigers, elephants, bears, monkeys, and various other wild animals of this kind, living in deserted and sandy places, are not fed on herbs, but on flesh. Likewise, kites, eagles, hawks, and birds that live by prey. Hence, although in the book of *Retractations* he tries to save the literal meaning, nevertheless another sense must be sought, to which perhaps the words rather point. It must therefore be observed that when all animals have been brought into the service of man, then food is prepared for all, signifying that when passions have been subdued, and all things brought into the service of reason and Christ, then they have for food seed-bearing plants and fruit-bearing trees: because all works in the grace of the Messiah are meritorious and fruitful. But to those who live like beasts, only the green of wild grass is given, neither cultivated nor seed-bearing. For foods are indeed distinguished in the literal truth, although our translation states, "that they may be for food for you and for all living creatures of the earth," without declaring any distinction between the foods of humans and the foods of animals. A peculiar and hidden food is also given to those who live purely under the Messiah, concerning which [Marginal note: Apocalypse] in the Apocalypse it says: "To him who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna, which no one knows except he who receives it." This food is also given to him while still living in this world, together with that living bread which came down from heaven, until he reaches that eighth (day/state) itself, where in the Father's house we may eat and drink with the Son at His table that new kind of food. But if anyone becomes rebellious or unfaithful to Christ, the animal powers dissent from him; hence, not content with his food, they feed on the pure green of herbs along with the cattle. Behold how the human race, through the course of six ages, finally comes to Christ, as to the true Sabbath, and rest, and the seventh (day/state); through whom it returns to that eighth (day/state) from which it had departed.

How a particular man, living regularly, comes to Christ through the six ages signified by those six days. Chapter XI.

The entire course of how these six stages of human life correspond to the seventh seems difficult to investigate, unless that light illuminates it, which variously and appropriately illuminates every man through his ages with its rays. Therefore, imbued with that light, we shall endeavor to equate the stages of man with those six days. For an infant, emerging from the mother's womb, where it dwells in darkness, is said to come into the light, so that what is said, "Let there be light," or "Let light be," illuminating even itself, may most fittingly apply to it. This also must be observed, that that age itself passes in silence, celebrating no work

--- Page 489 ---
**EIGHTH TONE. 175**

performing any notable work: indeed, if there is any, it is consumed by a flood of oblivion; because all those childish things are laid aside, and are forgotten, a small family saved; because few things remain in adolescents from infancy, namely, the seminal power and developing virtue. This is indicated at the beginning of the seventh year by the change of teeth, which signify the strengths and virtues of man, as we have declared elsewhere in a lengthy discourse. The second age follows after the course of seven years, in which always (as Chalcidius and Macrobius extensively relate) [Marginal note: Chalci. Macro.] some change occurs in man. In this age, therefore, the boy, freed from childish bonds, begins to be taught various doctrines and divine worship, just as the world was then taught by Noah. And the boy receives the dividing firmament, that is, discretion, which separates between waters and waters, namely, rational operations from animal ones. And because the age is completed, and no work is completed, but only begun, therefore it most aptly corresponds with that day, which the wise describer Moses, asserting it to be completed, thus says: "And there was evening, and there was morning, the second day." But in it, no work is indicated as perfected, since it is silent about what it says of other days: "And God saw that it was good." Hence, the boy is neither rewarded nor punished for work performed in this age, since it is not considered legitimate by any law, nor is it seen by God to be counted among other works. Nor should it be insisted that on the first day it was said, "And God saw the light, that it was good": because light is not our work, but produced by God for our benefit and aid. And although it is also said that on the second day the firmament, or the globe of the heavens, was made, the work was not yet perfect: because it was not yet adorned with the sun, moon, and its stars. The third age follows, in which man grows up, suited for both kinds of offspring, bodily and spiritual. For he becomes more apt for generation according to the flesh, and also according to the spirit: because then he begins to be watered by doctrine, law, and spirit, so much so that he is then judged by the wise to be fit for religion and spiritual burden. Whence it can deservedly be said to him: "Let the earth bring forth," namely, the earth of your mind, "green herb, and fruit-bearing tree." And this happens first by gathering the waters of his powers to their proper place, which at first were mixed, so that animal virtues were not distinguished from rational ones. For then a better separation of powers occurs, and it becomes clear to him how dry natural virtue is when left to itself. And here God sees in two ways that it is good: first, because the waters of powers are gathered together; afterwards, because the earth, moistened by supercelestial rains, produces fruit, so that he can say with the prophet: "For the Lord will give goodness, and our earth [Marginal note: David] will yield its fruit." The fourth age succeeds, which is called the most flourishing youth: where one who walks rightly is perfectly illuminated in mind, like the sun; and in the lower intellect, like the moon. For thus Plato teaches in the Symposium, that our intellect, united with divine light [Marginal note: Plato.] and made mind, is called the sun; but left to itself, it is the moon; and mixed with animal passions, it is the earth producing lower fruits. After youth, in the fifth place, follows virility, by which man ought to be a perfect man, adorned with perfect virtue and wisdom, which is called "salutary water" in Ecclesiasticus: [Marginal note: Ecclesiasticus] And because in wisdom it produces better sprouts, therefore it is said, pro-

**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

...And because in wisdom it produces better sprouts, therefore it is said, let the waters bring forth living soul. Also great whales are brought forth, that is, robust and strenuous works, and most solid counsels: which fear no assaults of the sea. Therefore they grow in strength, virtues, works, name, and fame: therefore it is said to those existing in this age: "Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea," that is, you should possess complete water-wisdom, by which it may be permitted to you to traverse all the gulfs of the sea. But unless man directs all these things towards God, he still lives somewhat as a beast, just as it happened to Solomon (although he was most wise): therefore it is said, that beasts and cattle were made, each according to its kind: But if [Psalm.] he lives for God, the sixth age immediately succeeds him with that old age, about which it is said in the psalm: "My horn shall be exalted like that of a unicorn, and my old age in the mercy of udders." In a wonderful way, when he was believed to fail in old age, he rejoices that he has received the strength of a rhinoceros: And when she was thought to be barren, he rejoices that she was most fruitful: Which we read has happened to few, that they became stronger in old age. There are, however, those who do not fail in old age from the strength of spiritual powers, as it is written concerning Moses, of advanced and mature age, at the end of the law, not without mystery, that when he was one hundred and twenty years old, his teeth were not diminished, nor did his eye grow dim: because he failed neither in speculative nor in operative [CHRIST.] virtue until the very end. And in this way, the sixth age and old age are most blessed: to whom our rest says: "I am with you until the consummation of the worldly age, and of yours." And just as the world in its last age was endowed with more perfect charisms, so also the human world (is endowed) with the grace of healings, virtues, miracles, and all kinds of perfection: which is given more at the end of life than at the beginning and in the middle. And these acquire a mind: which, as in most cases, arrives late: Having acquired this mind, they are also adorned with the perfect image and likeness of God: Whence it remains for them, that having completed the race, they receive the crown of righteousness [Paul] with Paul, who says: "Not only for me, but also for those who love his appearing." And they receive this in that seventh (age), and in perfect rest in Christ: through whom they may finally come to the eighth, from whence they proceeded, with the race completed, and perfect harmony, and a well-conducted, most sweet diapason. Nor is it without mystery that this seventh day, in which all things ought to rest perfectly, is placed without a succeeding evening: because then there will be no more night, nor sorrow, nor defect: but we shall rest in perfect and perpetual light, as our very rest [CHRIST.] prayed for us, saying: "Father, those whom you have given me, I wish that where I am, they also may be with me: and that they may see the glory which you have given me before the foundation of the world:" and it will always endure without any admixture of darkness: And He blessed this seventh age, for rest, according to what He promised He would say in the seventh age of the world: "Come, blessed [The Same] of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world."

Christ is true rest, and true sabbath. Chapter XII.

[Decorated initial V] Let us begin from the interpretation of the word: sabbath comes from שבת (Shabbat), which signifies rest: Since this cannot be had in the continuous movement and pilgrimage of this life, therefore Paul says: [Marginal note: Paul] Let us hasten to enter into that rest, which is the heavenly homeland, and eternal life, and who will give it, let us hear our Christ: I (he says) came, that they might have life, and have it more abundantly: And again: My sheep hear my voice, [Marginal note: CHRIST] and I give them eternal life, and they will not perish forever, nor will anyone snatch them from my hand: because that rest will be eternal, from which no one will be snatched, no one will be drawn out. And they will be (says Isaiah) in abundant rest, in tents of security: [Marginal note: Isaiah] By which words both abundance and security are denoted: And our Jesus, the true rest of all, will give both from that infinite shared essence. Hence after he promised life and happiness, and added this eternal [life/happiness]: My Father, [Marginal note: CHRIST] who is greater than all, gave it to me, namely the essence, as all interpret, and the object, in which all ought to be blessed: Which can be understood in the very mystery of the letters, if one has tasted the mysteries of the sacred letters: For in this word שבת (Shabbat) is the letter ש (Shin), which is the seal of supreme wisdom, who is God the Son: And ת (Tav) is the last letter designating the final reason, ש (Shin) however [designates] the beginning. שבת (Shabbat) is taken for the whole word, just as it is a common way of understanding among the Hebrews that sabbath signifies rest. If therefore the whole is woven together, this implies: wisdom, or God the Son, is the end, and the rest: How much these things agree with Christ, Paul, discussing with the Hebrews skilled in these mysteries, states: Let us enter (he says) into rest, [Marginal note: Paul] we who have believed: as he said: To whom I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest. It remains therefore for some to enter into it: but those, to whom it was announced earlier, did not enter because of unbelief. And since, with the works completed from the foundation of the world, it was said: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works: And here again, if they shall enter into my rest, and he determines a certain day by saying 'today', namely in David after so much time: For he says, Today if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts: For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never speak of another [day/rest]: Therefore on this day, Jesus remains the most sabbath-like for the people of God, who have entered, or will enter, into his rest: in which he himself rests, just as God [rested] from his works: Let us therefore hasten to enter into that rest. Behold how clearly, how lucidly the Apostle testifies and proves that Christ is our rest: Whom Augustine [Marginal note: Augustine] follows in a long discourse against the Manichaeans: For in Christ rests such a fullness of divinity, that all things which seemed divided by most diverse reasons in the old law—by many kinds of sacrifices, very many precepts, inexplicable ceremonies—are absolved by this one unique end, Christ Jesus: who (as the same Apostle teaches) [Marginal note: Paul] is the author and perfecter of faith: and in whom all things ought to be completed and rest: In him ages and times are fulfilled and closed: In him all who labor...

Thus the universe of the world is more beautiful and better than its parts and members: therefore, of the completed fabric, it was said that all things were very good, that is, perfect in their totality. This sense is indeed beautiful, but a more beautiful interpretation (if I am not mistaken) is found in the most beautiful Jesus: if the wise teach truly that things are good and finally beautiful only insofar as they participate in the highest being, the highest good, and the highest beauty (as the Acade [Marginal note: Academi.] mics add), how much more so is the highest being, the highest good, and the highest beauty itself, from which all beautiful things participate. Hence our Theolo [Marginal note: Theolo.] gians said that human nature is more perfect after the fall than before: because, united to Christ God, it has been adorned as with a royal necklace: and made beautiful by a divine lineage and ancestry through its regeneration in Christ himself, and by a greater communion with God. Since, therefore, each thing is more beautiful and better the more it participates in the highest beauty and the highest good, God, those things which come together in Christ, the most beautiful and best of all created things, are more beautiful and better: Therefore, to Christ, who, according to the Apostle, was predestined to be the Son of God, brought forth in power on the sixth day as the first of all [Marginal note: Paulus] creatures, and placed at the head of the eternal volume (as some wise men teach), and with all things brought back under his dominion, and all things renewed in him, in whom it pleased the supreme Father to make all fullness dwell, then all things were made more beautiful and better, and fruitful in him, to whom the Father gave all things: and in whom if anyone does not remain, he will be cast out like a branch, and will wither: and he will be cast into the fire, and burn. Thus also sacrifice, and priesthood, and all things pertaining to sacred rites, received increments of their goodness in him, as Paul says, "Christ, having come as a high priest of the good things to come, through a more ample [Marginal note: Idem] and more perfect [way]," And he proceeds with a long discussion with the Hebrews and Romans, demonstrating that the law, priesthood, and sacrifices were made more perfect in Christ, receiving better increments: For in him all things are perfected, magnified, and exalted, so that he did not speak without mystery when he said: "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] to myself," and by exalting them also. Therefore, whoever wishes to be perfected and exalted, let him adhere to him and serve him: who says: "If anyone serves me, my Father who is in heaven will honor him: for where I am, there also my minister will be." [Marginal note: Idem] The perfect diapason is completed in the octonary. Chapter XIV.

[Large decorative initial S] IF we wish to reach the eighth and true diapason, it is indeed necessary that we enter into the innermost sanctuaries: For then we reach the eighth, when we return to God himself, from whom we proceeded: so that we may say with Christ: "I came forth from the Father and have come into the [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] world: again I leave the world and go to the Father." For we too came forth from the same parent, having entered into this world, so that we might return to him through six days, or through six ages, or progressions: after which rest will be given, according to that passage of the Apo [Marginal note: Apocal.] calypse: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord," that is, by the death of the righteous, from now on.

**OF THE FIRST CANTICLE**

Now the spirit says that they may rest from their labors, namely in Christ, to whom those dead to the world live. After which rest (a wonderful thing indeed) follows an operation happier than the rest itself, yet very different from the primal operation, indeed, almost opposed to it: For the former concerns an exit from God into Christ, in whom we are perfected and rest; but this latter (concerns) a return with Christ into God, and union through Him with the Father. Appropriately indeed, between these two opposite movements, in the way we have said, a middle rest is given, which natural philosophers teach is found between any two contrary movements: For there are contrary movements of exit and return; and there are also contrary operations of those: because one is laborious, expecting rest, the other desires no rest, nor does it reach an end; since that operation, and continuous entry into God, is rest itself, and supreme pleasure, beyond which no other is given: And this second kind of operation makes not that material, inauspicious binary, but the most holy and true diapason, consisting in a double proportion, yet with seven intervals and eight limits. And when through the rest had in Christ, and through Christ we have arrived at this supreme operation, there is no longer for us a seventh day of rest, and a Sabbath to be celebrated: but that day, in which a better operation succeeds than the first, which was effected from the beginning on the same day. For the exit of all creatures from God, and the operation of God Himself in unfolding them into creatures, began on the first day; and the return into the same God through resurrection and stable union took its beginning on the same day, which is therefore called the Lord's Day, or Sunday: therefore the Sabbath itself, and the seventh, and the day of rest, has been changed into this eighth, and Lord's Day, a more celebrated festival indeed by mystery, and by a most profound secret. Therefore, rightly cease in us, for whom, through the true rest, Christ, a return to God is given, all sabbatical festivities celebrated by the ancients: who were expecting to come into the Sabbath, through which alone [CHRI STVS.] a return to the eighth is given, as He Himself says: "Without me you can do nothing." And again: "No one enters except through me." And because the Hebrews are unwilling to receive this Sabbath, which has already come, nor do they care to enter through it, therefore they cannot arrive at the [Idem] eighth, to which we arrive only through the Sabbath, Christ, who again says: "If anyone does not enter through me, he is a thief and a robber." But if anyone enters through me, namely to the eighth, he will enter into the divine inner chambers, and will go out to the vestibules of created things, not serving them, but through them praising the Creator; and everywhere he will find pastures. In which most sweet symposium he will perceive that harmony of glory, by which the Seraphim (as Isaiah saw) sang together that heaven and earth are full, the creator and the creature, the maker and the work, from love and mutual correspondence to each other.

That the heavens in their revolution perfectly lead to the diapason. Chapter 15.

[Decorative initial 'D']
Two things are to be considered in the diapason: One, that it always returns to the same tone from which it departs; the other, that that tone is not of the same key and nature. For it occurs from G to G, or from D to D, as musicians (know).

--- Page 495 ---
TONVS OCTAVVS. 178

let us use terms, and of this kind, as is clear: but one is of low natural, the other of
high natural, as newer musicians have in use: Or (if we follow the Greeks) one [Marginal note: Greek Musicians.]
is from proslambanomenos, which is called added because it was found after all others: the other is
in mese, which we call the middle: And from this up to nete hyperboleon, that
is, the ultimate excellence, is another diapason: And in the same order it is found in other terms:
in which there is some identity, or agreement, yet with a difference:
because there are different keys, and one tone is higher than another, but in nature
they correspond very greatly: Thus also the heavens in their daily circuit always all
return to the same place from which they had departed by a point of the circuit: yet it is not
the same revolution, nor of that day, degree, or minute: because every heaven
or planet changes its degree on any given day, or at least a minute, like Mars, Jupiter,
and Saturn: which do not exceed a degree on any given day, but some
minutes: But the starry heaven, even if (as many believe) it moves by some space
from its place, also completes its revolution every day, returning
to the same place by a point from which it had departed: All these heavens, by these their
revolutions, not only signify, but also favor, that all things into which they flow
follow this circular motion, and return to that from which they proceeded: Some
indeed by corruption to the earth, or the matter from which they are composed: others,
however, incorruptible, by separation from this gross matter, return
to that principle from which they emanated, yet under a different reason: For they
proceeded from Him, inasmuch as He is the beginning, and they tend towards Him, inasmuch as He
is the end: Yet the same God is the beginning and the end. They all also make
their diurnal revolution in 24 hours: which yield three octaves, or octonaries:
which, compared to each other, give a triple proportion: For 24 contains three eights:
And this proportion constitutes a diapason and a diapente: so that the circuit
of the heavens may also be harmonious, just like their distance, and the correspondence of their
motions to each other.

About the harmony of the heavens, both from distance and from the consonance
of motions. Chapter XVI.

The heavens are most consonant not only from motion, but also from distance
and mutual agreement, almost all antiquity attests.
Censorinus, Pliny, and Eratosthenes, assigning the distances of the heavens from the [Marginal note: Censorinus, Pliny, Eratosthenes.]
Pythagorean workshop, gather that the circumference of the earth is
two hundred and fifty-two thousand stadia: And they judged that as many stadia as there are on earth, so many
are there in each of the stars, although they are said to be of diverse magnitudes: But leaving aside this
controversy as less opportune, we say that these stadia are Italian, of one
hundred and twenty-five feet, not Olympic, which are of six hundred feet: nor Pythian,
which are of one thousand feet. Therefore, from the earth to the Moon are one
hundred and twenty-six thousand stadia, and they make an interval of a tone: But from the Moon to the star of Mercury -

[Marginal note: Pythag. Plato] and the authors we have cited, and all Pythagoreans affirm to be most consonant not only

auspicious numbers, but with the Moon in more, while Venus is joined with the Moon in all,
but with the Sun in more, therefore he decrees Jupiter to be the primary giver of good things, then Venus,

"So great is the harmony of the heavens from dissimilar motions, that while highest Saturn
cools, the star of Jupiter, placed between them, illuminates and tempers them." And he further discusses many things
about the agreement not only of their qualitative virtue but also of their consonant operations
for the safety of the world, and for the increase or stability of things, at least through succession.

some noise ought to be judged in comparison to that, if a comparison can be made between those things which are perceived by these coarser senses, and those which are perceived by better senses. And hence I gave credence with admiration, because those ignorant of mathematical things expounded so learnedly those things which they had foreseen by divine light, as not even the most skilled in those disciplines, no one doubts, would speak. **Concerning the consonant fecundity in the septenary number of the planets. Chapter XVII.**

Indeed it seems wonderful that the planets, through whom fecundity is supplied to all things, are distributed in the septenary number, which by experts in formal arithmetic, and especially by the Pythagoreans, is called an unfruitful number, because below ten it neither generates a number, nor is generated by any number; whence it is called sterile, and thence is considered unhappy and inauspicious.
[Marginal note: Pythag.]
If anyone, however, weighs this number with a straight balance, he will find it fruitful and most auspicious. For it is generated from the first even quaternary (four), as if from a female, and from the first odd ternary (three), as if from a male; whence comes all fecundity, beyond which no other is given. Hence, after one arrives at the septenary, no further progress is made, but always some change for the better up to the due increase. Concerning these changes, which occur in man through every septenary, Chalcidius, Macrobius, Galen, and others write most extensively.
[Marginal note: Chalcid. Macro. Galen.]
Which is most thoroughly proven in the fabric of the world, in which, when the Creator arrived at the septenary, he rested, not progressing further, but leaving all things made to produce through their own septenary courses. Hence it was not necessary for it to be composed of aliquot parts, so that it might generate, because from the first masculine and feminine number it had drawn perfect fecundity. Nevertheless, it is called sterile by Mathematicians, because it does not generate a number within the limits of ten, nor is it generated by aliquot parts. But by more secret wise men it is considered most fruitful, since from the feminine and masculine power which it contains, it gives fecundity and fruits to things. Therefore, the planets and signs provide fecundity to inferior things from the duodenary (twelve) and septenary (seven) number, both of which are composed of the first even and first odd, as if from masculine and feminine, but in different ways, as we shall presently say. And hence every planet and every sign partakes of a masculine or feminine nature, but Mercury partakes of both. But with perfect fecundity in the septenary itself, perfect rest occurs. For this number contains the first perfect senary (six), in which all things were made, and the seventh day of rest, which agrees with both Saturns, namely the celestial and the supramundane; and from both comes a Sabbath not unfruitful, but the end of the preceding course.

Z iij

--- Page 498 ---
CANTICLE ONE

after which immediately another follows, in which operations are again performed. And Christ, containing this septenary most perfectly, our true Sabbath, introduces us (as we [Marginal note: John.] said) to the eighth. Hence, not without great mystery, John, subject to the Spirit, saw seven golden lampstands, namely seven planets, and all septenary power: and in the midst, one like the Son of Man clothed in a *podere*, that is, a long robe covering everything down to the ankles, signifying that He covered all our sins, shame, and nakedness: and completed the work, and finishes it to the very end: and, existing in the midst, gives birth and fruit to all, both in the first generation of things and in their regeneration. Hence, declaring that He had perfected it, having brought the work to its conclusion, He cried out: "It is finished." Therefore, the septenary is most fruitful in things, although in numbers themselves it may seem sterile and unfruitful.

On the harmonious agreement of the septenary of planets with the twelve signs. Chapter XVIII.

[Decorative initial E] ND although a great discrepancy may appear in the numbers of the planets and the signs, nevertheless, there is a very great agreement in the root of both, which is the quaternary and the ternary: Which, if joined, constitute the septenary. But if one is squared by the other, by saying, "Three times four," or "Four times three," they yield twelve. Moreover, the planets agree with the signs in qualitative and elemental virtues, and in better powers, whence each of the planets has its domicile in some sign: and in some, its exaltation, receiving some power and nourishment from each of them. Nor do the seven intelligences presiding over the planets have less agreement with those twelve minds: which [Marginal note: John.] preside over the twelve signs. Of each of these, John makes mention in the Apocalypse, at the beginning of which he says: "And from the seven spirits who are before the throne of God:" whom I found also to preside over the planets. But at the end of the volume, where he describes the structure of the heavenly city, he testifies that in its twelve gates there were twelve angels: And therefore we have touched upon the agreement of these angels, planets, and signs: so that it may be understood how great a consonance both the ministers and instruments of the Creator lead us into the same. But the signs themselves are made and called the gates of the heavenly city, perhaps those twelve about which John writes in the same place. How these signs are the gates of the heavenly city, Plato touches upon in some way, saying that Cancer is the gate through which the soul descends to the body: [Marginal note: Plato.] and Capricorn is the gate through which it again ascends to God: Hence they called the former the gate of men, [Marginal note: John.] and the latter the gate of gods. But if there are twelve gates (as John testifies) equated with the twelve signs, or signifying them, each of those signs will be called a gate, but how, we will briefly run through. For Aries is a gate, and Taurus, which are offered for sin, without the purification of which no one can enter there. Hence one comes to Gemini, the acts of charity, namely of God and neighbor: Which twofold charity is strengthened in the strongest arms of Cancer, which—

On the true harmony of the heavens, which some, not understanding, falsely
deny. Chapter XIX.

<span style="font-size: 3em; line-height: 0.5em; vertical-align: -0.2em;">S</span>There are men of very grave authority who consider the modulations of the celestial
spheres utterly ridiculous: because that sound is not heard, nor perceived by any
sense, in no way persuading themselves how from that triple most swift motion in thick air
or fire, the celestial chorus does not resound, or the harmony is not heard. Hence they, along with Pythagoras,
removed harmony from natural motion; and against all Pythagoreans and Academics,
from violent and diurnal motion, adhering in this to their Aristotle, the principal enemy of this harmony.
But lest there be disagreement and discord among the supreme observers of this most consonant universe,
we will easily make them agree by attending to that in which they differ. The Peripatetics deny [Marginal note: Peripate.]
a vocal sound perceptible by these sensible ears: we grant them this. The Academics [Marginal note: Acade. Pythag.]
and Pythagoreans pass from vocal number to natural or formal (number), and arrange
the measures and numbers of the universe in the innermost sense of reason: and leaving behind
vocal harmony, which tickles the ears with drum, lyre, organ, and human voices, they
assumed a better one, which is in the numbers by which the Creator arranged the universe.
Which Plotinus clearly expresses when he teaches us to return to God through music, saying: [Marginal note: Plotinus]

Wherefore, after such sensible sounds, numbers, and figures, it is necessary to lead him thus, so that he may separate the matter in which are sensible proportions and their comparisons; and that beauty, namely formal consonance, which is in these, may be brought back. Moreover, let him learn that those things by which, full of wonder, he is vehemently affected, are not that beauty itself towards which we strive: so that it is not [Marginal note: Augustine, the same] this, or that beauty, but beauty only. And what Plotinus says about beauty, Augustine likewise pursues concerning the good, while he says: Take away this good, take away that: and consider the good in itself, if you can, and that is the highest good, towards which we strive. And between the highest good, the highest beauty, and the highest harmony, and this sensible good, beauty, and harmony, is that celestial middle, which is not sensible and vocal, nor most simple and divine, but middle and rational. Therefore, this external and vocal harmony is like a statue, and a certain image of a better harmony perceptible by reason: which statuary symphony, if anyone leaves it in the outer courts and scorns to adore it, he will be cast into the furnace of purging fire: where, enlightened and inflamed, he will adapt his three powers to the assembly of all things; and at the same time, running through each creature, he will attempt, together with all harmonizing things, to reach the highest maker, whom, as the threefold author of all things, intellect, reason, and will shall bless: and sometimes a fourth will appear, that is, this animal of ours made like the rational being: because, transformed for the better, and itself as if rational, and a legitimate son, it bursts forth into the praises of the Father, inviting all created things to do likewise, just like those three boys, as we read in Da- [Marginal note: Daniel, David] niel: and before them David had done so, inviting the elements, plants, hail, snows, rains, fish, animals, stars, heavens, and waters beyond the mundane, into the praise of the maker. And so that they might express divine, mundane, and celestial canticles in an appropriate style, they themselves, and other prophets, brought forth their writings in diverse meters: [Marginal note: Jerome, Eusebius, Jerome] as Jerome, Eusebius, and other most skilled attest. Job (as it pleases the same Jerome) begins in prose, proceeds in dactylic and spondaic hexameter verses, and because of the idiom of the language, frequently admitting other feet not of the same number of syllables, but of the same time: And sometimes the rhythm itself, sweet and ringing, is carried in numbers of feet that are free, which metrists understand more than a simple reader. But others strive to prove, by certain rules of metrical art discovered in that idiom, that that entire progress of Job is in hexameter verses: [Marginal note: The same] it was recently shown to me in Rome. But the aforementioned Jerome calls David a Pindar, Alcaeus, Flaccus, and Siren: because proceeding in diverse meters, together with the lyre, he proclaims Christ, and with the ten-stringed psaltery he would rouse Him rising from the underworld. [Marginal note: Solomon] Solomon, beloved of the Lord, sings in a most beautiful poem in that little work the epithalamium of the holy nuptials of man with God, of Christ with the Church, of both testaments with each other, of scripture with mystical meaning, the consonance resulting from the harmony of both worlds with the archetype, which he deservedly names the Canticle of Canticles. On the harmony of the heavens with the supernal minds. Chapter XX.

Beyond those things which have been said above concerning the agreement of the stars with the angels, I also deem it necessary to examine this: that the angels themselves are moved by the Father, who is the fount, and origin, and first mover of all. Hence Dionysius: [Marginal note: Diony.] "All rejoice when the Father moves." Therefore, those (angels), moved by God, move the orb; and these (angels) arrange our bodies and other lower things to that harmony which the first mover of all himself commands. So that therefore those motions and influences might be harmonious, He placed appropriate intelligences over each orb and over individual stars: those seven supreme ones over as many planets, as we have said, and twelve over the twelve signs, and over that entire orb and the planets, the Queen of the heavens, who is therefore said to be crowned with twelve stars for the number of the signs, and adorned with many sevens, and full of innumerable charisms, just as the star-bearing heaven is full of innumerable stars. And because she contains the power of all the heavens and of the angels presiding over them, she is therefore deservedly asserted to be exalted above all choirs of angels. But the Prime Mobile ought to be governed by the Prime Mover; and through it, the other orbs (are governed), to which, however, particular ministers have been appointed, through whom, and through celestial instruments, that supreme moderator arranges all lower and particular things, yet with this law: that the higher ministers, and those nearer to the supreme king, move with fewer motions, but those more distant move with more motions. And consequently, those are happier who adhere more to the supreme One, than these (who are more distant), as Aristotle, [Marginal note: Aristote. Albertus. Ptolema. Mesta. Acade. Diony.] Albertus, Ptolemy, Mestalac teach; but especially the Academics with our divine Dionysius. And although we lower beings are agitated by many motions, they nevertheless attain the same harmony, that of the first, unique, and uniform motion from the same unique mover. Hence, the Queen of the heavens herself adheres more to the first and unique (mover), agitated by fewer motions, yet collecting the power of all within herself, and diffusing that collected power first into the twelve Apostolic princes, and consequently, descending to particulars, into very many (individuals), just as that power of the star-bearing heaven is divided into the twelve signs, and consequently into innumerable stars; and just as the power of the soul, collected first in the brain, through the neck, a single channel, which in the mystical body of the Church bears the type of the Blessed Virgin (as Jerome teaches), [Marginal note: Hiero.] descends to the twelve... No less is the same virtue found collected in Christ the head, and diffused into twelves, and afterwards into very many parts, John saying: "From his fullness we have all received," [Marginal note: John.] as in the following volume, God favoring, we shall more broadly relate. Therefore through Christ, as through a masculine power, but through her, as through a feminine (power), this outpouring occurs: Who in this mystical body are joined, just as head and neck, or as spouses into one flesh, so those two into one spirit, as concerning all betrothed, or adhering to God, the Apostle says: [Marginal note: Paul.] "He who adheres to God becomes one spirit with Him." We have touched upon these things brought forth above so that readers may learn with what great harmony from all things, however diverse, yet moved by one, we are led into the same one: For just as a particular human is one individual, and directed to a single end, although distinguished by various members and motions, so this unique structure, and the mundane body, by diverse, and accommod...

with the supreme measures: so that from there a prudent and intelligent reader may perceive the congruence of all lower things with the highest: For infallible Truth testifies that there are very many mansions in the Father's house: but following the older Theologians, we will revere those ten, whence the denary number, beyond which no further is given.

The Moon therefore, inasmuch as it is the receptacle of all higher influences, corresponds to the last enumeration: or to the first in ascending: which is now called the land of the living, now the tabernacle, now the Moon, now the receptacle and bosom of all influences, now indeed the kingdom: concerning which it is sung in the psalm: "Thy kingdom is a kingdom of all ages." (David) And again: "His kingdom shall rule over all." In which mansion, He who is always everywhere, is called Adonai, or Melec, that is, Lord or King.

But in that the Moon itself is a particular planet, it has its power from the second enumeration, which is called Yesod, that is, foundation, and the living God, the life of the world, and the disposer of all things, just as the Moon is of lower bodies: And there God is called Shaddai, which we can interpret as omnipotent, or sufficient to satisfy all: concerning which we have in the psalm: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High, shall abide in the shadow of Shaddai:" (Psalm) where it is translated, "he shall dwell in the protection of the God of heaven:" Since that name seems to have been silent in a great mystery, therefore another name for that place must be assigned, which is called El Chai, which we have interpreted as the living God: since from there, or through it from a higher source, or from the supramundane sun, the life of all proceeds, just as through the moon the favor of life is poured forth from the sun.

Mercury corresponds to the particular second enumeration named Hod, which with us sounds like adornment, beauty, or renown: concerning which the prophet says: "Confession and beauty are in his sight," (The same) for which it would be better said: "Renown, or adornment, and beauty are in his sight:" And again: "Confession and magnificence are his work:" but as the truth of the letter has it: "Renown, or adornment, and beauty are his work:" And here the influencing God is called Adonai Tzevaot, that is, Lord of hosts: Which name is not of war, but of piety, and of harmony, and of sweetness: To which lower Mercury leads the lower, and to which higher Mercury leads the higher.

But Venus has its power from Netzach, which interpreted is called conquering, or victory, or perpetual: and this word is placed in the titles of most psalms: For love conquers all, and brings the work to completion, with all labor esteemed as little, and held for naught: There indeed the influencing God is called Elohim Tzevaot, that is, God of hosts: Which name is of God ordering, or fabricating, and avenging judgment through wars, or through other punishments. Nor should anyone wonder that Venus is placed in the virtue of war, because every unjust war proceeds from depraved Venus, that is, from excessive self-love, or inordinate love: So also every just war proceeds from right love, and good Venus: because one justly wages war out of zeal for God, or for relieving those unjustly oppressed, whom we love.

But the Sun, the heart of the heavens, corresponds with Tipheret, the heart of the archetype: Which beauty, or that beautiful thing, we interpret—

[Marginal note: Psalm.] ...is interpreted. from whom all things are beautiful: concerning which in the psalm cited above: "Virtue and Tipheret," that is, beauty in His holiness, or sanctuary: which is in the midst of the entire Divine temple as the Holy of Holies: For which in our translation we have sanctity and magnificence in His sanctification: And just as this sensible sun makes all things shine and appear beautiful, so that divine [power] makes all things beautiful with that beauty which [Marginal note: Socrates] Socrates sought from Hippias: In which glory and most beautiful throne, God is said to reside, יהוה (YHWH) tetragrammaton, and four-lettered: which, since it is ineffable and inexpressible, just like His beauty and glory, when read, is expressed under the name Adonai: But since this name is found elsewhere, another particular [letter] is prefixed, which is ו (vau), which, translated into our language, sounds like vau, which is the letter of life and knowledge, that is, of life and knowledge, and most appropriately, since therein is the tree of life and knowledge of good and evil, which is Jesus the Messiah. Mars, from גבורה (gebura), which signifies strength, [Marginal note: Dauid] has its strength: concerning which the prophet in the one hundred and forty-fourth hymn cited above says: "They will declare Your power": where גבורתך (geburateca) is found: And what is especially exercised there is called דין (din), that is, hard and severe judgment: [Marginal note: Psalm.] concerning which also in the psalm: "From heaven You made judgment heard": where "the earth trembled and was still" is found: because it is to be feared: And from that [place], through Mars, come severe punishments, and slaughters, and warlike men. Hence also God, exercising [Marginal note: Exodus Ierem.] His power by punishing the wicked, is called a man of war, as in Exodus, And in Jeremiah it is found: "The Lord is with me as a mighty warrior," or "as a strong breaker," properly interpreting that כגבור עריץ (chegibur bariz): Performing which office God Himself is called אלהים (Elohim): And the angels serving there are called sons of Elohim. Jupiter, however, so called because he helps everyone, always beneficent, corresponds with that dwelling which is called חסד (chesed): which can be interpreted as mercy, piety, or clemency: By which the Most High God, beneficent to all, always tempers hard and harsh things, spreading His kindness in all things, according to [Marginal note: Psalm.] that of the psalm: "His mercy is over all His works": And there God operating is called אל (el), which we have interpreted as God: because He cherishes all things, and helps all with the utmost piety and clemency: which is proper to Him. But we find Saturn to receive whatever he has from בינה (bina), which sounds like intelligence: [Marginal note: Ecclesia] where the Holy Spirit is especially said to reside: concerning which in Ecclesiasticus: "And the spirit of understanding will fill him": Who also gave to prophets and and apostles the understanding of secret things: From which place the Hebrews received their Sabbath, and the seventh day dedicated to both Saturns, namely the celestial and the supermundane: And from there come remissions, and years of rest, and jubilees through the simple or squared septenary: All of which God operating is called יהוה, that is, the letter ה (He) with the ineffable and four-lettered name: concerning which the magnitude of the mystery forbids us to speak. The starry heaven is subject to חכמה (chocmah), which is that supreme wisdom which is the Son of God, full of ideas and forms of all things to be produced, and

--- Page 505 ---
**EIGHTH TONE. 183**

of things to be produced, just as that heaven is full of stars, containing the power of all things within itself, as we said a little earlier. On which throne the Son, sitting at the right hand of the Father, is Himself called God YHWH, which is the very semaphoras, and the four-letter name together with Yod (י), the letter indeed signifying the simplest divinity itself. But the Primum Mobile corresponds to the First Mover and the source of all things: who, moving all things, draws all things to Himself, just as the center draws all lines of the circumference into itself: For it is the center and the circle and the sphere, embracing and filling all things, and drawing all lines into itself. I would not dare to ascribe this attraction to the Most High Father, unless His Son taught me, saying: "No one comes to me unless my Father [Marginal note: CHRIST] draws him." Since the Son has this attractive power from the Father, He therefore said: "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself." In which supreme seat residing, the Most High Father is called אהיה אשר אהיה (Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh), which we have interpreted as, "I am who I am," but it would be better said, according to the sense of the letter, "I may be who I may be." Or according to another way, His name is only אהיה (Ehyeh), which sounds the simplest being of divinity, about which it is not permitted to speak. Hence by the learned He is called ראה לא עין (Ayin lo ro'eh), that is, "the eye does not see," because no one knows the Father except the Son, and him to whom the Son wills to reveal Him. Therefore I will only say this, that when He is named "He who is," or "I am who I am," the Father of lights is understood: from whom (as James [Marginal note: James] testifies) every good gift and every perfect gift emanates, yet flowing through diverse channels into all lower things, He provides that all things may cooperate with Him, so that all things conducive may be led into Him. Hence all prayers ought to be directed to Him, as He taught, who alone knew Him, saying: "When you pray, say: Our Father." And repeating often, He exhorted that we should ask from the [Marginal note: CHRIST,] Father, the giver of all good things: Who by His clemency may direct us to the same end, for which, and to the contemplation of which, we were instituted.

**SECOND CANTICLE**

The second canticle, which IS CALLED NEW, IN WHICH WE WILL DEMONSTRATE THAT ALL THINGS IN CHRIST CORRESPOND WITH MULTIPLE HARMONY, with sweeter melodies than joints and members in a worldly or human body.

**PROEM.**

[Marginal note: David]
**S**INCE in many places, P.B., and often repeated, we see by the Royal prophet in his hymns that delightful (so to speak) refrain, "Sing to the Lord a new song," I was inquiring whether any new things have been made, to be sung with a new song: since we see no other heaven, or stars shining with new splendor: Nor other courses for the sun to traverse by day, and the moon by night: Nor the day to be distinguished by other hours, nor the summer season to advance with new increases, or to wane with recent decreases in wintry weather: Nor do we perceive any new living creatures, or any new kinds of things: And to conclude briefly with the Wise Man, nothing new under the sun: Nevertheless, by heavenly oracle we are taught that all things were made new in the time of the Redeemer: For He who sat on the throne said (says John in his most celebrated vision), [Marginal note: John] "Behold, I make all things new." [Marginal note: Paul] And Paul, in whose breast Christ himself resounds, speaking with the Corinthians, says: "The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." Hence he teaches us to praise God not only with a new song, but with new works and a new life, while he says: "Stripping off the old man with his deeds, put on the new: who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of Him who created him." Which knowledge is given through the word and the light, which illuminates every man coming into this world: so that it may enlighten and polish the defiled image, and in a certain way render it new: so that just as all things were made through Him, so through the same all things might be renewed in man: as [Marginal note: The Same] the same Paul teaches us in Colossians, saying: "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, for in Him were created all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers, all things were created through Him and in Him: And He is before all, and all things consist in Him:" And this much for the old; but concerning the new, he continues, saying: "And in Him it pleased [God] to make all fullness dwell, and through Him to reconcile, or to sum up (as the Greeks have it), or to renew all things, as is the truth of the matter, making peace and renewing through the blood of His cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven" with a sweeter sound and a more pleasant harmony than they had been in-

God, to whom, the Most High, be glory, who at last, by renewing all things through His Son, brought back God's ultimate
work into Himself with a new harmony, and a new and wondrous conso-
nance: which neither musicians knew, nor Pindar or Homer sang in verse, nor [Marginal note: Pinda. Homer.]
Ligystus with his lyre, nor Orpheus with hymns, nor Apollo with his lyre or tortoise-shell [Marginal note: Ligiſtus]
sang: Nor did the intellects of philosophers or the wise of the world devise it: But this [Marginal note: Orphe. Philoſo.]
only He knew, who brought about this harmony, and His Spirit, of whom it is
said, 'He will suggest all things to you, and will teach you all things': Who not only teaches
externally, but transfers Himself into holy souls, and establishes them as friends and harmonizers of God,
and of His secrets. He therefore assisted the most holy prophets, so that they might sing this new song as a most
sweet prelude: And He, teaching and
exciting new harmonizers, and them singing the new song with a clearer voice,
would somehow render us instructed in the same, so that, taught by them, and
strengthened by the same Spirit, we might extend our hands to the melodies of that song,
and with the clearest voice proclaim to the ears of all that Jesus Christ, the Son of the Most
High God, conceived in a new way, and born in a new way, has raised up a new
body for the Church: To this new militia He delivered a new sign,
taught a new life, and new customs, and a new doctrine:
He prepared new food: He instituted new sacraments:
He established a new dominion, and a new principate,
and a new way of rewarding:
Finally, He provided a new passage to God,
renewing all things: so that for those
writing about Him, a new song
is to be sung by us, and this
in eight tones, in our
manner,
as if with a new diapason, we
shall complete it.

THE TONES OF THE SECOND CANTICLE.

Christ is the life, and sustenance of all, vivifying all things, and drawing all things to himself. Tone II.
Christ is the true priest, true bread, host, and sacrifice purifying all things, and pacifying all things. Tone III.

Christ is King of kings, and supreme Emperor ruling all things, and moderating them. Tone VII.
Christ is mediator: through whom passage is given to all, that they may come to their end. Tone VIII.

HEADINGS OF THE FIRST TONE.

[Decorative initial M]Essiah's divinity is proven by reasons. Ch. First.
The same is corroborated by Prophecies. Ch. II.
How divinity, and the word are in him. Ch. III.
In the same word all things were contained. Ch. IIII.
Therein all things are in number, weight, and measure. Ch. V.
Exemplary cognitions in the mind of the supreme artisan are called ideas, and are. Ch. VI.
Who admitted these ideas. Ch. VII.
Who rejected them, and for what reasons. Ch. VIII.
They are errors, and not reasons, which seem to act against them. Ch. IX.
What we have from ideas. Ch. X.
That all harmony proceeds from the word. Ch. XI.
How these ideas are understood by us. Ch. XII.
The necessity of things, and all being depends on ideas. Ch. XIII.
Therein are also ideas of virtues, and rules, according to which we ought to live. Ch. XIIII.
There are reasons moderating honest, and base actions. Ch. XV.
Christ is true man full of divinity. Ch. XVI.
Just as Christ, in that He is God, contains all things by virtue, so in that He is man, He contains all the same things collected in the same most excellent note. Ch. XVII.

TONE ONE. 185

THE DIVINITY OF THE MESSIAH IS PROVEN BY
REASONS. Chapter One.

[Illuminated initial M] ESSIAH CHRIST, our Anointed One, was
and is God, we can prove not only by witnesses and oracles, but by the strongest
reasons: For we see the ready consensus of all,
and without disagreement, that blessed God,
existing of Himself, has all things from Himself, but nothing from another:
All other things, however, have their being and operation from Him:
therefore the great Theodorus said, with Proclus as witness: All things pray, except [Marginal note: Theod. Procul.]
the first, and they draw something from Him who is of Himself: and He is the fount and origin of all:
otherwise they would flow into nothing. Since, therefore, all things have both being, and natural power, and
glory, and adornment from God, all things participate in divinity itself, but
in diverse ways: All things (says Origen) have from God the Father, that they may be: from the spirit [Marginal note: Origen.]
of life, that they may live: from the Son, that they may understand and have a portion of reason: from the Holy Spirit, however
(who is nevertheless the same as the spirit of life), that they may be holy. Therefore, something divine
is inherent in all things: In this, indeed, to be only simple or composite: In that, to be
and to operate: In another, however, to be, to operate, and to understand. But leaving other things aside, let us speak of
man: to whom all things have been communicated, so that he may bear the most perfect image of God and the Father:
Hence, he can deservedly be called the Son of God, as the royal
prophet sings: I have said, "You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High." And since God communicates Himself more [Marginal note: David]
to him whom He wishes to make more exalted and perfect, it was fitting
that He should adorn him, whom He constituted head of others, redeemer, king, and eternal priest,
more with divinity, which is called oil in sacred scripture, as
the prophet again sings: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions," [Marginal note: Idem]
to such an extent that He made him more excellent than all in the communicated divinity itself:
Hence, by antonomasia and a certain hyperbole, he is called God. Another
reason is also readily available: because since man was made capable of divinity, in which alone he can
rest and be blessed, he ought at some time to have attained it: and to be united with
the same: by which union not only is God brought into man, but rather
man into God Himself, since it is of all-encompassing virtue and efficacy: And the more
this God is united with someone, the more He renders that person God. It is not surprising, therefore,
if He rendered this Messiah and Christ, to whom He offered Himself with that fullness, and which
man can receive, such that we can deservedly call Him God Himself: who
also gave to others the power to become children of God. Let us add another reason, that
just as all things are contained and recapitulated in man, so all things ought much more to be recapitulated
and united in God through man: Indeed, through that man
who ought to hold, and does hold, the first place among others: and who drew all things
to himself, so that he might lead all things back to God. Nor let some contend,
saying that this union does not argue for divinity in the united one, but only a conjunction—
AA

--- Page 510 ---
**OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

Indeed: for the highest Truth itself declares what this kind of union is, while saying:
[Marginal note: CHRIST.] "I pray, Father, that just as I and You are one, so also they may be one in You." But what their union is, He expresses elsewhere, saying: "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me." And again,
[Marginal note: Paul] "I and the Father are one." Which Paul also openly admonishes with his voice: "He who adheres (he says) to God becomes one spirit with Him." If therefore all can be made one spirit with God, why will not he be united with Him, who by antonomasia is called Messiah, Christ, and Anointed, namely by that divinity with which he was so full, that from his fullness we all receive?

Nor indeed (to proceed further) ought man, a creature of every kind, to be repaired by another than by him through whom he had been instituted: But all things were instituted and made through the Word, which was made flesh; therefore all things ought also to be repaired through that same one. And so that redeemed angels and men, and all things contained within them, might be indebted to the most honorable liberator: it was fitting that the liberator, to whom all things would be committed, should be the most excellent of all: which cannot happen except through a more fully shared divinity. Nor ought restitution and reparation, which are esteemed greater than institution, to be made by an inferior than by him through whom the institution itself had been effected: But this was done through the Word of God, therefore that also ought to be done through the same, since no greater means could be had, through which it could have been done.

Moreover, since the entire human creature had sinned, such a fall could not be repaired by a delinquent. Nor ought it to have been done by an angel, who is considered by the wise to be lesser than man, to whom it is given to transcend all angelic choirs: which could not be accomplished, unless man pre-existed in power greater than the angels themselves. Nor was there an angel, or any other creature, except man of every kind, capable of union with
[Marginal note: The same] the Creator of every kind; therefore the apostle said: "He nowhere takes hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham."

Moreover, sin itself, since it was against God, could not be repaired except by God: For ignorance was not involved: because this, given as a punishment for sin, ought not to precede the fault. Nor was it mere fragility, because sensuality had not yet rebelled: But pride was present, which caused both angels and man to apostatize from their Maker: because each had presumed to claim for himself a more eminent rank than was fitting for him: For it had been granted to man to emulate the condition of all creatures, but by no means that of the coming Christ. Hence all better and rational trees, or trees of virtues, had been permitted to him for food, except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which is Christ: who at the same time ought to experience, and did experience, the good of beatitude and the evil of our passions: This rank, he (man) desired to undertake, presuming not out of ignorance or fragility, but rather out of an excessive and most lucid knowledge: Whence his sin was as if against the Holy Spirit: which is complete despair, or excessive presumption, or stubborn malice, or the crime of lèse-majesté. Which crimes could not be expiated by any sacrifice, nor purged by the law, according to that
[Marginal note: Paul David] saying of the Apostle: "By the works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him." Hence David, perceiving that he had fallen into a lesser crime than lèse-majesté, while he sang psalms and prayed for his sin, said: "For if you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it, indeed;"

--- Page 511 ---
holocausts you will not delight in. And these are the sins by which man was so stripped bare, that no covering elaborated by art, or ingenuity, or human strength, or provided by nature, sufficed for covering. Hence, God, not content that man had covered his nakedness with a loincloth woven from fig leaves, clothed him with a tunic of skin, indeed made from the skin of that Lamb, of whom the Bap- [Marginal note: Ioã bap.] tist said: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world." And that that scripture speaks of Jesus our redeemer is manifest from the rearrangement of the letters of the Hebrew text of those words: "And he clothed them:" And this, according to the most celebrated doctrine of Hebrew Theology, we will nevertheless, God willing, refer to in its proper place: Hence neither human virtue, nor legal sacrifice could cover that sin: And since we are taught these things by sacred scripture, therefore it must be seen what it itself states concerning this nativity of Christ.

The same is corroborated by prophecies. Chapter II.

IF therefore we prove divine things by divine oracles, let us come to the divine prophets raging with the fury of the Holy Spirit. The royal prophet, a most elegant type of Christ, [Marginal note: David] sings in his person: "Adonai, or God, said to me, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'" For there is no other son who is "today," that is, continuously, begotten by God the Father, except God the Son himself, who is the Messiah and Christ: against whom the chief priests had conspired, and the nations and kings of the earth had gathered together, namely Pilate [Marginal note: Pilatus Herodes] and Herod with their attendants. And he is the one to whom the nations are given as an inheritance: and his dominion is extended even to the ends of the earth. Isaiah also, after he promised the birth of a young woman, or a virgin, [Marginal note: Isaias.] as a sign of the divine covenant, reconciliation, and peace, added: "And his name shall be called עמנואל Himmanuel, that is, God with us," indeed in a more excellent way than it ever was before. And again, while he prophesied concerning a child to be born, and a son to [Marginal note: Idem] be given, he said: "And his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Angel of great counsel (אל גבור El gibor), that is, Mighty God, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come." Nor let the Jews contend, saying that אל signifies "strong": because it would be an incongruous expression to say "strong strong": For in its proper meaning, גבור *gibor* is called "strong." But אל in common usage signifies God. Nor could any man be the Father of the age to come (which is the paradise of delights, as the wise Hebrews teach), nor an introducer to it, since the whole of humanity was expelled from it in the first man. But if the Father of the age to come is understood as the father and giver of blessed life, which I consider the same, no one can be this father, or of eternal life, except he who has it from himself, being the true Lord of blessedness, who is God alone in Christ saying: "I give eternal life to my sheep." [Marginal note: CHRI STVS. Ierem.] Jeremiah, however, foreseeing this same thing with clear insight, addresses God himself, who is to be made human, in familiar speech, saying: "Why will you be a settler and a stranger in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay in an unusual manner?" And because he was found in appearance as a fragile man, and subject to passions, therefore the prophet continues: "Why will you be like a wandering man, and strong, who cannot save?"
