**FIRST TONE.**                                                                    **189**

**How divinity and the Word are in Christ himself. Chapter III.**

[Decorative woodcut initial Q depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, at a desk] Although the manner in which the Divinity was and is in our Redeemer is difficult and almost impossible to explain, indeed not even perceptible to the intellect, since Damascene says that the incarnation of the Word was unknown even to the highest Seraphim, not only as to the time, but also as to the manner, nevertheless, as far as God has permitted us to speak, we will try to explain how divinity and the Word are in this man, the Redeemer. Something of the father is always found in the son through the seed by which he is generated: Hence Aristotle in his [Marginal note: Aristotle.] Ethics concludes that the father loves the son more than vice versa: because he feels something of his own in the son himself: whence in many things appears not only the paternal spirit, but speech, voice, manners, appearance, facial features, body stature, and the like. But God, although he is the parent of all things by a certain analogy, is in a more perfect sense the father of man: who bears his image, than of other creatures, who only enjoy his trace. Therefore, man feels and contains something of divinity more excellent than other created things: because we are his peculiar race: as the wise Aratus says: And before him Pythagoras says: A divine race is inherent in men: With whom that wavering semi-Pythagorean says: Man is born: whether that maker of things made him from divine seed, And a much, and incomparably greater gift of divinity ought to be in him, who is antonomastically called the Son of God, and through whom other sons of God are made.
[Marginal note: Aratus]
[Marginal note: Pythagoras. Ovid.]
Not only is the seminal virtue of God in all created things, and especially in man, but there is a continuous influx of that divinity, just as the continuous diffusion of the sun's rays illuminates and cherishes all places: to which it always comes beneficently, providing life and fruitfulness: Which we prove with clear light, while through its approach to us the earth is made fruitful: plants sprout: animals grow eager for generation and offspring: birds hasten to produce and cherish eggs: and fish, by scattering their eggs, provide the greatest increase to their kind: And conversely, when it recedes, generation seems closed: and plants lay down what they had previously produced when made fruitful: Hence, if the abundance of the sun itself were uniform, the same fruitfulness would always be equal in all things. But the highest and super-mundane Sun, since it neither approaches nor recedes, because it is always everywhere, is always diffused in all things according to their capacity: And always flowing in all things, it preserves their being, continuously bestowing and suggesting fruitfulness and the power of working, unless the weakness of the recipient obstructs it: Hence, the more disposed one is, the more one perceives the abundance of divinity: Knowing this, Jeremiah [Marginal note: Jeremiah.] said: But you are in us, O Lord, and your name is invoked upon us, that is, the power of the name, and of the one named, is perceived in us: For the name of God is the same as God himself: and the power of the divine name is the power of God, if the wise Hebrews, [Marginal note: Wise Hebrews.] interpreting thus, feel correctly: Just as concerning the angel sent for the protection and guidance of Moses, the Lord [Marginal note: GOD] testifies, saying: Behold, I send my angel, who will go before you: Observe him, and listen to his voice: for my name is in him,

**AA v.**

--- Page 518 ---
**OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

that is, the power of my name, and of my divinity: as those cited above explain. And so much had the power of God's name passed to Christ, that He himself obtained that name, in which all things bow the knee: and in which all wonders are performed: which used to be done in ancient times in El Shaddai (שדי) up to Moses: And from Moses up to Christ in that great four-letter name YHWH (יהוה): Christ, [Marginal note: CHRIST.] feeling the power of these names fused in Himself and in His name, said with great authority: "In my name they will cast out demons: they will speak with new tongues: they will take up serpents: and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not harm them: they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover." Therefore God flows into all things, filling all things according to their capacity, just as air fills every space not occupied by another body: because all things are full of Jove (God): which can be understood of air, and of God. And just as the whole body is filled by the soul, so that it is whole in the whole, and whole in every part, but in a certain more eminent way in the brain, and in the heart (as a medium for the senses), and lowest in the other members, So also in [Marginal note: Jeremiah.] this mundane body is God, saying through Jeremiah: "I fill heaven and earth:" Indeed, He fills the earth, and the elements, and other lower things more loosely, middle things more fully, but the highest things most fully: Which highest things are angel and man, whom He fills as heart and brain, not only with common life, but with rational, intellectual, and free, or loving life. Nor does God fill these mundane members with less power than the Sun fills the spaces of the world, and the soul fills all members of the human body. Therefore God is in man, but most especially in Christ through seed, through afflu- [Marginal note: Theologians.] -ence, and through repletion. He is also (as more recent Theologians teach) through hypostasis, or person, which they attribute to Christ Himself, and to our Anointed One: because they see works transcending the limits of human nature, which necessarily come from the individual subject: because actions belong to individual subjects, or particulars. He is also through in- [Marginal note: James] -sertion, as James says: "Receive the engrafted word." Indeed, it is an appropriate metaphor: because therein two natures united together by a certain natural, or divine, and supernatural glue produce fruit more according to the nature of the inserted shoot, than of the receiving trunk. But Christ himself said that He was united with us by a con- [Marginal note: CHRIST.] -tinuation, saying: "I am the vine, and you are the branches:" so also His assumed nature is united with the vine of divinity by a certain better-known continuation. Other examples could also be adduced of this union of divinity with that assumed human nature, but these suffice for the present.

Exemplary cognitions in the mind of the artisan are called ideas, and are. Chapter VI.

[Decorative initial D containing a scene with figures] We have learned from very many wise men that there are twofold rules in the divine mind and word:
Of which, some are of things to be made by Himself: and these are properly called ideas
from *eidos*, which signifies species and form: Others, however, are exemplars, to whose
goals our works are to be brought, which are also called ideas by a certain analogy.
Ideas are therefore eternal forms, species, and exemplars of things, always existing in the divine mind,
and before things came into being, so that each subject might be imprinted by them as by their
own seals: And now they persevere in their existence: so that the species themselves may always
be preserved, and be eternal: nor are they corrupted or transmuted by the corruption or
transmutation of the individual. And by a certain analogy, even the thoughts of things to be made
[Marginal note: Aug. li.] by us through art are called ideas and exemplars: as Augustine discusses at length on
John. But because they are not exemplars of species and essential things, they are not
properly ideas, but are called so analogically, through which we can conjecture those divine ones:
[Marginal note: Plato.] Which (as Plato teaches) in the paternal intellect is one and a simple idea, universal in
virtue and causality, and in itself, by its virtue, pre-possessing all forms in a certain more
excellent way. This, however, proceeding, shines forth multiplied in Him who has all things from the
Father: And further, it is diffused in some way, divided in diverse places or mansions of the
archetype. It then comes to the movers of the spheres and other intelligences, to whom it committed
the arrangement of lower things, offering them as it were a seed: and commanding them to
execute and bring forth according to the infusion given to them. They, however, unfold through
the heavens as through instruments with diverse irradiations and opportune aspects, trigons,
hexagons, and tetragons, now approaching, now receding: And finally, forms are infused
according to the disposition of the subjects, which they always desire, so that they may be
informed and perfected: just as a woman desires a man, so that she may receive offspring and
generation from him: or that she may enjoy his sex. But all those things are arranged by the

fertilize all things, as the seed, form, and life of all. Hence John said: "And the life was the
light of men": Because that supreme light is theirs, and of all

**Those who have admitted these ideas. Chapter VII.**

[Decorative initial F] Let Aristotle, Proclus, Porphyry, [Marginal note: Aristotle. Proclus. Porphyry.] and other wise men say how much authority the easy agreement of many wise men on the same opinion confers, and how much truth it demonstrates that opinion to have, who often prove the truth of a matter from the common consent of the wise. Therefore, in the matter of ideas, not only Catholics, or all Christians agree, but so many and such great external wise men, that all suspicion can rightly be removed that our people affirm them more by law than by truth. Zeno, the ancient Philosopher, [Marginal note: Zeno.] proclaims God as the principle and disposer of nature, whom he names "logos," that is, "word," which is the intelligence of Himself and of things to be made, and consequently, idea. Which I believe he received from the workshop of Mercury, [Marginal note: Mercury.] who says in Pymander: "Mind, God, most full of the fecundity of both sexes, life and light, by His word, brought forth another mind, the artisan." This God, of fire and spirit, then fabricated seven governors, who encompass the sensible world with their circles, and their disposition is called fate. Then the Word of God connected from the elements of God tending downwards a pure work of nature, and united it to the artisan mind, for it was consubstantial. Behold how piously, how learnedly, how clearly he teaches that all things pre-existed in that most fertile Mind or Intelligence of God, which he calls the Word, according to the doctrine of our John. [Marginal note: John.] But the Mind which it brought forth is another person, but of the same essence, in which artisan mind, that is, the produced Word, it fabricated all things. But first, those seven minds were fabricated, which are called the first separated intellects, according to that supramundane septenary, which septenary the Hebrews [Marginal note: Hebrews.] call "fabric," with which we have declared these intelligences and their orbs to agree. Which seven intelligences or Spirits (as we read in Apocalypse [Marginal note: Apocalypse. Tobit.] and Tobit) are always in the sight of the throne of the supreme Prince, who, disposing of lower things, execute what the supreme one commands, and hence their disposition is called fate. Afterwards he speaks clearly how the Word of God, that is, the conception of things to be made, or in which the conception itself exists, fabricated this mundane work to be united with the first artisan. Therefore, let ideas be in the mind or word of the supreme architect, as the causes of things: from which, Plato, proceeding, is deservedly said by Theophrastus to have assigned causes from divine providence above all philosophers. The Stoics, imitating their Zeno, said that anticipated notions in our souls are ideas: But these (notions) are analogical, while those (ideas) in the divine mind are truly so, because according to their likenesses, formless matters are shaped in a specific principle, as Plutarch says in 'De Placitis Philosophorum'. And before these, Timaeus Locrus teaches that the idea is innate, but externally an exemplar, and an assisting cause, or the form of all things that are transformed: with whom Epicharmus Sphaerus, and many other ancients agree. However, later Platonists, Iamblichus, Porphyry, Plotinus, Hermias, Numenius, Proculus, and his teacher Syrianus, expanded this doctrine: the last of whom (Syrianus) so extensively elaborated in his Apologetic for Plato that he published a very extensive volume. Alcinous also, explaining the master's dogma in the book titled 'On the Doctrine of Plato' and in his 'Epitomes', says: Plato held that ideas are not properly of artificial things, like a shield and a lyre; nor of those things that are contrary to nature, like fever and bile; nor of particulars, like Socrates or Plato; nor of very minute things, like dust or a straw; but they are of perfect beings, and immutable notions, always enduring; and certain immaterial measures existing, for the reason that the world is not from chance, but from the highest order, after the manner of those exemplars which were fashioned in the artisan: Which idea in the artisan is one, and a universal cause, virtually containing all things and pre-existing them, but multiplied with respect to the things ideated: because it is of many: Whence in origin it is one, but many from what is determined by it: Which opinion, approved by so many wise men and divine oracles, is judged worthy of greater assertion than Aristotle's heresy or derision: although the obscured Alexander and Averroes held the contrary. And it is remarkable (if Aristotle is well considered) that he himself, even if in words, by some spirit I know not, seems to disagree, yet in reality he thinks nothing else: For he concedes that active power and art pre-exist in the artisan before he comes to his work. Nor is the reason less in the artisan of the mundane fabric, whom, since they did not know when, why, and how he fashioned this mundane house, he denies the fabric itself, and the manner, and the order somewhere; which elsewhere, compelled by truth, he confesses. Perhaps he denied ideas and the world's fabric while, content within physical terms, he professes and teaches: For he asserts in that treatise 'On the World', which is ascribed to him, that this machine was fashioned by the supreme artisan; and in superior philosophy, freed from physical laws, theologizing quite well, he says that just as our intelligence is caused by things and known objects, so the science and knowledge of God is the cause of those things that are: But what, I ask, is the causative intelligence of God for things, if not His Word, through which all things were made? [Marginal note: Salomon]

**Who rejected ideas, and for what reasons. Chapter VIII.**

**T**he foremost among those who rejected ideas is Aristotle with his Peripatetics: and this man indeed of gravest authority among those who follow only sensible doctrine and inferior philosophy: who neither piously nor justly, but in the manner of an ungrateful disciple, deriding his master, says: "Farewell, ideas of Plato: for they are nothing, or they are monsters": deeming it superfluous, ridiculous, inconvenient, and false to admit ideas themselves.
[Marginal note: Ariſtoteles]
He indeed deemed it superfluous: since for the first agent, its object, which is its essence, through which it operates all things, and in which it contains all things, is sufficient. Ridiculous indeed, because God does not need an image or a paradigm through which to know something else, just as man needs a sensible or intelligible species. It also seemed inconvenient and absurd to them that corruptible and temporal things should be generated from those eternal forms. And since ideas are relative, because they refer to ideated things, they cannot exist in that most simple substance, alien from all imperfection. It is also absurdly said that they contribute to number, since equivocal things exist of a different nature from numbered things. Furthermore, they believed it false that through those exemplars, produced things are assimilated to the artisan: as the supporters of ideas assert.

Therefore, it confesses God to be the beginning and the end of all things, and the means by which all things are made, according to that saying of Paul: "From whom are all things, in whom are all things, through whom are all things." Which mystery was explained to Abraham the Chaldean, and to his descendants (who are called Hebrews from their crossing over), and committed to scripture in the book of Formation: which is inscribed to Abraham himself.
Whence also Aristotle, when he discoursed on the knowledge of God Himself in his first philosophy, venerated the Chaldean fathers, yielding to them: because they received it from oracles. Who (as Proclus says, illuminated by some light or other), feasting with God and living in pure splendor, were initiated into perfect and stable Phantasms on all sides, asserting opinions, and considered scientific reasons as trifles and old wives' tales, since those [opinions] are indeed uncertain and doubtful, and not far from an irrational life. But these [syllogistic reasons] are syllogistic and composite: and in no way can they touch the solitary and intellectual nature of the Creator Himself.

However, those easy and fallacious reasons, lest we seem to avoid their cunning, we will now unravel. And first, why Aristotle mocked or scorned ideas, let Themistius and Simplicius, his expositors, and Francis, distinguished among more recent theologians, adorned with the surname "the Illuminated," tell us: The first of these says: "Aristotle always tried to contradict appearances." The next one indeed says: "Aristotle argues more against words than against meanings." But the last, with greater license or zeal for the most divine theology, bursts forth against him with words of this kind: "Aristotle accuses Plato for two reasons: The first is envy, by which he falsely and impiously persecutes his master, from whom he learned much everywhere: as is manifest even to those moderately experienced in Plato's doctrines. The second, because even if he was a good philosopher, he was a very bad metaphysician. But neither in physics was he an inventor, but only a collector, as he himself confesses in the Elenchi, saying: 'If praise for inventions is given to anyone, it is due to me for the Elenchi.' Where, compelled by truth, he did not want to arrogate to himself what he had not done." Therefore, engaged in those rules of argumentation and sensible things, he willingly departed from the divine symposium: in which (says Simplicius) Plato, nurtured, always venerates divine things, and starting from those eternal species and ideas, descends even to the lowest things. But Aristotle, proceeding from sensible things, ascended only as far as his reasons, formed from sensible things, could lead him. "For there are diversities of gifts," says our Paul: "Therefore to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word..."

...knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, and suchlike. Therefore to some is given to know in human affairs;

To others also (as Cicero says) was given the faculty of speech: To others, access to the inner sanctuaries of doctrines: but to both (as he says) he had seen it happen to no one of the Greeks. They believe that His own object suffices for God: we grant this to them, but we say, that in Him, or in the Word produced by Him, which is the same as the object itself, are the ideas of things: Which is not an object under the aspect of the Son, or of the Word produced, or of ideas: but under the aspect of divinity, or of essence. Nor do the supporters of ideas propose anything ridiculous by saying that God needs an image, when He Himself has constituted Himself the exemplar of things to be made. On the contrary, self-content and sufficient: but ideas in Him are the same as Himself, also imparted to things, but not external. Nor is it inconvenient, according to the Platonic [Marginal note: Platon.]
and divine wise men, that what emanates from the supreme being and participates in it, is in some way one, and in some way not one: in some way the same, and in some way not the same, just as the sun is one in itself, manifold in its rays: and the heat proceeding from it is the same as the sun, and in the recipient not the same: So also a tree is one in itself, manifold in its branches: it is the same as its fruit, and not the same in taste, flavor, and nature: Which is learnedly [Marginal note: Procul.]
and wisely discussed by Proclus in his Commentary on the Timaeus and in his Theological Elements. Thus also John Scotus teaches that the object, as it is in [Marginal note: Ioā. Sco.]
the knower, is the same as the knower, but diverse in its own being. Nor does the Creator use the ideas themselves as an instrument, but as a seminal and impressive force (so to speak) of essential forms, from which an image is left in the recipient, just as a specific form is imprinted by a natural generator: For from a horse comes a horse, and not an ape: and from an eagle comes an eagle, and not an ass. And indeed I wonder why they doubted how that virtue of ideas, since it is like a seminal virtue, moves the passive recipient to receive the form: because the same doubt would exist about any agent, since there is no less application, or what is called virtual contact, in the primary cause than in secondary causes. We could pursue many arguments with such people, but we judge it superfluous, since these things are not to be brought into controversy: but rather to be received with all reverence, giving thanks to God who illuminates our intellect to receive His secrets and treasures.

**What we have from ideas. Chapter X.**

[Decorative initial E] And lest ideas be believed to be in vain, and fabricated by false imagination, let us see what utility we gain from them, which we so greatly revere. From them we have form and specific being, so that we may be preserved and understand: finally, we have our weight and measure. And as for the first point, many dispute about the origin and inherence of forms, whence they proceed: And by common consent the Peripatetics [Marginal note: Peripate.]
agree that corruptible and mortal souls emerge from the bosom of matter, to use their words. Concerning the intellective soul, since it is still doubtful among them whether it is mortal or immortal, nor have they determined whence it comes, but their Prince, [Marginal note: Ariftote.]
speaking doubtfully, says: If there is any form coming from outside, it is the intellective soul: but I truly do not know how one can imagine that a form is drawn out of matter, unless the true opinion ascribed to Anaxagoras holds, that anything is in anything. [Marginal note: Anaxa.]
But they say that there is a potentiality inherent, to be brought into act at some time. But O Peripatetics, who gave that potentiality to matter, and who brings it into act? Nature (they say) bestows this upon matter and the subject, and a particular agent brings it into act by seminal virtue. But what this nature is (as we have said elsewhere) they do not determine, but it cannot be anything other than the first Creator working all things in all, or secondary causes acting at His command and by His power.

**OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

He is therefore the first agent, and the first giver of forms, from whom is all life, form, and order. But since no one gives what he does not have (as the Peripatetics themselves teach), it is therefore necessary that every form be in the Creator, from whom it proceeded: And the forms existing there are ideas, to whose measures we have particular forms and being: And since that being continuously flows from Him who gave it, we have from the ideas, according to which He granted, whence we are sustained, lest we flow away into nothingness: since our being continuously flows: And that which flows, it is necessary that it be sustained in something permanent: For time and motion flow, and are sustained in the permanent heaven: Natural heat flows, and is sustained by food: Water flows in a river, and is sustained by its channel: Finally, every creature flows into nothingness, and is sustained by the divine word: in which all things were created.
[Marginal note: Paul] This is what Paul says concerning the Father, the source of all good things: "Upholding all things by the word of his power." From this we have: whence we may understand from those things which remain unvaried and unchanged: For from these things continuously flowing, and never remaining in the same state, nothing can be known, as Heraclitus of Ephesus, Cyril, Paron, and many others thought:
[Marginal note: Heraclitus, Cyril, Paron] because since the form of mutable things continuously flows, they believed that it was not always the same, nor did it have a determined being: so much so, that neither a definition, which is of permanent and necessary things, can be had concerning them:
[Marginal note: Parmenides] Wherefore Parmenides also asserted that nothing could be known about inferior things, except insofar as they depend on the supreme, concerning which there is true knowledge: Who, after he sang of divine things, then adds concerning inferior things:
Thus far both the mind of truth and undefiled words.
Now, mortal things, also take up a deceptive song.
Behold how piously, how justly, and with what an elevated mind he calls the knowledge of divine things true science, and discourse concerning them undefiled: because they are stable and firm: But the opinion of inferior and mutable things, and deceptive discourse, he judges:
[Marginal note: Aristotle, Averroes] Which Aristotle and Averroes did not see, or did not wish to see: because they did not wish to awaken and take up the eye, which (as Plotinus says) indeed all possess, but very few use: or they did not wish to admit what is taught only in that sacred bipartite scripture: from which, as from a true treasure, new and old things can be extracted, which we sing in a new and old canticle:
[Marginal note: Augustine] Augustine, weighing this, enlightened by sacred eloquence and subjected to the divine spirit, let us hear what he says about ideas, through which we have being and knowledge: "In ideas there is such power, that unless they are understood, no one can be wise." Which, since they are in the incarnate Word, not undeservedly does Paul declare concerning Him: "In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge."
[Marginal note: Paul, Philo] To this opinion the wisest Philo assents in the book which he wrote, that worse things are accustomed to insult better ones, saying: "It is fitting for all who seek knowledge to raise their mind to God the Father; but if they cannot, then at least to His image, namely the most sacred Word." Ideas also necessarily contribute to number: because in mutable things, and those subjected to continuous variation, enumeration cannot be verified or established. Nor otherwise did the Creator arrange all things in number, weight, and measu-

measure, except insofar as they are numbered in the Word, weighed by their own weights, and measured. **That all harmony proceeds from the Word. Chapter XI.**

[Decorative initial block with the letter C]INCE all things are numbered and weighed in the Word, and harmony depends on number and weight, we easily conclude that all things derive their harmony from the Word itself, in which the harmonious degrees of things are numbered and distinguished: Which are also necessarily harmonious, if Proclus, the principal illustrator of Academic doctrine, teaches truly: [Procul.] that every multitude descending from some one needs harmony: by which, namely, it may agree among themselves and with that one. But all things emanated from that one Word, and were indeed made harmonious, inasmuch as they receive from the same unique Word, and by its power tend towards the unity of the first: and are led by its attraction. Hence was received that portion, concerning which Plato says in Timaeus: [Plato.] 'In the beginning, the Creator received one portion from the universe:' For from the fount of the universe, and of all being, one portion was received, which is (if I am not mistaken) the very being of all things communicated by Him who said: 'I am who I am,' [DEVS.] having indeed being from Myself: and moved away from envy, I communicate it to all, distributed only according to their own degrees. Which communication: since it was made to prime matter produced by Him outwardly, therefore Plato follows, that from that one first emanates the dyad attributed to matter itself: because it first obtained duality: For just as from unity the first emanating number is the dyad (if it can be considered a number) so from that supremely one, being communicated was first determined in matter: And he doubles this dyad up to the cube, namely a threefold expansion, beyond which no other is given: Which Aristotle transmits from that workshop of Plato [Aristo.] in the beginning of the book 'On the Heavens'. From the other side, however, which belongs to the form produced second, and third from the producer, it proceeds through the ternary, even up to its cube: in which it concludes every kind of form: through which matter is reduced to act, and returns to the first: Whence form is inherent, as a familiar medium between the most perfect and the most imperfect, and having a certain symbol with the highest and the lowest, so that it may reduce the latter to the former: In which ternary, form, and the giver of forms himself, rejoices: therefore here, according to our most divine Theology, it is diffused into it, communicating it to us in some way: Which the Academics, [Academ.] excited by truth itself, profess: For Proclus [Procul.] says that the soul especially rejoices in this number, sen-

Therefore Moses (as Augustine [Marginal note: August.] understands) with wonderful artifice hints at how all things that were produced became manifest to angelic minds by a certain succession of that flashing light, saying: Just as the reason by which a creature is founded is prior in the Word of God than in the creature itself which is founded, so also the knowledge of that reason first occurs in an intellectual creature not subject to sin through the light of the Word, and afterwards in its own proper kind. From these two cognitions by the same light, as if from morning and evening, a day is completed: And granted that scripture begins from evening, it does so by resuming the succession from the latter part. Augustine pursues many arguments by which he demonstrates that angels do not understand those mysteries unless they have been imbued with divine light: much less can we, burdened by a bodily mass, be carried up to those spectacles, unless our eye is cleansed by divine grace and illuminated by its light: Therefore these things are hidden from the wise and prudent of this world: and are revealed to little ones made innocent of malice, disciples of the true light and eternal truth, which created and ordered all things. And it is indeed wonderful that many are unwilling to believe concerning the generation of the world and particular things to their progenitor and maker, and instead believe Aristotle and Averroes, who neither created them, nor knew their maker, nor the fabric itself, except insofar as it is subject to animal senses. It was enough for them to stay within the limits of their natural philosophy: which treats of things insofar as they are subject to manifold motion. But let them leave those things which are made by God to those who frequent God's own school: and are sometimes introduced into His inner sanctuaries: so that they not only hear, but see, and touch with their hands those things which lie hidden externally: How, namely, from that one proceeded this numerous multitude, From that good, all these things are very good, From that truth, that all these things might be true: From that Word, and supreme intelligence, that they might be knowable and known: From that life, that they might live: From that holy one, that those things which wish to be sanctified might be holy: From that beautiful one, that they might be beautiful: Which the very Word of God manifested in its own part by its goodness, saying: [Marginal note: CHRISTVS,] I am the way, the truth, and the life: And concluding summarily, He says: All things my Father has given to me: who is the immense fount of all good things, so that through me, namely, they may be produced and known.

The necessity of things, and all being, depends on ideas. Chapter XIII.

[Decorative initial E] From the workshop, therefore, of the supreme architect we have that from the ideas themselves we not only receive forms, and continuously flowing being, and the knowledge and number of things, weight, and measure, and consequently, that all things are harmonious, but they also have whence they are, and that they are necessary: which we can prove: For we consider it known to all that no one possesses those things which he strives to acquire and preserve: For we seek truth and wisdom, because we do not have it from ourselves: We seek goodness, and pleasure, and to advance in virtue, and to excel, since these are not in us, but from elsewhere com-

...to be acquired/prepared. We labor to preserve our very being, since we continually draw it from another; and finally, whatever good there is, we strive to acquire, as if it comes from elsewhere. But God seeks nothing, since He does not need our goods, says the prophet:
[Marginal note: David, Aristotle.] With whom Aristotle says in the Politics: God being witness, there is no happiness in external things: because He Himself is happy without anything outside Himself. Since God therefore has all things from Himself, but we have nothing, we expect to receive all things from Him, who distributes according to those most just measures which are in the archetype: Which some of the Hebrew wise men teach to be ideas, as the names agree: For an idea is an exemplar, a goal, and a measure of a thing to be made: For a fair and just distributor measures and weighs what he distributes: so that he may give to each according to his own virtue, or according to what he deserves: Thus also God, the most opulent giver, granted that He is of infinite goodness, nevertheless flows according to the exigency of the recipients: but in the primal distribution according to what the order of the universe required. Hence a curtain is placed in the midst of the superabundant waters, which are immense, and between these lower and finite waters. Therefore, through the supermundane heavens, all things to be given are measured, lest more be given to the recipient than is fitting: but all things measured and weighed are distributed by those weights and
[Marginal note: Augustine.] measures, which are not in the things measured (as we said above from the doctrine of Augustine) but in the measurer: And these are the eternal ideas and exemplars of things, from which each thing receives being and gifts, according to a degree and limit which cannot be surpassed: Whence, from the order given by the craftsman, and sealed by his idea, according to the king's command, is the very being of the receiving things and the necessity of being, according to the given form.
Likewise, there are also ideas of virtues, and rules, to which we ought to live conformably.

Chapter XIV.

[Decorative initial L]
[Marginal note: CHRIST.] That laws, rules, and goals of living are described in the Word, was sufficient to prove that of the eternal Word and infallible Truth saying: I am the truth and the way: from which, namely, it emanates, whence all created things are true beings, and whence each one holds the right
[Marginal note: Augustine.] path of living: and from which every judgment is right: Nevertheless, we will also bring forward Augustine explaining what Christ delivered in a few complex words, for he says this in his *De Trinitate*: "In that book of light, which is called truth, are written the rules by which one sees how each person ought to live: and there one recognizes what is just and unjust: There one perceives what one ought to have, but does not have:" Hence every law is described accordingly, and in the heart of the person who works righteousness, it is transferred not by migrating, but as if by imprinting, just as an image passes from a ring into wax, and does not leave the gold: For those [laws] are eternal and immutable. There are reasons governing honorable and base actions. Chapter XV.

[Decorative initial V] Since therefore in the divine Word are all the rules of living well and rightly, from which to deviate is sin, deservedly to the same, in whom these rules are, is committed the discernment of good or evil deeds, as he himself says: The Father has given all judgment to me. [Marginal note: CHRIST,] For he himself will judge the living and the dead, who knows how to discern the merits and misdeeds of all. Which also the oracle of Isaiah testifies, while treating of the Son to be born of a Virgin (who was to be called Emmanuel), saying: [Marginal note: Isaiah] He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good. [Marginal note: John.] And he needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man. Christ is true man full of divinity. Chapter XVI.

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 1; vertical-align: -0.25em;">S</span>I Christ was a true man, since all universally confess it, it is superfluous to dispute. Therefore, why he wished to redeem the human race in assumed human nature, remains for us to examine: The first reason for this is that since in the first man the whole human race transgressed, it was just that satisfaction should be made to the tribunal of God's supreme justice by man, in accordance with God's own law, that each should be punished,
<span style="float:right; margin-left:1em;">Exodus</span>
by that through which he also sinned: and satisfaction must be made by an equivalent, as we read repeated in Exodus
<span style="float:right; margin-left:1em;">Deuter.</span>
and Deuteronomy, that the one who harms another should render life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe: Therefore, man ought to be offered for man: but indeed a heavenly man, and innocent, and harmless from sin, for an earthly man, a transgressor, and a wicked one: so that not only the due penalty might be exacted, but also a legitimate redemption might be made by one not obligated for himself:
<span style="float:right; margin-left:1em;">Paulus</span>
Which Paul proclaims with his resounding words, saying: For indeed through man came death, and through man came the resurrection of the dead: And as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. Just as Christ, in that He is God, contains all things by virtue, so in that He is man, He contains these same all things collected in the same most excellent manner. Chapter XVII.

[Marginal note: Paulus]
[Decorative initial N, depicting figures in a landscape] Not without the deepest doctrine and sacrament, Paul, from the innermost sanctuaries, to which he had once been introduced, brings us the most celebrated eulogy of Christ, saying: It pleased God the Father to reconcile, or to recapitulate, all things in Him: as he expressly feels,

[Marginal note: Hieron.]
and at length Jerome discusses in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, lamenting that the Latin translation has 'instaurare' (to restore) instead of 'recapitulare' (to recapitulate): For Christ indeed recapitulates all things, containing all things in Himself: For just as in a summary and final repetition of a speech, an orator recapitulates and embraces all things which he had treated diffusely and individually throughout the entire speech, so the supreme Creator, having distinctly produced all creatures, on the sixth and last day produced man, in whom all things are contained. **SECOND TONE.**
**201**
**THE LIFE OF ALL IS MANIFOLD AND ONE.**
**Chapter One.**

[Large decorative initial N] Unless the Sun, which God lit to declare His majesty, and the soul, which He fashioned with such excellence, were to teach me how one can be manifold or many, I would not indeed dare to say that life is at once one and manifold. For the sun is one in itself, manifold in its rays, one in essence, yet of all kinds in power. The soul is also one in itself, but manifold in operation: For it hears in the ears: sees in the eyes: smells in the nostrils: tastes in the mouth: feels and works in the hands: understands in the brain: loves in the heart: walks in the feet: digests in the stomach, liver, and other digestive members: generates in the instruments appointed for this purpose, so much so that it appears manifold, though it is nevertheless one. Nor is it diminished by the fact that it seems to suffer a defect in some member: For if the eye or hand were weak, it is not thereby less in the brain or heart. From these things it will easily be recognized how that one life would be manifold in its members, if we were to admit that the world is an animal, as many wise men agree, even those who venerate the sacred scriptures, since these themselves seem to offer no obstacle: as Augustine, of most acute intellect and excellent doctrine, decrees: whence he also seems to assent to this opinion. [Marginal note: Augustine.] Origen, however, runs with swift feet to this same opinion: [Marginal note: Origen.] which he strives to prove both with reasons and with the testimony of sacred scripture, saying in his *De Principiis*: "Although the world is ordered with diverse offices, its state is not to be understood as dissonant or discordant: but just as our body is fitted together from many members and is contained by one soul, so too I think the entire world should be considered an immense and vast animal, which is held as if by one soul through the power and reason of God." Which I also believe is judged by sacred scripture through that which is said by the prophet: "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" says the Lord? And again through another Seer: "Heaven is My throne, and the earth My footstool." [Marginal note: Jeremiah.] Which the Savior also confirms, when He says: "Do not swear, neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God: nor by earth, because it is His footstool." [Marginal note: Isaiah CHRIST.] But also that which the Apostle, when he preached among the Athenians, approving the opinion of Aratus, said: "For in Him we live, and move, and have our being." [Marginal note: Paul Aratus.] And how is this, unless because God by His power binds, contains, and vivifies the entire world? How also is heaven the throne of God, and earth His footstool, unless because He fills all things in heaven and on earth? So far Origen. With whom Eusebius Pamphilus, reasoning in his *Theological Solutions* concerning the supreme artificer, says: [Marginal note: Eusebius.] "Life is there, and mind, so that being itself may perpetually remain life, and may fashion and contain for the mind those things which are." Hence, the first being must be vital and intellectual: whence all essence, life, and intellect are named more by participation than by species: For that very being is life in itself, and intellect in itself: Which

--- Page 542 ---

[Marginalia: Cardi. Cusa]
but besides these, everything is more non-being than being: because it was, when it was not being. And by this perpetuity, being remains, lives, and understands: For to that extent it is a participant of life, as much as that (being) has provided it; and it understands as much as that (being) has imparted. And he pursues many things in this matter, from which he concludes that there is one life of all living things, just as there is one soul in all the members of the body: which is not only diffused in its own members, but in some way is diffused even to external things: For into sweat flowing from a human, and condensed and arranged, a certain life is infused, weaker than human life, and lice are produced: But from a collection made from breath, the life of bedbugs and fleas is generated. What the tree of life is. Chapter III.

[Decorative initial O] It is common knowledge to all that Christ, our Messiah, has been celebrated with many kinds of mysteries and called by many names: For He is called Lamb, Lion, Cornerstone, Christ, Word, Truth, Life, and the like: Thus also He is called the tree of life, which is placed in the midst of the garden of delights, so that it may impart life to all, as we have revealed above. But why He is called a tree, now remains to be explained. A tree is rooted in the earth, from which it receives the increments of life: And Christ is a tree having its root in the land of the living, whence He drew His first origin, although He drew the body and organ of His divinity from a people already dry and arid, as Isaiah says: "He grew up like a sapling from the earth, and like a root from thirsty ground."

[Marginal note: Isaias]

A tree is divided first into larger and fewer branches, afterwards into very many smaller ones: And Christ's most abundant virtue and grace was first diffused into a few Apostles, but great and strong in virtue, and through them into very many others, to whom those [Apostles] are therefore deservedly to be preferred. The tree continually draws increments of life from the earth, to be communicated to shoots, twigs, flowers, and fruits: And Christ lives in that land of divinity and the Father, as He Himself testifies, saying: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father:"

[Marginal note: CHRI STVS.]

Which life, received from the Father, He imparts to others, so that they may live: whence He adds: "And he who eats me by taking food, like a branch from the trunk and root, he himself will live because of me." And again: "If anyone does not remain in me, that is, by drawing life from me, he will be cast out like a branch, and will wither." Flowers live and become beautiful on the tree, but if cut off, they immediately wither or rot: And the flowers of our thoughts live in that tree, which says: "Without me you can do nothing." Nor can we think anything of ourselves, as if from ourselves, says the Apostle. Fruits also ripen on the tree, continually receiving nourishment from it, just as the tree itself speaks, saying: "He who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit."

[Marginal note: Paulus CHRI STVS,]

CANTICI SECVNDI

Where this tree is planted. Chapter IIII.

[Decorative initial V] But where this life-giving tree has its roots, we have two testimonies from divine storehouses. One is, that paradise, or that garden of delights, had been planted by the Lord God מקדם *michedem*, which means "from the beginning" or "from ancient times": since the whole garden, and every true pleasure, is rooted in that most ancient eternal Father, the first origin of all good things: or the garden is planted in that divine essence, which is the true land of the living: from which all life, and all delights, and pleasures sprout forth. The other is, that the tree of life was in the middle of paradise: because the divine Word, which is the true tree of life, is the middle person in that most holy Trinity: and clothed in human flesh, conversing with men, it always held the middle position: For being born in the midst of animals, disputing in the midst of doctors, dying in the midst of thieves, rising again in the midst of disciples, he was found. And although he himself, as the Word, as the Son, as the wisdom of God, sits at the right hand of the Father, nevertheless, as teacher, as redeemer, as Messiah, as the tree of life, he stands in the middle of the archetype: just as the life of man, who is in his image, has its seat in the heart, which holds the middle position in the human body: from which life also flows into all members. And although God is whole everywhere, not divided by parts or members, nor consequently is there in him right and left, middle or extreme, according to these our bodily laws, nevertheless, there is a certain disposition, in a divine and excellent way not fully perceptible to us, not of the thing itself, which is most simple, but of an influx with respect to us, according to which we hold his image: and concerning which Scripture is verified, often reiterating about the right, left, middle, east, west, south, north, and similar dispositions of that divine influx, according to which that tree of life is said to be placed in the middle.

How that tree itself is formed. Chapter V.

[Marginal note: Heb. Wisdom] [Decorative initial F] The wise Hebrews figure this tree of life in the best way they can, by the shaft of the letter ו (*Vav*), which is straight like a tree trunk, with that upper part, which is like the letter י (*Yod*) united to that shaft, signifying the supreme fount of life, the eternal Father flowing into the Son: which the Hebrews themselves call the "upper crown": to which they wish א (*Aleph*) and י (*Yod*) to be dedicated: of which one signifies "one" and "beginning": the other "ten" and the completion of numbers: so that it may be intimated that the eternal Father is the beginning and end of all things. And by the continuation and union with that shaft, which figures the tree of life, is denoted the union which it has with the Son: into whom all things flow, so that he himself can also be called the beginning and the end: and all good be attributed to the Son. Hence, with great mystery, God commanded in Exodus to be carved on the columns of the tabernacle וויהם כסף *vavehem chaseph*, that is, "their *vavim* (hooks/clasps) of silver": for which we have "with silver capitals": Which either the translator did not know what it meant, or did not wish to reveal the mystery: For the column of the tabernacle, and of the whole world, after whose pattern it was made, is Christ, and the Incarnate Word: by whom also the heavens were made firm, and the Father carries and sustains all things. In this command, therefore

--- Page 548 ---
TOMVS SECVNDVS.

a letter of God was inscribed, which imports life: so that it might be denoted that the principle of life was placed in Him by the eternal Father, so that He might impart it to others, as Christ himself deigned to make clear, saying: "As the living Father sent me, and I [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.]
live because of the Father, so he who eats me will live because of me." And this tree is distinguished into root, trunk, branches, flowers, and fruits: For the root is the sprouting divinity itself: The trunk is the Word produced in it by the Father: The branches are the attributes communicated to Him by Him who gave all things to Him: Leaves and flowers are living ideas in it: But leaves are ideas of irrational things, which were produced for the service of intellectual creatures, just as leaves are constituted to cover flowers and fruits, and as if for their service. But flowers are ideas of intellectual things, from which due fruits are expected: But just as many flowers fall without fruit, so many angels and men have fallen and continually fall without fruit, and separated from that tree of life, they wither, to be burned by unquenchable fire. But fruits are the rules of good actions for us, and gifts, and charisms, with which we are continually endowed, so that living according to those rules, we too may present the fruits of our works to Him who planted both the tree of life itself and us, whatever little trees we may be, so that from that tree of life we may receive whence we may produce due fruits according to the spirit: of which Paul makes mention, saying: "But the fruit of the [Marginal note: Paulus]
Spirit is charity, joy, peace, etc.," which follow. Nor shall we proceed further concerning the figure of Him who is figured by no figure, yet gives to all things that they may be figured; nor is He enclosed by any boundary, though He encompasses all things within Himself. But let these few things be said, as we have been able to learn from the sacred scriptures.

To whom, and how communicated. Chapter VI.

[Decorative initial I] Beyond all doubt, we hold that all things which rejoice in life draw it from the fountain of life, or receive and eat from the fruits of the tree of lives: But it comes into controversy what are living things, and whether all things live. Indeed, angels, humans, animals, and plants live, each with its own life, as all agree: but concerning metals, stones, elements, and heavens, there is difficulty among some, because since their life does not appear, they judge them to live minimally, and call them inanimate: But if the world is an animal, as we discussed above, and as most wise men agree, there is no doubt that all these things live, just like all the members, flesh, intestines, nerves, blood, and bones in a human or animal body: although bones and such things, when separated, seem deprived of life. But in the body, bones grow, move, and support the body itself, like living columns. Flesh grows strong and is renewed, so that it does not fear a wound or incision; and broken bones are renewed, which certainly does not happen to dead things: Thus also the members of the great and mundane animal live, each with its own life, as Mercury says in that treatise which he calls "Concerning the Common": [Marginal note: Mercuri]
"Everything that is in the world moves either by growing or by decreasing; but that which moves, therefore lives." And since all things move, even the earth,

Thus also Paul divides the works of different ones according to the spirit, finally concluding: But all these are wrought by one and the same Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.

When, and why the tree was forbidden. Chapter VII.

**W**e have an explicit doctrine in the sacred scriptures, that God after Adam's transgression said: Behold, Adam has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil: And now, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and live forever, let Us cast him out: Which was also done. Nor should anyone wonder that God seems to have grieved that Adam had become a knower of good and evil: For He took vengeance not for his progress, but for his arrogance: since he wished to discern good and evil, and to decide what was just and unjust: which belongs to Elohim and to judges: in whose synagogue and assembly God stands judging: because man cannot do this without God Himself: Or because he wished to assume the rank and place of the Messiah: who (as we have said elsewhere) is the true tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore, He had forbidden anyone, by emulating the dignity of the Son of God and the Messiah, to claim it for himself, He who is the trunk of true life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But this is a mystery too deep to speak of, Therefore let us assign another reason: one that may be understood by all: And that is, lest man, infected with sin, unworthily receive the nourishment of life to his own destruction: For
CC v.

--- Page 551 ---
**OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

if he had fallen into uncleanness, he would have remained perpetually, and would remain unclean, if uncleanness can stand with that life. Or lest, being unprepared, partaking of the nourishment of life, it should turn to evil for him, just as the best wine harms one with a fever, and the most delicious meat, however well seasoned, harms a pleuritic person.
<br/>[Marginal note: The same] And this is what Paul says about one who is to eat the bread of life: "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup: For he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself." For what the tree of life was to our first parents, that is the bread of life to us; which is forbidden to the unworthy, just as that tree was forbidden to the transgressor Adam, and is forbidden to anyone unworthy and defiled by any crime. Because since crime and sin are the work of death, they can in no way agree with life.

**How all things live in that tree, and consequently in Christ. Chapter VIII.**

<br/>[Marginal note: John] <span style="font-size: 200%; float: left; margin-right: 0.2em; line-height: 0.8em; font-family: 'Times New Roman', serif;">I</span>terated often is that most famous saying of John, that all things, before they came into being, were life in the Word. Nor is it to be thought that, having been unfolded into their proper forms, they are deprived of that creative life by which they lived in the mind of the Creator: But beyond this, they acquire other lives according to their capacity. For life is manifold, therefore this tree is famously known as עץ חיים ez haiim, that is, "tree of lives," and not "of life" in the singular. Therefore all things live by that creative life; and they live by their own natural life, which nevertheless depends on that highest life, and is a ray or spark of it, in whom we live, and move, and have our being. Man also lives beyond his manifold natural life by a certain life of the spirit,
<br/>[Marginal note: CHRIST. Ezekiel.] concerning which it is said: "It is the Spirit that gives life." And this [spirit] favors a twofold life: Natural, according to that of Ezekiel: "And the spirit of life was in the wheels, quickening all things"; Spiritual, concerning which the same prophet [says]: "Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live." For they were dead in sin, and needed the
<br/>[Marginal note: Paul] life of the spirit: concerning which Paul [says]: "If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live."
<br/>[Marginal note: CHRIST.] Both of these lives, even if administered by the spirit of life, nevertheless proceed from the tree of life, which is the very Word of God made human, which says: "He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life." And again: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself." And often repeating, he affirms that he is life, to be communicated to others also according to their degrees; through which degrees he intends to lead us
<br/>[Marginal note: The same] into that blessed and eternal life, beyond which there is no other: "I (he says) give eternal life to my sheep." And again: "The Son of Man must be lifted up,
<br/>[Marginal note: Jeremiah.] that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." The source of this life is the Father, who says: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters." But the Son is the river of life proceeding from the Father's fountain, or the tree of life planted in the land of the living. But the Spirit is, as it were, a pool, receiving the water of life from the fountain and river of lives, and pouring it out into us also:
<br/>[Marginal note: Origen.] Which Origen discusses at length in his commentary on Matthew.

Christ is the support of all.                                         Chapter IX.
[Decorative initial E] ND if we have touched upon Christ sustaining this earthly fabric by His divinity and the power of the Word above, nevertheless, explaining more clearly, we will proceed: For Paul declares this in plain language, first saying to the Hebrews:
[Marginal note: Paulus] 'He upholds all things by the word of His power.' And again he says to the Colossians:
[Marginal note: Idem] 'For in Him were all things created, whether in earth, or in heaven.' And continuing, he again says: 'And in Him all things hold together.'
[Marginal note: Isaias] Which is also strengthened by the prophecy of Isaiah, when he says: 'And the government shall be upon his shoulder,' namely, of the whole structure, establishing Him as heir of all things, through whom He also made the ages. Therefore, He sustains this structure of the earthly house and all its inhabitants, like a column: He rules, like a prince: He feeds, like a shepherd, with the food of life, both of the body and of the spirit: For if all things were made through Him, then also foods are continuously produced through the same: But for spiritual life, He offered Himself as food,
[Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] saying: 'I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever:' And again: 'Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, ye have no life in you:' And again: 'For My flesh is meat indeed, and My blood is drink indeed.' But because we are continually washed, and fall by our iniquities, therefore He also offered Himself as a support for this ruin, making purification for sins, and bearing all our sins, as the Father had commanded,
[Marginal note: Isaias] as we read in Isaiah: 'The Lord hath laid on Him the iniquity of us all,' and 'with His stripes we are healed.' Nor content to have purged us from all defilements, but that we might build virtues, He offered Himself as a stable foundation, which would sustain our whole edifice.
[Marginal note: Paulus] 'No man (says Paul) can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ:'
[Marginal note: Isaias] Which also Isaiah had foretold: For speaking in the person of the Redeemer and suffering Christ, he recounts many things which He suffered, saying: 'I gave My back to the smiters, and My cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not My face from shame and spitting.' And after many things recounted, turning to the ignorant and blinded people, he says: 'Who walks in darkness, and has no light, let him hope in the name of the Lord, in whom alone is salvation: and let him lean upon his Lord God, who indeed saved the world in human flesh.' Nor can we lean upon any other than upon that staff which comforts and sustains all. This is what is said of the Queen of Heaven and Empress of the world: 'Leaning upon her beloved Son.'

and of preachers, the words of angels speaking inwardly and offering guidance, the words of Christ and the Holy Spirit speaking inwardly and inspiring. How He was exalted from the earth. Chapter XI.

[Decorative initial O] It is necessary (says God the Son Himself) for the Son of Man to be exalted, so that everyone who believes in Him may not perish, but have eternal life. Indeed, great is this mystery here, that eternal life is given in the exaltation of the Son of Man, and that He Himself is said to be exalted from the earth, like the serpent in the desert. Nor do I think this should be understood of the exaltation of the body, when, hanging on the wood, it was lifted from the earth and the mountain on which the cross was fixed. Nor do I think this is to be understood of that exaltation by which He is always exalted with the Father, sitting at His right hand: but of that exaltation which occurs in our sight, when, namely, the sublimity of His divinity is revealed to men: so that seeing Him as He is, they may venerate, exalt, and magnify Him, Just as at His death, the Centurion and those who were with him, seeing the air darkened contrary to the order of nature, the earth tremble, the rocks split, the dead rise, exclaimed, saying: "Truly this was the Son of God." Or of that exaltation, which through the cross itself Christ as man merited to be placed over every creature, as the Apostle speaks with open words, saying:
[Marginal note: Paul]
"Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross, therefore God exalted Him and gave Him a name that is above every name: so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth: and every tongue confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father:"
[Marginal note: CHRIST.]
Which the Savior Himself also confirms, saying: "It was necessary for Christ to suffer and so to enter into His glory:" By these words He openly demonstrates that He, insofar as He is man, acquired glory and a kingdom through the work completed in His passion and cross: But He is said to be exalted from the earth, because both the work He accomplished and the sublime and exalted kingdom He obtained were not earthly, but heavenly, sublime, and high: "My kingdom (He says) is not of this world," but it is that which the Father prepared from the foundation of the world: The possession of which He obtained for us, and for Himself the dominion, on the cross. But why the exaltation of Christ on the cross is equated with the exaltation of the serpent, which Moses erected at the Lord's command, is quite openly stated in the book of Numbers:
[Marginal note: Num.]
where it is read that when the people sinned by complaining about the food brought from heaven, God sent fiery serpents among the people: who, struck and wounded by them, came to Moses as suppliants, asking that those serpents be removed: Therefore, as Moses prayed for the people, the Lord said:

--- Page 555 ---
**OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

Make a bronze serpent, and place it as a sign: whoever, having been struck, looks at it, will live: which was also done. So also those struck by any kind of sin, by which the ancient serpent and his satellites are accustomed to wound mortals, if they look at Christ hanging on the wood, where he obtained the healing and salvation of all, asking for his help, they are healed. But here lies a mystery, why God willed the serpent to be exalted, which is the image of the enemy of the human race: and why Christ is likened to it: For what does a serpent contribute to healing? What agreement between the figure of the prince of darkness and the Prince of light? What symbol of Christ with that unclean and diabolical reptile? Indeed there is no agreement or symbol here, except in the erection. But healing is conferred in a varied, indeed, entirely opposite way: For those looking at Christ are healed effectively by Him, who, as the true physician, brought healing to all of us, according to that prophetic saying: [Marginal note: David] "He sent his word, and healed them." But those looking at the serpent were healed by an occasion taken (from it), not indeed adhering to it, or demanding healing from it, but abhorring it: For seeing the figure of the serpents, which had been sent by God as punishment for sin, they, being pricked in heart, returned to God Himself, praying for health and a remedy against the bites of the serpents: Just as among us the devil is painted as horrendous and terrifying in appearance, so that the people, seeing and contemplating his deformity and cruel rage, may dread him and be hostile to him, as much as they can. We could pursue other more secret mysteries about the serpent, revealing why the instigator of all evils, in his first encounter with man, assumed the form of a serpent: and how through the same image the figurative people obtained bodily health, which was a type of the health of both man (body and soul) given by Christ, who was assimilated to the serpent himself: but let these few words suffice, since it is not permitted to speak of all things.

How, being exalted, he drew all things to himself. Chapter XII.

[Large decorative initial E] Therefore, being exalted, he deservedly drew all things, because then he put on an all-encompassing attractive power: For goodness and love attract, so much so that they unite [Marginal note: CHRI] lovers together. But what greater, what more intimate, and more intense love [Marginal note: STVS.] could be shown, than to give life and soul for the beloved? "For no one has greater love than this, than to lay down his life for his friends," said Christ himself, so that he might signify to all: how much attractive power he received, being exalted on the cross. Wisdom and eloquence also attract. Hence the wise [Marginal note: Solomon] Solomon drew that queen from the ends of the earth, and wise teachers draw disciples from everywhere to their audience. Nor do hearers gather less from all sides to an eloquent preacher. But behold, more than Solomon, and more than Demosthenes, or Cicero, is Christ our king, exalted on the cross, in whom (as [Marginal note: Paul] Paul says) are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. And again: "We preach Christ crucified, indeed a stumbling block to Jews, but foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, the power of God and the wisdom of God." Which, being hidden, since not all see or know it, considering

--- Page 556 ---
TONE TWO: 208

thinking that] that work is foolishness and not wisdom, they are not attracted: Wealth and money also attract, to which all things obey, even unto death, as is clear in those who receive military stipends: To these, people flock from all sides more frequently, the greater the abundance in the one leading to military service. But our crucified one was so filled with true riches, especially on the cross, that from his fullness we all receive, and he is rich towards all who call upon him: And he cries out to everyone: "I advise you to buy, or acquire from me, refined gold, so that you may become rich:" For glory and abundant riches [Marginal note: CHRIST] are in his house. Power and victory also attract: For many supporters adhere to a victorious, great, and powerful prince; and even terrified enemies surrender. But no victory is greater, no triumph more glorious than this, which the Emperor of the Christian army reported in a duel fought on the cross against the enemy [Marginal note: CHRIST] of the human race, as he himself had predicted a little before he underwent the cross. "Now," he said, "the prince of this world will be cast out." Having conquered him, he plundered the spoils: he redeemed captives: he subdued the world, granting to all the faculty of conquering: he attracted so many thousands that there is no number of those who, imitating him, gave their lives to conquer: which they would certainly not have done, had they not been attracted by the virtue of him dying on the cross. Among attractive things is also novelty, to which both the common people and men of any gravity are drawn: But no novelty is greater than that which Christ, exalted on the cross, brought about, so that, sitting on the throne after his victory, he might say: "Behold, I make all things new," as John relates, [Marginal note: The same] as he had seen and heard in those highest and hidden inner chambers: Concerning these renewed things, we strive to speak in this new song. Also among the most attractive things are generosity and liberal distribution, especially of those things which are necessary for the needy: But Christ, hanging on that cross, forgave all our sins: and for us he paid every debt to the eternal Father: For since we were all debtors, no one excepted, he pardoned all, he forgave all, as the Apostle says: [Marginal note: Paul] "When you were dead in your transgressions, he made you alive together with him, having forgiven you all your transgressions, by canceling the record of debt that stood against you with its legal demands, nailing it to the cross." And concerning the Father's generosity, he says to the Romans: "He who did not spare his own Son, but [Marginal note: The same] delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?" Up to this point we have spoken of the manifold power of attraction which Christ, dying on the cross, acquired for himself: which is rooted in manifold acquired virtue: But now we will proceed to speak of his own inherent attractive power, which is connatural and consubstantial to him: For all acknowledge how great the attractive force is in stones. The magnet, for all to see, attracts iron: and the ruby, and rubbed amber, attract straw, and many such things. What then shall we say of that most precious stone placed at the head of the corner, indeed rejected by men, but chosen and honored by God? as Peter says: [Marginal note: Peter] Indeed, in him is not only the virtue of the ruby, the magnet, the diamond, and all precious stones, but the virtue of all plants, metals, animals, men, angels, and even of the eternal Father himself, who gave him all things: Therefore, he deservedly attracts all, especially

--- Page 557 ---
...especially the elect, and those who wish to have a symbol with him: Which indeed we can have, if we are willing to accept his institutions and teachings, and also sacred things, and all that he taught for our expiation and purification: Or if the Eternal Father, by his boundless power, deigns to draw us to the Son, to whom the rightly purified adhere. But let us pass on to other matters.

How virtues and divine powers seemed diffused into many things. Chapter XIV.

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.5; vertical-align: -0.2em; display: inline-block;">D</span>eity, as we have proven, operates in all members of the mundane body, enabling all to cooperate, lest the dissected parts of the world should fail without a unifying power, or so greatly oppose each other that they could not possibly stand. But the ancients, not perceiving this sacrament of unity, believed in many kinds of divine powers, multiplied according to the plurality of things, as Porphyry gathers, and after him Eusebius of Caesarea, from those things which ancient seers sang scattered and in many places: Which we will briefly touch upon.

Indeed, they called the power of the universal air Juno (because it helps mortals): But the effeminate air, the lower Juno, since nothing is softer: And the power of that lower air, which is illuminated by lunar light, they called Latona from "latendo" (hiding), because it makes souls hide and forget those things for which they were instituted, before they descended to the lunar orb: so that they appear as if blank slates having entered this lower air.

But they call the power of the earth Vesta: because it produces herbs and flowers: which are like garments and ornaments of the earth itself. And because this power is fertile, they wished to denote it in the form of a woman. But Rhea (whom the Latins called Ops) they judged to be the power of stony and mountainous land: But Ceres they called the power of fertile plains: but the female power they called Persephone: But Dionysius they called the mixed power of all plants, because herbs are always combined with both sexes: Which power the Egyptians named Isis and Osiris: There is also (as Plato says in Cratylus) Dionysius, as if "didos oinon," that is, giver of wine, and consequently of other fruits, ripening them with his fiery power, not indeed elemental, but solar:

For they called the elemental power of fire Vulcan: But the power of devouring fire they called Vesta, and this infertile: Whence the Poet [says]:
Nor do you understand Vesta to be anything other than living flame:
And you see no bodies born from flame.
Rightly, therefore, a virgin, who left no seeds.

But as Plato understands it, Vesta, whom they also call Vestia, they named the "ousia" of things, that is, their essence: because all things are clothed by her. And she is sterile, because essence neither generates nor is generated, but generates and is generated as an individual, not indeed by reason of essence, but by reason of the generative power existing in the generator: to which corresponds the passive potentiality in the generated. But let us proceed.

Therefore, in the Sun, this fiery power is called Apollo, from the movement of its rays, or by a fourfold etymology (as it pleases Plato) se-

-cording to the fourfold virtue dedicated to him, music, medicine, prophecy,

Furthermore, they judge that Atys and Adonis pertain to crops and fruits:

The effective power of waters, Oceanus: But its symbol,

And what Apollo is in the sun, that Minerva is in the Moon. And again, the Moon is called Hecate
because of the various figures of her body: to whom the Fates are associated: Clotho for generating,

not because the Moon alone does these things, but because it immediately pours out influences,
which it receives from higher sources, like a matrix, to be poured out. But the virtue of Saturn,
since it is cold and slow, they attributed to time, depicting him as an old man,
because all things grow old with time. They put fiery Mars in charge of war, from the impetus
which he displays in anger: Venus with her Cupid, to generation and love. The power
of speech and interpretation they called Mercury. Plato [Marginal note: Plato] pursues many things concerning the
etymology of these names, which he tries to demonstrate as congruent with the things themselves, as far
as that idiom allows: And before him Hesiod, [Marginal note: Hesiod.] where he treats of the genealogy of the gods,
and most later writers, All of which it would be long to adduce, nor do I consider them too necessary,
nor very congruent, because they are applied somewhat harshly: For Plato wished to
imitate the etymology of the first language, in which the protoplast imposed most fitting names on things.
But the congruence of names with things in the Hebrew language differs from that
which is in the Greek and Latin idiom, as much as the Hebrew language itself is more
sacred and divine than these, which follow it, though at long paces, and Latin
longer than Greek: because the latter (Greek) is immediately derived from Hebrew, but Latin from Greek.
But let us proceed. They called the symbol of the universe Pan, that is, the whole.
