**SECOND CANTICLE**

And this, spread into very many parts, they believed to be multiplied divine powers: Hence, for diverse needs, they implored these divine powers, which they believed to be diverse, with various prayers, many kinds of sacrifices, and incantations. For wisdom indeed they earnestly sought from Minerva, whom, born from the brain of Jove, they considered a deity favoring wisdom. To conquer in war they demanded from the deity of Victory, whom they believed to be born from Acheron and Styx, that is, from affliction and sadness: For Acheron signifies without joy, or without gladness, and Styx signifies sadness: because it is necessary for those who wish to conquer to abstain from many things and to inflict the greatest force upon themselves, whence sadness arises. But in punishing the wicked, they implored the deity of victorious Justice, whom they call Nemesis. They believed they obtained kingship from Jove, lord of all: And a happy union of marriages from Hymenaeus: But a prosperous navigation from the winds, sons of Astraeus the Titan and Aurora, as if born from the sun's heat refreshing the air, especially at dawn, when the sun begins to spread its rays over the ear- [Marginal note: Aristo.] th: Which Aristotle follows when in his Meteorology he says winds are produced from the heat of the sun: Nevertheless, they are said to have power from Juno, because they blow only in the air (which is called Juno). But whence the winds come, although the digressions of poets and philosophers are long, yet the truth is one: concerning which [Marginal note: David] the prophet says: He who brings forth the winds from his treasuries. But let us proceed. They believed they obtained graces from Venus, who is so called as if beautifying all things, [Marginal note: Cicero] or coming to all things, as it pleases Cicero. And if they hoped to receive any other benefit from the earth, sea, ether, plants, trees, heavens, and suchlike, they invoked those deities which they believed presided over them. The common people, however, whose concern is always to lean towards multitude, not content with these deities, divided them into more: For they believed in five Suns from various effects: four Vulcans: five Mercuries: four Apollos: three Aesculapiuses: three Dis: five Dionysuses: five Minervas: four Venuses: three Cupids. And wandering through many such things, even to harmful things introduced by evil angels, they not only gave names of gods, but also established sacred rites: for they publicly dedicated a temple to Fever in the Roman palace: and an altar to ill Fortu- [Marginal note: Pliny] ne in the Esquiline, as Pliny relates. And they came to such a degree of madness that they even wished to assign deities to thefts and crimes: And fashioning images of all these, they instituted sacred rites for them, despising the one God, from whom are all things. Hence they took cause for idolatry, each one composing for himself (so that I may jest with Pliny) Junos, Joves, Genii, Lares, Penates, and gods, whom they wished. Also led to extreme madness and darkness by the Prince of darkness, they did not blush to even in the underworld find gods whom they might worship, venerating the most miserable and lowest of all under three names: Whom from enriching they called Dis, and Pluto: For πλοῦτος (ploutos) in Greek, in La- tin is called rich: To whom they assigned three-headed Cerberus, as if devouring flesh: [Marginal note: Statius.] For κρέας (kreas) means flesh, and βόρος (boros) means devouring, they say: And rightly so, because he always goes about, seeking whom he may devour, sparing no one, but continually accusing, or harming: Whence the Poet (says).

And those skilled in secular literature beautifully describe him as placed in the depths of Tartarus, in a house indeed dark, and always with livid shadows, and opaque with dreadful gloom; whence he is called the prince of darkness, but also the prince of the world, because he is the instigator of evil desires which flourish in this world: For he dwells in the depths, that is, in the most filthy things over which he rules: For what is gold, what is this lowest silver, but the dregs of the earth? What is the lust of the flesh, but a certain heat and boiling of earthly flesh? And what is ambition, but the appetite for this filthy portion? To this calamity, therefore, mortals have come, that submerged in this most miserable dregs, they would adore the lord of the dregs itself: To which calamity almost all mortals have come, especially the Romans, lords of the world; with whom, as the chief authors of this crime, Paul, speaking, says: [Marginal note: Paulus] "And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image resembling corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed animals, and creeping things: therefore God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness, to dishonor their bodies among themselves: because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator." And they were so agitated by pernicious spirits that they sacrificed themselves to demons, and sought to appease wicked powers with the blood of their sons. The Rhodians (as Eusebius testifies) [Marginal note: Eusebius] sacrificed a man to Saturn, not indeed to the good one, but to the evil one. Also in Salamis (which in ancient times they called Coronea), up to the time of Diomedes, a man was sacrificed to Grauala, daughter of Ceclops. Manethus, the Egyptian historian, also narrates in his book "On Piety" that men were sacrificed in Heliopolis. How he called all other divine powers to himself. Chapter XV.

[Decorative initial V] ERILY, in order to remove idolatry and the worship of many divine powers from mortals, he called to himself the entire divine power, diffused into many (as the Father commanded): Which sacrament, indeed, revealing to those who understand, he said: "All things have been delivered to me by my Father," that is, the powers of all, the virtues of all, the divine powers of all, as Paul admonishes us with a clear voice, saying: "Having despoiled principalities and powers, he openly triumphed in himself," confidently transferring all the power of others to himself: And again: "He emptied every principality, and power, and virtue," so that we no longer seek necessary and opportune things from others, but from him to whom the Father has given all things. Hence he taught all, that henceforth they should ask the Father in his name: "Whatever (he said) you ask the Father in my name, he will give you." And this is the principality which (as the oracle of Isaiah attests) was placed upon his shoulders: which used to be upon the shoulders of various princes: but with them despoiled, all things were gathered into him: whom the Most High commanded to appear in visible flesh, so that the eyes of common people, who cannot behold spiritual things, nor are able to contemplate them, might have a figure offered to them, which they might behold: and in it adore the divine power and divinity: which lowly minds could not imagine.
Therefore, whoever desires true wisdom, not imagined Minerva, let him invoke Christ, the wisdom of God. Whoever desires life and health, let him not indeed implore Apollo or Aesculapius, but him who is the true life, and the physician healing all infirmities: concerning whom the Royal prophet sings: "He sent his word, and healed them." Whoever desires a prosperous journey on land and sea, let him not pray to Aeolus or the Astraei, but to him who commands the sea and winds: and they obey. Whoever desires an abundance of fruits or wine, let him no longer entreat Ceres or Bacchus, but him who immediately multiplied five loaves and satisfied a copious crowd of men and women, and by his sole command turned water into wine: who also said: "I am the true vine," providing indeed better wine than Bacchus or Dionysius. If indeed anyone needs water, let him not approach Oceanus, Achelous, the Nereids, Cymothoe, or Amphitrite, but let him fly to that most abundant fountain of life, from which water flows: which whoever drinks, will not thirst again. If anyone, however, wishes to delight in flowers, fruits, and vegetables, let him no longer invoke Attis or Adonis, but that true twin tree of life, which provides divine and human fruits: or feeds with bark and pith, so that we may find pasture in it everywhere. And if anyone desires riches, let him no longer approach Pluto, the lord of the earth, who holds riches with him, but the Prince of true treasures, which are preserved in the heavens: who also knows how to reward a hundredfold those who renounce having a share with Mammon: With which hundreds and thousands of monies given by God, and not by Mammon, li-

This dominion obtained, and the attraction of all deities to Himself, is proven by evident fact. Cap. XVI.

[Decorative initial E] And lest we seem to assert only with words what we are striving for, we will also review some most manifest effects that prove this: For Christ having died on the cross, on which He brought back triumph over the enemy, so that the powers of darkness were cast down: so much so that those [powers] which at first procured worship, giving responses from idols and temples as divine oracles, immediately fell silent, all power having been taken from them, not only of ruling, but also of speaking to mortals under the guise of Gods and disposers of this world: Which we not only see with our own eyes, but (what is wonderful) their chief worshippers themselves admit, marveling: For Porphyry [Marginal note: Porphy.] in his book 'On the Failing Oracles', compelled by truth, sings these words:

Indeed, Plutarch says even more, [Marginal note: Plutarc:] that a voice was heard from the Echinades islands at the time of Christ's suffering, that their great Pan was dead, his power having evidently been extinguished, both in ruling and in responding, although an oracle is brought forward in confirmation that demons die. This voice, spread by widespread fame, was even divulged to Emperor Tiberius, who, having examined witnesses, placed the deposition in the royal archives. Therefore, the most celebrated Delphic oracle ceased: and the Pythian, and all others, ceased. But also, a little after the death of the vanquisher of demons, all temples of Apollo, Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Diana, and whatever false gods there were, were destroyed, and temples of Christ were erected, and in honor of those who followed Him: so that we can exclaim:
Behold, our God CHRIST reigns through the ages:
And all created things offer prayers to the Creator.

And what Porphyry, that rabid dog against us, says in that book, which he published against our reli- [Marginal note: Porphy:] gion, let us hear: "Nor should we wonder (he says) if for many years now the city has been afflicted by plague, since Aesculapius and other gods are far from it: For since Jesus is worshipped, we can obtain no benefit from the gods." Indeed, wonderful is the power of truth, that the spear, which the fiercest enemy directs against us, turned by the force of truth against the one who directed it, strikes him who sent it. If the gods yielded to Jesus, O Porphyry, do you not unwillingly confess Jesus to be stronger than your gods? If you say: "They departed in indignation": Why (I ask) do they not suppress him who occupies their dignity, and his worshippers? "They punish (you will say) by afflicting with disease": But with the disease ceasing, and the worshippers of Jesus prevailing, have your gods, led by repentance, ceased from afflicting the worshippers of Jesus? For those worshipping Him, attacked by your gods and Roman princes for a long time, always received better increases, and His worship was so amplified, that the princes of the world were utterly vanquished: and the forces of the whole world yielded to a few poor messengers of the Gospel. Moreover, Aesculapiuses, and Apollos, and Plutos, and Serapises, and Minervas, and Pallases, and Venuses, and Cupids, and whatever kind of monstrous thing there is, or what were the names of idolatry, with Christ rising from the dead, collapsed as if having heard an earthquake: so that they could neither give responses, nor demand worship: nor demand human blood, nor favor auguries or any deceptions, nor obstruct the messengers of Jesus: to whom He gave power to easily subjugate and cast down those enemies, as it says in the Gospel which is titled according to Luke: "I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven. [An illuminated initial letter 'A' depicting a figure, possibly a saint or scholar, at a desk] As for the oracles, which preceded this matter, coming to them, we will begin with Moses, from whom we have in Leviticus, that Nadab, [Marginal note: Leviticus] and Abihu, sons of Aaron, taking their censers, put fire and incense upon them, offering strange or foreign fire before the Lord, which He had not commanded them: And fire went out from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord. This text cannot be read without wonder, unless its hidden and mysterious meaning is understood. Abraham, Moses, Aaron, and those chosen priests labored to extinguish idolatry: and to lead everyone to the worship of the Most High God: which they desired above all things. With this zeal, Abraham, when he taught the Chaldeans about the one God, was cast by them into the fire or furnace. With this zeal, Elijah obtained fire from heaven against the prophets of Baal. With this zeal, Nadab and Abihu, seized, wanted to offer with strange fire, that is, to offer sacred things for strangers: But since they arrogated to themselves the greatest work reserved only for the Messiah, and by no means committed to them, they were punished for their arrogance: Therefore, when Aaron grieved over his lost sons from a deed performed with the greatest good zeal, Moses [Marginal note: Moses] said to him: "Thus says the Lord: I will be sanctified in those who are near, or my relatives, and I will be glorified in the sight of all the people." The one near and close to God, first of all, was Christ His Son: Afterwards the Apostles: most of whom were relatives of Christ in the second degree of kinship according to the flesh: such as John, both James, Philip, Simon, and Thaddeus: But according to the spirit, all the disciples, especially the Apostles, in whom He was sanctified and glorified in the sight of every people and of the whole world: This glory those two priests wanted to claim for themselves, without the Lord commanding it, nor the time requiring it, therefore they were punished: Hearing this, Aaron was silent, yielding to reason and justice. How He will finally remove all things that distract, so that He may perfectly draw all things to Himself alone. Chapter XVIII.

**M**agna indeed, from what has been said before, a great wonder arises, why we do not see this drawing of all nations, and even of the Israelite people, as the oracles seem to have foretold: For the Royal prophet says: [Marginal note: David] And all kings shall adore him, all nations shall serve him: And Isaiah: [Marginal note: Isaiah] Arise, shine, Jerusalem, for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee: for behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and mist the peoples: but the Lord shall arise upon thee, and his glory shall be seen in thee: and the Gentiles shall walk in thy light, and kings in the brightness of thy rising: For mist and darkness covered the peoples, when they served idols and the powers of darkness: But when the Lord rose in the land of Jerusalem, and His glory was seen, the nations began to walk in His light, and kings in the splendor of His rising, His star having been seen in the East. There are also innumerable other oracles, by which it was foretold that all ought to be enlightened, directed, and led by this light exalted from the earth for our illumination and salvation. But this brings no small wonder to those who ponder, if this light (as has been said) has enlightened all, why do so many remain in darkness, and those who have received the mark of the most foul beast, and who, rejecting that light, are unwilling to depart from figures and enigmas? Are not also those who have only received the name, from which they are called Christians, but by their works fight against that name? For they contend among themselves with hatreds and disputes, and blaspheme God as if thrust into Tartarean prisons, they are enveloped in the allurements of the flesh, they adore idols of money, they savor earthly things, they hate spiritual things, they serve gluttony, they despise the worship of God, so much so that they seem not drawn, but utterly expelled from that light: Whence it might be judged that both the oracles of the prophets and the sentence of the Supreme Truth could be accused of falsehood: because neither do the nations flow together to Him, nor do all peoples adore Him, nor are all things seen to be drawn by Him: Satisfying these (concerns), we say that Christ worked salvation for all, delivered for the healing of all wounds, and risen and kindled as the true Sun into the light of all: Yet not all receive salvation, even those for whom salvation is prepared, until their time comes: For the Sun, in its primal creation, was filled with that light which is most sufficient for illuminating all parts of the world; yet it does not illuminate all parts simultaneously, but when its circuit is complete, no part remains deprived of the benefit of its light, and all things receive light in their own time. Christ, the Sun of justice, also rose with perfect light, by which He could illuminate every person: But there are darknesses which cannot comprehend it, either never or for a time: And those who will never wish to receive it, as enemies of light, will be given into the worst lot with the prince of darkness: But those who immediately, or at least sometime, it

have received it, these will also enjoy its benefit in the homeland of light. For the power of Christ, distributed into all members of the mystical and Christian body, is diffused like leaven into the whole mass, and like fire into many logs. But just as that whole mass is leavened with time, and the heated logs are kindled in their own time and transformed into fire, so also this mass of the human race, having received the power of Christ, will be entirely leavened with good leaven in its own time; and, heated by that divine fire, will be transformed into it, except for that part which, like dregs and parchment, will be cast into Tartarean latrines. But this will be when the course is completed, which the Eternal Father decreed for the purification of the mass to be transformed into Him. Concerning this, Sophonias says: "Wait for me, says the Lord, on the day when I rise up; for my judgment, that is, the decree given to me, is that I gather the nations and collect the kingdoms, and pour out upon them my indignation, all the wrath of my fury, for in the fire of my zeal all the earth will be devoured," that is, everyone who savors earthly things and lives according to the flesh and blood. "And I will purge all dross, both in works and in words; and then all will be pure, both in works and in words." [Marginal note: Sopho] From which it follows: "Then I will pour upon the peoples a pure lip, so that all may invoke the name of the Lord," that is, with that holiness and purity with which they ought to invoke it. And this as regards words. But concerning works it follows: "And they will serve Him with one shoulder," that is, with one heart, one worship, and conforming works. Which we have by no means seen yet. But we hope to see and rejoice when, the nations having been gathered and the kingdoms collected, fury, zeal, and holy indignation will be poured out, cleansing and purging all impurities, and gathering all dispersed things, and rendering a single lip, and that pure and clean. Which (say the Hebrews) will be that by which the law and oracles were given, and famous hymns dictated. [Marginal note: Hebræi:] Or let it be pure and clear speech, not according to idiom, but proceeding from a pure and single heart in all things out of binding charity. And then men will be led back from the multiplicity of rites and ceremonies, in which they are often confused, to a single worship; which will then be clearly unfolded according to God's good pleasure, with all discord and dissension ceasing. Whether these proceed from souls naturally disagreeing, or from bodies composed of contrary qualities, or from multiform shapes, or are fostered by varied worship, multiple influences, and diverse nourishments, indeed, a very deep investigation would be required to discern. Indeed, in man there are contrary qualities most diversely mixed, whence diverse temperaments. Various influences also intervene, disposing our bodies most diversely. There are also diverse regions, varied foods, multiple interactions, from all of which (as it pleases Ptolemy) man is led to diverse effects. [Marginal note: Ptole:] Nor does this proceed less from souls, which, if they proceed from the same source, yet passing through diverse media (as the Pythagoreans and Academics assert), [Marginal note: Pythag. Academ.] take on diverse natures and inclinations; whence dissension arises. TOMVS TERTIVS. 218
WHAT A PRIEST IS, AND HIS
office. Chapter one.

[Large decorative initial L] We enter a very wide field, and one which by its magnitude rises beyond our sight, while we wish to treat of the priest: who holds the middle ground between God and man: and is, as it were, a visible God: And especially Christ, the highest and true priest, whose priesthood we intend to explain to the best of our ability. Therefore, a priest (sacerdos) is so called, as if "giving sacred things" (sacra dans): For he administers to the people those things which he receives from the super-mundane sanctuary: Whence, how clean, how pure, how divine he ought to be, let the wise judge: For if he must administer all sacred things to us, we will presently run through seven things especially necessary for him.
First, therefore, he ought to pray for the people, as a mediator, as it is twice repeated in Le- [Marginal note: Leuiti.]
viticus, when treating of the faithless and perjured: "And the priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him:" or "he shall make atonement for him," or "he shall intercede for him for remission," as the truth of the letter sounds, which is thus written: וכפר עליו הכהן (uecaper alau ha-cohen). So also, where it treats of the purification of a woman after childbirth, it is said: "And the priest shall pray for her, and she shall be cleansed," and in whatever expiation or propitiation it is commanded by law that the priest intervene, as a mediator and obtainer of pardon and remission. So also James says: "Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the ec- [Marginal note: Iacobus]
clesiastical church, and let them pray over him."
Secondly, he ought also to offer sacred things, as Pau- [Marginal note: Paulus]
l, discoursing with the Hebrews, admonishes us, saying: "Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices:" and a little before: "It is necessary for priests to offer sacrifices first for their own sins, and then for the sins of the people:" And concerning this, we are most fully taught in the law.
Thirdly, he is constituted a teacher of the people, not indeed of vain and curious doctrine, but of the law and of those things which are of God: as it is said in Haggai: [Marginal note: Aggeus]
"Ask the priest concerning the law:" And through Malachi: "The lips of the priest guard [Marginal note: Malachi]
knowledge: and they shall seek the law from his mouth:" because he is the Angel of hosts, that is, the leader of the Lord's army.
Whence, consequently, in the fourth place, he is constituted a leader of the divine army: so that he may direct and strengthen the weaker people, and be the first to sustain the attack of enemies: as we are taught in plain language in Deuteronomy: [Marginal note: Deuter.]
"If you go out (He says) the Lord to war against your enemies, and you see cavalry, and chariots, and a greater multitude of the enemy's army than you have, you shall not fear them: because the Lord your God is with you in your midst:" And this with the priest intervening: Whence it follows: "The priest shall approach the people and say to you: Let not your heart be afraid, do not yield, do not fear them, for the Lord your God goes with you, and will fight for you against your adversaries, and will save you." Which also happened in Phinehas, the most zealous priest, who, by God's command, was constituted leader of an army of twelve thousand chosen men from every tribe of Israel, against a great multitude of Midianites: concerning whom he reported a glorious [victory].

That Christ was a true priest, and endowed with all things that pertain to a true priest and supreme pontiff. Chapter II.

[C]HRIST JESUS, anointed as king, prophet, and priest above all his companions, was deservedly King of kings, Prophet of prophets, Priest of priests, or Pontiff of pontiffs. But, leaving the first two to be declared in their proper place, let us see how well he performed the office of priest. For first, he prayed for the people, not only once, but many times, and throughout the whole time of his life, now on the mountain, now in a cave, now publicly, now secretly, as is recounted by most of the evangelists in many places. Nor was Paul silent, [Paulus] but discoursing with the Hebrews, he says: In the days of his flesh, he offered up prayers with tears and strong crying, and was heard because of his reverence: And especially at the end of his life, showing how much he loved them to the end, having taken the mysterious and last supper, he prayed to the Father, saying: Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me: but now I pray for them: And again: I will ask the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter [CHRI STVS.]. And again he prayed for the whole church, as we have in the gospel, which is titled according to Luke: I, he says, have prayed for thee, Peter, that thy faith [Lucas.] fail not. But even now, triumphing in glory, he intercedes before the face of God for us, as the Apostle says. He also offered holy things to God, and the most holy of all sacrifices, namely, himself, the immaculate Lamb: Concerning which offering, when Paul had discoursed much with the Hebrews, he finally added: But this man, having offered one sacrifice for sins [Idem], forever sits at the right hand of God, of which sacrifice, once offered,

To Christ, as the true priest, all priestly duties are owed. Chapter III.

[S]acerdoti (by command of the law) were given the first fruits with all things that were offered in the sanctuary: Likewise all sacrifices, and they were commanded by the people to be honored and revered. Concerning the first, it is said in the book of Numbers to [Marginal note: Numer.] Aaron: All the first fruits which the children of Israel offer, belong to the priest: and whatever is brought into the sanctuary by anyone, and delivered into the hands of the priest, is his: But afterwards in the eighteenth chapter the Lord says: Be- [Marginal note: Ibidem] hold, I have given you the keeping of my first fruits, as if He were saying: I have delivered my first fruits to be kept, as [Marginal note: Orige.] Origen rightly understands: Which can by no means be applied to the law of the letter: because these were consumed as food, and digested (as it is said in the [Marginal note: Euange.] Gospel) went into the latrine: Hence it must necessarily be referred to the law of the spirit, according to which the first fruits can be preserved: Those indeed, of which the Apostle says to the Romans: But we, having the first fruits of the Spirit: Which can be understood in two ways: Either the first fruits which the Holy Spirit gave to the Apostles in the primitive church, namely, manifold gifts and charisms: Or by these first fruits [Marginal note: Paulus] we understand the good beginnings of our works, or good inspirations: and these we ought to preserve, and offer them to Christ, the great priest, to be preserved by His grace, and to be increased by His merits, so that He may present them most pleasing to the Father. These, moreover, are said to be offered only by the sanctified of Israel, that is, by those who, having become princes of God, begin to fight against the enemy, against whom our JESUS, the High Priest, also fought, and by those who have been initiated and consecrated to God through baptism and other sacraments. The first fruits of our works, moreover, are the beginnings of love and charity: by which we embrace God and our neighbor: Indeed, among the fruits of the Spirit, charity is placed first by [Marginal note: Idem] Paul: Which our greatest High Priest also seeks above all other things, as true first fruits and tithes, concluding in it, as in the primary foundation, and without which all other precepts, and the whole law, and the prophets are without adornment, commanding by a special precept that it be observed with all diligence, saying: This I command [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] you, that you love one another: And again: By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, and sheep entrusted to me, the good High Priest, if you have love for one another. But so that all works may be done in charity, and be pleasing to God, their beginnings must be consecrated to Christ, as [Marginal note: Paulus] Paul teaches us in Colossians: Do all things (he says) that you do in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, we ought to present the first fruits, and all things that are brought into the sanctuary, to this supreme Pontiff: so that He Himself, sprinkled with His blood, and seasoned with His merits, may present them pleasing to the eternal Father with an everlasting presentation. And this is what is said: These were for the priestly office, by an everlasting statute. But since such things have failed in the priesthood of the law, lest the scripture be dissolved, it is necessary that they be fulfilled in our true priest Christ, into whom, and into his successors, namely presbyters or priests, all the priesthood of the law has been transferred: Also owed to this High Priest are not only the first fruits, which

CANTICLE TWO

The Hebrews call it תרומה *terumah*, but *terumah* of *terumah*, that is, the firstfruits of firstfruits:
Which were chosen thus: The people offered ten out of a hundred to the [Marginal note: Num.] priests:
But the priests offered one out of ten to God, as we read in the book of Numbers.
Therefore, to God, who is most simple, one was given; to the people, as material, a hundred:
But to the priest, who holds the middle ground between God and the people, ten: which is
the end of numbers, and the beginning of tens, and the middle between one and a hundred.
But to Christ, our High Priest, are owed one and ten: Ten indeed
as to a human priest, but one as to God: For he is mediator,
and the end that brings rest and refreshment. Moreover, to our Priest are owed not
only the firstfruits of virtues, but also of men. And these were the first innocents killed for him,
of whom John says: 'These were bought from among all, firstfruits to God and to the Lamb.' Nor
from this does he reject others, provided they wish to offer him firstfruits and tithes, that
is, the beginnings and completions of their works: Whence he says: 'He who perseveres to
the end will be saved:' For perseverance is the offering of true tithes.
He also seeks the firstfruits of days: For in the old law, God was content
that the last of the days and the seventh in the week should be sanctified: But to Christ,
together with God the Father, we give the first, which, because it is consecrated to the Lord,
is called the Lord's Day (Sunday): On which he also gave a beginning to the world,
and at the same time to spiritual life, Christ himself rising on that day, so that in it he might give a beginning to blessed life, just as in
it he began his creation. Hence some say that this will be the last day, on which
God will close the state of our pilgrimage, as if in a perfect octave derived

as is clear from their titles. To the priest also are owed sacrifices, just as
[Marginal note: Lev.] we are taught from the book of Leviticus, where it is said: 'As for sin, so also for fault, or
for transgression, as our translation has it, the sacrifice belongs to the priest:' For the text
here mentions two sacrifices: One is for the sin of commission, namely, where there is
some voluntary fault: The other is for transgression, that is, the sin of omission, as
[Marginal note: Origen] Origen understands. But if the truth of the letter is well weighed, it is for a fault committed through error.
Which sacrifice the Hebrews call אשם *asham*, as is clear in the fifth chapter of the same Levi-
ticus, where it is said: אשר שגג והוא לא ידע ונסלח לו אשם הוא אשם אשם ליהוה
which, interpreted word for word, says: 'Because he erred, and he himself did not know, and
it will be propitiated, or he will be spared, he himself will offer a guilt offering as a guilt offering to the Lord,'
that is, as a sacrifice for a fault committed through error. Such and other sacrifices belonged to the
priest, so that by receiving them upon himself, he might also receive the transgression, and the sin, and any
fault for which they were offered: and intercede with God for those
offering them: In whom the High Priest Christ was profoundly prefigured:
in whom the Father placed, and he himself received, the iniquities of all of us: and
having become himself the Lamb, and [Marginal note: Paul] the true sacrifice, he bore the sins of the whole world, just as the Apostle says to the Hebrews:
'Christ was offered once to take away the sins of many:' And again: 'We have been
sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all:' And again with the Ephe-

--- Page 582 ---
**THIRD TONE. 221**

Paul [marginal note: Paulus] says: "Christ loved us, and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God as a fragrant aroma." And in many places we have (accounts) of the offering made by Christ, the true High Priest, for us, so much so that we no longer need to offer animals, or other sacrifices, than ourselves in recognition of so great a benefit, and that, offered to the true priest, he may sanctify, purify, and present us to the eternal Father. And concerning the first offering, the Apostle, speaking with the Hebrews, says: [marginal note: Idem] "Through the Spirit let us always offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing His name: for with such sacrifices God is pleased." Concerning which also in the Psalmist [marginal note: Dauid] God says: "A sacrifice of praise will honor me." And this both in confession and praise of His name, as well as in thanksgiving. But concerning the second offering, the same Apostle, teaching us in Romans, says: [marginal note: Paulus] "I urge you therefore, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual worship." If we also wish to descend to particulars, in Leviticus [marginal note: Leuitic.] we read that the breast of the peace offerings and its right shoulder were given to the priest: In the breast is the heart: and the shoulder in Hebrew is called שוק (shoq) which among us signifies the arm, and concupiscence. Therefore, the heart which resides in the breast, and the arm in which is concupiscence and appetite, are given to the priest for judging and purifying. Hence also we expose to the priest in confession our thoughts and affections, and all those evils which (as Christ [marginal note: CHRISTVS.] says) proceed from the heart, and become evil desires: so that he may judge them, and by absolution and penance imposed, cleanse and purify them. And it is indeed very profitable that everyone should have their heart and affection in the hand of a good and wise priest, by whom they may always be cleansed and directed towards good: For (as we said above) the judgment of difficult cases, and discerning between leprosy and leprosy, and cleansing it (which is most difficult) belongs to the priest: who can by no means judge the cause of the heart, unless we present it open to him. And because the priest holds the place of God on earth, judging hidden things and those which pertain to divine judgment, therefore by divine precept honor is also due to him, as it is said in Deuteronomy: [marginal note: Deuter.] "Whoever acts presumptuously and will not obey the command of the priest, who at that time ministers to the Lord your God, that person shall die by the decree of the judge, and you shall purge the evil from Israel, and all the people will hear and fear, so that no one will again swell with pride:" Which, in summary, I say again, that God commands that the priest, as His minister, be held in such reverence by the people, that whoever despises him shall die: To which that of the Royal Prophet [marginal note: Dauid] assents: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm:" And this, because whatever the priest does on earth, performing his priestly office, he does it acting in the place of God: as Christ clearly declares, saying: "Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven: and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven." Moreover, there is in the priest either a certain character (as our Theologians [marginal note: Theolo.] say) or a certain divine power, or an impressed awe, which others should fear, just as in princes and kings...
EE v:

--- Page 583 ---
**SECOND CANTICLE**

To divine individuals there is a certain quality, which the people, in their fear, revere. There is also, or ought to be, in the priest a certain mark of virtue, and consequently divine favor, so that all should revere him. Hence Alexander (as Origen relates in *Contra Celsum*), while waging war against Darius, revered the great Hebrew priest of God, as he had been taught by a nocturnal oracle. Emperor Theodosius revered Ambrose even when he was rebuking him. Attila (as we have said) was terrified by Pope Leo. But it would be too long to adduce all that we find written about these and similar matters. But we must lament the calamity of these times, in which (I speak with shame and indignation) priests have so debased themselves by mixing with vile and wicked individuals, serving not heavenly but earthly things, that they are now a laughingstock to God, angels, and men. But to Christ, the true and greatest priest, distinguished not with a common priestly character, but with that of the supreme pontificate and empire, shining above all in doctrine, wisdom, and holiness, is due honor and glory above all others: Whence not only in His name every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bows, but even insensible things revere Him, and all things tremble at His nod: For He commands the sea and the winds, and they obey Him: He blesses bread, and it is immediately multiplied in a wondrous measure: He commands jars to be filled with water, and wine is made: He calls forth souls from the underworld, and they are reunited with bodies: He commands fevers, and they cease to trouble: And to conclude briefly, all things revere Him: all things obey Him: indeed, He has even given us power over all the strength of the enemy, provided we are willing to follow His footsteps, and become priests consecrating ourselves to God as a sweet aroma.

tightness, the linen tunic was drawn tight between the navel and the chest. The fourth kind of vestment is a round cap, like half a sphere, which the Greeks and our people call τιάραν (tiara), and others a galerus, but the Hebrews מצנפת (miznephet): Nor does it have a point at the top, nor does it cover the whole head, leaving a third part uncovered at the front: and it is bound at the back of the head with a band, so that it may not easily slip from the head: and it is of fine linen, so skillfully covered with a fine cloth, that no traces of a needle appear.

Of the remaining garments, however, which properly belong to the pontiffs, the first is ὑποδύμαβις (hypodumabis), that is, an ankle-length tunic, entirely hyacinth-colored on the sides, having sleeves sewn of the same color, and open at the upper part where it is put on the neck: which is commonly called a caputium (collar), with very strong borders woven into itself, so that they may not easily break off: However, towards the feet, on the hem, there are seventy-two bells, and as many pomegranates, succeeding each other alternately, so that his sound might be heard when he entered the temple, lest he die.

The sixth is אפוד (ephod), which the Septuagint calls ἐπωμίδα (epomida), that is, a shoulder-garment: Aquila calls it ἐπένδυμα (ependyma): But Jerome [Hiero.] calls it by its own name, ephod: which is twofold: one for priests, and this is a simple linen one, which Samuel the Levite and priest used: King David [Dauid] also used it when he wanted to consult the Lord, whether he should pursue the robbers who had attacked Ziklag and plundered it: for then he said to Abiathar the priest: 'Bring me the ephod': clothed with which, he consulted the Lord, and received a clear answer: The other ephod is woven from the four colors often repeated in the law: hyacinth, fine linen, scarlet, and purple, interwoven with gold, with a weft of hyacinth, scarlet, and purple, and with a warp of fine linen, having wondrous beauty, with twin stones enclosed and set in gold on each shoulder, which in Hebrew are called שהם (soham): which the Septuagint [Septua. Ioseph. Aquila. Symma. Theod.] translated as 'smaragdus' (emerald), Josephus as 'Sardonyx', but Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion as 'onychus', and rightly so, as we shall explain in its proper place: and on each of them were engraved the names of six Patriarchs: on the right shoulder the elder sons of Jacob, and on the left the younger ones were inscribed.

The seventh vestment is small in size, but more renowned than all the aforesaid: which in Hebrew is called חושן (hoshen), in Greek λόγιον (logion). From this, it is translated into Latin as 'rationale' (breastplate): Indeed, a short cloth woven from the four aforementioned colors, having the size of a span square, and doubled so that it might not easily tear: And it had four rows, or lines, in each of which were three precious stones: In the first, sardius, topaz, and emerald: In the second, carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper: In the third, lyncurium, agate, and amethyst: In the fourth, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl: In which were engraved the twelve names of the twelve sons of Israel. On the four belts of this breastplate were four golden rings corresponding to the four rings that were on the shoulder-garment, coupled with hyacinth bands and golden chains: so that the fastening might be firm, and it might appear as one texture. There was also (which is most important) in the breastplate of judgment itself, placed by God's command, האורים והתומים (haurim ve tumim), which we have translated as 'doctrine and truth'. And

What these vestments conferred upon the priests, and upon the High Priest. Chapter V.

[Marginal note: Hieron.] [Large decorative initial Q containing a figure] Wishing to discuss by what mystery or what figure these garments were commanded
to be made by the Most High God, we will not despise those things which the
Hebrew doctors set forth for declaring the mystical sense: Whom even [Jerome]
did not blush to imitate, as being most skilled in this matter: Afterwards, with the veil removed, and illuminated by divine light, we will declare in a mystical sense
what they represent in our priests, and what in our High Priest Christ,
[Marginal note: Sap. He.] to whom all things tend. Therefore, the [Hebrew Sages] say that the
four colors refer to the four elements, from which all things consist.
Fine linen, which is produced from the earth, is assigned to the earth: Purple to the sea, which is dyed from its
shells: Hyacinth to the air, because of the similarity of its color: Scarlet, as if burning,
to fire and the ether. For they judged it fitting that the High Priest should give
thanks to the supreme craftsman, to Him who produced both the elements themselves
and whatever was fashioned from them: and should represent the elements themselves,
and consequently all things made from the elements, to their maker. Therefore, the first garment,
with which the private parts were covered, was linen, signifying the earth from which we are drawn,
and from which our genitals must be covered: because from there we feel pleasure, to which a priest
should in no way condescend: nor should he do anything with those members, except insofar as
necessity, which we derive from the earth, compels. But gradually raised from earthly things
to heavenly ones, from head to heel they were covered with a hyacinthine garment:
which indicates the air diffused from the heavens to the earth: To which were appended
bells and pomegranates. Whose sound suppressed the thunder and lightning that occur
in the air, or by their sound terrified the aerial powers: Or (to speak more accurately)
they represented the harmony and consonance of the elements, and of all things compacted from them.
Which also the composition and wonderful order of the pomegranates signifies.
Ascending higher, they also say that through those seventy-two bells and as many
pomegranates, they also summoned the seventy-two princes of languages, six for each
of the signs, with all those entrusted to them, so that they might be present at the sacrifice which was being made

--- Page 586 ---
TOMVS TERTIVS. 223

by the Supreme Pontiff, Lord of the universe. But if this opinion of theirs is true, that summoning was figurative, sounding through bells as a kind of prelude, to indicate those things which were accomplished at the coming of the true Supreme Pontiff: as we will immediately declare. But the gold, with which the colors were interwoven, or those colored things, represents the vital bond by which elements are connected in composite things. But the ephod signifies the upper hemisphere, in which are two onyx stones, that is, two great luminaries shining from above. Moreover, the girdle, by which the priest's chest is bound, and the linen tunic, some wish to signify the Ocean, others indeed the Zodiac: but we can say both: For in that the linen garment, that is, the earth, is girded, it is the Ocean surrounding the earth: But in that it encircles the priest's chest, which is the center of the lesser world, the Zodiac is understood, encompassing all the central parts of the greater world. The breastplate, placed in the middle of the chest, they explain as representing the earth and its adornment, clothed with flowers, herbs, and fruits: Which, holding the center of this mundane body, receives the virtues of the twelve signs, which the twelve stones fixed in that breastplate represent. But by the four rows, in each of which are three stones, the four seasons of the year are distinguished, by which the earth is variously arranged, giving three months to each season. Or by the four rows are represented the natures of the four signs, since three are found in the property of each element. And so that all things which are in the breastplate may be applied to the earth, they also wish that by Urim and Thummim clarities and perfections may be signified: which are everywhere recognized on earth, where the effects of secondary causes appear: For here we somehow comprehend how clear and how perfect are the works of God and His ministers. Therefore, this very thing, which is in the middle, is beautifully called 'rationale' (breastplate): because in this middle earth the reason of secondary causes and the effects of the supreme God are perceived by purified minds: For all things here are full of reason, with earthly things corresponding to and connected with heavenly things. Hence the breastplate is said to be bound with the ephod, that is, the shoulder-garment. And explaining Urim and Thummim more clearly, they say they signify the truth and perfection of things, truth indeed, because everything that exists is also true: as the Metaphysicians say: In the same way, everything that exists is good, as Scripture says: God saw all that He had made, and [Marginal note: Metaph. Genesis.] it was very good, that is, perfect in its kind. Nor is it without reason that in the priest sacrificing to the Supreme Creator, His own creation is figured, with truth, or clarity, and goodness added in him who ought to instruct the people with the splendor of doctrine and the perfection of good works: so much so that his steps (as Jerome says), movements, and all that he does, are vocal. [Marginal note: Hieron.] Therefore, let him receive truth and divine splendor in his mind, and let him resonate with it in his whole habit and adornment, so that whatever he does, whatever he says, may thus be the doctrine of the people. But the miter and the hyacinth ribbon, beyond all controversy, show heaven: which ought always to be upon the priest's head, and presented to his eyes, and never to be laid aside: On which is a golden plate inscribed with the great name of God: From which we learn that in heaven is the great name of God

**OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

[Marginal note: Abraham] inscribed, presiding over, and sealing all twelve signs, and all corners of the world, as we are taught in the book of formation, which is ascribed to Abraham: From which name all things receive strength and nourishment. But the name is said to be inscribed on a plate of gold, which we find signifies natural and spiritual life. And not unfittingly, because it is solar, and consistent with the celestial sun, which is called the giver of natural life, and with the supramundane sun, which bestows spiritual life. The High Priest, therefore, bearing the trace of all creatures and of the whole world, indicated, when he sacrificed to God, that all things needed His mercy and favor, by which they ought to be expiated and cherished: And thus he prayed not only for his children, parents, and relatives, but for every creature, by voice and by attire. And the garments of this high priest [Marginal note: Exodus Leviticus] are commanded to be made in Exodus, but in Leviticus, Aaron is clothed with them by Moses (God commanding): because these things are to be learned from the law, and assumed by God's command. [Marginal note: Paul] For no one ought to assume honor for himself, unless (as the Apostle says) he is called by God, just as Aaron was: nor ought he to presume to judge what is pleasing to God, unless God Himself dictates it.

**What these figurative garments pertain to for the priests of Christ. Chapter VI.**

[Ornate initial C] Since all things happened to those fathers in figure, and all these sacred things (as Origen says) refer to Christ the High Priest, and to those things which He commands His Christian followers to do, we will first see how all these things come into the use of Christian priests, and afterwards we will discuss how all these same things are concluded and resolved in Christ. But here I deem it necessary to state beforehand that priests and pontiffs were washed before they put on any of those garments, as we read in [Marginal note: Leviticus] Leviticus: Where it is stated that by the Lord's command, Aaron and his sons were called to the door of the tabernacle with a bullock for a sin offering, and two rams, and baskets of unleavened bread, and the assembly of the children of Israel having been called before the doors of the tabernacle, Moses said: "This is the word which the Lord has commanded to be done:" And immediately he presented Aaron and his sons, and washed them, and clothed the high priest with a linen tunic, girding him with a belt, and putting on him a hyacinthine tunic, and over it he placed the ephod, which he fastened with a girdle, fitting it to the rational (breastplate), in which were the Urim and Thummim. He also covered his head with a turban, and on it, against his forehead, he placed a golden plate consecrated for sanctification, as the Lord had commanded. The priest, therefore, was washed before he put on any garment, but that washing was by the power and judgment of the law, which the Lord gave through Moses, therefore it is said that he was washed by [Marginal note: Jerome] Moses: Which, however (as Jerome says), prefigured the purification of the world, and the sacrament of baptism, or of penance: in which we are washed before we put on [Marginal note: Paul] that sacred garment, concerning which Paul says: "Put on our Lord Jesus Christ:" indeed, He Himself also willed to be washed in the Jordan, and to be clothed, and to be filled with the Holy Spirit, who ascended upon Him as He came out of the washing, in the form of a dove,

before he entered into sacred rites, and into the expiation of the human race: Which, being baptized,
he immediately began, having taken up the struggle in the wilderness against the enemy of the human race,
afterwards continuing to teach and heal; and finally offering himself as a sacrifice. The priest, having been washed,
therefore, was first clothed with an undergarment or breeches; because he who is about to sacrifice
must first observe this, that he gird his loins, since not even serving his wife by right
of marriage can he properly devote himself to God and sacred rites, unless he abstains from the marital act.
Hence the Apostle, teaching married people, that each should render to the other what is due (because   [Marginal note: Paul]
neither has power over their own body, but each over the other's) adds: Except that you may devote yourselves
to prayer for a time: Which would be nothing, unless it presupposed that no one could
serve marital matters, and prayer, and other sacred rites simultaneously: Because just as we cannot
serve God and mammon, so neither can we serve the spirit and the flesh, the ambition of the world, and the yoke
of Christ.

He was afterwards girded with a belt made of four colors, by which (as
we have said) the four primary elements and all things composed of them are understood,
signifying that all these things, which are called of this world, and are from corruptible
elements, ought to be bound and tied to the thigh and lower part: so that, left there,
they may not hinder the upper part of the priest, when acting in sacred rites, he is
about to sacrifice to God.

He is afterwards clothed with a hyacinth-colored tunic, so that from its color he may learn to become entirely
heavenly: For this, tending towards the sapphire heaven, invites the priest to the heavenly dwelling,
which Ezekiel saw to be of sapphire color: And this is to be declared in its proper place with a great mystery.   [Marginal note: Ezek.]

And a shoulder-garment was placed over it, of the same colors
as the belt, interwoven, so that these changeable elements with their composites
having now been dismissed to the animal part, he may raise his mind to better, heavenly, and
divine elements (of which we spoke above): Which also the stone *shoham*,
that is, onyx, bound with gold on each shoulder, designates: For this stone is
earthy around the center, but sapphire on the surface: by which it is taught that, with earthly things
now confined to the center and around the lowest parts, the priest may appear heavenly everywhere.

And because
it is the priest's role, as a mediating hierarch, to lead the lowest to the highest, and the people
entrusted to him to God, therefore it is said that on those stones were inscribed the names
of the sons of Israel, and consequently of all the tribes descending from them,
so that, presenting the whole people to God in sacrifice, he might reconcile them with Him.

But as for the names of the greater being placed on the right, and those of the lesser on the left,
I believe this signifies that greater things are given to the greater, not indeed
by age, but by virtues and merits: and lesser things are given to the lesser and less deserving.
Many things could be said about particular sons and tribes: and how, by God's
favor, they were figuratively placed in camps: and what is signified by the right and
left, which are not for the present discussion, therefore let us come to those things which
the priests of our time ought to bear: who bear not the names of the sons of Israel and the four-letter name,
but the names of the Apostles, who stand for the sons of Israel in the church;
and the name of JESUS, in which is the power of the Tetragrammaton. In the foundations of the holy and new
city descending from heaven (says John) were written the names of the Apostles.   [Marginal note: John]

of them, and of the Lamb: Whence any priest of this city, performing the office of a true

some are fruits which we produce on earth by God's grace, and others which we gather

and the earthly twelve to the heavenly twelve, and the evangelical twelvefold family

with the ephod, because our High Priest Christ made one out of both:
Which we leave to be explained in its proper place. Moreover, on that breastplate, or ra-
tional, were Urim and Thummim, which, somehow, they have interpreted as doctrine and
truth: For Urim (אור) comes from אור, which signifies light: Whence Urim (clarities
and illuminations of doctrine and spirit) seems to me to signify: which the priest ought
to have, who performs the office of mediator between God and man, and
provides leadership to the people towards God. For a leader will not know, nor be able to direct any-
one on a path he does not know: Nor will a blind man be able to provide good leadership to another: Nor
will he find propitiation with God who is not illuminated by the light of His grace:
because we can know neither God nor divine things without His light. Therefore,
the pontiff ought to be clear and illuminated by doctrine, knowledge of both testaments,
and spirit, so that he may know what he does, and understand by what way he leads the people, and
recognize what God demands from us for our purification and sanctification.
By this mystery, our pontiffs are said to wear that two-part miter, so that
the expertise which the pontiffs themselves ought to have in both testaments may be signified:
although in most cases of our time, the reality falls too short of the sacrament. To be

--- Page 590 ---
VOLUME THREE. 225

also the pontiff ought to be pure, clean, and perfect, lest, being hateful to God, he place an obstacle rather than a propitiation between God himself and the people: And this signifies that תמים tumim, which we can interpret as immaculate, perfect, complete, simple, and without defect. Hence such diligence is commanded that a priest not only guard against sins, but also be undefiled by a dead person, and also by a woman who has granted her body to another man: Likewise, that he be free from leprosy, from a flow of blood, from a hernia: and that he be whole in all his members, not blind, not lame, not hunchbacked, not with an excessively large and deformed nose: all of which are tolerated in others, but by no means in a priest: because he ought to be complete with every intrinsic and extrinsic perfection. Concerning the former, it is said verbatim in Leviticus: 'Let the high priest [Marginal note: Leviticus.] from among his brethren, on whose head the anointing oil has been poured, and whose hands have been filled, that is, with good works for vesting, namely, priestly vestments, not uncover his head, and not tear his garments, and by no means come near any dead body, even for his father or his mother he shall not be defiled: And he shall not go out from the sanctuary, and he shall not profane the holy things of his God: because נזר nezer, that is, a Nazirite, that is, separated, namely from the crowd, or crowned, namely with a crown of holiness: The oil of the chrism of his God is upon him: I am the Lord.' These words are full of mysteries: But let us briefly run through what they signify: The oil, which is poured upon the head of the priest, is divinity, with which the priest ought to be imbued above the crowd, especially in the head, where that supreme portion of the soul resides, which is divine: and by which we understand God, and by it we perform those things which are pleasing to God himself, provided it is sprinkled with His grace. Therefore, in Pontiffs, Kings, and prophets, who were anointed, it ought to be sprinkled with a particular outpouring. The filling of the hands, however, signifies the multitude of good works, with which the priest ought to be filled. Therefore, imbued with divinity, and made divine, and full of good works, he should also assume the habit of divine ministry, which is pontifical or priestly: He should not uncover his head by removing the turban, which (as we have said) signifies the upper hemisphere: by which the priest's head ought to be covered. And to speak more clearly, [Marginal note: CHRIST.] he should never lay aside heavenly things, but always direct his mind and soul towards them: For if it has been enjoined by Christ upon all to pray always and never to faint, then each one ought always to have his soul and mind in heaven, since he does not pray with his mind who does not have it elevated to God: Prayer (says Damascene) is the elevation of the mind [Marginal note: Damas.] to God. Much more therefore ought the priest, who prays for himself and for the people, always to have his mind and head raised to heaven, and overshadowed by divine covering. He should also not tear his garment. There are two kinds of garments that every Christian ought to wear: One is that of baptism, concerning which Jerome [Marginal note: Jerome.] says: 'I received the garment of Christ in Rome': for he was speaking of baptism: The other is that of penance, which is a second garment covering the nakedness of those who have lost the baptismal garment: And God clothed the first man with this, and all who, having fallen into sins, are saved: concerning whom the prophet says: 'Blessed are those whose sins are forgiven [Marginal note: David] FF

iniquities, and whose sins are covered. And with this twofold kind of garment was clothed our High Priest Christ, not for himself, but for all whose sins he bore: For one was the seamless tunic, which signifies the garment of baptism, indivisible, and never to be repeated: The other was divisible by part, and part: And this signifies the garment of penance, to be resumed as often as a person sins, as Christ himself said to Peter, to whom he had especially given the power of putting on this garment: [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] "I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven," that is, as often as necessary, as all explain: Moreover, both use the remissive number seven, but Christ multiplies by ten, and by that seven deduced from the complete ten, it squares, not without a mystery to be declared in its proper place: From all these repeated acts of penance, only one garment is made, which is unique: although divisible in the way we have said. However, neither of these should the priest and pontiff tear, but he should keep both untorn, lest his shameful nakedness ever appear with the garment torn by sin, because it is his duty to clothe the naked. Therefore, he ought to be unpolluted, holy, and clean. Nor does it hinder that he first offers for his own sin a calf, two rams, and a basket of unleavened bread, since no one is called clean from defilement, not even an infant of one day: because we are all born children of wrath, and subject to sin. Indeed there are sins, which are called venial, and do not tear the garments, and are worthy of easy pardon: from which nevertheless the priest ought to be clean, wishing to deal with a holy, clean, and pure God. Hence it follows that he should not approach any dead body, lest he be polluted and defiled by the dead, even if it were his own father or mother: From this it is understood how much greater purity is required in a pontiff than in a priest, since to the latter is granted at the beginning of the chapter access to the funeral of a father, mother, son, daughter, also brother, and virgin sister: But to the high pontiff access to any funeral whatsoever is forbidden. And what defilement a corpse contains, so that it can defile one approaching it, is not the subject of the present treatise: This, however, I will say, that the ancient Fathers, more skilled in spiritual matters than those who fantasize about finding relations and quiddities, which they never find, not without reason ordained that a corpse be buried in a sacred place, be accompanied by light as long as it remains above ground, be sprinkled with holy water, and be censed with incense: All these things were ordained not in vain, as the common people think, but for the expiation of the corpse, which is very unclean: And who would not be burdened by this defilement, defiled by a mortal, indeed, when it is justly incurred, when someone out of charity commits a dead person to the tomb, nevertheless, God commands the priest to be immune even from this defilement. He also commands that he never leave the sanctuary, but always (if possible) be holy, he who is about to minister to the Holy of Holies: For he is a Nazirite, that is, separated from the defiled crowd, and from common works defiling his dignity: Or a Nazirite, that is, crowned with the diadem of holiness, and infused with the oil of divinity. What all those vestments have to do with Christ, whom they pre-eminently prefigured. Chapter VII.
[Decorative initial I] Now we must come to Christ, to whom all things tend, and to whom all things look, as to the Lord of all things, for whom all those things were ordained, and in whom all things ought to be verified: Because Moses is always with Christ, and the law with the gospel: Therefore Peter is noted for error, who on Mount Tabor, when Moses was present with Christ, wanted to make three tabernacles, when one would suffice for Christ, Moses, and Elijah: For the law, prophecy, and gospel are one: and one so corresponding and connected to the other, that they are entirely the same: Which we can see, provided that God in His goodness removes the veil from us, so that with unveiled face we may be able to contemplate the glory of the Lord, transformed ourselves into the same image of the true Son of God, who was first contained under the enigmas of the law and the prophets: Whom, now revealed to us, we shall contemplate as we ascend from the clarity of the law to the clarity of the
[Marginal note: Leviticus.] gospel. he penetrated the heavens, having become better than them. For indeed, the heaven was the highest figurative covering of the ark, otherwise called the mercy seat, because from there propitiations were made, as we read in Exodus: In a similar, and better, way, from the body of our High Priest, that is, from those things which he bore in his own body, remissions are made for all of us. But in mind he penetrated the heavens, ascending to the right hand of the Father in the highest, so that he might be a mediator between the Father of all, and us: And he wore attached seventy-two pomegranates and seventy-two bells of each kind: Which bells we say signify the seventy-two princes set over seventy-two languages with the peoples entrusted to them, figured in as many pomegranates, because he called to himself all those divine powers and the virtues of those intelligences themselves, subjecting all things to himself, as the Apostle says: Because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily, so that just as through him God, and in him all things were created, so in the body he might be the head of the church, holding primacy in all things: And asserting with the Hebrews that that of the prophet was said of Christ: "You have subjected all things under his feet," he adds: "For in that he subjected all things, he left nothing not subjected to him." That there are princes of provinces and peoples, no one among those who study sacred letters doubts, as we are taught in many places, especially by Dionysius and Daniel; who commemorates an angel, prince of the Persians, and Michael standing for the Israelite people. But all those yielded to Christ coming, indeed, subjected to him, whatever they do thereafter, they accomplish by his command. The peoples also, entrusted to them, signified by the pomegranates, are disposed by the will of Christ our High Priest. Hence he not only cares for the Israelite family, but from every nation that is under heaven, and from all peoples (as John says), and from all tribes and tongues, he gathered his church. Therefore he rightly wore the ephod with stones, on which were written the names of the sons of Israel: because on his shoulders he bore the entire Israelite family, both cleansing and saving it: And what seems hard, he says: "I have not come, except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel:" Which however must be understood concerning both families, namely, the figurative and the true: which is the church, and the collection of all the faithful, as we shall declare below (God willing): And therefore the breastplate and the ephod are said to be bound together by their chains, passing through four rings on each side: From which it is hinted that both families are bound together by the quaternary of the great name, by which all things are bound, and in which all are saved. But these names are said to be written on onyx stones, which below, around the center, are earthly, but on the surface, heavenly: in which it is hinted that he intends to make that entire family, which was earthly and animalistic, heavenly. He also took the Choshen [Hebrew: חושן], which the Greeks call 'logion,' that is, the rational: and it is a breastplate ornament, in which were twelve precious stones with the twelve names of the sons of Israel. But those names were borne engraved on the two stones of the ephod, and on the twelve stones of the breastplate: From which it is expressly demonstrated our High Priest Christ: who ascended the altar of the cross to pray and to sacrifice for both twelve-fold families: Of which the figurative was contained on the back by two stones—

—of onyx, but the true [family] was inscribed on twelve precious and varied stones: This is why that family of Patriarchs was not gathered from every nation contained under the twelve celestial signs, but was begotten from one race, and from one Father, Jacob: Nevertheless, it is called bipartite, because from the same family there are those who ought to be placed on the right, and those who ought to be placed on the left. But this new family, and new bride descending from heaven, was gathered by our High Priest JESUS from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation that is under heaven, divided especially into twelve parts contained under the twelve celestial signs: Therefore it is said to be inscribed on twelve precious stones: because all things that have been done in this family can deservedly be called precious. But to each stone we could apply a twelfth part of this new family with its twelve leaders: But we will reserve this to be done in its proper place (God willing).

But why the breastplate itself is said to be woven from the four often-mentioned colors, we will easily be able to explain, if we remember that we said those four colors signify the four elements, from which all things are composed, and into which even heaven itself is said to be divided, and composed of them, not indeed from these corruptible elements, but from better ones. Hence, three of its signs are called earthy, three watery, as many airy, and the rest fiery: To which all corresponding things agree, so much so that all things, both celestial and terrestrial, are distributed to those elements signified by the four colors: Therefore, the type of both families is distinguished by those four colors.

But those two sacraments, which are called Urim and Thummim, so perfectly suit Christ our High Priest, that he not only bears them, but is entirely the very thing that is signified by them, however they may be interpreted: For if it is translated as doctrine and truth, he himself publicly proclaims: I am the truth: and my doctrine [CHRI STVS.] is not of my own origin, but of him who sent me, but communicated to me in such a way that by word and deed I am the doctrine of the peoples: because every action of Christ was our instruction. But if they are interpreted as clarity and perfection, he was the light illuminating every man, and so immaculate and perfect, that he might present us immaculate to God the Father by his grace and merits. And if the whole breastplate is called logion, that is, verbal, or rational, is he not the Word, in whom are all the rules both of created things and of those things which we ought to do? He also offers to all the reason for understanding and acting: And it is called double, because there were two natures: in each of which we find pasture for reason and understanding.

The breastplate and ephod were also bound with hyacinthine ribbons and golden chains in two sets of four rings, which were four on one, four on the other, corresponding to each other: But what better hyacinthine and celestial ribbon than he who is entirely celestial, who descended from heaven to make us celestial? And what is this golden chain, if not charity and love, by which our High Priest came to bind us, aiming at this with every word and work of his? Therefore he bound both families, the ancient and the new: he bound celestial and terrestrial things: he bound creation with God, just as in himself were bound two

Behold then how well that name of forty-two letters, in which the world was fashioned, agrees with JESUS: But we enter into so many and such great mysteries, that if we wished to explain all that would occur here, neither would my strength suffice for speaking, nor would readers perceive what was written. Nor is it fitting that those things which are to be communicated orally [Marginal note: David] among a few wise men should be committed to public letters: I have hidden (says the prophet) your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you. Lest, however, hungry readers be entirely dismissed, we will touch upon a few things. If all those elect and consecrated are said to have the name of the Lamb and the name of their Father written on their foreheads, it is no wonder if we say that the firstborn Son of God among many brethren, and to whom the Father gave all things, has the name of God himself in him. And here, I ask, let readers note why our great High Priest himself in the days of his flesh said: [Marginal note: CHRIST.] Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you: when afterwards, rising again, he says: In my name they will cast out demons: and other things which follow: Where, with careful inquiry, it must be noted why he is silent about the great name of God, in which Moses, the Fathers, and all the prophets from him up to Christ, whatever wondrous things they did, accomplished: And which is sung with such solemnity by the divine psalmist in many places: And nevertheless, with this passed over in silence, our Jesus proposes only his own name, in which he teaches us to ask and seek from the Father whatever we desire to have. Did he wish to arrogate to himself what he ought not? Far from it: For he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped. But he did this because he perceived the power of the great name given to him by the Father, and concluded within his own name. Therefore, he gave power to men, that they might perform miracles, speak in tongues, and such things, which were done by the power of the great four-letter name. But in the course of our time, from Jesus onwards, we ought to bear the name of Jesus himself, and consequently the great name of God enclosed within the name of Jesus himself: and this bound on our foreheads with a hyacinthine and heavenly ribbon, that is, by life, conduct, and mind.

Christ is a priest forever. Chapter VIII.
[Large decorative initial V] Therefore our Christ is the true Priest and High Pontiff,

[Marginal note: Dauid]

priesthood eternal in heaven, better than Michael, of whom it is said that he is a priest and prince over all souls to be received, and no less over bodies: For he even contended with the devil for the body of Moses, as Thaddeus relates in his canonical epistle: For the devil wanted to take it away, as being subject to sin; but Michael, on the contrary, wanted to present it to God, as purified by the law and cleansed by divine communion: whence he had brought his face to such brightness that the children of Israel could not gaze upon it because of the splendor of his countenance: Which we believe was also rightly done by our eternal priest, of whom Moses himself said many things, so that that soul and body, now purified, could be presented to God.
