And to conclude briefly, He showed mercy to all sinners with open speech, saying: "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners:" And what seems great, God permitted all to incur sin and wrath, so that all might feel mercy obtained through Christ, and not through the law, by which (says Paul) no one is justified: [Marginal note: Paul] Which I would by no means dare to assert, unless the same Apostle taught me, when he says: "He has confined all under sin, that he might have mercy on all:" although the Apostle says, "he has confined them in unbelief:" For that itself is the source of all sins, and true alienation from God. And so much does the Apostle ponder this word, although he knows it to be true, that immediately crying out [Marginal note: The same] he adds: "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!" But if those secrets have been entrusted to anyone, it was done on the condition that they should not be revealed to the unworthy. Hence Paul, faithful in the entrusted mysteries, did not explain, but hinted why God did this, saying: "For from him and through him and in him are all things:" for he wanted to imply: "Because just as all things were made through the very Word of God, so those very things, having been corrupted, might be restored through the same, so that from him, as from a head, we might recognize all influences and all good things to be received:" Therefore he adds: "Not to be wiser than one ought [Marginal note: The same] to be wise: because each one has, as God has divided:" For just as we have many members in one body, so also we have differing gifts according to the grace which has been given to us. And that the life and operations of all members proceed from Christ, he relates in a long discourse with the Corinthians and Ephesians, saying among other things: "To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ, according to what is said: 'Ascending on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men': For he gave some to be apostles, others prophets, and the rest that follow." Therefore, the Father willed that all things which we have, we should receive through the Son, and that we should obtain him himself, and all gifts, and charisms, and salvation, and mercy. Hence Zacharias said to his son, the recently born forerunner of the Lord: [Marginal note: Zacharias] "You will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, who indeed comes to give salvation to his people in the remission of their sins, through the bowels of his mercy, by which the dawn from on high has visited us," Therefore, no one is justified by the law, or by the blood of animals, but by him in whom the Lord has laid the iniquities of us all, by whose stripes we are healed. And Paul relates that not only men, but also all things have been brought into [Marginal note: Paul] due harmony through the blood of Christ, saying: "Making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven." What then remained in heaven to be made peaceful by the blood of Christ, unless we understand it concerning the eternal Father, and concerning all celestial powers made peaceful for us, when Christ, paying our debt in his passion, reconciled us to the Father, who had been provoked by the transgression of the first man? What the red heifer and its ashes signify in sacred rites, and in the expiation
of the defiled. Chapter VI.

**A**nd although all expiations were established by the Supreme Lawgiver in a wonderful
order, yet the mystery of the red heifer was considered most excel-
lent, and most celebrated above other sacrifices, since it
was ordained for the expiation of the most heinous crimes, and the trans-
gression of the first parents, and of the molten calf, erected by Aaron and by the
people in the desert: For expiation, I say, inasmuch as it was a figurative sac-
rifice: for all things are truly and fully expiated in Christ, as we recently touched upon: and
the more excellently this mystery of the red heifer prefigured the work of redemption,
the more celebrated it is. But if it was ordained for the expiation of the sin
of the erected calf, let us see: For the children of Israel, led out of Egypt, and freed from the
yoke of that dominion, which was ruled by the ram, still fearing that influence,
and deprived of their leader (as they supposed), wished to acquire a power stronger than
that of the Egyptians, namely the bull, which presides over the ram in the celestial circle:
Hence, by a certain more secret art, with things arranged, and metal melted in the usual way, a
calf was fashioned: And setting it up, still ignorant of divine matters, they thought to draw
a power superior to the ram, and thereby to prevail (if necessary) against those who were
ruled by the ram: But this was an error, and a very great sin, while they wished to attribute
favor to the celestial bull, which they ought to have received from the living God, as they had
hitherto received. The error was also increased because they erected the image of a beast
against the commandment of God their helper: For this crime, and wound, by God's own
command, two remedies were applied: One, because many were commanded to be expiated in their own
blood: Which was carried out by the sons of Levi, whence they earned the blessing,
of which that family had been deprived on account of the crime perpetrated against the Shechemites: The other
remedy was this red heifer: Whose mystery let us somewhat explore: Ob-
serve, I pray, the order: A cow, or heifer, is chosen against the sin of the adored
calf, so that purification may be made through that by which one sinned: But the weaker sex is assumed,
lest we believe that expiation is made by the power of the animal itself: for it was not from the ani-
mal, but from divine power that the purification flowed: Hence not more worthily

--- Page 646 ---
TONE FOUR. 253

animal, but a weaker one in sex is chosen: And so that the favor to be drawn might be proven, not from the animal itself, but from heaven, God commanded it to be burned with all its entrails, by that fire, namely, which was supplied from heaven for receiving burnt offerings, as we can learn from many places in scripture, and as is widely known by common report among the Hebrews: Which fire (as they say) was given from heaven throughout the entire time of the first temple, but was also sometimes supplied in the second, as we have from the second book of Maccabees: where it is read that Nehemiah, coming from Persia to offer sacrifice, sought the hidden heavenly fire, and did not find it, but thick water: with which he commanded the sacrifices to be sprinkled, since he did not have fire supplied from heaven.
Elijah however, in the time of the first temple, to prove that the worship of his God was better than the worship of the prophets of Baal, exposed his sacrifice to fire supplied from heaven, seeking that the prophets of Baal should do likewise: And when the fire by no means consumed the sacrifice of those false prophets, but burned Elijah's sacrifice and presented it transformed into fire to heaven, Elijah's worship was proven true and good, as is found in the third book of Kings. Therefore, the cow having been burned with all its entrails by this fire, the defiled were sprinkled with those ashes, according to that saying of Paul: For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled, sanctify the defiled for the purification of the flesh, and of blood, namely, according to which sin comes into man, therefore sin tastes of the nature of red blood: whence Esau, the sinner, was called Edom, that is, red, and sold his birthright for something red. The first parent also, through whom sin was introduced into all, was named Adam, which (as they say) means red earth in our language. But if we carefully consider those characters, that name signifies something sanguine mixed with divinity: For it is composed of א Aleph, which is a letter indicating divinity, and דם, dam, which signifies blood. Hence, especially for the expiation of the sin not only of the adored calf, but also of the protoplast, a red heifer is chosen, signifying, namely, not the redness of flesh and blood, but a better redness, concerning which it is said in the Song of Songs: "My beloved is radiant and ruddy: radiant indeed with innocence, ruddy with charity and fiery fervor." And just as Adam, through whom sin was introduced into the lower world, was called red or red earth, because he was drawn from האדמה adama, which signifies red earth, so David, chosen according to the heart of the Lord, was called אדמוני Admoni, that is, ruddy or red-haired, as we have in the first book of Kings: And Christ descending from him, a heavenly man indeed from heaven, the restorer of sin introduced by the first earthly man, was red, if painting teaches us the truth, and those who describe his physiognomy: Whose redness was so efficacious that just as the whiteness of his transfigured body overflowed into his garments, so that they appeared white as snow, so also the fervor of the same suffering one was diffused into his garments, so much so that (as Dionysius testifies) the angels, marveling, said that passage from Isaiah: "Why is your garment made red?" It is not surprising, therefore, if to prefigure the expiation to be made through

The heifer was also slaughtered outside the camp, as the Apostle says concerning it, and concerning the true holocaust, with the Hebrews [Paulus]: "Of which animals the blood is brought for sin into the holy places, their bodies were burned outside the camp: Because of this, Jesus also, so that he might sanctify the people through his blood, suffered outside the camp, so that he might expiate them, even those who through sin had been excluded from the assembly of the righteous, according to that which the supreme Redeemer says [CHRI STVS.]: 'I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.' And again through another Evangelist: 'The Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.'" Also from the blood of the slaughtered heifer, the priest, with a dipped finger, sprinkled seven times towards the doors of the tabernacle, indeed, in the number of remission, so that it might indicate the remission to be made in the blood of the true holocaust, who also alone is the door through which we enter to salvation and life. Afterwards it was burned by that fire supplied from heaven, so that it might be a fitting remedy, or at least a figure of a remedy, against the blemish derived from inferior fire and redness. Finally, from the ashes of the burned animal, the defiled were sprinkled not without mystery, because nothing more sanctifies the animal, and our redness, than its mortification and burning done by that holy fire which the Redeemer came to send upon the earth. But a wondrous sacrament arises: For if that ash sanctified and cleansed the defiled, why was the priest defiled who carried that ash outside the camp, or who burned it? Hence concerning this ash it was said, that it purified the defiled, and defiled the clean. From these things I infer that since the sacrament of this heifer, and of other sacrifices, is multifaceted and profound among all things which are found in sacred scripture, hence the question is resolved in multiple ways and for different meanings. Some therefore say that that defilement and cleanness was contracted by the priest burning it, because the thing was more sacred than that priestly rank, just as it happens to a layman or a woman touching sacred things and the body of Christ, which ought to be handled only by those existing in sacred orders: Others say, because sacred things received with devotion and reverence purify, but handled irreverently, or curiously investigated, defile: Still others say that as far as the letter sounds, the one burning it was unclean, that is, touching it, until that animal was expiated by fire: and whoever handled those ashes outside the camp, or in any way, as if anyone were handling a corpse: whence it immediately follows: "Whoever touches the corpse of a man shall be unclean for seven days: but sprinkled with water with those ashes on the third and seventh day, he shall be cleansed:" Others say that the place for those ashes was in the camp, therefore, touching them outside the camp was unclean, just as with consecrated things in an unsuitable place—

But if we wish to investigate this matter further, and reveal something of the hidden mysteries, we will say that this red heifer is the Blessed Virgin, of the lineage of ruddy David, through whom a blessing was introduced, expelling the curse and infection diffused by Eve into the human Race. And lest we be ashamed to assert this without reason, let us briefly see how much harmony all things converge in this sense. Eve, ruddy and earthly; Mary, ruddy and heavenly, and full of fiery spirit, and full of grace and virtues, as the heavenly oracle attests, so that she could say that from Ecclesiasticus: "My dwelling is in the fullness of the saints." [Marginal note: The Church.] Therefore it is said that that heifer had to be chosen perfect, whole, and without any blemish: Which had not been pressed by any yoke, just as the Virgin declared to the heavenly messenger, saying: "For I know not a man." Also, the sacrifice of this heifer, and all its mysteries, were celebrated outside the camp and the common assembly even of the chosen people, just as all of Mary's mysteries were celebrated outside the common law: For she was announced by an angel, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, made pregnant by divine power, and filled with grace not common, but that which was with God, the primary source of all good things: and she bore a son without pain, the enclosure of virginity being preserved, always proceeding beyond the laws of nature. Hence Solomon, seeking and investigating her, says in Proverbs: [Marginal note: Solomon] "Who can find a virtuous woman?" And lest he seem to have sought despairingly, he adds prophetically: "Far off and from the uttermost coasts," or "from the innermost parts" (as the truth of the letter has it), "is her price."

And so that we may relate something of the mysteries of a more secret Theology, we will also observe with what sacrament the numbers of the letters of the heifer and Mary agree: For the name of Mary, which is written thus in Hebrew מרים (Miriam), gives me 290: But the cow (heifer), which is written thus in Hebrew characters פרה (Parah), gives in number 285. But concerning this sacrifice, as a more celebrated and profoundly full sacrament, with the Spirit suggesting and impelling us, we will briefly explain how it was fulfilled in our Christ, so that through Him, all other things may also be understood as fulfilled. Let no one criticize me because I said that the heifer burned for the expiation of sin signifies the Blessed Virgin, as if I wished to imply that she was offered for our expiation: I do not mean this, since there is only one expiator and redeemer of all. **How the Doctrine of Christ is supremely true. Chapter VII.**

[Illuminated initial 'I'] IN Christ, not only was the law fulfilled, as we have somewhat shadowed forth from thousands (of examples), but also those things which He taught are proven to be most true. [CHRIST] First, because His doctrine emanated from the fount of truth, who is the Father, as He Himself explained, saying: "He who sent me is true." And again: "I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has Himself given me a commandment as to what I should say and what I should speak." This doctrine, therefore, emanating from the paternal fount, descended through the first channel of truth, creating a most profound sea of the highest [CHRIST] wisdom, who is the Son, to speak in the manner of the Hebrews. Hence, in repeated discourse, He Himself says: "My doctrine is not mine." Mine, indeed, because it was given to me by hereditary right; mine, because taught by me; but not mine, because it drew its origin from elsewhere. Hence, [Augustine] it is true because it is in harmony, indeed, identical with that of the supreme fount of truth. Therefore, it is always true, because existing in the Son, it has become the goal, the line, and the rule of all things that have been made in the world, since all things themselves pre-existed in Him, and were made precisely through Him, according to the idea of them that was in Him. And because it is the rule of all things to be done, both by us and by intelligences who consult it (as Augustine says) as the fount of life and truth, therefore, the more one conforms to that wisdom and rule, the more perfectly one is in truth; and the more one deviates from it, the further one departs from truth. [CHRIST] Hence, concerning the devil, Truth itself said: "That murderer, or killer, and having become death itself, did not stand in the truth from the beginning." This is because he departed from Christ, indeed, he presumed to rise up against Him and devour Him, when He was foretold in heaven as about to be born of a woman clothed with the sun and crowned with twelve stars. Moreover, it was true, because no falsehood was ever contained in His words: Perceiving this, He, the knower of all things, said: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." For (as we have said) there was no prophet whom opinion did not sometimes deceive,

--- Page 650 ---
**VOLUME FOUR.** 255

except Christ, in whom there is no error. For with this privilege he had been adorned by the Father, who was always with him, fulfilling all things that he said, according to that which he says: "He who sent me is with me, and has not left me alone, because I always do what is pleasing to him." For all of us (says [Marginal note: Isaiah] Isaiah) have strayed like sheep, but he never committed iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. Finally, it was true, because it was always derived from the first and most true principle of all, which says: "I [Marginal note: CHRIST.] am the beginning, who speak to you:" Indeed, the beginning of all things, the beginning of all perfection and salvation, and also the beginning of all truths: To whom all easily assent with known terms, understanding, namely, how that principle signifies him, through whom and in whom all things were made, and in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and all truths that can be demonstrated concerning any matter, so that Habakkuk rightly says of him: [Marginal note: Habakkuk] "He found every way of discipline, and delivered it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved." After these things, he was seen on earth teaching and explaining what he had previously foretold through the mouths of the Prophets.

**What about the truth of the law, those things which Christ taught. Chapter VIII.**

[Large initial S] But since the law has already been given by God with the highest truth through the angels of truth in the hand of the mediator, it is not foolish to ask what truth they contain, and what agreement those things which Christ taught have with the law: Whether it is something against the law, or different from the law, or from the law itself, or interpretations and perfection of the law. Indeed, the doctrine of him who came to fulfill the law even to the smallest jot contains nothing against the law. Nor is it different from the law, since he himself referred those who sought salvation to the law: Nor is it the law itself to the letter, because a double tradition of the law and a simple reiteration would have been superfluous; rather, those things which Christ taught seem to be something else from the law, from the doctrine of him in whose breast Christ himself resonates: who, placing a distinction between the law and the Gospel, says with the Romans: "By the works of the law no [Marginal note: Paul] flesh will be justified: for through the law comes the knowledge of sin: but now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, being testified by the law and the prophets." But if the law gives knowledge of sin and does not justify, while the Gospel justifies, and that apart from the law, although it was foretold in the law, the Gospel is entirely something else from the law, yet not diverse, since the law testifies concerning the Gospel. Therefore, this was a place occupied by shadow and darkness, until it should be illuminated by the succeeding light, which says: "I am the light of the [Marginal note: CHRIST.] world:" of whom Isaiah also prophesied, saying: "The people who walked in [Marginal note: Isaiah] darkness have seen a great light: and upon those who dwelt in the land of the shadow of death, light has dawned for them:" But when? When a child was born to us, and a son was given to us: whose name is Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Prince of Peace, Father of the Age to Come: who is our Christ, by whom we are regenerated and taught. Therefore, the Gospel is a light illuminating and interpreting the law: It is also the sweetest fruit of the hard trunk and bitter root of the law: For indeed, this was bitter, as Paul says [Marginal note: Paul]

--- Page 651 ---
**OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

lo: The Law works the wrath of God, because where there is no law, neither is there transgression: And again, which seems exceedingly harsh: The Law entered in, so that transgression might abound: Therefore [Marginal note: Paul] is the Law evil, is the Law sin? By no means! says the Apostle: For I knew sin through the Law, from which it itself took opportunity to enter in: The Law indeed is holy, and the commandment just, and good: And again: The Law is spiritual: And if I know evil through the Law, therefore the Law is not evil: And if, what I do not want, that I do, I consent to the Law, because it is good: to which indeed wishing to consent, I would not wish to do that evil, because against the Law. Therefore the Law is not evil, but bitter, because from it I feel the bitterness of sin: For I would not have known covetousness, unless the Law had said, "You shall not covet": For without the Law sin was dead: And then I lived without the Law: But when the commandment had come, sin revived, which indeed was contracted through the Law, by which to the first parent it was said: "From the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat." Nor were others bound by any law, except that which was written in their hearts, until the commandment was made public, which bound that Israelite family, and certain foreigners, who had received the Law: in whom sin revived, the occasion of sin having been given: because the strength of sin is the Law: Which was so bitter, and deadly, that from it itself all were subjected to death, just as to the first Progenitor, from whose seed all came forth, it was said: "In whatever hour you eat, you shall surely die." But the sweetest fruit of the Law is the Gospel, in which Christ is joyfully announced, and declared: to whom he who believes, it is reckoned to him for righteousness: Nor was this voice (Paul being witness) delivered for Abraham alone, but for all of us, to whom it is reckoned for righteousness, believing in Him, who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, who was delivered up for our transgressions, and rose again for our justification. Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: through whom we have access by faith into this grace by which we stand, and we rejoice in the hope of the glory of the children of God: Which glory, and consolation we have in Christ, who is the fruit of the Law, and the true interpretation of the Law itself, and its true perfection: For from that wisdom we have, from which we may be justified from sins contracted through the Law, and from which we may be freed from the servitude of the Law, and from which we may obtain mercy, and grace: which are the antidotes to the infecting Law: For from the Law we contract guilt, from the Gospel medicine: From the Law we feel punishing justice, but from Christ and the Gospel grace, and mercy. From the Law transgression, from the Gospel whence transgression may be forgiven: Through the Law all of us, like sheep, have gone astray, through Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life, our feet are directed into the way of peace: From the Law, whence our iniquities, like a heavy burden, weigh upon us: but in Christ the Father laid all our iniquities upon Him: Through the Law the soul is wounded, and weakened: but by the stripes of Christ we are healed.

By what rectitude of truth Christ God governs the world. Chapter IX.

[Large initial S] But before we come to those particulars which he taught according to truth, let us see by what rectitude he governs the world, to whom the Father gave all judgment, and all power in heaven and on earth, although it may seem contrary to those who do not fully perceive the things that are of God: and with what hidden wisdom the supreme governor himself permits many evils, so that from them he may extract a greater good, and the wisdom and goodness of him who governs may appear: Who, just as from the beginning in the worldly fabric he placed evil against good, the inverted and crooked against the straight, darkness against light, the passive against the active, cold against heat, and many such things, in like manner in the members of the true and mystical body, he placed one against the other, in the former the right against the left, but in the latter the angel of darkness against the angel of light, the wicked against the good: Among these, some are elegantly enumerated by Clement in the Recognition of Peter [Marginal note: Clemens]: namely Cain against Abel, the Giants against Noah, Pharaoh against Abraham, and against his family chosen by God, the Philistines and Gerarites against Isaac, Esau against Jacob, likewise he brings forward the Magi against Moses, the Tempter against the Redeemer, Simon Magus against Peter, the Gentiles against the faithful, the son of iniquity against Christ: Therefore he is now called by all Antichrist, as if against Christ. And thus all things have their contraries, so that, as if by a certain *antiparistasis*, a sweeter harmony of the worldly and human body may be achieved: Whence Dionysius, in that work in which he treats of divine names, discusses evil as something pertaining to Divine providence and to the harmonious disposition of things [Marginal note: Diony.]. Hence also Amos with great confidence broke forth: "There is no evil in the city which the Lord has not made" [Marginal note: Amos]: And Isaiah, speaking in the person of God, says: "I am creating evil" [Marginal note: Isaias.]. Yet God does not create punishment, as some explain, because the wicked person generates it from discordant morals and a troubled mind: since every disordered mind (as Augustine rightly believes) is a punishment to itself [Marginal note: Augusti.]. Therefore God is creating evil, because he created matter, which by its very nature is evil, and draws all things relying on it and adhering to it towards evil, because it causes them to recede from the first and highest act, which is the very rule of good and truth: He also makes all evil, who made nature mutable and annexed to matter, whence it becomes prone to evil. Nor can the Creator himself be considered evil on that account, since he has prepared a much greater remedy of goodness, and offers it to the willing, than is the proneness to evil. Nor could any creature be produced which by its very nature would not differ from the first rule, from which, differing in morals and will, it sins. Hence Anselm, and others following him, say that God could not have made an impeccable nature [Marginal note: Anselm.]: because he could not make another God, who would be the first rule of all things. But since I do not wish to be a judge of divine power, and to assert whether God could have done this or that, or not, since he himself can do many things which we cannot understand, therefore, abstaining from that judgment, let us say that it was entirely sought in the primal distribution of things;

CANTICLE THE SECOND

so that with a suitable limitation, a measure of good things might be given to each, lest anyone presume to claim for himself what had been bestowed by the supreme giver. Whence, because the first apostate had been endowed more than was fitting, he swelled with great pride, saying: "I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God, that is, above all the elect; I will exalt my throne. I will sit on the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds, namely, those higher ones in which the Lord is accustomed to dwell; and I will be like the Most High." And while he presumed to make himself like God by his own strength, the sinner departed from Him and became utterly unlike Him. Therefore, to crush and punish his pride, it is added below: "Nevertheless, you shall be brought down to hell, to the depths of the pit."

Moreover, it was fitting that every ra[Marginal note: Augustine.]tional creature, knowing itself, should say with Augustine: "When I stood, I stood by You; when I fell, I fell by myself; and had I fallen, I would have always lain in the mud, had You not raised me up." Finally, it was again fitting that each thing be governed in such a way that their governor would allow them to perform their own movements. But if they should fall, they would be led back to their proper order by the governor's providence. And in the first, the most wise maker appears as a distributor; in the second, a benevolent and free preserver; in the third, from the abundance of goodness, the best restorer. Therefore God made all things very good and ordered; and yet there is no evil that He does not make, by granting a mutable nature, and one inclined to fall by its own weight, unless they are sustained by that supreme good by whom they were also created, so that all things may learn that He who was also the creator is the same preserver and helper. And thus we would be bound to Him in two ways: both because He is the maker, and because He preserves and perfects. Therefore, there is no evil properly or formally (as they say) from the supreme good; but that in which evil is founded, namely mutable nature, and that by which we are drawn to evil, which is matter utterly removed from good, and especially by the most wicked tempter driving us, who, utterly removed from God, seeks to gather all with him to the center of his wickedness, and to tear them away from the sphere of good and happiness. Between these two, namely the supreme good and the most wicked perverter, man is placed in such freedom that God does not wish to be made the perpetrator of good or evil [Marginal note: Jeremiah.] from Himself, according to that of Jeremiah in Lamentations: "From the mouth of the Most High will neither good nor evil proceed," so that, namely, He might be the complete perpetrator of neither of them, although He is a cooperator of anyone who works well. Nor is any evil found to be effected by God, which man, desiring it, might commit as sin; because there is nothing outside the universe; and those things which are found within it are very good, yet contained within their own limits and distributed according to their own degrees; but evil is perpetrated when, [Marginal note: Dionysius, Hugh the Wise.] having scorned a greater good, we cling to a lesser one. Hence Dionysius, and Hugh his interpreter, and all true wise men agree that sin, both in angels and in humans, was and is when someone, departing from the supreme good or a greater good, wishes to delight in a lesser one. Hence God Himself encompasses the whole sum of sin, when He says [Marginal note: Jeremiah.] through Jeremiah: "My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, the Lord, and they have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold

--- Page 654 ---
**FOURTH TONE.** **257**

hold water. Nor is it only sin when a created good is preferred to the highest good, but also when, there being two created goods, the lesser is preferred, just as one who prefers his own convenience to the public or the many's utility: From which error the Apostle, turning away, said: "Seek not what is profitable for myself, [Marginal note: Paul] but what is profitable for many:" In like manner, when a bodily good and pleasure is preferred to spiritual delight. It is (to conclude finally) sin and error, when the due order is perverted, so that Augustine's saying is true: "Evil is the privation of order, or of due rectitude." [Marginal note: Augustine.] This error, or perversion of order, is not from any virtue granted by God, but from our weakness or obscurity contracted by idleness, which the Savior, and with him Dionysius, and Damascene [Marginal note: Savior] call night, or darkness, saying: "He who is in darkness does not know where he is going:" And again: "He who follows me," that is, the supreme guide, "does not walk in darkness," [Marginal note: Dionysius] that is, of sins: Which darkness is followed by the eternal night of hell: concerning which he again says: "The night will come, when no one will be able to work." [Marginal note: Damascene] And just as night, or obscurity, is the privation of light, so error is the privation of rectitude: Whence it is concluded that the proper essence of sin is the privation of good: into which man falls either by perverting the order in his choice, or by presuming from himself what he ought to have recognized from the supreme teacher. Therefore, fault is not from God, but from a will choosing badly, or presuming too much: But that which is badly preferred is from God, and the will, which errs by its own fault in choosing, is also from God. Therefore, Christ, both God-man and man-God, remains the true best moderator, while he exhorts and favors living well and rightly, as we most clearly prove in his doctrine and deeds.

**What Christ taught in truth concerning things to be believed. Chapter X.**

[Decorative initial Q containing a figure of a scholar at a desk] But concerning what our supreme Doctor taught regarding things to be believed, all agree on those which are called articles of faith: In which the Trinity, already explained by Christ, is expressly contained: For no one before Him had openly revealed the Trinity, clearly expressing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and the "circuminsession" (as they say) of these persons, just as Christ taught, saying: "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me." And concerning their productions, no one before had even spoken a word, but Christ openly explained, saying: "I came forth from the Father," as a Son, that is, begotten by Him. And concerning the Holy Spirit, that He proceeds from the Father, He says: "The Spirit who proceeds from the Father:" and that He also proceeds from the Son Himself, contrary to what some ignorant Greeks, misunderstanding the sayings of their fathers, falsely assert, He says: "He will receive from mine:" Not indeed did He merely receive doctrine, becoming a disciple of the very Word, like a little boy instructed in schools, but He received being and understanding, by which He instructed the Apostles, and before them the prophets: For the wisdom and understanding of the divine persons, and their other properties or attributes (as they say) are not distinguished, nor as accidents

are infused anew: whence whatever one person is said to have received from another, it is immediately concluded to have received the whole of what it is, and all things attributed to it: because neither can they be separated, nor received successively: Therefore, just as the Son confesses himself to exist from the Father, and to have received doctrine from the same in such a way, that he possesses the very doctrine of the Father and not his own, in like manner let us confess the Holy Spirit to be from the Father and the Son, simultaneously with doctrine, and to have received doctrine simultaneously with personal being. And since we have learned with sufficiently clear light from the words of our teacher Christ, those things which are attributed to each person, and those things which Christ himself had come to accomplish, we can easily profess or recite the articles of faith with the Apostles: For when we have learned that the Father is the first fount, from whom the Son and the Spirit proceeded, we can attribute the fabric of the world to Him as the chief maker, saying: I believe in God the Father Almighty, creator of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And when we have learned that wisdom is attributed to the Son, in which both the world and we were created, and by which we are all enlightened: and is called true water not only super-celestial, but super-mundane, to Him deservedly the restoration of the whole fabric, and especially of man, is attributed, so that all things might be restored by the same wisdom by which they were also created: and the human race might be washed by that laver emanating from the super-mundane fount, since it could not be washed by a mundane one, because the whole man was entirely infected: Moreover, we profess this restoration, while we unfold the principal acts of the Redeemer, namely, his conception by the Holy Spirit, birth, passion, burial, descent into hell, so that he might lead forth the captives from there, resurrection, and ascension, and return to the Father, from whom he had come forth, so that by him he might happily raise all his followers. And since we are taught to attribute love and connection to the Holy Spirit: hence when we have professed the Spirit himself, immediately we add: And the holy catholic church, namely, universal communion, and the bond of the faithful. And when again we have learned that remission is given through the Holy Spirit, our teacher saying, "Receive the Holy Spirit, whose sins you remit are remitted to them," therefore we also add, "The remission of sins." And through this the gathering of the faithful into one church, which they call mother, and the remission of sins are said to proceed from the Holy Spirit: because the place of both is the same in the archetype, and [Marginal note: Theolo.] of the remitting Holy Spirit, and of the rejoicing mother of sons, as ancient theologians teach: concerning which it is not permitted to speak in detail to those not initiated into such mysteries. And since we ought to return to the Father, from whom we departed, and to be united with Him, just as by our teacher we are taught, a transformation of our body for the better is necessary for us: hence we profess the resurrection of the flesh, and its renewal, before one comes to life, which is our ultimate and eternal end. And although some things are attributed to the Father, others to the Son, and others of those things which we profess to the Holy Spirit, nevertheless [Marginal note: The same] the divine persons are not separated in working concerning us, as all our Theologians proclaim: For even if the fabric of the world is attributed to the Father, as the chief parent, nevertheless the Son is not absent, in whom the Father produced and sustains all things. For the wisest Creator well knew that man was to be invaded and tempted by the angel of death and the virulent serpent, whence the human race was wounded by a deadly and irreparable wound: because sin was (as we said elsewhere) in a certain way against the Holy Spirit. Hence a remedy ought to be brought by a man who was not of that infected stock, but would descend from heaven, heavenly: By whose skin first the nakedness of earthly man, induced by sin (as we read), would be covered: Afterwards, by the flesh of that better serpent eaten by us, we would be healed from the wound inflicted by that most wicked serpent. And this is what our good serpent and heavenly man says: "Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who [Marginal note: The same] believes in him may not perish, but may have eternal life." That faith alone, which is pure credulity, is by no means sufficient for salvation. Chapter XI.

[Large illuminated initial F] Indeed, there were not only in our time, but much older, even among the Hebrews, those who wanted to assert that faith alone suffices for salvation: And they were called Rabbis: because they followed the opinions of certain teachers: against whom, on the other hand, another sect arose, which was called the Karaites: because they followed only the reading and text of sacred scripture, admitting no opinions of men, nor the sophistical reasonings of teachers: Omitting their reasons and inventions for the present, we will come to [Marginal note: Moderns.] our contemporaries, who, relying on many authorities from the Gospel and the Apostles, which seem to assert the same, have dared to attribute so much to faith, that they in some way condemn works: indeed, they seem to assert that faith cannot coexist with works, because if someone presumed to be justified by works, this would be to limp on two sides, to worship Baal, and to kiss the hand: which is the greatest iniquity, as Job says, Furthermore, they add and say: When you begin to believe, at the same time you learn that all things that are in you are utterly blameworthy, sins, and damnable, [Marginal note: Paul] according to that of the Apostle: All have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God: [Marginal note: Psalms.] And again: There is no one righteous, no one who does good, all have turned aside, together they have become useless: And pursuing many things of this kind, they finally infer this: Therefore, the first concern of any Christian ought to be, that, setting aside the opinion of works, faith alone may grow stronger and stronger, and through it may grow in the knowledge not of works, but of Christ Jesus, who suffered and was raised for him: in whom (as Peter says) believing, you will rejoice with inexpressible joy, obtaining the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls. **How those authorities are to be understood, which seem to attribute so much to faith. Chapter XIV.**

All those authorities, then, which the new dogmatizers have brought forward in excessive favor of faith, so that they do not obstruct the true doctrine which all right-thinking people profess, nor favor their heresy, we could prove with a single solution, saying that all those [authorities] attest to faith as necessary, as the door and beginning of salvation, and as the seed of good works, and their root: Whence all meritorious works, and those pleasing to God, are asserted by the Apostle to have been performed in faith: But the greatest teacher **[Paul]** admonishes us with an clear voice, that the word of God, which we must believe, is the seed of good works: How then do the Northern Theologians claim faith excludes works? For what is a door to us without a house, or a root and stem without fruit? What, again, is wrong with him who desires to be justified and to show himself pleasing to God by fruits, together with the root and seed? You limp, and everywhere stumbling, you fall, you who, content with only one foot, despise the other, and that most necessary one: For we wish to walk with both feet, namely of faith and charity, with a firmer step than you one-footed ones. Nor do we delight in kissing our own hand, but God's, relying on whose help we trust to undertake whatever work is destined for us: For not we alone, but the grace of God with us, imitating the Apostle, we strive to do good while we have time. And this is what we learn believing: because we are all born children of wrath, and we need not only glory, but also the grace of God, so that we may do good in the faith which we have received. Moreover, we know our prone nature, frequent falling, our weakness, and therefore what favor we need, so that we may do good. Nor should the importance of works be dismissed; indeed, we must aspire to them through the grace of Christ, who suffered for us, was raised, and by His merit always favors us: In whom we exult with inexpressible joy, obtaining the end of our faith, the salvation of our souls: And that, provided that faith itself is perfected through charity, with which the fruits of good works are produced, for which remuneration is promised. O good God, with what face, with what daring, with what (to tell the truth) rashness do these glorious more recent theologians presume to exclude works, when the royal prophet announces, the Apostle proclaims, and the Judge of all himself declares, that coming with his angels to put an end to human affairs, he will render to each one according to his works. Therefore be silent, and do not acquiesce to the spirit of error, but yield to the prophet, yield to the Apostle, yield to Christ, and to the Holy Spirit, by whom the holy men of God spoke, being inspired: Who, even if they exalted faith, nevertheless did not exclude works, except those which we do without the favor of Him who said: "Without me you can do nothing": Who to the Jews not yet initiated, and who had not yet received the seed of faith, nor had planted the root of good works, said **[GOD. / CHRI]**: "For it was the work of God,"

If, therefore, faith was sufficient, why was the observance of the law added? Why is Abraham commended now by faith, now by the observance of the law, and such a beautiful promise made to him? Not indeed because faith and works are the same, but because each presupposes or draws the other, nor can one be perfect without the other. For faith, in order to live, leads to works, and works, in turn, presuppose faith. Abraham, therefore, is commended as perfect in both, sometimes separately for faith, and sometimes for the observance of the commandments. These were revealed by God to Abraham himself no less than to Moses, although the latter, by God's own command, delivered them to the people and committed them to writing. And so Abraham kept the law, precepts, and statutes; therefore, these can be observed. Why then do you babble, saying that the law cannot be observed, and that Abraham was justified by faith alone and not by works? Search the scriptures, and adapt sentence to sentence, if you wish to perceive the truth. Indeed, Abraham's faith was credited as righteousness, and his works were also credited, because of which the blessing of all nations in his seed was promised, especially when he offered his son Isaac as a sacrifice. And even if he offered him in faith (as the Apostle says), that offering was not faith itself, but a work founded on faith, which is the foundation of the spiritual edifice.

but not with God: For what does scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, wages are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation. Therefore David also sings of the blessedness of the man to whom God [Marginal note: David] credits righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose transgressions are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. And although these words seem to favor a new doctrine, they are not alien to what the Apostle preaches as contrary in many places. For he, in whose breast Christ resonates, does not so rave as to assert one thing now and immediately begin to sing a recantation. For his discourse was to appease the Hebrews and the Romans: of whom the former trusted in circumcision and the law, while the latter trusted in uncircumcision and baptism. Hence he shows himself a most pious defender, now for the former, now for the latter. And he most fiercely opposes those things in which either the former or the latter, swelling with excessive pride, trusted.

For among them he places himself as a resolver of their questions, as Jerome rightly understands. He also tries to demonstrate that the salvation brought by the Messiah is not conferred either by circumcision, or by the law, or by works which we have done, but by the grace and munificence of God, who through his mercy and clemency sent us a savior. For we had done nothing by which we might extort or dispose God's clemency to give a redeemer, and to obtain the lamb who takes away our sins: Who by the decree of the Father was slain (as John says) [Marginal note: John] from the origin of the world for the universal salvation of all, but this was done out of God's pure grace. But for anyone to receive a portion of water and blessing from this universal abundance of salvation for his own and particular salvation, it is necessary that through faith he adhere to the one offering and bringing the saving water, so that he may drink, and by means of it, by working, grow immensely, and become in him a spring of water gushing up to eternal life. Therefore one must not stop at faith alone, but proceed further to the works which the received faith itself demands.

But if someone is unable to work, the will is counted for the deed, and in this sense that saying of the Apostle is understood: "Now to the one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness according to the purpose of God's grace," who accepts the will when there is an impossibility of working. And this is a singular grace, and a certain blessedness, according to what follows. David says blessed is the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose transgressions are forgiven, and whose sins are covered." Certainly God, who wills all men to be saved, could save all, even without works, but he does not save all, because not all obey him, nor do all wish to work according to the faith [Marginal note: Paul] received, concerning whom the same Apostle says: "No one is crowned unless he competes lawfully."

...according to flesh and blood: but that [salvation] which is according to God and spirit, according to which we also ought to work, since we cannot stand idle, nor ought we, being constituted children of God, to work merely according to flesh and blood. To which degree, and to obtain the reward according to it by merit (as they say) or according to a proportion of equality, to this we can never attain, but only through grace, and in geometric proportion: so that if for one, a hundred are given, for two, two hundred should be given, and for ten, a thousand are returned. Here several things are preserved, which at first glance seemed to fit poorly: For here it is preserved how the sufferings of this time, and our works, are not worthy of future glory: because those [sufferings/works] are performed by numbers [i.e., in simple units], but these [rewards] are returned by hundreds. Here it is also explained how we are saved by faith, since we ought to adhere to Him who brought it about that our works, exhibited by units, are remunerated by hundreds. Finally, it is stated here that even if we are saved by grace and faith, and although our works are not worthy of future glory, yet a just judge in rewarding will render to each according to his works: because this remuneration is made in an equal proportion, with the grace of the Redeemer, promised in the law and the prophets, always intervening nonetheless: And in this sense are understood those words of Paul: "If they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect." For it is most clear to all that salvation is not given by the law, or by the blood of animals, but through Christ and the Messiah: to whom sacrifices, prophets, and the whole law correspond: and in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell, and through Him to reconcile all things. And this, provided that we take up our cross, laboring, striving, working, and doing violence to ourselves, so that we abstain from vices: and work good to the best of our ability: The rest, however, will be supplied by Him who is most full of all good things, so much so that from His fullness we all receive. This is the true doctrine preached by Christ and the Apostles in many places, sincerely proclaimed to all, and which makes all the statements uttered by the same spirit through the mouths of various [people], and published in many places, converge into one. **VOLUME FIVE. 265**
**HOW GOD IS THE FATHER OF ALL.**
**Chapter One.**

[Decorative initial Q] HOW, first, the Eternal Father, and then Christ, is also called the father of all, if we wish to explain this, it will not be inappropriate to repeat those things which are said by natural philosophers concerning the generation of every animal, especially man, since in these lower things there are likenesses and images of divine things. Therefore, Hippocrates [Hippoc.] believed that the foamy and fleshy part of the semen emanates from the brain; Aristotle [Aristo.] from the heart, which is the principal seat of the soul; Galen [Galenus] from the liver, since in it the natural digestive and generative power is situated. But Avicenna [Auicena.] declares that it flows from three principal members, namely, the heart, brain, and liver, so that he may admit the opinions and reasons of all. Some, however (as Aristotle [Aristot.] mentions), are of the opinion that the semen itself descends from every member, on both sides, because pleasure is then felt in all members; also because from any mark of any paternal member, a similar one is generated in the son, and also because in many cases, any part of the begotten is formed with the likeness of the father; whence it is inferred that semen flows from every part of the generator according to the image existing in it. Some have wished to attribute all this to strong imagination, and falsely so: both because this happens without the imagination of the generator, and also because from an excessive emission of semen, every member of the generator itself is weakened. Therefore, let others say whatever they wish for the exercise of their intellect: it seems to me that a portion of semen descends from every member, from which the son is formed with the image of the generator, which represents the whole and all the members. And thus the heart of the begotten is from the heart of the generator, the brain from the brain, the eye from the eye, the hand from the hand, and so for each one: granted that the power and spirit are especially from the brain, heart, and liver, as from the principal and more spiritual members. Therefore, descending from the brain, it draws rational power, and passing through the veins which are behind both ears, to the *mica*, to which they are connected, it proceeds through the kidneys up to the seminal vessels and testes. But proceeding from the heart and from the liver, it draws power and the spirit of love and affection. Thus also Christ, the Son of God [CHRISTVS.], the perfect image and wisdom of the Father, emanated from all things that are in the Father, drawing all things with Him, therefore He said: "All things have been delivered to me by my Father," just as He proceeded from all things. For from the essence, piety, clemency, justice, goodness, infinity, and from the whole fount of all good things, He emanated and emanates; but especially in that which is wisdom, He proceeded from the brain, that is, from the paternal mind, so that Orpheus [Orph.] and after him the Gentile theologians did not inappropriately say that Pallas, that is, true wisdom, was born from the brain of Jove. But from the heart and the innermost paternal sanctuary He drew, so that together with the Father He might produce the spirit of love. According to whose example we also were first begotten by the Eternal Father, yet through the Son, into whom the seed of ideas had been poured. Afterwards, we were again regenerated through the Son made man. For this our seminal power first

It comes from the brain of the paternal mind, from which is the Word and the storehouse of all created things: For in Him were conceived, as if in a seminal power, all things, whether they are in the heavens or on the earth, visible and invisible. And these are unfolded with the image or likeness of the generating Father, as their perfection demands; whence they also emanate and are derived from all that they represent. Hence, since man has the image of the father, so that he may represent all that is in the father, he is formed from all things that are in the generating parent, yet not with that perfection with which the Son is, but with a more distant and obscure image, nevertheless sufficient for this, that he may be called a son, who [Marginal note: Aristo.] ought to be similar to the generator, as Aristotle teaches in the second discourse on the soul. [Marginal note: Dauid Moses.] With all these things, therefore, the prophet, exulting with a joyful spirit, sings: "I have said, 'You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High.'" And Moses, as if reproaching the people entrusted to him for their ingratitude, and consequently the entire human race, says: "Is He not your Father who made you, created you, and possessed you?" Concerning whom God Himself also [Marginal note: Malac.] complains in Malachi, saying: "If I am a Father, where is my honor?" And again, admonishing all mortals that they are brothers, he says: "Has not one God created us? Has not one Father created all of us?" But also our regenerator, preferring God Himself, the true Father of all, as if all others were fathers by similitude, says in the Gospel which is titled according to Matthew: "Call no man your [Marginal note: Matth. CHRISTVS.] father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven." To whom also He teaches us to approach with great confidence when we pray, saying: "When you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven." Whom Paul also calls the Father not only of [Marginal note: Paul.] rational creatures, but of all things, when he says: "From whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named."

**How Christ, regenerating us again in human nature, became a true father. Chapter II.**

[Large illuminated initial D] We have said that the son is similar to the one generating and producing. Therefore, since we have been made in the image and likeness of God, the supreme maker of all things, we are called, above all things produced by Him, sons of God. But with the image defiled and the likeness entirely lost, we were not deservedly called sons of the Most High Father, unless, being regenerated again, we reformed the dishonored [Marginal note: CHRISTVS. Nicod.] image and recovered the likeness that was entirely abolished. Therefore, He who had come to regenerate us said to Nicodemus: "You must be born anew." But Nicodemus, not understanding the mystery, said: "How can these things be? Can [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] one enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born again?" The new Father replied, teaching a new generation, affirming and declaring what He had said: "Amen, amen, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." He assigns water as the principle of regenera- [Marginal note: Moses.] tion, just as the waters are said by Moses to have been the principle of the primeval generation of animals, when he introduces God commanding and saying: "Let the waters bring forth, or let them teem with, a swarm of living creatures." Which also indicates the watery seed of an animal. As therefore...

266

the best philosopher, and the Son of God, well-versed in the ancient generation, spoke concerning the second generation, as if conforming to the first, that it is necessary for us to be reborn from water, so that just as the first generation flowed forth from super-mundane and celestial waters, so too regeneration might proceed from the same. Therefore, in the Son of God, who is the true super-mundane water, all things were created, and in Him all things are regenerated: For He was not speaking of elemental water when He said: Unless one has been reborn from water and the [Marginal note: CHRIST] Holy Spirit: For what has this foul water to do with that holy and divine Spirit? How can these utterly diverse things agree, so as to be one principle of regeneration? Therefore, He speaks of the water which is the Son of God, who together with the Holy Spirit regenerates humans: Of whom this watery element, which is placed externally upon the head of the one to be regenerated, is a sacrament, as is this word sounding outwardly: Of these, one signifies the seed, and the other the power of propagation. And because in this regeneration, from a fiery, warming, and disposing spirit, the power of the Holy Spirit is required, therefore He Himself is also signified by a sensible voice, as if by a sacrament from the minister and to the one being regenerated, while faith and the renunciation of diabolical and worldly impediment are sought and promised, when the one to be baptized is asked by the priest: What do you ask of the Church? And do you renounce the devil, the world, and its pomps? The one to be regenerated declares that he renounces all those things, so that, with the love of inferior things removed, he may be wholly gathered by the Holy Spirit into the love of God. He also demands faith, and the gift of the Holy Spirit itself, by which one can firmly adhere to Him by whom one is generated, and be connected with Him by the same Spirit, which is called the bond and chain of love. Therefore, we are regenerated by the Son and the Holy Spirit in baptism, of which regenerating agents the signs and sacraments are water, words, and those things which are done externally: Which signify not only the effect and grace to be given, but also the regenerator himself, as the true efficient cause. But since in natural generation a generating father, a seed that is infused, and a mother receiving it are required, one might justly say here: I have a Father, who is Christ regenerating, and a seed, which is His watery power and effective seed-bed, but I do not know the mother who receives the seed. Nor am I satisfied by what is commonly said, that the Church is the spouse formed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross, because the Church is nothing but a certain relation of aggregation, or the faithful themselves gathered: Who, since they are generated, cannot be both the generating mother and the generated sons: And even less can that aggregation or relation conceive and generate humans according to the flesh or the spirit. To this difficulty, we can respond in two ways. Firstly, just as the Eternal Father in that eternal and divine generation of the Son did not require a mother, nor in the primeval generation of the world and man, so too Christ, who regenerates us by spiritual and divine generation, does not require a mother. But if it is contended that by the voice of all the Church is called the spouse of Christ and our mother, we will say, lest there be contention where there ought not to be: The first marriage, which was between Adam and Eve, a great sacrament indeed (says [Marginal note: Paul] Paul) of Christ and the Church, teaches us how these things stand: For there

A woman was first a daughter, because she was taken from Adam's rib, as from material proportioned to him by a great mystery; but afterwards, as a wife formed from his rib, she bore sons. So also the first spouse of Christ, the Church—that is, the collection of Apostles—was formed into spiritual life from the rib, that is, from heartfelt love, because He chose them from the world; or from the water of grace and baptismal power flowing from the side and from the heart of Christ, especially as He slept on the cross. **FIFTH TONE.** **267**

And also (to bring forth something from the innermost recesses), such great diligence is required of the one being baptized, faith through the minister, so that, intent with firm adherence to those things which are performed in us, by a strong imagination through that regeneration, we may be better assimilated to the one generating us: For faith works much, which is a firm adherence and fixed intention of the cooperator in any matter, or of the one receiving the seedbed of doctrine and the health of instruction, or the generative seed. For Aristotle was of the opinion that the born child is assimilated to the one generating from the strong imagination both of the conceiving mother and of the generator himself. And Avicenna attributed so much to imagination that it operates not only on its own subject and fetus, but also often on external things, if it is intense: Into which opinion Aristotle also descended elsewhere, and with him Algazel, the wisest of the Saracens, and Galen: The first of whom proves his opinion by that which is trivial: that a woman bore an Ethiopian son from a strong imagination which she had towards a painting of an Ethiopian existing in her bedroom: Galen, however, urges that the eyes of the conceiving woman be fixed on such an image, and consequently her mind on the effigy, such as she desires the fetus to be: For if she desires a beautiful child, she should have Polycretus or Absalom before her mind, and a statue of the same before her eyes: if a valiant soldier, she should be carried away by Caesar, Alexander, Hannibal, or someone of that kind. If a philosopher is desired, she should consider Aristotle or Plato. These wise men perhaps learned from our most upright philosopher Moses, who narrates that Jacob cast rods into the troughs where the sheep drank, such as the offspring he greatly desired: white, black, or speckled. Nor is firm and certain faith, which our parent Christ demands of us not only in baptism but in whatever work we perform, anything other than a stable adherence and vehement application to Him who cooperates and gives strength, and to the work which we intend to do, so much so that it becomes in a certain way an idol in us of the virtue to be received, and of the thing to be done by us, or in us. And because this faith cannot be in an infant, hence in baptizing a non-adult, faith is required in the godparents, so that they may work in the same tender infant by disposing and cooperating with the mother—that is, the conceiving and giving birth minister—and with the principal generator Christ, by whose virtue the infant is regenerated. Therefore, this firm adherence with the generator, or principal cooperator God, or Christ Jesus, is very beneficial, so much so that Paul attributes all excellent works performed by great men to faith, as is evident in those things which he recounts in a long series with the Hebrews. But especially this faith is required in those receiving the divine seed in the field of their soul and mind, so that, wholly occupied in God through firm adherence of faith with Him, the enemy of man, coming upon them, may find no empty space where he may sow tares. For the fuller our soul's field is with divine seed, the less room is left for the enemy of the human race, who endeavors to sow tares: Therefore, not without cause is faith required, which ought to be not merely in pure credulity, but a firm and strong adherence of the mind, and a total application of the soul to the sower and regenerator.

Christ bringing it about, let him be male, divine, and happy, while we claim to be regenerated. He who is privy to secrets, and the messenger of the regenerating father, asks us, saying three times: "Do you renounce the devil, the world, and its pomps, so that, wholly devoted to God and adhering to Him alone, you may be happily regenerated?" He answers three times, promising namely with heart, mouth, and deed, "I renounce, I promise, and I pledge with firm adherence to dedicate myself to the regenerating Father, having removed everything else that might distract me from Him." Then, thus disposed, receiving that saving seed, he is most happily regenerated with such favor, that henceforth he cannot yield to the devil, as John says: "Everyone who has been born of God does not commit sin: for His seed is in him, and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God." [John] And again: "Everyone who has been born of God does not sin, but the generation of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him." [The same] And again: "Everything that has been born of God overcomes the world." And I cannot but wonder why those who reduce even the most minute points of our theology to neutral problems and questions have not discussed how John, whose testimony is true, could have truly said that one born of God overcomes the world, the devil, and sin: when we see so many regenerated in baptism who are wicked, unrighteous, entangled in sins, serving the world and the devil, indeed, made into devils, as our parent Christ said of the betrayer: "One of you is a devil," [CHRIST:] even though he, along with the other Apostles (as is fitting), had been baptized and regenerated by Christ. Here (unless I am mistaken) it must be said, I distinguish, that man is not reborn through water and the word of the priest, which are sacraments and external signs of what God works internally, but through that divine seed, as our John says: "Which (as we have said) is watery, made from that super-mundane water, [John] which is not given, nor does it remain in anyone, unless through faith he adheres to the regenerator, and, established by faith and firm adherence, preserves what he has received." By which faith, preserving that seed, he prevails over the world, the devil, and sin, as the Evangelist clearly states: "This is the victory that overcomes the world, our faith." [The same] But if someone does not adhere by faith, he indeed receives the sacrament, but not the reality or the power of it: For it is indeed given even to the unworthy, not for their benefit, but to their detriment, just as the sacrament of the body and blood was given to the betrayer at the Last Supper by Christ Himself. The same happens to those who receive that seed with faith, but believe for a time, and in time of temptation fall away from faith: which grants victory, in which the seed of God becomes fruitful, effective, and works those things that John narrates: For one is a true son of God only insofar as he adheres to God Himself in faith and firm adherence, as the same Evangelist says: "He gave the power to become children of God to those who believe in His name." [The same.] Therefore, those who fall away from faith in heart or deed are neither children, nor servants, nor friends of God and of Christ the regenerator: but they are erased from the book of children and heavenly courtiers, falling into a worse lot than if they had never been regenerated: because as violators of the oath and sacrament given in baptism, and guilty of the crime of lèse-majesté, they are to be punished with every torment. It is no wonder, therefore, if the Holy Spirit is not seen in the baptized.

Whence the likeness perfecting the image of the begetter in the begotten. Chapter V.

[Large decorative initial P] It is indeed beautiful when a son is like a good father in every
kind of likeness, which is manifold: For a son is formed according to the father's
form, first in a specific ratio arising from nature itself
in univocal generation: in which the begotten, according to species, is said to be most like the begetter,
a son. A son is also formed with the father's likeness in features,
exterior figure, voice, speech, gesture, and such things, which can arise from a strong imagination
and an "idol" existing in the heart of the begetter (as we have said):
Or from the vehement power of the seed and spirit emanating from the begetter through the
seed itself: Or it is (as some believe) from the influence of the heavens, which in some symbolic way
favor the begetter and the begotten. Furthermore, a son is assimilated to his parents in
morals, when he strives to emulate them: In all these ways, the son of Christ
can and ought to be assimilated to the Father. First, therefore, he is like Him in spiritual
generation, nature itself so demanding, as the Apostle says: "The first man is of the earth, earthly;
the second man is of heaven, heavenly. As is the earthly, so are those who are earthly; as is the
heavenly, so are those who are heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear
the image of the heavenly."

Which also had been commanded earlier in the law under the type of forming the tabernacle: "Look, and make it according to the pattern which was shown to you on the mountain." For on the mountain where Christ was affixed to the cross, an example was shown to us of forming the tabernacle of our soul, similar and worthy of a host, so that He might delight to dwell in it. For although our parent Christ always presented Himself as an example to be imitated by us, He did so most especially on the cross: to which, about to ascend shortly, He invites all to imitate Him, saying: "Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." By following Him precisely, we not only [Marginal note: CHRIST]
acquire His likeness for ourselves, but we are transformed into the same image, which is the Son of God Himself, the true image of the eternal Father.

How Christ nourishes all whom He generates. Chapter VI.

[Large decorative initial N] Or would it have been enough for our most pious Father to have generated us into a spiritual man, unless He had also prepared suitable foods for him. For His care for nourishing the spiritual man was no less than for the animal man, for whom He prepared such an abundance of things. For He filled the air, the sea, and the land with animals for its food; and He fertilized it with manifold influences of the heavens, adding the nourishment of winds, dew, and rains, so that it might produce manifold and most abundant herbs and fruits for its food. It remained to prepare foods also for the better man. Hence He prepared a paradise of delight, planted with trees of many kinds, most fruitful of all fruits. Moreover, He placed the tree of life in its midst, not for the animal man, but for the better man; and near the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, good indeed for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to behold. And to water all the trees, there was a river flowing out from the place of delight, which, afterwards divided into four heads, also watered all the lower parts. Which trees, which fruits, which waters were all granted to man, except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which is Christ, as we have said elsewhere. Man ought neither to emulate its rank, nor be nourished by it, or by the tree of life, which is the same, until the time predetermined by the Father should arrive, when the ripened fruit would be offered to us as food. But that was when He said: "Take, and eat; this is my body," and He offered not only [Marginal note: The Same]
the fruit, but the whole tree, yet without any diminution of Himself. Yet the spiritual man was not left without food from the first man (protoplast) until Christ: for He gave sacrifices and prayers, which Abel is read to have offered first. [Marginal note: Abel.]
Then all descendants also did this by God's command, as all who are wise rightly infer: because no one would have attempted to offer sacrifices and gifts to God that were not required by God. But in the time of captivity, when no place for sacrificing was given to them, they conveniently had prayers as that food, whose care it was to nourish the spiritual man. Egref
