**SECOND CANTICLE**

But to its own divine family, after the Egyptian servitude, manna was added, indeed the food of angels, or of the strong, as is contained in the literal truth. The sacrifice was also augmented, the law given, and hymns celebrated: All these are true foods for the spiritual and better man: From which family, degenerating and enveloped in many crimes, foods were withdrawn, it itself being destined for Babylonian captivity: from which, released but not fully restored, it became quite weak until the times of Christ: In which times the most pious and generous Father regenerated it, and the whole mass of the human race, preparing a better food than that shadowy one, as He Himself [Marginal note: CHRIST] says, revealing the mystery: "Amen, amen, I say to you, Moses did not give you bread from heaven; for I am the living bread, who came down from heaven. Your fathers ate manna in the desert, and died. But I am the living bread, who came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever." Therefore, the tree and fruit of life have been granted to us, which, lest the first man touch, he was expelled from that place of pleasure; and it is offered to us to be eaten under threat of death, while it is said: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, which is the same as the bread of life, and drink His blood, you will not have life in you." Therefore, both Fathers were most solicitous for feeding both types of man: both He who first begot us, and He sent by Him, who regenerated us: For He said concerning the animal man: "Be not anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, or for your body, what you shall put on. Look at the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?" Why then do you distrust the Father? Why do you doubt His providence to His injury? When did you see Him neglect the care of His children? If He cares for all those things which are produced for the service of man with such great providence, so that nothing is lacking to them, why do you doubt the provision for His children? Not only did He prepare food and clothing for animals, but He descended to the still viler flowers of the field, saying: "See the lilies of the field, or the roses, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, and yet they are clothed more beautifully than Solomon in all his glory:" because he used clothing woven with artifice and painted with adventitious colors; but the flowers, which nature prepared, put on garments and are painted with colors provided by nature, which is nobler than art: And He adds: "If the grass of the field, which today is, and tomorrow is cast into the oven, God so clothes, how much more you, O you of little faith?" Therefore, taught by this teacher, we can also argue: If He feeds the body, which is to be given to worms, with so many and such exquisite feasts, how much more the spiritual man, whom He begot from His own innermost being to be assumed as co-heir of the paternal inheritance, and to be united to Him in perpetual fellowship? Therefore, for this better man, He prepared special foods sent from heaven, heavenly and divine, by eating which man himself may be made entirely divine: Which foods He enclosed under bread, flesh, and wine, as under the principal foods and drink of human life. But blood, still digested in the mother's womb, and transformed by a wonderful metamorphosis into milk for infants, and

--- Page 680 ---
TOMVS QVINTVS. 270

is administered to tender ones: But to adults and older ones, the same blood, in which is heavenly life, changed into heavenly wine, is offered to drink, according to that of the Apostle: [Marginal note: Petrus] To you as infants we offer milk: But solid food is for the perfect, of those who by practice have their senses trained for distinguishing good and evil: To which Peter assents, saying: As newborn infants, desire pure milk without guile, so that by it you may grow into salvation: because then you will be able to taste how sweet the Lord is: And thus the same drink, which is given to infants in milk for food and drink, is given to adults under wine and blood, certainly not that [blood] in which resides the bestial soul, and which cannot possess the kingdom of God, but in which resides divine life, which the spiritual and divine human ought to live: And this was prepared as a special gift at the Last Supper, when he said: [Marginal note: CHRISTVS] Drink from this, all of you: For this is my blood of the new and eternal covenant, which will be shed for you and for many for the remission of sins: by which, cleansed through him, you may live a divine life. From this it is concluded that that blood was a washing and a drink: To which drink he gave conforming bread and flesh, and these cooked by fire, so that it might remove nausea, as we will say immediately: Which bread elsewhere he called the Word, which proceeds from the mouth of God, in which he also said that man lives, and not by bread alone: Because in this [bread alone] the animal man lives, and in the Word, the spiritual [man lives]. But if by this bread is understood that life, and spiritual [life], then we can say that by this bread the spiritual life of man is sustained: in as much as it is the Word and wisdom, that intellectual part is nourished: Yet it is the same, taking on diverse properties: For the same Christ in body is bread, in divinity is the Word, in soul is blood and wine: In each, however, is the virtue of each, whence he who receives the bread also receives the virtue of the blood and of the divinity, as we are taught by the common rite of the Church, which judges that laypeople are spiritually nourished by receiving only the bread and body, as if the virtue of the blood and the divine [virtue] is contained in it: Our parent, declaring what this multi-kind food is, said: I am the living bread who came down from heaven: And again: [Marginal note: Idem] My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. He also adds the effect of eating this food, saying: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. He also teaches that he is not only wine, but the vine from which it is born, saying: I am the true vine: And again he said: I am the truth, that is, the true Word of God, in which our inner man is nourished. Therefore, all things which pertain to this new doctrine and new food, he himself wished to express, knowing that we cannot have another teacher who might teach these things.

How, so that he might remove nausea, he cooked these foods. Chapter VII.

[Large decorative initial S] But lest the recipients should be nauseated, the most pious Father took care to cook these foods, as was observed in figurative foods by a happy omen: For when the Israelites were about to make the typical Passover, God commanded that they should roast the figurative lamb with fire. And to those offering bread in the law in-

--- Page 681 ---
**OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

it was said, that they should by no means present it raw, but cooked in an oven: Therefore our Father
and greatest priest Christ, observing and fulfilling all things which were set forth in the law even
[Marginal note: JESUS] to the smallest jot, cooked all the food which he prepared in the oven of the cross with that fire,
about which he said: I came to send fire on the earth, and what do I desire, but that it may burn?
Indeed it burns, not that it may consume, but that it may cook the prepared foods [Marginal note: Jeremiah]:
that it may melt us into one: that it may instruct and transform, according to that of Jeremiah in
Lamentations: From on high he sent fire into my bones, and instructed me: or dissolved, melting,
as the truth of the letter has it: or acquired me, namely, transformed from animal to spiritual:
for חרדה (charadah) is interpreted as 'acquired' or 'dissolved'. Therefore this fire dissolves us, that it may melt
and transform us for the better, so that Lateberacensis [Marginal note: Gui. Lo.] not inappropriately exclaims to this fire,
saying: O happy flame, burning and not scorching, illuminating and not incinerating, thus all
whom you touch, loving, you transform into yourself, so that they may deservedly be called by the name of the living God:
You warmed the Apostles, and leaving all things besides you, they became sons of God: You warmed the martyrs,
and they shed blood, so that their blood, mixed with your blood, might become one thing:
You warmed the virgins, and with the fire of love they extinguished the fire of stench, so that they might become
legitimate brides to be joined to you: You warmed the confessors, and they committed themselves to harsh
prisons, so that, dedicating themselves to you alone, they might easily be united with you. Therefore every
creature lives by the benefit of this fire, so that there is no one who hides himself from its heat,
if he desires to have fellowship with God. Therefore he kindled this divine fire in cooking the prepared foods,
adding fuel of woods suitable for it: Which are figured by the woods of the cross, the true oven,
where these foods are cooked. And these woods were cedar, cypress, olive, and palm, as is commonly asserted:
The first, therefore, is cedar, ignorant of corruption, and always enduring, denoting an indefectible
affection and effect, and the goodness of fiery love, a perpetually enduring fuel: because even the good
(one) always burns with love. The cypress, smelling of fragrance, signifies his virtues, always fragrant to
purified nostrils, so that perceiving it, one may say: We run in the fragrance of your ointments [Marginal note: Origen].
For with various ointments (says Origen) God the Father anointing him, made him Christ and a physician.
He also made him a pillar of smoke from the aromatics of myrrh, and frankincense, and all the powder of the perfumer.
Delighted by these fragrances, he was inflamed with desire that he might sprinkle us with them,
[Marginal note: Paul] and make us fragrant, according to that of the Apostle: We are the good odor of Christ. Indeed we are
fragrant with odor: when we offer our works to God, and ourselves as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God,
which he receives as a sweet fragrance: And this was the fuel of warming love, by which he was kindled
to undertake the work of our redemption. The olive tree bears forth mercy and benignity, by which, ever
benevolent towards us, he is carried by ardent love. The palm, however, designates the triumph to be won over the ancient
enemy, by the love of which he was also kindled: For martyrs carry the palm as a sign of constancy
and triumph, because the more its branch is laden with fruits, the more it rises, never bending.
These, therefore, are the four woods,

--- Page 682 ---
**FIFTH TONE. 271**

which provided fuel to that divine fire, by which our redeemer, made perfect, cooked, and seasoned, was brought into the best bread and flesh to be served to us as food. Moreover, with the same fire diffused in us, like a good baker and bread-maker, he cooks us and prepares us into bread and food to be eaten by him. "I will enter (he says in Revelation) to him who opens to me, and I will sup with him, and he with me." [CHRIST] For he was made man, that he might make man God: He also made himself the food of man, that he might make man his food, and that both might dine and sup together in that last and eternal supper: in which the foods, cooked and always warmed by that divine fire, are set forth as imperishable: Where also is that new wine produced from that vine which says: "I am the true vine:" And it was pressed in the winepress of the cross [The same] by the same one who said: "I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the peoples there is no man with me." For he alone trod the wine of merit, because he alone merited the grace by which we might work well, and the reward of glory, which is given to us. Therefore, these foods, cooked by divine fire, he prepared for feeding the children begotten from those divine and most sacred loins, lest they fail. So that just as the natural man lives on bread of fine flour, barley, wheat, and this *attolaganus* (primary, secondary, or baked under ashes, and the like), with many kinds of meats, fish, fruits, and various vegetables, and is drunk with manifold wine and various liquids, so the spiritual man might be fed with bread provided from heaven, having every delight in itself, and filled with the virtue of all foods, and kneaded with the sweet blood of the true Lamb: and might be fed with flesh, in which the most excellent virtue of all flesh is contained by a certain mark, not only because it is the flesh of man surpassing all others, but because it is the flesh of the Prince, because it is immaculate flesh, an ark existing of divinity, because it is the flesh of him who is the bond of all creatures. He is also fed with milk or butter, which he who eats, knows how to refuse evil and choose good: Which milk is pressed from those exalted breasts, of which it is said in the Canticles: [Canticles] "Your breasts are better than wine:" And again: "There I will give you my breasts." Also drunk is the water of saving wisdom, offered by that guest who, journeying with us, cried out saying: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink:" And again: "Whoever drinks of this [CHRIST] water that I will give him, a fountain of water springing up into eternal life will be in him." There will also be honey, which is the taste and sweetness of sacred words and divine wisdom then most clearly manifested: Which the Prophet, perceiving somewhat in this path of pilgrimage, said: "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey [David] to my mouth." But concerning these foods to be eaten in the heavenly nuptials, we will discuss more extensively in its proper place.

He who begot and feeds, also, like a good father, instructs us. Chapter VIII. [Eccles.]

**F** "Do you have sons (says that wise man)? Instruct them." Hence, Jesus, the wisest and best father of all, after begetting and feeding, with the greatest diligence took care to instruct us in every kind of doctrine, taught not only by words, but by deeds and examples. Of the doctrine made by word, all the gospels are full

We will strive to illuminate our eyes, adhering to the footsteps of the Evangelists, and we will hint at something about these wonderful things which are contained under the surface of the letter of both Testaments; concerning which the prophet said: *Reveal my eyes, and I will consider wonderful things from your law.* This law indeed, full of wisdom, was first given to Moses, but [Marginal note:] David by Christ transformed and brought into something better: just as if a potter would fashion the same mass, which was in the form of an ox, a ram, or a lamb, into the form of a man, with nothing added except a new form, the substance and material remaining the same. Our therefore father and teacher JESUS again subjected that law, which previously had been subjected by the blood of animals for sanctifying the animal man, as if some mass, enveloped it with his own blood, and fashioned it for sanctifying the spiritual and better man, losing nothing, leaving nothing which pertains to the substance of the law, but only changed the form and effect into a better state: and this is what he said: *One iota or one tittle will not pass from the law, until all things are done and fulfilled,* namely through the Gospel and the followers of the Gospel, which were spoken in the law. the authority of absolving, and the imposition of hands, and concerning the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment: All these things are contained in the outer shell of the Gospel, and are discussed by scholastic theologians daily in schools, and are reduced to problems for debate: But among the perfect (as Paul hints in the same place), these things pertaining to a better wisdom are discussed: Which is a heavenly gift, and hidden manna, which no one knows except he who receives it, therefore it is not to be discussed, except among the experienced: because others cannot grasp it: Moreover, how man is a partaker of the spirit of God, and one and the same with Him: How also the good and better word of God is tasted than that which sounds outwardly to the ears, and is disseminated to the common people in parables, according to that saying of our teacher to the more intimate disciples: **[Marginal note: CHRI STVS]** To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to others in parables: What, moreover, are the virtues of the future age, and of the happiness which we await, which neither eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, unless one has been lifted up by the power of the Holy Spirit to know those things which man cannot investigate by his own strength, as Isaiah cautiously speaks, saying: **[Marginal note: Isaias]** God will not see without you what you have prepared for those who love you: Nevertheless, these things were shown to the first parent, while he existed in the paradise of delight, which more intimate theologians, together with Paul, call the future age, that is, to be restored to us, who have lost it: **[Marginal note: Theolo. **A BRIEF EPILOGUE CONCERNING THOSE THINGS WHICH CHRIST TAUGHT CONCERNING THE MATTER OF MAN. CHAPTER X.**

Various things concerning man have been established by the wise men of the world, especially by those who are now at hand, touched upon but not decided, but most clearly defined by Christ: Who we are: From where we come: Where we dwell: Whither we tend: By what way. What man is, this alone we have determined by the Peripatetics, that he is an animal, and this a rational one, **[Marginal note: Peripate.]** produced by man and by the sun: But by the Academics (as they had deduced from the prophetic **[Marginal note: Academ.]** workshop) it is added, that beyond animal and reason, there is something divine in man, which Plotinus names intellect, or intellectual light, **[Marginal note: Plotinus]** by means of which we can know God, and do good pleasing to God Himself: Which

--- Page 686 ---
TONUS QUINTUS. 273

And Pythagoras draws from the same workshop, saying in golden words: "Trust, [Marginal note: Pythag]
because a divine nature is inherent in humans." But Christ, transcending further, taught
that we are sons of God, while he commends the prophet, who had said: "I said, 'You are gods,
and all of you sons of the Most High.'" But because we fell from this dignity, so much so [Marginal note: David]
that no trace of it remained in us, nor was anyone found who could either teach
or know anything about it, JESUS our teacher not only taught, but gave
power (says John) that we might become sons of God, by mortifying the flesh and blood, [Marginal note: John.]
which had torn us away from that dignity: Who also elsewhere, exulting, says: "See what kind [Marginal note: Idem.]
of love God has given us, namely through Christ, that we should be called sons of God,
and be so." He taught again, that we might become sons of God through sweet harmony with Him,
saying: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God." Which peace is certainly [Marginal note: CHRISTUS.]
not that of Octavian, or that which the world desires, so that everyone may more securely
possess their goods without robbers or assassins: but that which we ought to have with God:
which consists in complete harmony and concord with Him: so that we desire nothing,
accomplish nothing, except insofar as it is pleasing to Him, vices and concupiscences being completely overcome,
enemies vanquished, and affections pacified: Which to do we neither
knew nor were able, except through JESUS Christ our father and teacher,
Paul saying: "But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through JESUS [Marginal note: Paul]
Christ our Lord." Which peace and victory stands with all manner of external war,
persecution, and martyrdom: In which, being tormented, Vincent said: [Marginal note: Vincent.]
"I am carried on high, therefore I do not fear your torments." He taught moreover that the human condition
is finally to be assimilated to the angelic, while he says: "And they will be in heaven, like the angels [Marginal note: CHRISTUS.]
of God," perhaps not only with greater similarity, but with identity, than is supposed. He
also declared the value of the soul, while he preferred it to the whole world, saying: "What does it
profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers the loss of his own soul?"
All these things, and similar ones, if anyone has well considered them, will understand them defined concerning
the human condition, which the wise men of this world least of all declared. The second is:
Where we come from: Which we cannot learn from Aristotle, since he does not determine whence [Marginal note: Aristo.]
the rational soul emerges, whether from the very bosom of matter, or whether it comes from outside, but
speaks doubtfully and hesitantly, saying: "If there is any form coming from outside, [Marginal note: Pythag.]
that is the intellective soul." But Pythagoras, from the aforementioned workshop (Alexander [Marginal note: Alexan.]
and Laërtius relating), brought forth something more celebrated, saying: "The soul is immor [Marginal note: Laërtius.]
tal, since that from which it was torn away is indeed immortal." Where he professes two things:
One, that the soul is immortal; The other, that it emanated from God: both of which
are left doubtful by Aristotle, because he did not care to learn from the heavenly school,
whence all truth comes: in which Christ, taught above all others, openly instructs [Marginal note: CHRISTUS.]

Him Father, as He is; indeed, that we should acknowledge no other father, while he says:

concerning himself he says: "I came forth from the Father and have come into the world." But since we are brothers rather from

Furthermore, our teacher and Father showed, more by deeds than by words, that this is not our homeland, but a temporary lodging for pilgrimage, while he presented himself as a stranger to his disciples, in whose person the prophet says:
[Marginal note: David] "I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers." Hence it is concluded that the world is not to be loved, just as temporary lodgings for pilgrimage are not; indeed, we must most cautiously take heed, lest we be plundered, wasted, and wounded. Lastly, and what is the most difficult of all, by what way one must proceed to that end: There is no one (**[Baruch]** says Baruch) who can know the way to that kingdom: nor is there anyone who can devise its paths: Neither the giants, who were of great stature from the beginning, and men of renown: Nor any of the princes of this world, who are destroyed: Nor any of the philosophers, although in seeking they may have consumed their age and time (as **[Lactan.]** Lactantius discusses in a long discourse) and at the same time lost their industry, until this our teacher and Father was seen on earth, and conversed with men: Who not only taught, but made himself the way, not, I say, that of precepts, by which David ran with his heart enlarged, nor merely that of virtues, although he taught it in its entirety most fully, but he made himself the way and the staff, leaning on which we might proceed to the Father, not only sustaining, but leading, drawing, and carrying, as we are taught in the parable of the lost sheep, carried on the shepherd's shoulders: under whose person **[Augusti]** Augustine, disputing against five heresies, says: When you were an enemy to my Father, I reconciled you: When you wandered among mountains and forests, I sought you: among the stones and wood which you adored, I found you: I carried you on my shoulders to the Father, to whom I restored you. He also took upon himself all the burdens of our sins, so that, unburdened, we might proceed more easily, or be carried. He also taught how we ought to be renewed and transformed, so that, made lighter, we might not fail in the highest and most difficult journey, and lest, appearing in the form of a beast, which we had assumed through sin, we should be expelled from that court of minds and intellectual spirits much more severely than he is said to be cast out from the wedding who did not have a wedding garment. In what gymnasium, and from what chair he instructed us. Chapter XI.

[An illuminated initial 'E' containing a figure of a seated scholar or saint at a desk]
AND although this Father and our Teacher taught us in the temple, on the mountains, in the synagogues of Galilee, and in various places, nevertheless, he delivered the whole sum of doctrine, and more effectively, on the cross, so that
[Marginal note: Augustine. Paul] Augustine rightly says: The cross of the suffering Christ was the chair of the teaching master. Which he also knew, who said to the Corinthians: I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified: because placed on the cross he gave us all kinds of doctrine: which, running through superficially, we will say, that beginning from the elements of a better and mystical grammar, he led us up to the highest peaks of the deepest theology, leaving no intermediate doctrine untouched. For first he taught the eternal Word to agree with that name, which
[Marginal note: The same.] is above every name, given to him indeed through the power of the cross, if Paul teaches truly: who concerning this incarnate Word, who is called Christ, says: He became obedient for us even unto death, and that the death of the cross: therefore God also highly exalted him: and gave him a name which is above every name, that at the name of JESUS every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth: The power of this name, even if it was given on the cross, yet by virtue of the divine word united with and pervading this name JESUS, and the name itself, so much so that by antonomasia he is called Messiah and Christ, that is, anointed above all his companions. From this he also taught the participle, that is, the portion taken from both natures, by which Christ himself is constituted. He also explained another participle on the cross, while he shared with us grace, glory, and merit, which he acquired in it, so that he might make us partakers of himself, and unite us with him. The true pronoun is that surname Christ, which we use in place of the name JESUS, and we are called Christians from Christ, just as we ought to be called Je-

-suan from Jesus: Or let us say that even if Jesus is a noun, it can nevertheless be a pronoun, because it stands for us in place of the great name of God, which could not be expressed until the work of the cross was demanded: in which (as we said) power was given to this name, which we invoke in place of the great name of God, as we declared above. Moreover, he taught the preposition, by handing over his name to be placed before all our works, just as Paul expressed, saying: "Whatever you do, do it in the name of our Lord [Marginal note: Paulus] Jesus Christ." He also taught us to place the cross to be followed first, saying: "Whoever [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross, and follow me," I who am to be affixed to the cross, offering it to you as a staff and a guiding sign to be set forth in all works. He also explained the adverb, namely the mother standing next to the Word, when he said to the disciple, and consequently to all of us: "Behold your mother, whom I leave in my place, so that through her mediation: [Marginal note: Iedra] who stands continually next to me and before the face of the Father, you may obtain from the Father and from me whatever you wish." Therefore, the disciple then, in his own name and in the name of all of us, received her into his protection and as a refuge for Christ, and together with Him. But he also taught us to make the greatest interjections, providing a source from which we may utter sighs and all expressions of sorrow. Finally, that conjunction for which we were all instituted, namely with God making us blessed: For, sensing what he was soon to do on the cross, so that it might work more effectively, after the Last Supper he prayed to the Father, saying: "I ask, Father, that just as I and you are one, so also may these be one [Marginal note: Ibidem] in you." Indeed, he instructed us in a better logic than Aristotle, since we know how to discern truth from falsehood much more clearly through it than through this [logic] by which young people are instructed in schools and Peripatetic gymnasiums: For in the doctrine of the cross (if anyone wishes to consider it well) without doubt one will distinguish between true and false, just and unjust: For in it, man becomes spiritual, and consequently (as Paul teaches) judges all things: There, true milk and butter are eaten, so that everyone [Marginal note: Paulus] may know how to reject evil and falsehood, and choose good and truth. He also taught the highest Rhetoric, indeed he attributed all efficacy to prayer, by meriting, and he became the means through whom we obtain all things from the Father: For this name JESUS (in which we are taught to ask for whatever we desire) had (as we said a little earlier) its efficacy from the cross, from which it acquired that name which is above every name. He also offered two most pleasing things to reconcile the listener, the Father, in whose presence we must always pray: The first is the diligent care we must have, that a pure and clean soul be presented to God the Father, from whom we received it, which he taught to achieve by deed, when he said: "Father, into your hands I commend my spirit." The second is the love of enemies, in which he offered himself as an example to be imitated with singular efficacy, saying: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do," excusing them on account of ignorance. Moreover, coming to the prayer made for us, he offered [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] (says Paul) prayers with tears and a strong cry, instructing us, [Marginal note: Paulus] that we do the same when praying, namely with the cry of the heart, more than of the mouth. And this is the only way, that we be pressed under the winepress of the cross, and from being square-shaped and corporeal, we may become spherical and divine: For a sphere cannot rightly be given from a square or a cube, unless that square-shaped figure is resolved and reduced to a circle: Therefore, it is necessary that this corruptible, and quadrangular, or fourfold body be dissolved by the cross, to be mortified, if it ought (Paul) to become spherical and divine by putting on (as Paul says) incorruption, and immortality, and that only-begotten and spiritual nature: For through the cross he gave us the power to become children of God, by mortifying the very flesh and blood, and by being reborn through the virtue of Christ suffering, as we said above. Which to no one before or after was given to accomplish. Moreover, he taught true and better astrology, effectively producing and spreading heavenly and divine influences into all of us. Indeed, he opened himself as the true heaven, so that from his most abundant graces he might pour forth into all of us. He also expounded true philosophy, which teaches to abstract intellectual and spiritual things from sensible things, while he taught to despise these, and to desire those: (The same.) To which teacher Paul invites us, saying: "Let us run to meet [him], engaging in a struggle against ourselves, looking to Jesus, the author of faith and its finisher," who, having put aside the joy for himself, namely worldly and sensible, he endured the cross, despising the ignominy which followed from it, so that he might possess heavenly and divine delights. **OF THE SECOND CANTICLE**

**With what treasures, as a good father, Christ enriches us. Chapter XII.**

[Marginal note: M. Var.] [Large decorated initial N] It would not have been enough for our parent to have begotten us, and continuously nourished and instructed us, unless he also made us rich and provided for us in all things. For riches are so called (as Marcus Varro and other grammarians teach) because they make us divine, and in need of nothing, just as God is: To this state true riches lead us. But such a great error has grown among men, that they think they make themselves rich in those things which are dedicated to the lower kingdoms as dregs and refuse. For Pluto, the anti-god, also has his riches dug out of the earth, from which he is called Dis, because he is always twice rich in earthly things, as [Marginal note: Claudi.] Pluto himself says in Claudian: "and we always hold what the gods above once held." This Pluto (as we have said) is called Mammon by the Savior, as are the riches he possesses: These riches are opposed to true riches, just as their prince Mammon is opposed to our true Father, who is rich not only for Himself, but for all others, as [Marginal note: Paulus] the Apostle says: "Rich unto all who call upon Him." And so great is the difference between them, that no one can serve both, as our supreme teacher [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] Himself testifies, saying: "You cannot serve God and mammon," which are opposed as truth and falsehood. And therefore He admonishes us to despise false riches and seek true ones: "Do not (He says) store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal; but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither dig through nor steal." These treasures and riches are accumulated from many possessions.

For [Marginal note: Paulus] there is a treasure of grace, concerning which the Apostle says to the Ephesians: "We have the forgiveness of sins according to the riches of His grace, which abounded in us:" And again: "God, who is rich in mercy, because of His great love with which He loved us, made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved: and He raised us up together, and made us ascend into the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus, that in the ages to come He might show the abundant riches of His grace in His kindness toward us." And not without reason does the Apostle mix together the riches of God's mercy, grace, and goodness: because all those things come from the same super-mundane treasury. [Marginal note: Idem.] There is also a treasure of wisdom, as he says to the Colossians: "In Christ are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge," communicated to His friends, as he says addressing the Corinthians: "You were made rich in Him in all speech and in all knowledge:" He declares to the Ephesians that these treasures were entrusted to him to dispense, when he says: "To me, the very least of all saints, this grace was given, to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to make all see what is the dispensation of the mystery which for ages has been hidden in God, who created all things: so that now through the church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places according to the pre-

And for so long it is necessary for us to be under guardians and administrators, under the servitude of precepts, until (says Paul) we become a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ: [marginal note: Paulus.] so that we may no longer be wavering children, and tossed about by every wind, but joined together and firm through every joint, and to the measure of each member corresponding to divine precepts, as has been declared elsewhere. If, however, there are any who are not yet adult, Christ will supply, as such a great inheritance to be possessed demands. John [marginal note: Ioannes.] also twice testifies, saying: We saw his glory, glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. From whose fullness we have all received, so that we may be made co-heirs of that only begotten of the Most High Father.

**To whom, and how much he bequeathed. Chapter XV.**

**C**onsequently, since these things which happen in civil matters are consonant with divine and heavenly things, and one commonwealth is the image of the other, we can most aptly learn divine things from those things which are familiar to us. A civil testator can bequeath many things to many people, if however an heir has been instituted, by whom the hereditary legacies (as jurists assert) are owed. In a similar way Christ brought it about, as Ambrose well discusses, saying: The Author of piety, [marginal note: Ambroſ.] hanging on the cross, made a testament, distributing works of piety to individuals: to the Father his spirit, to the Virgin the Paranymph, to Nicodemus the body to be delivered to the earth, to the Apostles persecution, to the Sinner hell, to penitent Christians the cross; to the Thief paradise; and to all faithful children the inheritance of eternal life: Of which it is not given to speak, since those who saw it themselves protest

**With what solemnity he celebrated this testament. Chapter XVI.**

[Decorative initial I, depicting a seated figure, possibly a judge or scholar, with others standing nearby] N the solemnity of a testament, it is required (as jurists say, or as
is customary) that there be a competent testator, of sound and healthy mind, a notary having
authority, witnesses, and heirs. The testator was Christ, the Son
of the eternal Father, long since constituted heir of all things with the
fullest authority to make a will, to bequeath, and to appoint heirs, with such a division of assets
as shall seem fitting to each (by the judgment of the best Father). Concerning this testament,
it was indeed foretold in the oracle of Baruch the prophet with these words: [Marginal note: Baruch.] "I will make
with them another everlasting covenant, that I may be their God, and they may be my
people." Concerning which it is also said in Jeremiah: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and
I will make with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which
I made with their fathers, a covenant which they broke: For this will be a
new and eternal covenant and testament, and no longer to be removed
or to grow old." For in saying "new" (says Paul), [Marginal note: Paul.] "he has made the first old: And that which
is antiquated and grows old is near to perishing." Therefore, since that ancient testament [Marginal note: Idem.]
was old, it ought to be changed into a new one, and it has been changed into that beyond which nothing further
is expected. Nor should it trouble anyone that Jeremiah says "covenant" or "pact,"
because "covenant," "pact," and "testament" are taken for the same thing, as we can learn from Paul's
progress with the Hebrews: Thus also was called the ark of the covenant and testament.
And everywhere that promise made in the law, and confirmed by the death of animals, is
called the old testament. Therefore, this testator was competent, and he made his will so
composed of an excellent and sound mind, that no one equal to him has ever existed, as is clear from
his most celebrated doctrine, and in those things which he most prudently carried out when he made the
testament. There were also not just one, but four notaries, greater than all
exception, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, appointed by the supreme
Emperor: who wrote the life, doctrine, deeds, and testament of this
our Father. The witnesses were innumerable from every nation under heaven:
For to this spectacle had gathered Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamians,
Cappadocians, Phrygians, Egyptians, Arabs, Cretans, and others who are named in the Acts of the Apostles, [Marginal note: Actu.]
but especially from the three more celebrated languages, Hebrew,
Greek, and Latin, in each of which the cause of the testator himself was written
above: All of whom heard what the great man JESUS ordained before his death
in his testament: and saw those signs and wonders which in its corroboration—

were carried out for a reason, both then and afterwards. All are heirs who are born of God and are reborn, unwilling to live according to the flesh and blood. For if [Marginal note: Paul] anyone is not a son, neither is he an heir; but if a son, then also an heir, says Paul: But since we are sons, not indeed of a slave woman and illegitimate, but of a free woman and legitimate, we are consequently heirs. How the testament was confirmed. Chapter XVII.

[Marginal note: Paul] [Decorative initial V] Consultants of both laws, and all who deal with testamentary matters, agree on this one thing: that a testament is established upon the death of the testator, as Paul testifies with an explicit voice, saying: For where there is a testament, it is necessary that the death of the testator intervene: for a testament is confirmed upon death; otherwise it is not valid while he who made the testament lives: because human will is changeable until death, and mutable in any direction: Nor can anyone impose a law upon himself from which he cannot withdraw: And since the testator can change as long as he lives, and destroy the testament he has already made, therefore it has no force unless the testator comes to death, after which it can no longer be changed. Nor let anyone say that the ancient testament was a true testament, in which he bequeathed a land flowing with milk and honey, and yet was not [Marginal note: The same.] confirmed by death, because Paul has already satisfied this by saying: Indeed, not even the first testament was dedicated without death and blood: For when the command of the law had been read by Moses to all the people, taking the blood of calves and goats with water, and scarlet wool, and hyssop, he also sprinkled the book itself and all the people, saying: This is the blood of the testament which God has commanded to you. But the figurative testament was confirmed by the death of animals, symbolizing the death of him who was also represented by those animals, whence the Apostle continues: It was therefore necessary that the copies of the heavenly things be purified with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these, namely, by the very death of the true testator: Therefore at the Last Supper he said: This cup is of the new and eternal testament in my blood: Eternal indeed, because beyond that no other will be given, since it is sufficient and unchangeable, promising an inheritance that is not figurative, one that points to and culminates in the true, but the very true one itself, [Marginal note: John] beyond which we expect no other. Nor do I think it should be passed over why both testaments are said to be confirmed not only in death, but in blood, since the death of the testator seemed sufficient, as was presupposed: This was (unless I am mistaken) so that the heirs might become fit and capable of the bequeathed inheritance: for the defiled and polluted cannot possess it, as John says: Nothing defiled in-

TONVS QVINTVS. 280

will enter there: Nor will those living according to flesh and blood be able to attain that inheritance. Therefore, so that he might cleanse us from defiling blood, the testator willed to pour out his most pure blood, by which we might be cleansed from the defilement of our polluting blood, and again John says: Who washed us from sins in [Marginal note: Ioan.] his blood. Nor was there, according to divine justice, another way by which he might establish sons and they might be capable of so great an inheritance. But it troubles some when it is said that spiritual man is cleansed by blood, which is corporeal; and that by it even angelic minds are cleansed, Paul saying: Making peace through the blood of his [Marginal note: Paulus] cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven. To whom we reply, saying, that since life is (as scripture teaches) in blood, therefore, Christ's life existing in blood, angelic spirits and souls are purged; which blood, nevertheless, ought to be shed, as the occasion of all sin: For blood, and that earthly and sanguineous matter, is the fuel of all sins, as Dionysius defines in *On the Divine Names*: For sin is from self-complacency even to the contempt of God, as [Marginal note: Augusti.] Augustine most excellently judged: But the complacency which separates us from God is from the part of matter, that is, sensible appetite, to which man wishes to please himself, whence he is bound by the law of the members: for which Paul sighing says: I see another law in my members warring [Marginal note: Paulus] against the law of my mind, and leading me captive to the law of sin, so that I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish: So also in angels, the weight that diverts them from God is matter, whatever that may be, according to which, wishing to please themselves, they departed from that most pure act, which is God. And in those having an organized body and blood, concupiscence especially resides in the blood, which cannot have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, until our defiled blood has been purged by the most pure blood of Christ, according to the law by which it is decreed in the book of Wisdom: By those things through which one has sinned, by those things also will he be [Marginal note: Sapien.] punished. Therefore our blood is purged in the blood of Christ, since we have all been made one body, and he himself the head of all. Whence just as medicine, which is taken from the head through the mouth, purges the whole body, so also medicine taken from Christ the head healed all the members: For he drew to himself all our iniquities to be purged by his blood, so that that oracle of Isaiah might be fulfilled, where it is said, by his [Marginal note: Isaias] bruise we are healed.

In the body we have twelve principal joints: three in the right (arm), namely at the shoulder, elbow, and hand; and as many in the left: which are six. Also three in each foot, one at the hip or thigh, another at the knee, a third at the ankle joint, where the ankle bone is. Which, doubled, are six, and together with those six of the arms, they make twelve, as many as there are principal joints in the celestial body. **How Christ, as the true head, flows into all members. Chapter XIX.**

[Decorative initial C] We have already proven that Christ is the head of the whole mystical body; it remains for us to see how into all joints and limbs flows the nourishment of life, governance, movement, and whatever pertains to the sustenance and fostering of that body. And although life and movement (as some wise men believe) are principally in the heart, nevertheless, according to the opinion of Galen, Hali Abbas, and others who wrote about the nature and condition of the human body, [Marginal note: Galen, Hali.] all motive, sensitive, and rational power is in the head: For the motive power descends from the head itself through the nerves, which have their origin in the posterior part of the brain, and are diffused through various members. Nor would movement be regulated and rational, unless it proceeded from the place where reason resides, or a semblance of reason; I say semblance, because this exists in beasts instead of reason. The sensitive power is evident in the eyes, ears, mouth, and nostrils, all situated in the head. And although touch is principally in the hands, it is nevertheless not absent from the head, and from the whole body: And for there to be a rational judgment concerning what has been handled, it is necessary that the whole be referred to the head, where the judgment of reason resides. Also in the head are all the interior senses: the common sense, the fantastic faculty, the imaginative, the cogitative, and the leader of all, the intellect and reason: whence the members are said to be ruled by the head, as by a leader, and to be filled with power, just as streams and channels are filled from a source: All these things, according to a spiritual influx, must undoubtedly proceed from our head, Christ: For in Him are, and from Him are filled, all the senses of the inner man, since we can neither taste, nor see, nor smell, nor hear what belongs to God, unless through

What care Christ our parent has for us, his children, whom he be-

[Large decorative initial V]
THAT he might make us wholly divine, he wished to remove all solicitude for tem-

[Marginal note: Matt.] to Matthew, he says: Do not be anxious, saying, 'What shall we eat?' or

The first reason is, because this belongs to the Gentiles, namely, those
who do not admit God's providence, but ascribe all events to chance, or to their own ingenuity, and prudence.
The second: because the best Father, caring for all things,
is solicitous for us, and knows our need, whence if he provides for the birds,
and other living creatures, it is right that he should provide more happily for us. The last rea-
son is, because the order and rectitude of justice requires that we seek first the kingdom
of God, and his righteousness, so that we may find all these things succeeding it, prepared: Which
[Marginal note: Plato] Plato also teaches from the prophetic symposium in the first book of 'Laws,' saying: If anyone takes on greater things,
he will also possess lesser things: but if he lacks the former, he is deprived of both.

which lead to God: Human goods, however, are strength, beauty, health, rich-
[Marginal note: Cicero] es, and also civic virtues. Following him, Cicero says in his 'On Duties': Those who
prefer advantages to virtues, subvert the order and foundation of nature.
[Marginal note: Macro.] These are supported by what Macrobius adduces in 'On Scipio's Dream'. Plato, ob-

CHRIST IS THE AUTHOR AND END OF FAITH. Chapter One.

[Marginal note: Paul]
SO MANY things seem to be believed which are not
Christ Jesus, that I would in no way dare to call Him
the author and end of faith, unless Paul, in whose breast

fecter." But I believe this was said for this reason,
because while we could adduce some reasons for other articles,
for those, however, which treat of Christ Jesus, we can adduce absolutely none,
except fitting reasons, and these only as much as we are taught by divine oracles:
For we can investigate by natural dis-
[Marginal note: Aristotle.]
course that God exists, and that He was the maker of all things, although Aristotle,
as a natural philosopher and proceeding through sensible things, does not admit this: Yet, awakened
by these very sensible things, he does not disagree with other wise men who confess God to be the maker
of the whole world. But that He made all these things through the incarnate Word, who is Christ Jesus,
we have this only from the sacred scriptures, together with the other articles
pertaining to Him, so much so that some of the more recent theologians have asserted
that Christ is the subject around which all our theology revolves, since all
articles seem to refer to Christ Himself: For in the first it is said: "I believe in God
the Father": And indeed, a father cannot exist without a son, who is Christ Jesus.
And the second is: "And in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord." The
third: "Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary." The fourth: "He suf-
fered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried." The fifth: "He descended into
hell." The sixth: "On the third day He rose again from the dead." The seventh: "And He ascended into heaven,
sits at the right hand of the Father." The eighth: "From there He will come to judge the living and the dead."
The ninth: "I believe in the Holy Spirit." And because He proceeds from the Father and the Son, He cannot be
had or understood without the Son. The tenth: "The holy catholic Church, the communion
of saints, the forgiveness of sins." All these things, since they pertain to the mystical body, of which
Christ is the head, cannot at all be done or had without Christ Himself,
especially since both the unifying grace, and the life by which all members communicate, and the
spirit from which they obtain remission, are from the same Christ Jesus. The elev-
enth: "The resurrection of the flesh": Which cannot be, unless Christ,
[Marginal note: CHRIST.]
who is the firstfruits of those who sleep, has risen. The twelfth: "Life everlasting," which is given
by Christ, who says: "I give them eternal life." Behold then, how all things to be believed
either are about Christ, or emanate from Him, or are referred to Him: But all things to be
done, and all commandments, although they may seem external and separate from Him,
[Marginal note: The Same.]
nevertheless cannot be carried out without Him, who says: "Without me you can do nothing."
Christ therefore is the author and perfecter of faith, and of all things which pertain to it.

But if we wish to follow the ancient theologians, who say that the one precedes being itself, we will attribute that one to the first, who is the Father, the first origin of all things: but being to the Son, as is expressly held in their theology, namely that being belongs to supreme wisdom, which is the Son: that being, of course, is communicable, just as wisdom to be communicated to us is attributed to the Son, which, as it exists in the Father, is to be given only to the Son himself: And this is what he said: "No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him." Behold how we expressly have wisdom first existing in the Father, then in the Son.

And again with the Colossians: Christ is all in all, because he completes all things with a fullness suitable to each. But let us see how this Christ is something separate from all things, and all in all.

Christ is neither part, nor whole, and yet is whole, and part. Chapter III.

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.5em; vertical-align: -0.2em;">W</span>hen therefore Christ is all in all, it could rightly be asked whether he is as a part of anything, or a whole in all parts, or a certain divine power completing all things. Here, the revered Dionysius states the opinion of Hie- [Marginal note: Dionysius, Hierotheus] rotheus: JESUS is neither part, nor whole: And yet he is whole, and part, receiving and pre-possessing the part of all things, and the whole in himself: declaring which, he says, the divinity of JESUS is indeed perfect in imperfect things, just as a perfect gem in a rotten wooden box, which ought to be in gold: Yet it does not shine equally well, nor operate so perfectly, as if it were set in metal, or in a material proportionate to itself: But in perfect things, it is not with the perfect perfection by which those things are perfect, but super-perfect and pre-perfect, exceeding, that is, every lower perfection: And he is the form-maker, and introduces form into those things which lack it, as the true giver of forms, and the prince of form, not existing as a determined form, that is, but above all forms, just as the Sun favors the production of all herbs and animals, not itself being an animal or a plant, but having a superexcellent power for producing all those things: And he is a substance supervening all substances, illuminating all of them without defilement of himself: because he is separated from every substance, just as solar rays are in no way defiled when pervading mud, dirt, and whatever is vile, because they are separated from them: And he is ordering all principles, determining all orders, yet placed above every order, and every principle, and above every principality, just as an Emperor ought to order all his generals, existing above every dukedom, and just as the Pope orders all bishops, himself being a bishop, yet above every episcopate: And this is what the Apostle says with the Colossians: He is before all, and all things consist in him, since he is the head of the body of the Church: And he is the measure of all existing things, existing as duration above all duration, because he rejoices in eternity, which is the total possession at once: And he is the meter of all perfection: Therefore, the more one approaches him, the more perfect one is: And he is the full measure in those who have less, not failing on his part, so that he may fill all things with his fullness: But in those who are full, his fullness is not emptied, but is above all fullness: and it so exceeds that it is ineffable and inexplicable to us, and above all mind: And he is life vivifying all things, yet not living an inferior life, but he himself exists as the supreme life, which is above all lives: and he has all natural things supernaturally: Whence, although by his benevolence he came even to our nature, and truly became human substance, and man, and the highest man, yet he was called God:

From the sacred scriptures we have that Christ is all things. Chapter IIII.

**G**enerally, we have demonstrated that Christ is a certain whole in all parts, but what testimonies the sacred scriptures provide concerning this in particular, we will briefly review: And beginning from the lowest of all created things, we will say that God is the earth, that true earth flowing with the milk of higher wisdom, and the honey of divinity, or the taste of divine things, concerning which the prophet sang: "For the Lord will give goodness, and our land will yield its fruit." He is also water, as we explained more fully above. He is also air and breath, by which, breathing upon his disciples, he said: "Receive the Holy Spirit": for he would not give it unless he possessed it. He is fire, which he came to send upon the earth, that it might burn. He is a grain of wheat and a sprout of the earth, saying of himself: "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it bears no fruit; but if it dies," from which grain that living bread descending from heaven for our salvation was made. He is the tree (as we said) of the knowledge of good and evil, and the tree of life, providing wood for the flooring and planking of the entire true edifice to be built by us. He is also a stone and a rock, as Paul says: "Now that rock was Christ": Upon which the Church is founded, and also, placed in the corner, it joined together the whole edifice, and it is the rock that provided us water for washing and drinking. He is gold, which, promising to sell, he says: "I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire." He is silver, according to that prophetic saying: "The words, or utterances of the Lord, are pure words, silver tried in the fire, purified seven times": And what is the true word of the Lord, if not Christ, who is the Word made flesh? Among animals, he is the lion, king of beasts, concerning whom it is said in the Apocalypse: "The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered." He is a calf, or the chief of the herd, as doctors commonly explain that which is found in the Gospel according to Luke: "And he killed the fatted calf." He is the lamb, preeminent among tame animals, therefore the Baptist, knowing these mysteries, pointing to him, said: "Behold the Lamb of God." He is also the eagle, queen of birds, whose ascent into heaven, gazing at the sun with unblinking eyes, Solomon numbers among the four most difficult things. **That we still have from sacred scripture that Christ himself claimed for himself the names of many artificial things. Chapter V.**

[Large decorative initial Q containing a figure] What artificial names he also acquired, we can learn from the same scripture: For he is the great house of God, in which all forms and images of things were placed, before they appeared in their proper subjects: Whence the seal of himself, and of supreme wisdom in Hebrew theology, is assigned to ב (Beth), which, when explained, signifies 'house': And this house is typically said to be built without iron, axe, hammer, and every kind of iron tool, because it is entirely filled with clemency, piety, beneficence, without any iron hardness: In which house sacrifices, oblations, and prayers are offered to the Father: which is intimated in that which he said: "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you:" For to ask in his name is to work in his power, and within his scope. He is also called a tabernacle better than that made by hand, arranged by Moses, as God had commanded: For Christ is a tabernacle not made by hand, that is, not of this creation: Which is not only heaven, as we said elsewhere, but Christ himself is no less, indeed, a better tabernacle of God than we are, concerning whom the Apostle says: "You are the temple of God." And he is the door, as [Marginal note: Paul CHRIST] he himself says: "I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved." **That Christ Jesus also claimed for himself all divine names without usurpation. Chapter VI.**

[Decorative initial A] But coming to supermundane things, although God is unique and especially one, he is nevertheless called by many names, not indeed so that multiple essences or deities of his might be expressed by them, but properties, which, even if they emanate from the same fount of divinity, are nevertheless rooted there and are always one, but are called many with respect to us, into whom many benefits and diverse gifts distill through diverse channels. Therefore, God himself, most unified, is assigned diverse names, concerning ten of which Jerome [Marginal note: Jerome] compiled a short treatise to Marcella. But Dionysius, [Marginal note: Dionysius] proceeding further, collects forty-five names of God and of our Christ. But the Hebrew [Marginal note: Hebrew Doctors] doctors deduce seventy-two names from a certain text found in the fourteenth chapter of Exodus, [Marginal note: Exodus] from the name (as they say) of seventy-two letters. But others, proceeding still further, hint at so many divine names that both their number and what they signify are entirely unknown to us, but each speaks according to his own understanding, because not all secrets are revealed to all: Nor would we dare to say anything about them, except insofar as they are revealed to us by God

**SECOND CANTICLE**

...revealed by benevolence, as Dionysius teaches us, and with him other wise men, not only Catholics and Hebrews, but also Plato, who in Cratylus says: "Divine names were received from barbarians, that is, Hebrews, who received them from God, without whom we can in no way grasp true words, or what names God is called by." Therefore, as far as divine light has shone forth for us, we will touch upon some (names) which all agree with Christ, yet with this law, which Dionysius teaches, that we in no way presume to explain that supreme and ineffable substance, which neither our senses, nor imagination, nor speech, nor touch, nor knowledge reaches: because it is an uninvocable, super-nominable, and supersubstantial deity, contained in the most remote retreat of its divinity, and solitary withdrawal, concealing itself in the abyss of its own darkness: Also, in the supersubstantial thearchy, excellently separated from every state, movement, deliberation, name, word, intellect, placement, position, and end, utterly shunning our knowledge and explanation: which the [Marginal note: Hebrews] Hebrews call the infinite cause of causes, and substance above all substance: Nor do they presume to speak anything else about it, because it is infinite, and in no way perceptible by [Marginal note: Isaiah] our intellect: whom (if I am not mistaken) Isaiah wished not to explain, but barely to hint at with a certain general term, while he introduces him speaking these words: אני יהוה הוא שמי וכבודי לאחר לא אתן, that is, "I am the Lord, that very thing which is, is my name, my glory, this indeed I will not give to another, or to a stranger from me." For which our translation has: "This is my name," so that that relative "this" seems to refer to some name; for it indicates no name, but only hints at that which supremely is, and is utterly inexpressible by itself and by us, as we have it better interpreted a little further down, where it says אני הוא, that is, "chi ani hu": "Because I myself am," that is, from myself and through essence, whence it follows: "Before me no God was formed, and after me there will be none," from whom, that is, I could depend and receive being. So also that [Marginal note: David] Davidic passage ואתה הוא ושנותיך לא יתמו (ve'ata hu u'shnoteikha lo yitamu) is appropriately translated: "But you are the same, and your years will not fail." Therefore, that הוא (hu) there is not a relative (pronoun), but hints at that which is, namely from itself, and the first being, which is by essence. Concerning this name and the named, the more secret Theologians permit nothing further to be said at all, except that it is from itself, and infinite. But when God himself begins to open the fount of his goodness, and to diffuse it inwards (as they say) and outwards, then he acquires very many other names: Wishing to speak of these, we declare that we do so only by that law, by which [Marginal note: Dionysius] Dionysius deals with Timothy: that the secrets may not be poured into the ears of the unworthy, but may be kept among the wise with due reverence. Therefore, the first name of God the producer is אהיה אשר אהיה (ehieh asser ehieh), so fertile with mysteries, that all things are produced by it: For it is a name attributed to the superior crown, and to the fount, goodness, and origin of all things, whom Christ taught us to call Father. The translation, briefly explaining itself, has it interpreted as, "I am who I am": which would sound better to the truth of the letter as: "I may be who I may be," or "I will be who I will be," since that word is repeated twice in the Hebrew in the future tense: Nevertheless, it includes much longer mysteries than can be interpreted literally: But passing only superficially, we will say how from that אהיה is formed that great four-letter name of God, or tetragrammaton יהוה, attributed to the Son: so that just as the Son proceeds from the Father, so also His name is produced from the Father's name: For when אהיה is given אשר, which from one lesser number and two greater ones gives me six, which number is signified among the Hebrews by ו, and this [Vav] is placed in the position of ה, and if [a Yod] is prefixed, the tetragrammaton יהוה is constituted: Which is the name of the Son, bestowing life upon lower beings: Which is hinted at by that character ו, namely, life received from the Father, from whom all things have been delivered to Him: And thus, He who was unique in the Father, marked in א, which is the first letter signifying one, becomes ו, namely life, and the senary communicating being and life to all things, denoted in that senary in the works of six days: For all things were made through the Word, and without Him nothing was made. And lest it be believed that the Son is separated from the Father, that quadriliteral name of the Son is included in the seal of the house, measure, or Paternal dwelling, which is א, formed from ו and two י, which letters, when computed numerically, yield 26, the same amount that the quadriliteral name, which is the Son's, gives: By these numbers we do not understand vocal, or natural, or rational numbers, but divine ones, and properties of divinity, which are so reciprocally in communion in the Father and the Son, that the Son Himself says: [Marginal note: CHRISTUS.] "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me." And from the aforesaid name אהיה, one letter, namely ה, being changed into ל, and which letters in the middle numbers yield seven, that is, seven denarii, אלהים is constituted, which is the name of the Holy Spirit, to whom the septenary is always attributed: In which the ternary is connected with the quaternary, to denote that the virtue of the Holy Spirit unites corporeal quaternaries with the divine ternary. Also, to denote the connection that the Holy Spirit has with the Son, He receives two letters which are found both in the name of the Father and of the Son, namely, י and ה: Hence the Son says of the Spirit Himself: "He will take what is mine." And since the Son has received from the Father, therefore He proceeds from the Father and the Son, and receives. And since all those names [Marginal note: Idem.] are included in the quadriliteral, which is the name of the Son, therefore He claims for Himself, without usurpation, all the aforesaid names, and all others that pertain to divinity and the archetype: Thus, by the perfect production of persons, He opens the fountain-like splendor of His goodness into creatures to be produced by the Father in the Son, and through the Son, and through the Holy Spirit, as through an immediate artisan: therefore His name, operating and disposing, is always introduced by Moses saying: [Marginal note: Moses.] "And Elohim said, and Elohim made." And to denote that the Son also intervened in this production, in summing up all that was made, he introduces the name of both the Son and the Holy Spirit, saying: "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that Adonai Elohim made the earth and the heavens." How in the name of Jesus all names, both created and divine, are included. Chapter VII.

[Decorative initial N in a square frame] If the power of all names were not included in the name of Jesus, the Apostle would not say: He gave him a name which is above every name. For it is a great word, by which he says: He gave him a name which is above every name: It is indeed above every name of all created things, even of Angels, as the Apostle says elsewhere: [Marginal note: Paul.] Having become so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they. And because the power of all divine names is included in the name of Jesus, we will say with reverence that this name is above all names expressing attributes or particular properties: For just as the Father gave him all things, so also he bestowed upon him a name importing all those things, so that the name itself might be fitting for the one named. Let us also briefly examine with what artifice all things are included in the name ישו (Yeshu). Among those who are skilled in formal arithmetic, a simple number indicates divine things, a denary (ten) celestial things, a centenarius (hundred) grosser and corruptible things, while a millenarius (thousand) again indicates divine things, and God, whom [Marginal note: Cant.] finally all things repeat: Therefore at the end of the Canticles it is said: A thousand to you, Solomon, that is, to you, who are your peace, and two hundred to those who guard its fruits, that is, to us living in corruptible flesh, who seek to guard his commandments, from which we receive the fruits of eternal life: Which doctrine the wise Hebrews follow, while they declare that mystery of terumah, which we call tithing: in which the centenarius (hundred) is of the people: while the denarius (ten), which is the tenth of the centenarius, was given to priests, indeed celestial men: but the tenth of this denarius, which is one, is given to God. Behold then, that the simpler number is given to God, the centenarius to the grosser people, still unrefined and subject to corruption, but the denarius to the priests mediating between both: Now all these things are understood to be concluded in the name of Jesus: for it is composed of three letters, one of which imports a simple number, namely י (Yod): another, which is ו (Vav), a denary (ten), and the other, that is ש (Shin), includes hundreds. Nor is it to be wondered at, if the letter importing a number refers not to unity, but to six, because it was not done without a sacrament: For since the supreme craftsman came into creation through the senary (six), a number indeed perfect from the beginning, it is fitting that it be included in the name of the incarnate Word, through whom all things were made. But with what great mystery he proceeded into creation through the senary, besides those things which have been said elsewhere, these few

--- Page 718 ---
TOMVS SEXTVS. 289

we will briefly touch upon. The Monad, and the supremely fertile one, therefore produces another, from which the binary arises: and between the producer and the produced there is a mutual relation, behold the ternary: now combine three, and they will give the senary (six) by doing this: one and 2. make three: to which if three are added, they make 6. Of these, the first ternary, collected from the producer, the produced, and the mutual relation, or reciprocal love, is in God: the other ternary, however, is in created things, since all things contain a trace of God even in number: for they have matter, and form, from which results the composite, which they call a certain third thing. Nor should one insist concerning angels, because even they have their own matter, and their own composition. There is also another ternary in every creature, namely, beginning, middle, and end. And well among the letters signifying numbers in the name of Jesus is placed י (yod), by which the tree of life is designated, since He himself was both the tree of life, and life, and gives life to all. Behold then how beautifully in this name of Jesus it is indicated that all things were included in the one named, as the Apostle says: "For it pleased [Marginal note: Paul] the Father, namely, that all fullness should dwell in Him, and through Him to reconcile, or to recapitulate all things." But since all created things are contained in Christ as man, even the producing and operating reasons, which are in the archetype, are contained in Christ as God: Concerning all of which to write would be too long, and we would proceed further than the present work requires. How, however, the principal names of God, and those which are more frequently and openly repeated in sacred scripture, are contained in this name ישו (Iesu), we will sketch. This quadriliteral name is most famous, and most frequent, which is written thus יהוה and cannot be pronounced: but when it is read, it is pronounced Adonai. Therefore, two principal letters of this name, namely י (yod) and ו (vav), are contained in the name ישו (Yeshu). The two ה (he) letters, however, by a great mystery are changed into ש (shin): For the more secret theologians say that the supreme creator God produced all spiritual things through a certain force signified in the first ה (he): and corporeal things through the power signified in the second ה (he). And since all things were made through the incarnate Word, who is named Jesus, the virtues, or properties themselves, signified by those two ה (he)s, are included in Him. But because Jesus was given, and sent to us as a redeemer, and a guide to true rest, which is eternal life, indeed He became our very rest, therefore in place of those two ה (he)s, which signify the principles of the beginning in the name ישו (Iesu), ש (shin) is placed, which is the beginning of שבת (sabat), and itself signifies what is interpreted as rest. Behold how many and how great mysteries are imported in the three letters of this name ישו (Iesu): For י (yod) signifies divinity, as is most well-known among the theologians themselves; י (yod) the tree of life, and ש (shin) rest: and it is denoted that our Jesus is God, vivifying all with both lives, and finally beatifying in that eternal rest. That quadriliteral name also exists by another mystery in the name of Jesus, through the way, namely, of numbers, with the name of the mother added, from whom He drew the substance of His body: For the four letters of that name yield in number 26. and the name of the mother, which is מרים (Miriam), gives 290. Which number joined with those 26 constitutes 316, which number also the letters of the name ישו (Iesu) give. In which is denoted the named one himself

proceeded from God the Father and a human mother. By this same path of numbers, we conclude that the terrifying name שדי (Shaddai) is contained in Jesus: whose letters in number give 314. To this number, if the binary (two) is added, which signifies corporality, it constitutes 316, which is the number of the letters of the name ישו (Yeshu), as we recently said. To him [Marginal note: David] also was given the power of that name שדי (Shaddai), which was always terrifying to the enemies of the human race. Hence, in Psalm 90, which was made to terrify those enemies, the prophet says: "He shall dwell in the shadow of Shaddai." For which we have: "He shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven." [Marginal note: CHRIST] Therefore, when Christ recognized that the power of that name was contained in his own, he revealed the mystery to the Apostles, saying: "In my name they shall cast out demons," and the other things that follow.

There is also in the name of Jesus this name אל (El), which signifies God; and אלה (Eloah), which is the same as its plural אלהים (Elohim); although sometimes this name is singular and imports a singular God diffused and multiplied in many created things. Hence, in the creation of the world, when God, by diffusing himself into creatures, began to appear manifold, he is introduced as the creator under this name Elohim, with scripture saying: "And Elohim said, and Elohim made, and Elohim created." Which some, not understanding, wrongly translated by saying: "He created Gods." Others, however, join the singular name with a singular verb, saying that by it is understood the Trinity and a plurality of persons. But truly and properly explaining it, by that name Elohim is understood the craftsman diffusing himself into many things, or judging many through multiple ministers executing judgment. Hence, in scripture, sometimes both angels executing God's judgments and judges [Marginal note: Exod.] judging are called Elohim. As we have in Exodus, when thieves and those causing damage are ordered to be brought to Elohim to be judged by them; where we have translated: "Their case shall come before the Gods."

Therefore, not only the virtues of these names—which are to have mercy, to distribute, and to judge—are fitting in our Jesus, but also the mysteries of the letters. If we wished to declare these, I doubt we would proceed further than is permitted to write or speak. Nevertheless, we will touch upon something, even if superficially: In this name ישו (Yeshu), therefore, the first letter is י (Yod), which, when explained in its letters by saying יוד (Yod), signifies a thousand, which attribute we have already declared: to our Solomon, who is peace to himself, and a true peaceful King. But if the number of those three letters is calculated, a great mystery still arises: for י (Yod) gives 80, ל (Lamed) 30, א (Aleph) one. Which numbers, joined together, yield 111, namely a hundred, a ten, and a unit, of which we spoke above. And if attention is paid to the characters of the numbers, a mystery will still be foreseen: for there are three emanating from one character, which imports one, so that it is intimated that the Trinity of persons proceeds from and is contained in one unity, just as also in pronouncing א (Aleph) it is necessary to explain it into those three letters mentioned above. We have, therefore, in יוד (Yod) the mystery of unique deity and trinity. But to this is added ל (Lamed), which signifies 30 in number, that is, three tens, to denote celestial virtue fortified by the most holy Trinity, through which God, as through secondary causes, disposes all lower things. All these things, if found in Christ Jesus,
