Theol.] are elements and humors, mixed in due and harmonic proportions: from whose proper mixture comes health, and from imbalance comes illness. And all, I will not say parts of the body, but portions of the whole man, in one and the same soul vivifying all things, like the strings of instruments, or various melodies, agree in one consonance. And although the life of man may seem multifaceted—vegetative, animal, spiritual, intellectual, or whatever else it may be—yet there is a single principle of life in all. Hence, not without mystery, Scripture says that God, when he gave life to man, breathed into his face the breath, or soul of lives, which the Hebrews call נשמת חיים *nif-mat haiim*: it says "of lives," so that it may be intimated that in that breath, or soul, which was infused, every kind of life was contained, which pertains to the whole man himself.

Concerning that consonance which is between body and soul. Chapter II.

What kind of harmony there is between body and soul, which seem entirely different, the Pythagoreans, principal investigators of consonances, have attempted to conjecture from that most tranquil and sweet union which is observed by all. Among whom, Timaeus Locrus, a distinguished Pythagorean, in his usual manner outlined, saying: "For the soul to be well, the body needs to have its strengths, health, keen senses, vigor, beauty, the beginning of which external beauty is commensurability, which they call symmetry." For the members themselves, and for the soul, nature prepares a dwelling, as an instrument: and it is obedient, as it were, a certain adaptable thing to the principles of living and subjection: to which Proclus agrees in his commentary on Plato's Timaeus, saying: "The soul from the beginning was constituted according to harmonic principles: and every body is said to be joined to it according to proportions: and the whole universe itself is harmonically and fittingly bound together." And whence these harmonic structures arise, he continues, saying: "The principles of these are a force implanted by nature, or by the supreme artificer, so that man may be well-tuned with body and soul." Which Plato also explains quite clearly, while speaking of the soul of both worlds, whose principle is si-

--- Page 813 ---
**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

millima, he says: After the entire constitution of the soul was completed according to the Creator's mind, which is first in intention and in idea, He soon fashioned all that is corporeal within it, and adapting the middle to the middle, He joined it with fitting modulation. For a middle body suits a middle soul, an extreme (body) to an extreme (soul), and a supreme (body) to a supreme (soul): so that the disposition of the body may be adapted to the disposition of the soul, more than the reverse. Which holds true in both ways, since a nobler, a less noble, and a middle soul are found: for which, in this world's machine, a body is temporarily arranged according to the condition of the soul itself to be received. Also in the lesser world (man), the soul is disposed with a threefold difference, just like the body: like the typical ark, which Noah, not without great mystery, built at God's command. For there is a baser virtue of the soul in that lower part of the body which is below the diaphragm, represented by that lower three-storied part of the ark. There is a middle and animalistic power, above the diaphragm itself, up to the head, whose likeness was held by that middle station of the ark, in which the animals resided. There is a supreme and intellectual virtue in the head, denoted by the supreme part of the ark, in which Noah dwelt with his rational family. Of which each soul, or portion of it, with the dwelling in which it resides, is most proportionate. For unless there is a proportion between soul and body, human strength is easily led to dissolution and downfall: as Chalcidius says. [Marginal note: Chal.] The greatest incitement to vices is in the body; and in the concretion of humors and spirits, by whose abundance or deficiency, we are more prone to lust or anger. To these are added the strong danger of life itself to be lived, sickness, reproach, and lack of necessary things, by which occupied, we are led away from honorable studies to things consistent with an instituted life, and we are called without recognition of the true good. What this congruence is, is indeed most recondite, yet it has been somewhat outlined by the wise. Who, investigating the various dispositions of souls, judge that they obtain various fates according to the diversity of the means through which they have passage to us, and that these are joined with bodies proportionate to them. For in a body guided by a Jovian temperament, they believe a soul is infused, tempered by the divine power and intelligence, to which Jupiter responds and obeys. But into a body boiling with Martial impetus and bile, they believe a soul infused by the divine power and intelligence is poured, to which Mars, connected, is at hand. And thus they judge it should be decided concerning others. According to which disposition, if the soul, purified and expiated, operates well, it returns to the divine power, or the dwelling, from which it descended. And since there are many mansions (as Christ testifies) [Marginal note: CHRI- STVS.] in the Father's house, and these indeed are varied, otherwise they would not be many: souls are also varied, not only in gratuitous gifts, but in natural ones, which follow the gratuitous ones, if Gregory [Marginal note: Grego.] thinks rightly, who speaks of angels, and consequently says concerning men: Those who participate in the distribution of gifts, also agree in the disposition of natural things. In which sense are to be understood the words of the Savior saying, that to one were given five talents, to another two, to another one.

talent: or that (as another evangelist says) ten minas were given to ten servants, so that each might work [Marginal note: Luke.] according to the measure granted to him. According to this virtue, he who works receives a reward in proportion to the condition of the talent, or gift granted. But if he neglects to work, the gift is taken away and given to another worker, so that he may complete the place prepared for the influx and the granted gift.
Concerning this return of souls to places proportionate to them, and from which they departed, academics speaking with their [Marginal note: Academics.] Plato say that they return to their planets, perhaps speaking more profoundly than [Marginal note: Plato. / Theologians.] many readers might imagine. Our theologians, however, say that they return to those choirs of angels, to which they lived conformably. But (if I am not mistaken) they return to those supermundane abodes, to which the way and the gate is He who said: I am the way, I am the gate; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved. For through [Marginal note: CHRIST.] Christ, entry is not given to planets or angels, but to God Himself, and the eternal Father: in whose house, and in whose amplitude of divinity, are those many and eternal mansions.

Whence dissonance arises in the body. Chapter III.

[Decorative initial C] The body, though it be most temperate, sometimes feels a most vehement dissonance. We do not doubt that this happens primarily for two reasons. One is a distemperament of the humors, arising either from superfluity, or from diminution, or from intrinsic or extrinsic alteration. The other is that it is at odds with celestial influences, so that influences otherwise good, harm it. It is at odds, indeed, when the soul deviates from what the celestial influx requires. Many other disorders follow this disarrangement, because the dissenting [soul/person] is immediately subjected to an evil demon (says Proculus) [Marginal note: Proculus.] until it is purified by due expiations. What the distemperaments of the humors are, since this is the concern of physicians, leaving to them what is theirs, we will run through those things which pertain to our subject, and to the proper institution of a better human being.
For the humors are distempered, whence infirmities arise, not only from superfluous, diminished, or altered matter, but more often because the body is badly governed by the soul. For if it is fed with superfluous food, whence superfluous humors are generated, is this not the fault of the soul not curbing gluttony? And if harmful foods are eaten, is not the imprudence of the soul to be blamed? And if there is superfluous labor, whence weariness and various alteration of the humors, is not our ignorance to be blamed? And if a person commits something whence sadness arises, and black bile increases, by which the humors are infected, or if he grieves and is saddened more than is fitting about events, so that bile boils over, or melancholy is suppressed, is this not from a soul that is ill-disposed, which is absorbed by Aristotelian sadness, which corrupts the power of the one possessing it? But if the soul, like a leader in the entire human army, agreeing with the emperor or king, well moderates all lower appetites and forces, directing all against due enemies: if some sadness is brought back from battle or labor, that is evangelical, not harmful, but one that will immediately be turned into joy. For as to those who love God (as Paul says) all things co- [Marginal note: Paul] VV

--- Page 815 ---
**THIRD CANTICLE**

...operate for good, so to those dissenting from God, all things harm, all things turn to evil: because against such disobedient ones, every creature arms itself, namely for the vengeance of God's enemies: as it is said in the Book of Wisdom. Hence [Marginal note: Auguſt.] Augustine says: The cause of all evils is sin: which is a disorder and distemper of the soul, and of the human leader. When it rules badly, or is overthrown, all things rebel and become distempered, to the destruction of its own dominion. For then the animal spirits, having lost their bridle, rush into battle; evil humors arise, and even good ones, disordered, separated from each other by a certain alternation, vex and torment the body. Then celestial influences are harmful, just as the light of the sun to eyes poorly disposed. Then God's lictors, even they prepare themselves to torment [Marginal note: Dauid] men, according to that of the prophet: "And He sent forth plagues through evil angels," or (as the truth of the letter has it) "He sent distress through evil angels." Then (as [Marginal note: Iſaias.] Isaiah says) "The Lord will strike you with corrupted air." Knowing this, the royal pro- [Marginal note: Dauid] phet said: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, for all my bones are troubled," that is, my strengths and my virtues. And whence the strengths are troubled, and infirmity has arisen, he declares by adding: "And my soul is greatly troubled." Which (the soul) also sometimes becomes weak, so that it says: "Heal my soul, for I have sinned against You." From whose infirmity and rebellion, follows the rebellion and distemper of all things that ought to obey it. Nor should you say: "The good are often vexed more than the evil," because no one is vexed in that which he is good, but in that which he is evil. For take away the evil to be punished, the vexation will cease, because the mercy of God is over all His works. But the justice of God is over all evil works: which are not of God, but of man, or of the devil, or of both together. And just as there is no man who does not sin: so there is no man who does not need purification, and who is not subject to punitive justice. Therefore, man is purged by this momentary distress, so that he may flee the eternal: which is inflicted upon those who, having become children of the devil and completely separated from God's family, are handed over to that fire and torment which is prepared for the devil and his angels. Nor should anyone say that infirmities arise from those six natural causes which Avi- [Marginal note: Auicen.] cenna enumerates, namely inanition, repletion of food, or infected air, sleep, wakefulness, exercise: but most especially from accidents of the soul, namely anger, sadness, joy, and similar things: because all these (if one pays close attention) depend on and are governed by the soul, since it is in its power to give or withhold food from the body, to wake and sleep, and to exercise the body at will. For a wise person can admit or repel anger, sadness, and similar accidents of the soul, which are (as he says) the most powerful cause of the body's temperament and distemper, not only in oneself, but in others: asserting that a soul strongly elevated and inflamed by vehement imagination changes health or sickness even in the bodies of others. Nor should anyone blame complexion: because (as Ecclesiastes says) "God made man upright and most temperate:" namely, as to body and soul. But he himself has entangled himself in infinite questions, or (as the truth of the letter has it) "He sought out many thoughts." Whence, not content with the uprightness and perfect state in which the Creator had placed him, he wandered about many things,

We also see that proportionate things are very beneficial, while disproportionate things are harmful: so that we are compelled to believe that a harmonious force contributes much. Also beneficial for the temperament of the body, and consequently of the soul, are proper exercises and joyful and honorable occupations. Which Macrobius, explaining in 'On Scipio's Dream', says: "We say that souls have fallen from heaven into bodies, and that this is perfect wisdom of the soul, that while it uses the body, it recognizes whence it originated."
For thus all right-thinking people wish that that knowledge be sought, through which, with impediments excluded, the straight path to God may be taken.
Hence they judged that the oracle emanated from heaven rather than from a demon, as the Satirist sings: "From heaven descended 'know thyself'." [marginal note: Juvenal]
Indeed, from heaven and from the Holy Spirit sprang forth the teaching, as we have said: although it was uttered by a demon through the oracle to the Greeks.

For all things that are in the body receive nourishment from the heart, and the force of life and motion, which passes from the heart to the brain, which is lunar, and thence is diffused to all members of the body through veins and nerves descending from it. Therefore, following the Platonists, [Marginal note: Plato.] who agree in common opinion that the world is an animal, more one than anything else whatsoever, we say that the universal and particular members are connected in the same way, and are equal, and very similar, in influx, and mutual communication, in motion, quality, and every kind of correspondence. For it influences in both cases, especially the principal member, which is the sun in the mundane animal, and the heart in the particular. And the other superior members of both influence the inferior ones, according to the disposition of those receiving. Which is both inborn by nature, and is aided by the helps of prudence and art. But this, which is acquired by industry, even if slight, suffices for receiving the gifts of heaven, therefore not to be despised, since it contributes much both to the natural disposition, that it may be full, and to the disposing soul, since it itself favors by disposing, just as the celestial influences. And although man receives favor from the whole heaven, yet he draws most especially from the heart of heaven, which is the sun, since man is solar (as Arab astronomers say) [Marginal note: Arabes] and adorned with a certain peculiar gift of both suns, namely the celestial and the supermundane, as we gather from the theology of the Hebrews. Behold then, how you can receive favor from God, from His ministering angels, and from the heavens, His instruments. Now, learn how you may do this by a short and easy path.

By what short way we can draw favor from heaven, angels, and God. Chapter IX.

[Decorative initial 'E' within a square frame depicting a landscape with a celestial sphere or sun above] It would certainly be a long, arduous, and overly doubtful journey, if we wished to hunt for all the stars, and their influences, and favorable aspects, and through them to know who or what kind our guardian or genius is: since the professors of that doctrine have handed down long, very difficult, doubtful, and sometimes conflicting precepts. For Porphyry [Marginal note: Porphy.] seeks the genius from the planet ruling the nativity. Firmicus also [Marginal note: Iul. Fir.] seeks it either from there, or from him who has more dignities there: or from him whose domicile the moon is immediately about to enter, after the sign which it holds at the birth of a person. The Chaldeans [Marginal note: Chaldęi] rather auspicate the genius from the sun or from the moon. Others teach to seek it from some cardinal point of the heavens. And thus the professors of this doctrine wander through many things: either because they have not fully known the sacraments and order of the heavens: or because they have not wished to reveal and make common those things which are to be communicated among a few wise men. Since therefore that path, long and most hidden

--- Page 827 ---
**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

...is, a short journey must be undertaken, by inquiring of ourselves what we cannot do from the heavens. Indeed, we will do this if, with obstacles removed, we submit ourselves to our guiding spirit, who, if we do not resist, will show us the way to heaven, to our genius, indeed to where the supreme moderator leads. And this, if we pay attention to those things which, undisturbed by any corruptions from our earliest age, it suggests to us, or what, with a mind purified from vain care and perverse affection, we feel, imagine, imitate, and attempt more frequently, nature itself or the spirit dictating.

For nature feels: and our spirit feels the instinct and favor of heaven: it also feels the persuasions of its own genius: which is given to each person from the beginning of their birth: [Marginal note: Plato.] as not only the Platonists assert along with [Marginal note: Our Teachers (CHRIST).] our teachers, but infallible Truth openly declares in speech, when it says: "Their angels always see the face of the Father." For these (angels) favor their clients, leading them to where their star also inclines. Always indeed to good: unless man, deceived by these allurements, or by the persuasions of an evil demon, deviates from his path. For he who walks astray truly has no guide for his journey: because it is the duty of the stars and our guardians always to act rightly: and to dispose us towards what is right and more excellent. Therefore, assenting to the persuasions of heaven, and of one's genius, or proper angel (to speak catholically), one will act prosperously and live happily. Otherwise, one will feel heaven and the powers above to be hostile: and adverse fortune (which is the guidance of the divine ones) in all things to be done, having become estranged from the celestial patrons. To which perhaps [Marginal note: Zoroaster.] that adage refers: "Do nothing against Minerva's will." And thus (as Zoroaster teaches) fate is not to be increased, much less changed. For if you undertake something by your own will, against your genius and the continually inviting voice of the celestial beings: you will labor in vain, as [Marginal note: David] the prophet says: "Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain. And unless the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it." For it is vain for us to rise by ourselves, either before, or against the light that shines from heaven: and leads, and guides man, where he ought to go. Therefore, for those seeking a propitious omen for things to be done, it must be observed with all diligence: that we listen to what God speaks within us: or in His holy scripture and law: what the good guardian persuades, what the spirit suggests, and to what the star is favorable. Attention must also be paid to where they lead you. For place contributes much, because not without [Marginal note: GOD] reason did God, or the good guardian in His stead and name, say to Abraham: "Go to the land which I will show you, and I will make you into a great nation: and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name": where it is clearly understood how much place contributes to favor. And a little later it follows: "Abraham went forth, going and further advancing, or progressing towards the south." There he felt the most ample supercelestial favor: just as [Marginal note: Isaac.] Isaac in the north, of whom it is said: "Isaac came to Gerar, where he sowed, and reaped a hundredfold": or "a hundred measures of barley": as the literal truth has it. And the man became rich: and became very wealthy. Jerome seeks the mystery of this matter, but does not solve it: perhaps unwilling to reveal to the unworthy common people what place accomplishes, what barley signifies, by which Isaac so greatly prospered and grew, that

How much also the change of garments avails we can learn from the same scripture, which commands that priests and ministers of God, about to perform sacred rites, should be clothed in certain suitable and there determined garments. In like manner, how much the foods to be taken avail, we are instructed by the same [scripture]: which with the greatest diligence teaches its initiates from which foods they should abstain, and which they should admit. Whoever, therefore, has known his place, work, profession, star, genius, and spirit, possesses the surest pledge of his progress and happiness.

How man, a small world, can receive support from all members of the greater world (to which he is most similar). Chapter X.

[Decorative initial N] Nor only from heaven, angels, and intelligences, but from any member of the mundane body, we receive no small favor and protection. For man is divided by some wise men into five parts: into the intellectual, the rational, the irascible, the appetitive, and the senses, with all their instruments. The intellect, placed in the highest citadel, alone intimate with the supreme prince, draws from him what neither reason nor the senses can draw: since God himself and his ministers are not subject to the judgment of our senses, unless insofar as they themselves wish to be shown through sensible images, by their own will. Nor are they perceived by reason, except the movers of the spheres through their motion: as [Marginal note: Aristor.] Aristotle and other natural philosophers investigate. Much less is God perceived by sense or reason, except only His being. But if we perceive any secrets concerning God and his [Marginal note: Plato.] ministers, we do so by that supreme portion which the Platonists call intellect, distinct from reason. And this, by means of a certain divine light, by which [Marginal note: Dauid] the intellect itself, or that superior portion, is infused. Concerning which light the prophet says: 'In your light, we shall see light.' The rational [part], however, also placed on a higher throne, midway between the intellect and imagination, receives increase from all things about which it discourses: it is expanded by celestial, terrestrial, and human things, and especially by the presence of man, and is sharpened like iron by iron, as is the common adage. The irascible [part], dwelling in the abode of the heart, does not much need external favor, being sufficiently inflamed by the heart itself and bile, unless insofar as it externally receives the object at which it is angry. The appetitive faculty (Cupido), however, is twofold: one in the heart, which, supported by reason, is carried towards all things about which reason discourses: and from these very things, from which it is expanded and increased, it receives. But most especially from the supreme object of love, God: provided that it is led to Him through the intellect, illuminated by His light. The other, bound in the lower seats, and far removed from wisdom and reason, is constituted: lest

--- Page 830 ---
TOMVS PRIMVS. 345

troublesome proximity would disturb reason and all higher things. He receives so much increase of a true human from things, as much as he is obedient to and bound by the higher things themselves. But the means by which the higher appetite is fostered are institutions and teachings, which are contained in right laws and doctrines, especially in sacred writings, where all things are contained which pertain to directing and cultivating him. There are also sacred rites, by which he is purified, so that he may grow stronger. Finally, the senses, as ministers of reason and will, receive from all sensible things that by which they may delight, and may favor their protectors. For hearing, a participant of air, and an organ of those things which cannot be apprehended by other senses, a most accurate organ, and a magnificent minister of higher things, serves for acquiring wisdom, before all other senses. For it measures the rhythms of speech and all harmony, and the modes of things and of all discourse; from which it can itself become a modulator, and a musician, and semi-rational, since it alone among the senses perceives the discourses of reason. Also from composite and artificial instruments, and from the harmony of the world, which it perceives with better hearing, it receives wonderful delights and instructions, from which man composes himself, as the Platonists and Pythagoreans assert. With the eyes also it measures the sky, the most harmonious circuits of stars and constellations, their settings and risings, the most beautiful picture of the earth, the fertility of waters, and the composition of all visible things; from which the most abundant fount of philosophy is imbibed, from which one arrives at higher wisdom. No less nourishment for both aspects of man is gathered from there than doctrine. But between the eyes and ears, nature has placed the nostrils in the middle region of the face, by whose harmony odor passes with breath. These, receiving solace from well-smelling and well-composed things, also provide no small gain to man. The mouth also, in the middle of the face, fortified with teeth, palate, and tongue, bestows manifold profit upon man. For it receives all bodily nourishments, to be brought into the belly, as into a kind of storehouse, and into the whole body. But first they are committed to the judgment of the palate, so that it may reject harmful things and admit beneficial ones. And these the teeth chew, so that the food, now ground, may be presented to the cauldron of the stomach, easily to be digested. For the turning over of which food, the tongue is given, which also serves the spirit and soul no less than the body, bringing forth in speech what prudence and the heart conceive: so that it may both bestow benefit upon one's neighbor, and receive advantages from the same, indeed from higher beings, and from God himself, and acquire much wisdom through discussion. What therefore remains in the whole machine, from which man does not receive benefit through ears, eyes, nostrils, mouth, tongue, or mind? For nothing escapes but is subjected to the judgment of one of them. For those things which reject touch, sight, smell, and taste, are at least perceived by the ears and handled by the tongue: since these (tongues) can speak of all things, and those (ears) can hear of all things, whether sensible or intellectual. Hence hearing is the sense serving the intellect before all others, and its peculiar minister. After which are three other senses, placed in the royal court of the head, in the sight of reason: so that by its balance, all their judgment may be weighed. Touch

[Marginal note: Mercur.] For Mercurius proposed these things to his son Tatius for consideration, saying: "Note this, my son, that each genus of living beings inhabits its own province of the world. Wet creatures, indeed, inhabit water: terrestrial creatures, earth: winged creatures, air: but man uses all of these, earth, water, air, fire, and whatever is contained in them. [Marginal notes: Simplicius, Thomas] Nor does the opinion of Simplicius and Thomas please, that the statement should be understood only of artificial things, and that it made us the end only of artificial things, and not of others. [Marginal note: Aristotle] For he himself, explaining himself at the beginning of the Politics, says: "It is to be considered that plants exist for the sake of animals, and animals themselves for the sake of man: for domestic animals, that is, tame animals, which the Hebrews call בהמות *behemot*, are for use and sustenance: and wild animals, even if not all, yet most are held for our sustenance and convenience: from which clothes and many other things are supplied." And if nature makes nothing either imperfect or in vain, there is no one who does not know that these things were made for the sake of man. And although Aristotle himself would not admit that the heavens were made for man, since he prefers them to man in the Ethics: [Marginal note: Idem] nevertheless, as much as we can learn from sacred scripture, and from those who think correctly, they themselves were created for the service of man: granted that they receive God's influence more immediately. For they influence lower things, so that they may favor man without other mediation: or plants and animals, which are already conceded to be ordered for the service of man. Therefore, man receives increments of his progress from all things, provided he knows how to use all things and to dominate all things: just as it was instilled in him by the Creator, as we shall discuss in its proper place (with God himself favoring).

On the soul's agreement with itself. Chapter XI.

[Decorative initial N] And so that the soul may not dissent from anything, but receive sustenance from all things, [Marginal note: Origen] agreement with itself is necessary. For just as we feel (says Origen) the torment of immense pain, when the members of the body are dissolved, and torn apart from their mutual connections: so it is when the soul is found outside the order and connection by which it was created by God for harmony, for acting well, and for perceiving usefully. Whence, with the connection of rational movements dissolved, it inflicts punishment and torment upon itself. And the punishment for this disorder, all senses and all members, deprived or disordered

And the inventor of medicine is celebrated, not only of the body, but also of the soul. But the truer and super-mundane Apollo accomplishes this much better, resounding with a superior harmony, to which this artificial or natural harmony is far inferior, and even a dark image. For he himself provided and taught to give perfect health and balance to both parts of man, through those things which the experienced and wisest physician judged suitable for our infirmity and for tempering all parts: so much so, that all effort can be considered vain by which another doctrine or way, or rule, is determined or devised for instructing and perfecting the human race, than that which was delivered as most perfect by Christ.

But just as in healing bodies, harmony contributes so much, that not only natural, but also vocal harmony has brought healing, [Marginal note: Democ. Theoph. Pythag. Emped. Asclepia. Dauid Boëtius Terpan. Hisme,] as Democritus and Theophrastus seem to affirm; and Pythagoras and Empedocles, together with Asclepiades, demonstrate with words; which David and others proved by their deeds. For he cured Saul, raging with an evil spirit, with song and lyre. And as Boethius relates, Terpander and Arion of Methymna rescued the Lesbians and Ionians, afflicted with very severe diseases, by the aid of song. Hismenias the Theban is said to have wiped away all troubles by his melody for very many Boeotians whom the torments of sciatic pain afflicted. Many others also are recounted as healed by sensible harmony, [Marginal note: Boëtius] both by Boethius himself and by others. Therefore, natural harmony ought rightly to do this, being certainly stronger and more excellent than artificial harmony.

That (natural harmony) consists in the proportion and tempering of medicines to each other, and with the qualities of the body to which they are administered. Therefore, medicines ought to be tempered to each other and with the body, if they are to bring alleviation and the balance of health. [Marginal note: Demasc. Antiqui.] Hence, it was the most diligent care of Damascenus and other ancients who treat of such matters, in proportioning and tempering medicines, assigning in their mixture just and harmonious weights, leaving to the physicians administering them the care of proportioning them to the bodies they intend to heal. Which many ignorant people in this age, despising (this care), too often inflict such dissonance upon the internal organs: so that they shudder, grieve, and are tormented by the dissonance of the medicine, when a consonant temperament and health should have been brought about.

Nor otherwise ought virtues, which are the medicines of the soul, to be tempered among themselves and with the soul, if they are to bring health and delight to the soul itself. [Marginal note: Theolo. Thomas Henricus Scotus.] Our theologians dispute at length about the connection and structure of virtues: namely Thomas, Henry, John Scotus, and others. Since this connection cannot be made without harmonic agreement, setting aside whatever they may have thought about the connection of all or some particular ones, we will speak of our harmonic agreement. [Marginal note: Boëtius.] For just as vocal harmony (as Boethius defines it) is the concord of equal and unequal voices reduced to one, so the harmony perfecting the soul is the consensus of equal and unequal virtues reduced to one. For unequal virtues are liberality and faith, Frugality and hope, contemplation and the diligent work of charity in frequent ministry, and many of this kind. Which nevertheless all

But that into which all must converge is charity, and the love of God and neighbor: in which, as in the root, foundation, life, and soul of all virtues, all things contained in the law and the prophets are founded and depend: as the highest Truth teaches.
Which Paul also admonishes with an open voice, saying: "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and if I have faith so as to move mountains, and prophecy, and piety in distributing my goods, and all other virtues: but if I do not have charity (into which, namely, all other virtues must converge), I am nothing but a clanging cymbal, for the utility, namely, and delight of others."

But it profits me nothing, like a cymbal, which gains no advantage for itself from its sound, but rather is consumed and worn out, although it may soothe the ears of listeners.

Indeed, there is no progress in virtues, unless it is strengthened in the root and foundation of charity.

Nor is there delight, unless all converge into one, which Plato in the Epinomis calls piety, but our Paul and his teacher Christ call charity.
And although that common thing, into which all virtues must converge, Plato himself in the Republic (whom Macrobius follows, and Ambrose also, and Lactantius) seems to assert to be justice, and (as others say) temperance, which imposes measure on all virtues: nevertheless, these do not contradict what has been said about charity.

VOLUME ONE. 348

you can, do not despise [them]. In these matters, no rule can be given by which each person may measure where they have felt an easier progress of the soul. To which [progress] one arrives through that threefold kind of virtues, first described by Plotinus and most celebrated by all wise men [Marginal note: Plotin.], namely, political, purgative, and heroic. To these is added the exemplary [virtue], but this is not properly in us, but rather like a rule guiding and measuring the virtues that are in us. Therefore, that threefold kind [of virtues] brings about in us the most perfect harmony of virtues. For the political [virtue] is like the hypate, or proslambanomenos in an instrument, or a deeper and lower voice in song. The heroic [virtue] is like the nete hyperboleum, or a raised and highest voice. And the purgative kind is like the mese, that is, the middle string in an instrument, or the middle voices in song. And (as musicians teach) from proslambanomenos to mese is a diapason, and from there to nete hyperboleum, another diapason: and in both cases, perfect harmony. Thus, a person ascending from civil virtues is elevated to purgative ones, as if by the first diapasonic harmony; but carried from purgative to heroic virtues, another diapason brings about indeed the most consummate harmony. And how virtues make the soul harmonious, Plotinus, deservedly the foremost among philosophers of this doctrine [Marginal note: Idem.], explains quite clearly, saying: In man, two motions occur, disturbing the soul: Some, indeed, are certain unconsidered animal impulses, whether they are inciting or terrifying. The others, however, are when we deliberately and intentionally pursue those motions. Therefore, civil virtues temper these second motions with prudence and deliberation: so that one does not admit that which reason judges to be evil. Introducing this temperament, they begin to harmonize the soul. But purgative [virtues] not only curb those motions, but extirpate and eradicate them: and they so suppress the primary motions that the mere presence of reason, namely the mistress of the appetites, suffices to suppress them. These purgative virtues, when they have entirely freed the soul from those disturbances, render the instrument of the soul most temperate, so that nothing remains but to undertake a harmonious and excellent song and work. When the soul accomplishes this, applying itself to the greatest advancements, it becomes a hero. Again, political virtues compose our animal nature, or the outer man. Purgative [virtues], as if through the first diapason, purify the spirit and render it harmonious, so that man is called spiritual, and is so. But heroic [virtues] elevate the mind to the supreme harmony: uniting man with intelligences, indeed with God himself. To this Aristotle agrees [Marginal note: Ariſto.], saying that men are made Gods through excellence of virtue. But our Plotinus continues [Marginal note: Ploti.], saying that the aim and vow of the Heroic is not only to be free from sin, but to be God, and to return whence it proceeded: just as He who said: "I came forth from the Father and have come into the world; again, I leave the world and go to the [Marginal note: CHRISTUS.] Father [Marginal note: John.]." And since we are His brothers, having proceeded from the same Father, we must return to the same [Father]: though at a lower degree. But when we return whence we came, we complete a perfect diapason: in which the tone returns to the same [note] from which it had departed: although with a different key, as musicians say. So also we have emanated—

...ted from God, as from a productive principle: and we return to the same, but for another reason, namely, the beatifying end. Therefore, man (to follow the proposition from the mind of Plotinus), if he admits something erroneous, merely by inadvertence, following those first impulses, is a dual being, God and demon, since even demons, that is, wise intelligences (as the Platonists say) are touched by certain affections. And these are they, of whom Chrysostom says: "And if they are saints, nevertheless they are men: and if they cannot be overcome by evil, nevertheless they can be struck." But if man feels nothing of the first impulses, while he is thus, he is God alone. God, I say, from the number of those who follow the first, namely, the sons of God, of whom John says: "He gave them power to become sons of God." But Plotinus, progressing further, elevates men even to exemplary virtues, which he says are twofold. Some, indeed, are in the intellect: others, however, are in the soul. In the intellect, however, (the same author says) they are not properly virtues, but exemplars of virtues. In the soul, however, which is (as he teaches elsewhere) the proper form of man, they are properly virtues. For in the intellect they are, as it were, in God, and therefore they are called exemplars. For in God, and in the intellect, which is a certain divine thing infused in us, are the actions of that which is. In the soul, however, are perfecting virtues. For there, justice, temperance, and similar things are not properly virtues, but directing rules: which, while they are in the soul, are properly virtues. For there, justice is the conversion of one to oneself, namely, and nothing diverse from that in which it is. In the soul, however, it is directing itself to God. Temperance also is there the intimate conversion of the intellect to itself, as far as is fitting. But in the soul it is tempering its passions. Fortitude there is entirely constituted outside passion, prevailing in all things. In the soul, however, it is a participant in passion, by the likeness of that from which it received. Prudence there is a full contemplation, moderating all things. Here, however, it is a habit acquired from many experiences. There is charity (so that we may also discuss our theological virtues), a love and affection embracing all things, and pervading all things with their fitting degrees: In the soul it is a gift distributed, through parts, and parts. And that which is faith instructing in the soul, and a knowledge of certain things granted by divine light, from which a solid argument of non-apparent truths is made, in the intellect is the most certain knowledge of divine and all things. And those things which the soul holds by hope, the intellect (the same author says) possesses by firm apprehension. The soul also tends towards that which the intellect attains by contact. For the intellect (says Plotinus himself) has by a certain touch that which the soul desires and hopes for. And lest Plotinus seem to have dreamed here, let us hear what our John, who had ascended that degree, testifies. "What we have heard (he says) and seen, and touched concerning the word of life, this we announce to you." But he touches divine things who proves them by a certain experience, or by the higher part (which Plotinus calls intellect) adheres to God, leaning on Him and united by a certain contiguity. "We touch (says Proclus) the divine essence, and inclined towards it, we lean on the supreme head of the soul." And Paul says: "He who adheres to God becomes one spirit with Him." Which unity of spirit follows the union of the intellect itself.

After we have investigated the soul's harmony with the body, of which it is the form, and with the virtues, of which it is the subject, we must see what agreement it has with all things that it understands. For this purpose, I judge it opportune to see what the soul is, which has such a proportion with so many things that it can understand all of them. And omitting many opinions about it that we brought forward in the first volume, we will see what it is, as far as this faculty of understanding is concerned.

Aristote. Where indeed that very common definition given by Aristotle by no means satisfies me, that the soul is the actuality of a physical, organic body having life potentially. Because this only explains that the soul is the mover of the body itself, nor from it do we have how it can understand all things. Nor is another definition sufficient, which he himself handed down, saying, The soul is the principle of sensing, understanding, and moving according to place. Because from this we only have that it is the principle of understanding, but not how it understands all things.

Idem. Nor is it surprising if it failed, since knowledge about the soul (by his own testimony) is among the most difficult things. Which we do not doubt was drawn from Plato: who says in the tenth book of the Laws: "What kind of soul it is, and what power it has, almost everyone seems to have been ignorant of." Nevertheless, here, he handed down that doctrine about the soul itself, from which we can more easily investigate its symbol and proportion with all things. But because he himself did not wish to speak in plain language about the business of the soul, which he considered most difficult and almost hidden from everyone: hence his disciples defined it in various ways, as we brought forward in the same place.

Proculus And although Proclus rejects many who have tried to explain Plato's mind concerning the soul, neither did he himself wish to reveal what Plato thought. But (unless I am mistaken) he left it to readers to infer from many things, as the more recondite Theologians are accustomed to do in any arduous matters:

Theolo. whose footsteps and doctrine, no doubt, Plato followed.

Plato From him, therefore, we can hunt for this about the soul: that it is a certain divine substance, emanating from divine sources, bringing with it number, not indeed that divine number by which the Creator arranged all things, but a rational number: by which, having proportion with all things, it can understand all things.

Pythag. Nor should it disturb anyone that we have said the soul is something divine and emanates from divine sources: since Pythagoras, the father of philosophers, also asserted this, saying in golden words: "Be confident, for a divine race is inherent in humans."

Paulus. And what is more, Paul in the Acts of the Apostles adduces and approves the saying of Aratus, in which he says: "For we are indeed his offspring." Therefore, since we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold, or silver, or stone, the sculpture of art, and human industry. Behold how clearly he concedes that the human race is divine. And this is in part from that higher portion, which the Platonists always venerate as divine. Nu-

TOMVS SECVNDVS. 350

But that very number, by which the soul exists, Aristoxenus and Xenocrates said to be self-moving. [Aristox: Xenocr.] And this, because the soul itself is the principle of the body's motion (as Aristotle proves) and also of its own motion; although here, he [Aristotle] seems to attack both this opinion and equally all who say the soul is a number. And I believe Aristotle [Aristote.] did this rather to take up a subject for discussion than to destroy the truth. This is especially true, since they speak of a rational and formal number, but he speaks of a material and vocal number of merchants. And they speak of motion that belongs to the soul, but he speaks of the motion of the body, acquiring place through the succession of part and part. Hence, Aristotle's entire argument is equivocal in both respects. For from the doctrine of Augustine, which all theologians [August. Theolo.] revere, the soul, free will, or the will, which is the power of the soul itself, moves itself to whatever it wills. Nothing is (he says) so much in the power of the will as the will itself. Which [the will], also according to their common opinion, can command the intellect to understand, and itself, to will or not to will, carrying itself into whatever it chooses. Which motion, although it is not divisible according to parts (as Aristotle presupposes), is nevertheless a true change and motion, of which those speak who say it moves itself. And this motion is also of angels and intelligences, concerning whom Job [Iob.] says: "Behold, those who serve him are not stable, or are not faithful; and in his angels he placed change" (as the literal truth has it, for which we erroneously have "he found perversity"). The soul also moves while it moves the body, which if it did not do, Aristotle [Aristote.] could not, as a physicist, treat of it by that which he presupposes in physics, saying: "Whatever moves while moving, is placed under physical consideration; but whatever does not move while moving, does not pertain to physical speculation." But since he himself, as a physicist, treats of the soul moving the body, therefore, from his doctrine, the soul is moved by moving. Which motion, even if it is called accidental, is nevertheless a true motion, since it has the principle of motion in itself and is not moved by another. Nor do the reasons restrict, by which he strives to prove that the soul is neither a number nor a harmony, since they are founded in material numbers, without doubt, and sensible ones; and the soul is from formal numbers and harmony, extracted from the senses, from which Aristotle [Idem], unwilling to learn, does not want to admit it into his sensible doctrine. Nor is there (he says) in the soul a harmonic ratio of things composed together, because the soul itself does not have parts from which it might be composed. We grant this: But we say that there is a superior and rational harmony, having the species of things within itself, by which it understands them, and the numbers of things, by which it numbers them. Which numbers and species, indeed, are not merely adventitious and newly acquired, but are connatural to the soul itself, existing in it with a certain better quality than in themselves; just as all agree concerning exemplars or ideas: that they have a more perfect being in God producing and understanding, than in their proper genus; as John [Ioan.] says: "That which was made, in him was life." Life, indeed, creative and divine.

could have been made. No one, certainly, will teach it. And if anyone wished to correct something, they would either make it worse, or desire that which could not be made, or which is not fitting. Therefore, all parts of the world are so constituted that they could not be made better for use, nor more beautiful in appearance. So also individuals are distributed within the breadth of their species with a certain unequal equality and harmonious variety, especially human ones: each of which, and all together, bear the image of the mundane body. To these, therefore, differing by nature, various gifts have been assigned, to each according to their own virtue and disposition: To whom also rewards are given according to their works, yet by a geometric proportion, which is not concerned with number, but with the proportion of proportions: so that the proportion of gifts to gifts, and merits to merits, is the same as the proportion of rewards to rewards. And by this proportion not only does God give rewards to all, but also the civil Republic is governed: as Plato, Iamblichus, and Proclus write. [Marginal note: Plato Iambli. Procul.] Moreover, they add that for a Republic to be well governed, an arithmetic proportion is also necessary: by which, as by a certain justice moderating things, peace may be preserved. Nor is the Musical proportion lacking, which is a justice assigning a greater ratio to the greater, and a lesser to the lesser, as Proclus says. [Marginal note: Idem.] And this [musical proportion] is founded on both, taking from arithmetic, whence it equates number to number: from geometric, whence it compares proportion to proportion. From all these proportions (as we said in the first volume) this harmonious machine of the world is constructed. Therefore, it is ruled and ordered by the same, not only by those who hold the image of the supreme ruler, but by the supreme Moderator Himself: Who fashioned the human race with the same proportions: which holds the likeness of God Himself, and of this great machine. Just as therefore in this whole immense work there are unequal and equal degrees of things, from which all those proportions result, so in the human Republic there are equal and unequal degrees and ratios of individuals, from which, and likewise from their gifts and operations, all those proportions result: so that both the mundane and human republic may be harmonious and conformable.

Whether from the fact that He distributed mortals from the beginning in unequal degrees, and pursues them with various gifts and rewards, the Creator is to be considered a respecter of persons. Chapter IIII.

And since from that which appears to be an unequal distribution, people (especially superficial scholars) are accustomed to doubt whether the distributor is therefore to be considered a respecter of persons, giving greater gifts to one than to another. From this point, we have decided to address all doubts, first with the opinions of the Fathers, and then with reasons. And again in the Apostolic Acts he gives thanks to God, when he most certainly proved that there is no acceptance of persons with Him. For an acceptor of persons (as [Marginal note: Theologians] our Theologians teach) is one who, for some reason, owes to others, and when merits and offenses are equal, does not render equal rewards, or equal punishments. For a judge appointed to administer justice, having found two equally guilty of homicide, if he orders one of them to pay the penalty for his guilt, but absolves the other either entirely, or somewhat, from the due punishment, he is rightly called, and is, an acceptor of persons. No differently if he has two equally well-deserving of the Republic, and renders rewards to one according to his works, but to the other, by no means. Hence, when Peter [Marginal note: Peter.] saw that He had care for saving Cornelius the Gentile just as for the Jews, he said: "Now I have truly understood that God shows no partiality." But if a covenant had been made concerning rewarding each one according to their works, if He were to fall short in anything, He could be accused of partiality. But if He bestows something beyond what was promised out of His liberality, He incurs no mark of partiality.

For a living stone has been laid in Zion: "Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame, nor will he be a slave, but free:" by which liberty Christ himself freed us. He also willed to harden the heart of Pharaoh and the Egyptians: so that he might show his power in them: but when the Messiah came, he so softened those Egyptians that all their deserts were filled with monks serving Christ himself. Or let us say, that he hardens no otherwise than as clay is hardened by its own disposition by that sun which melts wax. For the same God [Marginal note: August.] (as Augustine argues in a long series) diffused the rays of his justice upon two kings and peoples, the Chaldean and the Egyptian. But the heart of the Babylonian was softened by the same sun, while that of the Egyptian was hardened. God daily softens the heart of him who hears his voice: but hardens and dries up that of him who disobeys, as the apostle himself testifies elsewhere. "But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, [Marginal note: Paul.] you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God." If anyone, therefore, is hardened, it does not happen without his own fault, for God sends his rays into us, so that by warming he may soften, but if anyone, being hardened, resists, he is hardened still more. He wills therefore to warm, but if hardness follows, it happens because the one receiving that warmth abuses it, just as some have abused the benefit of redemption, and it turned into ruin for them: which for others, well-disposed, was and is for the benefit of resurrection. For thus it happens to the sick who refuse to take medicine, or who take it without proper regimen: that the illness is aggravated, not indeed by the fault of the physician, but by the fault of the sick person himself: thus it happens to those who abuse God's benefit. But still we are pressed when considering with what pious and paternal care it has come to pass that some are born among the Hebrews, among whom was the learning of the divine law, or are born among Christians instructed in evangelical doctrine.         How the soul is bare in its origin, or appears so. Chapter VI.

**GOD.** All souls (says the heavenly Father and giver of all forms) are mine, and indeed begotten by me, and diffused into bodies.
**Wise Man.** As for birth, however, I am indeed (says the wise man) a mortal man, similar to all, conceived from the seed of man, and the fitting delight of the flesh. By what means we may attain the degree of knowledge prepared for us. Chapter IX.

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.5; vertical-align: -0.2em;">N</span>E lest anyone labor in vain about many things in order to reach that very degree of knowledge to which he can attain according to his own disposition, we will go to the supreme master of all wisdom and doctrine, Christ Jesus, and we will see from where he drew his doctrine. "My doctrine," he says, "is not mine, but of the Father who sent me." And making his disciples participants in this instruction, he says: "All things whatsoever I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you," that is, according to your capacity. For he reserved many things which, although they had been baptized and washed with the water of saving wisdom, yet they could neither grasp nor bear then, because not yet well cleansed and strengthened, they were offended by the superior light. Therefore he says: "But when that spirit of truth comes, whom the Father will send in my name, he, as it were, more familiar to you, by his fiery power will excite and sharpen your minds; and dwelling with you, and poured into you, will suggest all things to you, and will teach you all things whatsoever I shall have said to you." Nor let this be said only of the twelve apostles. For that spirit poured upon all who were together in the same place, whose number (as Luke had said a little earlier) was about one hundred and twenty men. This spirit had also poured upon many others, as Luke relates concerning the Samaritans. [Luke.] "When," he says, "the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them." **OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

[Marginal note: Arist.] Peripatetics: who in most places have repeated from their Aristotle: *Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.* Which we grant to those who have tasted only knowledge derived from the senses, and are content with their threefold way of knowing, through definition, division, and composition. But we are convinced that there are two other ways of understanding, not touched upon by the teacher of sensible doctrine. Of which one is the vision, and clear [understanding] of divine and natural things, I will not say speculation, but contemplation and contact: The other is the equation of truth itself, [Marginal note: Moses.] expounded by others with our intellect. TONE TWO. 360

...terior brings much fruit, by working, seeing, and tasting divine things. Which the apostle [Paulus.] explains somewhat, saying: "You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ." Therefore, by this death the prophets and all friends of God died, when they entered into those inner sanctuaries of God. By this death also John [Iohan.] was seized, when at the beginning of the most sacred vision he said: "I was in the Spirit on the Lord's Day," by which he was carried up and saw the throne of God, and the Lamb, and the seven spirits standing by, and all things that were decreed to happen in various past times. He also heard the songs of the saints and angels, and penetrated to many most recondite mysteries. Of this death also Paul [Paulus] makes mention, saying: "I know a man—whether in the body or out of the body, I do not know, God knows—caught up in this way, even to the third heaven, and he heard secret words of God, which it is not lawful for a man to utter." For then there occurs a separation of the soul from the body, and not of the body from the soul: because the latter is vivified by the soul itself, which neither operates in the body nor lives in it, except insofar as it vivifies it. To this mode of knowing also the apostles had come: and all who were imbued with that divine light and the Spirit suggesting all things, they too departed by this precious death. A sign of this was that they feared neither death, nor suffering, nor insult inflicted upon the body, which was already dead as an animal.

But those mysteries were shown to some less, to some more, according to their capacity, even though they had been seized by the same death. The other mode of knowing is through truth made equal with our intellect: just as a key is made equal to its lock. By this, even if we do not perceive in full light those things which are set forth by those who have beheld the mysteries themselves, yet a door is opened to us, so that from the conformity of perceived truth, and from the light which illuminates us from those opened inner sanctuaries, we may be rendered more certain than from the apparent demonstrations of the philosophers. I would call them "apparent" because they made either no, or very few, true demonstrations in natural things: but they are deduced from pre-accepted notions by Aristotle, or by whoever it may be, who had predicted those things beforehand. Therefore, this mode of understanding assigned by the Philosophers [Philoso.]: we have called the lowest of all, and less certain. The highest is that which is held by that clear intuition. The middle, however, is when it is given to us, not only to read and understand with external ears, but to perceive with better senses those things which are hidden in what is handed down under veils by those who beheld the same things with true intuition. For there are many, concerning whom the highest truth says, that "hearing they hear not and understanding they understand not." For it is sometimes given to us [CHRISTVS.], that we may clearly perceive the truth emanating from the marrow of the sacred scriptures, and that, with the veil removed and face unveiled, we may behold those things which are commonly hidden from the wise of the world: and with such certainty that all perplexity is removed, when we perceive them with better senses than external ones.

**THIRD CANTICLE**

**That interior senses are true and necessary, by which more and more certain things can be perceived than by exterior ones. Chapter XI.**

[A large decorated initial letter D set within a square frame with floral and scrollwork patterns] Therefore, it is about these interior senses, as better ones, that we must discourse: especially since the Peripatetics, who are primarily prominent in this age, have written most fully and minutely about exterior senses, but nothing about interior ones, except that there is a certain common sense, and phantasy, or imagination, which they placed in the anterior concavity of the brain: so that, receiving sensible species, it might judge between them, and, stripped of material conditions, might present them, now purified, to the intellect: And (as Algazel says) all senses would be joined in it, and emanate, and depend on it as parts from their whole. Or (as others say) it itself would result from the parts, as a kind of integral whole. Or it is (as held by others) a virtue or power more spiritual than the particular senses: and they proceeded no further concerning these interior senses. But Plato, agreeing with Mercury and Moses, asserts in the Symposium that man is twofold, and each part with its own senses: so that he has four eyes, two pertaining to the exterior man, others to the interior man, and as many ears, and nostrils, also hands, and feet as many. Likewise two mouths, and a double taste, and finally all things doubled: Which in the first homily on the Song of Songs by Jerome, or by Origen, or by whoever (whoever he was) who edited it (for its author is uncertain) are both presupposed and discussed. Whereby through many passages of sacred scripture we are reminded that man is twofold. For thus Moses wrote in the beginning of Genesis: "male and female he created them." Yet the female was not produced then, but afterwards, many other things having been produced in that interval, therefore that writing is about the twofold man, of whom the exterior and animal part is called feminine and inferior: but the interior and better part is called masculine. Concerning these, Paul, often repeating, teaches many things about separating the interior man from the exterior man who is corrupted. Also, the entire song of the divine epithalamium is about him. For it does not sing of the eyes, nostrils, mouth, teeth, breasts, chest, belly, legs, and other members of the animal man: but of the better and archetypal man, as we have discussed more extensively elsewhere. But continuing concerning the senses, we say that they do not recognize them: nor through them any better sensible things: except those who have them (as the apostle says), "exercised to discern good and evil." This discernment is by no means made through the exterior senses. For the boundaries of touch are hot and cold, hard and soft, rough and smooth. Sight, however, extends only to color and light, and darkness. Smell distinguishes between odors and stenches. Taste distinguishes between sweet and bitter: sharp and fatty: salty and pungent: austere and pleasant: tart and sour: hearing, however, only apprehends sound. None of them, therefore, makes a distinction between good and evil, but the better senses, by which not only moral—

Perhaps the Peripatetics will hiss and say: "With all study and all
diligence, we have investigated the lot of human nature, yet we have not perceived whether these
inner senses exist, indeed, we have not even heard of them." I am not surprised, since divine
and spiritual things of this kind are such that they mock the proud and those who presume upon themselves, [Marginal note: Plato]
and are utterly hidden from them. Concerning these things, Plato in his letter to Dio-
nysius [says]: "For whoever hears these things, at first glance rejects them: But after
these things have been well discussed and proven, we find them consenting with us."
For there are no things that seem more ridiculous to the common people and those addicted only to exterior senses,
nor things that are more to be revered and divine among the noble and experienced.
For very many have been, and indeed distinguished by sharpness of intellect,
and endowed with excellent judgment, who at first glance would utterly judge these things to be trifles (so to speak):
but afterwards, they not only assented but yearned for them in a wonderful way,
and what then seemed utterly probable, now seemed contrary to them.
Among these, that is most important, that the beginning of all truth arises through the exterior senses.
Indeed, all these are to be scorned, when we have come (as
Origen teaches against Celsus) to the exercise of the interior senses by which
we use, when we deal with God, who flees every grasp of the exterior senses.
Nor indeed (as I believe) is it sufficient for complete blessedness that the soul
understands and loves God: although intellect and reason are said, according to [Marginal note: Aristotle.]
Aristotle, to be the whole man. For the complete man is a certain whole resulting from soul and body,
having all the operations of both senses,
even existing in the body: But of the exterior senses in the body, and through a body
subject to corruption: Of the interior senses, however, in a better body, into which
this animal body will be changed, as the apostle says: "It is sown an animal body," [Marginal note: Paul.]
"it will rise a spiritual body: It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption:"
"It is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness, it will rise"
"in power." But (you will say) since we are in this valley of misery, clothed in this
corruptible body, we cannot use the interior senses. Hear (I pray) [Marginal note: The same.]
what Paul adds. "If (he says) there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one: just as
it is written. The first man, or Adam, was made into a living soul, the last,
or later Adam, into a life-giving spirit. The first man is from the
earth, earthy: the second man is from heaven, heavenly." "He speaks (you will say) of Christ."
Listen to what follows. "As is the earthy, so are those who are earthy: and as is the heavenly,
so are those who are heavenly: Therefore, if we have borne the image of the earthy, let us also bear the image of the heavenly."

I ask, will a grain ever become a plant, unless the living body of the plant has it at least in potentiality, as all Peripatetics agree? For this [plant] arises from a dead grain, and our spiritual body, in which we bear the image of the heavenly, arises from the animal and corruptible body that has been put to death: either by this common death, which all un-

we may be delighted in God himself. Nor indeed will we use corruptible senses there,
because nothing corruptible will be in those eternal and incorruptible dwellings.
Therefore, with better senses, we will perpetually be delighted in God himself.

TONE THREE. 363

WHAT SYMBOLISM, AND WHAT CONGRUENCE
man has with angels. Chapter One.

[Large decorative initial D in a square frame] MAN having been DISPOSED and tempered, and the
manner of his progress and reason assigned, as to the degrees
and gifts distributed to him, it must now be examined what
congruence he has with created beings: and especially with
angels, from whom, as from inseparable companions of his whole
journey, he may receive increments of progress. First, therefore, they agree by natural disposition,
since both are partakers of reason, capable of understanding, and tend to the same
end, servants of the same immediate Lord. Both likewise are incorruptible
and perpetual, but angels by an equal and continuous succession, man, however, according
to his better part, in the same way: but according to the other part, by a certain transformation,
concerning which it is said: "This corruptible shall put on incorruption." [Marginal note: Paul.]
Both also drink from the same fountain and rock, concerning which it is again said: "But they drank
of the spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ:" foreseen by them indeed,
but for us carved, erected, and filled with immense water, so that from its
fullness we may all fully receive. Because not only men, but also
angels draw from it, as Augustine says: "Angels consult Him, as [Marginal note: August. Peter.]
the fountain of life." Into Him also (as Peter says) angels desire to look:
so that they may always draw for themselves, and for us, whose care they have,
as long as we are confined in this bodily prison. And although they are said to differ
from men in appearance, nevertheless, they agree with them no less
than those (men) with horses, which they ride, and lead them at will with a small bridle,
and urge them on with a slight touch of the spurs, or a gesture of the body:
and instruct them, imparting a certain prudence for performing the journey.
Nor do they have less congruence with men, than they themselves (men) with birds,
which they train, either for hunting, or for singing, and for imitating human
speech. Thus they, presiding over us, guide, impel, and [Marginal note: Adam. Shem. Abraham. Isaac. Jacob. Joseph. Moses. Elijah. Peter.]
instruct us, so that we may capture the prey of heavenly things, and that we may bring back
divine words, more or less according to our capacity, and according to the diligence
we show, so that we may listen to them, and make them familiar to us.
Hence the ancient fathers diligently strove to adhere to them, and to have
familiar companionship with them. For thus (as I found in the most ancient Hebrew
monuments) Adam had familiar intercourse with the angel Raziel: Shem, son of Noah,
with Jophiel: Abraham, however, had Zadkiel as a familiar: Isaac and Jacob, Peliel: Joseph, Ga-
briel: Moses, Metatron: Elijah, Maltiel. And in the evangelical family, Peter had
an angel not only for himself, but also familiar to his other friends, so much so that when Peter came
from prison to the house of Mary, his hostess, knocking, she, with the other friends,
aware of his custom, which Peter had with an angel, said, "It is his an-

[Marginal notes: Iohan. Cecilia Agnes.] Thus John had an angel, who would show and teach him the sacraments of the most celebrated vision. Thus Cecilia had an angel, whom she would show to her husband and brother-in-law. Thus Agnes had a perceptible angel, so that it might even guard her in a brothel. And many others had familiar guardian angels, whom this brief summary of things does not permit to commemorate. Also from sacred writings we have that everyone has their own guardian angel, although they do not enjoy its domestic familiarity, because this is given to few and the purest. But if, knowing the symbol and congruence we have with them, and how pleasant and profitable their familiarity is to us, they would always seek their favor, taking them as friends to the best of their ability, so that now [Marginal note: Franci.] Francis might be set as an example for us. For he celebrated the forty days of blessed Michael the Archangel with strict fasting and careful diligence: he also chose places in which he believed them to be more propitious, namely the place of Saint Mary of the Angels, Mount La Verna, (as it is said) specially dedicated to angels. This is observed and sought by those who are wise in spiritual matters, and to whom the order of things in God, from whom they proceeded, is somehow known. For it is that those things which possess a lower place are led to the highest through intermediaries.

**Whether man is superior to angels, or vice versa. Chapter II.**

[Large initial E] And because we have said that man, as an inferior, is led to God through an angel, I deem it by no means to be omitted here to discuss whether the angel presiding over us, or ministering, is nobler, or man guarded by him and receiving the ministry. For that well-known sentence in the Davidic song [Marginal note: Dauid.], which the prophet sings when speaking of man, seems to press hard upon [this idea]: "Thou hast made him a little less than the angels." As well as those things [Marginal note: August.] which are said by Augustine, that He made the angel near Himself, as more worthy and excellent than other things created by Him. For those things which approach closer to the first and most perfect cause seem to be more perfect. And since angels, again, are above time, and produced with a certain aeviternity, and removed from burdensome matter, they seem nobler. Some add that an angel, because it is intellectual, is considered more worthy than man who is rational. And they try to prove it with the oracle of Ezekiel [Marginal note: Ezechi.], where it is said: "Thou art the seal of likeness." By which words (as some explain) something more seems to be attributed to the angel than to man, who was made in the image of God. For if they judge something more perfect to be implied [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] by the "seal of likeness" than by "image." Standing against these, we take from infallible truth that he who reclines is greater than he who ministers. [Marginal note: Paulus.] But concerning angels, Paul says: "Are they not all ministering spirits, not only indeed of God, but also of men, sent forth for those who are to inherit salvation?" Some say that angels minister to us, not as to nobler beings, but as to the weak and those in need of their protection. To whom we say,

**TONVS TERTIVS. 364**

that angels carried into Abraham's bosom the soul of Lazarus, not infirm,
but freed from the body and enlightened. And although a child sometimes needs
the guidance of a tutor, yet he is greater than the tutor, soon to possess a kingdom.
But we, whom angels serve, are to possess the kingdom prepared for us, not for an-
gels, from the foundation of the world. Whence also our condition is concluded to be
better than the condition of angels. Which also the order of creation declares: For
the last work of God was man: who was first and more excellent in the divine mind,
according to the common opinion of philosophers, by which it is said: What is first in in- [Marginal note: Philoso.]
tention, is last in execution. But man was the last work of God, intro-
duced into this world, as its steward, as into a house already built
and prepared. Since moreover Christ as man is considered nobler than angels,
we can conclude human nature to be nobler, by that Aristotelian principle
admitted by all: When the best in this kind is better than the best of that
kind, this kind is nobler than that. And unless Christ and the Blessed Virgin were
nobler than angels, they could never have transcended their choirs and ranks.
But concerning Christ, Paul says: "Having become so much better than the angels, as he has [Marginal note: Paulus.]
inherited a more excellent name than they." But omitting many things which are adduced
by some to save their opinion concerning the nobility of angels, I will address one
of their strongest points, namely that the soul of Christ was nobler by grace,
granted that by nature it was inferior. Which indeed, if well considered,
will seem to be far from the truth: since gratuitous gifts (as we explained above)
are given according to the dispositions of nature. And let that of the apostle be weighed (I ask),
that he is so much better than the angels, as he has obtained a more worthy name.
Which name, indeed, was not imposed by chance and improperly, as ours
are imposed daily: but was most fitting for the one named, and fashioned
in the college of the most holy Trinity: where both the ranks of things and all proper-
ties, even individual ones, are known. And if Adam, with a small light
imparted, knew how to impose names on things according to their property:
did not the Most Holy Trinity, and the origin of all light, know better? From this
indeed Gabriel was sent to announce the birth to the Virgin, with a command concerning
the name to be given to the son, whose conception he was announcing. God also took care
to add one character to Abraham's name, so that it might be more fitting for the one named.
What do we believe concerning the name imposed on the Son, and on Christ as man, whom He
loved and honored above all? If therefore He gave to this one a name more honorable than
to angels: He also made the one named more honorable. Indeed, I will not say
according to divinity, because angels could not be worthily compared to Him, since He
exceeds them by infinity and an immense interval. So much so that according to that
no comparison can be made. It remains therefore that Christ as man is more honorable,
just as He inherited a more excellent name. I will also add one thing, which greatly ex-
plains the nobility of man: because he contains within himself the structure of the world, ange-
