CANTICLE THE THIRD

Man, and the archetype, as we explained above, therefore has a more express image of God, in whom all His most beautiful characteristics shine forth. Nor is that prophetic saying compelling, by which it is said that man was made a little lower than the angels, since in truth the letters have ותחסרהו מעט מאלהים vate chasrehu mehat me-elohim. Which, if translated word for word, has: "Thou hast made him a little lower, or a little less than God:" for Elohim signifies God, although sometimes angels, and sometimes judges: but in this place (as the wise Hebrews commonly understand) it signifies God. Which is implied by the words that immediately follow: "And Thou hast set him over the works of Thy hands." Therefore man is not inferior to angels, because they themselves are also works of God's hands: And how much God Himself made [Marginal note: Paul.] man, Paul implies, when he says: "He took not on him the nature of angels, but the seed of Abraham," as if, namely, more capable of union than angels. Further, more esoteric Theologians proceed, explaining that [Hebrew letter] Ayin by numbers: For those letters yield 119: Ayin (ע) given as 40: Yod (י) 9: Nun (ן) 70: which numbers joined together yield 119. Where there is one hundred, one ten, and the whole number, up to the ten itself exclusively. Which is a great mystery, and is hidden among those who know the art of divine and natural numbers, about which it is not permitted to speak at present. As for Augustine saying that God made the angel worthier and more perfect near Himself. This is true as regards the immediate act, with which, however, it can stand that man was made nobler in potential, to be sometimes brought to act: and then man, having completed his course, will appear nobler, who, while he was under a tutor, seemed less noble. We will say the same regarding what was said about angels existing above time, because men also will be above time, when they enjoy eternal beatitude. But what is brought forward in the fourth place, that the angel is intellective, and man rational, is of no account: since man is also intellectual, as agrees [Marginal note: Aristotle. David. CHRIST.] Aristotle, saying: "Man is pre-eminently intellect, and reason." Nor would the royal prophet, unless he had felt himself capable of intellect, so often repeat: "Give me understanding." And the supreme truth, as if reproaching His disciples, says: "Are you still without understanding?" For there is a threefold intellect: divine and pure; likewise separate, and angelic; moreover mixed, and human. But when he will be freed from bodily bonds, he will not only attain to the angelic intellect, but transcending it, will apply himself to the divine, to be united with it, more happily than an angel: as many passages of sacred scripture resound. In which we have that man is made a son of God: and is transformed into the same image, which is God, and is united with Him: which things are nowhere read of angels. That also about the signet, or seal, collapses by itself. For in Hebrew it is found אתה חותם תכנית atah chotem tabnit, that is, "Thou seal of likeness." Nor have I ever found that a seal or signet says something [Marginal note: Augustine.] greater than an image. Augustine rightly says that the image of God is in man as if—

**VOLUME THREE. 365**

in the seal, but in Christ, as in a son. Into which image it is sometimes given to us to be transformed, while angels remain with the image of the seal, which is inferior. Or if it is said that an angel is the seal of the image, this is irrelevant, since that which is sealed is always nobler than the seal. Therefore, the seal in an angel argues nothing of nobility. Thus, man remains nobler, whom the angel serves, and rejoices in his progress: as we have learned from the Gospel: and reports some utility, since every agent acts for an end, indeed a useful and delightful one, unless there is an error in the operator. But since the angel is not deceived, he has that useful end which God knows, and to whom God wills to reveal it.

What envy there was and is between angels and men. Chapter III.

**W**hen, however, the angel saw a more express image, and greater perfection in man than in himself, from this perhaps he took the reason to envy him. For envy is sadness over another's good, with the desire either of depriving the one who has that good, or of surpassing him. Therefore, by this envy (as the Wise Man says) death entered into the world: because the angel of death seduced and subjected man, bringing death upon him, lest he should attain that lot from which he himself had been expelled. Nor is it to be thought that the angel envied God, who is so immensely exalted that there is no place for man or angel to emulate Him. But he knew the rank of man, and the most perfect end appointed for him, and the dominion that one man was to obtain. And this, when (as Paul says) God the Father introduced Him, the firstborn, into the world, saying: "And let all His angels worship Him." He also saw whence He would draw His origin here, and His future birth, as John testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: "A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun of divinity, and superior beauty, and the moon of light, and natural grace under her feet. And on her head a crown of twelve stars," that is, of all graces and gifts, since all heavenly things are divided by the number twelve. "And being with child, she cried out, travailing in birth," not indeed with a voice of pain, but of exultation, or of terror, which the one to be born ought to strike into all the powers and virtues of the world: whence it follows: "And she bore a son, who was to rule the nations with a rod of iron:" according to that psalm: "The Lord said to me, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession. And you shall rule them with a rod of iron.'" Hence, fearing and envying, the great dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that he might devour her son. And from this arose a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon and his angels, but these did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven. And lest anyone should doubt who this dragon was, it adds: "And that great dragon was cast out, who is the Devil and Satan." And since this son was not only to rule the world with a rod of iron, but, being exalted, to draw from—

...moving. But the examples brought forward concerning the pipe and the organ object, where from one source a breath sounds, from another a hand moves. And lest we seem by a witty example to wish to shake a solid (as they say) philosopher, let us bring forward a few, though from many, invincible reasons. It is pleasing what some bring forward to prove the numerousness of intelligences. For they presuppose order, without which the universe cannot stand: and this order is threefold, namely, for being, for operation, and for end. Or to superiors, inferiors, and equals, especially when the intermediates are ordered. For what glory is there for a Duke if, forgetting the emperor or king, he looks only to the soldiers? What does a bishop do with his clergy, having disregarded the supreme pontiff, or Christ, whom he represents? And what wise person will ever conceive of those celestial minds being so occupied with the revolution of the heavens that they look to nothing else? Or even (as some wish) that they are blessed in the influence and generation of inferiors, and not rather [Aristotle] in the Creator, from whom they receive: whence they influence? This is especially true since Aristotle himself teaches that if the soul were continuously moved, it would never attain a blessed life: because blessed life itself is rather in rest than in active or passive motion. Therefore, there is an order of intelligences not only to the heavens, which they move, and to themselves moving each other, but to God from whom they receive,

      *With what most just balance he has sent forth those who have transgressed*
      *from among them as enemies against us.*           Chapter V.

[Decorative initial E] And just as from among those who are faithful, a proper guardian has been assigned to each one, so from among the rebellious, an enemy is sent forth, so that from this, we may gain not ignominy and damage, but profit and glory. Hence, mankind unjustly complains about these assigned enemies:
[Marginal note: Paulus, Orige.] especially, since they contend with us with an equal balance and a compensated struggle. For (says Paul) "God does not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide the way of escape." Where Origen says: "Unless the virtue of those contending is equal, there will be no just palm for the victor." Therefore, those who preside over contests do not allow those who come to the struggle to enter into contests haphazardly among themselves, but with diligent examination, according to what they observe of their bodies or age, joining one with another with the most equal comparison, by this law and edict, that the victor be master, and the vanquished be a servant, according to that saying of Peter: "By whom one is overcome,"
[Marginal note: Petrus.] "by him he is enslaved." And the devil, vanquished and subdued, like a wasp with a broken sting (as I have heard from trustworthy sources), can no longer trouble another. Origen supports this,
[Marginal note: Orige.] saying: "I truly believe that the saints, fighting against these enemies and conquering, diminish the army of demons, so that it is no longer permissible for one who has been overcome by someone to attack another." Thus, the enemy fights against us, and our genius (guardian spirit) and guardian fight with us against that enemy: so that the struggle of flesh and spirit is the same: and that which is of the devil presiding over the flesh and its lust, with the angel strengthening the spirit. Hence, in that great contest, Michael fought for the prince, and his angels for his soldiers. But the Dragon fought against the prince of the human race himself, and against the prince of angels fighting for the same. And his satellites (followers) fought against the soldiers of the prince and their angels: so that the battle is always equal, prince against prince, and soldiers against soldiers. Therefore, man, in the midst of these contenders, grants victory to whomever he wishes, and thereby obtains it himself,
[Marginal note: Hiero.] as Jerome rightly says: "Weak is the enemy who does not conquer unless one is willing." For whatever great things are proclaimed about the enemy, that he is most cunning, and like a lurking serpent, or rages like a roaring lion, and that these are his names

**CANTO III**

Pythagoras and Plato speak of the most consonant influxes flowing into us,
[Marginal note: Pytha. Plato. Cicero. Macro.] especially in the republic; whom Cicero follows in a book under the same title. But Macrobius, in the first book of *On Scipio's Dream*, resuming their sayings, says: "When you gaze at the sky, you are amazed. That (I say) is what fills my ears, such a great and sweet sound. This (he says) is that which, with unequal intervals, but nevertheless in due proportion, distinct by reason, is produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves; and tempering the high with the low, it produces various equally harmonious sounds. For the starry heaven, whose revolution is more excited, makes a sharper sound; but the lunar (sphere) is the gravest, by a violent motion, by which the upper sphere moves more quickly. But by its own motion, the lower (sphere) is faster and sharper; the upper, however, is slower and graver. Which harmony is indeed most beautiful, and most sweet in its reciprocation; so much so that no song is sweeter than this, which is derived from numbers and measures, like the motion of the spheres: as we have clearly proven. Nor is there less harmony in the signs of the starry
[Marginal note: Plato.] heaven: to which (as Plato says) Sirens are appointed, who are called songs, because presiding over them, they render harmonious influxes."

From where the heavens receive the favor which they harmonically infuse. Chapter VII

[Marginal note: Idem. Apoca.] [Large decorative initial Q] What those Sirens are, Plato was silent, but from sacred scripture (if I am not mistaken) we can learn. For this (scripture) relates (as we read in the Apocalypse) that twelve angels preside over the twelve gates of that celestial city: who revolve with supreme and tireless harmony, and flow into those gates, which (as it pleases the Academics) are the signs of the starry heaven: of which Capricorn is the principal gate of ascent, and Cancer of descent; the other signs, however, agree with one or the other of these. But into these revolving signs flow many kinds of angels (arranged, however, under those twelve princes) that multiple and most sweet influx, and full of all kinds of harmony, which they receive from the divine name, revolved twelve times: as the Hebrews hold for certain.
[Marginal note: Hebræi Iohan.] Concerning which John (says) in the same place: "And in the foundations of that city are the names of the twelve apostles, and of the Lamb." For the Lamb does not have twelve names: but that great name (as we said above) in which alone it is necessary for men to be saved. Therefore, we obtain salvation in this name through Christ who inherited that very name: and this (salvation) through angels, through the heavens, and through every creature: because all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called saints according to His purpose. For to these, both the influxes of the heavens, and the power of angels, and every creature favors, just as conversely, the same every creature
[Marginal note: Sapiens.] arms itself to conquer the enemies of God, as we read in the Book of Wisdom. John also mentions the seven spirits who are before the throne of God, whom many affirm to preside
[Marginal note: Mercu.] over the seven planets. Hence Mercury calls these seven governors, because, namely, through the seven planets, which they move, they moderate all things, even the influx of the twelve signs. And how great the consonance, infer from this—

we can, because each number results from the same root. For three and four constitute seven. But one of them multiplied by the other yields twelve. Therefore the heavens receive from angels, whence they may flow in and favor good, but those [angels] from the great name of God: Whose virtue is primarily in God, afterwards diffused into those twelve and seven angels, through whom it extends into the twelve signs and seven planets: and consequently into all ministers and instruments of God himself. So also it is in this world, or the mystical spiritual body: For the virtue of the great name of God existing in Christ, and completing with all perfection, is afterwards diffused into those twelve apostles, as into twelve signs, and chief foundations after Christ of the celestial and spiritual edifice. By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and [Marginal note: Dauid] by the breath of his mouth all their host. And again: The heavens declared his [Marginal note: Dauid] righteousness, and all the peoples saw his glory. Behold therefore how both heavens, both of this machine and of the spiritual edifice, influence only as much as they are imbued and filled by supercelestial virtue: so that concerning both heavens that of the same divine prophet can be sung. For the heavens dripped from the face of God Sinai, from the face of the Lord Israel: Indeed, they dripped voluntary or spontaneous rain (that is, any influx whatsoever), because it is not diffused by any natural necessity, but by God's benevolence into his peculiar inheritance, when it has been capable of his influx. For not all receive spiritual charismata from God through the heavens and angels: although all rejoice in the common benefit of the rains, which the eternal Father commands to descend upon the just and the unjust: and they enjoy the bodily light of the sun, which he causes to rise upon the good and the evil.

What man has with the sacraments. Chapter VIII.

[Decorative initial letter Q depicting a figure in a landscape] Although the supreme moderator is most simple to each and omnipotent: yet many times he acts with us, with angels, heavens, and other suitable intervening means, which have a symbol with both. For the heavens, which are distributed by twelve and seven, derived from three and four, participate through three in divinity: but through four in the nature of lower things.

OF THE THIRD CANTICLE

Angels also have many things in common with God, and many things with man sojourning (on earth): therefore they are mediating ministers, until that better fortune shall be given to man himself, which may not need angelic favor. Yet not content with these, the most pious Father established other means, by which He might deal more intimately with us. And these are the sacraments and sacrifices, which partake of the nature of both, or analogically represent those divine things. For human defilements are washed away by that super-mundane water, which is the Son of God, and the Wisdom of God, and the Word of God, which sustains and heals all things: and He also who alone bore the sins of the world, making purification for sins. Hence, as a sign of this washing, this elemental water was ordained, whose purpose it is to wash away the defilements of bodies, and to signify that water which washes all stains of the soul and spirit. For these defilements could not be washed away, except by that water which is God's piety, cle-
[Marginal note: Hebrew Theologians] -mency, grace, and mercy; so much so that even the Theologians of the Hebrews are compelled to confess that the Messiah must purify man by water, who in the fiery law was purified by blood, justice thus demanding, which not
[Marginal note: John] omitting, but perfecting, Christ came (as John says) not in water only, but in water and blood. And since beyond washing, we also need to be strengthened, oil for anointing and strengthening was ordained: Which has such a correspondence with the divine name, from which is all delightful virtue,
[Marginal note: Song of Songs] and strengthening, that the name itself is called in the Song of Songs "poured out oil." And it has a correspondence with the Holy Spirit, who solidifies, binds, and anoints all things, so that it is called chrism, anointing, and bond. And just as the richness of oil and flesh together seasons all dishes and strengthens them for our nourishment, so the richness and chrism of this Holy Spirit seasons all our works: so that like well-seasoned dishes, they may be placed on the table of the highest king. For without His grace diffused in our hearts and sprinkling us, all our works are tasteless and of no nourishment. Therefore by this oil infants are strengthened, and those departing from us, and when someone is perfected as a king or priest, or constituted as a bishop. And because all created nature continually fails, it continually needs food and nourishment; hence He instituted another sacrament, namely bread and wine: which have the greatest symbolism with Him who is called the living bread and the true vine, given indeed as food and drink for nourishing our better man. Bread and wine also have such a correspondence and symbolism with us: that there is no more suitable nourishment for us. There remains the sacrament of penance, which is exhibited through the word, representing that Word by whose power all things are purified, and the purification of sins is effected. Which Word is also sought in the first sacrament, made complete both by word and by element: And if matrimony is a sacrament, that also is completed by a word. Therefore man has the greatest symbolism with the sacraments: which are means between God tempering souls, and this soul to be tempered, and finally to be united with Him. Habet

Moreover, man has a covenant with these by divine institution, since God's will does not have less power and efficacy in instituting anew than it had from the beginning, when it simultaneously imparted law, order, and being to things. What man has with sacrifices. Chapter IX.

[N] Not only, however, sacraments, but also sacrifices have been ordained as symbolic intermediaries for both. For they have a certain symbol with that to whom they are offered, and with those who are expiated: but so hidden that human intellects cannot grasp it: although all confess sacrifices to be necessary: and that they are certain quasi-natural intermediaries between God and man. For to sacrifice to God (says Ari- [Marginal note: Aristotle:] stotle) is from nature. However, the offering of this or that sacrifice, for this or that expiation, although it may be most fitting by natural order, is nevertheless instituted by law: since human intellects cannot discover or devise those things which God specifically requires for our expiation according to the order of celestial things, with the things to be expiated themselves, and the expiating sacrifices, so that the celestial powers may be rendered placated: and may restrain themselves from the execution of punishment, which those perpetrated sins deserved. For the blood of animals seems to purge the sin contracted in the flesh and blood of our animal nature: according to that of the Apostle. [Marginal note: Paul:] Almost all things are cleansed in blood. Almost (he says) because earthen and bronze vessels were cleansed with water. Nor was it without reason that man, who is the bond of all things, and contains all things, and has the greatest symbol in his lower part, in which and through which the beginning of sin is contracted, was purged with animals through the blood of immaculate animals: until the immaculate lamb was offered, supplying the place of all things that were offered. For he bore and purged the sins of all so much more perfectly, inasmuch as he himself is a more renowned bond of all creatures, rational and irrational, and insensible, and celestial. Therefore, the shed blood of animals was received into the holy places, together with the sins of those for whom it was shed: until he came, who by his own blood entered once into the holy places, having found eternal redemption.

What man has with words and prayers which support him. Chapter X.

[E] And because man is purged and perfected, not only by words expressed in the sacraments, but also in hymns, prayers, and however they may be duly expressed: therefore, what man also has with these words themselves must be surveyed. For words are intermediaries between the speaker AAA

...and the listener, conveying not only the concept but also the power of the speaker, with a certain energy into the listeners and those who are receptive. Hence they change not only the listeners but often other things as well. For Christ would not have said, "in my name they will cast out demons," unless there were a certain power in that name when expressed, over demons, and the sick, and such like. [Marginal note: CHRIST] Words also move wisely and in their own ways those who chant. And because Hebrew words, both divine and heavenly, and also natural, represent more expressly and more mysteriously, therefore Orpheus commands that "barbarian names" – i.e., Hebrew ones in sacred rites – are not to be changed, if we wish to operate effectively. [Marginal note: Orpheus] And beyond the efficacy that words have, whether from a certain power inherent in them, or from the divine and sacred things they represent, or from wherever it may be, another power is also found in complex prayers, from the truth contained in them, which has the greatest power of impressing, changing, and establishing, so much so that when agitated, it shines more, and when attacked, it is more strengthened and consolidated. Which truth is not in simple and uncomplicated words, but in enunciations, in which something is affirmed or denied. Therefore, from these true and sacred prayers, which we utter with mind, or inner sense, we acquire great power. This especially, when they are directed towards God, to whom, by applying ourselves, we move Him to direct towards us His words, full of favoring divine power, through a divine ray, by which (according to Dionysius) He speaks to us: but so secretly that few perceive it. [Marginal note: Diony.] But he perceived it who said: "I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me." [Marginal note: David] Therefore, prayers offered to God and hymns sung never return empty, provided that we do not utter those words empty of meaning, spoken only by mouth and not from the heart, to be quickly dissolved into the air; but if we direct them with full meaning and effective mind to God Himself, just as an arrow is directed by a powerful hand from a drawn bow.

CANTICLE THE THIRD
CONCERNING A CERTAIN HIDDEN HARMONY OF THINGS AMONG THEMSELVES, WHENCE ONE MIRACULOUSLY OPERATES UPON ANOTHER. Chapter One.

[Marginal note: Trisme.] [Decorative initial E in a square frame with floral patterns] The most excellent craftsman God fashioned (as Trismegistus says) two images of himself, namely the world and man, in one of which he might play, and in the other indeed he might enjoy delights. For in the world he plays with certain wondrous operations, not by qualitative, or elemental, or sidereal virtue alone: but by a certain power hidden from human intellects, unless insofar as he deigns to reveal it to his friends. Indeed, it is known to all that a certain virtue resides in the magnet, by which it attracts iron: and in amber and jet, that when heated by rubbing they draw straw. But whence it comes, or what it is, no one among those who fill immense volumes concerning the properties of things has yet revealed. Nor whence the Aetites (eagle-stone) has it, that it strengthens the fetus of women and plants when placed above, and draws them when placed below. Nor whence jasper stops blood, and the Echneis (which is also called remora) stops a ship. Nor whence coral, when hung, produces some joy in man, and the hyacinth, the best companion of travelers, confers strength. Nor whence rhubarb (which the Arabs call rauend) expels cholera from the human body: and many medicines draw out and expel very diverse humors: and many such things, concerning which it would be tedious to discuss each individually. We also see many animals, by a certain inherent, wondrous, and prophetic power. The rooster most skillfully indicates the hours by its crowing, and puts a lion to flight with open wings. Many birds also, by song and chirping, and flies by a sharp sting, announce future rain: and dolphins, by frequent leaps above the [Marginal note: Cicero] water, precede a storm. And (to touch upon particulars) roosters (as Cicero writes) in Thebaid, by crowing throughout the nights, foretold that victory for the Boeotians against the Lacedaemonians. [Marginal note: Augures] Whence the augurs interpreted that bird to be silent if conquered, but to crow if victorious. Also, a monkey showed a great omen to the Spartans, which the king of the Molossians kept as a pet. For when they had asked Jupiter Dodonaeus, inquiring about victory, and the envoys had placed that in which they had cast lots, it disturbed the lots themselves, and the other things that had been prepared for the lot, scattering one from another. Then the priestess, who was in charge of the oracle, is said to have said: The Lacedaemonians should think about their safety, not about victory. The liver of a chameleon [Marginal note: Democ.] (as Democritus attests), when burned on the highest tiles, excites rains and thunder. The Ligurian stone (as has been proven) removes wondrous veils from the eyes. It would be tedious to recount all the omens which the Phrygians, Pisidians, Cilicians, Arabs, Umbrians, Tuscans, and other peoples learned from birds, [Marginal note: Panę.] who followed auguries. And although Panaetius and Carneades ridicule them, since these auspices often [Marginal note: Carne.] fail: whom Cicero follows after many examples adduced concerning divination by birds and animal entrails. Those things which agree among themselves, much more fortunately meet in man, who is the most perfect bond of all things, and supported by divinity above all things. Chapter II.

[Large decorative initial E] X the mutual correspondence of things (as we have explained) one operates upon the other with a certain wonderful and hidden power. Therefore it is not surprising if man, since he has both the image and the symbol of all things, can operate in all things. This indeed he accomplishes, provided he enjoys his due temperament and presides over himself: so that he may deservedly rule among other things. For to the man who presides well over himself, God, operating all things, is present and inherent: as not only Paul, [Marginal note: Paulus] and our writings, but also external wise men assert. For Plato teaches this in Ion: [Marginal note: Plato. Mercur. Xistus.] and in Parmenides: Mercury in Pymander, and Xistus the Pythagorean, who says that man is the temple of God, and God is the guest. Which the Poet also twice sings in his verses: God is in us, and there are dealings with heaven: From ethereal abodes that spirit comes. For God himself transfers himself into holy souls: and constitutes his prophets and friends powerful in deed and in word. Perceiving this, Paul [Marginal note: Paulus] said: I can do all things through him who strengthens me. For God is the soul to us, the whole virtue, without whom (as he himself declares) we can do nothing. Which Aristotle [Marginal note: Aristote.] also admits in his Meteorology: and at the end of his Ethics, saying that there is no virtue, whether natural or moral, except through God. And in more secret doctrines he asserts that a good and sound intellect can penetrate the secrets of nature: provided the influence of divine power is present, otherwise not at all. We receive this influence so much more copiously, the more we are freed from the burdensome impediments of the flesh, and of earthly occupations, and of ambition, and of the mind unduly agitated towards our neighbor, or towards any other thing: as we have not only from our doctrines, but also Mercury [Marginal note: Mercur. Cicero.] and Cicero attest. For he (Cicero) says in his On Divination: "Nor does the human soul ever divine, unless it is so freed that it has plainly nothing, or very little, to do with the body." But he (Mercury) says to Tatius: "Let them indeed despise both bodies and all corporeal things: and let them be carried to the one alone: if they wish to attain mind and God. For it is impossible, O son, to attend to both at once, mortal and divine things." For the more we abandon the animal and human life: the more we live as angels, or God: United with these, and restored to our proper and better lot, we can do all things, ruling over all. And this is the honor, in which man, when he was before sin, did not understand: but obeying concupiscence, he became like the senseless beasts: [Marginal note: Trisme.] and from a master (as Trismegistus says) he became a most wretched slave. Therefore, again carried up by virtue, and restored to his pristine dignity through his own victory, he acquires for himself that dominion, of which it is written.

You have subjected all things under his feet. [Psalms. Genesis.] But this dominion is to be acquired in that order, which the supreme moderator established from the beginning, saying: Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it, and have dominion. Be fruitful, namely, in good works, and abound in much fruit: so that you may also fill the earthly body, through a certain superabundance, leading, namely, the animal man into servitude, and as far as possible into the nature of the spirit: and then you will have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and the beasts of the earth: which indeed, since they inhabit three elements, also testify that other things are subject to human dominion. That a man of good heart/mind sometimes becomes a prophet by the manifold support of inferiors. Chapter III.

[E] Many times a man, presiding over himself, becomes a sharer of the divine mind so that future things may be foreknown: which is proper to God according to that of Isaiah: [Isaiah.] Declare to us what is to come, and we will say that you are gods. To which Peter assents, saying: [Peter.] For prophecy was not brought at any time by human will: but holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit. The Stoics also acknowledge this, whom Cicero follows in the first book of *On Divination*, [Stoics. Cicero] saying: That the foreknowledge of future things belongs only to the Gods: because there is no determined truth about contingent future events, by the pure judgment, namely, of mortals: to whom Ptolemy agrees, he says in *Fructus*: [Ptolemy.] Only those inspired by divine power predict particulars. However, Cratippus testifies that there have been many prophets, and many true foreknowledges (to omit our own), who, by Cicero's testimony, was considered equal to the greatest Peripatetics. Zeno also testifies, [Zeno.] and many who proceeded from him with the old academy. But before them Pythagoras, [Pythagoras. Certain omens] and the Stoics who followed these, likewise assert. For Calanus the Indian predicted the death of Alexander, and the Asiatic Magi predicted that Alexander himself, born, would be the ruin of Asia. Socrates divined that death was imminent for Crito on the third day, the priestess Diotima, a prophetic woman, predicted a plague. Anaximander announced an impending earthquake to the Lacedaemonians: and advised them to leave the city and their homes. Which entirely collapsed, and from Mount Taygetus, the outermost part was torn away like a ship's stern. Epimenides the Cretan, a divine man, [Epimenides.] warned by an oracle ten years before the Persian war, came to Athens: and performed certain sacrifices prescribed by the oracle: and to the Athenians fearing the Persian fleet, [Various Prophets.] he predicted that the Persians would not come for ten years, and after they came, they would depart having accomplished nothing. Thales.] Thales of Miletus, in order to convince his detractors and show what a philosopher could do, bought up all the olive trees in the Milesian territory before they flowered, perceiving by a learned conjecture of nature that there would be an abundance of oil. Which happened, and he brought back a profit of money, not for the sake of money, but to the envy of his detractors. Many doctors, farmers, and sailors, each by his own art and probable signs, foresee many things, which we disregard as being most well-known to everyone. And because no small things to be foreseen come from those who are in charge, which cannot be foreseen by prudence and art, therefore, consulting prophets or God was a most diligent concern for very many ancient Gentiles, Barbarians, Greeks, and Romans, but especially for the Hebrews. The Athenians always employed certain divine priests (whom they called Mantes) in public councils. Hebræi.] to go to the Sibylline books. The kings of the Hebrews were accustomed to always employ their prophets, of whom very many flourished; and if they themselves were prophets, they consulted God Himself directly, as we often read concerning David. [Marginal note: Dauid] For there were Astronomers, who divined by the aspects of the heavens; Augurs, who observed birds, guided by the influence either of the heavens or of those who preside over them. Geomancers, by points, or by the first cast [of lots/objects], or by a certain force drawn by the arm or hand, as the ancients were accustomed to do, from which they skillfully composed celestial figures, through which they divined. Necromancers, [Marginal note: Necrom.] however (who are also commonly called Magi), invoked unclean intelligences, from whom they might inquire about the outcomes of events. **Who and whence a true prophet is made. Chapter IIII.**

[Large decorative initial E] TRULY, legitimate and true prophecy always (as we have said) proceeds from God and the favor of the superiors, and this is of many kinds. For sometimes it is effected through a dream: Sometimes through that vision which is between sleep and waking: And sometimes by frenzy and agitation of the spirit. All these modes converge in one type of divination, which the Hebrews call בת קול bat chol, that is, 'daughter of a voice,' which we call echo, that is, a reflection of a voice. [Marginal note: Hebræi.] For these are certain reflections of the divine and prophetic voice. But others divine through a clear vision, which a purified mind possesses. Others indeed, insofar as they receive from a living and true voice. All these kinds we see expressed in the sacred scriptures. For concerning dreams, Matthew says: "The angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, indicating indeed what he was to do concerning his wife and the child." [Marginal note: Matth.] Pharaoh also saw a dream, and Nebuchadnezzar: The former concerning the abundance and impending scarcity of food; the latter indeed concerning the most mysterious succession of kingdoms: And the former had Joseph, the latter Daniel, as a truthful interpreter of their visions, though they were by no means worthy to know the mysteries which had been shown to them, adorned as they were with royal lineage. Prophecy, however, through frenzy, we read to have happened both to gentiles and to our divine prophets. Democritus asserts that some, in a frenzy, proclaimed those things which neither their nature nor art had taught. Indeed, he did not think anyone endowed with great genius unless they were stirred by a certain frenzy. Plato mentions Tymnicus of Chalcis, who had composed no poem worthy of memory; but sometimes seized by a certain frenzy, he composed a hymn to Apollo, the most beautiful of all, so that it might be conjectured to have been a divine rather than a human work. And in Phaedrus he teaches that the poetic doors are knocked upon in vain without frenzy. This frenzy the Greeks call *Mantia*, from Manto, the founder of Mantua; although *Mantis* is more often taken for every kind of inferior divination. Defining frenzy itself, he says: "Frenzy is abstraction, alienation, and connection." Abstraction, indeed, and alienation from those shadows and images by which bodily senses are excited and often deceived. Connection, because alienated from the animal man and adhering to divine powers, they receive many things from them which cannot be narrated by intellect and strength. Whence Dicaearchus the Peripatetic, when he treated of divination, approves of dream and frenzy. Nor does Aristotle disagree, as we gather from his Problems. For wise men assert that this was done because the voice always raises him who is called to a higher rank: Therefore, the double voice indicates both the rank in which he was, and the rank to which he ascended when called. To this, therefore, come purified and good-hearted men, so that, having frequently become participants in the spirit of God and the holy divine power, they may prophesy, discern hidden things, and predict future events, which belongs to God alone, and to those with whom God has decided to communicate and make Himself familiar. Which He by no means grants, except to men who are well purified and composed.

An Apology for Prophecy. Chapter V.

[Large decorative initial E] ND although it is clear to all that there have been prophets and many prophecies, nevertheless, there are not lacking those who try to attack them: therefore, I judge it opportune to briefly refute their arguments. For they say (as Cicero gathers in the second book of *On Divination*): [Marginal note: Cicero] "To what does divination belong, to fortuitous or to fated things? Not to fortuitous things, because there can be no foreknowledge of those things which have no reason why they should be future. But what is chance, what is a fortuitous event, unless when something has fallen out thus, has happened thus, that it could either not fall out or fall out differently? How then can that which happens by chance, happens by blind chance and the fickleness of fortune, be foreseen and predicted? Nor does divination belong to fated things: because when they happen necessarily, foreknowledge of them profits nothing, indeed it torments, if a bad outcome is to occur. Nor can those things which are fated be guarded against. Nor indeed should it be said that all things will fall out more lightly if divine matters are attended to, because (as they say) since nothing is outside fate, nothing can be alleviated by divine intervention." They conclude therefore: "If nothing that happens by chance can be foreseen as future, because they cannot be certain, there will be no divination. But if they can be foreseen for that reason, because they are certain and fated, divination will profit nothing." Chrysippus, Diogenes, and Antipater add: [Marginal note: Chrysipp. Dioge. Antipa.] "If there are Gods, by whose auspices (as it is said) divination exists, why do they not openly explain what future things are to be guarded against, or embraced?" this especially when they are said to be gene-

--- Page 891 ---
**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

...beneficial and friendly to the human race, unless they think it makes no difference whether humans know or are ignorant of what is to come. And why do they hide so many and such great things from humans, so that what they know or foresee is nothing in comparison to what lies hidden? From this they seem to conclude that the Gods reveal nothing, but if anything is foreseen, it happens by skill, art, or chance. Some also attack the signs that seem to be given from heaven, relying especially on this reasoning: that winds, lightning, thunder, comets, earthquakes, vapors seen contending in the air, and such things, are natural, and not prognostication. A corroborating sign of this is lightning cast into the middle of the sea, or sent elsewhere in vain, and because those events which are said to follow comets and earthquakes do not always follow them. And many who pursue arguments against divination contrive in a greater manner, which indeed collapse utterly of themselves.

Nevertheless, we will respond to those things which have been brought forward. For [Marginal note: Cicero.] (to turn myself to Cicero and those who follow him) divination is of fortuitous and fatal things. And although fortuitous things seem to have no reason, yet there is reason in those to whom these things happen. For in the supreme moderator from whom they happen, [Marginal note: Aristo.] they are not without reason. For all fortuitous things are disposed by God according to His reason. But we (as Aristotle rightly thinks in *On Good and Bad Fortune*), since we do not see the cause of these things, which is God, attribute them to fortune, that is, to an unknown cause. Therefore these things do not happen beyond the intention of the supreme moderator, just as the iron of an axe falls into the water beyond the intention of the woodcutter. For it seemed by chance [Marginal note: Saul.] that the lot fell upon Saul when he was chosen as king, yet he had been indicated as king to Samuel by the Lord; and by Him who had indicated him, the lots were arranged to fall upon Saul, which, to those not understanding God's own disposition, seemed to have fallen by chance. So in many things it happens that they are judged fortuitous, which proceed from divine decree with supreme reason. And these in God are called divine provisions; which, if they are disposed through the heavens, assume the name of fatal things; but in those to whom they occur, they are judged fortuitous events. And prophecies of these are often sent beforehand, so that mortals may know that such things are foreseen and destined by God, whence they may dispose themselves to receive these influences well, and be grateful to the giver. Sometimes, however, things are disposed in such a series that their outcomes are in the disposition of the recipient, just as is the grace of one who works well, and manifold favor. Which are also promised under condition, as the supreme moderator often repeats in sacred scripture, saying: "If you hear me, if you do these or those things, I will be a generous rewarder." And although the supreme moderator knows what man will do, yet the vision does not pass into the past, so that from that vision, already had and elapsed, the matter may proceed with an infallible outcome. But how the same contingent event is infallible providence in God, and fate in the heavens (as Plato [Marginal note: Plato.] rightly thinks), that is utterly most difficult. And although we see and approve these things, yet no one has yet declared how they agree. Nevertheless, we can offer some example, by which we may be led to an explanation of this matter. A river flows by God's command ever-

--- Page 892 ---
TOMVS QVARTVS. 376

eternal and unfailing course passes through various regions: for the benefit of all inhabitants.
Someone takes care to receive the flow of water, by admitting as much as suffices him for irrigating his fields. Another, with fortified dikes, admits no water, for benefit or harm. Yet another, through his idleness, having built no dikes, allows all his lands to be flooded and all his crops to be destroyed. Thus, the course of the river is from God's providence and unchangeable command, or from the order of the heavens, or fate: but the benefit or harm is contingent upon the industry or idleness of the recipient. But if someone were to prophesy about that flood, perhaps one of the inhabitants would have better fortified his dikes to avoid harm, and another would have prepared himself to receive more abundant benefit. Behold then how that which is fatal is mitigated, but (to speak in our manner) that which comes from the infallible providence of God. To Chrysippus and his colleagues, however, we will say that the Gods, that is, Angels, by the command of the supreme moderator, reveal some things to us, as both the dignity of the Prince [Marginal note: CHRI] and our merits demand. And from these things declared by oracle, we can infer many other similar things, because God speaks once (says Job), namely in the same cause, to the limits of whose unique word, we may direct our actions in similar cases. [Marginal note: STVS.] And this is what the prophet Amos says: "The Lord will do nothing unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets," [Marginal note: Amos] either expressly, that is, or by analogy. But many things are hidden from the unworthy, just as much knowledge of things to be known by us [is hidden]. Nor is it fitting for a Prince to reveal his secrets to the common people, but to a few who are privy to his secrets, and these the most faithful: whose execution, however, is entrusted to the people in due time. And then all know those things which had been hidden among a few. And this is the order of things to be arranged, not indeed for harm, but for the benefit of the entire Commonwealth. But that they deny some celestial effects to be signs of future events, is groundless: since some effects are natural, and some happen by the immediate command of God. Those therefore which are natural, are not signs: but those which are commanded by God to terrify or punish peoples, such as those prodigies sent by Moses upon the Egyptians, and many similar things, can rightly be called signs, and are: from which man can conjecture the outcome of events. Therefore, the arguments brought forward do not so narrow [the scope] that a corner of truth to be evaded (as the arguers supposed) is closed off to us. Nor should anyone wonder if prognostications are obscure and require interpreters, since nothing, in a way, is accomplished in natural things without needing human aid. For gold and silver, and other metals, are dug up and excavated full of dross and mud, but are purified by human industry. The grape is born and ripens by the aid of nature: but it withers unless collected by human diligence and pressed into wine. Grains also, reaped with much labor, are threshed, ground, and often handled, before bread is made into food. Flax requires innumerable operations (so to speak), before cloth is woven for human use. And just as the works of nature are completed by art, so too are divine oracles offered to us for explanation: so that of nature, and of God

--- Page 893 ---
**THIRD CANTICLE**

having become co-workers, in both we may have the means to be exercised. But sometimes it is necessary to divine, so that we may understand what divine prophets have foreseen. Whence error often occurs, not indeed from a fault or defect of the prophecy, because what proceeds from the mouth of God does not become void: but it happens from the fault of a poor interpreter. Nor is prophecy therefore to be denied, because the interpreter is ignorant, or errs in interpreting: because medicine is not to be denied, although doctors are mistaken in many things. And farmers are mistaken, and ship captains, although they are considered good prognosticators from proven signs. Nor is prudence and reason lacking for governing the republic, although Gnaeus Pompey, Marcus Cato, Hannibal, and most prudent senators, and most illustrious leaders were sometimes deceived. So too it happens in the art of divination, which is brought about either by prudence, or by conjecture, or by the agitation of the spirit or by vision, that diviners are sometimes mistaken: either because what the spirit suggests, or the vision indicates, is not well perceived: or because some change occurs in that concerning which the prophecy was made: whence the oracle's sentence is either changed, if it was announced for harm: or if for good, it is delayed. [Marginal note: Jonah,] For Jonah, moved by a divine voice, announced to the Ninevites a future destruction on the fortieth day, yet this was delayed by the repentance of the Ninevites and the prayer of the prophet (as we said above). [Marginal note: Isaiah] Isaiah prognosticated that Hezekiah's death was imminent for the morrow: yet this was extended by royal weeping for fifteen years. [Marginal note: Moses.] Moses was chosen by God's oracle to lead the people from Egypt to the promised land: Indeed, he led the people out of Egypt: but erring at the rock, he by no means led them to the appointed place. [Marginal note: CHRIST.] Only Christ, free from error, uttered prophecy that could by no means be made void, who therefore said: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

Well-composed men draw all things to themselves. Chapter VI.

[Illuminated initial N depicting figures in a landscape] It has been proven by no small experience that well-tuned strings on stringed instruments, when one is struck, cause others to resonate. And it happens to oysters and all shellfish that they grow equally with the Moon, and equally decrease. Trees also in winter time are believed to age simultaneously with the Moon and Sun, and to shed their sap, whence they are thought to be opportunely cut. All things sprout and bloom in spring, and joyfully follow the course of the sun. Many such things also occur: in which the connection and correspondence of things is observed. Therefore, since man is the bond of all things, a well-composed man easily moves all things, and draws and leads them to himself: no less than a magnet draws iron, or rubbed amber draws straw. Hence He, who is the most perfect bond of all things [Marginal note: The Same] and rejoices in full harmony, said: 'When I am lifted up from the earth' – that is, most perfectly extended on the wood of the cross, and in harmony with all things that are in the length, width, height, and depth of this worldly machine – 'I will draw all things to myself, to dispose of all at will.' Whoever becomes more like Him, and is united with Him, obtains so much greater power of attraction, and therefore...

--- Page 894 ---
**FOURTH TONE. 377**

...and by that, it is further strengthened, reinforcing that power which is inherent in man by nature, of drawing from the correspondence he has with all things. This is inferred from the fact that while each animal has its own food – some hay or barley, some herbs, some legumes or seeds, some meats, and that kind – man alone, eating all foods, receives the growth and sustenance of life from all. Likewise, among living beings, some possess the earth, some the sea, some the air, and the more worthy ones, heaven. But man, using every element for his own benefit, draws pleasure and advantage from everywhere. Nor content with these, he strives to ascend into heaven, indeed into God Himself, so that there is no place he does not appropriate for his use; and deservedly so, that the saying of the highest Prince may be true: "Every place that your foot shall tread upon, shall be yours," [Marginal note: Deuter.] until, that is, you return to Me, bringing all things with you. And just as all things bring advantage to the man who is well-disposed with God, as Paul says: [Marginal note: Paul.] "All things work together for good to them that love God," so to him who is dissonant from God, all things turn to ruin, indeed, the son having become rebellious, to whom it is said: "Cursed is the ground in your labor." To the curse of this earth, which is the primary element and foundation of all corporeal things, follows the curse of all things which are made from it, or adhere to it. Hence, evil and dissonant demons lead away these rebels, concerning whom Porphyry says in [his work] 'On Good and Evil Demons': [Marginal note: Porphy.] "The bodies of the good consist in commensuration; but the bodies of the wicked are ill-proportioned; and with passive affection, they inhabit a place near the earth, indeed within the earth itself. There is no evil which they dare not commit. They have an altogether violent and unhealthy manner, being, that is, deserted by the guardianship of better demons." And therefore, they very much contrive and devise vehement and sudden ambushes. And while they make incursions, they are accustomed partly to lie hidden, and partly indeed to inflict violence. For this reason, the passions inflicted by them are sharp and swift. But cures and amendments become slower for better demons. And after he enumerated many evils which they commit, he adds: [Marginal note: The same] "For they are greatly delighted by all things thus wickedly and discordantly done." Therefore, those who live dissonant from God, from conscience, and from good spirits, having commerce with dissonant spirits, commit all things dissonant, disordered, and horrifying; so much so that, being dissonant with themselves, they agree with no one, but approve all things dissenting and disordered. But those who agree with themselves and with God, placed in their proper place, perceive all things corresponding to themselves and easily manageable; because (as Porphyry says in the same place) [Marginal note: The same.] every good thing is easy and equal in governance, because it proceeds from order, from which follows agreement, tranquility, and the easy consensus of all.

CANTICLE THE THIRD
Men placed in their proper place, and well-ordered, easily dominate all things. Chapter VII.

[Large decorative initial C] It has been widely spread by famous report (as we have often said) that man, by the testimony of the sacred scriptures, was preferred and constituted over all the works of God's hands. Which doctrines Sulmonensis sings, imitating them: "An animal more sacred than these, and more capable of a lofty mind, was still lacking, and one that could dominate the rest; man was born." Nevertheless, we see most people, and almost the entire multitude of men, enslaved rather than dominating. We do not doubt that this has happened because man, rebellious against God (as Trismegistus says), having fallen from the contemplation of the Father and from His fellowship, whence he received the power of dominating, to the sphere of generation, has become the most miserable servant of all. And (with the highest truth as witness) sinful man is made a servant of sin, that is, of Satan leading to sin, or of concupiscence, which is the parent of sin itself. For concupiscence [Marginal note: James.] (says James) when it has conceived, gives birth to sin. Hence, everything resists man who has fallen from his dignity, nor do they deign to have him as master, who has now become such a vile slave. And they themselves refuse to obey him, until he is restored to his pristine honor, from which he had fallen, and becomes of one mind with God, from whom he may resume the power of dominating, just as he had already received it from the beginning. Then he will not fear poisons and [Marginal note: First Kings.] enemies, then he will not dread wild beasts: but he will shake them with terror, just as we read of David in the first book of Kings: who said to King Saul, who was terrifying him and recalling him from the encounter with the giant: "Your servant has pursued a lion and a bear, and I struck them, snatching the prey from their mouth. And when they rose up against me, I seized their chin and strangled them." Daniel killed a dragon, and stood intrepid among hungry lions. Paul shook off a viper clinging to his hand as if it were straw, fearing nothing of its bite or its harm, over which he had already obtained full dominion. For that power did not fail Paul, which He who [Marginal note: CHRIST.] said to the other Apostles: "Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you." John drank poison gladly and [Marginal note: Augustine.] steadfastly, and escaped unharmed from boiling oil. For (as Augustine, in my judgment, rightly determines in the third book *On Genesis According to the Letter*) animals were not produced venomous, hostile, and troublesome to the human race from the beginning: but after sin, they were constituted hostile and inimical. Which was brought forth from the Lord's sentence as punishment for the unjust rebellion of the first parents. For to the serpent, the most hostile of all animals to man (so that we may understand what was said thence to apply to other hostile animals), He said: "I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed." And scarcely had the sentence been uttered, when, providing also for a remedy, He said: "It, namely the seed of the woman, shall crush your head: so that you may not be able to harm either it, or its true followers." Hence not only the Apostles, but also their successors prevailed against hostile animals. For Jerome brought a fierce lion, a most bitter enemy, into his own service. And many hermits

Whence comes the power of dominion, how it was lost, and how it was restored.
Chapter VIII.

[Large decorative initial D] We have said long ago that the power of dominion was implanted in man by the supreme Creator.
But what it itself is, and how we possess it, I deem it necessary to examine.

and placidly even show the way. The same, noticing human footprints

to snort with anger;" by these and other signs which the natural historian adds there,
man is feared most of all, but whence he is feared, we could not easily comprehend.

[Marginal note: Hebrews.] The Hebrews, moreover, call this terror פחד *pachad*. And this (terror) is stronger in some, weaker in others. But it was greatest
[Marginal note: Isaac Jacob.] in Isaac: therefore Jacob, to whom his father had granted it by hereditary right, said to Laban the Aramean, his uncle and father-in-law: *“Unless the Lord God of my father Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, perhaps you would have sent me away naked.”* Where in Hebrew, instead of "fear," that *pachad* is found. And there again Jacob swore by the fear, that is, the *pachad*, of his father Isaac. For this is like a terrifying sign for whatever is subject to man: be it a servant or an animal: otherwise, neither would a boy rule oxen, horses, and elephants, nor would a king terrify the people of an entire region. Nor does man only have a sign by which he is feared, but another by which he is loved: in this too, he is made an image of God, who is encompassed by both tribunals, of love and of fear. In this way, he also becomes an imitator of Christ, of whom it was said: *“He shall reign in the house of Jacob, who, participating both in the benevolence of Abraham and in the terror of Isaac, possessed a tempered moderation.”* And with both these royal insignia, the first man was adorned.
[Marginal note: Adam] Hence, all animals are said to have been brought to him, as to their lord, so that he might give them all suitable names, by which he could call them at will. For they were subject to him by terror and attracted by his gentle mildness. And this lasted until he transgressed and lost his pristine dignity, and from being a lord, he became a most wretched servant. And the more sin is aggravated in man, the more he falls from that dignity, which instilled terror and attracted benevolence, into fear and servitude to others. Hence the first fratricide, who, adding homicide to the sin of his parent which he had contracted, felt himself cast down from that dignity, so much so that, fearing, he said to the Lord: *“Everyone who finds me will kill me.”* For he feared beasts or demons, not men, since the family of humankind was very small: his father, mother, wife, and sister-in-law, whom Lamech later took as his wife, who alone is said to have had two wives among those who lived before the flood. And because he raised up seed for Abel, which
[Marginal note: Cain.] Cain was bound to do, therefore he is said to have killed Cain, the despiser of the sign given by God, so that he might indeed raise up his brother's seed. Because he scorned to do this, he is rightly said to have been killed by Lamech, who raised it up, as a despiser of the law given specifically and later to be promulgated to the people. A great mystery lies hidden here, but let us proceed.
[Marginal note: Noah.] Noah succeeded, who was called righteous in his generations: therefore, let us see with how much favor he was restored to his pristine dignity. Some, not content with art, having become very accurate investigators of nature, studied how to bring about those things which were prepared by nature, applying active principles to passive ones, before the time ordained by nature itself: Whence they were commonly seen to perform miracles: which nevertheless are natural works, with only the anticipation of time intervening.

But those who [Marginal note: Magi.] used to perform these things were called by the Persian word "magi," that is, "wise men": although that name is by some abuse taken for a necromancer by many. For they were wise and knowledgeable of hidden things: among whom were those who, seeing the star at the birth of the Redeemer of the human race—beyond and contrary to the order of nature, which was very well known and familiar to them—concluded (as was right) that someone had been born who would transcend the order and limits of nature. Moved by this, they came from Persia and the regions of the East (that is, however, to the Bethlehemite city of Jerusalem) to adore the child, demonstrated by a wondrous and supernatural prodigy. For those who are called magi first studied medicine: so that they might know what was suitable for expelling cholera, what for phlegm, what for black bile: what for tempering the heart, liver, or stomach, and suchlike. And to do this better, they added astronomy, believing that infirmities, and the natures of herbs, roots, and other medicinal things, could be easily judged from the planets and stars with which they correspond, as we confirm Hermes did. And with him Zoroaster, Charundas, Ostanes, Zamolxis, the Brahmans, the Gymnosophists, and many among the ancients and later ones, whose fame (though they excelled) is obscure. But for many reasons to be passed over here (lest we digress more than is fitting), the knowledge of that natural order and the application of things has been lost. Whence some sought to adjure evil demons by divine names. Others, having become obscene and detestable, wished to consult them by adoring them, a crime indeed punishable by every penalty. But they consulted evil and unclean ones, because the pure and higher powers do not readily present themselves: but await purity of heart, sanctity of life, and the command of God. **Daniel** Sacred writings tell (as we have in Daniel) that Nebuchadnezzar was changed into an ox, not by the enchantments of women,
**Nabuc.** but by the command of God to crush his pride, and that he ate hay for seven
**Regum.** years. Also in the first volume of Kings, we read that a Pythoness, a woman
**Samuel.** who was in Endor, had summoned Samuel the prophet; whom
**Saul.** Saul understood to be truly Samuel, having inquired from him about the outcomes of his affairs, who confirmed all that he had said before he departed from among men. And it was the true spirit of Samuel, easily to be summoned before a full year after his departure from the body,
**Hebræi.** as the Hebrews say, although most interpret the text in different senses.
**Exo.** Also in Exodus it is reported that Pharaoh's magicians had changed rods into serpents,
**Magi** that a multitude of frogs was brought forth, and that water was turned into blood, to the destruction of fish and the loss of the Egyptians. And if magicians, pythonesses, necromancers, sorcerers, and enchanters, and such like, had not truly existed, the oracle of the living God would not have commanded in many places that they be exterminated from the land. But there is a great difference among magicians, or those who work wonders. For there are those who work by ingenuity, art, and learning, supplementing, or accelerating, or augmenting the work of nature, if it is permissible.
**Zoroa.** If it is permissible (I say), because Zoroaster, the inventor of the magical art (as the writings of the Gentiles attest), says in his oracles: "Do not augment fate," that is, do not extend yourself more than what is given from above, or what the series of things demands,
**Gemi.** as his interpreter Gemistus Plethon writes. And these magicians are called wise men, or true philosophers. There are also those who attempt things that transcend human powers and knowledge. And these inquire about things they do not know and cannot do, and demand that they be done by unclean demons, sometimes submitting themselves and adoring them, guilty of a double crime, namely idolatry and the most vile subjection, especially to those (demons) to whom they themselves are by nature far superior. Others, however, adjuring by the power of divine names, compel the demons themselves. And these, although they do not commit the crime of idolatry and abasement, nevertheless expose themselves to manifest dangers, because even if the demons are compelled, they always watch to deceive the one who errs. Others, truly, not content with unclean demons, enlist better and pure intelligences, or God himself immediately, which is given to few or none.
**Moses.** For God spoke even to Moses, the greatest of all prophets, through angels,
**Paulus** as Paul says: "The law was given through angels by the hand of a mediator." But because the angel was acting in God's stead, therefore, speaking, he said: "I am Adonai," which is the four-letter name, appropriate only to God.
**Abrahā.** To Abraham also (as we read in Genesis) angels spoke, foretelling Sarah's conception and the burning of the Pentapolis, although Abraham, adoring the sender, said "Adonai" to the messengers, which name was more appropriate to the sender than to those sent. And what the angels did for those fathers, the power of Christ works for us, who (as we have said) drew all divine powers to himself, and who has a name to which every knee bows, and every name of celestial, terrestrial, and infernal beings. Hence it has been commanded to us that we do all things in that name. For in our time no other way of performing miracles has been left to us.

What are natural works, and what are false, and what are true miracles, and what is legitimate power to rule. Chapter X.

[Decorative initial C] Since therefore (as we have said) some are content, as much as art, ingenuity, and our nature permits, to unite the world and apply active principles to passive ones, these are called wise men, true philosophers, or mages, exploring the secrets of nature and the symbols of things. Nor are these to be held worthy of censure or any injury, but of all veneration: whom the Lord of all wished to have as witnesses and supporters of His most blessed nativity. But when they consult evil demons, imploring their help to bring about things which neither art nor human ingenuity permits: then whatever things are accomplished by their favor, those are not miracles, but deceptions: because they happen either only according to appearance, or to the harm of those who undertake them, or who perform them. For asses appear, or horses, or any other animals, seen as transformed only by fascinated and deluded eyes. Hence that woman, who was judged a mare by the common people, to Hilarion she appeared a woman, as she was. Indeed, we confirm many obstacles brought about or removed by God, angels, and demons: for sometimes they disturb the eyes of those looking, and sometimes the medium through which they look. For demons stand (as we have learned by clear experience) before ten or twenty people, seen only by one or two, but not at all by others. And this is because they hide themselves at will, and present themselves as visible at will. Likewise, many will judge an ass, a lion, or a rooster, a goat, or a man to be present. But others see absolutely nothing: and this happens by the art and illusion of evil demons. But let us come to the heavenly beings. When Elisha was besieged by the army of the king of Syria surrounding Dothan, his servant feared, seeing chariots and horsemen around the city: To whom Elisha said: Do not fear, there are more with us than against us. And when he prayed to the Lord, that He would open the eyes of his servant, behold, he saw a mountain full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha. Praying again against the enemies, that the faculty of seeing might be taken away from them, he was also immediately heard. Wherefore, just as the eyes of the boy were opened by his prayer, so the eyes of the enemies were closed, so that they could see nothing: and made blind, they were led by Elisha saying: This is not the way, nor the city: follow me, and I will show you the man whom you seek. And he led them into Samaria. When they had entered it, Elisha prayed again, saying: Open, O Lord, the eyes of these, that they may see. At his prayer, the Lord opened their eyes, and they saw that they were in Samaria. Which the holy man by no means sought to the harm of the Assyrians: but to the glory of his God. For when the king of Israel wished to strike them, he said: By no means: for you did not capture them with your sword: but set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink, and go to their master. Behold how, at the prayer of the man of good accord, the visual faculty was increased beyond natural limits in the boy: and diminished in the Assyrians and again restored. But let us return whence we digressed. Therefore, some apparent miracles have been performed by soothsayers and illusionists, by whatever name they may be called,

Some things were also done by the art of demons, either by transferring, as we have already said about harvests moved to other fields: or by applying active to passive [forces], just as when Pharaoh's magicians enchanted, frogs and flies were brought forth, made by demons by bringing about in a short time what would have required a long time to achieve: or by transmuting: just as they did, converting waters into blood. And concerning prophetic women transmuting many things, it has been said. But they neither confer any benefit, nor can they do things that are above nature. For frogs, flies, and blood were to the detriment of their Egyptians. But those things which are performed above nature, and for a benefit, are called true miracles. Moses therefore, by God's command, by bringing forth lice, for which there was no material to be approximated, performed a miracle. Moreover, by bringing forth water from the rock, manna
[Marginal note: David] from heaven, preserving the people from sickness, as the Psalmist sings: "And there was no one sick among their tribes." Also the preservation of garments, so that they were not worn out, and many such things were true miracles: Some of which, even if performed to the detriment, indeed as punishment for the unbelief of the Egyptians and their stubbornness, nevertheless redounded to the benefit of the liberated people. But the illusions of the Egyptians were for no one's benefit. Elijah and Elisha performed miracles, raising the dead, multiplying oil and flour, healing the sick, and such things. But above all, Christ performed miracles, commanding as the true Lord of all things: and always for benefit, but never for harm. And what his followers have done in his name has already been spread throughout the whole world by famous report, and we have touched upon it above. From this, indeed, it seemed that in those immediate, or close, disciples of his was the true kingdom of God, which he had promised to give: indeed, which he had given, when he said: "The kingdom of God is within you:" And again: "Behold, I have given you power over all hostile and resisting power, namely: For friendly power you will easily have at your beck and call."
[Marginal note: CHRIST] He, therefore, restored to us the lost kingdom: provided that, being well-tuned, we follow his footsteps with a straight and perfect pace.

A well-tuned person is heard in his desires, whatever he may ask for. Chapter XI.

[Marginal note: The same] There exists a saying of the Highest Truth. "Whatever you ask the Father, it will be done for you." But to whom this will be done must be considered, for he says. "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them," afterwards he adds: "Concerning whatever they agree upon, those namely who are gathered and have come together in my name, it will be done for them." A great, indeed, and very clear word. Gathering and agreement must precede for those who are about to obtain [something]. Agreement, indeed, is not only of two or three people: But (as Origen rightly understands) the concord of two is that of the animal man with the spiritual: but the concord of three is that of both of them with God. And this is that temperament which

we seek out, indeed what God himself expects from all: if he is to receive pleasing and sweet prayers. For then man, like a well-tuned lyre, renders every voice and sound of his work pleasing and most sweet to God, so much so that He himself, resounding among them, provides strength and energy, so that prayers may be pleasing and effective to the paternal source of all good things, from whom all good things are drawn, and whatever is asked is obtained.

Here the prayer of Moses, or Moses praying, prevailed so much that he changed the divine sentence. [Marginal note: Moses.] And God saying, "Leave me alone, that my wrath may burn against them, and I may destroy them, and make you into a great nation:" Moses did not care about the promised exaltation, already in harmony and united with God, but about His glory, from which he prayed, saying: "Let not (I pray) your wrath burn against this people, lest the Egyptians say: 'He led them out cunningly, to kill them in the mountains, and to destroy them from the earth.' Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: 'I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and all this land, of which I have spoken, I will give to your seed: and they shall possess it.'" Hence the Lord was appeased, hearing Moses praying, as a true, faithful, and well-attuned servant, who, zealous for the Lord's honor, put forward those things which the nations could bring to the Lord's injury, and brought up the oath already given, lest ill-wishers accuse Him of infidelity in His promise. And this one, so well-tuned with God, had such power with Him that he overcame Him, so that He could not punish the rebels against Moses' judgment and consent. Hence He said: "Leave me alone:" And what is wonderful, God came into Moses' judgment, lest He should disagree with him who was so well-tuned with Him.

Through Isaiah also He made known to Hezekiah the sentence already passed, that he should set his house in order, as he was soon to die. [Marginal note: Isaiah Hezekiah. GOD.] Hezekiah prayed and wept, so that the Lord immediately changed the sentence, and through the same prophet signified, saying: "I have seen your tears, and I have heard your prayer. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your days, and I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians: and I will protect it." Hezekiah prays for himself, and not only obtains for himself, but also for the city and the people to be delivered from the Assyrians. And by what virtue (I ask) was he supported, or by what reason strengthened? Certainly because he had felt himself well-tuned with God. Hence he said: "Remember (I pray) how I have walked before you in truth, and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes."

The Lord had delivered Drusiana, an Ephesian woman, to death, and her corpse was already being carried to the tomb. At the insistence of the supplicating people, John prays: and he calls her back to life again, deferring the sentence already pronounced, to another time, emulating his Master, who, recalling the lethal sentence of Lazarus, already stinking, prolonged the interrupted life for a longer period, with a prayer poured out to the Father.

Paul prays for those suffering the onslaught of the raging sea, and delivers them from imminent shipwreck, the Lord Himself granting them. Clement prayed, and the Lord opened a fountain of living water for all who were on the island to which they had been exiled with him. Catherine, seeing the torment of wheels prepared for her, with her eyes raised to heaven, silently prayed—
