...prayed, and that mass was shattered with a violent impact. This is because he was a faithful vicar of Christ, and she a most united bride. There are innumerable examples which prove that the prayers of the faithful, and of those well-tuned with God, are heard according to their wishes. But since all proof stands in the mouth of two or three, these few out of many suffice.

Only man, well-tuned with God, lives happily. Chapter XII.

**A**nd it is indeed wonderful that, while all seek to live happily, nevertheless very few attain it. This is because they seek outside themselves the happiness placed within themselves: For within us is the kingdom of God, within us is true joy and happiness, provided that we receive the guest, from whom comes all happiness and blessedness, according to what he says: "If anyone opens, I will enter and dine with him," that most happy and eternal supper, namely. Nor is there any other door through which we can enter except He himself, to whom we enter, and whom we receive coming into us through reciprocal love, and a man well-tuned, by which we not only converse with Him and He with us, but we are united with that joy, than which no greater can be expected.

And just as it is the greatest sorrow, and a pledge of Tartarean punishments, to disagree with oneself, and consequently with God: so true happiness is harmony with both.

But what sorrow there is for the discordant and impious, Trismegistus explains in "Clavis ad Latium," saying: "Impiety, my son, is the soul's gravest torment: For there is no flame of any fire more ardent than impiety: Nor does any fiercer beast so lacerate the body, as impiety, which is discord from God and oneself, lacerates the soul. Do you not see by how many evils the impious soul is oppressed? Alas, my son, thus cries out the wicked soul: 'I burn, I am consumed, I know not what to do, what to say. Evils flowing in from all sides devour me, wretched as I am.'" However, Proclus assigns the reason for these torments in "On the Soul and the Daemon," saying: "The wicked man cannot agree with himself, and, being at odds with himself, he cannot agree with others. Hence it is clear that from a disturbed imagination he is ignorant of many things, and, disagreeing with himself, he is tormented." Repentance, coming when disturbances are dismissed, declares this; in it, he blushes and is tormented by those things which, blinded by pleasure, he cannot recognize while committing them.

I will add that saying of Hierocles in "Pythagorean Verses": "Fools are afflicted on all sides by their vices and by the deprivation of divine affection." And because they refuse to adhere to the good, hence minds are carried towards evil affections in this life, as if into storms. In these matters, the heavenly oracle through Jeremiah makes us cautious with paternal love, while it says: "My people have committed two evils: They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that can hold no water." They have also changed their glory into an idol: For the glory, good, and happiness of man is to adhere to God. But he makes an idol who, neglecting God, worships himself or something viler, with great discord and disordered arrangement. And since tranquility arises from order, he who lacks order also lacks tranquili-

**THIRD CANTICLE**
**WHAT SPIRIT IS. Chapter One.**

[Decorative initial C containing an illustration of a scholar at a desk] Since the entire evangelical law deals with perfecting man according to the spirit, always concerned with spiritual matters, it is therefore right and opportune that we should discuss something about the spirit: which is understood so variously in sacred scripture that it is comprehended with no small difficulty what it is. For it is among the most recondite things of nature, and nothing about it is to be discussed except what we can infer from sacred scripture, edited by the principal and chief spirit, or deduce from the characters of the word of that language in which all names were imposed on things according to their properties. For the Hebrews call spirit [Marginal note: Hebrews.] רוח Ruah. In this word there are three letters. One is ו (Vav), which is the letter of divinity, signifying the number six, according to which the supreme spirit itself, the artificer of all things, first brooding over the fertile waters, arranged (as was fitting) this whole machinery of the world. For the principle of all things is threefold, going forth into work, adorning, and cherishing, and each of these through an intermediate spirit, from which the number six results in the greatest unity. Hence the most recondite theo [Marginal note: Theologians of the Hebrews.] logians of the Hebrews said that letter of divinity, which is ו (Vav), signifying beginning and end—since it is the end of numbers and the beginning of tens—has six barbs: because in that respect, in which God himself is the principle, signified by that letter, it is a ternary: from whom, in whom, and through whom are all things. But in that respect in which it is director, cherisher, and restorer, it rejoices in another ternary, namely a spiritual one: not because [Marginal note: Abraham.] there are three spirits of God (although Abraham in the book of formation says spirit from spirit) but because its operation is threefold, according to which the royal prophet in the [Marginal note: David] fiftieth psalm calls it the principal spirit, the right spirit, and the holy spirit. Therefore, in that word and name, there is the letter of divinity, which is ו (Vav). There is also another letter of life, which is ח (Chet). For life is called חי (chai). The third is ר (Resh), which signifies two hundreds, and matter, or a certain corporeality: For the bi [Marginal note: Jerome.] nary (number two) signifies matter, hence (according to Jerome) it is always inauspicious, unless joined with another number it is made fortunate: For the material, when associated with life and divinity, [Marginal note: Canticle.] is fortunate. For the two hundreds signified by ר (Resh) are those about whom it is spoken in the Canticles. Where, after א (Aleph), and one, and a thousand are attributed to divinity, it is added: "And two hundred to those who guard its fruits:" For we are placed as guardians in the vineyard of the Lord with a binary corporeality. Where if we guard the fruitful precepts of the Lord: finally we shall be united with Aleph itself, prepared for all truly peaceful things, and with Him who has peace in Himself. The spirit, therefore, is a certain bond, binding and connecting two extremes together: itself vivifying and strengthening, according to the condition of the uniting spirit. Hence it partakes of the nature of the two extremes which are united, and of its own connecting middle, as is hinted at by the letters of its name already explained. For it vivifies since it contains life within itself, whence it is sometimes called the spirit of life. Cor-

--- Page 908 ---
TONE FIVE. 384

but it strengthens, giving power to operate, according to that of the Apostle: To be strengthened by his spirit. [Marginal note: Paul.] And concerning Samson it is read in the book of Judges: The spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson, [Marginal note: Samson] and he tore the lion apart. And whatever strength proceeds in a living being comes from the spirit of life, which is in it: But the spirit of man is a certain bond, and a medium partaking of intellectual and corporeal nature, binding and connecting the animal and coarser soul with the intellectual faculty, which is called the higher part. Indeed, the spirit is corporeal, yet not having a gross, tangible, or visible body, according to that of the highest truth: Feel and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones. [Marginal note: CHRIST.] But that body is most subtle, and easily unifiable with the higher mind, and with that divine [part] which is in us. Hence, those who become divine are called spiritual by a common and ordinary name, because their endeavor is to lead the body into the nature of the spirit tending towards the divine. Or because they strive to be led back into God Himself through the spirit of God: Hence it is clearly inferred that the spirit differs from the supreme soul, which is called intellect, mind, light, and the higher part: and also differs from the animal [soul], from which the Apostle teaches to separate by the power of the word of God, saying: For the word of God is living [Marginal note: Paul] and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit. For the word of God teaches that we remove all rational affection, which pertains to the spirit, from concupiscence and animal pleasure: and lead it back into God through that supreme and divine [part] which is in us by the grace of God: with which the spirit ought to be united not only by affection, but in reality itself. Nor can it be entirely united with the higher [part], unless it is separated from the lower [part]: just as fire proceeding from wood is not united with the higher and ethereal fire, unless it is separated from the coarser subject. But that which is separated, is also distinguished. And if they say that the spirit is the rational soul, we indeed grant it: For it is a certain medium (as it pleases Plotinus and the Academics) [Marginal note: Plotin. Academ.] between the lower animal [part] and the divine, which is higher, connecting both, and unifiable with both. But lest readers be offended, while they hear that the soul is something corporeal, we say that it has, or partakes of, something of corporeality, while it is in the body, and uses the body, as a necessary instrument for itself. But if it is entirely separated from the body, it is united with that higher divine [part], indeed with God Himself, with all corporeality entirely removed: finally drawing with itself the body, which is glorified, of which it was the immediate form. And since the soul itself is the medium leading the body into a better state, it is necessary that it partakes of the nature of both. And this is as much as we can say about our spirit at present.

How many kinds of spirit there are. Chapter II.

[Illuminated initial E] AND because spirits are found not only in man, but also in other things: therefore let us explain the various natures of spirits. For there is a natural spirit, celestial, demonic, human, angelic, and divine. The natural spirit is both in the greater world and in the lesser world that medium by which one member operates upon another. In man there is the power of imagi-

--- Page 909 ---
THIRD CANTICLE

...native, or fantastic, power in the head, so that it moves the hand or foot, and it is immediately moved: although it is quite distant from the head, where that cogitative power is. How this happens is through multiple spirits, which are between the head and the hand or foot. Concerning these natural, or vital, spirits, authors of medicine discuss much: which we leave to be read in their books. For through them the soul is united with the flesh and body, whence it lives: and through the body itself, by means of those spirits, the soul operates.

In the same way, there is a manifold spirit in this lower mundane body: through which one thing operates on another: just as a magnet on iron, attracting it: and multiple stones on humans, gladdening, strengthening, and inducing multiple dispositions: and whatever operates on another, not only by means of primary qualities intervening, but from a (as they say) hidden virtue. Since this is a medium, so that one thing operates on another, it can rightly be called a spirit.

There is also a celestial spirit, by means of which lower things are bound with the heavens: so that from them, through that spirit, they may draw and receive celestial influences. There is also an evil demonic spirit, and a good angelic spirit, both given to every human. Whose office it is to seek union with our spirit, so that each may call forth and draw it to themselves. But the evil one strives to render those who are similar and united to himself through evil works: as the highest Truth testifies concerning the traitor, saying:
[CHRIST.] "I have chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil," that is, turned into a diabolical spirit through his iniquity, and united with it and made the same: For these spirits are mixed together like water and wine, or two wines, or two waters together. But the good one, through good works and those symbolic of himself, strives to lead us into angels: as God testifies concerning John in
[Malachi.] Malachi: "Behold (he says) I send my angel before your face."

Finally, there is the divine spirit, which by sacred and true doctors is called the bond, binding namely our soul with God himself, first made one with that spirit,
[Paul.] according to that Apostolic saying: "He who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him." And this is the consummated union, which finally we hope to attain. And because all things must finally be reduced to their principle, from which they proceeded: because all things are through Him, from whom all things emanated (as
[The Same.] the Apostle teaches) therefore that spirit, by whom brooding over the waters all things were brought into light, is required, so that by the same they may also be reduced to that from which they came forth. Hence concerning Him it is said: "The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world": And again. "And the spirit of his mouth, all their power":
[Wisdom.] For by Him not only the heavens, but this entire universal machine is sustained, lives, is strengthened, strives, and finally is reduced to where all things tend. But this divine spirit is entirely absolved from all corporeality, and is like a consuming fire, melting, converting, and leading those whom it touches into its own nature, and making them divine. And until it completely deifies them, it always flows into them, and pervades them, being a fire and a channel through which it flows.

**FIFTH TONE.** [Page number:] **385**
**What the spirit does in man beyond the soul. Chapter III.**

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.5; vertical-align: -0.2em; display: inline-block;">V</span>erum if we wish to follow the Peripatetic dogma, from which we have that man is composed solely of soul and body, it will be difficult to explain what the spirit is, and what it does in man beyond the soul, since both are considered by them to be the same. If, however, we listen to the Platonists and the Hebrews, [Marginal notes: Platon. Hebræi Plotinus Paulus] who distinguish those things and place more in man, we will easily write down what the spirit is, and what it does: for Plotinus places three things in man: the supreme, the lowest, and the middle. The supreme is that divine (part), which our (authors) call the superior portion. The lowest is what Paul calls the animal man. The middle is the soul, or the spirit connecting both. All Hebrews call these three: נפש רוח נשמה nephes ruah nessamah. [Marginal note: Hebræi] Which we, interpreted, call the soul, the spirit, and a certain divine (part), for which we have no more suitable word than the superior portion: or as we have translated in Genesis, the breath, [Marginal note: Genesis] breathed into us by God, namely, or by His spirit. Which, united with the lower soul through our spirit, the whole is called by the common word, נפש nephes, that is, soul. Therefore, that middle (part) is what Plotinus calls the rational (part), [Marginal note: Plotinus] and the Hebrews call the spirit, but our (authors) call the soul, from the mixture it has with it. That supreme (part) also always prays for the best, never sinning, but murmuring against sin and error. The lowest (part) is always immersed in evil and concupiscence, according to what the apostle says: [Marginal note: Paulus] "I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin: so that I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want." But the middle spirit, which is also called the rational soul by Plotinus, [Marginal note: Plotinus] can adhere to either at will. But adhering to the superior (part), it merits (reward); and adhering to the inferior (part), it turns itself away from God. But that superior (part), since it never assents to sin, never sins at all; therefore it is neither damned but departs unharmed from its punishable companions, just as when a window is closed, the sunlight departs, leaving the space dark: thus, with that light departing, the soul and spirit remain, to be cast into inner darkness, [Marginal note: CHRISTVS] to which outer darkness will be added, according to that testimony of the Supreme Truth concerning the damned: "Go into outer darkness." And because man performs a twofold work through that superior (part): namely, he understands God, and merits (reward) by doing good: hence, with that (part) departing, he can neither understand God nor merit anything. Therefore, he becomes impenitent, never to return to God. But the middle soul, which I believe to be the same as the spirit, either consents to that superior (part), and merits (reward), and is finally united with it, and made happy: or consents to the inferior (part) drawing towards evil, and agitated by an evil demon, and then merits badly (i.e., punishment): and is so depraved that it becomes the same as the evil demon itself. Therefore, the spirit differs from the power of the superior and inferior soul, though capable of being united with both at will: but proceeding on the proper path, it must be separated from the inferior, and united with the superior.

**What covenant man has with the Spirit of God. Chapter 4.**

It also has a very great connection with that divine [part] which is in man. Hence the disciples were better taught by the Holy Spirit, as if by a nearer person, and having a clearer connection with man, than by him who

**What man has with the diabolical spirit. Chapter VI.**

[Large decorative initial H] Man (as Mercury testifies), consisting of all powers, has commerce with all: from intellect with the supernal and good; from matter with the infernal and evil. [Marginal note: Mercury.] Hence Michael, prince of good spirits, [Marginal note: Michael.] is said to have dominion over all souls already expiated and to be received by God; and the evil demon, the ancient serpent Azazel, or As

--- Page 913 ---
**THIRD CANTICLE.**

had proclaimed before, was saying: "Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." Nor is a dwelling less to be prepared than a way, and both must be arranged with rectitude, since the guest who is to dwell there is supreme truth and rectitude. But the evil demon, being by nature false and crooked, procures that things be arranged for himself with error and falsehood. Nor is the dwelling of our heart ever left empty: for when one guest departs, another immediately enters, as it is said of Saul [Marginal note: Saul.] in the first book of Kings: "The spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul, and an evil spirit tormented him, sent by the Lord, as the order of things required." As it is also held in the Gospel, which is titled "according to Luke," [Marginal note: Lucas.] concerning that man possessed by an unclean spirit, which, having been expelled, the world entered. The expelled one, returning here to re-enter, cannot do so until, through the uncleanness brought in by seven more evil [Marginal note: Paulus.] spirits, the good guest is put to flight: Once he is put to flight, the evil ones entered. For neither God, angel, nor demon dwells in anyone, or does anything with him, except through spiritual power. Hence Paul, after remembering many things which God bestows and works with us, adds: "But all these are produced by one and the same Spirit." Which, however, is sometimes (as we touched upon above) called the Spirit of the Father, according to that saying of the Savior: [Marginal note: CHRI- STVS] "But the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." Sometimes it is called the Spirit [Marginal note: Paulus. Act. apo.] of the Son, concerning which the apostle says, addressing the Galatians: "God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts." Sometimes it is spirit from spirit: as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: "All were filled with the Holy Spirit:" Which, however, did not depart from its dignity and deity: but by a certain spiritual power sanctified and deified the spirit of the apostles whom it had infused.

What harmony is to be established between spirit and soul. Chapter VIII.

**T**herefore, in order that a good spirit, whether angelic or divine, may be introduced into us, a harmony must be established between spirit and soul, not indeed that [soul] which is the same as spirit, but with a better one. From which harmony it may at last come to union with it, and as a medium may draw down with itself that which is inferior, transmuted into spirit, to a better lot. For just as in the art of transmutation (as the more secret [Marginal note: Philoso] philosophers say) there is a medium, as it were a certain spirit clothed, and first imbibing the nature of gold, afterwards by a certain immense and very swift force draws other metals into gold. And because the spirit of man is transmutable into diverse natures, hence the Chaldeans said that man is an animal of a dissolutory nature, having no determined [Marginal note: Chaldei.] image, but very many adventitious and extraneous ones. For the spirit is transmuted not only into a superior and inferior nature, which are in man, but into a demon, an angel, and God, as we have touched upon. And when transmuted into a better lot, it draws down the inferior with itself, it refines this by itself, just as gold is refined when drawn through a very narrow opening: so that it may be drawn out like a silken or linen thread at will, and from animal become spiritual. Hence not without mystery רוח, which is spirit, with letters inverted, by 'sirup' in the manner of the Cabala

--- Page 914 ---
SIXTH TONE. 387

mystically renders `חור hur`, which signifies a hole, through which passing, the
animal body becomes spiritual, so that, united with the higher, it may be beatified.
And this happens when the spirit is first united with that divine, and higher [part].
But if, falling, it is glued to the lower [part], then through it, as through the
holes of a sieve, it distills, and whatever can be corrupted from the higher [part]
is lost. If therefore man desires to become divine, it is necessary that his spirit
agree with that divine [part] which is in him, into which he may finally lead back
the lower soul, first having been made spiritual. But we make the spirit consonant
with that divine [part], when, obedient, it adheres to that which is called synderesis,
always murmuring against evil, and imploring for good. Consenting to which, and
in no way disagreeing, there follows in man peace, and tranquility, and thence
joy of heart, jubilation of mind, and the pledge of blessedness: so that he may

**CANTICLE THE THIRD**
**MAN BY NATURE EMULATES GOD.**
**Chapter One.**

[Large decorative initial P] OUR purpose being to explain in what way man agrees with God and is assimilated to Him, as we are persuaded and invited in many places, we have deemed it opportune to repeat with what image of Himself the supreme Creator produced man. For it is already a commonplace to everyone that man was made in the image of God and brought to His likeness. But in what this image consists (with due respect to those who have written about this), since it has not yet been clearly explained, let us investigate. For it is said by common and old-wives' doctrine that the three divine persons are represented in the three powers of the soul: memory, intellect, and will. Nor indeed can this be called an image, whose role is to represent the whole and the complete likeness, as is most excellently determined by our more perspicacious theologians. But it is the role of a trace (vestige) to represent not the full image, but some aspect or part of it. And although the whole divinity is comprehended in the three persons, and also in the very nature of deity, yet more things can be explained in God which man most fully represents in other parts than in the aforesaid three powers. Hence, some more acute among the newer theologians, not content with that simple assigned reason of the image, say that it consists not only in those three powers, or (to speak in their manner) in primary acts only, but also in secondary ones. For there is in us intellect, memory, and will: and these same three represent in God. Moreover, there is a word produced by our intellect, and love emanating from the will, by the former of which the divine Word, and by the latter the Holy Spirit, who is a certain love, is signified. But the intellect, having a present object and producing, portrays the Father. But this image in man falls short of the portrayed God no less than a painted image of a man falls short of the true man himself. For the word produced in us, and likewise love, which are called secondary acts by them, are accidents in us; but in God they are substance, and identical with God Himself. And memory, which in us is the recollection of past things, in God is the most complete intuition of all past, present, and future things. But we can still hunt for a more expressive image of God in man, comparing to God not only the soul, but the whole man, in whom shines forth every kind of image of God Himself. Therefore, God is full life, vivifying all members of the mundane body. There is also in the soul a certain fount of life, emanating from the supreme and divine sea, and bestowing life upon all members of its own body according to their condition. Hence it is said in the sacred page: "And He breathed into his nostrils the breath, or soul, of lives," so that it may provide life to the body.
[Marginal note: Scotists]

--- Page 916 ---
TONVS SEXTVS. 388

vegetative, sensitive, rational, intellectual, and divine. God is [marginal note: Salom.] by His power containing all things; and of man, the Wise Man says in his discourse: God made man dust from the earth, and gave him the power of containing all things. God knew all things. Man also can know all knowable things, since for an adequate object (as theologians and philosophers say) he has truth, [marginal note: Theolo. Philoso.] or being in common; but the image differs from that which is imaged: He understands all things by a single act, but man by a certain succession. Moreover, God is a certain circle, drawing origin from nowhere else than from Himself, and tending towards Himself, He leads all things thither with Him. Man is also a circle proceeding from God, and tending towards Him: leading all things thither since he contains all things. Nor does he ever rest until he reaches God Himself, from whom he proceeded. He also emulates God Himself as far as he can in duration. But since he cannot have the entire possession of his duration at once, he endures at least by perpetual succession; and he is so similar and (so to speak) connatural with God, that at last he is united with Him: as we shall declare in its proper place, God favoring. Finally, God is free from passions, except insofar as He suffered in the assumed body: no passion indeed passing to God Himself; just as He does not undergo passion when (as Jeremiah says) filling heaven and earth, He is altered in the members of the mundane body which He fills. [marginal note: Ieremię.] In which sense perhaps not foolishly can be understood all those sayings by which God is said to be angry, to repent, to grieve, to desire, and the like. For He does not repent: except insofar as it appears in the members, or things, which He fills: from which, when He withdraws Himself and turns away His face, all things are disturbed: and empty of the vivifying God, they return to their dust: so that those members, indeed God in them, seem to grieve, to be sad, and to be indignant, and to repent: that is, ceasing from His accustomed influence. But when His spirit returns, which fills the whole orb of the earth, all things are recreated and seem to rejoice. Nor does our soul behave differently, concerning which Aristotle and Plotinus say, [marginal note: Aristote. Plotin.] whoever says the soul grieves or rejoices: he said it weaves or spins. Therefore the soul does not rejoice or grieve: just as it neither weaves nor spins: except insofar as it is joined to the body. For it is characteristic of the animal (as Plotinus follows) to suffer and to act, but not of the rational soul, nor of the intellect: but it is the role of these to direct the animal which acts: just as it is God's role to moderate the world, whose members are secondary causes operating with such agitations and passions. Nor is any disposition found in man, but that something of divinity shines forth in it, nor is there anything in God that is not represented in man: but let us come to the figure.

**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**
**Man portrays the archetype in figure. Chapter II.**

[Large decorative initial S] If, however, man is to contain the true image, it is necessary that he possess a figure similar to it. But alas, where do we enter? What figure shall we assign to Him who is enclosed by no boundaries, figured by no lines, painted with no colors? Hence, with such diligence, it is provided by divine law that no image whatsoever should be made, neither of God Himself, nor of any heavenly things: lest visible creatures be adored through those idols: and also lest that which cannot be depicted be falsely expressed. But even if no figure can be derived, nor any found in lower things, in which the likeness or image of God may be recognized: nevertheless, supported by the testimony of God, in man we shall seek out His likeness and figure, at least through a certain analogy, by which indeed the supreme artificer Himself deigned to ascribe it to Himself, just like all the divisions and members of the human body.

For He said He has a right hand, as
[Marginal note: David] is sung in the Davidic psalm: The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand. He also has a left hand, to which the wicked to be condemned will be placed at the last judgment. He is also said to sit sometimes like a man, as it says in Isaiah:
[Marginal note: Isaiah] Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. He is also said to walk in Genesis towards midday, or the coming of the Day. And concerning His eternal journeys, the Psalmist says: They have seen your goings, O God, the
[Marginal note: David] goings of my God and my King who is in the sanctuary. Which steps and journeys sometimes cause terror: so that by them (as Habakkuk testifies) the mountains

With His heart, He loves us most tenderly. With His breast, He receives us, and embracing us most dearly, He cherishes us. His back: which sometimes turning, He shows Himself indignant; and sometimes shining in created things, He offers Himself to us for contemplation, just as He said to Moses, "you shall see my back parts." With the feet of His affections, He sometimes comes to us; and sometimes, our sins demanding it, He departs. Behold then how God has shown Himself similar to us in all things; indeed, making us, He has rendered us conformable to Himself in members and figure, if there is any in Him. For it is, but not confined by any limits, nor circumscribed by lines; but it is the fountainhead and origin of all properties and figures. Which members (as we have said) He puts on better garments than ours are clothed with. A body is no less fitting for God clothed than for Him naked, pure and unadorned matter. Chapter III.

[Large decorative initial E] We have already explained above how harmoniously matter, the purest potentiality first created, corresponds to God, the purest act, and the first cause of all things. Now is to be explained that correspondence which man, the most perfect work of God and the most renowned of the entire mundane machine, has with God Himself, now clothed with all perfections, which are internal or external (as they say). Nor should this unusual mode of speaking about the garments of God among our theologians terrify anyone, since we have from sacred scripture, the mother and fount of all theologians, most ample attestations concerning these very garments. David sings in the ninety-second psalm: "The Lord has reigned, He is clothed with beauty; the Lord is clothed with strength, and has girded Himself with power." [Marginal note: David] Moreover, the theologians of the Hebrews enumerate up to ten garments, not without mystery. I would not believe them, unless that same sacred scripture taught me. For they assert God to be naked when He Himself (blessed be His name) is considered in His solitary nature, entirely removed from every relation (as they say) arriving intrinsically and extrinsically; and as He is supremely "this." Who, as He is understood thus remote, speaks in Isaiah, saying, "אני יהוה הוא שמי Ani adonai hu semi." [Marginal note: Isaiah.] Which we have interpreted as: "I am the Lord, this is my name," but it would be better said: "That very thing, namely, which is my name." For that "hu" (הוא) is not something relative referring, but a word importing that very thing which is supremely "this." Who, as such, communicates Himself to no one, therefore it follows: "My glory, which I have in my supreme unity, I will not give to another." He, therefore, supremely "this," before He diffused Himself into creatures, begot the Son, with whom He simultaneously produced the Holy Spirit. When therefore He decided to generate the Son,

Since in man there are the lowest, the highest, and the intermediate, all things are easily reconciled with God through man himself. Chapter IV.

**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

Why the soul has been placed in the body, as if in a melting pot, to be purified before it returns to Him from whom it came. Chapter 5.

[Large initial S] But before the soul returns to this unity with God, it is enclosed in the body, so that it may perfect it: and may be perfected by it. And I do not know whether it perfects first, or rather is perfected, or whether both happen simultaneously. And perhaps both are perfected simultaneously in those who proceed well and rightly. The soul is (say our Peripatetics and theologians) in the body as a form perfecting the body itself: not indeed giving only movement, and the power of sensing, vegetating, and understanding: but perfecting and purifying it: so that it may be able to be transformed into a better state. Nor does it dispose the body to be transmuted, unless it itself has been purified. For not all of us will be transmuted (says the apostle) although all of us will rise again. But only the bodies of those will be transmuted whose souls are found purified. The soul, therefore, has been placed in this body as in a melting pot, to be melted down and purified by the fire of charity, and by the divine [fire] poured throughout the whole person by the grace of the infuser, and according to the disposition of the recipient, with sacrifices and sacraments especially intervening. Hence, that supreme sacrifice having been offered, to which all other things assist and yield, by the high priest JESUS, redeemer of the human race, that fiery Spirit was sent, for melting, purifying, and forging the hearts of the disciples, and of those who were to believe through them. Nor did any space of time intervene after that supreme sacrifice had been offered, except fifty days: a number indeed suitable for sending that fiery spirit. And He would not have been sent, unless the Son of God had been offered as a sacrifice, He himself testifying, who says: Unless I depart, offered, that is, to the Father as a burnt offering, the Paraclete will not come to you. And this sacrifice was indeed often prefigured in the old law: And that when, a sacrifice having been offered, fire was expected from heaven, which, coming, and the sacrifice already kindled and changed into fire, would lead it back with great mystery to the sublime place from which it had come: and would pour that fire upon the offerers, about which it is said in Deuteronomy: God is a devouring fire, or one who eats and consumes. For just as one eating consumes food, and changes its substance into himself: so God, accepting the true sacrifice of one offering it duly, is nourished both by the sacrifice and by the offerer, transforming both into Himself. But the true sacrifice, which we ought to offer together with the sacrifice offered by the high priest Christ Jesus, is that each person, according to apostolic teaching, offer himself as a living, immaculate, holy, God-pleasing victim with rational service. And thus not only souls will ascend into God Himself: but also the mortal and corruptible body, putting on (as the same apostle says) incorruption and immortality: And then it will be a true burnt offering, that is, consumed by that divine fire which transmutes all things. But the Hebrews [call] this sacrifice עולה hola, that is, ascending

Why God placed the soul and a changeable mind here. Chapter VI.

[Decorative initial E] And since the soul is in this melting pot for the purpose of being purified and perfected, some, even lesser ones, whose constant endeavor is to strike down their superiors with their own judgments and words, wonder why God sent the soul here, not only changeable, but also to be continuously assailed by a most bitter enemy. And as if constituting themselves as God's counselors with impudent rashness, these bats dare to accuse the highest light and highest wisdom. But let dust and ashes blush even to name Him: whose beautiful form shines from the rising of the sun to its setting. And if (from the monument of the wise) young people ought to be silent in the midst of great and old men: what are we in the sight of the Ancient of Days, and of Him in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge? Nevertheless, we can, not to accuse: But to be enlightened, ask: why the wisest creator did not make man stable, and continuously proceeding on a straight path. Here Anselm answers: because [Marginal note: Ansel:] he could not. But (to speak better) it was not fitting to make another God: who alone is by nature impeccable and immutable. Alexander attempts to adduce reasons for this saying: [Marginal note: Alex:] Which John Scotus decided to support as weak, yielding however [Marginal note: Ioan. Sc.] more to the opinions of the saints than to his own reasons. Therefore, leaving these as invalid by the judgment of their own author, to be read in his books, we will confess with Augustine to Volusian, [Marginal note: Augusti.] that God can do many things which we are unable to understand, since the whole reason for the deed is the power of the doer: which is infinite, and transcends all human and angelic intellect. Therefore, for the discussion of this matter (as the Lord shall enlighten our eyes) we will say something, presupposing what the order of things requires: which (as Aristotle also teaches) [Marginal note: Aristo.] is twofold in every army, namely, of the soldiers among themselves, and of all of them to the leader and head: if they agree with him, all things are done correctly: but if they disagree, they become discordant and confused. But just as all soldiers can defect from an emperor, however good: so all creatures can defect from God: for there are many distracting objects for us, by which we are carried now to the highest, now to the mediocre, now to the lowest. Now too we are distracted from an inferior good, now from an apparent one, now (as they say) from a predetermined one: And by these continuous games we are deluded: until our heart, always restless, always unstable, is established in the Prince: who alone is stable: whence if we are sometimes made stable: this is not of nature (says Augustine) [Marginal note: Augusti.] but by the grace of Him whose it is to establish all things. How fittingly, however, it has been done, that man has been placed in the field of struggle with a two-edged battle, Gre- [Marginal note: Grego.]

--- Page 925 ---
CANTICLE THE THIRD

Gregory, inspired by the divine spirit, declares: "In the toils of scourges and the struggles of vices, not only does our weakness become known to us, but we also learn how much we advance in virtue. Indeed, no one knows his strengths in peace. For if battles are lacking, the trials of virtues will not profit. He is an improvident soldier who boasts himself strong in peace: For no one knows how much he has progressed, unless [Marginal note: Firmianus.] amidst adversities and uncertainties." To whom Firmianus assents, saying: "Above all, God willed there to be diversity in us, and did not reveal the mystery to the common people, but revealed it to very few. This diversity, however, contains every secret of the world. For this makes virtue, without which one could not only not exist, but not even desire it: because virtue cannot exist unless there is some adversary, in overcoming whom it may either exercise or display its power. For just as victory cannot exist without struggle, so neither can virtue without an enemy. Therefore, when He gave virtue to man, He established an enemy for him on the contrary, lest virtue, languishing in idleness, should lose its nature. The reason for this is that being assailed and undermined, it may be strengthened. Nor could it otherwise reach the highest peak, unless, always stirred by an assailing hand, it should establish itself in the zeal of fighting for its own salvation: For the Lord did not wish that that blessedness and reward be attained by an easy path. Therefore, being about to give virtue, He also gave an enemy, who would inject desires and vices into the minds of men, and hold them in uncertainty, existing as the author of evils and the contriver of all errors: so that while He calls man to life, that one, on the contrary, may seize and lead him to death. Hence our path is left doubtful, the battle uncertain, and very many misfortunes. For that enemy leads astray or deceives those who strive for truth. Or if he cannot by deceit and cunning, he assumes a manly spirit, with which he tries to undermine the vigor of the exalted, contriving things obscene to speak of and execrable, he harasses and kills: And yet, as he overthrows many, so by many he is conquered and overthrown, he departs: For great is the power of man, great his reason, and great his mystery." Origen also, in his 'On First Principles', pursues this matter, saying: "For if God had granted that we could in no way be overcome, what cause for struggle would remain for him who cannot be overcome? Or what merit of the palm, where the reason and faculty of resisting and conquering are not admitted? Therefore, those things are sufficiently good for him which are adverse to him, which, when he has overcome them, become a cause of greater glory for him. For Job received double after the victory over the enemy, who had received power to fight against him. Nor indeed is a crown owed to us, unless a struggle precedes it. For what glory and what praise belongs to the crowned one, unless he has earned it by some race or battle? For this is the condition of earning, that he may prevail from that point whence he could have been shipwrecked. And it is the praise of victory that he conquers from that point whence he [Marginal note: The wise man.] could have been defeated." Hence the wise man praises him who could transgress and did not transgress, do evil and did not do it: His goods shall finally be established in the Lord, so that he may no longer depart from order, peace, and quiet.

TONVS SEXTVS. 393

How man is at variance due to sin. Ch. VII.

[Marginal note: Licentius.]
[Decorative initial C] ONSEQUENTLY, when man often recedes from God, then he errs, sins, and falls short of the order which God values so highly: as the wise Licentius says in Augustine's book 'On Order': "I accept something manifest: but nothing seems to me to happen outside of order: For whatever things are from God, are ordered: But whatever things are apart from God, or without God, or beyond God, are disordered." And consequently, guilt, disorder, dissension, lack of rectitude, defect, sin, and nothingness. But alas, we enter a most foul and dreadful forest, describing that which is nothing: And declaring disorder to be evil in that work which is governed by the supreme moderator ordering all things. Indeed, disorder is evil, and a defect from that which is: and that which is good. Nor is evil a substance: because its being is to be in another. Nor is it an accident: because it is contrary to good, and consequently in the genus of good: since contraries are of the same genus: and true good is a substance in itself. Nor is it an existent thing: because whatever is of this kind has the nature of good. Nor is it above all existent things: because that is God, and the supreme good. Nor is it absolutely nothing: because evil is contrary to good: and vice to virtue. But nothing is not contrary to anything: because things that are contrary are something. Nor is good contrary to itself. Therefore, evil is a medium between being and nothing, having being in which the defect itself exists, founded on the rectitude which ought to be in that which is. Which defect is a certain privation founded in being, but tending towards nothing. Therefore, just as good is above all being: where whatever tends towards it is perfected: so evil is below all being: into which tending, it fails. And just as by thinking of good, which is above all being (as it pleases the [Marginal note: Academics. Dionysius.] Academics and Dionysius), we are finally resolved into being: so also, thinking of evil, we arrive at a certain privation. Therefore, evil in nature is a defect and a privation of natural order and perfection. Hence woman is evil (as [Marginal note: Pythagoras.] Pythagoras used to say) because she falls short of the perfection of man. So too darkness, because it falls short of light: and anything orphaned or monstrous: because it falls short of the order instituted by nature. And evil in morals is a defect from rectitude: which ought to be in the act and operation which we perform: or a dissension from the supreme good, to which we ought to adhere. And it is found in privation, a fugitive from the region of light and being, weak, miserable, tearing, destroying: and not only dissenting from good, but leading away from it.

Just as man falls short of God and is at odds with Him through sin: so through penitence he is brought back and tempered. Ch. VIII.

[Decorative initial D] HEREFORE, man, falling short of God and being at odds with Him through sin, has a unique antidote, that he may return and agree with God Himself. And this is true penitence: which is not (as some assert) the holding of punishment, or sorrow for sins voluntarily assumed, but a return to God, from whom he had receded: as the etymology of a more perfect language indicates: For penitence is called in Hebrew *teshuvah*, which means 'return'. Many, for

**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

who grieve and are tormented by very great punishments because of the sin committed, yet they are neither freed nor justified, because they do not have the antidote for sin, which is to return to God, from whom they departed, and to agree with God, from whom they dissent. Hence the voice of the oracle always thunders to the sinner: "Return, or convert."
[Marginal note: Zechariah. Jeremiah.] "Turn to me" (he says in Zechariah) "and I will turn to you." And through another prophet: "But you have played the harlot with many lovers, nevertheless return to me, and I will receive you." And this is the same as that which the Savior laid as the foundation of his sermons: "Repent, and the kingdom
[Marginal note: CHRIST.] of heaven will draw near." For what is the kingdom of heaven if not God, who turns to us when we turn to him? And because then he dwelt with us in a special way, and now, having assumed human nature, he offered us an easier way of returning to God himself, therefore he said that the kingdom of heaven, and God himself, to whom we tend through true penance, was drawing near to us. If, however, to this conversion, which presupposes withdrawal and fasting from all illicit pleasure, sorrow and affliction follow, this is by accident, and not of the essence of penance or of that conversion. For many afflictions follow sin, from which, however, a man is not called penitent. Nor should anyone think someone to be penitent because he assumes voluntary sorrow, because this is sometimes in sin. For just as sorrow follows the act of conversion, so it follows sin, because every disorder brings with it affliction and punishment. For no one can directly will sorrow, because sadness (as
[Marginal note: Augustine.] Augustine says) is that which arises from things we do not want. The occasion of sorrow differs, however: because in the penitent there is progress towards good, but in the sinner there is a fall and a headlong rush, or evil. True tempering of the soul, therefore, is a return, application, and adaptation with God in truth and affection, just as the Lord seeks through Joel,
[Marginal note: Joel.] saying: "Return to me with all your heart," that is, with full affection, "in fasting from things that lead away from God himself, in weeping and lamentation," so that by tears drawn from your eyes, you may move the divine eyes and the fount of his clemency to distill grace for your watering. For our weeping eye moves the fount of divine piety, which in the mystical language is called by the same word as the eye. For both are called `ayin` [ע]. Hence, just as in name, so also in reality they have a symbol, and from this, the movement of one easily leads to the movement of the other, as we have said elsewhere concerning the strings of a well-tuned lyre.

Through Sacraments man is made more perfect in himself, and more resonant with God. Chapter IX.

[Decorative initial E]
AND if this return to God sufficiently tempers man with Him, nevertheless something more remains to be tempered, since it is a great, indeed a very great thing, for him who by nature, as it were, dissents, to agree with Him who is by nature harmonious. For man, born from the beginning a son of wrath and subject to sin, dissents, and in the course of life, even if he is just, seven times (as he says

wise man says) falls daily: And he who thinks himself immune from sin, deceives himself [marginal note: Wise man.]

which is true agreement, and harmony with the highest truth. But God, since He is the first rule moderating all contingent things, is always harmonious: indeed, that one, and harmonious virtue: through which all things that agree are rendered harmonious. Hence sacraments are ordained as signs of a sacred and divine thing: and in a certain way, effective causes. For they are efficacious signs of divine grace and favor: which is granted to man in them, so that he may be led to due harmony with God. Since therefore man is born a son of wrath, and discordant with sin, for his tempering, the sacrament of baptism has been given: in which he is washed, and tempered with God, not only by the virtue and efficacy of the sacrament itself, but by the favor of the institutor: provided that the recipient is well disposed. Man also disagrees, and fails in daily operations, in which neither the whole mind, nor the whole soul, nor all powers agree, as the law commands: therefore, daily defect and disharmony. For the tempering of which, the sacrament of penance has been given: by which, both by reason of conversion to God (as we have said) and by the efficacy of the sacrament and absolution, discordant things are made to fit together. And because we are infected and distempered by continuous nourishment, the sacrament of the Eucharist has been ordained: by which we repair that which has been infected by other foods: and we dispose the body of our humility, so that it may be fitted and conformed to the body of His glory. And that which in the generation of offspring is defiled by the enticement of the flesh, and becomes discordant: that is repaired by the sacrament of matrimony, duly observed. Two other sacraments have been assigned, quite opportune: one of which is confirmation, or the strengthening of that which was done in baptism: especially in those who received it with weak virtue and no positive disposition, namely, in their first and infantile age. The other is called extreme unction, in which we intend to abolish, and perfectly cleanse man from all contagion, and from all (if any remains) discord. There is also another sacrament, by which the hierarch is instituted in this mystical body, and is raised to be its head with a beard: from whom, and through whom, the sacred chrism, anointing all things and tempering all things, descends even to the hem of the garment of that body itself: as it is said in the Davidic psalm: "Like the precious oil upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard: that went down to the skirts of his garments." [marginal note: David.] Which chrism, or which influx, is called by another metaphor the dew of Hermon, that is, of that place from which sadness has been anathematized: for Hermon is interpreted as "anathema of sorrow," Which dew first descends upon Mount Zion, that is, upon those who are placed as watchmen over others: And from there it is diffused to the whole city, and the assembly of the faithful. Whence also through that chrism, or dew, blessing and life even unto ages is bestowed.

**It is expiated by sacrifices. Chapter X.**

[Large initial P] After man has been tempered by penance, and furthermore led by the fuller
dignity of the sacraments, it remains that through sacrifices
(with which he also has no small affinity), thoroughly,
**Heracli.** expiated, he may be found worthy of God. For sacrifices are (as Hera-
clitus says) certain remedies for souls instituted by the supreme physician: For an
**Proculus** evil demon possesses man (says Proculus) until he is expiated by sacrifices.
And then, the evil demon having been put to flight, he returns to God. But the true sacrifice,
purifying, tempering, and uniting, is twofold. One is that which the high
priest Christ offered for the remission of all sins, making
peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth. Which
pacification renders man, now expiated, harmonious with God in supreme concord,
and most sweetly attuned. The other sacrifice is to offer oneself pure,
immaculate, and perfect to God as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing
**Porphy.** to God. Concerning this, Porphyry also says in "On Abstinence from Animal Food": Let us worship
God with silence, care, religion, with pure and true opinions about Him, striving
to be assimilated to Him, and to be united with Him;
and to offer the sanctity of our life as a sacrifice, and to adapt it to sacred things.
Our Christ indicated that He expected this, while speaking with the Samaritan woman,
**CHRISTVS.** saying: "There will be true worshipers who will worship the Father in spirit
and truth." For God is spirit: and He seeks worshipers conformed to Himself:
But so that we might be conformed to Him, having become spiritual, indeed, converted
into a better spirit, Christ willed to mortify Himself, offered as a supreme burnt offering:
so that He might offer us to God, indeed mortified in flesh,
**Idem.** but vivified in spirit. Therefore, so that we may be conformed to God and united,
our animal (nature) must be mortified: so that the spiritual may rise and grow strong.
And this is what He says, John reporting: "If a grain of wheat falling into the earth
dies, namely according to the flesh and blood, it brings forth much fruit." And again:
"It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing." Hence the high
priest Christ offered Himself, and taught us to be offered together with Him, when
He said: "Do this in remembrance of me, and in imitation, namely offering
yourselves, just as I was offered." For He commanded the mystery of the
body to be commemorated, already offered as a sacrifice, mortified by the passion, and now
vivified in spirit: so that what He said about the sacrament of His body, to be eaten by us,
and to be offered by Him on the cross, and for a commemoration to be made for Him, could be applied to it.
"The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life."
Into which spirit and into which life all our things must be brought back, if we wish to attain God.

It is cleansed by alms. Chapter XI.
[P] Oſt temperate penance, harmonious sacraments, and expiatory sacrifices, so that man may not be led away by any defilement from communion and union with God, there follows an ablution, which, after that baptismal one, is performed through alms. I would by no means dare to assert this, unless the highest truth taught me this, saying: "Give alms, and all things are clean for you." For it is a certain water flowing from super-mundane springs, just as it is said in Ecclesiasticus: "As water extinguishes fire, so alms extinguish sin." [Marginal note: Eccleſi] The same thing Daniel taught the king of Babylon in other words, saying: "Redeem your sins with alms." And the angel Raphael in Tobit: "Alms deliver from sin and from death." [Marginal note: Thobi.] My reason, however, is, because (as Rabbi Simeon Benoicai says) [Marginal note: Si. Ben.] even if every rule sometimes fails, this one never fails: "With the same measure you have measured, it will be measured back to you." [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] For this is the rule of the highest Truth, which again says: "Give, and it will be given to you." And again: As a guarantor, it teaches that we may confidently say to the Father: "Forgive us, as we forgive: Give, as we give." Therefore, just as a man is pious towards his neighbor, remitting debts, spending, and giving from his own, so he feels God to be most pious and a most generous giver towards him, and so much more abundantly, the more munificent he who spends is. Hence the munificent rewarder himself said: "You will receive a hundredfold for one, and you will possess eternal life."

Man Resounds with Virtues. Chapter XII.
[A] Bluted, therefore, and temperate man, and with instruments arranged, desires to render harmonious melodies. But at first glance, he feels difficulty, [Marginal note: Plato.] because (as Plato says) our soul, coming from God and enclosed in the body, suffers dissonance. To compose which, harmony was given by the Muses, which render the movements of our soul harmonious and kindred, provided that man uses them well, embracing suitable virtues. Explaining this, [Marginal note: Chalcid.] Chalcidius says: "When the Creator fashioned the soul in the higher realms according to harmonic reason, and commanded all its actions to consist of rhythms and modes, but these things are accustomed to fade away due to the companionship of the body, which it necessarily obtains, whence the souls of many will be without measure. Therefore, for the remedy of this defect, he established music: not that by which the common people are delighted, and which excites to pleasure, and often to vices, but that divine music, which is never separated from intelligence." For Plato [Marginal note: Plato.] considers this to recall wandering souls from the right path to their ancient harmony. Furthermore, the best harmony is in our morals and in the justice of all virtues by moderation, through which each of the other virtues performs its duty and work: so that reason indeed may be the guide, and the inner vigor, similar to wrath, may offer itself as an aid to reason. Furthermore, these things cannot arise without modulation. But modulation without harmony is nothing: But harmony itself is intelligence, and a concert of virtues adorning the soul, and rational-
DDD iij

--- Page 931 ---
**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

again recalling it to its ancient nature, and finally making it such as God the Creator had made it from the beginning, namely, so that it might resound with virtues. Although these are fourfold, all are nevertheless found to be harmonious, like the strings of a lyre: some of which are lowest and deeper, some in the middle, and some higher and sharper. For virtues are all works proceeding from a well-strung instrument, indeed named from *vir* (man). Or because it is harmonious, it is thus defined by grammarians: Virtue is a disposition of the soul consistent with the mode of nature. However, in the sense in which it is named from *vir* (man), they describe it thus: Virtue is a constant and fitting affection of the soul, making those in whom it is praiseworthy; or, Virtue is a strong and unconquered patience in enduring things: for *vir* (man), as they say, implies strength or fortitude. If, however, we approach the sacred and proper idiom and wish to name it, it will be necessary to observe by what words in that language *homo* (human being) and *vir* (man) are called. For *homo* (human being) is called אדם Adam, אנוש Enos, and גבר Geber, for diverse reasons to be passed over for now. And this alone must be noted: that in any of those names there is either one or no letter of divinity. But *vir* (man) is called איש Ish, in which word there are two letters of divinity, namely א aleph and י iod, where they imply that a man endowed with virtue is twice divine: namely by nature, by which he contains the image of God; and by virtue, by which he contains the likeness. According to this mystery, virtue can thus be defined: Virtue is an operation assimilating man to God, and deifying him.

Another thing to be observed in this word אדם Adam is that there are two quadrarian letters: namely ד dalet, which signifies four, and ם mem, which signifies forty. From which they imply that man is composed of two quadratures, and imbued with some divinity, denoted by the א itself. Which is indicated clearly enough in those words: "God made man dust from the earth" (for which we have "from the clay of the earth"), "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of lives." Where three things are touched upon: dust, earth, and breath. For earth is one of the four lower elements; עפר Aphar, which we call dust, or better, Atomos, indicates a more subtle body suitable for the spirit, as is known to the learned. But that divine breath is poured into us, which our people call the higher portion. From which, with our animal nature (as Plotinus holds), the rational soul sprouts forth. [Marginal note: Plotinus] But when, from this double quadrature, through the mediation of virtue, the whole man is reduced to that divine (state) and passes into God, then he changes the quadrarian and elementary letter into a mark of divinity; and with great mystery, he reduces another quadrarian letter to the triple hundred denoted by ש (shin) in the third letter of the word signifying *vir* (man). And to put it briefly, through virtues and other purgative means, the animal and earthly man is made spiritual and celestial: according to that of the apostle: "The first man is of the earth, earthly. The second man is of heaven, heavenly." And again: "As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly." [Marginal note: Paul] This transition from earthly man to heavenly man is made through fourfold virtues, as if through four steps: through civil or moral virtues,

--- Page 932 ---
**TONE SIX. 398**

[Marginal note: Plotin.] through purgative, heroic, and exemplary virtues. About which Plotinus, and others, treat very extensively. But we, briefly summarizing, say: that man toils in moral or civil virtues: In purgative virtues he prevails: In heroic virtues he rejoices: In exemplary virtues he shines, and attains divinity. And although there is labor in the first three kinds of virtues, according to what the [Marginal note: Paulus.] apostle says to Timothy: "Toil as a good soldier of Christ": nevertheless, especially in civil and moral virtues, there is labor unredeemed by any delight: which is present in the other, better virtues. Whence it is widely proclaimed to the novice on the path of virtues that it is [Marginal note: Basilius.] arduous and difficult, the journey of virtues itself. Therefore Basil [says]: "The way of virtue is at first rough, and almost impassable, and full of continuous sweat and labors." Therefore great strength is required because of the arduousness of undertaking it: nor is it [Marginal note: Lactan.] easy for one striving to ascend to its summit.

another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind: and leading me captive to the law of sin, but let him say: I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection. Then, freed from the most unhappy bond, he rejoices even in any adversity, which harms the purged man minimally, but the flesh: which he now hates, and has brought into subjection, as a most cruel enemy. Hence he rejoices as a righteous man, who has seen the enemy pay the penalties deserved by God. Thus the apostles, purged and strengthened by that holy spirit, went rejoicing from the presence of the council: because they were considered worthy to suffer ignominy for the name of JESUS. And [Marginal note: Paulus. Petrus.] Paul with the Colossians: Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you. And Peter: Rejoice, partaking in the sufferings of Christ. And this is true heroic virtue, to rejoice and be glad in every adversity brought upon the body, and upon our animal (nature), indeed a most bitter enemy. And so much is it to be rejoiced in: that we now consider it a pledge and guarantee of blessedness. To this therefore Christ speaks, when he says: [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] Blessed are the poor in spirit, that is, fasting from the desires of lower things, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven: and the delight of heavenly and divine things: Blessed are the meek, that is, gentle and giving no offense to anyone, with the impulse of anger and vengeance extinguished, or at least suppressed, which is in the flesh and blood crying out from the earth, that is, from this earthly body, for they shall inherit the earth, that is, of the living, from which evildoers and defiled ones are expelled. Blessed are those who mourn, either from nearby adversities or also indignant about the prolonged dwelling in this most miserable worldly valley, in which, already purged, he lives impatiently, always aspiring to heavenly things, having now shaken off the weight pulling him down. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness: How excellently these degrees of perfection succeed one another. The purged man abstains from the desire for lower things: Hence, envying no one and desiring nothing, he becomes meek. Afterwards, sympathizing and mourning over the evil of another, he is saddened, and also about the prolongation of this prison (of life): whence he hungers and thirsts for God's righteousness, and all heavenly things: by which he may truly be satisfied. Afterwards he becomes beneficent towards his neighbor, and inflamed with true charity, he would wish to draw everyone with him: whence it follows: Blessed are the merciful, compassionate, and pious towards their neighbor, for they shall obtain mercy and piety. Finally, perfectly purged, indeed adorned with purity and cleanliness, they are introduced into the presence of the king: whence it follows: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. They shall therefore see, united and in harmony with Him, in perfect peace and complete tranquility, which we obtain from peace: concerning which it is added: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God, now raised to a sublime degree, and fortified by perfect charity, which casts out fear. For intrepid and secure, they dare to undertake all arduous things: and [Marginal note: Idem.] they endure all things with a joyful spirit, having already obtained the kingdom of heaven: which (to teach with the highest truth) is within us. Hence he says: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. These therefore are deified through exemplary virtues, and shine for others. Nor would I dare to assert that men attain to divinity...

...attain divinity, unless John taught me with open speech, saying: He gave them the power to become children of God. Hence we shall be silent about many things that we could say concerning the splendors which proceed from those perfect ones who have already attained exemplary virtues.

By reading, man imbibes that by which he can modulate. Chapter XIII.

**H**aving been purified, adorned, and made harmonious, man ought now, introduced before the king, to modulate something harmoniously. But that which must be sung occurs, which man knows least, unless he learns it from him who seeks harmony: for he composed all the songs to be recounted there, and presented them to us to be easily read, though many are obscure and difficult. [Marginal note: Baruch 3.] There is none (says Baruch) who seeks the ways of the Lord, nor who devises His paths: But He who knows all things, knows them. He found every way of discipline, and delivered it, written indeed to Jacob His servant, and to Israel His beloved: opening to some the most hidden and wondrous sacraments contained therein. [Marginal note: David.] Among whom was he who said: "Reveal my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of Your law." Baruch continues: After this, He was seen on earth, and conversed with men, delivering the same discipline in a better form: which four wrote down, who were close to Christ, yet with this law and form, that according to [Marginal note: CHRIST] the teacher's edict, what is holy should not be given to dogs, nor pearls exposed to be trampled by swine: for the secrets of the Most High King are not to be revealed. Hence the divine psalmist sings: "I have hidden Your words in my heart, that I might not sin against You." And because strangers, and those not well initiated in divine and sacred matters, cannot grasp them: [Marginal note: David.] but like strangers hear someone speaking in a language unknown to them: and stand (as they say) like donkeys at a lyre: therefore the prophet again sings: "How shall we sing [Marginal note: CHRIST] the Lord's song in a foreign land?" Therefore, our wisest preacher Christ spoke with this law and reason, that only the more intimate disciples would understand the mystery of the kingdom of God: while the others would perceive only parables. For sacred scripture is like a human body: in which there is skin, flesh, and bones with marrow. Many see the skin, but not the flesh: much less the bones with marrow. The literal sense, indeed, is like the skin, known by all: and hidden from no one who looks. But the moral or allegorical sense is like the flesh covered by the skin, nevertheless perceptible by one who looks within. The anagogical, moreover, and divine sense is like...

**THE THIRD CANTICLE**

'But the anagogical and divine is as if the most hidden bones, covered by flesh and skin, and full of marrow. Nor indeed is the marrow explainable, which is contained most richly in the bones, and [which is] the power of the sacred scriptures: because it is that which transcends all human intellect, nor is it perceptible: unless He who delivered it declares it. Therefore, in the very ancient books of the law itself, in which it was given, as well as in the newest, where it is explained by the commentaries of Christ and the disciples, and nowhere else do we look or receive, from where we may sing all hidden and more secret canticles. From here, therefore, the sweetest songs must be sought by us, of which it is said: "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth:" And again: "The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves: more desirable than gold, and precious stone: and sweeter than honey, and honeycomb." For they are right, and consistent in themselves, and from this gladdening the heart, and enlightening the eyes: and so delighting the whole person, that blessed is he who dwells in them: as the same prophet sings elsewhere: "Blessed is he whom you have instructed, O Lord: and taught him from your law."

He introduces with meditation. Chapter 14.

[Decorative initial E depicting a figure in a landscape] Indeed, the holy scripture blesses, converts souls, and grants wisdom to the little ones, provided that the reader meditates on it, and is admitted as a ruminating and clean animal, which is offered as a sacrifice to God through the study of sacred scripture. Hence in a Davidic song it is proclaimed blessed is he who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night: And in another song: "Blessed are those who search his testimonies." Which not only praises, but observes: while it says: "My eyes anticipated you at dawn, or my eyes anticipated the watches, or vigils, that I might meditate on your words:" And that is what is commanded in the repetition of the law: "The words which I command you today shall be in your heart: and you shall meditate on them sitting in your house: and walking on the way, and sleeping, and rising up: and you shall bind them, so that they may never be moved from your eyes." Indeed, they are not to be bound with linen or silk thread, as superstitious observers of the law were accustomed to do, but with firm tenacity of mind: so that you may always have from where you are stirred, and led to the sweetest harmony, which is contained in them, manifold, indeed, of every kind. For there are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden, from there, therefore, we can meditate, from where we may sing not only of the wandering moon, and the labors of the sun; of which the latter, like a rooster, impregnates the whole heaven: while the former, like a womb, receiving effects from all the stars, explains them to us: but from where we may make resound the melody of the whole machine, and of its guests, and of its archetype, and of its maker, and of all things together. For all things are accustomed to be sung in it in wonderful ways, provided we know how to search it thoroughly: and it is given to us, that with unveiled face we may behold the glory of the Lord contained in it, proceeding from clarity to clarity, until, supported by the grace of God, we reach the fount of light inaccessible to our powers. Hence, meditating in the scripture itself is considered blessed, not only in the Davidic hymns, but also by Plato, who says in Phaedrus: "Divine medita-

-tations he who rightly uses, and is always imbued with perfect mysteries, truly alone becomes perfect. He orders by prayer. Chapter XV.

[Ornate initial S] o he recognizes his indigence, procures what is necessary, and asks for that which he still lacks. For since we are all parts of the universe, we need the universe: as Proclus teaches from the sources of Porphyry [Marginal note: Proclus] and other wise men. And since for every nature, salvation and preservation most truly depends on its conversion to its own totality, he who desires to possess virtue must insist on prayers, and frequently make supplication, that He may infuse it, who contains all virtue in Himself, and is the supreme good: and the cause of every goodness, existing not only by a certain series and succession, but immediately producing all things, even if you consider matter itself. Nor is divinity removed or distant from anyone: but it is equally present to all: since each thing exists by the gift of God. Nor is there anything outside God: since He Himself embraces and comprehends all things: And whatever we imagine outside God, is utterly nothing. Iamblichus adds the necessity of prayers beyond all expectation: because all [Marginal note: Iambli] things are produced and guarded by the Gods, by the command of the highest. Therefore, he who desires to be saved must pray to those who save: from whom things cannot be separated: For every created thing torn from its parents and root, immediately slips into non-being and perdition: especially those things which, although they have proceeded into themselves, nevertheless remain in their parent: such as all created things, which begin from God, and end in God Himself, according to the perfecting trinity, by which they proceed from God, exist in themselves, and tend towards God Himself. For all created things form a certain circuit (as Proclus explains from the mind of Plato), [Marginal note: Proculus] beginning from God, and ending in God Himself, like the line of a circle, which closes where it begins. But that they may return, they need the favor of those from whom they proceeded: And favor is obtained by prayers, whose purpose is to persuade both angels and also God, that He may command, and they may guard with perpetual protection: and may lead it back to where we came from. For what is (he says) each thing without consent and return to God: and without that harmony which they call sympathy? And although prayer is necessary for all, yet especially for upright men, since it is a certain application and conjunction of them to God: For like is naturally inclined to be intertwined and joined with like: But the upright and whole man is similar to God: hence he must be intertwined with Him, so that he may obtain help: by which he may be drawn away from the blind prison and chains of the body, in which existing, he wanders from Him to whom he is similar: and to whom he came to be united. And just as children taken away from their parents implore, driven by nature, until they re-

...until they return: thus we, separated and alienated from the true Father of all, so that we may be led back, it is necessary to pray to Him and supplicate Him. Hence some academics called those orphans and lacking both parents, who, despising prayers and supplications, neglected to turn to the higher and divine nature. Therefore, among various nations of men, whoever, led by virtue, claimed a name for themselves, exercised themselves in the study of prayers and supplications: such as the Brahmins among the Indians, the Magi among the Persians, the theologians among the Greeks, the Chaldeans in Assyria: who established the festivals of the Gods and hidden mysteries, venerating them with prayers:

However, for composing those songs as perfectly as possible, Proclus offers five most precise instructions: The first of these is the knowledge of the divine orders: to which he who prays approaches: For he cannot properly and readily approach who is ignorant of their properties. Therefore the oracle, or divine responses, command that the first notion in the sacred worship of God be the kindling of fire:
[Marginal note: Leuitic.]

After this, the second place is held by our kinship and affinity to God Himself, according to our multifaceted sincerity, purification, and faithfulness in what has been entrusted to us:
