according to that which the supreme teacher says: 'Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, sister, and mother.' The third in order is contact, according to which we touch the divine essence with the very highest part of the soul, and, inclined towards it, we rely on it.
[Marginal note: Ioannes.]
In which sense (as I believe) John says: 'That which we have heard, and seen, and touched concerning the word of life.' Fourth in place follows
[Marginal note: Dauid.]
application, or adherence: for thus the oracle calls it. Which we also have expressly in the Davidic psalm, where it is said: 'But for me, to cling to God is good.' In the oracle, however: 'A mortal adhering to fire will have the light of divinity:' For this offers us great communion and a more evident participation in the divine light: and it leads through similarity of character and intense affection. The last is union, which places that one thing which is in the soul into the unity of God: and renders us stable, reducing us to one act: according to which we are not our own, but God's, remaining in the divine light: and embraced by Him in a circle: And this is the best end of true prayers, that it may apply the conversion itself to abiding: and may place and establish everything that proceeds from the one God, back in the one. This also is the true and perfect harmony: which only a righteous and truly good man can possess. This is also an easy and most expeditious path to a happy and blessed life, while we are elevated by prayers and ascend to God.

**TONVS SEXTVS. 399**
**Contemplation is introduced. Chapter XVI.**

[Decorative initial V] But when we ask in prayer, we do not yet have what we desire; but after prayer has been heard, and the desired gift has now been obtained, we are introduced to the inner sanctuaries, in which it is permitted to gaze upon those eternal spectacles with full delight of the soul. And this is true contemplation, just as Richard well defines it in his book *De Arca Mystica*, saying: Contemplation is the free perspicacity of the mind suspended in admiration at the spectacles of wisdom. For the Lord, moved by prayers, sometimes opens one of very many chambers, into which, having entered, with eyes enlightened, one sees the spectacles of divine wisdom, most hidden from the common folk. And because they extend infinitely, the mind of the beholder, unable to penetrate all, remains suspended in admiration. For (as it is said in Ecclesiasticus): "Exalt the Lord as much as you can, for he is greater than all praise. For who can magnify him as he is? Many things are hidden, greater than these." For even the blessed see few of his works and his infinite magnificence, who, although they see him as he is, do not see how great he is; because he is infinite. But they have determined degrees of their virtue. Hence Isaiah, speaking intimately with God himself, says: "Truly, you are a hidden God." Hidden indeed, and manifest; for God is in all things, hence manifest to all. And he is hidden in himself, as if covered in an abyss of his own darkness, hidden from all, as it is said in a Davidic psalm: "He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies." Behold how he is covered by darkness, a pavilion, and dark waters. And sometimes, with impediments broken, he appears open and manifest; whence it follows: "At the brightness before him his clouds passed, hail stones and coals of fire. The Lord also thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice," making himself manifest to whom and when he wills; not only in this immense machinery of the world, but dealing with a particular man, he sometimes hides his face from him, and says: "No man shall see me, and live." Sometimes he speaks face to face, acting very intimately; whence the royal prophet prayed, saying: "Show your face, and we shall be saved." Which face God shows us especially in prayer, as Job says concerning God approaching: "He will pray to God, and he will be gracious to him: and he shall see his face with joy." Therefore, man returns to God through prayer. Having arrived there (says Plato in *Phaedrus*), he stops his horses and enters the chamber of the symposium, where he is fed ambrosia and drinks nectar. This ambrosia is that manna, of which it is said: "To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it." But that nectar is that of which the heavenly teacher says in the Gospel: "I will drink it new with you in my Father's house." For this (Plato continues) is the life of the gods and of happy men: that, reflected in God by a circular motion, they may be fed with his food, and, turned towards him, may rest in him. For the progression is direct (as Dionysius holds) when it is from God to creatures; but the reflection or reversion of the creature is circular in

God: which occurs when the course of life is completed, and sometimes even before the soul is fully separated from the body; and this is when it is given to man, that with the veil removed, and the face revealed, he may behold the glory of the Lord, ascending from glory to glory. And this is true contemplation. For that reflection which occurs through riddles or images, is a kind of speculation or discourse; but that which occurs immediately concerning God, as in a clear mirror, is contemplation, as Augustine rightly believes. Therefore Rachel, whom they interpret as "seeing the beginning" or "seeing God," is most aptly taken for the contemplative life or mind, which beholds not through riddles, nor through creatures, but God Himself, and the principle in which all things shine forth. And this is the best portion, indeed the end and completion of the entire course which we await; to which Philip, imbued with some supernatural light, [Marginal note: Philip.] aspired when he said: "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us." And because the Father and the Son are the same, therefore He will answer here saying: "Philip, he who sees me, sees also my Father," because whatever shines forth in one, shines most fully in the other also.

United by Love. Chapter XVII.

[Decorative initial 'I'] NTO the mirror of divine clarity, therefore, the subjected mind also feels a fiery heat, which follows from that reverberating light; whence it melts, dissolves, and finally is fused into one with God Himself, who illuminates it. Nor let the pedants oppose this truth, who wish to bind Him who is absolved from all laws with the laws of inferior mathematics, ineptly saying that there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite, and consequently no union. Moreover, since God is most simple, He admits no union or mixture. For He Himself is one, most simple in many, perhaps in a better way than the sun, which is unique in all the illuminated places of the whole earth. And since this (sun), illuminating and warming all things, admits no mixture, much less does He, who is most simple, pervading all things and transforming all things into Himself at will. Nor is it surprising, because if this lowest fire, burning wood, converts it into itself, suffering no mixture, much more does that fire, of which it is said in Deuteronomy: [Marginal note: Deutero] "God is a consuming fire," convert into itself without mixture those whom it ignites. For consuming with fiery and vital power, it converts food into the nature of the consumer. Nor is a proportion of quantity or virtue required in the first cause, entirely absolved from every law of secondary causes, such as is required in secondary causes themselves, which are subject to their own laws; for that first cause, although it is of infinite power and exceeds the proportion of all inferior things, nevertheless extends to producing even the smallest thing. Which also unites to itself at will, although it infinitely exceeds. For what in inferior things is a proportion of greater inequality in the agent, that in the first cause is an all-encompassing excess; yet the agent is the first cause itself, according to the virtue determined by itself, [Marginal note: Theolo.] because it operates freely (as our entire theology pro-

--- Page 940 ---
TONVS SEXTVS. 400

proclaims) and not according to all-encompassing virtue, as those falsely assert [Marginal note: Philosophers] who opine that God acts necessarily. Therefore, the law of proportion holds in those things which are of determined virtue, and not in the most excellent agent: who exceeds all natural power: and to whose nod all things are ready: both before they exist, that they may come into being: and after they have been made, that they may be reduced back into Him: but especially man, who is capable of Him: and by his very nature born to be united: provided that that power of love intervenes, which unites the lover with the beloved: and makes two, I will not say into one flesh, but into one spirit, as Paul says: [Marginal note: Paul] 'He who adheres to God becomes one spirit with Him.' Which union occurs not only through love and affection, concerning which [Marginal note: John] it is said: 'God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him.' But also through transmutation, which occurs through a certain ecstasy and excess.

He is transmuted by ecstasy and excess. Chapter XVIII.

[Large decorative initial N] ot therefore content (as some do) to lead man up to union with God, we will endeavor to lead him to a further and ultimate degree: namely, to the transmutation of the body into spirit: and of the spirit into God. Concerning one of which the apostle says: [Marginal note: Paul] 'We await the Savior, our Lord JESUS Christ: who will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of His glory.' And what kind of reformation this will be, he declares elsewhere, when he says: 'It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body.' But concerning the other, the evangelist says: [Marginal note: John] 'He gave them power to become children of God: namely, while men are transformed into the same image: which is the Son of God.' Which transformation occurs through an excess of the mind and a certain ecstasy: [Marginal note: Hebrews David. Canticles.] which the Hebrews call the death of the kiss, concerning which it is said in a Davidic song: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints.' For in the excess of the mind, one dies through that kiss: concerning which the Wise One says in the Canticles: 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.' For man, existing in an excess of mind, dies to the body, so that its life then scarcely lives, nor does it use its aid: although the body is by no means deprived of the soul's life-giving power. Which soul, leaning on God in that excess, is united to God by a certain kiss, so delighted by Him, that, forgetting all external things, and even the body itself, it leaves it living but deprived of senses, and half-dead, Which Paul explains, when he says: [Marginal note: Paul] 'You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ.' Who so receives the soul itself, and unites it with Himself, that it lives rather of Christ, than its own life, as the apostle again says: [Marginal note: The same] 'I live, yet not I; but Christ lives in me.' But since this transformation occurs not only through the illumination of the mind itself, but also through unifying love, which is a certain divine fire, melting, uniting, and transforming: I have deemed it opportune to publish a special tone on this: which we will append to this one.

**SEVENTH TONE. 401**
**WHETHER RESURRECTION IS POSSIBLE. Chapter One.**

O MAKER, that supreme one, whose spirit is the sweetest artisan of all, just as the highest harmony came forth into creation, and disposes and moderates it with tranquility: so at last will He lead it to a perfect and complete concert, by a happier and more perfect lot: and that will be, when all noisy and dissonant matter, which by its very nature tends to dissolution, has been laid aside, man, the most perfect work of God, will be fitted together with divinely perfect harmonies: so that he may always render to Him due and harmonious praises. For we lay aside that dissonant and horrid matter by death, so that we may take it up again, changed into a better lot: and sometimes by a certain most vehement power of the spirit we change it for the better: as first happened to Enoch, who walked with [Marginal note: Enoch.] God: and was not seen thereafter, namely in a perishable flesh, and subject to corruption. Elias also achieved this, who was carried up in a fiery chariot. Moses also: [Marginal note: Isaias Moses.] whose face, while still living among men, shone so brightly from divine communion: that the children of Israel could not look upon it because of the splendor radiating from it. Which was a most evident sign of a body already transformed for the better. Hence he did not see corruption: nor is he found among men, nor was he left to the power of the devil, like other corpses: but transformed into the nature of spirit, according to that of the Apostle, [Marginal note: Paul.] "It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body." Therefore, it is also indicated by Thaddaeus that he was brought back into the dominion of Michael, who is appointed prince over all souls and spirits to be received. And this is that dispute and altercation, which is said by the same (Thaddaeus) to have occurred with the devil concerning the body of Moses.

But since this transformation has been granted to very few, therefore, through the laying aside of this tabernacle, and the fiery power of the supreme arch-musician in the work of resurrection, we must arrive at that harmony: Concerning which Ambrose [Marginal note: Ambrose.] touches upon somewhat, when he says: "Let those who have tasted the first fruits of the resurrection make known to you, how the dissipated organ of the body will have been refitted into its former state of nerves: nay, rather, it will have been led into a better state with sweeter melodies, and such harmony, that it will never again be dissolved: but without any interruption, they will bless and praise the artisan of all with continuous praises." But before we describe this concert, virulent doubts must be removed from the minds of men, which infect the wholesome food of truth: which concerning our state and end are to be ruminated upon by us with continuous meditation: For the entire life of the wise and happy is a meditation not on bodily death and the dissolution of this our tabernacle, but on the death of the saints: which is precious in the sight of the Lord: and through which we live to God, and, transformed into a better lot, begin to taste that blessedness which we await. Hence we have deemed it necessary to preface how this resurrection and transformation is possible and true. Here

**THIRD CANTICLE**

Indeed, I cannot but marvel at the great many who give so much credence to the asser-
tion that it would be impossible for that which has once been destroyed to be able to return again, when
we daily observe these returns, repeatedly reiterated in most things, now
under one specific form, now under the same specific form. For from the body of a bull, beaten with clubs
and enclosed in a cell and buried in the earth, in a few, that is, about twenty days more or less,
bees are generated. But from an equine cadaver, beetles (are generated). But from the bodies of any
animals whatsoever, diverse worms (are generated), so that what was just now the matter of an ox, or of a
horse, becomes a bee, or a wasp. And often the same specific form is restored.
For lettuce, cabbage, wild thyme, parsley, and suchlike, produced from the earth,
yet by seminal virtue, are again resolved into the earth, with the seed preserved, in which
the virtue remains: by which, with the earth, they again produce the same things, so that they seem to rise
again every year. Yet they are not said to rise again: because they are not gods...

TONVS SEPTIMVS. 401

Afterwards they are changed into butterflies, which produce eggs as certain seeds; but these, warmed at the appointed time, again break forth into the same worms. Nor does the reiteration of man differ from these (as more secret theologians assert), whose bone, which they call Luz (לוז), of the size of a cleaned chickpea, subject to no fire, nor any corruption, is always preserved unharmed: from which (as they say) the whole animal body sprouts again, like a plant from a seed: with which, the same spirit and soul, which the Hebrews themselves call Nessaman, being resumed, a superior and spiritual man is constituted: just as the inferior man is constituted from reason and discourse, with our animal (nature), or with a celestial body, as it pleases the Platonists: into which body this heavy and corruptible (body) will be transformed according to the Apostle's opinion. For neither the sex of the body, nor grosser matter, is of the substance of man, as they suppose. Which we can prove from those things which happen in the transmutations of alchemists: where we see the whole substance of a thing, and its spirit, and life, reduced into a small amount of matter, and this (matter) liquid and rare, and freed from the fecal portion. No less, that which is animal and foul being left behind, that which is spiritual will rise again (as the Apostle says), indeed sufficient for man's integrity, nay, man will return equipped with a far better lot, transformed namely into an angel and into the very Son of God.

An resurrectio fuerit. Cap. II.

[Decorative initial S] But whether any resurrection of men has occurred, since it is merely contingent, it cannot be proven except by witnesses and the evidence of the fact: For we have many who attest that Christ rose from the dead, and gave pledges of his true resurrection. For he showed himself visible not only to the Apostles and women, but also to five hundred brothers at once or more, as Paul relates, and to many who were present when he ascended into heaven not without the admiration of those watching; moreover, he showed himself palpable and impassible to Thomas, when he fearlessly offered his wounds to be touched, without any fear of pain arising from the touching of the wounds themselves. Hence that cry of Thomas, arising with the greatest reason, by which he said: "My Lord and my God!" "Now (he said) I have known you as a faithful guarantor and patron, while you demonstrate the reward promised to faithful soldiers for their labors and death endured for your love. Now I know you as God, while you have changed this mortal and passible body into an immortal and impassible one, and this as a pledge of our body also to be changed. Which I infer from this, because I touch this fresh wound of yours with my fingers (as you commanded), without at all renewing any pain for you: But to perform such things, because it belongs only to God, hence I confess you, who have done these things, to be my God." The heavenly spirits also attested to Christ's resurrection, who said to the women: "Jesus, whom you seek, is not here; he has risen: and he will precede you into Galilee." But lest the testimony of the angels should be known to us only by the report of women: Therefore, as Christ ascended, the same (angels) addressed the astonished crowd with these words.

**THE THIRD CANTICLE**

“Men of Galilee, why do you marvel, looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will so come in the flesh, or in a body already glorified, to judge the world, and to give you the same glory, just as you saw Him ascend into heaven, already glorified.” Which, along with other deeds performed by Christ, the Apostles attesting, as they had seen, proved it not only with words, but with many miracles, and finally with the peril of their lives. And to remove all suspicion of rashness and fraud, which could be ascribed to the Apostles from this testimony, Paul [marginal note: Paul] wisely argued, saying: “Unless Christ had risen, and had provided us access to resurrection, we would be more miserable than all other creatures, who enjoy their fitting pleasures.” For just as brute animals, so the unbelieving man shamefully indulges his lower appetite; but a true Christian abstains from all such things, so that he may enjoy those good things which are prepared for the blessed soul, either separated from the body, or endowed with a better lot along with it. Hence, deservedly, the Apostles and all evangelical men, who abstain from all pleasures so that they may receive that incorruptible crown, unless they were to obtain that very thing promised after the resurrection, to be most fully enjoyed by the whole person, would truly be more miserable than all other creatures, who at least enjoy some pleasure. Nor does this truth lack strength, which is embraced by all who are not depraved, is asserted by every law, is expected by all, unless there are some so defiled by such great and many crimes, that they persuade themselves of no future life, no tribunal, no judge for such great crimes. For horrible crimes (as Hierocles [marginal note: Hierocl.] says) take away all faith, all God, and finally all judge, from the minds of the blinded. By every law, I say, the resurrection [marginal note: Mahum.] is asserted, since not only the Christian [law] confesses this, but also the Muhammadan and the Hebrew [marginal note: Hebrews]. For the chief among the Hebrews, who were called Pharisees, that is, separated and removed from the common crowd, asserted this beyond all doubt. Hence Paul [marginal note: Paul] did not blush to profess himself a Pharisee, and to embrace their dogma concerning the resurrection of the dead. “For I am (he says) a Pharisee, and the son of Pharisees; and concerning the resurrection I am judged.” Indeed, the Pharisees were anciently the truly religious among the Hebrews, and were called ‘separated’ from the common people, from [Hebrew text] Paraz, which means ‘he separated’, although with diminished spirit and fervor (as very often happens) they mingled with the crowds, committing things that were not right. But when Christ, the true Pharisee, and utterly separated from the world and from all that is in it, rebuked them as guilty of their profession and name, hence they rose up against the teacher of truth, which by common law begets hatred. Those therefore among the Hebrews themselves who think well, profess the resurrection, await the world to come, and celebrate it in many volumes, greatly esteeming those who have diligent care for the coming age. Nor will I bring forward what Muhammad asserts about the resurrection in his theology, since he received by theft every truth he professes from the Mosaic or evangelical law. Nevertheless, I considered it opportune to bring up his sect, since at present the entire human race is divided into these three principal sects: Hebraic-

--- Page 946 ---
**SEVENTH POINT.**                                **403**

Christian, and Mahumetan, so that all may understand that there is no religion or dogma that does not profess and teach this truth about the resurrection.

        **Whether the future resurrection can be proven by reasons.        Chapter III.**

[Large decorated initial E] ND although (according to Plato) divine things are to be received by oracles rather than investigated by intellect or proven by reasons, nevertheless, since the oracles themselves are such that they teach nothing absurd, nothing not consonant with nature, I judge it not unfitting to thoroughly examine the agreement of these divinely revealed things with our reason and intellect: which kind of knowledge is most elegant in my view, namely when something is in harmony with the intellect, which feeds on truth alone and delights in it, provided it is purified. For a darkened intellect cannot receive the light of truth, as John says: 'And the darkness did not comprehend it.' Therefore, acting with purified minds, we will propose that the soul is immortal, as not only laws assert, but all true wise men profess; and reason persuades that it should indeed attain that end which it can in no way achieve in this earthly pilgrimage, as the Apostle wisely says: 'As long as we are in this body, we are pilgrims from the Lord.' Moreover, the soul is a partaker of divine and eternal light, just like an angel: For God himself (as John says) was the true light, which enlightens every man: that light, indeed, which is the Word and the splendor of the Father: to which even angels (as Augustine says) approach, as to the fount of life. And (to proceed further) everyone who is a partaker of something, perceives the nature of that of which he is a partaker. For the eye, capable of this sensible light, is considered to be of the same nature, even if some see less, and some more, and some more acutely, and others more obtusely. It is no different with hearing and other faculties. Therefore, man will not be alien from the nature of the angel and of God, since all (though in different degrees) enjoy the same light. And since they are incorruptible and immortal, without doubt the soul will also be immortal, since it has communion with them: this especially, because the soul itself immediately draws its origin, together with the angel, from that immutable and perpetual parent, who whatever he produced immediately and without other aid, undoubtedly brought forth as eternal: as Plato teaches, and Plotinus confirms. For he produced heaven, earth, which stands eternally, man as to the soul, and great dragons immediately, and without the aid of a second cause, or presupposed matter: all of which are perpetual and permanent. Nor do I understand by these dragons, those creeping upon the earth, but both angels, good and bad: as some more recondite theologians not unfittingly interpret, as we have said elsewhere. Nor does that saying of the highest Truth stand in the way: 'Heaven and earth will pass away': because that passing away will be according to some effect: or it will be a transformation into a better state, without its destruction. By the same law, the ideas of things, or universals (if they truly exist) are eternal: because immediately, and without any

CANTICI TERTII

With the cause having been brought forth, this soul is therefore immortal and perpetual, so that it may perpetually enjoy the eternal God and be a partaker of Him. From whose fellowship, a wanderer, even if it sometimes falls away through negligence and does not fully and purely receive Him, yet it has within itself certain seeds, from which, with the favor of that supernal sun, it can repair and recall its suppressed powers, until it attains His perfect likeness, image, and complete union. Since, as a wanderer and clothed in this heavy mass, it cannot do these things perfectly, it is necessary that its body be transformed, configured to the body of glory of Him who gave beginning to resurrection and life, so that it may enjoy His full fellowship. For the transformed body will become, like a seed into a living plant, a companion and vehicle of that prince of blessedness, just as He Himself became living bread and was presented to us as food. And this is that [Marginal note: Apocal.] mutual banquet, about which He, both food and guest, speaks in the Apocalypse, saying: "I will sup with him, and he with me." For He will indeed eat me, the living bread, and the hidden manna, by which He will be continuously sustained. But I will delight in him, marked with a better life and made like unto me, to whom I, who am the resurrection and the life, will continuously grant that better life.

Nor is it necessary for us to labor here in bringing forth sentences from sacred scripture, since the same faith ought to be given to one as to many, as any one of them emanates from the face of unmixed and infallible truth. Paul, [Marginal note: Paulus.] who saw the mysteries of God and in whose breast Christ resonates, brings forth these things, taught by the master and in the gymnasium of truth: "Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall all indeed rise in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." Behold how clearly he reveals the mystery and manner of the resurrection, with which all agree who have been taught in the same academy.

Nor are there wanting those who suggest that the resurrection can be proven from the stars, if it could be shown that the aspects and places of the planets are the same as when the world was created, and that those surfaces upon which the stars revolve are not incommensurable, like the diameter of a square to its side, but symmetrical, so that all things might at last converge as they were. Which, however, is nothing, since the universal resurrection of the dead does not require the exact same condition of the stars that the world held when it was first created, because human bodies were not fabricated then, nor was the union of souls with them made; but (this happened) in many and successive courses of years. Hence, this truth about the resurrection is to be sought only from Him who will bring it about at will, and who gave to man the means by which he can rise again, just as He gave to plants and certain animals the means by which (as we have said) they are renewed in their seasons. From these things alone (beyond what the oracles say) can we conjecture about the resurrection.

Who first gave access to the resurrection, and how fittingly. Chapter 54.

Who indeed gave the beginning to this true resurrection, and access to it for us, is not to be doubted in the least, as Paul's truthful trumpet of the highest prince resounds: [Marginal note: Paulus] "Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep; for since by man came death, by man also came the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ all will be made alive." And again: "The first man became a living soul," which is also granted to other living beings. "But the second man became a life-giving spirit," which is granted to man alone by the grace of God, through Him who provided the beginning of the resurrection: [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] as He Himself expresses in the Gospel which is titled according to John, saying: "This is the will of the Father who sent Me, that of all He has given Me, I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day." And again: [Marginal note: Idem.] "This is the will of Him who sent Me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him may have eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day."

Indeed, it is fitting that man should be restored by Him through whom he was instituted; and just as through the lower man he had descended into death, so through the higher man he should rise to life. For concerning the earthly man it was said: "The Lord God created man from the dust of the earth"; and thence it is inferred: "Dust you are, and to dust you shall return," until, that is, you rise adorned with a better lot. But at the generation of the second man, Gabriel, His angel, who was the maker of both men, said to the mother of the second man, soon to be: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you." Hence you will conceive and bear a son, not indeed earthly, as the former was, but heavenly, divine, and the savior of the former and of all human offspring. From this the messenger added: "He will save His people" (whom, namely, He will regenerate by a new generation) "from their sins," and consequently from the death which they had contracted therefrom.

From the earthly man, therefore, we have the means by which we return with him to the earth from which he was taken; but from the heavenly man, the means by which we are led back to heaven, from which He Himself descended, to lead us there. Since this cannot happen with this garment subject to corruption, it is necessary that, having laid it aside, we put on the incorruptible, according to that saying of the Apostle: [Marginal note: Paul] "But when this mortal will have put on immortality, and this corruptible will have put on incorruption, then will come to pass (as is subjoined) the saying that is written: 'Death is swallowed up in victory.'" For death, indeed, not only that which is our dissolution and the separation of the soul from the body, but also the very angel of death, who is called death, especially in this place: whose power and strength will be utterly swallowed up, when, having achieved victory, we shall obtain triumph in the resurrection. For then no power of the enemy will be left against us, when his instrument, which is our animal nature, will have been changed into that state which it can in no way harm. Therefore, its power will be emptied, and utterly extinguished, just as fire is extinguished when its fuel is removed. So death will be swallowed up, and its author with all its power, when we shall attain in the resurrection immortality, incorruption, and perpetual life. Which, however, having been conquered -

If by any conjecture it can be known when this resurrection will be. Chapter VI.

[Decorative initial Q] Therefore, when this resurrection will be is very difficult to define, [Marginal note: The same.] as Christ says: It is not for you to know the times or seasons, which the Father has placed in His own power. And again in the Gospel, concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, but the Father alone. And (as Mark adds) neither the Son, but the Father alone: and to whom, of course, it is revealed by [Marginal note: Mark.] the Father Himself, in whose power it is to determine all these things. For this, and all other things, the Son confesses to have received from the Father, when He says: The Father has given all things to me. And again, [Marginal note: CHRIST,] concerning the knowledge of things, He says: My doctrine is not mine, but His who sent me, the Father's. Therefore, those who have been taught by the Father of lights can prognosticate something about that final judgment and the solemn change of things. Among whom is the Son of God Himself, who, when the Apostles questioned Him about this matter, although He did not openly state the time, nevertheless mentioned some preceding things, saying: [Marginal note: The same.] For you will first hear of wars and rumors of wars: and He adds many things that will precede them long before: among which He enumerates false prophets, who indeed presume to prophesy things which the Holy Spirit has not suggested, or who, to gain some reputation, falsely strive to persuade the common people of certain unheard-of sects and things, which are not conducive to the truth of the Gospel, nor to the unity of the spirit, nor to the bond of peace left to us by Christ in a solemn testament. Afterwards, He adds concerning the son of iniquity, who himself will precede that last day for some time, as He Himself relates, saying in the Gospel titled according to Luke: These things must first happen, but the end is not immediately. [Marginal note: The same.] Finally, He adds closer signs, saying: There will be

signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and on earth distress of nations, and because of the roaring confusion of the sea and waves, men fainting from fear and expectation of what will come upon the whole world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken, namely, to execute those things which will happen everywhere beyond all natural order. But although he mentions many things of this kind, he hints at nothing about the time, except in those words which he finally added, saying: Amen I say to you, that this generation will not pass away until all these things happen. Which word is quite obscure, since it can be understood in different ways. For instead of 'this generation', we can interpret 'human generation' (mankind): But would it not have been superfluous to say of the human race, that generation will not pass away until those things which are to be accomplished in that generation are fulfilled? Also, 'generation' is the common life of man, according to which meaning that sentence has no place at all: since the life of man from the time of the flood onwards has been confined within the space of one hundred and twenty years: and already one thousand five hundred and more years have passed since that threat. Nor can that word be interpreted concerning the great life of man, which was appointed from the beginning to be extended up to a thousand years: although no mortal has reached that limit (not without mystery), but some have come close to it, such as Adam, Methuselah: and others. Adam indeed lived nine hundred and thirty years: The other indeed nine hundred and sixty-nine: For this generation or life also fails from the time already elapsed after those words. Nor could it be understood as 'age', because 'sæculum' [Marginal note: Exo.] (age) is sometimes taken for the common span of life, as that which we read in Exodus: And he shall be a servant forever, until namely he completes the span of life. And sometimes 'sæculum' is extended up to a thousand years, beyond which limit [Marginal note: Hebræi.] (as the Hebrews assert) it can by no means be extended. Hence (if I am not mistaken), by 'this generation' the Savior understands the third part of the fluctuating course of the world. For (as we can conjecture from some not weaker passages), the labor of the human generation is completed in six thousand years: but in the seventh it will rest: Just as the supreme craftsman built the world in six days, and rested on the seventh. Nor do we inappropriately equate thousands of years with as many days, because among more profound [Marginal note: Theolo.] theologians, a thousand years is often counted as a day, according to that [Marginal note: Dauid] of the Davidic hymn: For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed. Also the six of labor, and the seventh of rest, both in days and in years, is corroborated by divine law. For six days of the week are granted by law for performing works: but the seventh is dedicated to rest. And again, six years being [Marginal note: Exodo.] granted for cultivating fields, in the seventh, rest is proclaimed for both the field and the cultivator, as we read in Exodus. It is not surprising, therefore, if after the human race has labored for six thousand years with various inconveniences and diverse agitations brought about by Satan, that is, the adversary, it will rest in the seventh millennium, as the beloved Apostle [Marginal note: Ioannes.] of Christ describes in the Apocalypse. And this, with Satan himself and our adversary first bound, who is the ancient serpent: so that he may not deceive, nor disturb in that blessed

nations in the millennium: but let men be true priests of Christ, dedicating themselves to God, so that they may now reign in that kingdom which is established within us, and which, having attained, they truly rest. The first of these times, and the first generation, directed only by the law of nature, without sacrifices and the influx of grace, was in a way barren and empty. This generation, therefore, according to this kind of calculation, is of two thousand years, which are to be completed under the Messiah: in which all things predicted by Christ will be fulfilled, before we come to the great day, and the sabbatical space of a thousand years. These are the things which, from conjectures drawn from lower things, can be held concerning the determined course of the end time. I say from lower things, because also from revolutions and measurements determining lower things, which are in the archetype, the same could be conjectured: which, however, we omit, because our Latins have neither the elements of that doctrine nor its progress from them at hand.

**By whose virtue the resurrection will be brought about. Chapter VII.**

**T**herefore, the course of times having been completed, every cause and instrument will converge to bring about the renewal of things, which had been instituted by the same. For God is the Father, from whom as from the first origin, and the Son, in whom as in a solid foundation all things were skillfully made through the Spirit, the artisan of all created things: concerning whom it is said in scripture: [Marginal note: Genesis] "The Spirit of the Lord hovered over the waters," so that from them particular for-

--- Page 953 ---
**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

might bring forth into light. To bring about these things, however, the Creator assumed things already created as co-workers, or as instruments, commanding the earth that it should bring forth green herb: and the waters that they should teem, and bring forth living creatures according to their kind: And the other things which follow. Which, after the first foundations were laid, he brought forth, with certain powers intervening, through which he governs all things: and finally he will bring all these things to their proper end. Therefore, in the same order, that succession of times being completed, which the Father placed in his own power, he will command that in that word, in which he sustains all things, these same things be restored to complete perfection by the same artisan, and through the same means, through which they were brought forth from the beginning. And although the sacred scriptures seem to attest concerning man alone being resurrected, and being restored to his first, and highest parent: nevertheless if anyone carefully considers the words of the highest
[Marginal note: CHRIST] Truth, he will clearly perceive that all things are to be renewed, for it says, "Heaven and earth will pass away:" Nor (as I think) will they make any transition, except to a better state. For to pass away is not to perish: but to change place, state, or some condition. Therefore, the movable heavens will pass away to a state and rest, towards which all motion tends. And the ever-changing earth will pass away, to that state where it may receive a certain lot of the land of the living. And men, in whom all things are contained, will pass into an angelic and divine nature: so that truly that heavenly oracle, recently
[Marginal note: Apoca.] brought forth, may have its place: "Behold, I make all things new." For indeed, in the first advent of the Redeemer, the human condition had been renewed by signs, sacraments, law, worship, and all disposing means towards a perfect, complete, and evident renewal. But in the second and more glorious advent, that renewal will be consummated, by which it will appear what new sacraments, what new signs, and new rites have accomplished. Therefore, the author of this universal resurrection and renewal will be God, three and one: by whose command all these things will happen. But it will deservedly be ascribed particularly to him, who is the principle of resurrection, and who, rising first, provided the way of rising to others.
[Marginal note: Paul] But the executors will be angels, and ministers of God himself, as the Apostle openly relates, saying: "The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, namely his own, and with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God." "And the dead in Christ will rise first." In like manner also Christ, from whom Paul had learned, in the gospel, which is titled
[Marginal note: Matthew] according to Matthew, explains the same, when he says: "They will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with much power and majesty." "And he will send his angels with a trumpet, and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest heavens, to their uttermost bounds."

**What this angelic voice and trumpet of God is. Chapter VIII.**

**B**ut it must be observed, why this trumpet is called "of God" by the Apostle, and is ascribed to angels by Christ. For this is done, so that we may understand that voice, by whomever it is uttered, is brought to us by the command of God who ordains. For often we read that angels spoke in the person of-

--- Page 954 ---
TOMVS SEPTIMVS. 407

of God: so much so that that precept and word is uttered by an angel, and yet is ascribed to God. For the Law (says the Apostle) was given through angels: nevertheless, God is always introduced as commanding and ordaining. [Marginal note: Paul] And this, because the angel conveyed all those things to Moses by the command and power of God. Therefore it is said: And the Lord spoke to Moses: For an angel, always receiving influence and command from God, moves at His nod, speaks, cries out, and sounds like a trumpet: Hence, when the command of God and Christ concerning the raising of the dead is announced by angels, they will be like trumpets, conveying not only the voice, but the very power of God to raise corpses, or to clothe souls anew. Therefore, the trumpet will be angelic, because an angel will convey the voice and command: but it will be of God, who will command and blow, or give a sign through angels (as some think) or bring about some effect through them, whoever it may be. And it is rightly called a trumpet, which conveys the voice of God to the ears of men as a kind of channel. And just as trumpets, receiving breath and force from the trumpeter, rouse horses to move camps, incite men to war, and invite soldiers to receive a bounty, and to all celebrated acts of military service, so angels, receiving the voice and power together with the command from God the prince, will rouse the horses of our bodies, together with their riders, to that terrible judgment, to invade new dwellings, and to receive rewards for deeds well done.

What change of bodies is to come. Chapter IX.
**W**HEN, therefore, this trumpet sounds, the greatest change of things will occur, but especially of our bodies, as the Apostle says: "For the trumpet will sound, [Marginal note: Idem] and the dead will rise incorruptible: and we shall be changed." But to those wishing to inquire how and with what kind of body the dead will rise, the Apostle answers, saying: "You fool, who indeed do not believe, or do not understand: Do you not see how the dead will rise, and be changed? For what you sow is not quickened, unless it first dies. And observe what you sow: you do not commit to the furrows the body that will be, but a bare grain of wheat, or of some other plant: but God gives it a body as He wills: and to each seed its own body. So to each man being raised, He will give a body suitable to his state: and whatever kind of body it may be, it will be a true body (although that of the blessed will be a celestial, impassible, and glorious body, while that of the reprobate will be passible and heavy) just as both an earthly body and a celestial body are each a true body: Which bodies differ, just as the flesh of different animals, according to the Apostle's opinion, who adds: "Not [Marginal note: Idem] all flesh is the same flesh, but there is one of men, another of beasts, another of birds, and another of fish: so also celestial bodies, and terrestrial bodies: But there is indeed one glory of the celestial, and another of the terrestrial: And among celestial bodies, there is one brightness of the sun, another of the moon, and another of the stars." And again, establishing a difference among sidereal bodies, he adds: "As star differs from star in brightness, so saint from [Marginal note: Genes] saint in glory." And so that he might more clearly explain those things which he had shadowed forth by metaphors,

--- Page 955 ---
CANTICLE THE THIRD

he explains in plain language, adding: It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incor-
ruption: It is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory: It is sown in weakness,
it will rise in power: Finally, an animal body is sown, a spiritual body will rise:
so that we may always be conformed to the eternal Father. For the first man was made into a living
soul: The last man into a life-giving spirit: although this heavenly one, in order to lead that earthly one into the heavenly, assumed an earthly and passible body: according
to which he suffered, died, and was buried. After which he rose impassible, heavenly,
and spiritual, having now become the second parent: to whom it is necessary that we also
[Marginal note: Paulus.] be made conformable in body, if we are to reign with him, as the Apostle adds. Therefore, just
as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly. And so
Paul determines this transformation to be necessary, that he declares the opposite impossible, saying:
But this I say, and proclaim: that flesh and blood cannot inherit the
kingdom of God, nor will corruption inherit incorruption: this flesh, of course, is
corruptible, mortal, and passible: but especially subject to sin, and
[Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] to the tempter. Hence he most clearly concludes that this flesh must be transformed into another,
adorned namely with a heavenly and spiritual nature. But those words which
Christ uttered about himself when risen seem to greatly object, saying: Handle me, and
see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have: Which would
have been nothing, unless his risen body had palpable flesh and bones: It is true,
I say: but incorruptible flesh, and bones that cannot be diminished, yet a body palpable
and visible at will: For he entered to the eleven disciples with the doors
closed, which could by no means have happened, unless that body had been able to be attenuated at will,
like wind and spirit. Nor otherwise, while he was with men for
forty days after the resurrection, did he now show himself visible and palpable,
now did he flee human touch and gaze. Again, he can present himself as
large and small at will, and without any circumscription of place, as happens in the sa-
crament of the altar: which all wise men approve: although some think it happens
by a miracle, with the respect of the parts to the place removed, yet with the
relation of the same parts to the whole remaining: But (unless I am mistaken) this happens from the nature of the spirit
into which he was transformed when rising. Therefore, the change of these corruptible
bodies will be into the nature of heavenly bodies, and spirits.

Who are to be changed, and who not, and why. Chapter X.

[Marginal note: Paulus.] [Large decorative initial S] Now, whether all will be changed, or not, is not to be doubted in the least, since
we have the heavenly trumpet openly proclaiming it: Indeed,
we shall all rise, but not all shall be changed. For those will be changed into
a heavenly nature who, trampling down corporeal and earthly things, lived
heavenly lives: and who are to possess the heavenly regions. But the others, who willingly
submitting themselves to the earth and the dregs of the earth, have been enslaved to infernal
and Tartarean regions, are to be thrust down into the lowest center of the machine: if they
will retain flesh and an earthly body conformable to their dwelling, yet freed from further dissolution, so that

--- Page 956 ---
TONE SEVENTH. 408

...deprived of perpetual light and the grace of God, and always turned away from God, they may be tormented in dark fire perpetually, according to the Emperor's edict, now promulgated by him: "Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire." Therefore, only those will be changed into a better state who, raised beyond men, will attain the condition of the Gods and the fellowship of the supreme craftsman himself: which, clothed in this corruptible garment, they cannot achieve. For by this law, war was declared upon us from the beginning between flesh and spirit, and between body and soul: so that whoever conquered would endow the vanquished with their own laws. For if the flesh, or the animal body, conquers, it imparts heaviness to the spirit and rational soul, so that it descends to the lowest parts of the world. It also envelops it in darkness, so that it can no longer perceive that divine light in whose splendor well-instructed souls rejoice. Moreover, it renders that soul capable of suffering, which by itself could not be sad, just as it could not weave or spin: so much so that it suffers even from corporeal fire. Finally, it provides grossness with its weight, so that it can in no way depart from the infernal dwellings, but, enslaved by perpetual chains and prisons, always with the heaviest weight prepared by its own crimes, it lies perpetually in the lowest part of the world. But if the spirit prevails, it will bestow its own laws, and these better ones (which theologians [Marginal note: Theologians] call "gifts" or "endowments") upon our inferior part, according to that Apostolic saying [Marginal note: Paul]: "When this mortal shall have put on immortality, and this corruptible shall have put on incorruption." To which immortality follow agility, subtlety, clarity, and all the endowments which they attribute to glorious bodies: which bodies are said to "put on" by an accommodated term. For just as our body puts on a garment of another nature to cover its nakedness and defend itself from cold, in a similar way, the body itself clothes itself in the condition of another and better nature, so that, immune from all labor and passions, it may always rejoice in a better lot. Therefore, the body will be made agile and light, so that it can easily ascend to the highest heaven. It will be subtle, so that it can penetrate all things. It will be lucid and shining like a spark, indeed like a star, so that it may be a worthy inhabitant of the region of light and splendor. It will also be impassible, so that it may feel nothing that impedes blessedness and that full joy. Finally, it will be immortal, so that it may always enjoy those eternal joys.

**With what flesh, and with what body, the sleeping are to be raised. Chapter XI.**

[Large decorative initial E containing a figure] And although we have touched upon many things concerning the transmutation of our body, and in what condition it will rise again, nevertheless, satisfaction must be given to some who subtly inquire whether it will be this same body, and with the same form after the resurrection, which we use in this pilgrimage. For Jerome and Rufinus of Aquileia, discussing this matter, say [Marginal note: Jerome, Rufinus] that for each soul, not a confused or alien body, but its own, which it had, will be restored, so that consequently, for the struggles of the present life, its flesh, either chaste, may be crowned with its soul, or unchaste, may be punished. For a greater expression of this matter, Rufinus says [Marginal note: The Same] that by the church itself, where the resurrection of the flesh is commonly held in the creed, there was added "the resurrection of *his* flesh, or *their* flesh": undoubtedly *his* flesh which he who professes it has, with the sign of the cross imposed on his forehead.

--- Page 957 ---
CANTICI TERTII

Others, however, on the contrary, cry out and say: How can flesh, which, having putrefied, dis-
solves, or is turned into dust, and even absorbed into the deep sea, and scattered by the waves,
be gathered again, and joined together into one, and a human body be restored from it?
How again can the same flesh, which is now corruptible and dissolvable,
immediately or after some time be incorruptible, immortal, and entirely free from all
change: when corruptible and incorruptible (as they say) differ more than in kind?
The first of these is easily solved, if one looks to the majesty of the supreme creator and ruler.
For divine power is not so limited and weak, that it cannot gather the scattered dust of each flesh into its proper form, and restore it:
when we see mortal ingenuity exploring veins of metals submerged deep in the earth,
where the eye of the diligent artisan sees gold, which the unskillful considers earth.
Why then should we hesitate to grant these things to Him who made man, when he who
was made by Him can achieve so much? And when mortal ingenuity discovers that there is a proper vein for gold, and another for silver, and one for bronze also far different, and a diverse one for iron and lead, lying hidden within the species of earth, shall not divine power be thought able to find and discern the proper essence of each flesh, and gather it into one, if it appears scattered, by the power of its own fire, just as miners gather the very smallest particles of metals themselves with this common fire which we use?
As for what is objected secondly, whether the form of the incorruptible body, and already converted into the nature of spirit, will be the same as that corruptible one which it has here, we ought not easily assert that: since the form subject to corruption does not appear to be the same as that which is entirely free from all change: This is especially so,
[Marginal note: Paulus] as the Apostle says: "We await the Savior, our Lord JESUS Christ, who will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of His glory."
By these words (if one rightly understands), the Apostle implies another form, and another figure of the body to be resumed by those who are raised, just as he says again: "because we shall be changed, because a spiritual body will arise, because this corruptible [body] will put on incorruption, and because from the sown body there will be a new sprouting." For one is the form of the sown grain, another of that which sprouts: For that dies, and remains dead in the earth: But this revives and lives. The body also, which will rise, will assume a life that will always endure.
Therefore we shall be raised in flesh and body, which sprouts from that which dies, perhaps in a better state than that which dies, as the Apostle says again. "Christ has risen from the dead, He dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over Him." So that we may
[Marginal note: Iob.] follow Him, our bodies will rise with the same endowments. Nor does that passage from Job hinder, where he says: "Again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my savior." For even if it will be different, it will still be that of the one rising, so that each one can say: "This is my flesh, and my skin."

Which hair will not perish. Chapter XII.
[Large decorative initial S] But since sacred scripture makes mention of hairs, something must also be discussed concerning them. For Christ says: "All the hairs of your head are numbered." Concerning these words, Jerome says: "They mock understanding-"

--- Page 958 ---
**SEVENTH TONE. 409**

...ecclesiastical understanding in this place, which denies the resurrection of the flesh: as if we say that all hairs which are numbered and cut by the barber will rise again, since the Savior did not say: 'All the hairs of your head are to be saved,' but 'are numbered.' Where there is a number, the knowledge of the number is demonstrated, not the preservation of the same number. By these words, Jerome seems to refute that we will resume our hairs again. But what shall we say to that which is found in the Gospel, whose title is according to Luke: 'A hair of your head shall not perish'? Therefore (unless I am mistaken), Christ does not speak of these hairs which are cut off and wasted or burned by fire, but of better hairs, which are commended in the Nazirites and are forbidden to be cut. In these was the power of the Holy Spirit, for casting down foreigners, as Origen rightly understands. For these hairs are the virtues of the soul, and manifold senses, which were produced from the nobler part of the mind, from the head of the Apostles. Hence, for Nazirites and others familiar with God, not only was cutting forbidden: but also that no razor should come upon their head: as we read of Samuel, Samson, and others: because the thoughts of the righteous are not to be cut off, but to be preserved. For whatever the righteous do, prospers, and their leaf does not fall. But every work, every word, and every thought of sinners, as evil, ought to be cut off and removed. Hence in Deuteronomy it is commanded: that if any woman from among foreigners, that is, captive by gentile errors, is led [to be married], she should shave her head: or, as the literal truth has it, she should shave the hair of her head and cut her nails: so that nothing of gentility or error may remain in her who is joined with a true Israelite. In Isaiah also, after the prophet prophesied concerning the conception and birth of the virgin, it is added: 'In that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor, from those who are beyond the river, by the king of the Assyrians, the head, and the hair of the feet, and the whole beard,' openly signifying that in the time of the Messiah, all things that were of idolatry and error ought to be cut off in the Gentiles coming to the faith. And this with a hired razor, that is, by the merit of the Redeemer: by which all things that are of sin and error were shaved away. Therefore, the hairs of sinners and those who err are to be shaved. But those of the righteous and Nazirites are to be preserved: according to that which is mysteriously written in the Canticles: 'The locks of your head are like royal purple, joined to channels.' For what it had said before, 'your head is like Carmel,' it now says, 'the locks of your head are like purple.' For this [purple] is born from a worm, which is called *chermel*: whence it is sometimes used for purple: just as we read in the second volume of Paralipomenon (Chronicles): when Solomon sent to Hiram, king of Tyre, to send him a skilled man who knew how to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, and purple: For which in Hebrew is found כרמיל *charmil*. For it does not speak here of Mount Carmel, nor of the worm generating purple: but of purple itself, which by its proper name in Hebrew is called ארגמן *argaman*. Therefore, it means that the locks, that is, thoughts and works, should be like royal purple, enriched and shining with grace and the merit of our supreme king, our redeemer. So that these may be fruitful, it is necessary that they be joined to those heavenly channels flowing from that all-irrigating fount, from which...

For it punishes the wicked with a constricted, tormenting fire, by no means illuminating or consuming. Hence, those who are tormented by that fire are said to dwell in darkness. And this, if the dogma of the Pythagoreans is true, [Marginal note: Pytha.] namely, that there is one fire everywhere: In heaven, expanded and illuminating: But in hell, constricted, dark, and tormenting: While in the midst of the whole universe, it partakes of both. Malac.] For a soul dissolved, or destroyed by the wound of sin, unless it has been lamented, is bound up by an antidote, consolidated, and restored to health, either by the very revolution of harmony, as Plato asserts at the end of Timaeus: [Marginal note: Plato.] Or by the application of fires, according to the Apostle who says: "He will be saved, as if passing through fire," [Marginal note: Paulus.] according to that which we read figuratively in the book of Numbers. "Everything that can pass through the flames, shall be purified by fire." For the discourse was about the vessels of the tabernacle, which prefigured those vessels, of which the Apostle says: "In a great house of God there are not only vessels of gold or silver, but also fiery and earthenware." [Marginal note: Idem.] And again with the Thessalonians: "Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor." But that fire transforms the purified. Therefore, in Deuteronomy it is said: "God is an eating fire:" for which we have "consuming." For he does not consume and destroy friends: but he "eats," that is, he takes them into himself, and transforms them into himself as food. Which Plutarch also testifies (as he had gathered from various ancient sources) [Marginal note: Plutarc.] saying: "God is an intellectual fiery spirit, having no form: but transforming into himself whatever he wishes, and making himself equal to all things, and all things to himself." And he accomplishes this not through elemental fire, but through himself, or through a seraphic burning close to the divine fire itself.

By what peculiar fire the wicked are to be burned. Cap. XV.

[Large decorative initial M] Therefore, that the wicked are tormented by fire, and are to be tormented, almost all confess and agree with the Supreme Truth saying: [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] "Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire, and it burns, indeed, with that fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels." For that fire is not ordained by God for our destruction: Nor will anyone be tormented by it, unless he himself has kindled it: as we can learn from the oracle of Isaiah saying: [Marginal note: Isaias.] "Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled: This has been done for you by my hand, you shall lie down in sorrows." The prophet touches on both: that it is accomplished by God, and that we ourselves kindle that fire. For although it is prepared by God, nevertheless no one will be tormented by it, unless he himself kindles it with the fuel of sins: as Origen rightly believes. [Marginal note: Orige.] For just as we kindle fiery fevers in the body with harmful foods and immoderate labors, so shall we kindle them in the soul and in the body-

**THIRD CANTICLE**

we will receive (when they are united) fiery torments, from the superfluity of evil works, and crooked affections: whose abundance, gathered in man, in its own time, boils up to the punishment and penalty of those who ignited it. And thus (as we follow the dogma of Pythagoras) that fire which, expanded and illuminating, beatifies him who
[Marginal note: Pythag.] has a heart expanded in the way of God's commandments: so too, fire constrained by the evil disposition of those who have a constrained heart, and hardened to good like a stone, and an anvil of a smith, and a darkened effect (for they themselves, darkened by the immense wickedness of their crimes, cannot receive divine light) becomes obscure and tormenting: just as the same sun or fire hardens or liquefies according to the variety of subjects receiving that light and heat. This doctrine concerning the same fire, beatifying and tormenting, is not alien to the sacred scriptures. Since that fire, which in Deuter-
[Marginal note: Deuter.] onomy is called consuming: and consequently beatifying and transforming, and which
[Marginal note: Exo.] in Exodus gave the fiery law in a visible flame, and which makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire, is in Isaiah called a reproving, judging,
[Marginal note: Isaias.] and punishing flame: For the prophet says: "Behold, the Lord will come in fire: and like a whirlwind his chariots, or his tribunal, to render his fury in indignation or burning rage, and his rebuke in a flame of fire: for in fire the Lord himself will judge:" Which fire he prepared for the just and orderly from the foundation of the world for splendor, joy, and gladness: But he prepared it for the wicked for torment and punishment, as their crimes and evil disposition, induced by the multitude and immensity of their sins, demand. This beatifying fire will be perpetual: but the purging fire will be extinguished in a short and appointed time. But the tormenting fire will also be eternal: as we have not only
[Marginal note: CHRIST.] from the word of the supreme Judge saying: "Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire:" But from the prophecy
[Marginal note: Isaias.] of Isaiah, who, while speaking of the corpses of those who gravely transgressed against God, says: "Their worm shall not die: and their fire shall not be quenched." By these words, the prophet refers to both torments of the damned, namely the intrinsic and the extrinsic, as being perpetual.

How the wicked are to be tormented. Chapter XVI.

[Decorative initial S] But since we have said enough about the tormenting fire, we must also consider how the wicked will be tormented by that fire. This presents no small difficulty, presupposing that fire to be corporeal (as is the common opinion) and our souls, and evil intelligences, to be entirely separated from the body. And this topic appears all the more difficult to us, the more numerous and varied are its critics. For Gregory, quickly dispatching the matter, considers that fire
[Marginal note: Grego.] to torment the wicked as an instrument of divine justice: But how it is an instrument, and whether it inflicts torment by its own form, or is guided by another like a saw or a hammer, for the cutting or striking of the wicked, he left this to be explained by posterity. But it is to be wondered how Gregory hesitated in such a matter, when elsewhere he asserts that angels and demons have bodies: but so subtle that, in comparison to our bodies, they are said to be incorporeal. The Lord says to the pious: Behold how the prophet describes the punishments of the wicked following from disorder and the deprivation of peace, which is the tranquility of order in things. Therefore, the soul, not feeling the coherence of rational movements to be in harmony with itself, must necessarily endure punishment and torment: and let it feel the penalty of its own discord, inconstancy, and disorder. Also, those authors whom we mentioned above describe another kind of torment: which is generated from an evil idol. And thus He Himself, who is for the well-disposed unto resurrection and joy, is for those who are ill-disposed unto ruin and punishment. And this is what Ezekiel [Ezechie.] reports having seen the Lord, namely, from the loins upward in the appearance of shining amber: but from the loins downward in the figure of burning fire. That Lord, indeed, is He who, filling heaven and earth, sits in heaven, gladdening the good: But on earth (which is the footstool of His feet), holding feet of burning fire, He torments and afflicts earthly people and those alienated from heavenly things. And unless sacred scripture taught me this, I would by no means presume to declare it, that the same Lord is now light and a beatifying fire, and making the just shine like stars, and like sparks of fire: Now therefore He is a refining fire, and purifying the sons of Levi: But now He is a fire consuming wood and stubble: which we have badly built: and devours and destroys (as Joel [Ioël.] says) the beautiful things of the desert, that is, whatever works which seem glorious, perpetrated by those who are deserted by grace and heavenly influence: And now He is a tormenting and burning fire. Hence again Joel [Idem.] says: "Before His face is a devouring fire: and behind Him a burning flame." The meaning of these words is: He Himself, for those who are worthy to see His face, is a fire consuming and transforming into Himself: as we touched upon above: But for those who are abandoned to the delight of posterior, that is, lower affections, He is a burning and tormenting flame, either by Himself (although in Himself He is most excellent) just as it happens to any ill-disposed persons, for whom light, wine, meat, and similar bodily goods are harmful. Or He does this through ministers, whom He makes (as the prophet [Dauid] testifies) a burning fire, but for the good unto joy, and for the wicked unto torment. Or likewise He does it through something corporeal fashioned for the torture of the wicked: so that it may satisfy those who contend that that fire is corporeal. But whether it is corporeal or not, God knows: but it is well proven to be invisible by Origen [Orige.] from the Apostolic saying: "That fire (he says) is of such a substance: that it burns visible things, being itself invisible," as the Apostle [Paulus.] says: "For the things which are seen are temporal: but the things which are not seen are eternal." If therefore that fire by which those who depart from God are punished is eternal, it is also necessary that it be invisible: since, according to the Apostolic saying, only invisible things are eternal. Nor should you wonder (as Origen [Orige.] continues) that fire is invisible and tormenting, when you do not see the heat affecting bodies, and severely tormenting in those who are most severely afflicted by it. Therefore, this tormenting fire is of another kind than that which we have in common use, yet that supremely tormenting one is compared to it, since nothing among us is more tormenting than this visible fire: If we desire to avoid this eternally tormenting fire, let us beware lest there be in us an eternal evil disposition: but let it be such that we may receive that supreme fire unto joy, or at least unto the consumption of wood and stubble, and unto the purification of dross: so that we may be beautiful vessels of pure gold, to be placed in the heavenly nuptials and those blessed and eternal mansions.

--- Page 967 ---
**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**
**CONCERNING THE SWEETEST HARMONIES,**
*and that eternal pause in acquired blessedness. Eighth tone.*

[Large decorative initial letter E containing a figure playing a stringed instrument]

Putting the finishing touches on this last song of the newest canticle, we will imitate the more excellent musicians to the best of our ability: who always strive to make the newest harmony sweeter; and sometimes they are drawn by such sweetness that, were they not subject to temporal movements and did they not fail, exhausted by labor, they would prolong the song perpetually. But enduring as long as they can, now with continuous, now with alternating turns, they do not cease from beginning to end.
But the supreme choirmaster, whose song we attempt to describe, since he both transcends time and rejoices in eternity, now distributes and divides his songs through temporal periods, now leads them to eternity itself. For this harmonic machine (by some wondrous artifice, I know not what) he both subjected to temporal succession and freed from time itself: For all these elemental things are generated by daily and annual changes. And the heavens move in time, or (as we might more correctly say) being moved, they generate time itself. Nevertheless, the earth stands forever, and the heavens will never cease to be, quanquam quo ad motum & influxum (ut canit psalmographus) peri [Marginal note: Dauid] although as regards movement and influence (as the psalmist sings) they will perish.
He also completed the sweeter harmony of redemption in a few (I will not say) months, but days: nevertheless, abundant redemption remains perpetually with him: ma [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] and the eternal fruit remains. If anyone (says the Redeemer) eats of this bread, offered, namely, for your redemption, he will live forever, enjoying the fruit of that eternal redemption itself. He also wished to bring together the sweetest song of union, from merits acquired through time, to draw all to eternity itself with perpetual rewards, and he determined to make them co-eternal with himself. Hence he will free all from temporal succession whom, being lifted up from the earth, he will have drawn to himself with a better harmonic power quã Or [Marginal note: Orpheus Amphio.] than Orpheus and Amphion, placing them in most harmonious mansions, where (if we believe Augustine, once enticed by that sweetness) even numbers and corporeal harmonies, now hidden, together with other harmonizers, will be heard to resound around in public praises of the Creator and of that supreme beauty. Therefore, with the greatest diligence, those heavenly scribes of both testaments, Ezekiel and John, described those mansions with most exact figures and most harmonious measures and divisions, prout [Marginal note: Ezechi.] just as the Holy Spirit taught them. But Ezekiel describes only the measurements of the structure, its arrangement, its division for the twelve tribes, the sacrifices, and the name of the city. Ioan. [Marginal note: Ioan.] John, however, intimate with the Prince, admitted to the more secret inner chambers, brings forth sweeter songs. Both, however, are obscured by such a mist that unless the supreme sun with its heat thins out its density and with its light dispels its darkness, we will not be able to hear what they say, nor see what they describe and measure, to any extent: for they transmit such things wrapped in sensible enigmas, or so that from those things which the mind knows, it may be able to rise to the unknown:
