and to discern invisible things through such sensible ones; or because, neither to us who hear,
nor to them who speak, has He yet delivered words by which those things can be expressed:
just as those who have seen them openly affirm that it is not lawful for a man to speak of them. Or
because the mind, still weighed down by the burden of its bodily mass, cannot ascend to these supreme things:
as Isaiah and Paul agree, that neither has eye seen, nor ear heard, [Marginal note: Isaiah Paul.]
nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him. Therefore;
if we too do not explain those mysteries, you will grant pardon: since they are to be treated
which transcend all our intellect: they escape all memory:
they surpass all eloquence. Yet, relying on a single aid, we will undertake this most arduous work:
since we have guides to whom God has revealed these things: as the same Paul [Marginal note: The same Isaiah.]
adds: But God has revealed these things to us through His Spirit. Hence more cautiously
speaks Isaiah, saying: Eye has not seen, O God, besides You, what You have prepared for those who await You.
Therefore, following these divine guides closely, as much as the supreme light
has illuminated our eyes, we will unravel in our words those things which they have entangled in their enigmas:
and we will especially pursue the more secret and fuller canticles of John:
who, resting on the Pegasean breast of Christ, between the two peaks of divine and human
nature, was so suffused with light, and so filled with that rapture: that he easily
became a prophet of divine things. Afterwards, from Patmos: an island, drawn by the divine spirit to the supracelestial
continent, now taught by an angel, now by the supreme harmonizer Christ
Jesus, now by various surrounding voices, he delivered to us those perfected
canticles: and with wondrous artifice, moving hither and thither, now ascending, now
descending, with full musical laws, he left no module of the supracelestial instrument,
nor any voice of musical distribution untouched. For by twenty degrees
musicians distinguish the entire harmony invented by them: which they placed upon the hand
so that practice might be easier and memory more tenacious. John touches upon just as many
modules, in which the entire supracelestial harmony is perfected. And
this under the figure of a city, which is presented as a celestial lyre, in which, when
all these voices are tempered, and touched by the supreme arch-musician, that harmony
transcending all others is perfected. All rejoice (says Dionysius) when the [Marginal note: Dionysius.]
Father moves: for the Son has become the organ of God, since in Him exist the ideas of all things created:
and in Him all are placed as pipes, whence
if anyone does not remain in Him, he can bring forth nothing useful or harmonious. The breath
moreover is the spirit filling all things: as it is said in the book of Wisdom: The Spirit of the Lord [Marginal note: Wisdom.]
has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of a voice.
The Father, however, is the first and principal mover of all, especially in that supernal city,
in which all things correspond to Him as pipes, strings, or modules of an instrument:
Declaring these modules, and dividing them into harmonies, we will follow John:
and with him, we will make Ezekiel agree as far as possible.

**FIRST MODULE, MATERIAL.**
*Why that city is said to be built of gold. First Harmony.*

[Large Roman numeral I in margin]
**T**herefore, John, making the foundation of the heavenly building, describes it as made of gold and precious stones. For gold is not only for lithocolla for cladding walls, but for cement and glue for stones, for particles and nails binding the building: And what is wonderful, that gold does not obscure the brilliance of the precious stones, since it enjoys perfect transparency. Hence our composer says that gold itself is like pure glass: But precious stones are for the foundation, for the gates, and for the entire structure of the walls: so that both the stones and the glue may be most precious for that most precious dwelling: and incorruptible for those eternal mansions. And entering the inner chambers, as far as it will be right and permitted by the archimuseum, we will explore the mysteries and more secret harmonies, which are described under the type of precious stones and gold, which a ribbon signifies, according to that saying of the wise man: Before the golden ribbon runs out: [Marginal note: Sapien.] which ribbon, or golden thread, signifies true life. To do this, we must examine the properties and nature of gold and the stones themselves: For gold is beautiful and comely, hence called as if *horaios* (as some prefer) or from *aura*, which signifies splendor: although Hippocrates thought it was named from *aro* its inventor: [Marginal note: Hippoc.] For it is beautiful, and it makes other things beautiful: yet not all things (as Hippias, once deceived, had said), but those to which gold itself is fitting: [Marginal note: Hippias.] And it is of more perfect value among all metals and molten things. It is also by its very nature most constant, so that when extended into the thinnest foils, it is hardly broken: For from a denarius' worth of gold, one hundred and twenty-four foils of four digits on each side are produced in our times, whereas the ancients extended it to only seventy. Moreover, it is most tenacious with a certain yielding, for it yields to him who strikes and folds it, but it is not consumed by fire at all, not by rust, not by verdigris, not by the juices of vinegar and salt, conquerors of all things, nor by sublimated arsenic, which (according to Albertus) [Marginal note

Why walls of jasper. Singer II.

**T**he structure of all the walls (says our singer John) [Marginal note: John] was of jasper: which the wise celebrate exceedingly. For it (jasper) delights in both sexes, rejoices in a beautiful appearance, excels in multi-faceted virtue, and glories in manifold variety and name. For Aaron, Pliny, Albertus, and other more recent writers who write about stones, [Marginal note: Aaron. Pliny. Albert.] report that up to seventeen kinds of jaspers are found: although Albertus only mentions ten. Of these, the principal one is green and luminous, having red veins. Next is the red one, like fire, and translucent: another, however, is opaque red: This one excels in utility, while that one in price. Another is like an emerald, encircled with a white line: which they call gramantia. Another is distinguished by several lines, and is called polycalamos: which more reclusive philosophers say is useful for singers. Its virtue is manifold, as Bocus, Aaron, Thetel, Zenothemis, Arnoldus, and Albertus report: [Marginal note: Bo. Aa. Th Ze. Ar. Al. Pliny.] but above all, it stops bleeding, renders the wearer chaste and pleasing: it is hostile to phantoms, and favors those who sing together, especially the polycalamos, as we have said. And Pliny, and Thetel in his work, pursue many other things about jasper, and how it is a most anticipated kind of stone, which we omit. Therefore, the heavenly singer very aptly describes the woven dwelling of the singers as being made of jasper, glorifying in the beauty of both sexes. since those living stones described by him, from which the city itself is built, are gathered from both sexes: so that they may draw forth the praises of Him who is (as Mercury says) [Marginal note: Mercury.] most full of the fecundity of both sexes, And His beauty most beautifully figures the beauty of all citizens and those fiery stones: For nothing but what is beautiful and comely ought to stand before supreme beauty. Moreover, its precious variety designates the royal splendor of that most beautiful city, which is surrounded by the variety of many precious things. For a Cherub differs from a Seraph: virtue differs from power: and an angel from an archangel. No less does saint differ from saint in glory (as Paul says) than star differs from star [Marginal note: Paul.] in brightness. Indeed, there are various kinds of jaspers, yet one species

There are also those who assert that the interpretations of stones were not made according to the literal truth: And among others, concerning יהלם (yahalom), which they interpret as jasper, some contend that it signifies the diamond: and if this does not please others, for the reason stated above. THE THIRD CANTICLE

Zacharias also the Babylonian, writing to Mithridates, says: "Great power and
human fates are in stones." But whence these come, a deeper speculation is sought.
Alexander the Peripatetic, not departing from his senses and qualities, opined
that these proceed from the elements, or from the qualities of the elements
composing the stones themselves. Which can in no way stand, since qualities are
of the same species, but the operations of stones are many and are proven to
agree neither in species nor in genus. Therefore, the Academics, ascending
higher, some of them attribute these things to the formative ideas of things:
Hermes, however, to the stars: Avicenna to the Intelligences: but Albertus
reduces such operations to the specific forms of things. And although these wise
men seem to oppose each other, yet if the matters are well considered, none of
them deviates from the truth, provided that their sayings are rightly understood:
For diverse things, as in many cases, converge to the same effect. For God, in
the first place, as the fount and origin of all virtues, bestows the seal of
ideas upon His ministers: But the Intelligences, as faithful executors, seal the
things entrusted to them with no other seal than the royal one: And the Heavens,
as instruments, dispose matter to receive those forms which (as Plato says in
Timaeus) reside in divine majesty to be led down through the stars, and the giver
of all forms distributes them through the hands of ministers, whom He has
appointed as rulers and guardians over His works. For the Creator does not need
them as co-workers: but He has them as ministers, just as royal and imperial
majesty requires. Nevertheless, the supreme moderator committed to them that
faculty in the things entrusted to them, so that all virtue of stones, herbs,
metals, and the like might be from these presiding Intelligences, as some wise
men assert: because the work and motions which we see in stones and metals
cannot proceed from a non-living thing with that life which their effect and
virtue demand. Therefore, the form and virtue of stones agree with the idea,
with the ruling Intelligences, with the disposing aspects of the heavens, and
with the disposed complexions of the elements corresponding to the influxes of
the heavens, by which the elements themselves are disposed. Thus, such operation
exists in this lower world through expressed forms, in the heavens through
disposing virtues, in the Intelligences through moderating reasons, in God
through ideas and exemplary forms. And thus all agree, both the executors of
effects and the describers of the causes themselves, although by understanding
each of them individually, we would have imperfect knowledge: but if sayings are
added to sayings, we will achieve the best knowledge in this matter and in many
others.

But since they have a certain stability, so that they sustain the upper waters, they also seem to participate in earth: and also in air, so that respiration can occur there.

**SECOND MODE ARRANGEMENT.**
**Concerning the general division of Ezekiel and John. Part I.**

[Decorative initial T] Speaking in accordance with the measure of our harmonious city, we will proclaim why it seems to be divided in various ways by Ezekiel and John: For Ezekiel, in his first division, divides the structure into the temple, the city, and the whole promised region: And this [region] into twelve parts, for the twelve tribes, with twelve gates. But he also divides the temple into vestibules, chambers, courtyards, treasuries, porticos, the holy of holies, and other parts for the kitchen and special uses. John, however, entirely excludes the temple: [Marginal note: John] "I saw no temple in it," he says. Very fittingly and aptly, Ezekiel, describing the buildings of a figurative family, includes the temple necessary for it for prayer and making sacrifices. John, however, describes the house and city of the Christian assembly: who do not need another temple, than themselves already built into God's temple, according to the apostle's teaching. Therefore Christ says to that Samaritan woman: [Marginal note: CHRIST] "The time is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father not on this mountain, or in the temple: but in spirit and truth." And thus we, purified here on the way, are made God's temple, receiving Him through piety, purity, and good works, just as the host Himself promises, saying: "If anyone keeps My word, My Father will love him, and We will come to him, and make Our dwelling with him." How much more shall we ourselves be a temple, when, namely, received into those eternal tabernacles, with open contemplation, face to face, and by mutual custom, we shall enjoy [Him] as citizens of that supernal city? Now, however, we domestically receive God as a guest, but then we shall be received by Him of whom John says: "For the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb:" Indeed, of that city, and of the assembly of the blessed ascending there. He also describes the gates, through which entry is open to all: provided they are willing to hear the one inviting. He also describes its splendor, by which all are enlightened: as well as the river of the water of life, and the tree of life in the midst of its street, for continuing the life of those dwelling there forever. He also narrates the throne of the Lamb, who will reign there forever with His co-heirs.

**What the magnitude of this city is. Part II.**

[Decorative initial M] Great, indeed very great, is that house of God and of the blessed: so much so that Baruch exclaims, saying: "O Israel, how great is the house of God: [Marginal note: Baruch.] and the immense place of His possession. Great, and having no end, exalted, and immense:" as Pliny and some other wise men most aptly say, [Marginal note: Pliny.] that those who presume to measure it are filled with insane madness. Nevertheless, our John seems to comprehend it within a few stadia: [Marginal note: John] "And he measured," he says, "the city with a golden reed, twelve thousand stadia on each side, completing the whole city"

--- Page 986 ---
CANTICI TERTII:

forty-eight thousand stadia: which are six thousand miles. Ezekiel, however, measures it as four thousand five hundred reeds on each of the four sides: which, when calculated, yield eighteen thousand reeds: Which are forty-four thousand three hundred and forty [Marginal note: Hieron.] Roman paces, more or less according to Jerome: but they are thirty-one thousand five hundred and forty Venetian paces. For the Roman pace (as Jerome understands it) contains fifteen palms or a little less: the Venetian [contains] twenty palms exactly: whence this [the Venetian] is greater than that [the Roman] by a fourth part: a reed, however, contains thirty-seven palms, that is, six cubits and a palm: for a cubit is made up of six palms. Therefore, the entire circuit will be in total thirty thousand paces above one thousand five hundred, more or less, if the measurement is made with the Venetian pace. Nor should anyone wonder if John found the circuit of that city to be six thousand miles, which is described by Ezekiel as approximately thirty-one miles: because this new city built by Christ, like a bride adorned for her husband, ought to be so much greater than that ancient, and Israelite one, as this Christian family is greater than that figurative one: which was contained in the small land of promise. John also measures the height of the walls as one hundred and forty-four cubits, and all these things with a golden reed, the measure of a man, which is of an angel: and perhaps (God willing) we will explain these things in their proper place. Now, however, let us proceed concerning its magnitude, in comparison to which that described [city], indeed the entire circuit of the earth, which is thirty thousand miles, is considered as nothing, or like a grain of millet compared to a huge mountain: where no proportion is found. Nor indeed does reason admit that for so August a kingdom the city should be so narrow: and that in so humble a dwelling so many thousands of the elect should be received with that great multitude from every tribe, and from every nation, which no one could number. Therefore, if we wish to explain Ezekiel and John, this literal number must necessarily be abandoned by us. For sacred scripture [Marginal notes: August. Pythag. Acade.] (as Augustine rightly perceives), and the Pythagoreans, and the Academics care little about it, intending towards the proportion resulting from it, which they call the natural or formal number: and towards the divine, and the sacraments emanating therefrom. Observing this, we will easily make Ezekiel and John agree with other wise men [Marginal note: Ezechi.], who speak of the immensity of that heavenly city. For the sum of the entire circuit (as Ezekiel describes it) is terminated by eighteen thousand reeds. For the explanation of which it should be noted that the millennial number pertains to the ultimate completion, since it is a cube and a solid of the complete number: which is ten, beyond which no further [number] is given, but a repetition of the preceding numbers. Nor can a number be extended beyond a solid, which grows in length, width, and depth. Therefore, this number signifies the consummate perfection of that dwelling. Therefore, Ezekiel measures the city, the temple, and the space of the entire region with thousands of reeds: And John [measures] the same city

Why this city is said to be placed in a square. Conclusion II.

**F**IGURE of this city both describe as square to demonstrate solidity, which is denoted by a square figure, and by the quaternary number, from which that figure is derived: For this number is the foundation and root of all other numbers: whence also all foundations, both in artificial and in natural, moral, and divine things, are square: as we have touched upon elsewhere. [Marginal note: Plato.] Hence Plato said that the first foundations of this world machine were laid fourfold by the supreme artificer so that it might be solid. For solids (as he says) are always joined not by one, but by two means, between which means there is a corresponding proportion, just as between fire and air, air and water, and earth, and again between earth and fire. By which wonderful harmony the creator of the world connected them, so that they cannot be dissolved by another, except by Him by whom they were bound together. Therefore, so that the holy city might be firm and harmonious, full-

excellent Trinity: and the Trinity in the quaternary. From which, when deduced into one another,

**EIGHTH TONE. 425**

Nevertheless, as he who revealed to the prophet, if he has enlightened our eyes, we will at least sketch out those hidden mysteries. And first of all, I think this should be stated beforehand, so that access to those inner sanctuaries may be easier for those striving, that Ezekiel begins with the divine tribunal, and after a varied description of things, finally concludes with the measurements of those things that have been touched, as if the ultimate effects are to be joined and united with the first through those measurements. Therefore, at the beginning of the vision, he sets forth God and His tribunal with wonderful artifice and hidden mystery; afterwards, under the name of a manifold structure, he measures man by proportioning him with God, as well as those things that pertain to him. But before we reveal the secrets, we will briefly explain what that measurement is, about which he speaks literally in the text. "And in the hand of the man was a measuring reed of six cubits, a cubit, and a palm." We have this precisely in the letter (text): the meaning of which words is: The reed contains six cubits, to each of which a palm is added. But since a cubit contains six palms, with that one added, there will be seven: And calculating the total measure of the reed as seven times six palms, the number of palms amounts to 42. And this calculation differs from that of Jerome, adduced above, in which there was no hesitation, when [Marginal note: Jerome] the measure of the reed was only six cubits and a palm: but not six cubits: and as many palms. Therefore, following the true interpretation according to the mind of the prophet, we say that that measure was not 37 palms, as our translation sounds, but 42, and with a most hidden sacrament, concerning which we will relate only what the divine oracles permit. For by palm and hand, or fingers, work is carried out: and this under the auspices of the number forty-two, by which God went forth into work, and measures all things, as is common among the wise. Hence, not without mystery, the more secret theologians said that the name of God of 42 letters is extracted from the first [Marginal note: Theologians and Moses] words by which the fabric of the world is narrated and described by Moses with a hidden mystery: And again, through the stations of the same number (as Jerome prudently observes), it leads the people, brought out of Egypt by such a celebrated mystery, to the land [Marginal note: Jerome] of promise, bearing the type of a better land. But with this measure, which is unique and 42, it sometimes multiplies all things by numbers, sometimes by hundreds, sometimes by tens, and thousands, distributing them with their own mysteries. Therefore, with this measure, the prophet first measures himself: And consequently [Marginal note: Paul] every man: and this under the figure of an unexpressed building, so that the mystery may be kept silent. Afterwards he measures that temple, concerning which the apostle says: "You are the temple of God." After this, the treasuries and storehouses, that is, the powers of the soul, in which heavenly treasures are received. Then the gates and vestibules, which are the exterior senses, and all things that lie externally to man: yet pertaining to the integrity of man. After these things, he measures the whole city, that is, the inner man, who has become a city and a dwelling receiving God as a guest, and the holy angels. After which he also measures the suburbs, that is, those external things that belong to man: and through which there is an entrance to God, and of God to us, and union with Him. Finally, he comes to the first fruits or tithes, namely good works, which are offered to-

--- Page 992 ---
CANTICI TERTII

...which we offer to God, which must be measured, so that a good and abundant reward, suitable for them, may be proportioned.
[Marginal note: CHRIST] For with the same measure (says the prince of all things) with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you, yet with a geometric proportion, each thing returning a hundredfold from God's greatest liberality. Very beautifully, therefore, he who demands tithes, returns the same to us in thousands of gifts, as will be clear to one calculating from the hundredfold retribution of the Gospel. Or let us say, that tithes received by God from numbers come to thousands: because with the added grace of God, to whom the thousand is attributed, those things which were previously tens, become ten thousands, and so on for the rest. This also must be noted, that at the end of the vision, he measures by thousands of measures, what he previously measured by unity, a ten, and twenty-five. Nor must this be omitted, that he measured the thresholds of the gate with one reed, and a little later he adds that the threshold of the gate was ten cubits. All these things, the prophet, not ignorant of the sacraments, described by their mystery. For the measure of all things is made by one, which denotes the beginning, and by ten, the completion of all simple numbers: because the remuneration and reward of all is He who is the beginning and the end: And from this, first fruits and tithes are rightly owed to Him. Then from ten, he passes to a hundred, assigning the distance between gate and gate by hundreds of cubits: because the reward differs by a hundredfold multiplication for those who enter through one gate, and those who enter through another. And yet he comes to a thousand, namely the cube of the complete number ten: in which he encloses and consummates all measure, although he does not fully express it: rather, he frankly confesses that he is immersed in such a deep sea: for when he came to the east, from where is the origin of all measures, he says that the waters were overflowing too much from the right side, from where mercy, grace, and all gifts [come], denoting that those things which the giver of all good things has imparted to us are so great that we cannot comprehend them. And he said, that the man coming from the east (where is the fount of all good things, although they are communicated through the power of the right hand) measured a thousand cubits with a cord: And the said waters reached up to the ankles: And he measured yet another thousand, behold the waters up to the knees: And he measured again a thousand, and was led through the water up to the loins. But when the measurer proceeded further, the waters grew so much that he could not cross: because the waters were too deep. But, to relate something of the secrets (which nevertheless may be spoken of): as long as the measurer measured those things which pertain to the animal man, whether they be ankles, knees, or loins, or kidneys, he could cross the deep waters of wisdom, by which man himself is disposed and proportioned. But when he proceeded further, namely to those things which pertain to the inner man: no further passage was given to him. Since, therefore, these things are so great that the prophet's shoulders succumbed under the burden, much less will our shoulders sustain such a burden of wisdom: because while man is spiritual, God, who is infinite, dwells in him. For the measure of the temple and the city being completed, and the sacred rites perfected, the prophet adds: And the name of the city is יהוה שמה Adonai Sama, which
[Marginal note: Ezekiel] interpreted, means: The Lord is there, that is, in man already made into a city...

--- Page 993 ---
TONVS OCTAVVS. 426

and the temple of God having been established: from which the Lord himself will never depart, just as he completely departed from the synagogue, and from many in the church: yet not from all, since he promised, saying: I am with you until the consummation of the age. These things, as far as the measure of the city according to Ezekiel, have been very lightly touched upon: so that readers may perceive whither such exact measures tend: which assuredly do not refer to that land often promised in the past, but in our time and the prophet's time stripped bare, and despoiled of sacrifices, ceremonies, treasuries, suburbs, tithes, and first-fruits. Therefore, it measured us, and our works, and corresponding rewards: all of which are subject to God's balance and measure.

De mensura primitiarum, aut decimarum. Con. II.

[Decorative initial N depicting a figure, possibly a saint or scholar, in a landscape] I also do not think the measures should be omitted, by which the prophet measures the first-fruits, or (as we better say) the tithes to be offered: which are called תרומה *teruma* in Hebrew, as we read most fully in the book of Exodus. [Marginal note: Exodus.] For the prophet says: "And upon the border of Judah from the eastern side, even to the side of the sea, there shall be first-fruits, which you shall separate, twenty-five thousand reeds in length and width: as individual parts, both from the eastern side to the sea, and in other sides: or both in length and in width, so that the entire circuit is by one hundred thousands" – I will not say of reeds, because 'reed' is not found here in the Hebrew text, but is added in our translation at will, and not according to the mystery. For here the reward is measured by one hundred, by which those are rewarded who offer to God the true first-fruits of their body, kept purely and chastely. For these (as Jerome thinks) [Marginal note: Hieron.] are crowned with the number one hundred, which is multiplied by the prophet by a thousand, always attributed to God: so that the reward corresponding to a work pleasing to God may be understood as divine. But the first-fruits of the other tribes are measured by twenty-five thousand from the northern side, and the same from the southern side. But from the eastern side by ten thousand: and from the west by the same number, which, brought together into one, yield seventy thousand. The root of this number is seven, indeed the number of remission, led by ten, a complete number: and again brought back by the divine thousand denotes the works, offerings, and rewards of penitents, who expect remissions from the true seven: afterwards the reward of completed works supported by the divine thousand. Hence, those who cannot dedicate themselves with Judah, the royal tribe, inasmuch as they have been quite faithless and rebellious, at least let them offer the oblations of penitents through the hands of a priest, not just any priest, and rather one polluting the offering than offering it, but through the hands of those who are of the sons of Zadok, which means 'just' or 'righteous': concerning whom it follows: "Who kept my ceremonies, and did not err, when the children of Israel erred, as also the Levites erred." But this Zadok (as Jerome thinks) [Marginal note: Hieron.] is Christ, a priest forever, and just: therefore it is said, "according to the order of Melchizedek": who is interpreted as "my righteous king". Concerning whom

Concerning the measure of this city according to John. Con. III.

**S**The measure of John seems to differ considerably from that of Ezekiel: For the latter (Ezekiel) measures with a wooden reed those things which pertain to the figurative family, not yet freed from the burdens of stones, wood, and straw: but John describes the merits of the blessed, and the fabric of that city, which we declared above to be woven from gold and precious stones: therefore it is rightly said to be measured with a golden reed. However, he does not express how great the measure is: because neither can those things which he measures be determined: since the glory of the blessed is about an infinite and interminable object, continually filling those who receive it according to their capacity: and that place is immense and truly terminable by no measure. Nevertheless, with his reed, he leads that circuit to twelve thousand stadia: and the walls through twelve square cubits, namely one hundred forty-four thousand, running through both in some way with great mystery. He says therefore that he who spoke with him measured the measure
John. [marginal note] of a man, which is of an angel: but how great it is, he does not declare even in this place. In that, however, which he says, that the measure of a man, and the measure of an angel, he implies the reward in which each is blessed. Which, since (as we have said) is God: its measure can neither be terminated nor expressed. Nevertheless, the measure of an angel and of a man is said to be the same, because it is given in the same proportion, provided that their capacity and merits demand it. Therefore, with that measure, the angel who spoke with him measured the city, by twelve thousand stadia: which is set in a square, and its height is as great as its width, since these are equally related to each other. And he measured its walls one hundred forty-four cubits. Many things occur here which present no small difficulty: And first, how the city can be equal in width and height, when the width is said to be twelve thousand stadia, but the height only 144 cubits. And here we briefly say: because we do not have other words at hand, by which divine things may be more suitably explained, than these of ours, which are certainly most suitable for the things we wish to express, to God not without mystery, both Noah's ark and the tabernacle of the covenant are said to be measured by cubits: and the immense edifice of the heavenly city is said to be measured by stadia. For the cubit imports the arm and hand simultaneously: by which we outwardly distribute and perform good work. The stadium, however, is completed by a Herculean race in a single breath (as it is said): Whence by this stadium every possible affection is signified to us, by which as if by feet we are carried to God. For by feet in sacred eloquence, affections are always mystically designated. And these ought to be of strong, great, and vigorous spirit, and carried by a single breath, that is, by a single intention. But by the cubit, arm, and hand, the work to be rewarded is understood. And since the reward and glory of that heavenly city correspond to work and affection by geometric proportion, therefore things pertaining to that city and glory are said to be measured by cubits and stadia. But how many cubits and stadia themselves there are, is not expressed: because those heavenly things cannot be terminated by our number: although they are said to be commensurate with our works,
[Marginal note: CHRIST.] and affections by geometric proportion. Both of which Christ, the prince of that city, explains in the Gospel, saying: "You will receive a hundred for one," behold a geometric proportion: "and you will possess eternal life," behold an unending measure. Because affections and works, when sprinkled with accepting grace and embraced by God's charity, smell of God himself: and therefore they rejoice in that divine millennium: And through Him they are multiplied as many times as that divine name, from which is all virtue, is invoked.

**FOURTH MODULE. STRUCTURE.**
Who built it. Con. I.

[Decorative initial 'V' containing two figures in a landscape] Who built this city and our harmonious dwelling, and full of all harmony and joy, John clearly declares, while he says: "I saw the holy city, Jerusalem, de-
[Marginal note: John.] scending from heaven, prepared by God, as a bride adorned for her husband." So it itself descends from heaven, and its Calotechnius, that is, good architect, builder, and adorner: so that looking up to it, he might lead us back to heaven itself.
[Marginal note: John. The Church.] For John speaks of that structure woven from living stones, as the Church sings: "Blessed city, Jerusalem, called vision of peace: which is built in the heavens
[Marginal note: CHRIST.] from living stones: and adorned with angels, as a betrothed companion:" It is certainly prepared in the mind of the builder from the primal constitution of the world, as it is said in the Gospel: "Come"

--- Page 998 ---
**TONVS OCTAVVS. 432**

ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For the supreme architect prepared a threefold dwelling for the human guest: one indeed is that heavenly kingdom, and the dwellings of the blessed. The second is this earthly one for our pilgrimage: from which, most elegantly arranged, we can easily conjecture how great and of what kind that is, which he prepared for our eternal dwelling. The third is this one constructed upon a foundation, which indeed is Christ, and upon the twelve apostolic foundations, made from living stones, and measured by the measures of Ezekiel and John, concerning which we touched upon above. And so great is the harmony of these three, that from one we can infer another, provided we well understand the nature and arrangement of each building: that this one, which we now inhabit, is defiled and lowest: and that one to which we tend is purified and most exquisite: that also which is in the middle, and under whose auspices we hasten to that supernal one, is spiritual, namely the house and city of the church, within whose bosom or embrace it is necessary for us to be contained, if we wish to ascend to the heavenly and supernal. For these structures are similar, constructed by the same artisan: and each bears his image according to its capacity: Hence there is a symbol and likeness among them, from which, by treating of one, we can also understand something of another. Nor was there any other maker of these buildings, except Him of whom it is said: For He is the artisan of all, possessing the power of all, foreseeing all things.

How, and with what glue, this structure is compacted and united. Con. II.

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.8em; float: left; margin-right: 0.1em;">O</span>MNIA multiple things which come together into one, must be joined either by art, or by nature, or by divine mystery. For stones in a house are connected by cement, lime, and iron or bronze clamps, over poured lead. Wood, however, is joined by nails, or by glue made from cheese, or fish, or ox-hide, which is considered the most perfect. But bones in the human body are bound together by nerves, flesh, and skin. And sometimes stones, and diverse bodies, by a certain natural force, I will not say are glued together, but are united: like two trees by grafting: and oysters with stones by a certain more hidden force of nature. I have also seen human bodies turned into stones, and so united with the stones, that they already seemed to have become one body, and that a homogeneous one. And because the force of nature is stronger than art, therefore it binds more strongly. But since the divine power is the strongest of all, therefore it not only connects but also unites. And this force is of His holy and great name, of which it is said: O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name in all the earth: namely, both in the upper and lower, binding, connecting, and uniting all parts and their members together in both. In imitation of which, in Jerusalem (which bears the type of that supernal city which we describe), God commanded that a temple be built: Afterwards he added in that volume, which in Greek is called Paralipomenon, but in Latin "words of days" (Chronicles): "I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name may be there: which I have chosen: that a temple may be built in it for my name." But not only the stone temple, and the whole great machine of the world, but also the rational

      [ornament] FIFTH MODULE, ORNAMENT.
    Typical description of ornament according to Ezekiel. Con. I.

[Illuminated initial O] The ornament of this city is extensively described by Ezekiel under the type of a bride elevated by the Lord from a humble state to a glorious one: which [Marginal note: Ezekiel.] John does not express, but hints at, when he says: Prepared by God, as [Marginal note: John.] a bride adorned for her husband. Therefore, the Lord is introduced by Ezekiel in such words complaining about the synagogue, which after such noble ornaments had fallen into many crimes: from which ornaments, described metaphorically, we will easily be able to understand those ornaments with which she herself will be clothed for the supreme prince and the Lamb, perpetually to be espoused in those very nuptials, concerning which John says, 'Let us rejoice and exult, and give glory to God: for the marriage of the [Marginal note: The same.] Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself; and it was granted to her to be clothed in shining and white fine linen, for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.' And John does not proceed further concerning the ornament: but Ezekiel, in a long discourse, recounts with what ornaments and gifts the former bride, the synagogue, was endowed by the bridegroom: and with what lamentations he complains of her ingratitude, saying: 'I made you multiply like the growth of the field,' which indeed cannot be numbered: just as the multitude of the blessed cannot. It follows: 'You multiplied and grew large, and you came to the ornament of ornaments:' for which we have 'woman's adornment:' for the ornament of ornaments is placed at the time of weddings. Your breasts swelled: those very breasts, concerning which in the Song of Songs. 'Your two breasts are [Marginal note: Song of Songs.] like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, or a hind, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline.' Indeed, hinds and gazelles are exalted, by which he adjures all the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken the beloved. Which breasts receive milk flowing and emanating from that land once promised, but now described by our John. To which milk Isaiah, in the name of the bridegroom, invites, saying: 'Come, and buy wine and milk without any exchange.' [Marginal note: Isaiah.] And concerning her who does not have this milk, nor breasts, that is, the capacity to receive it, the bridegroom complains in the Song of Songs, saying: 'Our sister is little, and she has no breasts.' [Marginal note: Song of Songs.] Blessed therefore are those who have those full breasts, which are better than wine. Hence, for a great gift, he brings forth that: 'Your breasts swelled full of that milk, which he who sucks knows how to reject evil and choose good.' And your hair grew: that indeed, which in Nazirites is not shaved, but grows, and is counted with all the hairs, which are numbered. But it is exceedingly damnable that with breasts swollen with that heavenly milk, and with flourishing hair, that is, with increasing vigor and strength of youth, she was naked, and

three names he indicates the sacrament of the Trinity: not that there is one substance
and another, but that diverse things figure the diverse properties of the persons.
For fine flour, which is the marrow of wheat, commanded to be offered in sacrifices in many places, signifies Christ,

[Marginal note: David.] concerning whom the psalmist follows: "And from the rock, He satisfied them with honey." Therefore, by the influence of these persons, united nonetheless in one essence, every rational creature is truly adorned and nourished: Which, without their influx, is destitute in poverty and starvation, weak, deformed, and hungry. Therefore, with such great diligence, God required those three in offerings, namely fine flour, honey, and oil, so that, receiving these sacramental offerings, He might return certain divine gifts, accumulated with no small increase, just as Christ asked for water from that Samaritan woman, so that He might return from His own abundance eternal life: The soul, fed and made beautiful by this food and influx, it follows: "You have become exceedingly beautiful, and you have prospered in the kingdom: And your name went forth among the nations because of your beauty." For thus the Israelite people prevailed over whomever, while it stood in its beauty, indeed in the beauty bestowed by God: whence it follows, "You were perfect in My beauty, which I placed upon you," says the Lord. And because the prophet first prophesies concerning the synagogue, in which many transgressed: therefore he subjoins complaints, which God Himself makes concerning the fornications, debaucheries, adulteries, and idolatries perpetrated by that ungrateful people: Whence also He judges its crime more grievous than the wickedness of Gomorrah and Sodom. But if we wish to understand the true adornment of that bride, who is bound to the bridegroom by an indissoluble bond, through that figurative (description): then all falls, and crimes, and abominations are far removed, [Marginal note: John.] since in that city, and among those perpetually betrothed to the heavenly bridegroom, these things are by no means found, as our John says: "Nothing defiled or unclean will enter into it, namely into those most chaste bridal chambers: but outside will stand all the unchaste, sorcerers, murderers, liars, and whoever has been defiled in any way." Therefore, you have the adornment of the structure declared above, from gold, jasper, and various precious stones: And here you have the mystical adornments of the living city, built from living stones, or the adornments of the guests of that city: Nor can we express further adornment with our words.

Why John does not express adornment as Ezekiel does. Con. II.

And thrice the prophet Ezekiel and John compare the adornment of that city to the adornment of a bride prepared for her husband, since a more accurate preparation than that is not found: then also because the union of that city, or of its guests with the prince, is called a certain celebration and a connection of nuptials, [Marginal note: Ezekiel. Idem.] as John expressly says: "Let us rejoice and exult, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His wife has prepared herself." But Ezekiel continues this adornment...

--- Page 1006 ---
**EIGHTH TONE. 432**

chiel, but John kept silent: and this because the former, speaking of a figurative bride, could borrow from this analogous adornment, from which he might describe that figurative worship. [Marginal note: Ezechie.] But John, since he treats of the true bride, now freed from all shadows, figures, and enigmas, often lacked words and images by which he might describe that true splendor and glory, which surpasses every eye and human intellect. Therefore, I now seem to have arrived at the goodness of silence, which (as Dionysius says) is in the hidden and inmost divine places: [Marginal note: Diony.] Where the glory and beauty of all things is especially in the contemplation of God, who is all things so eminently that nothing can be compared to Him. Hence, those who have attained that glory considered it better to be silent than to speak inadequately, and to fail through inept examples and words for so great a thing, or to wish to express those things which it is not lawful for a man to speak. Nevertheless, John left a way for contemplatives, by which they can pursue many things, while he says in a single word: "As a bride adorned for her husband." Than which adornment none is more careful, none more celebrated, nor any marital union more intimate. These things argue for the greatest charity of the prince of that city towards us, since he seeks us not as servants and handmaids, but as most beloved brides for himself, to be bound by the bonds of heavenly nuptials, concerning which we shall immediately discourse, God being our guide.

**SIXTH MODULE, LIGHT.**
**What light is in general. Con. 1.**

[Decorative initial P] After the adornment of the city, light is treated very elegantly: by which the adornments themselves can be seen, and those who behold them can be delighted in it, from which they receive all good things. For just as (as the Phoenicians teach in their theology, with Iamblichus relating it) [Marginal note: Iambli.] we receive all corporeal good things from the light of the sun without any intermediary, or from the planets and stars, to which that Phoebean light is communicated: so in the heavenly city, whatever good things those citizens have, they receive from the Father of lights, and from that sun who says: "I am the light of the world." Or from higher minds, [Marginal note: CHRI STVS Diony si.] who, acquiring stronger illuminations from the supreme light, afterwards illuminate the lower ones, as Dionysius, conscious of those mysteries, hands down. Concerning which light, however, when I have decided to say something, I shudder at first glance: because the most obscure of all things offers itself to me, which indeed, the more it shines, the more it is also contracted by a darker gloom, and enveloped in a denser mist, so that eyes not well purified are offended rather than enlightened. Hence, that supreme light spoke to Solomon, the prophets, and Moses himself in darkness, until their eyes, freed from lower darkness, could endure that light itself. Whence Moses, sometimes freed from bodily impediments, transcending the darkness, saw the supreme light and the good itself face to face: whence his face shone so brightly that the children of Israel could not look intently at his face (as Paul says) because of the splendor of his countenance. For descending from the mountain, he had from con-

--- Page 1007 ---
**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

the divinely shining face: although our translation has 'horned'. Which error arose from the similarity of the word. For the Hebrews say קָרַן (karan) for 'shining' and קֶרֶן (keren) for 'horn' with indeed the same letters, but varied points (vowels). But let us return to our subject. Many are there who cannot bear that light, just like that common people: whence it is necessary that a veil be interposed: otherwise, offended by their own darkness, unable to comprehend that light, when they presume to speak of it, they utter many absurdities. For some say, and think to prove, that light is not a substance: because it sometimes happens to someone (as an accident): and because it cannot be the specific form of any form: Which things are childish, and bound by Peripatetic laws: for we have from our John: that life was the light of men. But since life is called light, it is inferred that light itself is also a substance, just like life. We also have from Augustine, from the great Plotinus, and from Aristotle himself in the second discourse on the soul, that this light, which is seen by the eyes, is a certain corporeal form. This light (says Plato), after the matter of heaven and earth was produced, the Creator immediately commanded to be present: so that it might vivify, distinguish, and illuminate all things, lest all things be confused, but distinct. For this [light] is so clear that it makes

**EIGHTH TONE.** 433

referring to them: The people who sat in darkness saw a great light. Concerning this, elsewhere, inspired by prophetic fervor, he exclaimed: Arise, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. For the glory of the Lord is no other light than this, which once rose in the world, and was begotten by the Father from eternity: This generated light, together with the unbegotten, brought forth the creating mind (says Mercurius), [Marginal note: Mercur.] that is, it produced the Holy Spirit, the artisan of all things: to speak in our manner. For this [Spirit] is heat, which, proceeding from light and splendor, exists as light itself: For those three most holy persons are like three rays existing in one splendor, as Dionysius teaches; [Marginal note: Diony.] yet these rays are not confused. Which we also prove in three lights, while we perceive the Trinity in the shadows emanating from those lights. But unity is present when they form one light and one splendor. However, the example fails, because those multiplied splendors of lamps provide a greater light, since by their termination one increases the light of the other; but those infinite supramundane rays cannot be increased; yet they communicate their infinite light to inferior beings as much as they please. In shadows too they are distinguished, that is, in the effects produced by them, since from the Father of lights we have being; from the Son, understanding; from the Spirit, warmth and love. They are also distinguished among themselves as light, splendor, and heat, which nevertheless are the same in substance: Not indeed qualitative splendor and heat (as logicians say), [Marginal note: Logici] but essential light, splendor, and heat: which subsist by themselves, without being in a body, and without emanating from a body: such is that divine light, splendor, and heat of which we speak: from which all life and all things emanate. This light John explained in a few words, [Marginal note: Ioannes] as is the custom of those who are closer to the light itself. For just as light, the closer it is to the shining and diffusing source, the more intense it is and less spread out. And the more remote, the more spread out and less intense. In the same way, those teaching it and diffusing it, the more they have approached it, the more intensely they understand, and explain it in fewer words. But those more distant from the light and doctrine, since they do not know well how to express what they do not well perceive, multiply words and entangle those listening and reading. Therefore, John, [Marginal note: Idem] being very close to that illuminating one, and reclining on his breast, received intense and less diffused light, whence he also expressed himself concisely concerning it. But we, being much more distant from that light, and acting with those sitting on lower benches, it is necessary that, just as we have received it through more rays, we also explain it to our inferiors with more words: yet pursuing those things which we have learned from John, admitted to the inner chambers of light, delivered in few but most sweet harmonies, both concerning the light itself and concerning those things which emanated from it and continuously emanate.

How all created things proceed from light. Con. III.

[Decorative woodcut initial L]That first-begotten light, therefore, is unique, and vibrating within itself with a single and most simple ray, it offers a single idea to the divine eye. But according to the multiplicity of those who behold it, it becomes multi-faceted: And the more it descends, the more rays it seems to have. Which
Ioannes. John, embracing all things, says in a single word: "All that was made, in Him was life."
Augusti. "life it was," a creative life, says Augustine. And immediately he adds: that this life
was light, from which all things were made: which he calls by another name, the Word. There are also
Moses. those who believe that which was prescribed by Moses, "Let there be light," refers to angels, as the first lights emanating from God: through which, as through glass (as Iamblichus
Iamblic. draws from the Pythagorean workshop), that supreme light transmits its light into other lower things: And let them be, as it were, transparent, and the first intermediaries, the higher
angels beholding that light itself, by which all lower beings are illuminated in their respective degrees,
Dyoni. as it pleases Dionysius. But each of the lowest things [is illuminated] through a medium, or suitable media, corresponding to them, as we touched upon above. But each of mankind receives that portion of light whose nature is the medium to which it is exposed: or with which it is connected. For if the soul emanates from that supreme light through Seraphic intelligences, it becomes seraphic: and strives to reach seraphic mansions (by the auspices of nature, but primarily with God's favor and attraction). But if through Cherubic minds the soul receives the splendor of knowledge, having become familiar with that light, it strives to reach Cherubic seats: whose nature it has already assumed through the penetrating light: and so let it be said of any other orders whatsoever. For just as light passing through glasses of different colors also diffuses multicolored rays, namely red ones through red, green ones through green, white ones through white, and so it must be said of the others. In a similar way, the intellect, or soul, assumes that nature through whose transparency it passes. Nor is the transparency of spiritual light air, but spirit,
CHRI STVS. and intelligence: which can receive and transmit that light. And perhaps of these the supreme teacher speaks, when he says: "Their angels always see the face of the Father." And who are their angels, if not those appointed for their guardianship? And how are they suitably appointed, unless they have some affinity with those to whom they are destined? But since above we have equated all lower things with the heavens, and the heavens with angels, and angels indeed with that supreme light: we can easily understand how all things themselves emanate from the same light.

**How light itself kindles and excites. Con. V.**

[Decorative initial H] THIS light, however, not only illuminates, but also kindles; and through its splendor, separating, rarefying, and heating (as Avicenna [Marginal note: Avicenna] says), it separates the pure from the impure, the good from the evil, the beautiful from the deformed: destroying and consuming the former; perfecting the latter. But there is a difference between light and heat: For light remains in the illuminated object, yet illuminating and penetrating what is illuminated; Heat, however, passing into what is heated, mixes with it. Hence the Holy Spirit, whose role is to heat, is said to dwell in us and mix with us more than the Son, who is properly light. For He (the Son) taught and illuminated the Apostles, and ascended into heaven; But He (the Spirit), sent and destined by this light, descends, entering, inflaming, and remaining, so that one and the same spirit may be made with those whom He inflames, or they themselves one with Him. And if He ascended to heaven, He does not, however, abandon us; but is with us until the consummation of the age, vivifying and illuminating. Nor is He therefore said to be diffused in us, like the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Apostle says: "The love of God has been poured out in your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us." [Marginal note: Paul] Which we can also prove in the sun, a sufficiently clear image of God: whose light illuminates us, but is not diffused in us, like heat. For when the sun recedes, or a person moves away from it, or a window is closed, light no longer provides splendor; but diffused heat remains for a time: Thus also charity remains in our hearts, even if that light does not actively illuminate.

Therefore, that light excites, which in its solitary nature is entirely separated from us, but sent through the Son as through rays, and through the Holy Spirit as through heat: which excited those ancient fathers through that enigmatic splendor: who nevertheless was the Son and wisdom of God, veiled in enigmas and figures: Afterwards, appearing in the flesh, He excited us with clear light, according to that of the Apostle: [Marginal note: The Same] "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son: whom he appointed heir of all things, as to his humanity: through whom he also made the ages, as to his divinity." Paul continues: [Marginal note: The Same] "Who being the brightness of His glory." Behold therefore, that this light, this splendor, is the Son of God: who taught and excited the ancient fathers through various enigmas, and at last demonstrated Himself in the flesh with a clearer light. In the homeland (heaven), however, there will be a most manifest and continuous light for all, without any interruption, or overshadowing, or concealment under dark veils: And therefore John says: [Marginal note: The Same] "And there was no night there, for the Lamb was its lamp." Hence, sometimes the prophet implored the excitation that occurs in this pilgrimage, saying: [Marginal note: David] "Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp!" for which we have: "Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp," for עור (Hur) means to excite/awaken, not to arise. Therefore, he prays to that begotten light, which was the psaltery of the Old Testament, and the evangelical harp, and the glory of all, that it may excite him: since we are not excited from elsewhere, nor do we have exciting light from elsewhere.

**THIRD CANTICLE**

**How this light amplifies and expands. Consideration VI.**

[Decorative initial M]ruly wonderful is this light, which at first offered itself as obscured, but as soon as it began to illuminate my eyes, it leads me to such spacious chambers, and so entices the eye of my mind by piercing through, that I cannot depart from it, even though I cannot fully conceive even its smallest portion. For it expands my heart to such a magnitude that I am unable to retreat, but I am compelled to run with loose reins into the path of its rays, when it has expanded my heart and my mind. Nor is it truly wonderful if that light amplifies and expands, since white color, which is a kind of opaque light (as we touched upon above), disperses and expands; and the purer this corporeal light is, the more it extends visual rays widely, lengthily, and broadly. But that light is always most pure, so much so that the more our inner eye receives it, the more it is purified. Hence, the wise who have purified their inner eye by faith and doctrine see more than the common people; and the purified simple ones see more than those entangled in human doctrines and cunning, as the true light itself says: [Marginal note: CHRIST] "I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones." And prophets, having a purer eye of the mind, saw even more than the wise of this world. For in the pure splendor of light, the truly purified behold, as the same supreme light says: [Marginal note: The Same] "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." The vision of which light is followed by joy, as the same light says: "These things I have spoken to you, illuminating you, so that my joy may be in you, and your joy may be fulfilled." Nor can he feel this joy who is deprived of that light, as that good old man Tobias said: [Marginal note: Tobias] "What joy can there be for me, when I do not see the light of heaven?" Therefore, by this light, the heart and intellect of Solomon were expanded, so that he might observe natural things and discourse from the cedar of Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. [Marginal note: Moses. Paul.] Expanded by this, Moses gave the law of most divine wisdom. Expanded by this, Paul saw the secrets of God, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. By this, all the prophets saw not only hidden things, but also those things which were done in times long past, and those which were to be done after a long time. [Marginal note: Benedict. Francis.] By this, Benedict, Francis, and many others, whose eyes were illuminated, saw absent things and things remote from corporeal sight. Finally, expanded in this perfect amplitude, we blessed ones hope, where we shall behold all things we desire with clear and open sight.

**How this light gladdens and beatifies. Consideration VII.**

[Decorative initial P]inally, this most holy light gladdens and beatifies those things which it had already vivified, illuminated, aroused, and expanded. For those things which shine and are illuminated are joyful, just as those things which lie in darkness mourn. And since there is no night in that most blessed kingdom, therefore there is no sorrow or horror there, whence our divine John, testifying to this, says: [Marginal note: John] "And there was no night there, for its lamp was the Lamb." And the more that heavenly and divine light ex-

--- Page 1014 ---
TONVS OCTAVVS. 436

...excellent it is than ours, the more joy it brings to the mind contemplating it. Indeed, our eyes rejoice in that solar light; our soul rejoices, and the spirit itself, as if in a light most familiar to it, from which spirit and life, most similar to light, emanate. For the Father of all (says [Marginal note: Mercur.] Mercurius), existing as intellect, life, and splendor, created man in His own likeness, a partaker, namely, of light and life. Therefore, when man returns to the light akin to him, he rejoices much more than one who, having long sojourned abroad, returns to his own and desired homeland. And so much does our spirit and mind befriend light, and delight in being suffused with light, that when it rejoices, it seems to emit it; so that just as the spirit rejoices within, so outwardly it smiles with the face, and shines with a certain exhilaration. And the eyes, which are most friendly to light, shine, and in that smile they create a circular motion like the heavens, and they dilate. In those who mourn, however, on the contrary, they are constricted and darkened; and as if adhering to a center of darkness, they are fixed. For we rejoice in this light, as if suffused with the smile of heaven. But if that light were seen in angels (as happened to some), we would rejoice much more. But in that supreme light, the blessed rejoice so much, that the overflowing joy converts the body itself into a celestial nature, and makes it glorious, luminous, and clear. For the eyes of all the blessed, both of body and mind, now converted into the nature of light, permeable and shining, by a mere glance, impress rays of intelligence upon their companions, sparkling in both with that emanation. And this supreme light shining so abundantly and felicitously in all things, just as this Sun in the stars; and much more: for the stars of the blessed will pass into the nature of that sun, as the Savior says: The just shall shine like the Sun in the presence of their Father. [Marginal note: CHRI STVS] Hence, a better and more harmonious harmony and joy is born there, than arises in the heavens from their consonant distance and most orderly motions, with the stars corresponding from the due convergence of rays. For those converging rays of the blessed united in the supreme light produce a sweeter melody. Moreover, those citizens smile and rejoice in the light itself, which illuminates all things, however diverse; because, having now become children of light, they are converted in mind and body into the same light. All things also become beautiful by that light; which is so beautiful that, with all deformity put to flight, it brings a wonderful delight to those who behold and receive it. The blessed, therefore, now in that evening light dispersed into many things, now in the morning light collected in the Word, behold all forms gathered there in most sweet harmony. Now turning themselves to that one thing shining in the midday light, from there too they draw what makes them rejoice, perceiving especially in that light, whence all things become beautiful and harmonious; and whence comes the congruence and harmony of colors, tastes, smells, spirits, and all things. Therefore, eyes turned to that midday light are so absorbed, that those who were formerly celestial then become divine, having drunk the nectar of divine pleasure. Therefore, nothing remains that they can desire; because, admitted to those inner sanctuaries, they are completely intoxicated by the abundance of that light, which immediately fills whatever is in that kingdom. And this is what Peter says: [Marginal note: Petrus] He has called us into His marvelous light; which was first diffused into the Son, who is the splen-

of the Father: afterwards into Christ, the man, prince of the whole city: then into the God-like queen, where she shines more splendidly than the others. Then it passed to the angelic choirs arranged in due order, down to the lowest dwelling of that supernal city: so that in it, all who see the Father of lights may always praise and glorify Him.

**THIRD MODULE, DIVISION.**

**That the house and that heavenly family are divided. First Harmony.**

[Marginal note: John. Ezekiel.]
**W**e are most fully taught by John and Ezekiel that the city and heavenly commonwealth are divided into many parts: who describe now foundations, now gates, now streets, now suburbs, now the temple, now treasuries: into which that structure is divided. Thus also Paul openly testifies that the inhabitants are divided into several ranks, saying: "In the church, which is this holy ci-
[Marginal note: Paul.]
-ty, which we describe, first indeed He gave some to be Apostles, then prophets, but others Evangelists, others pastors, and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ." To these ranks correspond distinct portions of rewards, dwellings, and se-
[Marginal note: CHRIST.]
-ats, as Christ says: "In my Father's house are many mansions." And since these things are hidden from us, and Christ has been silent as to for whom they are prepared by the eternal Father, indeed, He even confessed that it was not His to distribute them, but that they are given to those for whom they are prepared by the Father Himself, we too shall revere in silence, except insofar as the Son Himself deigned to reveal to His prophets and intimates. We shall follow those who treat of such matters, considering first that if in this earthly house there is a varied division into diverse seats for guests and lodgings for travelers, no less should it be thought concerning the blessed and Heavenly kingdom, from which, without doubt, these lower things emanate. There, therefore, are eternal mansions for all, not succeeding one another through time, but now dwelling together, having been admitted as heavenly citizens and members of God's household. Some of whom are assessors and judges. But the souls of some are brides and queens: but of some, concubines and young women, with a mystery more sublime than sensible words can express. The rest, however, are distributed into so many ranks that I dare not pursue the series of things in any way: Nevertheless, we will subjoin a few excerpts from those who have been taught by divine oracles.

**Concerning the particular mansions and seats of the blessed. Harmony II.**

[Marginal note: Isaiah.]
**T**he first seat, therefore, is that of the supreme Emperor, which is sometimes described by the name of the whole heaven, according to that of Isaiah: "Heaven is my throne." Sometimes it is a particular throne, on which Christ also se-
[Marginal note: Paul. Stephen. John.]
-ats, as Paul, Stephen, and John testify in many places. For here (John) in the beginning of the most sacred vision introduces Him speaking these words: "To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with Me on My throne, as I also overcame and sat down on"

my Father's throne. Concerning whom Isaiah also says: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and elevated throne: and the whole earth was full of his glory." [Marginal note: Isaiah.]
Before this throne stand seven spirits, as John says: "And to the seven spirits who are in the presence of his throne." [Marginal note: John.]
But first let us speak of the queen and empress of all: who, clothed with the sun and crowned with twelve stars, treads the moon under her feet like the sun, and she herself sits at his right hand: as the prophet, once admitted by the Holy Spirit to those inner chambers, addressing the king sitting on the throne, exclaims with these words: "The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded by variety." [Marginal note: David]
She has the moon, that is, the synagogue, or the assembly of all the elect, under her feet: because she is exalted above all creatures. And she is clothed with the sun, that is, Christ, above all who put him on according to the Apostolic teaching.
Afterwards are the twelve seats of the Apostles, who will obtain a more worthy place than others, and a seat on the thrones of judgment, as the Prince says: "You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." And when the twelve fathers of the figurative family correspond with these, 24 are formed: [Marginal note: CHRIST] because (as John says) "And around the seat of the Lamb, namely, there were twenty-four seats. And upon the thrones, I saw twenty-four elders sitting, clothed in white garments, and on their heads golden crowns." [Marginal note: John.] All of whom with mutual voices praised Him who lives forever and ever, and said: "You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory, and honor, and power: for you created all things."
There follow the seats of the prophets: who (as the Apostle teaches) [Marginal note: Paul.] hold a more sublime place, yet after the Apostles, and the first founders, and the principal fathers of both families, the twenty-four so often celebrated. Among the first are the four major prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, and the twelve minor prophets, and many others, of whom mention is made in the four books of Kings. These are therefore called by the Hebrews the books of the former prophets, because all of them are interspersed with the deeds of some prophets, beginning with Samuel, after whom Nathan, Ahijah, Elijah, Elisha, and many others flourished: among whom, without doubt, are many whose names and deeds are not written: and very many who were called sons of the prophets.
Next succeed the Evangelists, whom He chose from among His intimates in the order in which Paul instructs us. Who were figured (as it pleases Gregory and most others) [Marginal note: Gregory.] by the four animals full of eyes, also furnished with six seraphic wings. For they were full of eyes illuminated by divine light, so that they might describe the gospels in a wondrous way, consonant with the law: so much so that there is no apex or iota in the law that is not contained in the gospel by a wondrous artifice. But of these, it is not necessary to speak in detail. They also have six seraphic wings: because they were always carried by fiery love in their narration. And they extended their wings in six parts of that structure, namely, before and behind, to the right and to the left, upwards and downwards. Concerning which the Apostle says: "That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints (especially with the Evangelists, who fully wrote those things which pertain to holiness and perfect life) what is the length, and breadth, and height, and depth." [Marginal note: Paul.] For length is before and behind:
