breadth is extended to the right and left: which are four extensions: Afterwards height, and depth, which complete the six. And this extension is according to the moral sense. In the natural sense, however, seraphim extend their wings to all the aforesaid parts: because their warming power is sought everywhere in length, breadth, and depth, just like the sun's. Nor are the seats of others mentioned by John, although there are many in the house of the eternal Father, and we are taught by Dionysius about many orders of angels, about which we have explained above.

Concerning the Merkabah, or tribunal of God, according to the Hebrews. Con. III.

[Decorative initial E] There also exists in the theology of the Hebrews the tribunal of God, which they call Merkabah: as we have from Ezekiel, and from diverse places of scripture, but explained by the doctors, especially in the book of formation, which is inscribed to Abraham: [Marginal note: Abrahā.] To which they say belong Ophaninim, Seraphim, angels of ministry, and animals of holiness. Which, because they are not in use among our Latins, no one doubts, will seem foreign, not to say inept, because they savor of nothing trivial at all. Nor do I think we should desist from this, but that I should touch upon some things worthy of knowledge, besides those things which we have touched upon above. Therefore they say Ophaninim are angels whose care it is to dispose the matter of things, so that form can be introduced. For matter does not dispose itself, since it has no active power: therefore it is necessary that it be disposed by an external force. Seraphim, however, they say are warming powers, by which life and form are supplied. The angels of ministry, however, are of many kinds, just as the ministries entrusted to them. But the four animals of holiness are concordantly mentioned by Ezekiel and John, namely, the lion, the calf or ox, the eagle, and the man. What these animals are, however (although diverse [authors] have understood diverse things in the allegorical and moral sense, as Jerome recounts in a long series on Ezekiel [Marginal note: Hierōn.]), we, interpreting the anagogical sense, will follow the ancient fathers, saying that these four are, as it were, kings of four kinds of animals. For among herds and domestic animals, the ox is king: among wild beasts, the lion: among birds, the eagle: And among all rational beings, man: who also holds primacy over angels, and this applies to both sexes. For in the male sex, Christ exceeds them, as Paul says: "Having become so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they." [Marginal note: Paulus.] In the female sex, however, she who is said to be exalted above all choirs of angels: To whom it was said more particularly (as it pleases some wise men), before man was formed from the earth and Eve was extracted from his rib: "Have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the other creatures." But to what purpose in that tribunal are the lion, the ox, and the eagle? I say, that if all things emanate from Him, ought not all things also have their image and idea in Him, and be written in the book of the supreme God's reckoning? For if, as in the books of royal reckonings, and of good rulers, all things are noted, both men, and cities, and revenues, and whatever pertains to the kingdom: so also in the book of God (as the prophet says) all will be written. And lest it be contended, that ho... [Marginal note: Dauid]

--- Page 1018 ---
TONE EIGHT. 438

men alone are written there, he prefaced by saying: "My frame was not hidden from you, when you made me in secret: Your unformed substance your eyes saw." [Marginal note: Jerome] Where Jerome says: "Even the elements, from which man is composed, God knows before he is formed, and all elemental parts: but also He numbers the stars, calling all of them by name: He also numbers the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, having in Himself the archetype of all these. Much more does He know the animals sometimes shown to the prophets, and contains their image in His most abundant court." And therefore John, [Marginal note: John, Daniel, Ezekiel] Daniel, and Ezekiel, who sometimes returning to us from that same court, reported that they had seen there horses, serpents, dragons, leopards, lions, calves, and various beasts. However, those royal animals are not without reason (as it seems to me) held more particularly as images and singular ideas of those things which are here, just as the insignia of individual kingdoms and principalities are held by the Emperor. And since these animals are in that kingdom, as are also their seats, and [the seats] of all those whose type they bear in this world. But since we do not have other things expressed by the prophets concerning the division of that city, and concerning the seats of its inhabitants, nor shall we, progressing further in this manner, come to the guests, through whom that division will be better known.

[Ornamental symbol] MODULE EIGHT, GUESTS.
How many guests there are in that city. First Harmony.

Beyond the threefold and unique supreme prince, and the queen, how many guests there are in that dwelling, who always sing together there in praise of the prince, it is impossible to define, as John says: [Marginal note: John] "I saw a great multitude, which no one could number." And concerning the seed of Abraham, to be saved for the most part, God said to Abraham himself: [Marginal note: GOD:] "Count the stars, if you can: So shall your seed be," which indeed will come forth from Isaac, who indeed was born not according to the flesh (says Paul) [Marginal note: Paul] from the slave woman, but from the free woman, according to the spirit through the promise, which things are spoken by allegory. This number, however (as Dionysius says), [Marginal note: Dionysius] transcending the faculty of human calculation, is known to Him alone, who numbers all the hairs of the head. Nevertheless, some are of the opinion that they have discovered the number of angels, and consequently of those who are saved: whom they estimate to be as many as the angels. For they say that in each choir, of which there are nine, there are as many legions as the number of units a legion itself comprises, by squaring the number of the legion. A legion, however, contains (as they say) six thousand six hundred and sixty-six, which number, if it is squared and multiplied by itself, yields 44,435,556, and these are forty-four million, four hundred and thirty-five thousand, five hundred and fifty-six: But collected from all nine choirs, it would be 399,920,004, which are three hundred and ninety-nine million, nine hundred and twenty thousand, and four: but we shall leave these as founded in mere imagination. Others, however, estimate the number to have been calculated from the words of Daniel, who says: "Thousands of thousands"

--- Page 1019 ---
**THIRD CANTICLE**

ministered to him: and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. And thus there will be in the computation already made two thousand thousands: who indeed some of our most recent theologians dared to assert, that ten times one hundred thousand are more than thousands of thousands: Which proceeds from complete ignorance of numbers and calculations. From none of these, finally, can we have a true computation of angels or of the blessed: For the former presuppose what they ought to prove: And those who rely on Daniel would indeed have a computation already made, if the prophet had declared that there are no more angels than those two thousand thousands. Hence, Jerome wisely and learnedly says: "Not from this saying of Daniel is the number of God's ministers defined, but human speech was unable to explain a greater multitude." For these are the thousands, and these the myriads,
[Marginal note: David] of which, as it is said in the psalm: "The chariots of God are ten thousands, thousands of those rejoicing, the Lord is among them." Therefore, the number of both, angels and saints, remains unknown to us: but known to Him to whom the drops of rain and the grains of sand are known. However, we do not doubt that there are three kinds of guests, namely, divine, angelic, and human. But first we will speak of the lower ones, afterwards we will say what those supreme ones accomplish among the lower ones with harmonious sweetness.

Concerning angelic guests. Conclusion II.

Angelic minds are said to be divided, namely, into those assisting and those ministering. But first stand seven spirits, to whom is entrusted the dispensation of the entire celestial kingdom and of hell: which (as they say) is beneath the lunar sphere.
[Marginal note: Theolo.] For these (as more secret theologians say) govern all things by a certain succession of hours, days, and years: just as it is said by astrologers concerning the planets over which they preside.
[Marginal note: John.] And of these our John speaks, when he says: "And seven burning lamps before the throne of God, which are the seven spirits of God," through whom, as through principal ministers, He distributes all things: both the higher things, which delight in the number three: and the lower things, which delight in the number four: and are composed of the four elements: from which three and four that seven is completed. And that they preside over the seven spheres, and consequently over those things which are disposed by them,
[Marginal note: The same.] John clearly indicates, when he continues: "I saw in the midst of the throne, and in the midst of the elders, and of the four living creatures, a Lamb standing, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth:" that is, extended by power wherever, so that with eyes they may see all things, and with horns they may strike all things that are to be struck: for they stand in the sight of God, so that they may hear and grasp all things that the prince commands. But they are sent, and go, or are extended by power, so that they may execute the commands entrusted to them, either by themselves or through the inferior ministers of the celestial militia designated for their governance.
[Marginal note: Mercury.] Who (as Mercury teaches) were created immediately after the mind and the divine spirit. The Mind (he says), God, most full of the fecundity of both sexes, life, and light, with His word, created another mind, the artificer: which God indeed is the divine power of fire and spirit. He then created seven governors, who encompass the sensible world with their circles: whose disposition is fate

Concerning human guests.		Con. III.

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.8; vertical-align: -0.2em; display: inline-block;">S</span>There are also in that super-exalted city human guests distributed and gathered with such wonderful harmony that any ordered lower kingdoms do not even reflect a shadowy image of it. There is she who is the daughter and wife of the eternal king, and also the mother of the supreme prince. Also present are the Evangelists, as if privy to the eternal king's secrets, depositing in the archives the deeds of the prince and his soldiers: And these are chosen from different orders: for Matthew was an Apostle, and Luke was from the disciples. Concerning divine guests.                                             Con. IIII....

[Ornate initial E in a decorative square frame] There are also divine guests, from whom is all harmony, praise, glory, even being and living, and every good: and to whom all hymns and praises are directed. For from the Father they have that they exist, who praise: From the Son they know the measures, and the art of singing together, and the rules by which they move heart, hands, tongues, and all things, into true praises: since in Him are the rules directing all things: But from the Holy Spirit they draw breath, by which they render their voices sonorous. For spirits in that language which is called holy, and is proper to sacred eloquence, are named רוח ruah, which signifies wind and breath. For He himself gave [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] to the fishermen, and to all followers of Christ, breath, voice, and the ability to speak, Christ attesting to this, who says: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. For He filled the boy lyre-player, and made him a psalmist: He imbued the shepherd of sheep, and established him as a lawgiver: He filled the herdsman plucking sycamore figs, and made him a prophet: He filled the fishermen, and made them Apostles and singers together: He touched the persecutor, and appointed him teacher of the Gentiles: He inspired the tax collector, and promoted him to Evangelist. He visits the unlearned and simple day by day, and they become most enlightened teachers: For it is the same Spirit, distributing to each, who works all things in all. And if, filling these strangers, He made them singers together for God, what will He do for those who are already citizens and members of God's household

And if they are, will they never depart from that place and rank? No less does the Son continually impart from his fullness, so that they may have whence to grow: or at least persevere in continuous praise. And the Father, the most exuberant fount of all, gives so that they may be strengthened, moved towards God, and blessed, according to that saying of Dionysius: "All rejoice at the Father's prompting." Just as therefore all the blessed receive whatever they have from that Trisagion, so all tend towards Him, and look towards Him like lines to a center, from which they emanate. Which return to that very same [source] from which they proceeded renders a perfect harmony.

**MODULE NINE, THE MARRIAGE.**
*How, and when, the marriage between God and the soul was initiated. First Harmony.*

**I**ndeed, the sacrament of marriage is of the greatest importance, so much so that, with the creation perfected and its own high priest introduced into it, marriage was immediately celebrated: and marriage was ordained by God for our first parents: For the Creator, placing the final hand on his work, decided to give to man, now made, a helper that would stand before him, concerning which our text has: "He made a helper like himself." Hence, a deep sleep having been cast upon Adam, He took one of his ribs, and forming it into a woman, brought her to Adam, and assigned her as his wife: so that the human race, from the application of the active to the passive, might feel its own harmony: and might rejoice in a fruitfulness so much more celebrated than other living beings, as man is better than them. Therefore, Adam himself received this woman, formed from the rib of the man, saying: "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife." Which words Paul, quoting to the Ephesians, adds: "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church:" And just as sacred scripture, having recounted creation, first deals with marriage: In the same way, it will end in the sacrament of marriage, as John says, at the end of his most celebrated and final vision, while relating the person of the exultant blessed: "Let us rejoice and exult, for the marriage of the Lamb has come." And again: "Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." Also, the prince and Lord of that city, while he lived among humans, compares the kingdom of heaven and the sum of all human endeavor to marriage. Since therefore the most celebrated of all marriages are conducted there, let us see who is the bridegroom, who is the bride, by what marriage song, by what feasts, by what contract, by what auspices they are celebrated. The bridegroom, there is no doubt, is He who says through Hosea: "I will betroth you to me in faithfulness, and you shall know that I am the Lord." Which bridegroom is more clearly expressed in the Gospel by Himself, when He says: "The kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding feast for his son." Now the Son of the supreme King of all ages is Christ, and He Himself is king: for He has long since received the scepter from the Father. Now the bride is any soul consenting to this contract: And consequently the whole church

And since marriage is initiated, contracted, ratified, and consummated, first we will see how, and when, it took its beginning. Therefore, these nuptials were initiated by the Holy Spirit, when, at his dictation, God so often invites us through the prophets to this contract: according to that which is openly found in Hosea: I will betroth you to me forever: I will betroth you to me [Marginal note: Osee.] in righteousness, and in justice, in mercy, and in compassions: for which in Hebrew is found וברחמים (ube rahamim): which we can interpret as, 'in benevolent loves,' or 'in pieties.' For under the Law, the severe groom betrothed in judgment and justice: but in the Messiah, showing himself most benevolent, he betrothed in mercy, piety, grace, and all blessings signified by that word 'rahamim': And through Ezekiel, inspired by the divine spirit, he says: And I swore to you, and [Marginal note: Ezech.] entered into a covenant with you, and you became my bride, namely by the consent which every soul readily gives, which by its very nature desires the blessedness encompassed by these nuptials. You have, therefore, how these nuptials were initiated, to which he first invited angels: But he found many of them unworthy: whence he also ordered them to be expelled as rebels and rash ones. He also invited all men, but most, immersing themselves in follies, and almost base and bestial things, unworthy of such great companionship, were not unjustly rejected and left to wallow in the mire of sordid pleasures. Hence, with them cast out, he called others to the nuptials through angelic, prophetic, and Apostolic heralds and messengers: who, all solicitous for our salvation, invite to those nuptials whomever they find at the ends of the roads, or at crossroads and the world's intersections.

How it was contracted. Con. II.
</center>

<p style="text-indent: 2em;">
<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.5em; vertical-align: -0.2em;">C</span>ontracted is marriage by words (as they say) of the present, an indissoluble bond among Christians; although it was permitted to those who lived according to the law to give a bill of divorce, which the Mahometans also observe. But marriage, which is by words of the present between spouses immediately assenting, differs from betrothals, which are made by words of the future, and by parents, or by intermediaries, and any sponsors, while the betrothed are still underage; who, when adult, often rescind such agreements. But the marriage between Christ and the soul, initiated by the prophets, is contracted by words of the present in baptism; when the one to be baptized asks for faith, and gives full consent, by which a true marriage is contracted. And because customarily they join right hand to right hand, this is represented by the sensible water, in which one is immersed, with the word accompanying; from these a sensible sign of this contract is provided. But the word is interposed, just as it is accustomed to be said in carnal marriage, "I want you as mine (wife)," and "I want you as mine (husband)," so here it is said: "I renounce the devil, the world, and its pomps, so that I may fully adhere to my spouse Christ." Who also confirms this kind of marriage by an oath, according to that passage of <span style="margin-left: 2em;">Ezechiel</span>Ezekiel: "And I swore to you, and entered into my covenant with you, says the Lord, and you became my bride." But when? Hear what he adds: "And I washed you with water, and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil." All these things happen in baptism. Of which, no one doubts, the prophet speaks under the type of a figurative bride, who herself was washed with water, but not with that perfect water with which we are washed. But we are joined to Christ in baptism by an indissoluble bond and covenant, which no one is ever permitted or able to break without express adultery. Nor indeed did he ever repudiate any wife, even if he made a divorce from his once dearest spouse, the ungrateful synagogue, of course; as we have in the figure of Vashti, who, despising the royal command, deserved a bill of divorce. Hence also the custom had prevailed (with the law nevertheless assisting) that marriages were often dissolved. This is by no means granted to Christians, to whom <span style="margin-left: 2em;">CHRIST</span>it was said by the spouse: "I am with you until the consummation of the age, never to repudiate you, even if you commit a thousand adulteries, yet not with impunity." For, the indissoluble marriage with the whole Church persevering, every immodest soul will not unjustly pay the penalty of adultery, when it is expelled by perpetual <span style="margin-left: 2em;">The same</span>separation from the spouse saying: "Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire." Hence this universal bride, which is called the Catholic Church, will never be repudiated. But if a particular one is rejected, another will be brought in, so that that number may be full, by which this betrothal assembly is concluded. For in Job it had been foretold: "God will crush many, and will make others stand in their place." And in Revelation: "Hold fast what you have, lest another take your crown." Nor are these repudiated by the spouse, except insofar as they themselves despise

**How it is ratified. Con. III.**

**C**arnal marriage is confirmed and held valid before the priest: who exists as a witness and minister of that sacrament: So also this spiritual betrothal is ratified before the Bishop, from whom we receive the sacrament (as they say) of confirmation: because the covenant and the oath made in baptism are confirmed. It is also called the sacrament of chrism: because the recipient is anointed with a particular anointing of divinity. Also, the nuptial covenant contracted in baptism is confirmed and ratified whenever we receive the sacrament of confession or the Eucharist: or are endowed with any other gift by Christ the groom. But we receive true confirmation when we are so solidified in the grace of God that we may complete the course of this life in it: for which reason no divorce is to be feared by us in the future. Which confirmation the **David** prophet desired, saying: "And confirm me with a principal spirit:" or with a willing, liberal, generous, or munificent spirit: For that is what נדיב (nedib) signifies, which we have translated as "principal." The prophet also foreseeing what the groom was about to do with his bride, the Church, prays and says: "Confirm this, O God, which you have worked in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem," or this lower (Jerusalem), where he celebrated this covenant on the cross, and confirmed it by the infusion of the Holy Spirit: or in the heavenly Jerusalem, where these most celebrated and whatever other nuptials are completed, **CHRIST** saying: "What God has joined together, let no man separate." If God therefore effects these marital conjunctions and unions, let them be made in heaven, where He himself dwells. Whence we ask to be confirmed (says **Jerome**)

Concerning wine. Con. II.

[V]ine indeed he offered us something wonderful in the Last Supper: yet promising something better in our resounding kingdom, and in the heavenly nuptials, while he says: "From now on I will not drink of this fruit [CHRI STVS,] of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father." Since therefore we speak of that kingdom, and of those nuptials, it must also be explained by us, what that wine is, which is promised to be given there. Wine indeed is pressed from the grape, and is born from the vine: Nor can it come from any other vine than from that one, of which he said: "I am the true vine." [Idem.] And it is prepared in those heavenly nuptials, which were prefigured by those nuptials, in which the heavenly bridegroom, first showing himself above man, and above the order of nature, immediately made wine from water, and by a mere command: which nature does with an interval of time, and by suitable means. These water jars, Jerome (Hieron.) in his commentary on Ezekiel, and some others elsewhere, interpret as six ages, as vessels capable of holding water both super-mundane and inferior: Which water, if it passes through Christ, the true vine, with the super-mundane sun boiling it down, is converted into good wine, which that figurative transformation signifies. But if the water jars are filled only with inferior water, that is, with graces which they call "freely given," then, with the evil heat of concupiscence boiling, they are often converted into wine, concerning which Moses (Moſes.) says with indignation in the Canticle: "Their vine is from the vineyards of Sodom, and from the suburbs of Gomorrah: Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster most bitter. The venom of dragons is their wine, and the incurable poison of asps."

With this wine, that great harlot, that is, worldly concupiscence, has made all nations drink: Therefore, that wine is said to have come from the vineyards of Sodom and the suburbs of Gomorrah: which, just as they burned with their most wicked concupiscences, so also they burned with the fire of divine justice. And this is the vineyard of the lovers of the world, whose grape and cluster is most bitter gall: because it is bitter to have abandoned the Lord for concupiscences. Hence, one must lament bitterly twice, as Jeremiah (Ierem.) says in Lamentations to his people enveloped in worldly affections: "Make for yourself the mourning of an only son, a bitter lamentation." And Hezekiah (Ezechie.), realizing to what this wine had led him, said: "I will recount to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul." And this worldly wine is rightly called the gall of dragons, because it was offered by the dragon, and the ancient serpent, for our irreparable ruin, whence it follows: "And the incurable poison of asps," that is, by human strength, without the help of the heavenly redeemer.

And to this corresponds the most bitter wine of divine judgment, concerning which the prophet David (Dauid) says in the psalm: "A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine, mixed, or with a mixture:" because the Lord Himself has dominion and judgment, power and justice, to reward the good and punish the wicked. And He poured out, or made it overflow (for which our translation has "inclined"): "It overflowed, and the malice of the one committing evil overflows upon his own head," thus divine justice decrees. Nevertheless, all the wicked of the earth shall drink its dregs: for the good taste the wine of divine justice, but sinners and the wicked drink the dregs. But let us return to those who drink good wine here, for a better and heavenly refreshment. Therefore, the wine which to drink here...

What bread, and what flesh.                                        [Banquet III.]

[Decorative initial C containing a figure] Since we have spoken above of bread alone, now it must be seen how bread, having become flesh, is given to us in the banquet of the heavenly nuptials, just as the bridegroom said: "The bread which I shall give, is my flesh for the life of the world." And what is it that he says, "bread is flesh"? For bread is eaten so that it may be transmuted into flesh, and become flesh. But since this heavenly bread is not transmuted, but transmutes the one eating it, we eat this bread so that we may be transmuted into the flesh and body of Christ, and become two in one flesh, so that the true Adam may say of us: "Bone now of my bones, and flesh of my flesh." Therefore we eat this bread, by which we are transformed into the body and flesh of Christ, when we receive his doctrine, which is the bread of life and understanding, and is the water of saving wisdom; and also when we duly eat the very body of Christ. But no nourishment and transmutation occurs through any of these, unless that fire of the Holy Spirit and love is present, by which the food may be prepared before we receive it, so that we do not receive it out of habit, or hypocrisy, or any other indirect cause, but with sincere love and affection. By which fire also we may prepare and digest the received food. For then a true transformation [Academics, Epicureans] will be effected in us by the fire of love, which (as the Academics, Epicureans, but most especially [Dionysius] our Dionysius teaches) transmutes the lover into the beloved. Therefore the flesh especially prepared in the heavenly nuptials is the flesh of our bridegroom, and of the immaculate Lamb [CHRIST] sacrificed for the life of the world. And besides this flesh, in the Gospel, where the heavenly nuptials themselves are discussed, mention is made of certain other meats by the bridegroom saying: "My oxen, and fatlings killed," that is, the magnitude of doctrines through oxen (as [Jerome] Jerome understands it) and the profundity of God's doctrine through fatlings. But the wise [Hebrews] Hebrews say that God prepares for the just in the banquet an ox, a bird, and a fish: of the first of which Christ makes mention. For the ox is our animal, which was purged by the legal ox: The bird is that supreme portion of the soul, which by flying always seeks high things, interpreted elsewhere by Jerome as the eagle: But the fish, which is nourished in the waters of the spirit, is our middle or rational part: which is nourished and delighted in the waters of wisdom and doctrines. And all these things are prepared in that banquet to be eaten by the bridegroom and the guests, just as he himself says in the [Apocalypse] Apocalypse: "I will sup with him, and he with me." He certainly delights to sup with us, not because he needs our goods, but so that by eating, he may change us into himself, so that we may become one and the same with him, eaten by him, digested, and nourished into his body. But [Ezekiel] Ezekiel touches upon fish, saying: "There will be very many kinds of its fish, like the fish of the great sea": because there will be multiple, I will not say merely species, but genera of these fish, that is, of rational spirits and souls: which spirits will be assumed

Concerning the Fruits of this Feast. Con. IV.

[Marginal letter: C] Our harmonizers Ezekiel and John also narrate the fruits prepared for this feast: for Ezekiel says: On the banks of the river, [Marginal note: Ezekiel] which passes through the city, is every fruit-bearing tree: its leaf shall not wither, and its fruit shall not fail. It shall bring forth its firstfruits every month, because its waters issue from the sanctuary. And its fruit shall be for food, and its leaves for medicine. But John [Marginal note: John.] echoes the same as Ezekiel, but more clearly: because perhaps he had seen more clearly. He therefore says: In the midst of its street, and on either side of the river, was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations. Great are the mysteries here, and heavier than our weak shoulders can bear: nevertheless, we shall say something (with the Lord's favor). First, they concordantly recall the river passing through the middle of the city, concerning which perhaps the royal prophet [Marginal note: David.] says: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God. This river is the abundance of all good things flowing from that unfailing source, from which comes all good: which gladdens the city of God itself, and all its citizens. But the tree of life is that from which the promised and eternal life is supplied to them. But what these fruits are, which are said to be produced every month, O good God, unless you, who planted the tree, teach us, I would dare to affirm nothing rashly. Nor do those fruits of the spirit, which Paul mentions, seem to me to be the same: because they belong to travelers (on earth), and are not to be placed at heavenly weddings. And if that tree is the tree of life, which is the Son, those fruits would more appropriately be called fruits of the Son than of the spirit, although they could also be called fruits of the spirit: because they are spiritual, and produced by His power. Nevertheless, this tree is God the Son Himself, who, planted in earthly flesh, produced every kind of fruit. But mention is made of twelve principal fruits, because they are primary, and are said to be produced every month. And so that it may be understood what is signified by months and days (since in that eternal succession there is no distinction of years, days, or months), another meaning must be sought than what the letter sounds: in which that monthly...

the monthly production of those fruits. We have said that the twelve Apostles are appointed over a twelvefold family, both figurative and true, which is divided: to the goal of the twelve celestial signs: through whose spaces the sun, running its course, distinguishes twelve months. Therefore, there are months in those eternal abodes according to a division of distribution, and not according to the courses of time, described by these lower divisions, as causes by effects, or true forms by pictures. Since, therefore, the twelve Apostles will preside over those families, whose marked and principal members are distinguished by twelve thousands: from this, the principal fruits of this tree of life are numbered twelve, and monthly: which primary and special fruits the tree of life itself produced as food, and for the shepherds of the whole family. Indeed, we have declared that the prince already set forth is food and nourishment, and that all of us are likewise. For the leaves are, as it were, certain coverings in the type of sacraments, which cleanse sins and cover the nakedness of sinners. But those fig leaves could not cover Adam's nakedness, because they had not received power from the tree of life: nor were they leaves of this tree. For if Adam had taken of its leaves, perhaps he would have covered his nakedness. In these fruits the bridegroom will delight, and the Most High Father will also delight, as in the offspring of his most beloved son. All those fruits will also congratulate each other, considering that they have proceeded from such a great tree, and have been placed at such a most celebrated banquet: these also (which is wonderful) will not only be dishes, but also guests, nor will any diminution occur from eating.

MODVLVS VNDECIMVS, INSTRVMENTA.
De primo instrumento qui est cælorum globus. Concentus primus.

[Large decorative initial Q]uite sufficiently have we already explained with what harmony the celestial spheres resound: But let us add this, that those ascending harmonies of the heavens resound in that whole celestial hall, where are the performers, namely their intelligences ruling them, which stand (as we have said) always before (Plato. Orpheus) the throne of God. And these, like Sirens (as Plato says), sitting upon those spheres, make their melody resound everywhere. But he makes them sound in the first place, to whom Orpheus said: "You tune the heaven like a melodious lyre." And that place is so tempered by harmonic proportions, that it renders the voices of those singing there much more sonorous than theaters or stages constructed with musical proportions, so that spectators might more easily perceive the voices of the actors, or players: who recited comedies or whatever else they presented on that stage or platforms: so that just as they were seen by everyone, both those in the orchestra and those sitting in the periphery of the semicircle, so their most consonant voices might be heard, with vessels resounding here and there, adapted with wondrous artifice for conducting harmonic voices. For art cannot surpass nature; indeed, it imitates it, and by long strides. Therefore, the harmony of the heavens is better than human constructions and instruments crafted by art. But beyond all ambiguity, it must be believed that among all the works of the supreme artisan, that is more beautiful and sweeter in which His throne resides: and the seats of all His banquets: In which not only is no dissonance felt, but all things are most consonant, (Augusti.) all joyful, all festive, all pleasant. Which (as Augustine says) David, learned in such songs, who had loved musical harmony not with common pleasure, but with faithful love and reverence, revealed through the mystical image of the thing itself, and through various rational sounds and moderate harmonies: and depicting the compact unity of the most orderly supernal city with harmonious variety, he sang it with many modes, various harmonies, and more secret mysteries of instruments, than is thought by the wise of the world. Hence, although some have applied their utmost industry to sing a psalm or hymn similar to Davidic odes, they are separated by a very long interval (begging their pardon) from our divine Lyre-player, who always seeks the sublime, to which he does not ascend unless carried by the same Holy Spirit, by whom he himself was inspired.

De secundo instrumento, quod est humana lingua. Con. I I.

[Large decorative initial A] tongue is necessary, assigned and ordered to song, which emits a voice, and that a sonorous one, by means of its instruments, which are the fauces, palate, teeth, lips, throat, lung, the spiritual artery, which they call the trachea: and above all, the pectoral muscles (Avicena.), which obtain the principle of this motion from the soul, as is held by Avicenna, and

--- Page 1036 ---
TONE EIGHT. 447

...from others who write about the disposition of the body. This tongue, even the bodily one, will be exercised in praise of the Prince, with the Holy Spirit testifying in David, who says: "The exultations of God are in their throats." [Marginal note: David.] For no distinct and sonorous voice resonates in the throat except through the movement of the tongue: for this [tongue] has been, or will be, restored to all bodies that have risen, or will rise, with all their arteries and instruments, in a much better harmony than anyone has had or could have in this earthly journey. For just as all members that were deformed, or distorted and maimed, will be repaired and perfected, so that everyone may meet the supreme Prince (as the Apostle says) as a perfect man. In like manner, also, what was previously a dissonant and discordant voice, or a lisping tongue, will be restored, polished and most harmonious, so that nothing base, nothing unseemly, nothing ungraceful may be seen there. [Marginal note: Paul.]

But since two media for forming voice and sound seem to be granted by nature (as those who treat of natural things say, namely air and water, in which elements sound occurs, though more aptly in air), it must be seen what water or what air there is in that supercelestial region, in which the voice can be established. [Marginal note: Physicists] This will be difficult to define by those who admit elements only in the lower regions, which are beneath the orb of the moon. But those who acknowledge elements even in higher regions (as touched upon above) will more easily determine this matter. [Marginal note: David.] For there are waters of which the wisest philosopher David [says]: "And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord." [Marginal note: Moses.] Moses had taught this same thing before, namely, that there are waters above the globe of the heavens, divided from those that are beneath it. And we have already said that some of the heavens are watery, and some are airy: For if the ninth heaven (which astronomers call the *primum mobile*, but some call 'crystalline') is watery, then following the order of the elements, we will say that the upper heaven, where the seats of the blessed are, is airy, yet with a certain solidity, so that the seats of the blessed and the throne of the Prince may be firm, as required by those who sit there, and all the guests now glorified. [Marginal note: Astronomers.] Nor will solidity prevent sound from resonating everywhere in a fluid transparency. And although some say that heaven is fiery, and therefore called empyrean (for πῦρ is fire), it is not so fiery that it is not also airy: whence others say that it is called empyrean more from its fiery splendor than from the nature of fire itself. [Marginal note: Theologians.] Certainly, sound will resonate there, as some of our theologians assert.

From this, it must be seen in what language, or in what idiom, they will speak. And as far as reason can persuade me, if they use any idiom, it is Hebrew: in which the law was given, the Gospel was preached by Christ, divine hymns were written, and all oracles were given, with the sole exception of that revelation which is called 'apocalypse' in Greek, written and delivered in the Greek language. [Marginal note: The same.] Then, because it is a most mysterious language in its figures, points, accents, and numbers carried by those letters: so much so that the more recondite theologians promise to explain everything from the permutation of letters and apices, and from the computation of numbers signified by the letters. Then, because those letters are said to be written in the seat of God, which is heaven: the letters themselves, which Moses first used in giving the law, are formed in the likeness of its figures.

Moreover, just as this was the first language, and emanated from heaven, and existed before the confusion of languages arose in Babylon, so it will be the last (language) to be eradicated by that confusion, which was inflicted as punishment (as [Marginal note: Auguſti.] Augustine says) for such great rashness and pride. For this variety of languages is a very severe punishment, because of which no one can make known his thoughts or ask for necessities, either to a tent-mate or a traveling companion:
[Marginal note: Idem.] so that it is better (says the same Augustine) to be with one's puppy or horse than with a companion of a foreign idiom, because the puppy will understand what the other will not understand. Therefore, [Marginal note: Idem.] this language persisted either in Eber (as the same Augustine thinks) or in some pious family that had not consented to Nimrod's arrogance, who presumed to erect a tower into heaven so that, removed from atmospheric change (as is said of Mount Olympus), they might, with every impediment removed, devote themselves to contemplation and, elevated, surpass others beyond what nature provided. Nor was there ever lacking a pious family not assenting to such rashness, from which Abraham descended, who was first called a Hebrew in the sacred scriptures from עבר babar, which means 'to cross over', as we explained above. Therefore, just as this was the first language, always persevering unchanged, so it will also be the last in the homeland (heaven), if any vocal speech is granted: The sign of this is that intelligences, when they speak to men who know that language, use the Hebrew language: Although some assert that demons, or wise intelligences, use the languages of each of the nations with whom they dwell. But (if I am not mistaken) what we have said is more probable, since almost all authentic oracles have been delivered in that idiom. It is therefore most fitting that just as any victorious city imposes not only a yoke upon conquered peoples, but often also its idiom, so the Emperor of that heavenly city, and the attendant princes, will decree that all who are brought up there speak in the language and speech originating from there, and which the prince of that kingdom used to employ while he dwelled among men. Which perhaps (as we have said) will be before we arrive there, or at least after the future judgment by fire, according to what the Lord says in the prophet Zephaniah: [Marginal note: Soph̃. 3.] "In the fire of my jealousy, all the earth will be devoured. And then I will restore to my people a pure language, that they may call upon the name of the Lord, and serve him with one shoulder."

**Concerning the third instrument, which is our body. Consideration III.**

[Large decorative initial C containing a figure of a man]
[Marginal note: Auguſti.] We have stated above that the human body is ordered with the most perfect harmony, so much so that in no other body is it better and sweeter. Which Augustine says exists not only in those things which are outwardly apparent, fitted together by their numbers and measures, but also in those things which the human eye does not reach, derived with such numerosity and consonance, that no one could discover it, however diligent the investigation of anatomists might have been. Concerning which Boethius also says: [Marginal note: Boëtius] "That vivacity of reason in the body is mixed with a certain fitting together, like a harmony of grave and light voices tending towards a single consonance." Which (harmony), being brought together, man feels better than he understands, according to that saying of Zoroaster: "Man rejoices because of the harmony which he feels within himself." And what is more to be wondered at, it does not ha-

--- Page 1038 ---
**TONVS OCTAVVS. 448**

...the human body has not only harmony between its members, and humors with each other, and between the soul and the ruling spirit, but also between divine and supramundane things. Hence, by a great mystery, so many affirmative precepts were given in the Mosaic law as there are bones in the human body, namely two hundred and forty-eight; and so many negative ones as there are nerves in the same body, which are, not without reason, three hundred and sixty-five, by which number the days and nights of the year are comprehended; which, joined together, amount to six hundred and thirteen. This number is likewise yielded by the letters of the name of God אלהים if they are filled in a cabalistic manner, and the name יהו with one added, signifying that which results from both: For if the letters composing the name אלהים are filled, they yield 296, and the letters of the name יהו give 316, which, joined together, make 612. And that one, which results from them, brings the number to 613. Which indeed, according to the doctrine of those who theologize by numbers, denotes by a great mystery that the fullness of judgment contained under the name Elohim was given to JESUS, who said: "For the Father judges no one" [Marginal note: CHRI] after, namely, this transfer of judgment was made, "but has given all judgment to the Son." [Marginal note: STVS.] He who is about to judge all things again said: "For every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment"; much more concerning everything that shall have been done against precepts, both affirmative and negative, in all of which we ought to completely agree and concur with God. From which we are not exempt, since all those things are concluded in a brief, but mysterious evangelical word, in which the whole perfection of all precepts is absorbed, Christ saying: "On these two commandments, [Marginal note: Idem.] namely the love of God and of neighbor, depend all the Law and the Prophets." Whoever fulfills these will feel that which is said in the oracle of Ezekiel: [Marginal note: Ezechie.] "The bones came together, bone to bone, each to its joint." Those very bones about which the divine Harper [Marginal note: Dauid] sings: "Then shall the bones which thou hast broken rejoice"; and again: "My soul shall rejoice in the Lord, and shall be delighted in his salvation," to whom, namely, he harmoniously said: "All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like unto thee, who hast so well fitted all things by bringing them together, especially indeed the bones which seemed utterly scattered here and there?" And with these fitted together, Ezekiel continues, saying: "And I beheld, and, lo, the sinews and the flesh came up upon them," so that all members and internal organs, most harmoniously, may rejoice in the Lord. [Marginal note: Augusti.] Hence, in a magnificent sense, Augustine says that all the nerves and members of resurrected bodies will resound in praise of the prince of that city, and with a much better harmony, the more consonant men have been with God in observing His precepts and ceremonies.

**On the fourth instrument, namely the angelic tongue: Con. IV.**

[Decorative woodcut initial I] Angelic spirits are also present in those harmonies, concerning whom indeed we would doubt whether they speak in tongues and praise the Creator, unless Paul, taught in that heavenly gymnasium, and in whose breast [Marginal note: Paulus.] Christ resonates, were to say: "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels."

Concerning the second, it is manifest how by the tongue we offer to others the food of the word of God: And what man does with a sensible voice, an angel accomplishes by impressing a concept. Concerning angelic and blessed minds, which are themselves
resonant instruments. Harmony V.

[Decorative Initial P] Therefore, since the discourse of that heavenly homeland is conducted more by mind than by sound, minds themselves will be certain resounding instruments, producing a sweeter harmony than that which is produced by vocal sound. We can conjecture this harmony from those things which we continuously prove by experience: For when, concepts having been revealed, harmony is felt among those conversing, a certain delight filled with sweetness arises from that consonance: just as horror, weariness, displeasure, and pain are felt from the dissonance of voices, and especially of minds, so much so that from such things the odor of hell is perceived. Therefore, in that supracelestial chamber, where there is the highest concord of all minds, both divine, human, and angelic, with each other, and of all with the Prince himself, the highest joy will be entirely conceived, [Marginal note: Augustine.] which Augustine believes and asserts to be the cause of blessedness, which lies in consonant adherence with God, just as dissonance from Him is the cause of misery. And this is the true consonance, namely, of the mind, to which every vocal harmony, whether made by natural instruments, or that which is made by adventitious and artificially crafted ones, is directed, as to the principal instrument of all praises. Therefore, first of all, the minds of all the blessed sing the praises of the Creator with their high-sounding voice: because we can contemplate more and higher things with the mind than we can utter with the mouth: Nor is any melody more pleasing to the Prince [Marginal note: Augustine.] than the concord of the mind, in which He is especially delighted: concerning which Augustine, on that psalm, says: "Sing praises wisely:" He sings wisely who praises with the illumination of the mind, because no one does wisely what he does not well understand. For no praise is elegant unless it proceeds from the mind and heart. Hence, that which does not proceed from the heart is despised by God: as it speaks most clearly in Isaiah, saying: "This [Marginal note: Isaiah.] people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." Therefore, the divine harmonizer, [Marginal note: David. Blessed Virgin.] to render pleasing praise to God, says: "I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart." And the God-bearing Virgin, already instructed in heavenly songs by the Word she bore in her womb, intoned: "My soul magnifies the Lord. And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior." For she joins soul and spirit in praise of the Prince and

[Decorative flourish]

**Epithalamium for the bride,**

a You shine beautifully, and your face, my friend, is as joyful
as the palaces of Jerusalem.
b And you are formidable in contrast, when your brow gathers its clouds,
like a martial host arrayed.
c Look down a little, I pray, and turn away your eyes for a moment,
by which I swell with pride.
d Your hair, arranged in order around your temples,
like flocks of goats.
e As a snowy flock of sheep when it comes forth from the river,
so do your teeth gleam.
f And your cheeks shine with red and white color,
like a split pomegranate.
g And your white navel is the image of a crater
made by an artisan's hand.
h And your belly is like wheat, among whose sprouts
a spike of roses gleams yellow.
i And soft breasts cling to your slender bosom,
like fawns resting.
k Sixty queens and eighty concubines
speak such things of you.

[Bottom Section]

a The bride is called beautiful like the heavenly Jerusalem, to which she tends, having a symbol with it; whence Jerusalem figures both that heavenly city and the particular bride or collection of all brides, who descends from heaven as a bride adorned for her husband, nor had anything more fitting to compare a friend to.
b Who, though so beautiful, yet because of her modesty and the fortification of virtues and charisms, is terrible to the enemy, like an army's battle line. c He prays her to turn away her eyes in a flattering manner, when he is too proud, so that the bridegroom may grow in the sight of such a bride.
d The hairs are like flocks of goats, but not those kids which were given for the lot of Azazel, or who will be placed on the left for judgment, but of those who are placed from Gilead, that is, who are placed before the Lord as a heap of testimony; for a good kid and numbered hairs are the same, and can be considered by the same Hebrew word.
e Ivory teeth are innocent and pure, like sheep ascending from the washing.
f The cheeks are painted and arranged like a piece of pomegranate.

**OF THE THIRD CANTICLE**

[Left column marginal notes]
n Therefore, finding the bride in a fall, he calls her back from it, saying: "Return, return, O Shulamite," that is, pacified, and perfected by my merits, and constituted victor over enemies. Whence she is to be applauded, according to what follows: "What do you see in the Shulamite, but choirs of camps no longer warring, but dancing for joy?"

o Therefore, raised up and fitted with proper morals and affections, all looking on and recognizing her blessed state, she induces such great admiration that they say: "How beautiful are the steps of your affections and works in sandals, by which, namely, your feet are defended, lest they be offended by an evil stone, O daughter of the prince?" For she is called bride and daughter.

[Main text]
Thus, intertwined in mutual bonds,
h *Among the beautiful coverings of the bed we shall lie:*
*Which, sprinkled with various perfumes, is fragrant,*
i *And around, sixty men keep watch:*
*Who surpass all Israel in strength.*
k *Soon, gently, sleep will come to our eyes*
*Peacefully diffused through all our limbs:*
l *Nor, I pray, let anyone awaken us before.*
*By creaking footsteps, or obstructing murmur:*
*Than quiet itself spontaneously takes itself from our eyes.*

a ¶ The affections of true heavenly marriage are expressed in every possible way by mystical words. First, reciprocal love is declared when one is shown to be solicitous for the other, while they mutually embrace each other in love, and between breasts – not indeed feminine ones, but those better ones from which milk is offered, which he who drinks knows how to reject evil and choose good.
b Nourished by this milk, both burn with a common love: For the breasts in the archetype are fountains flowing prophetic streams. They are also the legal books offering us the true milk of wisdom.
c To suckle at these breasts one comes through a kiss, in which the soul, dying to the world, lives for God alone, content with that milk, which is far better than all wine of the wisdom of lower things. But sometimes we also suck wine from the same breasts: concerning which it is also said, "your breasts will be like clusters of grapes."
d Therefore, the kiss given and the milk drunk, one is introduced to the mother's chamber, not indeed of this lower and mortal one, but rather of that better one who is called the mother of children, rejoicing and gladdening, namely, in a most fruitful offspring from whom we must be reborn if we wish to enter the kingdom of heaven, concerning whom the Apostle says, "That Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother:" Into whose chamber are introduced those who have received the true kiss and have partaken of that good milk.
e Thither also, the introduced soul drinks pure wine and the nectar of love seasoned with the juice of pomegranates, that is, of true charity, so that it may be preserved from the intoxication of wanton and perverse love.
f Therefore, burning with that love, the spouses come to mutual and holy embraces, through the arms of virtues and good things, which are accustomed to be common among true friends.
g In this embrace, the left hand, and all that pertains to it, are subjected to the head and reason: just as it was once commanded: "Your desire shall be subject to you," which is according to blood, and wise in its nature: which also in the archetype receives influence from the left, But the right hand rejoices in the embrace of love and all propitious and anointing influences. These two, namely fear and love, are accustomed to thrive in lovers, so that the latter (love) may grow warm and advance, while the former (fear) may take care not to offend, and thereby provoke the beloved to anger: But fear ought to be subordinate to love.
h Embraced, connected, and joined by this love, each, having now attained the end, ought to lie down and rest upon those beautiful and fragrant coverings and beds of true heavenly marriage: Whereupon the bride, ascending, sings, "In peace, I will both lie down and sleep."
i Therefore, so that one may rest securely, those chambers and beds are surrounded by sixty strong men, not just any, but from the strongest of Israel, that is, those fighting for God in that militia of the heavenly army: Who are chosen in the number sixty, derived from the first perfect number six and the complete number ten, to signify the complete perfection of the guardians: All of whom hold swords, indeed from those of whom it is said, "My sword is drunk in heaven:" And they are taught for wars, and that warfare by which Michael fought against the dragon. Therefore, each of the warriors

having a sword on his thigh, as is customary, מִפַּחַד בַּלֵּילוֹת mi pacad belelot, that is, from the fear or terror of the night, so that they may indeed defend from the powers who are accustomed to terrify us in both the night of time and of sin. Therefore, from these, those guards defend those resting in those tabernacles of trust and security, so that they may not be troubled by any terror.
**k** In which security the soul rests so placidly, in Him from whom it received a kiss, that in that slumber it may be transformed into that very thing in which it rests, and become one and the same spirit with Him.
**l** Therefore, when in that sleep the soul is lifted up and ascends to God, all companions are adjured not to excite or awaken one thus resting, until the spirit, which has seized it, has prolonged that sleep. This is especially so since it inspires when it wills, and is not in the power of the recipient, but of the very one inspiring and coming; therefore, it must be left undisturbed until it has departed. CANTICLE THE THIRD
[ornament] MODULE THIRTEENTH: TRIUMPH. [ornament]
What is a just fight. First Harmony.

[Decorative Initial N, depicting a figure in a landscape]A noble and glorious triumph first requires a just fight,
and a beautiful victory: And then a fight is just, when there is a le-
gitimate reason for fighting, with war also having been declared beforehand: Likewise, with the
authority of the Prince intervening, whose role it is to declare war, and that it be fought justly,
not however for the sake of evil vengeance. If however our Emperor Christ
had a just cause in the war which He undertook against the enemy of the human race, it is manifest:
since that most monstrous robber, the ancient serpent, who is the devil,
held the human race itself under the harshest and most horrible yoke of servitude:
Which indeed he had subjected by deceit and manifold fraud. Against
this one, therefore, Christ, fighting with truth and piety, and also with zeal for divine
honor and the salvation of souls, was most just in war. And lest the enemy (though unjust)
could have any just complaint, war was declared against him by the ancient
fathers and prophets, to whom this had been entrusted as if they were heralds. Among whom
[Marginal note: David.] the most solemn royal prophet of God, a herald, proclaimed, saying: He delivered the
poor from the mighty, and the poor who had no helper. Indeed, the Prince Himself
[Marginal note: CHRIST] publicly declared, saying: Now the prince of this world will be cast out, because I am
about to contend with him: and what is more, the enemy himself attacked Him while He was fast-
ing in the desert. Indeed, He had the authority to wage war from the Father, who Him to
[Marginal note: Isaiah.] this war destined, commanding that He should conquer the enemy by His wounds, just as
He had said through Isaiah: 'For the sins of my people I struck him,' that is, 'I handed him over to be struck
and wounded': For in this new kind of battle, victory was to be achieved
by wounds: In this war, indeed, no fraud or deceit intervened, nor
any evil desire for vengeance: but rather, the piety of liberating those unjustly oppressed. He fought therefore
with truth against the lying enemy: He fought with zeal against the envious one: with goodness
against the malicious and wicked one: with meekness against the proud one. For this
battle, all soldiers of Christ, who received His pay in baptism,
ought diligently to gird themselves, just as Michael, the guardian of souls, had done against the same
enemy, as John narrates, saying: Michael and his angels fought with the dra-
gon: Which battle he had undertaken for Christ the Prince, and by the same laws

the stars of God, that is, I will exalt my throne above the saints, I will place my seat to the north, as if standing opposite him who comes from the south. And rightly he turns himself to the north, from where all evil spreads, and from where all ruin and fall (come). Against whom Michael and his angels rose up for Christ, receiving [Marginal note: Dauid] that decree sung by the divine fellow-singer: "And let all his angels adore him." All of whom undertook war against the dragon for Christ and the laws of Christ. For the serpent fought with stubbornness, these with obedience; that one with hatred, these with love; that one with envy, these with zeal; that one with pride, these with piety; that one presuming on his own strength, these supported by divine power. By this justice and this favor Michael and his army prevailed against the dragon and his followers, even to their complete extermination and irrevocable expulsion from that kingdom in which Christ, the peaceful king, reigns in peace. Therefore the dragon, vanquished and cast out, directed a threefold battle line against us, which are the monstrous things of the world, of which the dragon had become the prince and tyrant. Which battle lines John mentions in his epistle, and are now known [Marginal note: Ioannes] to all, namely, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. And this is what the same John continues in the Apocalypse: "And the dra [Marginal note: idem.] gon, enraged, went to make war with the rest, who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus Christ." And a little later: "And it was given to him to make war with the saints and to conquer," unless Christ had prepared victory for us, by whose favor he is often conquered by us.

Concerning the great victory obtained by Christ for himself and for his soldiers. Second Harmony.

[Illuminated initial I] N this war our emperor Christ was so victorious that the enemy could not inflict even the slightest harm or wound upon him; hence he joyfully declares: "For the prince of this world comes, and he [Marginal note: CHRI STVS. Isaias.] has nothing in me." The entire praise for this victory must be ascribed to him, who alone fought with the enemy, just as it had been said in the prophecy of Isaiah: "I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the peoples there was no man with me." And for this reason, when Peter, with drawn sword, wanted to rush out against the enemies, he said: "Put your sword into its sheath. Do you not think that I could ask my Father, and he would send me more than twelve legions of angels? But I do not want to, because I alone must enter this battle." Hence, not without the admiration of those listening, and those attentively trusting, in the conflict itself he cried out to the Father: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — alone, that is, in a duel with the fiercest enemy. Which, Paul, conscious of the secrets of God, understanding, explained the mystery to the Colossians, [Marginal note: Paulus.] saying: "When you were dead and plundered by sin, Christ made you alive together, forgiving all transgressions, blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, contrary to us; and he took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross. Stripping principalities and powers, he led them out confidently, triumphing openly—

--- Page 1051 ---
CANTICLE THE THIRD

...triumphing over them openly in himself. Did not Paul here expound and explain the mystery and order of the entire war and Christ's victory over the adversary of the human race? For he showed why he fought, namely, to deliver us from death, that is, from the angel of death, and from sin, remitting the debts for which we were liable and slaves, erasing the bond which we had made to the devil by our evil-working hands: And that through the cross he paid the debt, enriching us with the spoils of the principalities and powers of darkness: And finally he concludes that he achieved this victory and triumph through himself, whence he was deservedly most glorious. But as far as we are concerned, he fought alone, so that we might owe (our redemption) to him alone who redeemed us, as Ambrose [Marginal note: Ambro.] discusses at length in the book 'On the Patriarchs'. And he did not achieve this victory [Marginal note: Paulus.] only for himself, but for all of us, thereby showing his magnificence: Which the apostle openly states, saying: "But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord," provided that we are willing to faithfully fight against the same prince of the world and of darkness: and against his evil persuasions and battle lines: as many have done, considering all earthly things as dung, so that they might rush into the battle line of Dis, taming the flesh and pleasures, so that they might avoid the allurements of Azazel, subject to the laws of obedience, and enslaved to humble things, lest the pride or arrogance of Asmodeus find a place to inflict some wound. Which threefold battle, namely, in the spirit, in the sensitive man, and in the delight of external things surrounding us, has been declared, so that, with the three-headed beast defeated in this threefold combat, we might attain that exalted ternary, or in some way merit it. Indeed, we are rightly united with the Holy Spirit when, having laid aside the pride of our own spirit, nothing at all remains in us that would hinder complete subjection and adherence, by which we are able not only to obey, but to be united with that Spirit. Appropriately also does one attain to the Son, Christ, who crucified his own flesh with its vices and carnal desires. Finally, we best come to the most pious Father when, having piously cast aside or expended all things, or at least having destroyed them with all our might, we pursue Him with religion, piety, and the most vehement ardor of soul: then He Himself, who sees in secret, will reward us. He also cherishes us, embraces us, and nourishes us, according to what the Son testifies, saying: "For your heavenly Father knows what you need." For this exalted ternary is against the lowest and most terrible (ternary), indeed, by that divine ordinance, by which all evil things opposing good have been so established, that with those rejected, we may come to these (good things) with no small glory.

On the triumph of various leaders after Christ's departure. Con. IIII.

[Decorative initial Q] Although victory over the entire world was achieved by Christ in his blood, to whom praise and glory are owed by all: nevertheless, by his command and favor, others triumphed (especially the twelve apostolic princes) over the twelve parts of the world, through the virtue of the Holy Spirit, with which he had filled them. Therefore, they are called prefects over the twelve tribes, in which (as we have said) the entire human race is encompassed. Nor was Paul excluded, who labored more than all: For he too (as is clear) triumphed with them over many cities and provinces, which he brought under the dominion of Christ: For example, over Antioch, Seleucia, Rhodes, Perga, Pamphylia, and Cilicia: Likewise over Phrygia, Philippi, the Macedonians, and Corinthians, the Thessalonians, Athenians, and Ephesians, and over many islands of Greece. Also over Italy and Spain, to which regions (as we have said) he carried the name of the Lord JESUS; to Paul himself, especially, the triumph is to be awarded. To Peter, however, over Rome, which began to serve under Christ's empire by his admonitions: To John over Asia: To Thomas over India: and to the rest over the provinces assigned to them by lot for preaching. Having achieved this victory, they deservedly ought to obtain triumph, and crowns with the emperor, and to be placed as his assessors upon twelve thrones, so that they might preside and judge the true twelve tribes of Israel, concerning which enough has been said above. Hence the prophet sings of them: The princes of the peoples are gathered with the God of Abraham, [Marginal note: David.] who saw the days of our emperor, and rejoiced. And he is called the God of Abraham, because his coming was first promised to Abraham. Also, the God of Abraham, because, having indeed become a new man, as that changed name indicates to those who understand the mystery, he was constituted Father of a new family to be regenerated by the redeemer. The twelve princes also are so united with Christ our God, that the prophet adds concerning them: The Divine ones of the earth, or the Divine ones who are shields, or protectors of the earth, have been greatly exalted: because they have been exalted above all tribes of the earth, and placed [Marginal note: The same.] upon the chief seats of glory. And concerning these, the divine Psalmist sings in another psalm, saying: Two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance upon the vanquished enemies, who had prevailed against the human race, and against all nations. This vengeance they have executed, and do execute together with Him, of whom John says: [Marginal note: John.] That a two-edged sword proceeded from His mouth, therefore, armed together, they will execute the judgment written and determined in the divine mind, binding hostile kings in fetters, and their nobles in iron manacles. This triumph, therefore, was given especially to the apostolic princes, and consequently

☞ FOURTEENTH MODULE: THE REWARD.
How great and precious is the reward of those who fight.
First Harmony.

[Large decorative initial S]
[Marginal note: Paul.]
Under many metaphors, the reward has been promised to those who contend lawfully.
For first, God promised it under the type of a land flowing with milk and honey:
But Paul sometimes calls it a crown, saying: "No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully:"
And again: "They indeed, that they may receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible." Sometimes He calls it a prize,
[Marginal note: CHRIST. GOD.]
saying: "All indeed run, but one receives the prize: So run, that you may obtain it."
But Christ sometimes calls that reward a daily denarius:
sometimes nuptials, sometimes the tree of life, sometimes hidden manna.
But to His most familiar friend Abraham, God explained it more clearly, saying: "I am
your exceedingly great reward:" Than which nothing greater, more precious, or equal could be given
or conceived: because it is the highest good, in which are all good things. Which
[Marginal note: CHRIST.]
nevertheless is the same, although named in different ways: for God the Father Himself is named
"crown" by Hebrew theologians: For He is indeed our crown and reward,
since He is the principal object of blessedness, as the Son says: "This
is eternal life, that they may know You, God the Father." And because the Son is the same as the Father,
it follows: "And Him whom You sent, His Son:" Who indeed is the true land of the living
promised to us, from which flowed and flows the milk of divine wisdom and honey, that is,
the sweetness and taste of divine things, which is concerning the true manna: which is nothing else
to say than a certain admirable food. For the children of Israel, seeing that food
of angels, or of the strong, sent from heaven, having every flavor in itself,
said to one another, wondering: מן הוא *man hu*, which interpreting
we say, "What is this?" Hence that food was called *man hu*, but we in Latin say *manna*:
for that is rather the exclamation of one wondering, than the name of the food. For since that food
sufficiently transcends the grasp of the weak, it is therefore called the food of the strong, although
our translation has "of angels." And because no one can understand it
or taste it unless he has experienced it, Christ says in the Apocalypse: "No one knows it, except he who
receives it." This reward is also called a daily denarius: a denarius, that is,
a true and complete reward, just as a denarius is a complete number: "Daily,"
however, from the illumination of the object, and the clear intuition of the blessed. It is also called
a prize, promised namely to those who run, as a reward. This reward is therefore...
