EIGHTH TONE. 457

reward (by whatever name it may be called) a good never failing, nor diminished by
sharing. Nor, because it is communicated more to one than to another, does it leave
room for envy to the one having less, since all rejoice together in the glory and good
of the co-heirs. For those who were found envious were irrevocably expelled from that
fellowship and communion of that reward.
      That that reward is pleasant and eternal. Consideration II.
[Decorative initial D containing a small landscape scene] Concerning this reward, how pleasant it is, he who had approved it
explains, saying: "Taste and see how sweet the Lord is." But hoping for greater
things, he says again: "You have made known to me the paths of life," namely in the [Marginal note: David.]
resurrection, as Ambrose says. "You will fill me with joy, or pleasantness, with your [Marginal note: Ambrose. Peter.]
countenance," as Peter alleges in the Acts of the Apostles. What delights will be at the
right hand of God, where there is piety, mercy, grace, and everything pleasant and
delightful. Which delight will be unto the end, that is, eternal and unfailing: And this
results from multiple causes, because, namely, the object is beautiful to the sight,
delightful to the sense, sweet to the taste, and perfectly proportioned to all faculties,
with the added covenant of perpetual possession. For God is that beauty, from whom
all beautiful things are made: as the Platonists rightly perceive, along with Dionysius [Marginal note: Platonists. Dionysius. Hierotheus.]
and Hierotheus, who say: Just as each thing is called good because it participates in
the highest good, and being because it participates in the highest being: so it is beautiful
by participation in the first beautiful, which is now called יפית *iaphit*, now הדר *hadar*,
now תפארת *tipheret*: Although they differ, if we carefully consider the force of the
words. For *iaphit* signifies true beauty coming from within. *Hadar*, however,
indicates grace and beauty in appearance, attire, adornment, and manners. But
*tipheret* signifies beauty itself, and intrinsic majesty resulting with a certain glory and
apparent triumph. For *iaphit* is called in the forty-fourth psalm, where we have [Marginal note: Psalm.]
translated: "You are fairer than the sons of men:" For in Hebrew it is יפיפית מבני אדם
*iaph iaphita mibeni Adam*. Which, translating word for word, we would say: "Beautiful
with beauty from, or above the sons of Adam." We have *hadar* in the ninety-fifth
psalm, where it is said: "Confession and beauty are before him," when in Hebrew it is
הוד והדר לפניו *hod ue hadar lepanau*: We also have *tipheret* there, ותפארת במקדשו
*hoz ue tipheret bemicadso*, that is, "strength and beauty in his sanctuary:" For which
we have, "holiness and magnificence in his sanctification:" We have these three words
in many other places. But it should be noted that that majesty and beauty, which is
called *tipheret*, is sometimes indicated by light: Whence he who dwells in it says: "I
am the light of the world." Sometimes by the sun, according to that of the psalmist:
"He has set his tabernacle in the sun." For Abraham had pitched his tent towards the [Marginal note: Genesis.]
south, in which he had greatly prospered. Isaac also, but he was not too enriched there:
Which is hinted at in what is said:

--- Page 1057 ---
**THIRD CANTICLE**

Isaac sowed in that land, and found in that very year a hundredfold, but the Hebrew truth has it: He found in that year a hundred measures of barley, and the Lord blessed him, and the man became great: and he went on progressing and growing until he became very great. (Hierony.) Jerome wonders how he could have become so great through a hundred measures of barley found. The truth is, that he prospered in that northern influence indicated by [Hebrew: שעורים] seharim, which signifies both barley and many other things. But Jacob pitched his tent in the middle, where Tipheret is, that is, beauty, and the supramundane sun. Concerning which tent, or tents, it is said in the book of Numbers: How beautiful are the tents of Jacob, and the tents of (Num.) Israel. Therefore, it is the same to say, beautiful in form above the sons of men: He was the true light illuminating all: He placed his tabernacle in the sun: He will reign in the house of Jacob forever: And many similar things, which agree, as is known to those who understand what is conveyed by such things. Therefore, God is beautiful, our reward and object, and consequently delightful to the inner sense through divinity: and to the outer (sense) through assumed humanity: (CHRIST. Peter. David.) as Christ himself, our redeemer, reward, and rest, says: He will enter, namely, to divinity, and will go out to humanity, and in both places he will find pastures. He is also sweet and pleasant to the taste, as Peter says: If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious. And David in the psalm: The Lord is good to all. Finally, it is proportioned to all powers, although it is infinite, exceeding all powers: because by that excess it by no means corrupts, but grants as much as the capacity of the recipient power allows: And this is true joy, which results from proportion and suitability. Which joy, which delight, which sweetness, which finally full happiness would be nothing, in a way, unless it were continuous with the security of the possessor. Therefore, our supreme (CHRIST.) emperor, in order to make us certain about this joy never to be lost, said to his disciples, and consequently to all: Your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.

**FIFTEENTH MODULE, DOMINION.**
Concerning the ample dominion of the prince. First Harmony.

[Large decorative initial P] After the triumph, dominion was given to this triumphant one, since he is King of kings and Lord of lords. What kind of dominion this is, (Paul) Paul explains in very few words, saying: Whom he appointed heir of all things. Nor can it be extended further, since all (Isaiah) things are subject to him. Concerning whom Isaiah also, when speaking of his birth, prophesied, saying: His dominion will be multiplied, and of his peace there will be no end: for he will be the prince of peace. Nor should anyone be disturbed if multiple wars still exist in the lower kingdom, which is called the Church Militant: because not all his enemies have yet been placed under the footstool of his feet, (Paul) according to that of Paul: He sits at the right hand of God, from now on waiting until his enemies are made his footstool.

--- Page 1058 ---
**EIGHTH TONE. 458**

...stool for his feet. But when the time is given for hostile death to be destroyed, then it will rejoice in perfect peace in all its members. The prophet continues: "He will sit upon the throne of David, and over his kingdom." Indeed, he is rightly said to sit on the throne of [Marginal note: Dauid.] David, who was the first king, and the only one pleasing to God among those who reigned in all Israel. And he was from the tribe of Judah, which was adorned with a royal lineage. [Marginal note: Moses.] For each of the tribes of Israel had its own peculiar privileges, as Father Jacob, [Marginal note: Iahac.] and after him Moses, [Marginal note: Moses.] hint at in their blessings with a hidden and profound mystery. Therefore, it refers to the royal scepter having been designated for the tribe of Judah, saying: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah." And for this reason, Jacob did not trust any son guaranteeing for Benjamin to be brought down to Egypt, except Judah, as a king, whose word ought to be truthful. And although the kingdom did not always appear in the tribe of Judah, it was nevertheless always adorned with the royal scepter in its archetype. For David [Marginal note: Dauid] had been chosen as king over all Israel, and anointed by Samuel, yet before he actually obtained the kingdom, which was already decreed in the divine mind, he served under Saul for many years. And because of his merits and glorious deeds, he was indeed most famous among the people, but hated by Saul, and watched with many snares; so much so that he thought it necessary to yield to envy, preferring to serve foreigners rather than an envious king. And after he began to reign, he reigned for seven years, confined to his own tribe of Judah alone. This was shown to us as an example, so that no one should be saddened if they do not immediately obtain the promised kingdom. However, this royal scepter endured in the tribe of Judah, either under the name of king or leader, until Christ. When he arrived, it was by no means taken away (although the oracle says: [Marginal note: Genesis.] "Until the Messiah comes"), but under him, it was changed for the better, since he is King of kings, and for all of us, he acquired that true and eternal kingdom. Therefore, when Pilate asked if he was a King, he replied: "You say that I am a king." [Marginal note: CHRI] But my kingdom is not of this world, but having a super-mundane root in the [Marginal note: STVS.] archetype, from which descending I brought with me the kingdom, which is mysteriously hinted at in this name יהודה Iehuda, from whose truly royal lineage I am. In this name are contained all the letters of the great four-letter name, or Tetragrammaton, with the letter ד dalet inserted, which signifies four in number. From this is hinted that the divinity and royal majesty, which is contained in the Tetragrammaton, was found in human form, a squaring from the four elements of which it is composed. Therefore, since that sacred four-letter name belongs to the Messiah, and he was true man, we easily understand that he is also the true super-mundane king, and from the true tribe of Judah; although for the time of his pilgrimage, he lay hidden in a four-square human body. But now he reigns with royal splendor on the heavenly throne, with which he will appear to mortals also in his second coming. Of whom he himself says: [Marginal note: Idem.] "When the Son of Man comes in the seat of his majesty with his angels." And again: "All will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty."

**THIRD CANTICLE**
How just is the rule of this prince. Con. II.

[Large initial S] But since one receives imperial or royal dignity by a twofold right, namely by inheritance and by just war: I think it must be seen how Christ our emperor claims that empire for himself not tyrannically, but by both rights: For he had in it an hereditary right, since he was the son of the supreme prince, with whom he had also created all things which he subjected to him, as Paul, the revealer of mysteries, said: "Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages."
[Paulus. in margin]

But this would have been little just for him, unless by military virtue and skill (in a just war, however) he had again acquired a distinguished empire. For the kingdom is proposed as a reward for those running or contending, who have overcome the enemy in the struggle of this mortal life. Indeed, the course of life itself is like a gymnastic race, by which each person can arrive at reward or punishment. But for the contest, war has been declared against vices and Tartarean enemies, as explained above...

--- Page 1060 ---
TONVS OCTAVVS. 459

...it is that he might pay the debt for us, but strenuously fighting, he snatched the whole human race from the hands of the enemy. But since one redeemed from captivity (as laws decree) is bound to the redeemer, therefore, Zacharias, inspired by the divine spirit, sang: *That, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.* [Marginal note: Zacha.] And thus that divine wisdom, which as the author of all things rightly rules in all things, as we read in Ecclesiasticus: *In every people and in every nation I held the primacy*, [Marginal note: Ecclesia.] so also in the assumed humanity, struggling, warring, conquering, and triumphing, might also justly rule by the right of a just war.

De regno commilitonum. Con. III.

[Large decorative initial N]or let it be believed that this is because we are called servants, condemned to vile servitude, since we serve him for whom to serve is to reign. Hence the Emperor declares us destined for the kingdom, to which he also invites, saying: *Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.* [Marginal note: CHRI STVS.] For if the emperor of this world presides over many kings, much better does the heavenly emperor have fellow-soldiers who are kings, to whom Peter speaks, saying: *But you are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition.* [Marginal note: Petrus.] Indeed, that conjunction of kingdom and priesthood is greatly to be pondered, because it is called a royal priesthood, to imply that every Christian ought to shine with both, namely, kingdom and priesthood, so that he may be a true soldier of him who was a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedech, who is interpreted as a righteous king. Therefore, it testifies that he was a royal priest, just as each of us ought to be. For as a true king ought to rule over all earthly things and his own body, reducing it (as often as necessary) to servitude. But as a true priest, everyone ought to offer his own body as a sacrifice to the living God, as Paul teaches, saying: *I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God:* [Marginal note: Paulus.] To which if we add a third, namely wisdom, there will be a perfect man, as it is said, not by trivial doctrine, of Mercury, [Marginal note: Mercu,] who was thrice greatest, in wisdom, priesthood, and kingdom. But much more elegantly did our high priest Christ shine in wisdom, kingdom, and priesthood: which indeed every Christian ought to have, but especially he who holds the place of that supreme wisdom. Hence not without reason is his triple tiara or miter (which is commonly called a kingdom) distinguished, as if he were crowned with a triple diadem of wisdom, kingdom, and priesthood. For unless he is wise, he cannot be good, because every ignorant person is evil, as the Peripatetics say. [Marginal note: Peripat] Nor should only the supreme pontiff excel in doctrine, but every bishop, so called from *epi*, which is "above," and *scopos*, "intending," as if he were "intending over" the people, as Augustine interprets; [Marginal note: August.] or from *scopos*, which is "speculation" (watching), as others prefer: whence it is understood that a prelate is placed on a watchtower over his flock. But neither should any other priest lack wisdom and knowledge, because through Hosea the Lord threatens: *Because you have rejected knowledge,* [Marginal note: Osee.]

[Three leaf-like ornaments] MODULE SIXTEEN, PEACE.
What peace is. First Harmony.

[Marginal note: August.] [Large decorative initial P containing a figure] eace indeed (as Augustine rightly perceives) is the tranquility of order: which order is the disposition of equal and unequal things, assigning to each its own: For when all things are rightly ordered, tranquility and peace follow: which, since it is manifold, is explained by a manifold definition. For the peace of the body is the ordered composition of its parts, which is called health. The peace of the irrational soul is an ordered and quiet appetite. The peace of soul and body is an ordered life, and a harmonious union, and a consistent operation of both.

--- Page 1063 ---
TOMVS OCTAVVS. 462

Rational peace, however, is ordered knowledge and complete agreement of choice. And this is that most blessed gathering of two or three, in which the king of peace promises to dwell, namely when our animal nature agrees with reason, and reason with will, and will with reason. From this follows true peace with God, which is the pure and manifest observance of God's law and will: and not only that the rightly tempered mind be the temple of God, but whoever is thus composed, whatever he asks for, will immediately be heard, because he in no way deviates from what God has established. To such a one, the yoke of God and Christ is also sweet and delightful. And in such a state, the hymn sung by the angels at the birth of the Prince of Peace finds its place, saying: "And on earth peace to people of good will," [Marginal note: Angel.] namely to those whose will is in harmony with reason and God. These indeed are deemed worthy to ascend to that peace of God which surpasses all understanding, and to arrive at that celestial and sublime city, in which (according to Job) [Marginal note: Iob.] God made such concord that the city was called a vision and enjoyment of peace. And because only the peaceful can reach this kingdom of peace, its prince therefore commands his ministers that wherever they arrive, they should bring and announce peace. And He, departing from them, left this peace to be kept by testamentary right, saying: "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you." [Marginal note: CHRISTVS.] Whoever neglects to observe this testament will in no way be able to attain the inheritance of peace, because what is dissonant (even in the slightest) ought not, and cannot, be admitted to harmonious concert and melodious sweetness. So also those who serve the smallest sin, or in some part serve pleasure, cannot attain the kingdom, since they are servants of sin, nor that peace which some wise men define as the tranquil freedom of the soul.

From whom peace is given. Harmony II.

**S**ed since no one can be free from sin without God, therefore neither can one [Marginal note: Ecclesia.] enjoy peace without God, nor make progress in it. Hence the Church prays: "Give us that peace which the world cannot give." For the dwellings of the world are threefold: supernal, infernal, and middle. The supernal dwelling is most harmoniously ordered and filled with complete peace. The lowest is where no order, no rest, no peace, but eternal horror dwells, says Job. The middle, however, is mixed from both, in which man is first placed, with a crossroads set before him, and is continually invited to the extreme dwellings. But to the infernal dwellings one runs easily, with loose reins, no bridle, no moderation, no order observed, but everything prepared by wantonness. The descent to Avernus is therefore easiest: where mortals fall without help, so separated from themselves and from an orderly God, and so discordant, that they can no longer possess any peace or tranquility. But those who strive towards the supernal dwellings and the upper breezes undertake a difficult and arduous journey, such that without God's divine power it absolutely cannot be accomplished, as attested by the infallible truth which says: "Without me you can do nothing." For just as instru-

**THIRD CANTICLE**

CHRISTUS. An instrument needs a tuner, who adjusts the strings or pipes, and makes them harmonious, and afterwards tunes them with due sonority: so also we, as instruments (and would that we were good ones), need a tuner, who adjusts our nerves and pipes: who doubtless are soul and body: our animal nature and spirit: the superior part and the inferior: will and reason: and finally may all things harmonize with God himself. Thence therefore is the fitting together of instruments: thence sonorous and harmonious operation: thence tranquility, peace, sweetness, and every good.
How sweet and harmonious this peace is. Con III.

Peace is sweet and pleasant to God, as some wise men say, that in nature nothing is thought more excellent, nothing sweeter. Because true peace is tranquility of mind, simplicity of heart, a bond of love, a chain of charity, a solace for the commonwealth, a joy for homes: domestic to angels, hostile to demons, pleasing to God above all things, and the harmony of all things. And where there is concord, there is harmony, there is sweetness, there is joy. Hence sings the prophet: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity."
Dauid. Brothers, namely soul and body, when they are in agreement: or men together, or a man and his guardian angel: because then God and Christ (whose name in the canticles is called ointment, or poured out oil) is diffused into those who thus come together, sprinkling all things with the sweetest odor and fragrance: whence it follows: "As the ointment upon the head," namely Christ, "which descends upon the beard," namely of Aaron the great priest: because through the hands of priests divine charisms are administered to the people. Therefore this ointment descends even to the hem of the garment, namely that which Christ our anointed one bought and wove for us: so that it might cover the sins of all. Therefore He pours ointment upon this garment, so that He might also heal the wounds of all. There is also this divine influx upon those dwelling together in peace, like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion. Indeed, dew is a heavenly influx, indeed divine, in which Isaac blessed his sons, saying to each: "In the dew of heaven shall your blessing be." For it descends from heaven, indicated by Hermon, which they interpret as an anathema of sorrow: And here it descends

dew on Mount Sion, that is, on those who are placed on watchtowers, and in the governance of others: for Sion denotes a watchtower. But if we wish to imitate the more recondite theologians, the dew, which in Hebrew is called טל (tal), by way of numbers carries the surname of a great hidden name, from which all things flow: And thus by the ointment it is indicated that we have an influx of the name, which is properly a poured-out ointment: and by the dew an influx of the surname: so that nothing is lacking to those dwelling together in peace and unity. And explaining more clearly, the prophet adds: For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever. But what is life, if not eternal blessedness? And what is blessing, if not the gift by which one may attain that blessedness itself? Therefore, those to be introduced to that kingdom of glory are called blessed by the Prince saying: "Come, blessed of my Father." From peace, therefore, one arrives at blessing, and from blessing to life and kingdom, but from life to union, concerning which (as far as is right, and as much as the weakness of our small intellect can achieve) we shall attempt to draw forth something.

**SEVENTEENTH MODULE. UNION.**
On the union of the blessed with God. Unique Harmony

**F**ROM the most sacred paternal treasuries, Jesus, the Son of God, when about to depart from here, had given a pledge of His greatest love towards us, He also bestowed this monument, hidden from almost all human intellects, saying: "Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we are." And again: "I pray not for these alone, whom I sent to preach, namely the apostles, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, and they in us may be one." By these words He not only explains our future union with God, but also hints at the manner, while He says: "As you, Father, are in me, and I in you." Concerning which union, when Plotinus, the most eminent expounder of Plato's most recondite doctrine, indeed of divine wisdom imbibed by Plato, wished to treat, as far as the prophets had offered, he said: "Therefore, the institution of such mysteries indicates that it forbids revealing it to men not yet initiated and purified." Namely, it forbade revealing what is divine to another, unless it was granted to that person to see it. Hence, because Parmenides said that all things are one, the Peripatetics themselves are truly laughable, because they dispute against all things that Parmenides did not say: and what he did say, they left untouched, firm on its own feet, and utterly unshaken. Aristotle argued (says Simplicius) against the words, not against the meanings of Parmenides, who spoke divinely, and beyond the bounds of natural philosophy: to which Aristotle was devoted in physics. For all things proceeded from the One, and that all things may be the same, it is necessary for them to participate in that One. And just as all things proceeded from the One into many, so all things which tend to return to that One from which they proceeded, necessarily must shed the multitude, which pertains to imagination, discourse,

**THIRD CANTICLE**
[floral ornament] **MODULE EIGHTEEN: FELICITY.** [floral ornament]

Who is happy and blessed. First Harmony.

[Marginal note: Augustine. / Plato.] As for what is considered happy and blessed, Augustine defines it by saying: Blessed is he who has whatever he wants. Plato, however, in the Philebus, does not differ much, when he says: Blessed is he to whom nothing is lacking: But in the Euthydemus, he agrees with Augustine, saying: Felicity is the attainment of things according to one's desires. But no one possesses all the things he desires, unless he adheres to and is united with the source of all good things, from whom he can draw all things at will. Therefore, blessed and happy is he who is united with God, in whom he sees all things, possesses all things, and enjoys all things with a better lot than he perceives in their proper kind:
[Marginal note: Augustine.] although the vision of those things, which by Augustine is called 'vespertina' (evening vision), is not denied, nor their enjoyment, which we declared spurious above, provided that all things are referred to God with that relation and consonance which is fitting. From whose harmony the great glory of the creator is seen, which vibrates and shines in creatures, which well-illuminated eyes contemplate, like those seraphim who (as Isaiah relates) sang, 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts, the whole earth is full of His glory.'
[Marginal note: Isaiah.] If this shines in created things, much more happily does it shine in the Creator Himself, whose vision is given to those who, dead to the world and to themselves, live for God alone, who said: 'No man shall see me and live.'
[Marginal note: GOD] It is therefore necessary, if anyone wishes to be happy, that he die the death of the righteous, either through complete separation from the body and conversely, as all the blessed whose souls have attained that celestial glory: Or through the transmutation of the body into a better state, as we read of Elijah, translated in a fiery chariot, his body now changed into the nature of spirit; and as Enoch, who walked with God in soul and body, and was no longer seen by bodily eyes: And as many others whose bodies rose with Christ and entered the holy city, happy together with Him: Or through a temporary departure from the body, as Paul in his rapture; Moses, who saw the Lord face to face; Isaiah, who saw the Lord sitting on a high and exalted throne; and not a few others, whom to enumerate would be too long, not to say impossible.

In what felicity consists. Harmony II.
Although in the first volume we brought forward many opinions of those who wished to define in what felicity and blessedness consist, here, however, determining the matter definitively and conclusively, we say that felicity cannot exist except in God, and not in any external things,
[Marginal note: Aristotle.] as Aristotle wisely decrees in his Politics, saying: 'God is my witness, there is no felicity in external things, because He Himself is happy and uses none of external things.' Here Cicero falls, struck by his own battering ram,
[Marginal note: Cicero.] while he places the blessed life in the emptiness of all things: which must be placed in God alone.

Nevertheless, progress towards God sometimes occurs through creatures, as Paul says. [Marginal note: Paul.]
The invisible things of God, understood through those things which have been made, are perceived from the creation of the world: From

Therefore the apostle says to the Colossians: "See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men." Therefore, true knowledge is to be expected from the supreme fount of truth with purity of heart. Hence the same Mercurius introduces the Mind speaking to him in these words [Marginal note: Mercury. Mind]: "I am the Mind, that is, the divine splendor illuminating your intellect, for those who are good, pious, pure, religious, and holy: And my presence brings them aid, so that they immediately discern all things." And exhorting his son to grasp this mind, he says: "Whoever are supported by the gift of God, so that they have attained the Mind, they, O Tat, are considered immortal among mortals, according to the comparison of their works, [Marginal note: Idem.] having embraced all things by their understanding, which are on earth, which are in the sea, and whatever else is above heaven: and therefore they raise themselves up to behold that very good, in which they indeed see all things." When they truly perceive this, they consider the life we live here to be a kind of misery: despising indeed both bodies and all corporeal things, they are carried towards the one alone. This, O Tat, is the meaning of the mind, namely the contemplation of divine things, and the understanding of God, the divine crater existing, that is, the soul being disposed to receive in the intellect that splendor from which the mind is formed, having indeed the intellect itself illuminated by divine radiance. Which illumination John indeed

--- Page 1071 ---
EIGHTH TONE. 464

calls it an anointing, saying: "You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things; and you do not need anyone to teach you, for His anointing teaches you about all things." Which anointing, or illumination, or mind is given (as the more secret [Theologians] Theologians say) in the death of the kiss, concerning which the prophet says in Psalm [number omitted]: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His [David. CHRIST] saints." To which death Christ and [SAINT Paul.] Paul openly provoke us. Indeed, the other mystically says: "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." For it is necessary to die to the world and to the animal man, if one wishes to live to God and to discern those things which pertain to divine life, as [GOD] God Himself testifies, who says: "No man shall see me and live," that is, live an animal life. Therefore [Paul.] Paul says: "Mortify your members"; and again: "You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ." Therefore, a person dying to the senses, in a certain ecstasy and separation of the intellectual faculty from its engagement with sensible things, is elevated into God, where he sees all things. Which, even while still pilgrims, they attain by the gift of God, provided they have become pure in heart, as the supreme [CHRIST] Truth teaches. From whose workshop, [Plotinus] Plotinus says: "Those who are pure, dwelling with themselves, having no impediment to becoming one, but having become divine, beautiful, and God-like, then ascend into the Mind where they contemplate all beautiful forms, and recognize them to be the ideas which indicate the true essences and quiddities of things." To this had come the prophets, Paul, and he who said: "What we have heard and touched concerning the word of life, this we announce to you"; and again: "We have seen His glory, glory [Paul.] as of the only begotten from the Father." In which Word, since all things shine and have their exemplars there, consequently all things are beheld there. But this way, familiar to the ancients, and known even to some, or very few, of our time, who can say with the [David.] prophet: "You have made known to me the ways of life"; is, however, utterly obliterated among the common people, each one being addicted to his own concupiscence, or to doctrine perceived by the senses, which do not at all reach such things, being entirely alien to them. Hence, to them it seems hard, strange, and perhaps deviating from the truth and inaccessible (as they say) for this present state. Therefore, for them it is enough to await the time when our heavy body will be reformed and made conformable to the body of Christ's glory; which they estimate will happen only after the resurrection and in the state of glory, not paying attention to what the saints attest: and how (as authentic scripture testifies) some, while still pilgrims, have seen these things, speaking with God face to face: as it is said of Moses, and of Jacob, and of others through other words. Since, therefore, all agree that this perfect knowledge will be given to those who have diligently applied themselves to the goal of the race, we will also briefly discuss them.

--- Page 1072 ---
**THIRD CANTICLE**
**To whom perfect happiness is given. Con. III.**

**E**T if to those living in this life an entrance is sometimes given to the paradise of delights, where we can eat of all the trees planted there, and delight in that which [Marginal note: Paulus.] Paul, and other wise Hebrews call the future age, nevertheless, its perfect [Marginal note: Paulus.] possession is given to those who have completed the course of life. For before, even very few [Marginal note: Hebręi.] perfectly initiated in such things arrive there, as Paul himself, with the Hebrews not moderately instructed in this matter, says: "But solid food is for the perfect, for those who by reason of custom have their senses exercised to discern good and evil." Therefore, speaking with these, we will interpose the introductory discourses of Christ, which indeed are about works of penance, baptism, the authority to absolve, the resurrection of the dead, and such like: so that we may be carried to perfect doctrine among the perfect, and to those who have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, to be communicated in such a way: in which is treated the heavenly gift, the hidden manna, the better word of God, namely, that which is hidden and to be communicated to the perfect, and concerning the virtues of the coming age: To which (God helping) when we arrive, then we see, even as pilgrims, at least in part, those things which are hidden: But if, freed from the body, we are carried to God, then that which is in part is made void, the perfect having been attained, in which we are fully blessed: But whether the soul, freed from this bodily mass, immediately reaches the goal and end to which it will eventually come, or if it still progresses, [Marginal note: Theolo.] there is a varied opinion among the wise: For more recent theologians incline towards the former opinion: But Origen, and with him other wise men, are of the opinion that [Marginal note: Orige.] the blessed still progress, [Marginal note: Celsus.] as he, in a long discourse against Celsus, says: "When the saints arrive at the heavenly places, then they will know more amply and perfectly what they did in their pilgrimage." In which knowledge, rational nature will grow through individual things, not as in the flesh, or body and soul, in which life grew, but the mind, now initiated, augmented in mind and sense, is led to perfect knowledge, by no means to be hindered in the future by these carnal senses, but augmented by intellectual increments, always with every veil removed, and purely (so to speak) face to face will contemplate the causes of things: where it will first attain that perfection by which it ascended to Him, and then that by which it remains: having as food, by which it may feed, theorems, and the understanding of things, and the reasons of causes: For just as our bodies in this life, by the aid of food, while we are still in our youthful years, continuously grow and are fully perfected: but when nature has brought them to their full stature with suitable proportions, we use food, no longer to grow, but to live and be preserved in life through sustenance. So I believe the mind, even when it has come to perfection, nevertheless feeds and uses its own proper and competent foods in that measure, to which nothing should be lacking, nor should it abound. But in all things, this food is to be understood as contemplation, and

--- Page 1073 ---
TOMVS OCTAVVS. 465

the understanding of God, having its own proper and suitable measures for this nature, which has been made and created; which measures each individual, beginning to see God and understand Him through purity of heart, must observe. This progress, indeed (in my judgment), the Apostle wished to show you, where after he discussed the ascent on high, and captivity led away by Christ, and about the degrees distributed in the church, by which some were made Apostles: others Evangelists, others doctors, and of this kind, he adds: Until we all meet in the unity of faith, and knowledge of the Son of God unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, that we may no longer be children tossed to and fro, and carried about by every wind of doctrine. [Marginal note: Paulus. CHRI STVS.]
However, if anyone asserts that there is no progress in the heavenly homeland, because on the journey each person reaches the measure destined for them (as the doctors of the Church commonly hold, and we are with the Church and with Christ here and everywhere); nevertheless, it seems to some (unless this contradicts the truth) that those adhering to the infinite always draw from it the means by which they grow, until they become one with it, as we hinted above, and then, having attained the perfect portion by which they grow, they rest in peace in that very thing. For (as they say) if anything obscene and unclean defiles those who have completed the course of life, they have a place in which they may be purged, before they come to that light illuminating and perfecting, lest the very weak and infirm be offended by its clarity. Thus the eye must be accustomed, before it fixes its gaze on that most full light: because (as Plotinus says) an eye infected with filth, not yet well purged, or weak, if it is directed towards a most pleasant spectacle, will immediately grow dim: for it is necessary for the one who is to see, to first become akin and similar by seeing, before it is applied to seeing: For the eye would never see the sun, unless it became solar: nor again will the soul, unless it becomes beautiful and divine, behold beauty itself, and God: nor will it receive light unless it becomes luminous and clear. [Marginal note: Plotinus]
Hence Solomon in Proverbs says: The path of the just shines like light, going forth, or progressing and shining unto the perfect day. Hence concerning the most blessed Christ it is said: But the child grew, and was strengthened, full of wisdom: And again: And JESUS advanced in wisdom, age, and grace with God, and men. Nor should it be said that that progress was according to appearance, because they would accuse scripture of falsehood when it itself says, that he progressed in wisdom, not in appearance, nor only for the sight of men. Nor does he solve it well, who says that he progressed by experience: because there it is said, that he progressed in wisdom: For scripture itself never speaks incongruously, except by the fault of the translator. Therefore, that man, even united with God, progressed, just as he deserved, up to that fullness to which the Father had preordained. [Marginal note: Salomon]
The just also grow up to that same perfection, which is noon, or the 'meridional vision,' as Augustine called it, when the blessed clearly beholds God face to face as He is. In this vision there is infinite breadth, just as the object seen is infinite. Nor should those who hold this opinion consider the state and progress of the blessed as inconvenient: for it is indeed a state in which none of them can fall in any way; but progress, however, when always [Marginal note: Augusti.]

**CANTICI TERTII**

**Petrus.** Let them become more intimate with God, until they become one with Him: whence even angels (as Peter says) desire to look into God. For they desire what they do not yet have, nor do they desire in vain, because they would be defrauded of their desire and would grieve, which is contrary to the nature of blessedness. Therefore, it seems that they sometimes obtain what they do not yet possess, even though they are blessed.
**Theolo.** Or if it is asserted (as theologians commonly believe) that the blessed, immediately introduced to that vision, are found at an already predetermined end, so that they do not progress further or become more intimate with God, since, once introduced there, they are already perfectly blessed. But however that may be, perfect happiness is given to those who have already reached the ultimate goal of their progress, and the full measure according to their capacity, so that they cannot receive more. And this is what is said:
**CHR-** "Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full."

[Three leaf-like ornaments] **NINTH MODULE. ALL GOOD.**
*What the good is, which is called the supreme and true good. A single harmony.*

[Decorative initial V in a square frame] Since no dispute can be made about that which is not subject to the senses, or to composite reasons, because it is most simple, therefore a simple discourse must be made about it, taught only by divine light, just as true wise men instruct us. For Trismegistus, imbued with that very light, says: "God is goodness itself, and nothing else besides goodness; all other things are distinct from the very nature of goodness. Indeed, body and soul, since they are finite, have no place by which they can grasp goodness, because goodness is as vast as the existence of all corporeal and incorporeal, sensible and intelligible things, and that which is above all existing things. Beware, therefore, lest you ever say that anything else is good; for it would be a profane error, according to that which the supreme teacher says:
**CHRI-** "No one is good except God alone." Nor must it be said that God is indeed anything other than the sole good, because into the same impiety

--- Page 1075 ---
**VOLUME EIGHT. 466**

He extends all things, nor does He receive anything: but man and all things together with him receive all things, but give nothing: therefore none of these can be called good. Christ therefore, in that He had received all things from the Father, did not wish to be called good: but in that He gave, He performed the office of good. Therefore God is all good, and the supreme good, receiving nothing, because He needs none of our goods, but gives to all, that they may be good, as the Divine lyre-player sings, saying: "When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness." [Marginal note: David] And this is true humility, and true self-knowledge, to understand oneself to be pure nothing, and to have received all things from God, and to be what they are from this, inasmuch as God diffuses Himself into them: And he who participates more in God, is better, since God is good itself: and is more beautiful, since God is beauty itself. For this is (as Dionysius and the Academics teach) true beauty, to participate, namely, in the supreme beautiful: and true goodness, to participate in the supreme good, just as true being is, insofar as it participates in that which is from itself, and the supreme being, as is most commonly held in all schools: [Marginal note: Diony: Academ:] For (as the same Dionysius says) because God is substantial good, He extends His goodness to all existing things, just as the sun by its being illuminates all things which can participate in its light. [Marginal note: Diony:] Therefore the supreme good, through its very essence, sends forth the rays of all goodness to all existing things by a certain measure and wonderful proportion. Not otherwise does he say a little further down about beauty: [Marginal note: Idem] For the most beautiful itself, and always above beauty, and existing in every part, is the cause of all beautiful things. From this beautiful, therefore, it comes to all existing things that each one is beautiful in its own way: And this beautiful creates the congruities, and friendships, and societies of all things: and to this beautiful, as to an efficient cause and end of all things, all things pertain: for all things exist for the sake of the beautiful. It is also the exemplar, and goal, by which all things are defined. And the same is beautiful and good, which all things desire, and to which all things are related, because there is nothing in the substances of things that is not in some way a participant of the beautiful and the good. And since it is the primary and immense fount, from which all things desire to receive, therefore all things (as the great Theodorus says in Proclus) pray except the first itself, because all things are in need: [Marginal note: Theologian] And while they know that they ought to receive from Him those things of which they are in need, they ask Him: Hence the supreme teacher Christ taught that we should direct our prayer to the Father, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes, when He says: [Marginal note: CHRIST] "When you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven." And we must always pray until the measure of gifts, which are prepared for us, is completed, and until our joy is full. For then nothing remains that we can obtain, but prayers are poured out of charity for others, that they may obtain what we have already obtained. And therefore (as John testifies) the Saints pray, and the Son of God Himself: [Marginal note: John] "If anyone," He says, "has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is the propitiator for our sins, and for the sins of the whole world," To whom Paul assents, saying: "Jesus entered into heaven itself, to appear before the face of God for us, and as a true mediator, to bring all things back to the supreme good itself," [Marginal note: Paul.]

**TWENTIETH MODULE: SILENCE.**
Concerning pause, rest, and silence, to which one arrives once the good, towards which we strive, has already been attained.

[Illuminated initial V] When therefore we have arrived at the first and highest, one must rest, nor must one proceed further, since nothing beyond the highest can be given. And this which Jeremiah says: "He shall sit solitary and be silent, because he has lifted himself above himself." By these words is declared rest in that which he says, "He shall sit"; divestment from the multitude, because he says, "Solitary"; silence, while he says: "he shall be silent"; and transformation into God in that which he concludes: "And he shall lift himself above himself." For above man there is nothing but God. In harmony the prophet sings, saying: "In peace, in the same, I will sleep and rest." With this said, let him be silent, because he has now arrived at the place where there is silence, inasmuch as there each one has become most intimate, and most intimate with the highest, so much so that, having forgotten all external things

Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine, namely
by revealing God's most precious secrets to the unworthy and incapable. Add to this that sometimes,
out of reverence (as Mercury says), silence offers a fertile pregnancy
of truth, so that in its proper place, he who has preserved those
secrets with reverence may speak all the more effectively and sublimely, the more faithful a servant he has been in concealing them. Acceptable
ones are also found more to praise the ineffable in silence than those who unworthily utter something,
stained by deceit contrary to true praise. Therefore, the soul, with senses closed,
which are delighted by colors, odors, tastes, sounds, and sensations, and with the discourse
of reason closed, whose food and sustenance is truth and the knowledge of lower
things, and gathered entirely at the apex of the mind, whose food is also supramundane
light, is silent to others: and, being free, speaks to that one alone who is the supreme and unique good, and
renders praises: Let us also (as far as it is right to reveal) render a hymn to God, the best and greatest.

A Hymn to be rendered in silence to God alone with a pure and elevated mind.

**T**o You, Holy Lord, and supreme King of all, praise is due,
which no one can render, since You are immense, eternal, and ineffable:
Therefore, if not worthy, yet as much as is right for me, and as much as
my strength allows, indeed, as much as You, speaking within me, shall command, I will render it.
You, enclosed by no boundary, circumscribed by no reason, and accessible to none, containing all things

CANTICLE THE THIRD

Indeed, carrying all things, a hidden dwelling in things, being, life, foundation, & beginning of all things & end, You, holy, blessed, the very high God, seal, form, spirit, bond, & life of the world: Great are You, & very praiseworthy, & of Your greatness there is no end: For You, with that immense goodness by which You created, by the same You also preserve all things, & with Your arm You protect all things: And You are the origin from which every light shines, & every good arises: You are powerful, & who resists You? And let him who is wise understand these things, for this is the hidden manna, which no one knows, except he who receives it: whence it is least permitted to speak of such things: For these things are not perceived by vocal hearing, but by that eternal light, by which those words are conceived, which are to be hidden in the heart, lest as unfaithful & unworthy praisers we sin before the king, whose sacrament it is good to hide: which we can neither reveal, because it is ineffable: Therefore, since words are insufficient, He is to be praised in silence, with a pure & fervent heart: for in silence, & hope will be our strength, says the oracle: with which that of Jeremiah especially agrees: 'It is good to wait in silence, until seeing face to face as He is, our true tongue may be loosed in due praises, as it is again written: "Those who dwell in Your house will praise You forever and ever." Amen.
